How English works

English is a big language, but its core is small. A few word jobs and one main word order build most sentences. This chapter gives you the map: the six levels, the parts of speech and the shape of a sentence. At the end you get a daily plan.

  • Name the six CEFR levels and say what a person can do at each one.
  • Find the eight parts of speech in a real sentence.
  • Find the subject, the verb and the object in a clause.
  • Put words in the normal English order and avoid the common order mistakes.
  • Tell a clause from a sentence, and plan a 30-minute study routine.

Six levels: from A1 to C2

Read three messages. Three people send the same news to a manager. Each person has a different level of English.

Message 1

Hello Tom. Train stop. I am late. Sorry.

The idea is clear. The grammar has gaps.

Message 2

Hi Tom, my train stopped, so I'm about ten minutes late. Please start without me.

Clear, correct and polite. It uses two clauses.

Message 3

Hi Tom, apologies. My train is stuck outside the station. Could you start without me? I'll read the notes and join as soon as I can.

What changed?

The writer of message 3 is softer and more exact. Every sentence has a clear job. That is a higher level.

Teachers and exams describe levels with the CEFR. The letters mean Common European Framework of Reference. The Council of Europe made it. Today schools, exams and employers all over the world use it.

The CEFR has six levels in three groups. Each level is a list of can-do statements. They say what you can do with the language. They do not list grammar rules.

The six CEFR levels (British Council names in brackets)
LevelGroupWhat you can doAt work, for example
A1 (Elementary)Basic userUse everyday phrases. Introduce yourself. Answer simple questions about you."I am a developer. I work in Osaka."
A2 (Pre-intermediate)Basic userHandle simple, direct exchanges. Describe your background and your needs.Ask for a file. Say that you are late.
B1 (Intermediate)Independent userUnderstand the main points on familiar topics. Write simple connected text. Give reasons.Explain a bug in a stand-up meeting.
B2 (Upper intermediate)Independent userUnderstand the main ideas of complex texts, also technical texts in your field. Speak with some fluency.Discuss a design choice with a native speaker.
C1 (Advanced)Proficient userUnderstand long, hard texts. Speak fluently without searching for words. Use English flexibly for work and study.Lead a design review. Write a design document.
C2 (Proficiency)Proficient userUnderstand almost everything. Express fine differences in meaning precisely.Negotiate a contract. Give a conference talk.

How long does each level take? Cambridge English gives a rough guide in guided learning hours. The numbers are totals from zero. The chart shows the top of each range.

Look at the steps between the bars. Each step is about 200 hours. The last step, from C1 to C2, is longer. Your own time can be shorter or longer. It depends on your first language, your practice outside class and your goals.

Do not think you have one level for everything. Many engineers read at B2 but speak at A2. They read documentation every day, but they rarely speak. Your level is a profile, not one letter. Plan practice for your weakest skill.

In 2020 the Council of Europe published the CEFR Companion Volume. It adds a Pre-A1 level and describes plus levels, like A2+, B1+ and B2+. It also adds scales for online interaction and for mediation.

IELTS, TOEFL, Cambridge and other exams link their scores to the CEFR. A school may ask for "B2 or higher". The chapter CEFR and the exam map shows which score means which level.

Words have jobs: the eight parts of speech

Read this sentence. Then look at the job of each word.

Wow, my new teammate writes clean code very quickly, but she rarely talks in meetings.

Each word in a sentence has a job. Grammar books call these jobs parts of speech. Traditional grammar has eight. Modern grammar books use the name word class.

The eight traditional parts of speech
Part of speechIts jobExamplesIn our sentence
NounNames a person, thing, place or ideaAna, laptop, Tokyo, ideateammate, code, meetings
PronounStands in for a nounI, you, she, it, they, themshe
VerbShows an action or a statewrite, run, be, have, knowwrites, talks
AdjectiveDescribes a nounnew, fast, clean, brokennew, clean
AdverbSays how, when, where or how muchquickly, often, here, veryvery, quickly, rarely
PrepositionLinks a noun to the rest of the sentencein, on, at, to, with, fromin
ConjunctionJoins words or clausesand, but, or, so, because, ifbut
InterjectionShows a feeling or a reactionwow, oh, oops, heyWow

What about my? Modern grammars add a ninth class, the determiner. It comes before a noun and its adjectives. The articles a, an and the are determiners. So are my, this, some and every. The UK national curriculum glossary lists determiners as a word class too.

The tree puts the classes in two big groups. Content words carry the meaning. New ones appear every year, like "to google". Function words build the structure. This group almost never gets new words.

Look at the two kinds of conjunction in the tree. A coordinating conjunction joins two equal parts: "tea and coffee". A subordinating conjunction starts a clause that depends on another clause: "because it rained". You meet both again in the next chapter.

One word, many jobs

English often uses the same word in two classes. Only its place in the sentence tells you the job.

  • test: "Run the test." (noun) "We test every change." (verb)
  • fast: "a fast laptop" (adjective) "It runs fast." (adverb)
  • work: "I love my work." (noun) "I work from home." (verb)
  • after: "after lunch" (preposition) "after I finish" (conjunction)

Do not use an adjective to describe a verb. An adjective describes a noun. An adverb describes a verb.

She speaks English very good.

The app runs slow.

She speaks English very well.

The app runs slowly.

Note: good is an adjective and well is its adverb. "Her English is good" is correct, because good describes the noun English.

Subject, verb, object

Read this short sentence.

The tester found a bug.

Ask three questions about it.

  1. What is the action? found. This is the verb.
  2. Who did it? The tester. This is the subject. It comes before the verb.
  3. What did the tester find? a bug. This is the object. It comes after the verb.

The subject and the object are often more than one word. "The new tester from Kyoto" is one subject. "A serious bug in the login page" is one object. A group of words with one job is a phrase.

The rule: every clause needs a subject and a verb

English almost always needs a subject. The verb must show time or person, like works, worked or is. This kind of verb is a finite verb. The words to work and working are not finite. They cannot make a sentence alone.

There is one big exception. An order or request has no subject. This form is the imperative: "Close the ticket." "Please send me the link."

When there is no real subject

Sometimes nothing does the action. English still puts a word in the subject place. This word is an empty subject.

  • It for weather, time and distance: "It is raining." "It is nine o'clock." "It is 5 km to the office."
  • There to say something exists: "There is a bug in line 20." "There are three new tickets."

Many languages can drop the subject. English cannot. Do not start a statement with is or have.

Is very hot today.

Have a problem with the server.

My manager she is busy.

It is very hot today.

There is a problem with the server.

My manager is busy.

The third mistake is the opposite. It has two subjects. "My manager" is the subject, so she is extra.

Not every verb has an object

Compare: "The server crashed." and "The update crashed the server." The first verb has no object. A verb with no object is intransitive. A verb with an object is transitive. Some verbs, like crash, can be both.

After be, seem and become there is no object. There is a complement. It describes the subject: "The build is green." "She became a team lead." Extra information about time, place or manner is an adverbial: "at nine", "in the office", "carefully".

The normal word order

Read the example. Then look at the picture.

She fixed the bug quickly in the office yesterday.

English uses word order to show meaning. Many languages use word endings for this job. In English, only the order changes the meaning here:

  • "The dog bit the man." The dog did it.
  • "The man bit the dog." The man did it. This is surprising news.

Six order rules

  1. In a statement, the subject comes before the verb.
  2. The object comes right after the verb. Put nothing between them.
  3. Manner, then place, then time: "carefully, at my desk, every day".
  4. An adjective comes before its noun: "a fast laptop".
  5. Words like often and never go before the main verb but after be: "I often work late." "I am often tired."
  6. In a question, a helping verb comes before the subject: "Do you use Git?" "Is the build green?"

The most common order mistake is a word between the verb and its object. Move the extra words to the end.

I like very much Python.

She speaks very well English.

Yesterday I in the office worked.

I bought a laptop new.

I like Python very much.

She speaks English very well.

Yesterday I worked in the office.

I bought a new laptop.

Clauses and sentences

Look at these three examples. Count the verbs.

  • "I was tired." One verb.
  • "I was tired, so I went home." Two verbs.
  • "Because I was tired, I went home early." Two verbs.

A clause is a subject plus a verb, with its other parts. A sentence is one clause or more. In writing it starts with a capital letter. It ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.

A main clause can stand alone. A subordinate clause cannot. It starts with a word like because, if, when or although. It needs a main clause.

Three kinds of sentence
KindWhat it hasExample
SimpleOne main clauseThe tests passed.
CompoundTwo main clauses joined by and, but, or, soThe tests passed, so we released the app.
ComplexA main clause and a subordinate clauseWhen the tests passed, we released the app.

A fourth kind mixes the last two. It is called compound-complex: "When the tests passed, we released the app, and the client was happy."

A fragment is a subordinate clause alone. A comma splice joins two main clauses with only a comma.

I went home. Because I was tired.

The tests passed, we released the app.

I went home because I was tired.

The tests passed, so we released the app.

The tests passed. We released the app.

In speech, short answers like "Because I was tired." are normal. In writing, join them to a main clause. The next chapter, The 15 sentence patterns, gives you fifteen safe shapes for clauses and sentences.

Expert view: seven clause patterns

Here are seven clauses. Each one has a different shape.

The seven basic clause patterns
PatternExampleTypical verbs
S + VThe server crashed.arrive, sleep, crash, happen
S + V + OThe team released the app.find, build, like, need
S + V + CThe tests are green.be, seem, become, look
S + V + AThe meeting is in room 4.be, live, stay, go
S + V + O + OShe sent me the link.give, send, show, tell
S + V + O + CThey made Ana the team lead.make, call, find, keep
S + V + O + APut the laptop on the desk.put, place, keep

S is the subject, V the verb, O an object, C a complement and A an adverbial. A famous reference grammar by Randolph Quirk and his team (1985) uses these seven types. Every longer clause is one of them, plus optional extras.

The verb chooses the pattern. A good learner dictionary shows it. It marks verbs as transitive or intransitive, often with T and I. It also gives example patterns, like "send somebody something".

In two patterns the adverbial is not optional. "The meeting is." and "Put the laptop." are not complete. They need the place.

Verbs like explain, suggest and describe do not take the S + V + O + O pattern. Use to before the person.

Can you explain me the plan?

She suggested me a new tool.

Can you explain the plan to me?

She suggested a new tool to me.

She sent me the link. She sent the link to me.

How to use this book

This book goes from A1 to C2 and to exam level. The language stays easy all the way. Only the ideas get harder. Each chapter has the same parts, so you always know where you are.

  • Level badge. Basic is A1 to A2. Intermediate is B1 to B2. Hard is C1 to C2. Certified means exam level.
  • Word help. A dotted word has a short meaning. Tap it or hold the mouse over it.
  • Example first. Every section shows real sentences first. Then it gives the rule and the common mistake.
  • Wrong and Right tabs. Read the wrong version and find the problem. Then open the right one.
  • Patterns to remember. One table near the end of each chapter. Copy the models into your notebook.
  • Practice. Quizzes, gaps and short writing tasks. The answers are hidden. Try first, then check.

Do the chapters in order if you are at A2. Start with The 15 sentence patterns and Sounds and spelling. Then go to Present simple and present continuous. For exams, go to CEFR and the exam map. For your job, read Writing at work. Each time you make a mistake, look in The error clinic.

A 30-minute daily routine

Short daily practice beats one long session a week. Memory works better with many short sessions and short gaps. Researchers call this the spacing effect. Here is a routine for one half hour.

Review

Look at yesterday's flashcards. Say each word or pattern aloud. Put hard cards at the front.

Learn one thing

Read one section of this book. Learn one pattern. Write three of your own examples about your life or your job.

Listen

Listen to a short clip, like a tech talk or a podcast. Use English subtitles. Find your new pattern in it.

Speak

Repeat one sentence right after the speaker. Copy the rhythm. This is called shadowing. Then say your three examples aloud.

Write and plan

Write a short message of three to five sentences. Check it against the patterns. Make two new flashcards for tomorrow.

Change the focus each day of the week. Keep the five steps the same.

One week of focus
DayFocusSmall task
MondayGrammarOne pattern, ten examples
TuesdayVocabularyTen work words with collocations
WednesdayListeningOne clip, two times, with notes
ThursdaySpeakingRecord two minutes about your work
FridayWritingOne email or one pull request text
SaturdayReadingOne article or one documentation page
SundayReviewRedo the week's practice items

Review old cards on a growing schedule. For example, review a new card after one day, then three days, then a week, then two weeks. Apps with spaced repetition do this for you.

Study at the same time every day, like after lunch. Link it to a habit you already have. Then you do not need to decide each day.

Many learners only read grammar. They never speak or write. Grammar becomes useful only when you use it. Say every new pattern aloud and write it at least three times.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the basic shape of English
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + verbSay that something happensThe server crashed.Every clause needs a subject and a finite verb.
Subject + verb + objectSay what someone does to somethingThe tester found a bug.Put nothing between the verb and the object.
Subject + be + complementDescribe the subjectThe build is green.Use an adjective after be, not an adverb.
It + be + weather or timeFill an empty subject placeIt is nine o'clock.Never drop it. "Is nine o'clock" is wrong.
There + be + noun + placeSay that something existsThere is a bug in line 20.Do not start with "Have".
Subject + verb + object + how + where + whenAdd detail in a safe orderI read the logs carefully at my desk every day.Place comes before time.
Adjective + nounDescribe a thingI bought a new laptop.The adjective goes before the noun.
Helping verb + subject + verb?Ask a yes or no questionDo you use Git?The helping verb goes before the subject.
Verb + thing + to + personExplain or suggest something to someoneCan you explain the plan to me?Never say "explain me".
Main clause + so or because + clauseJoin two ideas in one sentenceThe tests passed, so we released the app.Do not join two clauses with only a comma.

Practice

Quick quiz

At which level can you understand technical discussions in your own field?

  • A2
  • B2
  • C2

B2 learners understand the main ideas of complex texts, also technical texts in their field.

In "She rarely talks in meetings", what part of speech is rarely?

  • Adjective
  • Adverb
  • Preposition

It says how often she talks. It describes the verb, so it is an adverb.

Which sentence has the normal word order?

  • I check carefully my code.
  • I check my code at my desk carefully every day.
  • I check my code carefully at my desk every day.

The object comes right after the verb. Then how, where, when.

Which group is a complete sentence in writing?

  • Because the build failed.
  • The build failed because a test was wrong.
  • The build failed, a test was wrong.

The first is a fragment. The third is a comma splice. The second has a main clause and a subordinate clause.

Fill the gap

? is very cold in the server room.

? are three new tickets in the queue.

In "The tester found a bug", the object is ?.

The app runs very (slow) on my old phone.

A clause that cannot stand alone is a ?.

Think and write

  1. Put the words in order: every morning / I / my email / at home / check.
    Answer

    I check my email at home every morning. You can also say: Every morning I check my email at home.

  2. Name the part of speech of each word in bold: "Oh, the new update works well on my phone and it is fast."
    Answer

    Oh: interjection. the: determiner (an article). new: adjective. update: noun. works: verb. well: adverb. on: preposition. my: determiner. and: conjunction. it: pronoun.

  3. Correct the three mistakes: (a) Is a meeting at ten. (b) My boss he wants the report. (c) I like very much this tool.
    Answer

    (a) There is a meeting at ten. (b) My boss wants the report. (c) I like this tool very much.

  4. Fix the comma splice in two different ways: "The API was slow, users complained."
    Answer

    The API was slow, so users complained. Or: The API was slow. Users complained. Or: Users complained because the API was slow.

  5. Which clause pattern is each sentence? (a) The office seems quiet. (b) She gave me her notes. (c) We keep the keys in the drawer.
    Answer

    (a) S + V + C. (b) S + V + O + O. (c) S + V + O + A.

  6. Expert. Why is "Please describe me the problem" wrong? Write it correctly.
    Answer

    The verb describe does not take two objects. The person needs to. Correct: Please describe the problem to me.

  7. Plan your own week. Which skill is your weakest? Change the weekly table so that skill gets two days.
    Model answer

    My weakest skill is speaking. I keep Monday for grammar and Friday for writing. Thursday and Saturday become speaking days. On Saturday I record a two-minute talk about my project.

What are the three CEFR groups?

Basic user (A1, A2), independent user (B1, B2), proficient user (C1, C2).

Name the eight traditional parts of speech.

Noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.

What does a clause need?

A subject and a finite verb. Only the imperative has no subject.

What is a comma splice?

Two main clauses joined by only a comma. Use a full stop, or add and, but or so.

What goes first: place or time?

Place. "I work in the office on Mondays."

Key takeaways

  • The CEFR has six levels in three groups: basic (A1, A2), independent (B1, B2) and proficient (C1, C2).
  • Your level can be different for reading, listening, speaking and writing.
  • Words have jobs. The eight traditional parts of speech are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection. Modern books add determiners.
  • Every clause needs a subject and a finite verb. Use it or there when there is no real subject.
  • The core order is subject, verb, object. Put nothing between the verb and its object.
  • A sentence has one clause or more. Do not write fragments or comma splices.
  • Thirty minutes every day is better than three hours once a week.

The 15 sentence patterns

Fifteen sentence shapes build most of what you need to say and write. Fourteen come from your own favourite table, with the same words. One pattern is new. Learn the fifteen, and you can write clear English from A2 up to exam level.

  • Build each of the 15 patterns as a statement, a negative and a question.
  • Join two ideas with because, so, although, however, if, while and not only ... but also.
  • Choose the right connector for the meaning, from the 30 connectors in this chapter.
  • Punctuate joined sentences without comma splices.
  • Combine several patterns into one clear paragraph for work or an exam.

Three families of sentences

Watch one idea grow. Each line adds one pattern.

  1. People commute.
  2. People commute by train every day.
  3. Many people commute by train because it is cheap.
  4. Although trains are often late, many people commute by train because it is cheap.

The first line is complete. It has a subject and a verb. The last line has three clauses. It is long, but it is still clear. Each part follows a fixed pattern.

A sentence pattern is a shape you can reuse. You keep the shape. You change the words. "People commute" and "Servers fail" have the same shape.

The fifteen patterns belong to three families. The picture shows the shape of each family.

  • Simple: one clause. It can stand alone.
  • Joined: two equal parts with a connector, like so or however. Each part could stand alone.
  • Complex: a main clause plus a subordinate clause. The subordinate clause starts with a word like because, although or if. It cannot stand alone.

The tree groups the fifteen patterns by family. The numbers are the pattern numbers in this chapter. Open a branch to see its patterns.

Simple means one idea. Joined means two equal ideas side by side. Complex means one main idea and one helper idea. Long is not the same as complex. A long sentence can still be simple.

Patterns 1 to 5: the core

These five patterns are the base of English. Every longer sentence contains one of them.

Pattern 1: Subject + verb

People commute.

This is the smallest complete sentence. It has a subject and a verb. The verb must be finite. A finite verb shows time or person: commute, commutes, commuted. Verbs like arrive, wait, sleep and fail often use this pattern.

Commute every day.

People commuting.

I commute every day.

People are commuting.

The first wrong line has no subject. The second has no finite verb. Commuting alone does not show the time.

Pattern 2: Subject + verb + object

I read technical documents.

Now the action goes to a thing. That thing is the object. Keep it close to the verb. Put details like time and manner after the object.

I read every day technical documents.

I like very much this library.

I read technical documents every day.

I like this library very much.

Pattern 3: Subject + be + adjective

The timetable is flexible.

This pattern describes a state or a quality. After be, use an adjective. Do not use an adverb. The same is true after seem, look, sound, feel and become.

The timetable is flexibly.

The timetable flexible.

Your plan sounds well.

The timetable is flexible.

The timetable is flexible.

Your plan sounds good.

The second wrong line has no verb. Many languages drop be here. English never does.

Pattern 4: Subject + verb + object + place + time

I study English at home every evening.

This pattern adds practical detail. The order is safe and neutral: first the place, then the time. You can move the time to the front for focus: "Every evening, I study English at home."

I study every evening at home English.

I study at home English.

I study English at home every evening.

Every evening, I study English at home.

What about "I study English every evening at home"? It is not wrong. People say it. But place before time is the safest order, so use it when you are not sure.

Pattern 5: There is or There are + noun + place

There are several courses in my area.

Use this pattern to say that something exists. The word there is an empty subject. The real subject comes after the verb. So match is or are to the noun that follows.

  • There is a bug in line 20. (one bug)
  • There are two bugs in this file. (two bugs)
  • There is some information on the wiki. (uncountable noun)
  • There is a desk and two chairs. (a list: match the first noun)

There is many courses in my area.

Have many courses in my area.

In my area has many courses.

There are many courses in my area.

There are many courses in my area.

My area has many courses.

In fast speech, people often say "there's" before a plural noun. In writing and in exams, use there are.

Patterns 6 to 9: reason, result and contrast

Now we join two ideas. These four patterns give reasons, show results and balance two sides. They are the most useful patterns for opinions.

Pattern 6: Main clause + because + reason

I practise daily because I need more confidence.

The clause after because gives the reason. It must be a complete clause, with its own subject and verb. Before a noun alone, use because of.

I practise daily because my exam.

I practise daily. Because I need more confidence.

I practise daily because of my exam.

I practise daily because I need more confidence.

The second wrong line is a fragment. In speech, "Because I need more confidence" is a fine answer to a why-question. In writing, keep it with its main clause.

British spelling: practise is the verb and practice is the noun. "I practise daily. Practice helps." American English uses practice for both.

Pattern 7: Reason + so + result

The bus was delayed, so I arrived late.

This is pattern 6 turned around. The reason comes first. So introduces the result. When so joins two clauses, put a comma before it.

Because the bus was delayed, so I arrived late.

The bus was delayed so, I arrived late.

The bus was delayed, so I arrived late.

I arrived late because the bus was delayed.

Choose one connector for one relationship. Because and so show the same link from two sides. Never use both in one sentence.

So that is different. It shows a purpose, not a result: "I left early so that I could catch the bus." There is usually no comma before so that.

Pattern 8: Although + contrast, main clause

Although remote work is flexible, it can feel isolating.

This pattern balances two ideas. The although clause gives the weaker side. The main clause gives the side you want to stress. When the although clause comes first, put a comma after it.

Although remote work is flexible, but it can feel isolating.

Although remote work is flexible, however, it can feel isolating.

Although remote work is flexible, it can feel isolating.

Remote work is flexible, but it can feel isolating.

Some languages say "although ... but". English uses only one contrast word for one contrast. Use although or but, never both.

Three close relatives:

  • Even though is stronger. Use it for a surprising contrast.
  • Though is more informal. In speech it can go at the end: "It's flexible. It can feel lonely, though."
  • Despite and in spite of take a noun or an -ing form, not a clause: "Despite the rain, we went out."

Pattern 9: Main clause. However, contrast.

Remote work is flexible. However, it can feel isolating.

This is the contrast of pattern 8, but across two sentences. However is not a joining word like but. It is a sentence linker. Put a full stop or a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

Remote work is flexible, however it can feel isolating.

Remote work is flexible however, it can feel isolating.

Remote work is flexible. However, it can feel isolating.

Remote work is flexible; however, it can feel isolating.

The first wrong line is a comma splice. It is one of the most common mistakes in learner essays. Examiners notice it quickly.

In careful writing, however can also move inside the second sentence: "It can, however, feel isolating." The commas go on both sides.

Patterns 10 to 14: condition, detail, focus and balance

These five patterns make your English more exact. They are common at B1 and B2. Exams reward them when they are accurate.

Pattern 10: If + present, can or will + base verb

If cities improve transport, fewer people will drive.

The if clause gives a real, possible condition. The main clause gives the result. Use the present simple after if, even for the future. Use will or can plus the base verb in the result. Grammar books call this the first conditional.

If cities will improve transport, fewer people will drive.

If cities improve transport, fewer people will to drive.

If cities improve transport, fewer people will drive.

Fewer people will drive if cities improve transport.

You can swap the two clauses. The meaning stays the same. When the main clause comes first, you do not need a comma.

The table says "do not normally use will". There is one polite exception. Will after if can mean "be willing": "If you will wait here, I'll get the manager." This is a request, not a time. For the full system, see Conditionals.

Pattern 11: Noun + who, which, or that + information

I need a course that fits my schedule.

The second part tells you which course. It is a relative clause. Without it, "I need a course" is too general. Use who for people. Use which or that for things.

  • I need a teacher who gives clear feedback.
  • I need a laptop that can run this software.
  • This is the ticket which caused the outage.

I need a course what fits my schedule.

I need a teacher which gives feedback.

This is the laptop that I bought it.

I need a course that fits my schedule.

I need a teacher who gives feedback.

This is the laptop that I bought.

In the third line, that already stands for the laptop. So it is extra. Also note: when the relative word is the object, you can leave it out: "the laptop I bought". More in Relative clauses.

Pattern 12: Passive: be + past participle

The laptop was damaged during delivery.

The passive puts the thing that changed in the subject place. The form is be plus the past participle. Use it when the action or the result matters more than the person.

Name the agent with by only when it matters. "The laptop was damaged by the courier" is useful in a complaint. "The data is encrypted by someone" adds nothing.

The laptop damaged during delivery.

The laptop was damage during delivery.

The laptop was damaged during delivery by someone.

The laptop was damaged during delivery.

The laptop was damaged during delivery.

The laptop was damaged by the courier.

Technical writing uses the passive a lot: "The data is encrypted at rest." "The request is sent to the server." See The passive for every tense.

Pattern 13: While + clause, clause

While offices support teamwork, home working saves travel time.

Here while compares two ideas. Both ideas are true at the same time, but they point in different directions. Keep both clauses complete, each with its own subject and verb.

While also has a time meaning: "While the tests were running, I made a coffee." Make the meaning clear from the context.

While offices support teamwork, but home working saves travel time.

While offices support teamwork, saves travel time.

While offices support teamwork, home working saves travel time.

Offices support teamwork, whereas home working saves travel time.

Pattern 14: Not only + verb, but also + verb

Online learning not only saves time but also increases access.

This pattern adds two points with balanced emphasis. The second point feels stronger. The two sides must be parallel. A verb after not only needs a verb after but also.

Online learning not only saves time but also it is increasing access.

Online learning not only saves time but also access.

Online learning not only saves time but also increases access.

Online learning saves not only time but also money.

In the second right line, both sides are nouns: time, money. That is also parallel.

At the start of a sentence, not only changes the word order. The helping verb comes before the subject, as in a question: "Not only does online learning save time, but it also increases access." This is C1 grammar. See Inversion and emphasis.

Pattern 15: the new question pattern

Your table had fourteen patterns. Pattern 15 is the one new pattern. It fills a gap. The first fourteen are all statements. But at work you ask questions all day.

Ana: Do you work from home on Fridays?

Ben: Yes, I do. Does the new course include speaking practice?

Ana: No, it doesn't. But it includes writing feedback.

To ask a yes or no question in the present simple, put do or does before the subject. Then use the base verb.

  • Do with I, you, we, they and plural nouns: "Do they use Docker?"
  • Does with he, she, it and one person or thing: "Does the build pass?"
  • The -s moves to does. The main verb has no -s.

Does she works on Fridays?

Do she work on Fridays?

She works on Fridays?

Does she work on Fridays?

Does she work on Fridays?

Does she work on Fridays?

The third wrong line is possible in speech, with a rising voice. It shows surprise. In writing and in exams, use does.

Three limits of pattern 15

  1. With be, there is no do: "Is the course online?" not "Does the course be online?"
  2. With can, will, should and other modal verbs, there is no do: "Can you share your screen?"
  3. In the past, use did for every subject: "Did the deployment work?"

Short answers repeat the helping verb: "Yes, I do." "No, it doesn't." "Yes, she did." Do not answer with the main verb: "Yes, I work" is not a short answer. Questions with who, what and why come in Questions and negatives.

Each pattern four ways

A pattern is only useful if you can turn it. Each slide shows one pattern four ways: a statement, a negative, a question and a longer version. Say all four aloud.

Subject + verb

Statement: People commute.

Negative: People don't commute.

Question: Do people commute?

Extended: Most people in my city commute by train every morning.

Subject + verb + object

Statement: I read technical documents.

Negative: I don't read technical documents.

Question: Do you read technical documents?

Extended: I read technical documents in English for an hour every day.

Subject + be + adjective

Statement: The timetable is flexible.

Negative: The timetable isn't flexible.

Question: Is the timetable flexible?

Extended: The timetable for the evening course is very flexible this term.

Subject + verb + object + place + time

Statement: I study English at home every evening.

Negative: I don't study English at home every evening.

Question: Do you study English at home every evening?

Extended: I study English with an app at home for thirty minutes every evening.

There is or There are + noun + place

Statement: There are several courses in my area.

Negative: There aren't any courses in my area.

Question: Are there any courses in my area?

Extended: There are several cheap evening courses for adults in my area this year.

Main clause + because + reason

Statement: I practise daily because I need more confidence.

Negative: I don't practise daily because I have no time.

Question: Do you practise daily because you need more confidence?

Extended: I practise speaking daily because I need more confidence in client meetings.

Reason + so + result

Statement: The bus was delayed, so I arrived late.

Negative: The bus wasn't delayed, so I didn't arrive late.

Question: The bus was delayed, so did you arrive late?

Extended: The bus was delayed by heavy snow, so I arrived twenty minutes late for my interview.

Although + contrast, main clause

Statement: Although remote work is flexible, it can feel isolating.

Negative: Although remote work is flexible, it doesn't suit everyone.

Question: Although remote work is flexible, can it feel isolating?

Extended: Although remote work is flexible and cheap, it can feel isolating for new team members.

Main clause. However, contrast.

Statement: Remote work is flexible. However, it can feel isolating.

Negative: Remote work isn't always easy. However, it saves a lot of time.

Question: Remote work is flexible. However, does it feel isolating?

Extended: Remote work is flexible for parents. However, it can feel isolating when the whole team is online.

If + present, can or will + base verb

Statement: If cities improve transport, fewer people will drive.

Negative: If cities don't improve transport, people won't stop driving.

Question: If cities improve transport, will fewer people drive?

Extended: If cities improve buses and cycle lanes, fewer people will drive into the centre.

Noun + who, which, or that + information

Statement: I need a course that fits my schedule.

Negative: I don't need a course that starts at 8 a.m.

Question: Do you need a course that fits your schedule?

Extended: I need an online course that fits my schedule and gives feedback on my writing.

Passive: be + past participle

Statement: The laptop was damaged during delivery.

Negative: The laptop wasn't damaged during delivery.

Question: Was the laptop damaged during delivery?

Extended: The new laptop was badly damaged by the courier during delivery last week.

While + clause, clause

Statement: While offices support teamwork, home working saves travel time.

Negative: While offices support teamwork, home working doesn't waste time on travel.

Question: While offices support teamwork, does home working save travel time?

Extended: While offices support teamwork and quick questions, home working saves travel time and money.

Not only + verb, but also + verb

Statement: Online learning not only saves time but also increases access.

Negative: Online learning neither saves time nor increases access.

Question: Does online learning not only save time but also increase access?

Extended: Not only does online learning save time, but it also increases access for people in small towns.

Do or Does + subject + verb + ?

Statement: The course includes speaking practice.

Negative: The course doesn't include speaking practice.

Question: Does the course include speaking practice?

Extended: Does the evening course include speaking practice with a native speaker every week?

Most negatives add don't, doesn't, didn't or n't after be. Pattern 14 is special. Its negative uses neither ... nor. Pattern 5 often uses any in the negative and the question.

Expert level: from patterns to paragraphs

Real writing mixes patterns. Here is a short opinion paragraph. The numbers show the pattern in each sentence.

  1. There are several good reasons for remote work. 5
  2. It not only saves travel time but also reduces office costs. 14
  3. Although home working is flexible, it can feel isolating for new staff. 8
  4. New employees need a team that answers their questions quickly. 11
  5. If companies plan regular office days, these problems will become smaller. 10
  6. Overall, a mixed model is more practical. 3

Six sentences use six different patterns. The paragraph is easy to read, but it is not childish. This mix is what examiners call range.

Five rules for combining patterns

  1. Accuracy first. A correct simple sentence is better than a broken complex one. IELTS marks grammar with one criterion: Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Both words count.
  2. One connector for one link. Do not stack them. "Although ... but" and "because ... so" are errors.
  3. Old information first, new information last. Start with what the reader knows. End with the new point. The end of a sentence carries the most weight.
  4. Vary the length. After two long sentences, write a short one. Short sentences make strong points.
  5. Join only related ideas. If two ideas have no clear link, keep them as two sentences.

Patterns inside patterns

Advanced sentences put one pattern inside another. Here are some safe combinations.

  • 6 + 11: "I chose a course that fits my schedule because I often work late."
  • 10 + 12: "If the laptop is damaged during delivery, the shop will replace it."
  • 8 + 5: "Although there are several courses in my area, none of them fits my schedule."
  • 13 + 3: "While the office is noisy, it is good for quick questions."
  • 9 + 12: "The code is clean. However, it was not tested on mobile."

The same patterns work for a status message at work:

Update: The release was delayed, so we moved the demo to Thursday. Although most tests pass, two payment tests fail on mobile. There is a fix in review. If the review is approved today, we will release tomorrow morning. Does anyone need the old build for testing?

That message uses patterns 7, 8, 5, 10 and 15. It is clear, short and polite.

Patterns to remember

Here are all fifteen patterns in one table. The first fourteen rows are your own table, word for word. Row 15 is the one new pattern.

Sentence patterns from complete ideas to controlled complexity
PatternPurposeModelAccuracy note
Subject + verbComplete basic actionPeople commute.Every sentence needs a subject and a finite verb.
Subject + verb + objectAction directed at a thingI read technical documents.Keep the object close to the verb.
Subject + be + adjectiveDescribe a state or qualityThe timetable is flexible.Use an adjective, not an adverb, after be.
Subject + verb + object + place + timeAdd practical detailI study English at home every evening.This is the safest neutral order.
There is or There are + noun + placeIntroduce existenceThere are several courses in my area.Match is or are to the following noun.
Main clause + because + reasonExplain whyI practise daily because I need more confidence.Because must introduce a complete clause.
Reason + so + resultShow a direct resultThe bus was delayed, so I arrived late.Use a comma before so when it joins two clauses.
Although + contrast, main clauseBalance two ideasAlthough remote work is flexible, it can feel isolating.Do not add however to the same sentence.
Main clause. However, contrast.Contrast two sentencesRemote work is flexible. However, it can feel isolating.Use a full stop or semicolon before however.
If + present, can or will + base verbCondition and resultIf cities improve transport, fewer people will drive.Do not normally use will in the if-clause.
Noun + who, which, or that + informationAdd defining detailI need a course that fits my schedule.Choose who for people and which or that for things.
Passive: be + past participleFocus on action or resultThe laptop was damaged during delivery.Name the agent only when it matters.
While + clause, clauseCompare simultaneous or contrasting ideasWhile offices support teamwork, home working saves travel time.Keep both clauses complete.
Not only + verb, but also + verbAdd balanced emphasisOnline learning not only saves time but also increases access.Keep the grammar parallel on both sides.
Do or Does + subject + verb + ? NewAsk a yes or no questionDoes the course include speaking practice?After do or does, use the base verb with no -s.

Learn the table one row a day. Write the model sentence. Then write three new sentences about your own life with the same shape.

The 30 connectors

Read these three sentences. They link the same two facts in three ways.

  • The plan is expensive, but it may be necessary.
  • Although the plan is expensive, it may be necessary.
  • The plan is expensive. However, it may be necessary.

The meaning is the same: contrast. But the grammar and the punctuation are different. A connector belongs to one of four grammar groups. Learn the group, and the punctuation follows.

Four groups of connectors and their punctuation
GroupConnectorsShape
Coordinating conjunctionsand, but, or, so, yetClause, but clause.
Subordinating conjunctionsbecause, since, as, although, even though, whereas, while, if, unless, when, before, afterAlthough clause, clause. Or: Clause although clause.
Relative wordswhich, who, thatNoun that clause.
Sentence linkershowever, therefore, consequently, moreover, in addition, for example, on the other hand, as a result, in conclusion, overallClause. However, clause.

Punctuation in four rules

  1. Coordinating conjunction between two clauses: comma before it. "The salary is attractive, but the commute is long."
  2. Subordinate clause first: comma after it. "If I practise, I improve." Subordinate clause second: usually no comma. "I improve if I practise."
  3. Sentence linker: full stop or semicolon before it, comma after it. "Demand increased; therefore, prices rose."
  4. Relative clause: no comma when it tells you which one. A comma when it only adds extra information.

Rule 4 needs an example. Compare these two sentences.

  • "Employees who receive feedback can improve faster." Which employees? The ones with feedback. No commas.
  • "The council opened a clinic, which improved local access." The clinic is already clear. The extra fact gets a comma. Use which here, not that.

Choose by meaning

Ask yourself one question first: what is the link between my two ideas? Then pick a connector from that row.

The 30 connectors grouped by meaning
MeaningConnectorsSafe first choice
Additionand, in addition, moreoverand. In formal writing: in addition.
Choiceoror
Contrastbut, yet, although, even though, whereas, while, however, on the other handbut, although or however
Reasonbecause, since, asbecause. It is the clearest.
Resultso, therefore, consequently, as a resultso. In formal writing: as a result.
Conditionif, unlessif. Unless means if not.
Timewhen, before, after, whilewhen
Extra informationwhich, who, thatwho for people, that for things
Example and summaryfor example, in conclusion, overallfor example. At the end: in conclusion.

Too many formal linkers make writing heavy. Do not start every sentence with moreover or furthermore. In a good paragraph, many sentences need no linker at all.

Here is the full list of 30 connectors from your table, word for word.

Conjunctions, relative words, and discourse linkers
ConnectorRelationshipModel sentenceAccuracy note
andadditionThe course is practical, and the timetable is flexible.Join equal ideas; do not use it to connect an unlimited chain.
butcontrastThe salary is attractive, but the commute is long.Use a comma when both sides are complete clauses.
orchoicePeople can drive, or they can use public transport.Make the alternatives clear.
soresultThe train was cancelled, so I worked from home.Do not combine because and so for the same relationship.
yetunexpected contrastThe method is simple, yet it is effective.It is slightly more formal than but.
becausereasonI chose the course because it includes speaking practice.It needs a complete main clause.
sincereasonSince housing is expensive, many adults share flats.It can also mean from a past time, so check clarity.
asreasonAs demand increased, prices rose.Because is often clearer for learners.
althoughcontrastAlthough the plan is costly, it may reduce pollution.Do not use but or however in the same structure.
even thoughstrong contrastEven though I was tired, I completed the practice test.Use it when the contrast is surprising.
whereasdirect comparisonCity life is convenient, whereas rural life is quieter.Best for two clearly contrasting facts.
whilecontrast or timeWhile technology saves time, it can reduce privacy.Make the intended relationship clear.
ifconditionIf I practise consistently, I can become more fluent.Use present simple for a realistic future condition.
unlessnegative conditionPeople will continue driving unless transport improves.It means if not.
whentime or conditionWhen employees receive training, they often feel more confident.Use for a likely or repeated situation.
beforetime sequenceCheck your verb endings before you submit the essay.It can begin either clause.
aftertime sequenceAfter I finish a draft, I check articles.Do not confuse it with afterwards, which is an adverb.
whichrelative informationThe council opened a clinic, which improved local access.Use a comma for extra, non-defining information.
whorelative information about a personEmployees who receive feedback can improve faster.No comma when the information identifies the group.
thatdefining informationI need a laptop that can run this software.Do not normally place a comma before defining that.
howeversentence contrastThe plan is expensive. However, it may be necessary.Use a full stop or semicolon before it and a comma after it.

consequentlyresultThe road was closed; consequently, traffic moved elsewhere.Use it only when the cause is already clear.
moreoverstrong additionThe policy is affordable; moreover, it is easy to implement.Do not overuse formal linkers.
in additionadditionIn addition, the new library provides free internet access.Add a genuinely new point.

Practice

There is at least one task for every pattern. The pattern number is in brackets. Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the correct sentence

(Pattern 2) Which sentence is correct?

  • I read every morning the news.
  • I read the news every morning.
  • I every morning read the news.

Keep the object close to the verb. Time goes at the end.

(Pattern 3) Which sentence is correct?

  • The new office is quietly.
  • The new office quiet.
  • The new office is quiet.

After be, use an adjective. And do not drop be.

(Pattern 5) Which sentence is correct?

  • There is three open tickets.
  • There are three open tickets.
  • Have three open tickets.

Match the verb to the noun after it. Three tickets is plural, so use are.

(Pattern 8) Which sentence is correct?

  • Although the app is fast, but it uses a lot of memory.
  • Although the app is fast, it uses a lot of memory.
  • Although the app is fast. It uses a lot of memory.

Use one contrast word only. The although clause also needs its main clause in the same sentence.

(Pattern 9) Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

  • The design is simple, however it is slow.
  • The design is simple however, it is slow.
  • The design is simple. However, it is slow.

Put a full stop or semicolon before however and a comma after it.

(Pattern 15) Which question is correct?

  • Does your manager speaks English?
  • Do your manager speak English?
  • Does your manager speak English?

One manager means does. After does, use the base verb with no -s.

Fill the gap

(Pattern 1) My train usually (arrive) at 8.15.

(Pattern 6) I work late on Mondays because ? have a meeting with the US team.

(Pattern 6) The flight was cancelled because ? the storm.

(Pattern 7) The server was down, ? we used the backup.

(Pattern 10) If it (rain) tomorrow, we will work from home.

(Pattern 10) If you finish the review today, we (release) the app tomorrow.

(Pattern 11) We need a designer ? knows accessibility well.

(Pattern 12) The invoice (send) to the client yesterday.

(Pattern 15) ? the meeting room have a screen?

(Pattern 15) ? your colleagues use English in meetings?

Choose the connector

The method is simple, ? it is effective. (unexpected contrast)

People will continue driving ? transport improves. (if not)

City life is convenient, ? rural life is quieter. (direct comparison)

The road was closed. As a ?, traffic moved elsewhere.

Check your verb endings ? you submit the essay.

Think and write

  1. (Pattern 1) Each line has one mistake. Fix it. (a) Arrived at nine. (b) The tests running. (c) My laptop it crashed.
    Answer

    (a) I arrived at nine. (b) The tests are running. (c) My laptop crashed.

  2. (Pattern 4) Put the words in order: in the office / every Tuesday / I / my team / meet.
    Answer

    I meet my team in the office every Tuesday. Or: Every Tuesday, I meet my team in the office.

  3. (Patterns 6 and 7) Join the two ideas twice. First use because. Then use so. "The documentation was unclear. I asked a colleague."
    Answer

    I asked a colleague because the documentation was unclear. The documentation was unclear, so I asked a colleague.

  4. (Patterns 8 and 9) Write the contrast in two ways. "The new laptop is light. The battery is weak."
    Answer

    Although the new laptop is light, the battery is weak. The new laptop is light. However, the battery is weak.

  5. (Pattern 11) Join with who, which or that. "I work with a tester. She finds every bug."
    Answer

    I work with a tester who finds every bug. You can also use that.

  6. (Pattern 12) Change to the passive. Leave out the agent if it is not important. (a) Someone stole my bike. (b) The team released version 2.0 in May.
    Answer

    (a) My bike was stolen. (b) Version 2.0 was released in May.

  7. (Pattern 13) Join with while to compare. "Trains are fast. Buses are cheaper."
    Answer

    While trains are fast, buses are cheaper.

  8. (Pattern 14) Rewrite with not only ... but also. "The tool finds bugs. It also suggests fixes."
    Answer

    The tool not only finds bugs but also suggests fixes.

  9. (Pattern 15) Make a yes or no question. Then give a short answer. (a) The app supports dark mode. (b) Your team uses Slack.
    Answer

    (a) Does the app support dark mode? Yes, it does. (b) Does your team use Slack? No, it doesn't. Or, thinking of the people: Do your team members use Slack? Yes, they do.

  10. (Connectors) Find and fix the two mistakes. "Because the price rose, so many customers left. However the company kept its plan."
    Answer

    Because the price rose, many customers left. However, the company kept its plan. Remove so, because one link needs one connector. Add a comma after however.

  11. (Expert) Start with not only and change the word order. "The new process not only saves money but also reduces errors."
    Answer

    Not only does the new process save money, but it also reduces errors. The helping verb does comes before the subject. The main verb loses its -s.

  12. (All patterns) Write a paragraph of six sentences about your job or your city. Use six different patterns. Write the pattern number after each sentence.
    Model answer

    I work as a backend engineer in Osaka. (2) There are many tech companies in my area. (5) Although the salaries are good, the hours can be long. (8) I chose a company that allows remote work. (11) If the project goes well, we will hire two new engineers next year. (10) Does your company use English at work? (15)

Key takeaways

  • Fifteen patterns build most English sentences. Fourteen come from your table. Pattern 15, Do or Does + subject + verb + ?, is the new one.
  • There are three families: simple (one clause), joined (two equal parts) and complex (main clause plus subordinate clause).
  • Every sentence needs a subject and a finite verb. Keep the object close to the verb.
  • Use one connector for one link. Never write "although ... but" or "because ... so".
  • Punctuation follows the connector group. A comma before but and so. A full stop or semicolon before however.
  • Turn every pattern four ways: statement, negative, question and a longer version.
  • At the expert level, mix patterns, keep them accurate and put new information at the end.

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Contrasting ideas. Although, even though, though, despite and in spite of.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Conditionals: zero, first and second. If with the present simple and will.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Questions and negatives. Yes or no questions with do, does and did.
  • UK Department for Education: English glossary. Clauses, conjunctions, relative clauses and the passive.

Sounds and spelling

English has 26 letters but about 44 sounds. So one letter can have many sounds, and one sound can have many spellings. This chapter gives you the sounds, a short key to the phonetic symbols and the spelling patterns that work most of the time.

  • Say and spell the 26 letter names, also on a call.
  • Read the phonetic symbols in a dictionary entry.
  • Use the magic e, double consonant and i before e patterns.
  • Count syllables and put the stress in the right place.
  • Say -s and -ed endings correctly and avoid homophone mistakes.

The alphabet and the letter names

Listen to this call. Ana spells her email address.

Ben: Could you spell your surname, please?

Ana: Sure. It's Kato. K, A, T, O.

Ben: Thanks. And your email?

Ana: ana dot kato at example dot com. Ana is A, N, A. All lower case.

Ben: Is that one T or double T?

Ana: Just one T.

Every letter has a name. You need the names to spell words aloud. English has 26 letters. Five are vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u. The letter y is sometimes a vowel too, as in my and gym. The other letters are consonant letters.

The easiest way to learn the names is by sound. Letters in the same row rhyme.

Letter names grouped by their vowel sound
SoundLettersRhymes with
/eɪ/A, H, J, Kday
/iː/B, C, D, E, G, P, T, Vsee
/e/F, L, M, N, S, X, Z (British "zed")bed
/aɪ/I, Ymy
/əʊ/Ogo
/uː/Q, U, Wyou
/ɑː/Rcar

A few names need care:

  • H is "aitch", /eɪtʃ/. Some speakers say "haitch". Dictionaries give "aitch".
  • W is "double u". It has three syllables.
  • Z is "zed" in British English and "zee" in American English.
  • R is /ɑː/ in British English. Americans add an r sound at the end.

Learners often mix up three pairs: G /dʒiː/ and J /dʒeɪ/, E /iː/ and I /aɪ/, and A /eɪ/ and E /iː/. Practise them with real words: "GitHub is G, I, T." "JSON is J, S, O, N."

Words for spelling aloud

Saying symbols in an address
SymbolSayExample
@atana at example dot com
.dotexample dot com
-hyphen or dashmy hyphen app
_underscoreuser underscore id
/slash, or forward slashapi slash v2
ttdouble TMatt: M, A, double T
A or acapital A, or lower-case acapital K, a, t, o

Sounds: vowels and consonants

Say these words: cat, cake, car, ball, about. They all have the letter a. They have five different sounds. Now say see, sea, me, key, piece, receive. They have one sound with six spellings.

A sound that changes meaning is a phoneme. Change /p/ to /b/ and pin becomes bin. Standard British English has 44 phonemes. The usual model accent is called Received Pronunciation, or RP. Other accents have a few more or a few less.

  • 24 consonant sounds.
  • 20 vowel sounds: 7 short, 5 long and 8 diphthongs.

Voiced and voiceless

Put your fingers on your throat. Say "ssss". Then say "zzzz". With /z/ you feel a buzz. With /s/ you feel nothing.

A sound with the buzz is voiced. A sound without it is voiceless. Eight consonant pairs differ only in this way. All vowels are voiced. This idea seems small, but you need it for the -s and -ed endings later in this chapter.

Many learners say /s/ for /θ/ or /z/ for /ð/. Then think sounds like sink. For /θ/ and /ð/, put the tip of your tongue between your teeth. Blow gently.

A short guide to the phonetic symbols

Look up computer in a learner dictionary. You see /kəmˈpjuːtə/. These symbols come from the International Phonetic Alphabet, or IPA. Each symbol is one sound. Once you can read them, a dictionary tells you exactly how to say a new word.

The vowel symbols
SymbolExampleSymbolExample
/ɪ/sit, busy/iː/see, team
/e/bed, head/ɑː/car, father
/æ/cat, app/ɔː/door, talk
/ʌ/cup, love/uː/food, blue
/ɒ/hot, what/ɜː/bird, work
/ʊ/book, put/eɪ/day, name
/ə/about, server/aɪ/my, file
/ɔɪ/boy, join/əʊ/go, code
/aʊ/now, cloud/ɪə/near, here
/eə/hair, there/ʊə/pure, tour

Most consonant symbols look like normal letters: /p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /k/, /m/. Only a few are new. Learn these eight.

The consonant symbols that look new
SymbolSound inSymbolSound in
/θ/think, month/ð/this, other
/ʃ/she, session/ʒ/usually, vision
/tʃ/check, watch/dʒ/job, page
/ŋ/sing, string/j/yes, use

Three marks complete the system:

  • ː after a vowel means it is long: /iː/ in sheep, but /ɪ/ in ship.
  • ˈ before a syllable shows the main stress: /kəmˈpjuːtə/.
  • ˌ low down shows a weaker second stress: /ˌæplɪˈkeɪʃn/ (application).

The schwa: the most common sound

The symbol /ə/ is called schwa. It is a short, relaxed "uh". You hear it in about, computer, problem and to in fast speech. Schwa is the most frequent sound in spoken English. In RP it is about 10% of all speech sounds. It appears only in syllables without stress.

Do not read IPA like normal letters. The symbol /j/ is the sound at the start of yes, not the j in job. The symbol /e/ is the vowel in bed, not the letter name E.

Books do not all use the same symbols. American dictionaries write /oʊ/ where British ones write /əʊ/. The UK school curriculum writes /ɛ/ for the vowel in bed. Some newer phonetics books write /ɛː/ for air, because many speakers now say it as one long vowel. Also, many younger British speakers say tour like tore. The sounds are the same. Only the symbols change.

Silent letters

Say these words aloud: knife, write, climb, hour, listen, walk, sign, night. Each word has a letter you do not say. It is a silent letter.

Many silent letters were spoken hundreds of years ago. In old English, people said the k in knight. The sound went away, but the spelling stayed. Other silent letters came from Latin, Greek or French.

Common silent letters
Silent letterWhereExamples
kbefore n at the startknow, knee, knowledge
wbefore r, and in a few wordswrite, wrong, wrapper, answer, who
bafter m, and before tclimb, thumb, debt, doubt
gbefore nsign, design, align, foreign
ghafter i, and in other wordsnight, light, high, through, daughter
hat the start of a few wordshour, honest, honour
lbefore k, d, m, fwalk, talk, could, should, calm, half
tafter s, before en or lelisten, castle, fasten
nafter m at the endautumn, column
pbefore s and t in a few wordspsychology, receipt
sin a few wordsisland, aisle

Software English is full of silent letters. You meet design, align, sign in, debt (as in technical debt), column, knowledge base, wrapper and receipt every week.

A silent letter often comes back in a related word. Use the long word to remember the spelling: sign and signature, column and columnist, muscle and muscular, bomb and bombard.

Do not say the silent letter. "K-nife" and "wal-k" sound strange. But do not drop letters that are not silent. In keyboard and help, you say the k and the l.

Spelling patterns that work

English spelling is not random. A few patterns cover thousands of words. Learn these three first.

Pattern 1: the magic e

hat, pin, hop, cut

Short vowel sounds: /æ/, /ɪ/, /ɒ/, /ʌ/.

hate, pine, hope, cute

Long sounds. The vowel says its letter name.

An e at the end of a short word is silent. But it changes the vowel before it. Teachers call it the magic e. The UK school curriculum calls the pair a split digraph. Think of code, note, file, save, use, type.

When you add an ending that starts with a vowel, drop the e: make, making; hope, hoped; write, writer; nice, nicest. Before an ending that starts with a consonant, keep the e: hopeful, careless, movement.

Some very common words break the magic e pattern: have, give, live (the verb), love, come, some, done, gone. Also, keep the e in being, and in noticeable and changeable, where it keeps the c and g soft.

Pattern 2: double the consonant

Compare hoping (from hope) and hopping (from hop). The double p keeps the vowel short. That is the job of a double consonant.

Use these four questions before you add -ed, -ing, -er or -est.

  1. Does the word end in one vowel letter plus one consonant letter? stop, plan, big: yes. need, help, rain: no, so do not double.
  2. Is the last consonant w, x or y? Then never double: fixed, showed, playing.
  3. Does the word have one syllable? Then double: stopped, planning, bigger, hottest.
  4. Longer word: is the last syllable stressed? Then double: begin, beginning. commit, committed. prefer, preferred. If not, do not: visit, visited. open, opened. develop, developed.

travel, travelled, travelling

cancel, cancelled

model, modelled

label, labelled

travel, traveled, traveling

cancel, canceled

model, modeled

label, labeled

British English usually doubles a final l after one vowel, even without stress. American English usually does not. This book uses British spelling. Note: cancellation has double l in both British and American English.

Two software words break rule 4. Program and format have stress on the first syllable, but they double: programmed, programming, formatted. Learn them as exceptions.

Pattern 3: i before e

Look at these words: believe, piece, field, chief, achieve. After c: receive, ceiling, receipt, deceive.

The old rhyme says "i before e, except after c". It only works when the sound is /iː/, as in see. The UK school curriculum teaches it with this limit. Three exceptions with /iː/ are protein, caffeine and seize.

For other sounds the rule does not help: their, height, weight, foreign, science, efficient. Learn these by sight.

More patterns in one table

Other useful spelling patterns
PatternExamplesWatch out
Consonant + y: change y to icity, cities. try, tries, tried.Vowel + y keeps y: day, days. play, played.
Ending -f or -fe: change to -vesknife, knives. half, halves.Some keep -fs: roof, roofs. chef, chefs.
Hissing sound: add -esbus, buses. fix, fixes. push, pushes.The -es adds a syllable.
c before e, i, y says /s/city, centre, cycle, processc before a, o, u says /k/: cat, code, cut.
-ck after one short vowelback, check, stack, lockAfter a long vowel or a consonant: bake, desk.

British and American spelling also differ in some groups: colour and color, centre and center, licence (noun) and license, programme (a TV show) and program. For computer software, British English also writes program. Many British writers use -ise (organise). Others use -ize. Choose one and keep it.

Syllables and word stress

Clap as you say com-pu-ter. You clap three times. Each clap is a syllable. Now say it again. The middle clap is stronger: comPUter. That strong syllable has the word stress.

A syllable has one vowel sound. Count sounds, not letters. Worked has one syllable. Wednesday has two: WENZ-day. Vegetable usually has three: VEJ-tuh-bul.

The stress can move inside a word family. Look at the picture. The big circle is the stressed syllable.

A stressed syllable is longer, louder and higher. Unstressed syllables are short and weak. Their vowel often becomes schwa. Listen to the o in photograph and photographer. It changes from /əʊ/ to /ə/ when it loses the stress.

Five stress tendencies

English stress has no perfect rule. But these tendencies are right most of the time.

  1. Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives: stress on the first syllable. TAble, HAPpy, SERver.
  2. Most two-syllable verbs: stress on the second syllable. deCIDE, reLAX, dePLOY.
  3. Endings -tion, -sion, -ic, -ical and -ity: stress the syllable just before. inforMAtion, deCIsion, ecoNOMic, seCURity.
  4. Compound nouns: stress the first part. KEYboard, LAPtop, PASSword, DAtabase, FEEDback.
  5. Endings -ee, -eer and -ese: stress the ending. employEE, engiNEER, JapaNESE.

Rules 1 and 2 explain pairs with the same spelling. The noun has early stress. The verb has late stress.

Same spelling, different stress
WordNounVerb
recorda REcordto reCORD
presenta PREsentto preSENT
objectan OBjectto obJECT
increasean INcreaseto inCREASE
contracta CONtractto conTRACT

Wrong stress can make a word hard to understand, even with every sound right. Learners often stress these work words wrongly: deVELop, ALgorithm, aNALysis, comPOnent, TECHnical, eVENT. Check the ˈ mark in the dictionary for every new word.

Endings: -s and -ed

Say these three words: books, files, pages. Listen to the end. You hear /s/, then /z/, then /ɪz/. The spelling is almost the same. The sound is not.

The -s ending

Three sounds of -s and -es
Last sound of the wordSayExamples
Voiceless: /p/, /t/, /k/, /f/, /θ//s/stops, gets, books, laughs, months
Voiced, or a vowel/z/runs, bugs, files, servers, plays, goes
Hissing: /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ//ɪz/ (extra syllable)buses, fixes, pushes, watches, pages, changes

The same three sounds work for every -s: plurals (bugs), the third person (she runs), possessives (Mark's, Ana's, Alex's) and short forms (it's /s/, he's /z/).

The -ed ending

Follow the questions on the slides. The order matters.

Say the base verb

Say the verb without -ed: work, play, start. Listen to its last sound.

Find the last sound, not the letter

Fix ends in the sound /s/. Laugh ends in /f/. Change ends in /dʒ/. Save ends in /v/. The final e is silent.

Is it /t/ or /d/? Say /ɪd/

Add a syllable: wanted, started, needed, added, deleted, updated.

Otherwise: voiceless or voiced?

Voiceless gives /t/: worked, stopped, fixed, pushed, watched. Voiced or a vowel gives /d/: played, called, opened, saved, logged.

Only /ɪd/ adds a syllable. Worked is one syllable: /wɜːkt/. Played is one syllable: /pleɪd/.

I work-ed late and fix-ed the bug.

The page load-d slowly.

I worked /wɜːkt/ late and fixed /fɪkst/ the bug.

The page loaded /ˈləʊdɪd/ slowly.

A few -ed words used as adjectives keep the old /ɪd/: a naked eye, a wicked plan, a learned professor, a beloved friend, an aged parent. As normal verbs they follow the rules: "I learned /lɜːnd/ Rust last year."

Homophones

Their going to there office, but there laptops are still hear.

A spell checker finds no mistakes in this sentence. Every word is a real word. But four words are wrong. The correct sentence is: "They're going to their office, but their laptops are still here."

Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings. They are a top source of mistakes in writing, even for native speakers.

Homophones you meet every day
WordsMeaningExample
there, their, they'rea place; belongs to them; they areThey're in their office over there.
its, it'sbelongs to it; it is or it hasIt's a good library. Its docs are clear.
your, you'rebelongs to you; you areYou're right about your test.
to, too, twodirection; also or more than enough; 2I sent two files to Ana too.
here, hearthis place; use your earsCan you hear me? I'm here.
right, writecorrect; put words on paperPlease write the right version.
whether, weatherif; rain and sunCheck whether the weather is OK.
site, sight, citea place or website; seeing; quote a sourceCite the site in your report.
cache, cashfast stored data; moneyClear the cache. Pay in cash.
wait, weightstay until; how heavyWait for the model weights to load.

Some pairs are near-homophones. They are close but not the same: accept and except, affect and effect, advice and advise, lose and loose.

The opposite also exists. A homograph has one spelling but two sounds: read /riːd/ today and read /red/ yesterday. A lead /led/ pipe, but lead /liːd/ a team. Live /lɪv/ in Osaka, but a live /laɪv/ demo.

The most common homophone mistake is its and it's. Test it: can you say "it is" or "it has"? Then write it's. If not, write its. "The function returns its value." Not "it's value".

In IELTS Listening and Reading, an answer with a spelling mistake is marked wrong. British and American spelling are both accepted, but use one style. Learn to spell common words for days, months, numbers and places.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for sounds and spelling
PatternPurposeModelNote
Letter, letter, double letterSpell a name aloudMatt: M, A, double T.G is /dʒiː/ and J is /dʒeɪ/. Do not mix them.
Short word + silent eMake the vowel say its namehop, hope. cut, cute.Drop the e before -ing: hoping.
One vowel + one consonant + endingKeep the vowel shortstop, stopped. begin, beginning.Only when the last syllable is stressed: visited.
Vowel + l + ending (British)Spell British past formstravel, travelled. cancel, cancelled.American English uses one l: traveled.
ie, or ei after cSpell the /iː/ soundbelieve, piece. receive, ceiling.Only for the /iː/ sound. Learn protein and seize.
Last sound /t/ or /d/ + ed = /ɪd/Add a syllable for -edwanted, needed, updated.Never say "work-ed".
Voiceless sound + ed = /t/Say most -ed endingsworked, fixed, stopped.Listen to the sound, not the letter: laughed is /t/.
Hissing sound + es = /ɪz/Say the extra -es syllablebuses, fixes, pages.After other sounds, -s is /s/ or /z/.
Noun: early stress. Verb: late stressSay word pairsa REcord, to reCORD.Most two-syllable words follow this.
Stress before -tion and -icStress long wordsinforMAtion, ecoNOMic.The syllables around it often become schwa.
it's = it is; its = of itChoose the right homophoneIt's fast. Its API is clear.Say "it is". If it fits, write it's.

Practice

Quick quiz

Which letter names have the same vowel sound as day?

  • A, H, J, K
  • B, C, D, E
  • F, L, M, N

A, H, J and K all have /eɪ/.

How many syllables does worked have?

  • One
  • Two
  • Three

After /k/ the -ed is /t/. Only /ɪd/ adds a syllable.

Which word has the -ed ending /ɪd/?

  • pushed
  • logged
  • deleted

Delete ends in /t/, so -ed is /ɪd/.

In which word is the -s pronounced /ɪz/?

  • servers
  • branches
  • commits

Branch ends in the hissing sound /tʃ/, so -es adds /ɪz/.

Which word has a silent letter?

  • keyboard
  • align
  • help

The g in align is silent. You say the k in keyboard and the l in help.

Where is the stress in the verb record?

  • REcord
  • reCORD

Two-syllable verbs usually have late stress. The noun is a REcord.

Spell the new form

stop + ed = ?

make + ing = ?

begin + ing = ?

visit + ed = ?

travel + ed, British spelling = ?

try + es = ?

I can't find the (r_c__pt) for the new monitor.

The library is great, but (its / it's) documentation is old.

Think and write

  1. Spell this address aloud, in words: dev_ops@my-site.io.
    Answer

    d, e, v, underscore, o, p, s, at, m, y, hyphen, s, i, t, e, dot, i, o. You can also say the words: "dev underscore ops at my hyphen site dot i o".

  2. Sort the verbs by the sound of -ed: /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/. asked, tested, opened, watched, loaded, cleaned, helped, decided.
    Answer

    /t/: asked, watched, helped. /d/: opened, cleaned. /ɪd/: tested, loaded, decided.

  3. Find the silent letter in each word: knowledge, debt, listen, column, hour, wrapper.
    Answer

    knowledge: k. debt: b. listen: t. column: n. hour: h. wrapper: w.

  4. Mark the stress with capital letters: computer, deploy, information, password, engineer.
    Answer

    comPUter, dePLOY, inforMAtion, PASSword, engiNEER.

  5. Fix the homophones in this code review comment: "Your right, but its to slow. Lets check weather the cash is working."
    Answer

    You're right, but it's too slow. Let's check whether the cache is working. (Let's means let us, so it needs the apostrophe.)

  6. Read the IPA and write the word: (a) /ˈdeɪtə/ (b) /ʃeə/ (c) /θɪŋk/ (d) /ˈjuːzə/.
    Answer

    (a) data. (b) share. (c) think. (d) user.

  7. Expert. Why do we write preferred with rr, but preference with one r?
    Answer

    In preFERRED the stress stays on -fer, so the r doubles. In PREference the stress moves to the first syllable. The -fer is not stressed, so the r does not double.

  8. Expert. Say why fixed ends in /t/, though the letter before -ed is x.
    Answer

    The rule follows the sound, not the letter. The letter x in fix makes the sounds /ks/. The last sound /s/ is voiceless, so -ed is /t/: /fɪkst/.

"___ in a meeting." (they are)

They're in a meeting.

"The app saves ___ data locally." (belongs to it)

The app saves its data locally.

"I'm not sure ___ it will rain." (if)

I'm not sure whether it will rain.

"Please clear your browser ___." (stored data)

Please clear your browser cache.

"Did you ___ the new rule?" (to receive or agree to)

Did you accept the new rule? Except means "not including".

"The change will ___ performance." (verb: to change something)

The change will affect performance. The noun is effect: "a big effect".

Key takeaways

  • English has 26 letters and about 44 sounds: 24 consonants and 20 vowels in standard British English.
  • Learn the letter names in rhyming groups. Do not mix G and J, or E and I.
  • IPA symbols show the exact sound. The schwa /ə/ is the most common sound, and it is never stressed.
  • Silent letters are history in the spelling. Related words often show them again.
  • Magic e makes the vowel long. A double consonant keeps it short. The i before e rule works only for the /iː/ sound.
  • Every word with two or more syllables has one main stress. Check it in the dictionary.
  • The -s ending sounds /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/. The -ed ending sounds /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/. Follow the last sound, not the letter.
  • Spell checkers do not catch homophones. Test its and it's with "it is".

Sources
