  • Greg Brooks: Dictionary of the British English Spelling System, chapter 2. The 44 phonemes of RP, the schwa and word stress (open textbook).
  • UK Department for Education: English glossary. Definitions of vowel, consonant, digraph and split digraph.
  • IDP IELTS: Common spelling mistakes. Why spelling counts in the Listening and Reading tests.

Nouns and articles

Nouns are the names of people, things and ideas. Small words like a, an and the often come before them. The word the is the most common word in English. This chapter shows you how to use these small words with confidence.

  • Make the plural of regular and irregular nouns.
  • Tell countable and uncountable nouns apart.
  • Choose a, an, the or no article.
  • Use first mention and second mention in a short story.
  • Use some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few and a little correctly.

One or more: singular and plural

One

I found a bug.

She has one laptop.

We need a new file.

More than one

I found three bugs.

She has two laptops.

We need some new files.

A noun names a person, a thing, a place or an idea. Developer, laptop, city and idea are nouns.

A singular noun is about one. A plural noun is about two or more. Most plurals end in -s.

Some nouns are the name of one special person, place or company. They are proper nouns. They start with a capital letter: Ana, Japan, Monday, GitHub. Other nouns are common nouns.

How to spell the plural

Spelling rules for regular plurals
The noun ends inWhat you doExamples
most lettersadd -sbug → bugs, file → files, user → users
-s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -zadd -esbus → buses, class → classes, dish → dishes, match → matches, box → boxes
consonant + ychange y to -iescity → cities, query → queries, library → libraries
vowel + yadd -sday → days, key → keys, array → arrays
-f or -fe (some words)change to -vesknife → knives, life → lives, leaf → leaves, half → halves, shelf → shelves
-f or -fe (other words)add -sroof → roofs, chef → chefs, belief → beliefs, safe → safes
-o (a few words)add -espotato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes, hero → heroes, echo → echoes
-o (most other words)add -sphoto → photos, video → videos, radio → radios, logo → logos, demo → demos

The words with -ves and -oes are a short list. There is no simple rule for them. Learn them as a list. A one-syllable word that ends in one z doubles it: quiz → quizzes.

How to say the -s

The plural ending has three sounds. You hear /s/ in laptops and chats. You hear /z/ in bugs, files and users. You hear /ɪz/ in boxes, pages and classes. The /ɪz/ ending adds one more syllable. The chapter Sounds and spelling explains the three sounds.

After a number bigger than one, the noun is plural. After one of, the noun is also plural. Short forms like API and URL take a plain -s, with no apostrophe.

I worked there for two year.

She is one of my colleague.

The app calls three API's.

I worked there for two years.

She is one of my colleagues.

The app calls three APIs.

Irregular plurals

  • One child, two children.
  • One person, many people.
  • One sheep, ten sheep.

An irregular plural does not follow the -s rule. These words are old. Many of them are very common, so you must know them.

The main groups of irregular plurals
GroupExamples
The vowel changesman → men, woman → women, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, goose → geese, mouse → mice
Add -en or -renchild → children, ox → oxen
A new wordperson → people
No change at allsheep, fish, deer, aircraft, series, species

The word women sounds like "wimmin". The first vowel changes in speech, but not in spelling. The computer device is also a mouse, and its usual plural is mice.

Always plural, or plural without -s

  • Some things have two equal parts: trousers, jeans, glasses, scissors, headphones. They are always plural. To count them, say a pair of: "a pair of jeans", "two pairs of glasses".
  • Clothes is always plural. There is no "a clothe".
  • People, police and cattle have no -s, but they are plural. Say "The police are here."

Singular, but with -s

Some nouns end in -s, but they are singular. News is the most important one. Say "The news is good." School subjects like maths, physics and economics also take a singular verb. "Maths is my favourite subject."

Words from Latin and Greek

Science and software use many words from Latin and Greek. Some keep their old plural.

Old plurals in technical English
SingularPluralNote
criterioncriteria"The criteria are clear." Not "a criteria".
phenomenonphenomenaMostly in science writing.
analysisanalysesAlso crisis → crises, thesis → theses, hypothesis → hypotheses.
matrix, vertexmatrices, verticesCommon in maths and graphics.
indexindexes or indicesDatabase people usually say indexes. Maths uses indices.
mediummedia"Social media is everywhere" is now normal.
schema, formulaschemas, formulasThe -s form is normal. Schemata and formulae are old or formal.
status, virusstatuses, virusesRegular plurals. Not "stati" or "viri".

The word data was the plural of datum. Today most people use it as an uncountable noun. "The data is ready." In software this is almost always the form. Some science journals still write "The data are ready." Both are correct. Follow the style of your team or journal.

Countable and uncountable nouns

I have a question.

I have two questions.

How many questions do you have?

I need some advice.

I need some information.

How much time do we have?

A countable noun has a singular and a plural. You can put a number before it. One question, two questions, ten questions.

An uncountable noun has only one form. It has no plural. It never takes a or an. You cannot say "an advice" or "two informations".

Uncountable nouns are often a substance, a feeling, an activity or a group of things. Furniture is a group of chairs, tables and beds. You count the chairs, but not the furniture.

Many learners find this hard. In your language the same idea may be countable. In English, these words are uncountable: advice, information, news, knowledge, homework, money, traffic, weather.

Countable partners

Many uncountable nouns have a countable partner with a similar meaning. Use the partner when you want a number.

Uncountable nouns and their countable partners
UncountableCountable partnerExample
worka job, a taskI have a lot of work. I have three tasks.
advicea tip, a suggestionShe gave me some advice. She gave me two tips.
travela trip, a journeyI love travel. It was a long trip.
luggagea bag, a suitcaseMy luggage is heavy. I have two bags.
softwarea program, an app, a toolWe use free software. We use three tools.
codea line of code, a script, a functionThe code is clean. I wrote two scripts.
feedbacka commentThanks for your feedback. I left five comments.
researcha study, a paperWe did some research. We read four papers.
moneya coin, a note, a dollarI have no money. I have three coins.

Unit words

You can also count an uncountable noun with a unit word. The unit word is countable. The noun after of stays the same.

  • a piece of advice, two pieces of furniture, a piece of software
  • an item of news, three items of luggage
  • a bit of help (informal)
  • a cup of coffee, a bottle of water, a slice of bread, a bowl of rice
  • a line of code, a gigabyte of data

Nouns with two meanings

Some nouns are countable with one meaning and uncountable with another. The meaning decides.

One noun, two meanings
NounUncountableCountable
coffeeCoffee grows in Brazil. (the drink)Two coffees, please. (two cups)
paperThe printer needs paper. (the material)I read a paper about AI. (an article)
timeI don't have time today.I called her three times. (occasions)
experienceShe has experience with Rust. (knowledge)The trip was a great experience. (an event)
roomIs there room for one more? (space)We booked a meeting room.
codeThe code is on GitHub. (program text)The server sent an error code.

An uncountable noun takes a singular verb. Say "The information is correct" and "Your feedback was useful."

Do not add -s to an uncountable noun. Do not put a or an before it. Use a singular verb with it.

Can you give me an advice?

We need more informations.

We installed two new softwares.

I have a good news.

The news are bad.

Can you give me some advice?

We need more information.

We installed two new programs.

I have some good news.

The news is bad.

A or an?

  • I need a laptop.
  • She is an engineer.
  • The meeting takes an hour.
  • He studies at a university.

A and an are the indefinite article. They mean "one". Use them only with a singular countable noun.

The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter. Use a before a consonant sound. Use an before a vowel sound.

Tricky first sounds
WordFirst soundArticle
hour, honestthe h is silent, so a vowel soundan hour, an honest answer
user, university, URL, UI"you", a consonant sounda user, a URL, a UI
one-time password, European"w" and "y" soundsa one-time password, a European city
API, IDE, LLM, HTTP, XML, SSHthe letter names start with a vowel soundan API, an LLM, an HTTP request, an XML file
JSON, CSV, PDFconsonant soundsa JSON file, a CSV file, a PDF
SQL"ess-queue-ell" or "sequel"an SQL query or a SQL query

Look at the last row. Both forms are correct. The article follows the way the speaker says the word.

An adjective can come between the article and the noun. Then the adjective decides: an old bug, a new error, an unusual problem.

Other uses of a and an

  • Jobs: She is a data engineer. He is an architect.
  • One of a group: Python is a programming language.
  • Per: twice a week, three meetings a day, 100 kilometres an hour.
  • Feelings: What a nice view! It was such a long day.

A and one are similar. Use one when the number is important. "I have a question" is normal. "I have one question, not two" puts the focus on the number.

A job needs a or an. Choose by the sound. Never use a or an with a plural or uncountable noun.

She is engineer.

It takes a hour.

He works at an university.

I need a information.

They are an good team.

She is an engineer.

It takes an hour.

He works at a university.

I need some information.

They are a good team.

The: first mention and second mention

Read this short story. Look at the articles in bold. Each slide shows one step.

Something new

Yesterday I found a bug in an old script.

The listener hears about the bug and the script for the first time. So we use a and an.

Now we know it

The bug was in the login function.

Now the listener knows which bug. It is the bug from step 1. So we use the.

One more new thing

I wrote a test. The test failed.

First mention: a test. Second mention: the test.

A new person

I asked a colleague for help. The colleague found the problem in five minutes.

We knew there was a problem, so it is the problem.

The answer

The problem was a missing comma.

The comma is new information. So we use a.

The end

Now the script works, and the test passes.

Everything is known now. Every article is the.

The is the definite article. It means "you know which one". It works with every kind of noun: singular, plural and uncountable.

The first time you talk about something, use a or an. This is the first mention. After that, the listener knows it. Now use the. This is the second mention.

Other reasons for the

Sometimes you use the at the first mention. The listener already knows which one, for another reason.

Six more reasons to use the
ReasonExample
There is only one.the sun, the moon, the internet, the world
Everyone in the situation knows which one.Can you close the door? Is the server down again?
Superlatives and order wordsthe best tool, the first step, the last line, the next slide, the same problem
A phrase after the noun tells you which one.the name of the file, the woman in the red coat, the bug that I found
Some place namesthe Thames, the Pacific, the Alps, the Netherlands, the UK, the United States
Decades and instrumentsthe 1990s, play the guitar

A superlative like best means there is only one top thing. So it needs the.

Most countries have no article: Japan, France, Brazil. A country takes the when its name is plural or has a word like Kingdom, States or Republic. The chapter Advanced articles and prepositions has the full rules for place names.

How to say the

Before a consonant sound, say /ðə/, like "thuh": the bug, the user. Before a vowel sound, say /ði/, like "thee": the error, the API, the hour.

Do not forget the when both people know which one. Do not use a after the first mention.

I bought a book. A book is about Rust.

Sun is very hot today.

This is best tool for the job.

Can you open window?

I bought a book. The book is about Rust.

The sun is very hot today.

This is the best tool for the job.

Can you open the window?

No article

  • Developers drink a lot of coffee.
  • Water is free here.
  • I speak English and I write Python.
  • We have lunch at one.
  • She goes to work by bus.

English often uses no article. Some books call this the zero article. The main reason is a general meaning. You talk about all things of one kind.

A general meaning uses a plural noun or an uncountable noun. It has no article.

General: no article

Coffee is expensive these days.

Users want fast apps.

Life is short.

Specific: the

The coffee in our office is bad.

The users of this app want dark mode.

The life of a startup founder is hard.

On the right, a phrase tells you which coffee, which users, which life. So we use the.

Groups of nouns with no article
GroupExamples
Names of people and companiesAna, Dr Lee, Google, Microsoft
Most countries, cities and streetsJapan, Berlin, Oxford Street
Languages, including programming languagesEnglish, Japanese, Python, Rust
Days, months and mealson Monday, in May, have breakfast, after dinner
School subjects and sportsmaths, history, football, tennis
Next and last with time wordsnext week, last year, next Friday

Fixed phrases

Some common phrases have no article. Learn them as one unit: at home, at work, go to work, go to bed, by car, by bus, by email, on foot, on time.

With school, university and hospital, there is a small difference. No article means the normal purpose of the place. The means the building.

  • My son goes to school. (He is a student there.)
  • I went to the school for a meeting. (I visited the building.)
  • She is in hospital. (She is a patient. This is British English.)

American English says "in the hospital" for a patient too. It also says "in college" more often than "at university".

Do not use the for a general meaning. Do not use the with languages, sports, meals or fixed phrases.

The life is short.

I like the coffee. (in general)

I go to the work by the bus.

She speaks the Japanese.

See you the next week.

Life is short.

I like coffee.

I go to work by bus.

She speaks Japanese.

See you next week.

Now you know three choices: a or an, the, and no article. Use these steps to choose.

Some, any, much, many and other quantity words

Kim: Is there any coffee left?

Leo: Only a little. And we don't have much milk.

Kim: How many people are coming to the workshop?

Leo: A lot. About thirty. We need some snacks.

Kim: OK. I can buy a few bags of fruit.

A quantity word says how much or how many. Grammar books call it a quantifier. Some quantity words go with countable nouns. Some go with uncountable nouns. Some go with both.

Which quantity word goes with which noun
Quantity wordPlural countableUncountableExample
some, anyyesyessome bugs, some time
a lot of, lots ofyesyesa lot of tests, lots of work
no, enough, plenty ofyesyesno errors, enough memory
manyyesnomany users
a few, few, severalyesnoa few questions
muchnoyesmuch traffic
a little, little, a bit ofnoyesa little help

Some and any

  • Use some in positive sentences. "I have some questions."
  • Use any in negatives and most questions. "I don't have any questions." "Do you have any questions?"
  • Use some in offers and requests. You expect the answer yes. "Would you like some tea?" "Can I have some water?"

Much, many and a lot of

  • Many goes with plural nouns. Much goes with uncountable nouns.
  • Use them mostly in negatives and questions. "We don't have much time." "How many tickets are open?"
  • In positive sentences, a lot of is more natural in speech. Say "We have a lot of time", not "We have much time".
  • Lots of means the same as a lot of. It is a little more informal.
  • At the end of a sentence, drop of. "Thanks a lot." "Do you travel much?"

Use How much for uncountable nouns and prices. Use How many for countable nouns. "How much memory does it use?" "How many servers do we have?"

A few or few? A little or little?

These pairs look the same, but the feeling is different.

  • A few and a little mean "some, enough". The feeling is positive. "I have a few ideas. Let's talk."
  • Few and little mean "not many, not enough". The feeling is negative. "Few people read the manual."
  • Little alone sounds formal. In speech people say very little or not much. "We have very little time."

Check the noun first. Is it countable or uncountable? Then choose the quantity word.

There are much people here.

I don't have many time.

There aren't some errors.

We have a lot of informations.

I have few money, but it is enough.

There are a lot of people here.

I don't have much time.

There aren't any errors.

We have a lot of information.

I have a little money, and it is enough.

More words for amounts, like each, every, all and both, are in Pronouns and determiners.

Common article mistakes

These are the article mistakes that teachers see most often. Read the wrong form, the right form and the reason.

Ten common mistakes
WrongRightWhy
I have car.I have a car.A singular countable noun needs an article or a word like my.
He is doctor.He is a doctor.Jobs need a or an.
The money is not everything.Money is not everything.General meaning: no article.
I play the tennis.I play tennis.Sports have no article.
She is the best in a team.She is the best in the team.We know which team.
It is an useful tool.It is a useful tool.Useful starts with a "y" sound.
Can you give me an information?Can you give me some information?Information is uncountable.
I'll see you in the next Monday.I'll see you next Monday.No article before next or last with time.
Most of people agree.Most people agree.General meaning: most, with no of.
I usually have a lunch at one.I usually have lunch at one.Meals have no article.

Look at row nine again. Most people means people in general. Most of the people is also correct, but it means a group we know. For example, it can mean the people in this room.

Every singular countable noun needs a small word in front. This can be a, an, the, my, this or one. When you check your writing, find each singular countable noun. Then look in front of it.

  1. Find every noun in the sentence.
  2. Is the noun countable or uncountable? Is it singular or plural?
  3. Does the reader know which one? If yes, use the.
  4. If not, and it is singular and countable, use a or an.
  5. If not, and it is plural or uncountable with a general meaning, use no article.
  6. Read the sentence aloud. Check a and an by sound.

Expert uses

These uses are above A2 level. You will meet them in books, news, documentation and exams.

The with a singular noun for a whole kind

"The smartphone changed how we live." This is not one phone. It means all smartphones, as one idea. This use is common for inventions, animals and instruments. It sounds formal. In normal speech, a plural with no article is easier. "Smartphones changed how we live."

A with a singular noun for any example

"A good test checks one thing." This means any good test. It is a typical example of the kind. Use it for definitions. "A compiler is a program that translates code."

A with some uncountable nouns

A few uncountable nouns take a when an adjective or phrase comes with them. "She has a good knowledge of SQL." "He has a deep understanding of networks." Learn these as fixed phrases. "She has a knowledge" alone is wrong.

The with an adjective for a group of people

"The rich", "the young" and "the unemployed" mean groups of people. They take a plural verb. "The young are often better with new apps."

Articles in titles, headlines and commit messages

Short texts often drop articles to save space. A headline says "Server down in Frankfurt". A commit message says "Fix bug in login form". This is normal in these texts only. In emails and documents, use full sentences with articles.

Stressed the

Sometimes a speaker says "thee" with stress before a consonant. It means "the famous one" or "the best one". "Is that the Ana Silva, the author of the book?" "This is the place for pizza in town."

Some and any with a special meaning

Stressed some can mean "a part, but not all". "Some tests pass, but others fail." Any in a positive sentence means "it does not matter which". "Any modern browser works."

In formal writing much can appear in positive sentences. "Much work remains." After too, so and very, much is normal in every style. "There is too much code in this file."

Articles and quantity words are small, but examiners notice them. In IELTS Writing and Speaking, they count under the criterion Grammatical Range and Accuracy. In Cambridge B2 First, the open cloze task often tests small grammar words like these.

Before you finish an exam essay, use the six checking steps above on every paragraph.

For the 60 most common learner mistakes, see The error clinic.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for nouns and articles
PatternPurposeModelNote
a or an + singular countable nounTalk about one thing for the first timeI found a bug in the code.Choose a or an by the first sound.
the + noun (second mention)Talk about a thing the listener knowsThe bug was in the login form.Do not use a again after the first mention.
Subject + be + a or an + jobSay what someone doesShe is an engineer.Not "She is engineer".
Plural noun with no article + verbSay something about all things of one kindUsers want fast apps.The users means a group we know.
Uncountable noun with no article + singular verbTalk about a substance or idea in generalSecurity matters.Not "The security matters" for a general idea.
a piece of + uncountable nounCount an uncountable thingCan I give you a piece of advice?Not "an advice".
the + superlative + nounSay which one is the top oneThis is the fastest server.Superlatives always need the.
some + plural or uncountable nounTalk about an amount in a positive sentenceWe need some test data.Also in offers: "Would you like some tea?"
not + any + nounSay there is nothingThere aren't any errors.Or "There are no errors".
How many + plural noun + ?Ask about a numberHow many users do we have?Not "How many user".
How much + uncountable noun + ?Ask about an amountHow much memory does it use?Also for prices: "How much is it?"
a lot of + plural or uncountable nounTalk about a large amountWe have a lot of work this week.More natural than much in positive sentences.
a few + plural noun or a little + uncountable nounSay there is a small but useful amountI have a few ideas.Few and little alone sound negative.
one of + the or my + plural nounPick one from a groupShe is one of my best colleagues.The noun after one of is plural.

Practice

Choose the right answer

She works as ___ engineer.

  • a
  • an
  • the

Engineer starts with a vowel sound. Jobs need a or an.

Which noun is uncountable?

  • suggestion
  • laptop
  • furniture

Furniture is a group of things. You count chairs and tables, not furniture.

Which plural is correct?

  • childs
  • children
  • childrens

Children is already plural. Do not add -s.

We don't have ___ time before the demo.

  • many
  • much
  • a few

Time is uncountable here. In a negative sentence, use much.

I read ___ interesting article yesterday. ___ article was about chips.

  • a ... A
  • an ... The
  • the ... An

First mention: an, because interesting starts with a vowel sound. Second mention: the.

Which sentence means "not enough"?

  • A few people came to the talk.
  • Few people came to the talk.
  • Some people came to the talk.

Few without a has a negative feeling. It means not many.

Write the plural

  • box → ?
  • query → ?
  • key → ?
  • knife → ?
  • photo → ?
  • tooth → ?
  • criterion → ?

Complete with a, an, the or nothing

Write - for no article.

It takes ? hour to get there.

Can you send me ? URL for the docs?

? Cats sleep a lot.

This is ? worst bug of the year.

She plays ? football on Sundays.

I bought a new chair. ? chair was cheap.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistakes. (a) I need an advice. (b) He is architect. (c) The news are good. (d) I go to the work by the car.
    Answer

    (a) I need some advice. Or: I need a piece of advice. (b) He is an architect. (c) The news is good. (d) I go to work by car.

  2. Make each sentence countable. Use a partner word or a unit word. (a) I have a lot of work. (b) She gave me some advice. (c) We wrote some code.
    Answer

    (a) I have five tasks. (b) She gave me two tips. Or: two pieces of advice. (c) We wrote three scripts. Or: 200 lines of code.

  3. Explain the difference. (a) I like dogs. (b) I like the dogs.
    Answer

    (a) is general. I like all dogs. (b) is specific. I like some dogs that we both know, for example my neighbour's dogs.

  4. Write a short story of four sentences about a problem at work. Use first mention and second mention.
    Model answer

    Last week a customer sent us an email. The email was about a slow page. We checked the page and found a large image. We made the image smaller, and the page is fast now.

  5. Why do we say "a university" but "an hour"?
    Answer

    The choice depends on the first sound. University starts with a "you" sound, which is a consonant sound. In hour the h is silent, so the first sound is a vowel sound.

  6. Expert question. Explain the difference. (a) Most people use a phone. (b) Most of the people use a phone. (c) The phone changed the world.
    Answer

    (a) is about people in general. (b) is about a group we know, for example the people in this office. (c) uses the with a singular noun for the whole kind. It means phones as an invention, not one phone.

A or an: "___ API key"?

An API key. The letter A is said "ay", a vowel sound.

What is the first mention rule?

First time: a or an. After that: the. "I wrote a test. The test failed."

Name five uncountable nouns.

Advice, information, news, furniture, software. Also work, code, feedback, money.

How do you count an uncountable noun?

Use a unit word: a piece of advice, a line of code, a cup of coffee.

When do we use no article?

For a general meaning with a plural or uncountable noun. Also with names, languages, meals and sports.

Much or many with "people"?

Many. People is a plural countable noun. In positive sentences, say "a lot of people".

What is the difference between "a few" and "few"?

A few means some, enough. Few means not many, not enough.

Is "The data is ready" correct?

Yes. Most people use data as uncountable. Some science writing uses "the data are".

Key takeaways

  • Most plurals add -s or -es. Irregular plurals like children, people and teeth must be learned.
  • Countable nouns have a plural. Uncountable nouns like advice, information and software have no plural and no a.
  • Use a or an for one thing at the first mention. Choose by sound, not by letter.
  • Use the when the listener knows which one: second mention, only one, superlatives.
  • Use no article for a general meaning with plural and uncountable nouns.
  • Many and a few go with countable nouns. Much and a little go with uncountable nouns.
  • Some is for positive sentences and offers. Any is for negatives and questions.

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Count nouns. Singular and plural forms and plural spelling.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Uncount nouns. Common uncountable nouns and unit words like a piece of.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Quantifiers. Which quantity words go with countable and uncountable nouns.
  • Purdue OWL: How to Use Articles. Articles by sound, abbreviations, and place names with and without the.
  • Purdue OWL: Count and Noncount Nouns. Plurals, articles and quantity words in one chart.

Pronouns and determiners

Pronouns are short words like she, it and mine. They stand in place of a noun, so you do not repeat it. Determiners are short words like my, this and every. They come before a noun and tell you which one or how many. You use these words in almost every sentence.

  • Use subject, object, possessive and reflexive pronouns in the right place.
  • Show who owns something with my, mine and 's.
  • Choose this, that, these or those, and one or ones.
  • Use there is, there are and the empty subject it.
  • Use each, every, all, both, either and neither.

Subject and object pronouns

Ana is a tester. Ana works in my team. I like Ana. Ana's tests find many bugs.

Ana is a tester. She works in my team. I like her. Her tests find many bugs.

The second text sounds natural. It uses pronouns. A pronoun stands in place of a noun. The listener already knows the noun, so you do not repeat it.

English pronouns change their form. The form shows the job of the word in the sentence. The first job is subject. The second job is object.

All the personal pronouns
SubjectObjectPossessive + nounPossessive aloneReflexive
Imemyminemyself
you (one person)youyouryoursyourself
hehimhishishimself
sheherherhersherself
ititits(rare)itself
weusouroursourselves
you (more people)youyouryoursyourselves
theythemtheirtheirsthemselves
  • The subject pronoun comes before the verb. "She fixed the bug."
  • The object pronoun comes after the verb. "The manager thanked her."
  • After a preposition, use the object pronoun. "This is for you." "Come with us."
  • In short answers, use the object pronoun. "Who wants coffee?" "Me!" "I'm tired." "Me too."

It and they

Use it for one thing, one animal or one idea. Use they for more than one person or thing. "The tests are slow. They take ten minutes."

English also uses they for one person. You use it when you do not know the person's gender, or when the gender is not important. "Someone called. They left a message." The verb stays plural: "they are", not "they is". Many style guides, for example the APA guide, accept this use.

Two subjects together still use subject pronouns. Two objects together still use object pronouns. A polite habit is to put yourself last.

Me and Tom wrote the report.

This is between you and I.

Her is my manager.

My manager she is very kind.

Tom and I wrote the report.

This is between you and me.

She is my manager.

My manager is very kind.

Look at the last example. Do not use a noun and a pronoun for the same subject. Choose one of them.

Not sure about "Tom and I" or "Tom and me"? Remove "Tom and". "I wrote the report" is right, so "Tom and I wrote the report" is right. "The email is for me" is right, so "The email is for Tom and me" is right.

Who owns it? My, mine and 's

  • This is my laptop.
  • This laptop is mine.
  • This is Ana's laptop.
  • This laptop is Ana's.

English has three ways to show who owns something. They all have a possessive meaning.

Three possessive forms
FormPositionExamples
my, your, his, her, its, our, theirbefore a nounmy code, their office, its name
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirsalone, with no noun after itThe red bag is mine. Is this yours?
noun + 'sbefore a noun, or aloneAna's idea. The idea was Ana's.

The words in the first row are determiners. A determiner always comes before a noun. The words in the second row are pronouns. They replace the noun.

How to write the 's

Spelling the possessive 's
The nounWhat you addExamples
singular noun'sthe user's password, my boss's office
plural noun with -s' onlythe users' passwords, my parents' house
plural noun without -s'schildren's books, people's opinions, the men's team
name that ends in -s's or 'James's car or James' car
two names, one shared thing's on the last nameAna and Ben's project (one project)
two names, two things's on each nameAna's and Ben's laptops (two laptops)

Look at the first two rows. "The user's password" is one user. "The users' passwords" is many users. In speech they sound the same. In writing the apostrophe shows the difference.

's or of?

  • For people and animals, use 's: my sister's job, the dog's name.
  • For things, of is more usual: the end of the film, the top of the page.
  • For time words, use 's: today's meeting, last year's results, a week's holiday.
  • For companies, teams and countries, both are fine: the company's rules, the rules of the company.
  • For things, a noun + noun is also common: the file name, the page title, the door handle.

The 's form can also stand alone for a shop or a home. "I'm at the doctor's." "We had dinner at Ana's."

Its means "of it". It's means "it is" or "it has". Possessive pronouns never have an apostrophe. Do not put a or the before my.

The app saves it's data in the cloud.

Is this pen your's?

She is a my friend.

This is the car of my brother.

This is my.

The app saves its data in the cloud.

Is this pen yours?

She is a friend of mine.

This is my brother's car.

This is mine.

Other pairs sound the same but have a different meaning. Your (of you) and you're (you are). Their (of them), there (in that place) and they're (they are). Whose (of who) and who's (who is). Check them every time you write.

Myself, yourself and each other

  • Be careful with the knife. Don't cut yourself.
  • The laptop turns itself off after an hour.
  • I built this website myself.
  • She often works by herself.

Words with -self and -selves are reflexive pronouns. Singular forms end in -self. Plural forms end in -selves. They have three main uses.

Three uses of reflexive pronouns
UseExampleMeaning
The subject and the object are the same.He taught himself Rust.He was the teacher and the student.
Emphasis: this person, not another personI wrote the code myself.Nobody helped me. I did it.
by + reflexiveShe lives by herself.alone, with no other person

Emphasis makes a word stronger. You can also put the reflexive right after a noun. "The CEO herself answered my email." This means "the CEO, not her assistant".

Verbs with no reflexive in English

In many languages these verbs need a reflexive pronoun. In English they normally do not: relax, feel, meet, concentrate, worry, wake up, get up, sit down. For daily routines, English often uses get: get dressed, get washed, get ready.

Themselves or each other?

themselves

Ana and Ben looked at themselves in the mirror.

Ana looked at Ana. Ben looked at Ben.

each other

Ana and Ben looked at each other.

Ana looked at Ben. Ben looked at Ana.

Each other is a reciprocal pronoun. The action goes both ways. One another means the same and is a little more formal.

Do not use myself as a polite word for me. This mistake is common in work emails. Also, do not add a reflexive to verbs like relax and meet.

Please send the file to myself.

My colleague and myself will join the call.

Relax yourself and enjoy the weekend.

We meet ourselves every Monday.

Did you enjoy at the party?

Please send the file to me.

My colleague and I will join the call.

Relax and enjoy the weekend.

We meet every Monday.

Did you enjoy yourself at the party?

Look at the last pair. Enjoy always needs an object. "Enjoy yourself!" and "Enjoy the party!" are both right.

This, that, these and those

Ana: Is this your mug, here on my desk?

Ben: No. Mine is that one, over there by the window.

Ana: And these cables here?

Ben: They're not mine. Ask Tom. Those boxes over there are his too.

This, that, these and those point at things. Grammar books call them demonstratives. The choice depends on two questions. How many? Near or far?

Near and far can mean place or time. This week is now. That day is in the past. "Do you remember that day in Kyoto?"

Other uses

  • Introduce a person: "This is my colleague, Ben."
  • On the phone: "Hi, this is Ana from the support team."
  • Talk about an idea: "That's a good idea." "That sounds great."
  • Point to what comes next: "Listen to this. The server is back."
  • Point to what came before: "The test failed. This means the fix is wrong."

The four words can be determiners or pronouns. As a determiner, the word comes before a noun: "this file". As a pronoun, it stands alone: "This is important."

The word and the noun must agree. Use this and that with a singular or uncountable noun. Use these and those with a plural noun.

Can you review this files?

These information is useful.

This are my notes.

I like this kind of tools.

Can you review these files?

This information is useful.

These are my notes.

I like this kind of tool.

There is, there are and the empty it

  • There is a bug in the login page.
  • There are two tests that fail.
  • It is ten o'clock.
  • It is raining again.

An English sentence needs a subject. Sometimes there is no real subject. Then English uses an empty subject. The two empty subjects are there and it.

There is and there are

Use there is and there are to say that something exists. Use them for something new, the first time you talk about it.

The forms of there is and there are
Singular or uncountablePlural
PositiveThere is (There's) a problem.There are three problems.
NegativeThere isn't a problem. There's no time.There aren't any problems. There are no problems.
QuestionIs there a problem?Are there any problems?
Short answerYes, there is. No, there isn't.Yes, there are. No, there aren't.
PastThere was an error.There were two errors.
FutureThere will be a meeting.There will be two meetings.

The verb agrees with the noun after it. With a list, look at the first noun. "There is a desk and two chairs." "There are two chairs and a desk."

In fast speech, people often say "There's two problems". In writing and in exams, use "There are two problems".

There first, then it or they

First, there is introduces the thing. Then a pronoun talks about it.

  • There's a new café near the office. It opens at seven.
  • There are two failing tests. They are both in the payment module.

The empty it

The empty it has no meaning. It only fills the subject place. Use it for these things.

Uses of the empty it
UseExample
Weather and temperatureIt's cold. It's 30 degrees today.
Time, days and datesIt's half past nine. It's Monday. It's the 3rd of May.
DistanceIt's two kilometres to the station.
How long something takesIt takes ten minutes to build the project.
Opinions + to or -ingIt's easy to make this mistake. It's nice working with you.
A situationIt's very quiet in the office today.

Look at the opinion row. You can say "To make this mistake is easy". It is correct, but it sounds strange. English prefers to put the long part at the end. The empty it goes first.

Many languages can drop the subject. English cannot. Do not start with is. Do not use have or has to say that something exists.

Is raining.

Is important to test your code.

In my city has many parks.

Have a problem with the server.

There is many bugs in this code.

It's raining.

It's important to test your code.

There are many parks in my city.

There is a problem with the server.

There are many bugs in this code.

One and ones

  • I don't like this shirt. Can I see the blue one?
  • My headphones are broken. I need some new ones.
  • "Which laptop is yours?" "The one on the left."
  • "I need a pen." "There's one on my desk."

One and ones stand in place of a countable noun. Use one for a singular noun and ones for a plural noun. This way you do not repeat the noun.

They often come after:

  • an adjective: the red one, the new ones, a cheap one
  • the + a phrase: the one on the left, the ones I bought yesterday
  • which: Which one do you want?
  • this and that: I'll take this one.

Look at the last example in the first list. "There's one on my desk" means "there is a pen on my desk". One alone means a + the noun. Do not say "a one" here.

Do not use one for an uncountable noun. Do not use ones after a number. After my or your, the pronoun mine or yours is better.

I like white bread more than the brown one.

I have two old phones and three new ones phones.

I bought two ones.

Your laptop is faster than my one.

I like white bread more than brown.

I have two old phones and three new ones.

I bought two.

Your laptop is faster than mine.

In British speech, "my one" and "these ones" are common. In careful writing, "mine" and "these" are better.

Each, every, all, both, either and neither

  • Every test passes.
  • Each user has a password.
  • All the servers are online.
  • Both answers are correct.
  • You can use either browser.
  • Neither answer is correct.

These six words talk about the members of a group. Three of them are for a group of exactly two: both, either and neither. The others are for a group of any size.

Every and each

  • Both words take a singular noun and a singular verb. "Every developer knows this." "Each file has a header."
  • Every looks at the whole group. It is close to all. "Every room has a screen."
  • Each looks at the members one at a time. "The teacher spoke to each student."
  • Each can be for two things. Every is for three or more. "She had a bag in each hand."
  • Each can stand alone or take of: "each of the files", "each of them". Every cannot. Say "every one of them".

All

  • All takes a plural or uncountable noun. "All tests passed." "All the data is safe."
  • Before the, my or these, you can drop of. "All the tests" or "all of the tests".
  • Before a pronoun, you need of. "All of them", "all of us". Or put all after the pronoun: "We are all ready."

Be careful with time words. "I worked all day" means the whole day, from morning to night. "I work every day" means Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and so on.

Both, either and neither

Three words for two things
WordMeaningNoun and verbExample
boththe first and the secondplural noun, plural verbBoth servers are down.
eitherthe first or the second, it does not mattersingular noun, singular verbEither day is fine for me.
neithernot the first and not the secondsingular noun, singular verbNeither option is cheap.
  • With of, use the or a pronoun: both of them, either of the rooms, neither of us.
  • The pairs join two ideas: both A and B, either A or B, neither A nor B. "We can meet either today or tomorrow."
  • Neither is already negative. Use it with a positive verb. "Neither answer is right", not "isn't".
  • For three or more, use none and all, not neither and both. "I asked five people. None of them knew."

After neither of and none of, a singular verb is the formal choice. "Neither of them is ready." In speech, a plural verb is also common: "Neither of them are ready." In exams, use the singular verb.

Every and each take a singular noun. Every never takes of. Both is for two only. Do not put not with neither.

Every users have an account.

Every of the tests failed.

I have three brothers. Both live in Osaka.

Neither of the tools don't work.

The both answers are wrong.

Every user has an account.

Every one of the tests failed. Or: All of the tests failed.

I have three brothers. All of them live in Osaka.

Neither of the tools works.

Both answers are wrong.

Putting it all together

Here is a short tour of an office. It uses many words from this chapter. Each slide shows one place.

The entrance

This is our office. There are forty desks on this floor.

This points to a near place. There are introduces the desks.

The kitchen

That's the kitchen, over there. There's a coffee machine, but there isn't any tea.

That points to a far place.

Our desks

These are our team's desks. Mine is the one by the window.

Mine means "my desk". One means "desk".

The meeting rooms

Those are the meeting rooms. The big one is called Atlas. It has a large screen.

It refers back to the big room.

The lockers

Each person has a locker. Every locker has a key. Keep yours safe.

Each and every take a singular noun.

The printers

Both printers are on the second floor. Neither of them is fast, so print early.

Both and neither are for two things.

Articles are determiners too. You can read about them in Nouns and articles.

Expert uses

These points are above A2 level. They help in technical writing, emails and exams.

Make it clear what "it" means

"The client sends a request to the server, and it logs it." What does each it mean? The reader cannot be sure. In technical writing, repeat the noun when two nouns could match. "The client sends a request to the server, and the server logs the request."

This + noun is clearer than this alone

"The cache was full. This caused the crash." Here this can mean the cache or the full cache. "This full cache caused the crash" is clearer. Many writing guides give this advice for reports and design documents.

Their after each, every and everyone

"Every user can change their password." The word every is singular, but their is normal here. It includes all people. The older form "his or her password" is correct, but long.

Companies: it or they?

In British English, a company or a team can be it or they. "The company has changed its policy." "The team are happy with their new office." American English usually uses it and a singular verb. Choose one form and keep it in the same text.

The general you and the formal one

"You should always back up your data." Here you means people in general. It is normal in speech and in documentation. Very formal English sometimes uses one for this. "One should always back up one's data." It sounds old in most situations.

Than me or than I am?

"She is faster than me" is normal in speech and most writing. "She is faster than I am" is more formal and always safe. "She is faster than I" is very formal and rare.

Not ... either

Either also ends a negative sentence. It means "also". "I don't like it." "I don't like it either." For positive sentences, use too. See Questions and negatives for "neither do I".

In IELTS Writing Task 1, you may describe a map or a plan. You need there is, there are and there was a lot. "In 2010 there was a car park. Now there are shops." In the Cambridge B2 First open cloze, small words like each, either, its and there are good candidates for a gap.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for pronouns and determiners
PatternPurposeModelNote
Name and I + verbTalk about you and another person as the subjectTom and I wrote the report.Not "Me and Tom wrote".
Verb or preposition + me, him, her, us, themUse a pronoun after a verb or a prepositionPlease send it to me.Not "to myself".
my, your, our + nounSay who owns a thingOur team uses Rust.No a or the before my.
Noun + be + mine, yours, hersSay who owns it, with no noun afterThe blue mug is mine.No apostrophe in yours or hers.
Person + 's + nounShow that a person owns or has somethingThis is Ana's laptop.Plural with -s: the users' data.
Subject + verb + myself, yourselfThe subject does the action to itselfHe taught himself Python.Not with relax, meet or feel.
this or that + singular nounPoint to one thing, near or farCan you check this file?Plural: these files, those files.
There is + singular or uncountable nounSay that one thing existsThere is a problem with the build.Not "Have a problem".
There are + plural nounSay that many things existThere are three open tickets.Not "There is three tickets" in writing.
It + be + adjective + to + verbGive an opinion about an actionIt's important to test your code.Do not drop it.
It takes + time + to + verbSay how long something takesIt takes five minutes to deploy.The subject is it, not the person.
the + adjective + one or onesAvoid repeating a countable nounI prefer the smaller one.Not with uncountable nouns.
Every or Each + singular noun + singular verbTalk about all members of a groupEvery test passes now.Not "every tests". Not "every of".
Both + plural noun or Neither + singular nounTalk about two things togetherNeither option is perfect.Neither already means not.

Practice

Choose the right answer

My colleague helped ___ with the report.

  • I
  • me
  • myself

After the verb helped, use the object pronoun me.

The app updates ___ settings every night.

  • its
  • it's
  • it

Its means "of it". It's means "it is".

Can you send me ___ files from yesterday?

  • this
  • that
  • those

Files is plural, and yesterday is far in time. So we use those.

___ a meeting room on the third floor.

  • It is
  • There is
  • Has

We say that something exists, so we use there is.

I have two monitors. ___ of them are new.

  • All
  • Both
  • Every

There are exactly two monitors, and the verb is plural. So we use both.

Which sentence is correct?

  • Every developers use Git.
  • Every of the developers uses Git.
  • Every developer uses Git.

Every takes a singular noun and a singular verb. It never takes of.

Complete the sentences

This is not my bag. It's (she).

The (children) toys are everywhere.

Did you build this table (you)?

? very windy today.

? any questions?

These shoes are too small. I need bigger ?.

Ana and Ben help ? a lot. Ana helps Ben, and Ben helps Ana.

I tried two keys, but ? of them worked.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistakes. (a) Me and Ana are in the same team. (b) Please call myself tomorrow. (c) In the office has a gym. (d) Is this pen your's?
    Answer

    (a) Ana and I are in the same team. (b) Please call me tomorrow. (c) There is a gym in the office. (d) Is this pen yours?

  2. Explain the difference. (a) the student's books (b) the students' books
    Answer

    (a) is the books of one student. (b) is the books of two or more students. The apostrophe position shows the difference.

  3. Rewrite the text with pronouns, so you do not repeat the nouns. "Ben has a new phone. Ben bought the phone last week. The phone has a great camera. Ben loves the camera."
    Model answer

    Ben has a new phone. He bought it last week. It has a great camera. He loves it.

  4. Describe a room you know in four sentences. Use there is, there are, it and one.
    Model answer

    There is a big table in our kitchen. There are six chairs around it. It is the warmest room in the house. My favourite chair is the one by the window.

  5. What is the difference? (a) I worked all day. (b) I worked every day.
    Answer

    (a) means one whole day, from morning to evening. (b) means many days, one after another, like Monday to Friday.

  6. Expert question. This sentence is not clear: "The service calls the database, and it returns an error." Why? Rewrite it.
    Answer

    The word it can mean the service or the database. Repeat the noun to make it clear. "The service calls the database, and the database returns an error."

Tom and I or Tom and me: "___ fixed the bug."

Tom and I. It is the subject. Test it: "I fixed the bug."

Its or it's: "The team changed ___ name."

Its. It means "of it". It's means "it is" or "it has".

Where does the apostrophe go for many users?

After the s: the users' passwords.

What does "by myself" mean?

Alone, with no other person. "I live by myself."

This, that, these, those: which two questions decide?

How many? Near or far?

How do you say that something exists?

There is + singular noun. There are + plural noun.

Which words are for exactly two things?

Both, either and neither.

Is "every" singular or plural?

Singular. "Every test passes." Never "every tests".

Key takeaways

  • Subject pronouns go before the verb. Object pronouns go after a verb or a preposition.
  • My, your and their come before a noun. Mine, yours and theirs stand alone, with no apostrophe.
  • Add 's to a singular noun and ' to a plural noun with -s.
  • Reflexive pronouns point back to the subject or add emphasis. Do not use myself as a polite me.
  • This and these are near. That and those are far.
  • Use there is and there are for things that exist, and it for time, weather and opinions.
  • Each and every take a singular noun. Both, either and neither are for two things.

  • British Council LearnEnglish: one and ones. One and ones after adjectives, the and which.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Quantifiers. Each, every, both, either and neither, with their verbs.
  • APA Style: Singular they. Why many style guides accept they for one person.

Everyday vocabulary

Grammar gives you the structure. Words give you the meaning. This chapter gives you the words for daily life: numbers, dates, time, money and seven common topics. It also gives you 120 key verbs, the most useful word partners, polite phrases and a simple way to remember new words.

  • Say and write numbers, dates, times and prices correctly.
  • Use basic words for family, home, food, travel, health, work and technology.
  • Learn 120 high-use verbs in ten groups.
  • Choose make, do, have, take or get in common word partners.
  • Use polite phrases, and keep a word notebook and flashcards.

Numbers

  • The meeting room has twelve chairs.
  • Our office is on the third floor.
  • The project costs two hundred and fifty thousand euros.
  • The test takes two point five seconds.

English has two kinds of numbers. A cardinal number counts things: one, two, three. An ordinal number gives the order: first, second, third.

How to say numbers
WrittenSaidNote
13, 30thirteen, thirtyStress the end in thirteen. Stress the start in thirty.
105one hundred and fiveBritish English says "and" after hundred.
2,400two thousand four hundredNo -s on hundred or thousand after a number.
1,000,000a million, one millionA billion is a thousand million.
3.75three point seven fiveEnglish uses a point, not a comma. Say each number after the point.
0.5nought point five, zero point fiveNought is British. Zero is used everywhere.
½, ⅓, ¼, ¾a half, a third, a quarter, three quartersTwo thirds has an -s.
40%forty per centBritish spelling is per cent. American spelling is percent.

In English, a comma separates thousands: 12,500. A point separates the decimal part: 12.5. Many European languages do the opposite. Check this when you read a report or a price.

Ordinal numbers

Most ordinals add -th: fourth, sixth, seventh, tenth, hundredth. Learn the special ones: first (1st), second (2nd), third (3rd), fifth (5th), eighth (8th), ninth (9th), twelfth (12th), twentieth (20th).

After twenty, only the last part changes. Write 21st, 22nd, 23rd and 24th. But write 11th, 12th and 13th, with -th.

Years, phone numbers and maths

  • Years: 1998 is "nineteen ninety-eight". 2008 is "two thousand and eight". 2026 is "twenty twenty-six" or "two thousand and twenty-six".
  • Phone numbers: say each number alone. British speakers often say "oh" for 0 and "double" for two same numbers. 0844 is "oh double eight four four".
  • Maths: 2 + 3 = 5 is "two plus three equals five". Also say minus, times and divided by.
  • Versions: software version 3.14 can be "three point fourteen". Here the number after the point is a whole number.

After a number, hundred, thousand and million have no -s. Use hundreds of only when there is no exact number.

Three hundreds people came.

The price is 4,99 euros.

My birthday is on May three.

Three hundred people came. Hundreds of people came.

The price is 4.99 euros.

My birthday is on the third of May.

Dates and time

Ana: What's the date today?

Ben: It's the fifteenth of November.

Ana: And what time is the demo?

Ben: At half past two. It finishes at quarter past three.

Days and months always start with a capital letter: Monday, November. Seasons do not: spring, summer, autumn, winter.

Dates

One date, written and said
British EnglishAmerican English
Written in full15 November 2026, or 15th November 2026November 15, 2026
Saidthe fifteenth of NovemberNovember fifteenth
Numbers only15/11/2026 (day, month, year)11/15/2026 (month, day, year)

Look at the last row. 03/04/2026 is the 3rd of April in Britain. In the United States it is March the 4th. This difference causes real mistakes with deadlines and flights.

At work, write dates as year, month, day: 2026-11-15. This is the ISO 8601 format. People in every country read it the same way. Computers can also sort it.

Telling the time

Two ways to say the time
TimeClock wordsDigital way
9:00nine o'clocknine
9:10ten past ninenine ten
9:15quarter past ninenine fifteen
9:30half past ninenine thirty
9:40twenty to tennine forty
9:45quarter to tennine forty-five
9:53seven minutes to tennine fifty-three
  • Use a.m. for the morning and p.m. for the afternoon and evening.
  • Midday is 12 o'clock in the day. Midnight is 12 o'clock at night. "12 a.m." and "12 p.m." often confuse people, so say midday or midnight.
  • Timetables often use the 24-hour clock. 17:30 is "seventeen thirty".
  • With numbers that are not 5, 10, 20 or 25, add minutes: "seven minutes to ten".

Time words

  • the day before yesterday, yesterday, today, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow
  • in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening, at night
  • this week, next week, last week, a fortnight
  • a deadline: "The deadline is Friday at 5 p.m."

The little words at, on and in go with times and dates. "At three", "on Monday", "in May". The chapter Prepositions explains them.

Do not say "half to". In British speech, "half nine" means 9:30, not 8:30. Do not use the with next and last for time.

Money

  • "How much is this coffee?" "It's three pounds fifty."
  • I paid twenty euros for the ticket.
  • We spend a lot of money on cloud servers.
  • "Can I pay by card?" "Of course."

In Britain the money is the pound (£). One pound has 100 pence. People often say p for pence: "ninety-nine p". The United States uses dollars and cents. Many European countries use euros and cents.

How to read prices
WrittenSaid
£3.50three pounds fifty, or three fifty
99pninety-nine p, or ninety-nine pence
$12.99twelve dollars ninety-nine, or twelve ninety-nine
€1,200one thousand two hundred euros, or twelve hundred euros
$2.5mtwo point five million dollars

We write the symbol before the number: £20, $20. We say the money word after the number: "twenty pounds". Before a noun, the money word has no -s: "a twenty-pound note".

Money verbs

Verbs for money and their partner words
VerbPatternExample
costsomething costs + moneyThe course costs 300 euros.
paypay + money + for somethingI paid 10 pounds for lunch.
paypay by card, pay in cashCan I pay in cash?
spendspend + money + on somethingShe spends a lot on books.
borrowborrow something from someoneI borrowed 20 dollars from Ben.
lendlend someone somethingBen lent me 20 dollars.
earnearn + moneyHe earns a good salary.
affordcan or can't afford somethingWe can't afford a new server this year.

Other useful nouns are price, cash, change (the money you get back), receipt, discount, refund and invoice. In a British restaurant, ask for the bill. Americans say the check.

Borrow is to take. Lend is to give. Pay takes for before the thing you buy. Spend takes on.

Can you borrow me your pen?

I paid the coffee.

I spent a lot for my phone.

It costs 20 £.

Can you lend me your pen?

I paid for the coffee.

I spent a lot on my phone.

It costs £20.

Words for seven daily topics

The picture shows seven topics that you meet every day. Open a topic to see some key words. Then read the word lists below.

Family

Words: parents, mother (mum), father (dad), son, daughter, brother, sister, grandparents, husband, wife, partner, uncle, aunt, cousin, niece, nephew.

Your siblings are your brothers and sisters. Your in-laws are the family of your husband or wife. A partner is the person you live with or love.

Useful sentences: "Do you have any brothers or sisters?" "I'm an only child." "My parents live in the countryside."

Home

Words: house, flat, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, living room, rent, bills, furniture, neighbour, landlord.

A flat is British English. Americans say apartment. The rent is money for a home that you do not own. The landlord owns it.

In Britain, the floor at street level is the ground floor. The next one is the first floor. In the United States, the street level is the first floor.

Useful sentences: "I live in a two-bedroom flat." "The rent includes the bills." "My neighbours are very friendly."

Food

Words: breakfast, lunch, dinner, snack, vegetables, fruit, meat, fish, rice, bread, menu, order, tasty, spicy, sweet, salty.

A snack is a small amount of food between meals. A takeaway is hot food that you buy and eat at home. Americans say takeout.

Useful sentences: "Could I have the chicken, please?" "I'm vegetarian." "I'm allergic to nuts." "Is it spicy?"

Travel

Words: ticket, single, return, platform, gate, boarding pass, passport, luggage, delay, cancel, book, check in, check out.

A British return ticket takes you there and back. Americans say round-trip. A single is one way only. A delay means late. A train leaves from a platform. A plane leaves from a gate.

Useful sentences: "Excuse me, how do I get to the station?" "Is this seat free?" "My flight is delayed by two hours." "I'd like to book a room for two nights."

Health

Words: headache, stomach ache, cold, flu, cough, sore throat, temperature, doctor, appointment, pharmacy, medicine, prescription.

An appointment is a fixed time to see a doctor. A prescription lets you get medicine. In Britain a pharmacy is also called a chemist's. "I have a temperature" means your body is too hot.

Useful sentences: "I don't feel well." "I have a headache." "I'd like to make an appointment." "I need to take a sick day."

Work

Words: job, colleague, manager, team, meeting, task, project, deadline, office, salary, contract, day off, holiday.

A colleague is a person you work with. A holiday in British English is time away from work. Americans say vacation. A contract is a written work agreement.

Useful sentences: "I work as a backend developer." "I'm responsible for the payment system." "Can we move the meeting to Thursday?" "I'm taking Friday off."

Technology

Words: laptop, screen, keyboard, mouse, charger, battery, Wi-Fi, password, account, app, update, file, folder, link.

A charger fills your battery. You log in to an account with a password. You log out when you finish.

Useful sentences: "My battery is low." "The Wi-Fi is down." "I can't log in to my account." "Can you send me the link?"

Oxford Learner's Dictionaries publish the Oxford 3000. It is a list of 3000 core words for learners from A1 to B2. Oxford chose the words by how often they appear and how useful they are for learners. It is a good list to check your basic vocabulary.

120 high-use verbs in ten groups

Verbs are the heart of a sentence. Learn them in groups, not in a long alphabetical list. A group helps your memory, because the words share a meaning.

The verbs in bold are irregular. Their past form is special. For example, go becomes went, not "goed". The other verbs add -ed in the past.

120 verbs for everyday English
GroupTwelve verbs
1. Basic actionsbe, have, do, make, get, go, come, take, give, put, keep, let
2. Movingwalk, run, drive, fly, ride, move, leave, arrive, return, travel, follow, carry
3. Senses and the mindsee, look, watch, hear, listen, feel, think, know, understand, remember, forget, believe
4. Talkingsay, tell, speak, talk, ask, answer, reply, explain, call, discuss, agree, repeat
5. Feelings and wantswant, need, like, love, hate, prefer, hope, wish, enjoy, worry, care, miss
6. Daily lifeeat, drink, sleep, wake, wash, cook, clean, wear, buy, pay, spend, live
7. Work and studywork, study, learn, teach, write, read, try, finish, plan, meet, help, decide
8. Changebecome, change, grow, stay, seem, happen, begin, start, stop, continue, increase, improve
9. Giving and gettingbring, send, receive, find, lose, sell, borrow, lend, share, use, show, choose
10. Computersopen, close, click, type, save, delete, download, install, update, check, fix, test

In British English, learn has two past forms: learned and learnt. Both are correct. Show has a regular past, showed, but its third form is usually shown.

Look at the chart. 49 of the 120 verbs are irregular. The oldest and most common verbs are often irregular. New verbs, like download and click, are almost always regular. So the irregular verbs are few, but you use them all the time. The chapter Past simple and past continuous lists their past forms in sound groups.

Pairs that learners mix up

Six verb pairs with different meanings
PairDifferenceExample
say and tellTell needs a person after it. Say does not.She said hello. She told me the news.
speak and talkSpeak is for languages and more formal. Talk is for conversations.I speak Japanese. Can we talk later?
see, look and watchSee happens. Look at is on purpose. Watch is for things that move.I saw a bird. Look at this graph. Watch the video.
hear and listenHear happens. Listen to is on purpose.I can hear music. I listen to podcasts.
bring and takeBring moves toward the speaker. Take moves away.Bring your laptop here. Take this to Ana.
remember and remindRemember is in your head. Remind makes another person remember.I remember his name. Please remind me at five.

Word partners: make, do, have, take and get

  • Can you make a decision by Friday?
  • I do the shopping on Saturdays.
  • Let's have a short break.
  • I'll take a photo of the whiteboard.
  • Did you get my email?

Some words often go together. They are called collocations. In English we make a decision, but we do homework. Often there is no logical reason. Native speakers just say it that way.

So learn the verb and the noun together, as one unit. Do not translate each word from your language.

Make or do?

There is a useful idea. Make often creates something new. Do often describes an activity, a task or work. You do the cooking, and you make dinner.

make

  • make a decision
  • make a mistake
  • make a plan
  • make a call
  • make money
  • make a noise
  • make an appointment
  • make progress
  • make an effort
  • make coffee

do

  • do homework
  • do a task
  • do your job
  • do an exam
  • do the shopping
  • do the dishes
  • do exercise
  • do a course
  • do business
  • do someone a favour

A good test: if you can say "something" or "nothing", use do. "I did nothing today." "Can I do something to help?"

Have, take and get

Common partners for have, take and get
VerbMain ideaCommon partners
havemeals, events, experienceshave breakfast, have lunch, have a meeting, have a break, have a party, have a shower, have a problem, have fun
takephotos, transport, time, actionstake a photo, take a bus, take a taxi, take a break, take a day off, take notes, take a look, take a risk
getreceive, become, arrive, buyget an email, get a job, get tired, get better, get home, get to work, get a coffee, get ready

The verb get has many meanings. Here are the main five. Receive: "I got your message." Become: "It's getting dark." Arrive: "I get home at six." Buy or fetch: "I'll get some milk." Understand: "Sorry, I don't get it."

British English uses both have a break and take a break. American English prefers take a break. Both are correct.

These mistakes often come from translation. Learn the correct partner as one unit.

I made my homework.

I did a mistake in the code.

Can you make a photo of us?

We take breakfast at eight.

We need to do a decision.

Let's do a party on Friday.

I did my homework.

I made a mistake in the code.

Can you take a photo of us?

We have breakfast at eight.

We need to make a decision.

Let's have a party on Friday.

You will learn many more partners in Register, collocation and idiom and in Phrasal verbs.

Polite phrases

Give me the report.

I want a coffee.

What? Say it again.

No. I can't come.

Could you send me the report, please?

Could I have a coffee, please?

Sorry, could you say that again?

I'd love to, but I'm busy on Friday.

The sentences on the first tab are correct grammar. But in English they sound rude. English speakers make requests softer. They use questions with could and would, and they add please.

Being polite is very important in English. Often it matters more than perfect grammar.

Polite phrases for common situations
SituationPhraseAnswer
Meeting someone newNice to meet you.Nice to meet you too.
Saying thank youThank you so much. Thanks for your help.You're welcome. No problem.
Asking someone to do somethingCould you check this, please?Sure. Of course.
A bigger requestWould you mind checking this?Not at all. (This means yes, I'll do it.)
Asking for somethingCould I have the bill, please?Of course. Here you are.
Offering helpShall I open the window? Can I help you?Yes, please. No, thanks. I'm fine.
InvitingWould you like to join us for lunch?I'd love to. Thanks for asking, but I can't today.
Saying sorrySorry I'm late. I'm sorry about the delay.No worries. That's OK.
Not understandingSorry, I didn't catch that. Could you repeat it?Of course. I said ...
Getting attentionExcuse me, is this seat free?Yes, it is. Sorry, it's taken.

Look at the request rows. After Would you mind, the verb takes -ing. The answer "Not at all" means "No, I don't mind. I'll do it."

Excuse me comes before you disturb someone. Sorry comes after a mistake, or when you did not hear. In British English, cheers is an informal way to say thanks.

The carousel shows polite English through one work day.

Arriving

"Good morning! How are you?" "Fine, thanks. And you?"

A short greeting is enough. Answer and ask back.

A request

"Could you review my pull request when you have a moment?"

"When you have a moment" makes the request softer.

An offer

"Shall I book a room for the meeting?" "Yes, please. That would be great."

Shall I offers help.

An invitation

"Would you like to join us for lunch?" "Thanks, I'd love to."

I'd love to accepts warmly.

Saying no

"Can you help with the release today?" "I'm sorry, I can't today. How about tomorrow morning?"

Say sorry, give a short reason or a new time.

Not understanding

"Sorry, I didn't catch the last part. Could you say it again?"

This is polite. It is also normal in video calls.

Leaving

"Thanks for your help today. Have a good evening!" "You too. See you tomorrow."

A thank you at the end of the day is always welcome.

A word notebook and flashcards

You will forget most new words in a few days. This is normal. Your memory needs to see a word many times. A word notebook and flashcards give it these chances.

Keep a word notebook

Do not write only a word and a translation. Write the word in a small context. Use these steps for each new word.

  1. Write the word and its type. deadline (noun, countable)
  2. Mark the stress and the sound. DEAD-line, /ˈdedlaɪn/
  3. Write a simple English meaning. The last time or day to finish something.
  4. Add its partners. meet a deadline, miss a deadline, a tight deadline
  5. Write your own sentence. "We missed the deadline because of a bug."
  6. Add a translation in your language, if it helps.

The stress is the part of a word that you say louder. Mark it, because a wrong stress can make a word hard to understand.

Organise your notebook by topic, not by date. Use one page for work words, one for travel, and so on. Leave space to add partners later.

Flashcards and the box system

A flashcard has a question on the front and the answer on the back. Write the word on the front. Write the meaning and your sentence on the back. Or do it the other way round to practise speaking.

A smart way to use flashcards is the Leitner system. A German science writer, Sebastian Leitner, described it in a book in 1972. Here is a simple version with three boxes.

  1. All new cards start in box 1.
  2. Test yourself. A right answer moves the card to the next box.
  3. A wrong answer sends the card back to box 1.
  4. Study box 1 every day, box 2 every three days and box 3 every week.

In this way you spend your time on hard words, not on easy ones. This idea is called spaced repetition. Flashcard apps, for example Anki, use the same idea with a computer. The chapter How to grow your vocabulary explains it in more detail.

Say each word aloud when you test yourself. Use it in a real sentence the same day: in a message, a meeting or your notes. A word you use is a word you keep.

The IELTS Listening test often asks you to write numbers, dates, prices and names. A small spelling mistake makes the answer wrong. Practise writing what you hear, for example "the 21st of March" and "£14.50".

In speaking tests, polite phrases help too. If you did not hear a question, say "Sorry, could you repeat the question?"

Patterns to remember

Patterns for everyday vocabulary
PatternPurposeModelNote
number + hundred or thousand + nounGive an exact large numberWe have two thousand users.No -s on thousand after a number.
the + ordinal + of + monthSay a date in British EnglishThe launch is on the fifth of June.Write 5 June or 5th June.
minutes + past or to + hourTell the time with clock wordsIt's twenty to four.Use past up to 30 minutes, then to.
It costs + moneyGive a priceThe ticket costs twelve pounds.Write £12, say twelve pounds.
pay + money + for + thingSay what you paidI paid five euros for the sandwich.Not "I paid the sandwich".
spend + money or time + on + thingSay where money or time goesWe spend a lot on cloud costs.Spend takes on, not for.
Can you lend me + thing?Ask to use something for a short timeCan you lend me your charger?Or "Can I borrow your charger?"
make + result nounCreate something or decideWe need to make a decision.Not "do a decision".
do + task or work nounTalk about an activity or a dutyI'll do the code review after lunch.Not "make the review".
have + meal or eventTalk about meals and meetingsLet's have lunch at one.Not "take lunch" in most cases.
take + photo, transport or timeTalk about photos, buses and days offI'm taking Friday off.Not "make a photo".
Could you + verb + , please?Make a polite requestCould you share your screen, please?More polite than "Can you".
Would you mind + verb-ing?Make a bigger, careful requestWould you mind waiting a minute?The answer "Not at all" means yes.
Would you like to + verb?Invite someoneWould you like to join us?Accept with "I'd love to".
Sorry, I didn't catch that.Ask someone to repeatSorry, I didn't catch your name.Better than "What?".

Practice

Choose the right answer

How do you say 9:45?

  • quarter past nine
  • quarter to ten
  • half to ten

After 30 minutes, we count to the next hour. 9:45 is fifteen minutes to ten.

Which number is correct?

  • five thousands people
  • five thousand people
  • five thousand of people

After a number, thousand has no -s and no of.

I ___ twenty pounds for this book.

  • paid
  • spent
  • cost

Pay + money + for + thing. Spend would need on.

Oh no! I ___ a mistake in the report.

  • did
  • made
  • took

The partner is make a mistake.

Which request is the most polite?

  • Send me the file.
  • I want the file.
  • Could you send me the file, please?

A question with could and please makes the request soft and polite.

Your colleague says, "Would you mind closing the door?" You are happy to help. What do you say?

  • Not at all.
  • Yes, I mind.
  • No, thank you.

"Not at all" means "I don't mind". Then you close the door.

Complete with make, do, have, take or get

Can you ? a photo of the whiteboard?

I usually ? the shopping on Saturday.

Let's ? a short break.

What time do you ? home after work?

We need to ? a plan for the release.

Write the words

  • 12th → ?
  • 3rd → ?
  • The plural of thousand after "five" → ?
  • The opposite of borrow → ?
  • Two weeks in British English → ?

Think and write

  1. Write these in words. (a) 1,250 (b) 0.75 (c) £8.99 (d) 21/06/2026 in British English.
    Answer

    (a) one thousand two hundred and fifty. (b) nought point seven five, or zero point seven five. (c) eight pounds ninety-nine, or eight ninety-nine. (d) the twenty-first of June, twenty twenty-six.

  2. Correct the mistakes. (a) Can you borrow me your pen? (b) I made my homework. (c) She said me the news. (d) We take dinner at seven.
    Answer

    (a) Can you lend me your pen? (b) I did my homework. (c) She told me the news. (d) We have dinner at seven.

  3. A colleague writes the deadline as 04/05. Why can this be a problem? How can you avoid it?
    Answer

    In Britain 04/05 is the 4th of May. In the United States it is April the 5th. Write the month as a word, like 4 May, or use the ISO format, like 2026-05-04.

  4. Make these sentences polite. (a) Repeat that. (b) I want the menu. (c) Come to my birthday dinner.
    Model answer

    (a) Sorry, could you repeat that, please? (b) Could I have the menu, please? (c) Would you like to come to my birthday dinner?

  5. Write a notebook entry for the word "invoice". Use the six steps.
    Model answer

    invoice (noun, countable). IN-voice, /ˈɪnvɔɪs/. A paper that says how much a customer must pay. Partners: send an invoice, pay an invoice. "We sent the invoice to the client on Monday." Then a translation, if it helps.

  6. Expert question. Why are most of the 12 basic verbs irregular, but all 12 computer verbs regular?
    Answer

    The basic verbs are very old and very common. People used them so often that their old special forms stayed. New verbs, like download and install, come into the language with the normal -ed rule. So common old verbs are often irregular, and new verbs are regular.

How do you say 2008?

Two thousand and eight.

Is 03/04 March or April in Britain?

April. British dates are day, month, year: the 3rd of April.

How do you say £4.50?

Four pounds fifty, or four fifty.

Borrow or lend: "Can I ___ your charger?"

Borrow. You take it for a short time.

Make or do: "___ a decision"?

Make a decision.

Name five meanings of get.

Receive, become, arrive, buy or fetch, understand.

What does "Would you mind ...?" need after it?

A verb with -ing. "Would you mind waiting?"

In the box system, where does a card go after a wrong answer?

Back to box 1. You see it again tomorrow.

Key takeaways

  • Say "and" after hundred in British English. Hundred and thousand have no -s after a number.
  • British dates go day, month, year. At work, the ISO format 2026-11-15 avoids confusion.
  • Say past for the first half hour and to for the second half hour.
  • Write £20, but say "twenty pounds". Pay for a thing, and spend on a thing.
  • Learn verbs in meaning groups. The most common verbs are often irregular.
  • Learn collocations as units: make a decision, do homework, have lunch, take a photo, get an email.
  • Use could, would and please to be polite. Keep a topic notebook and review flashcards with the box system.
