Present simple and present continuous

English has two present tenses. The present simple is for habits and facts. The present continuous is for actions in progress now. This chapter shows you how to form both and how to choose.

  • Use am, is and are in statements, negatives and questions.
  • Form the present simple with the right -s, do and does.
  • Put words like always and never in the right place.
  • Form the present continuous and spell the -ing form.
  • Choose the simple or the continuous form, also with state verbs.

Two tenses, two meanings

Read these two sentences. The verb is the same. The meaning is different.

Present simple

I write code.

This is my job. I do it again and again.

Present continuous

I am writing code.

I am in the middle of it now. Later I will stop.

A tense tells us when something happens. English has two tenses for the present. Each one answers a different question.

  • Present simple: What is true in general? What happens again and again?
  • Present continuous: What is happening now? What is different these days?

The picture shows the idea. Each line is time. The small mark in the middle is now.

A habit is many points on the line. A fact covers the whole line. An action in progress is a short bar at now. A temporary situation is a longer bar around now.

Do not mix the two forms. In the present simple, do not put am, is or are before another verb. In the present continuous, you need one of them, and the verb ends in -ing.

I am write code every day.

I writing code now.

I write code every day.

I am writing code now.

The verb be

We start with be. It is the most common verb in English. You also need it for the present continuous.

  • I am a developer.
  • She is my manager.
  • We are in the same team.

The verb be has three present forms. The form depends on the subject. In speech we use the short form. A short form is also called a contraction.

The present of be
SubjectPositiveShort formNegativeQuestion
II amI'mI'm notAm I late?
he, she, itshe isshe'sshe isn'tIs she late?
you, we, theythey arethey'rethey aren'tAre they late?

For a question, put be before the subject. For a negative, add not. You can also say she's not and they're not.

The form "amn't" is not standard English. Say I'm not.

Ana: Are you free at three?

Ben: Yes, I am. Is the big meeting room free too?

Ana: No, it isn't. But the small room is.

A short answer repeats be. After yes, use the long form. Say "Yes, I am", not "Yes, I'm".

What we use be for
UseExample
Name and jobI am Dana. I am a tester.
AgeHe is 34. He is 34 years old.
CountryThey are from Japan.
Feelings and statesI am tired. The server is down.
PlaceThe keys are on the desk.
Time and priceIt is ten o'clock. It is five euros.

English uses be for age, not have. A sentence also needs a verb and a subject. And agree is a verb, so it needs no be.

I have 30 years.

She a developer.

Is cold today.

I am agree with you.

I am 30.

She is a developer.

It is cold today.

I agree with you.

You can read more about the empty subject it in Pronouns and determiners.

Present simple: the form

  • I work at home.
  • Ana works in an office.
  • We start at nine.
  • The build takes ten minutes.

The present simple uses the base form of the verb. There is one change. After he, she, it, one name or one thing, add -s. Grammar books call this the third person singular.

How to spell the third person -s
The verb ends inWhat you doExamples
most lettersadd -swork → works, run → runs, write → writes
-ch, -sh, -ss, -x, -zzadd -eswatch → watches, push → pushes, pass → passes, fix → fixes
consonant + ychange y to -iesstudy → studies, try → tries, copy → copies
vowel + yadd -splay → plays, pay → pays, deploy → deploys
four special verbslearn themhave → has, do → does, go → goes, be → is

The ending has three sounds. In works you hear /s/. In runs you hear /z/. In fixes you hear /ɪz/, so the word gets one more syllable.

Two verbs also change their vowel sound. Does sounds like "duz" and says sounds like "sez". The chapter Sounds and spelling explains these endings.

The -s is small, but listeners notice when it is missing. Check it every time you write he, she, it or one name.

She work in a bank.

My manager have two teams.

People works too much.

Everyone know the rule.

She can speaks English.

She works in a bank.

My manager has two teams.

People work too much.

Everyone knows the rule.

She can speak English.

  • People is plural, so it takes no -s on the verb.
  • Everyone, everybody and nobody take the -s form.
  • After can, must and should there is never an -s. See Modal verbs.

In British English, a group word can take both forms. "The team is ready" and "The team are ready" are both correct. Choose one form and keep it in the same text.

Do and does: negatives and questions

Kim: Do you work on Fridays?

Leo: Yes, I do. But I don't work late.

Kim: Does your team use Rust?

Leo: No, it doesn't. It uses Python.

For negatives and questions, the present simple needs a helper verb. Grammar books call it an auxiliary verb. The helper verb is do, or does for he, she and it.

I use Linux.

She uses Linux.

I don't use Linux.

She doesn't use Linux.

Do you use Linux?

Does she use Linux?

Yes, I do. No, I don't.

Yes, she does. No, she doesn't.

Look at the sentences with she. The -s moves to does. The main verb goes back to the base form. One -s is enough.

Questions with a question word

Put the question word first. Then use the same order: do or does, subject, base form.

  • Where do you work?
  • What does this function return?
  • How often do you deploy?
  • What does "deprecated" mean?

There is one exception. When who or what is the subject, we do not use do. We say "Who uses this API?" and "What happens next?". The chapter Questions and negatives explains this.

Do not put -s on the main verb after does or doesn't. Do not use no to make a verb negative. Do not forget do in a question. And remember that be makes questions and negatives without do.

She doesn't works here.

Does he likes coffee?

He don't know.

I no like meetings.

Where you live?

What means this word?

Do you be tired?

She doesn't work here.

Does he like coffee?

He doesn't know.

I don't like meetings.

Where do you live?

What does this word mean?

Are you tired?

When to use the present simple

Here is a short text about one person. Every verb is in the present simple.

Omar works for a small software company. He lives near the office, so he walks to work. He starts at nine and he usually finishes at six.

He knows three programming languages. On Fridays his team has lunch together.

Nothing in this text is special to today. It is all true in general. That is the job of the present simple.

Six uses of the present simple
UseExampleWords that help
A habit or routineI check my email every morning.every day, on Mondays, usually
A fact that is always trueWater freezes at 0 degrees Celsius.no time word needed
A situation for a long timeShe lives in Berlin. He works for a bank.no time word needed
A thought, a feeling, a thing you haveI know the answer. This laptop belongs to me.see the section on state verbs
A timetableThe train leaves at 8.15 tomorrow.at 8.15, on Friday
Steps and instructionsFirst you open the terminal. Then you run the tests.first, then, next

A situation for a long time is permanent. The speaker does not expect a change soon. The timetable use talks about the future. You can read more in Talking about the future.

Technical documents use the present simple a lot. "This function returns a list." "The server listens on port 443." These are facts about the software, so the present simple is right.

Do not use a present tense with since for a time up to now. "I work here since 2020" is wrong. English uses the present perfect here: "I have worked here since 2020." See The perfect tenses.

Adverbs of frequency

  • I always test my code.
  • She is usually on time.
  • We don't often work late.

An adverb of frequency answers the question "How often?". These words are very common with the present simple.

The position is the hard part. There are three places.

Where the adverb goes
PlaceExample
Before the main verbI usually start at nine.
After beHe is never late.
After the helper verbWe don't often work late. I can never remember it.
  • Usually, often and sometimes can also start a sentence. "Sometimes I work at night."
  • Sometimes and often can also end a sentence. "I work at night sometimes."
  • Always and never stay in the middle of a statement.
  • In an instruction they can come first. "Never share your password."
  • Longer phrases go at the end. "I back up my files once a week."

More words follow the same rules. Normally means usually. Rarely and seldom mean hardly ever. They are more common in writing.

Some useful end phrases are every day, on Mondays, twice a month and three times a year.

To ask, use How often or ever. "How often do you back up your files?" "Do you ever work at the weekend?"

Never and hardly ever are negative words. Use them with a positive verb. Say "I never eat meat", not "I don't never eat meat".

Do not put the adverb between the verb and its object. "I drink often coffee" is wrong. Say "I often drink coffee."

Present continuous: form and use

  • I am fixing a bug.
  • The tests are running.
  • She isn't answering her phone.
  • Are you listening?

The present continuous has two parts. The first part is am, is or are. The second part is the verb with -ing. Here be is the helper verb, so you do not need do.

I'm working.

She's working.

They're working.

I'm not working.

She isn't working.

They aren't working.

Am I working?

Is she working?

What are they working on?

Yes, I am. No, I'm not.

Yes, she is. No, she isn't.

Yes, they are. No, they aren't.

How to spell the -ing form

Spelling rules for -ing
The verbWhat you doExamples
most verbsadd -ingwork → working, test → testing, study → studying
ends in a silent -edrop the ewrite → writing, make → making, use → using
ends in an e that you saykeep the esee → seeing, agree → agreeing, be → being
ends in -iechange ie to ylie → lying, die → dying, tie → tying
short verb: one vowel + one consonantdouble the consonantrun → running, sit → sitting, stop → stopping
long verb, strong last partdouble the consonantbegin → beginning, forget → forgetting
long verb, weak last partdo not doubleopen → opening, visit → visiting, listen → listening
ends in -w, -x or -ydo not doubleshow → showing, fix → fixing, play → playing
ends in one vowel + l (British)double the ltravel → travelling, cancel → cancelling

"Strong" means the part of the word that you say louder. Teachers call this stress. In begin the stress is on the last part. In open it is on the first part.

American English writes traveling and canceling with one l.

When we use it

Six uses of the present continuous
UseExampleWords that help
An action at this momentI can't talk. I'm driving.now, right now, at the moment
An action around nowI'm reading a book about Rust.this week, this month, these days
A temporary situationTom is working from home this week.this week, for now, today
A changePrices are rising. My English is getting better.more and more, slowly
A fixed plan with other peopleI'm meeting Sara at six.tonight, tomorrow, on Friday
A repeated action that happens too oftenMy laptop is always crashing.always, constantly

"Around now" is important. I am not reading the book this second. I started it and I have not finished it.

The fixed plan is a future meaning. See Talking about the future.

Do not drop be. Do not forget -ing. In a question, be comes before the subject.

I working now.

She is work at the moment.

What you are doing?

Do you coming with us?

I am working now.

She is working at the moment.

What are you doing?

Are you coming with us?

State verbs

I am knowing the answer.

This bag is belonging to me.

Are you wanting a coffee?

I know the answer.

This bag belongs to me.

Do you want a coffee?

Some verbs do not describe an action. They describe a state. You cannot see a person "doing" it.

A state verb normally has no continuous form. Use the present simple, also when you talk about now.

These state verbs are useful at work: depend, contain, matter, mean and need. "It depends on the version." "The file contains ten lines." "What does this error mean?"

Verbs with two meanings

Some verbs have a state meaning and an action meaning. With the action meaning, the continuous form is fine.

State meaning and action meaning
VerbState: present simpleAction: continuous is possible
thinkI think it is a good idea. (my opinion)I'm thinking about the design. (my mind is busy)
haveI have two monitors. (I own them)I'm having lunch. (an activity)
seeI see what you mean. (I understand)I'm seeing the doctor at four. (a meeting)
tasteThis soup tastes good.The cook is tasting the soup.
lookYou look tired. (you seem tired)I'm looking at the logs.
weighThe box weighs two kilos.I'm weighing the box.
beHe is kind. (always)He is being kind today. (he acts like that now)

For your senses at this moment, use can. Say "I can hear you" and "I can't see your screen". This is very useful in video calls.

Simple or continuous?

Now compare the two tenses side by side. Each pair uses the same verb.

The same verb in two tenses
Present simplePresent continuous
I work in Tokyo. (my normal job)I'm working in Osaka this month. (temporary)
What do you do? (What is your job?)What are you doing? (now)
It rains a lot here. (in general)It's raining. Take an umbrella. (now)
The service runs on port 8080. (a fact)The service is running slowly today. (now)
He always calls on Sundays. (a habit)He's always calling during meetings. (too often)
  1. Is it a state verb, like know, want or belong? Use the present simple.
  2. Is the action in progress now or around now? Use the present continuous.
  3. Is the situation temporary, or is it changing? Use the present continuous.
  4. Is it a habit, a fact or a timetable? Use the present simple.

Time words help, but the meaning decides. Every day and usually point to the simple form. Now, at the moment and this week point to the continuous form.

On the way to work

Mina usually takes the bus.

Today she is cycling, because the sun is shining.

Usually shows a habit. Today shows something different.

Start of the day

She starts work at nine.

Right now she is reading her messages.

The start time is a routine. The reading is in progress.

Team meeting

Her team has a short meeting every morning.

This week they are having it online.

Here have is an activity, so the continuous is fine.

Lunch

She often eats at her desk.

Today she is eating outside with a new colleague.

The adverb often goes before the main verb.

Helping

She knows the code very well.

She is helping the new colleague with a bug.

Know is a state verb. It stays simple, also for now.

After work

She finishes at six.

Tonight she is meeting a friend for dinner.

This is a fixed plan, so the continuous talks about the future.

A stand-up is a good place to hear both tenses. Read this one and find them.

Lead: What are you working on today, Dana?

Dana: I'm fixing the login bug. It only happens on mobile.

Lead: Do you need any help?

Dana: No, thanks. I understand the problem now. I'm writing a test for it.

Lead: Good. Omar, you usually deploy on Thursdays.

Omar: Yes, but this week I'm waiting for the security review.

"It only happens on mobile" is a fact about the bug. "Understand" and "need" are state verbs. "You usually deploy" is a habit. The other verbs describe work in progress.

Expert uses

These uses are above A2 level. You will meet them in books, news and meetings.

Stories and film plots

We often tell the story of a film or a book in the present simple. "A young engineer finds a strange bug. She follows it and discovers a secret." The present makes the story feel close.

Demos and sports commentary

For quick actions, one after another, speakers use the present simple. "I click Run, the tests pass, and the page opens." For a longer action in the background they use the continuous. "The logs are still loading."

Verbs that do the action when you say them

With promise, agree, suggest and apologise you do the action by speaking. Use the present simple. "I promise." "I suggest a short break." "I apologise for the delay."

News headlines

Headlines often use the present simple for a past event. "Company opens new office in Seoul." The event is finished, but the headline feels fresh.

State verbs in the continuous

Sometimes a speaker wants to show that a state is temporary or changing. "You're being very quiet today." "I'm liking this job more and more." This is common in informal speech. In exams and formal writing, keep state verbs simple.

Always with the continuous

"She always helps me" is a neutral habit. "She's always helping me" has a feeling in it. It means very often, more than you expect.

With a problem it sounds like a complaint. "He's always losing his keys."

Part 1 of the IELTS Speaking test asks about familiar topics. Examples are home, work and studies. Use the present simple for your habits. Use the present continuous for things that are different these days.

One of the four marking criteria is Grammatical Range and Accuracy. A missing -s counts as an error there.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the two present tenses
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + am, is or are + noun, adjective or placeSay who, what or whereThe server is in Frankfurt.Be makes questions and negatives without do.
Subject + verb (+ -s for he, she, it)Give a habit or a factShe tests every change.Check the -s after one person or thing.
Subject + don't or doesn't + base verbSay what is not true in generalThe app doesn't save the file.No -s on the verb after doesn't.
Do or Does + subject + base verb + ?Ask a yes or no questionDoes the API return JSON?Not "Does it returns".
Question word + do or does + subject + base verb + ?Ask for informationWhere do you keep the logs?Keep do or does. Not "Where you keep".
Subject + adverb of frequency + verbSay how oftenI usually start at nine.The adverb goes before the main verb.
Subject + be + adverb of frequencySay how often with beHe is never late.The adverb goes after be.
How often + do or does + subject + base verb + ?Ask about frequencyHow often do you back up your data?Answer with once a week or every day.
Subject + am, is or are + verb-ingDescribe an action in progressThe tests are running.Do not drop be.
Subject + am, is or are + not + verb-ingSay what is not happening nowI'm not using the big screen.Say I'm not. "I amn't" is not standard.
Am, Is or Are + subject + verb-ing + ?Ask about nowAre you sharing your screen?No do or does here.
Subject + be + verb-ing + this weekDescribe a temporary situationI'm working from home this week.The simple form means it is normal.
Subject + state verb in the present simpleGive a thought, a feeling or a needI understand the error now.Not "I am understanding".
Subject + be + always + verb-ingShow that something happens too oftenMy laptop is always freezing.For a neutral habit, use the simple form.

Practice

Choose the right answer

My colleague ___ from home on Fridays.

  • work
  • works
  • working

"My colleague" is one person, so the verb takes -s. "On Fridays" shows a habit.

He ___ long meetings.

  • don't like
  • doesn't likes
  • doesn't like

With he we use doesn't. After doesn't the verb has no -s.

Which sentence has the adverb in the right place?

  • I check always my email first.
  • I always check my email first.
  • Always I check my email first.

The adverb goes before the main verb. "Always" does not start a statement.

Listen! Someone ___ at the door.

  • knocks
  • is knocking
  • knock

"Listen!" tells us the action is in progress now.

Sorry, I ___ what you mean.

  • am not understanding
  • not understand
  • don't understand

"Understand" is a state verb. It stays in the present simple, also for now.

My sister lives in Paris, but this month she ___ with us.

  • stays
  • is staying
  • stay

"This month" shows a temporary situation. "Lives" is her normal situation.

Write the form

Write the form for he, she and it.

  • fix → ?
  • study → ?
  • have → ?
  • go → ?

Write the -ing form.

  • write → ?
  • run → ?
  • lie → ?
  • open → ?

Complete the sentences

Use the present simple or the present continuous.

The Earth (go) round the Sun.

Please be quiet. I (try) to think.

Ana (not / work) on Saturdays.

Look! The build (fail) again.

How often (you / update) your laptop?

This book (belong) to my manager.

Think and write

  1. Find the mistake in each sentence and correct it. (a) She don't use a mouse. (b) I am usually start at eight. (c) What you are reading? (d) He is having two brothers. (e) Where does she lives?
    Answer

    (a) She doesn't use a mouse. (b) I usually start at eight. (c) What are you reading? (d) He has two brothers. (e) Where does she live?

  2. Put the words in order: late / is / the / never / train.
    Answer

    The train is never late. The adverb goes after be.

  3. What is the difference? (a) What do you do? (b) What are you doing?
    Answer

    Question (a) asks about your job. A good answer is "I'm a data engineer." Question (b) asks about this moment. A good answer is "I'm writing an email."

  4. Write three sentences about your normal work day. Use always, usually and never.
    Model answer

    I always read my messages first. I usually have lunch at one. I never work on Sundays. Check that each adverb is before the main verb.

  5. Write a short stand-up update with four sentences. Use both tenses.
    Model answer

    This week I'm working on the search page. Today I'm fixing a slow query. It takes five seconds, and users don't like that. I need a review from Omar before I deploy.

  6. Expert question. Explain the difference: (a) You are rude. (b) You are being rude.
    Answer

    Sentence (a) describes the person in general. It says the person is always like that. Sentence (b) describes the behaviour now. It says the person is acting badly at this moment. That is not normal for them.

When does the verb take -s?

After he, she, it, one name or one thing. "The server runs."

How do you make a present simple negative?

don't or doesn't + base form. "She doesn't work here."

Where does "always" go?

Before the main verb, but after be. "I always test." "He is always late."

How do you form the present continuous?

am, is or are + verb-ing. "The tests are running."

What is a state verb?

A verb for a situation, like know, want or belong. It stays in the present simple.

Habit or now? "I'm staying with a friend."

Now, and temporary. The speaker's normal home is somewhere else.

What does "He's always calling me" tell you?

He calls very often. The speaker thinks it is too much.

Which is right: "I'm here since Monday" or "I've been here since Monday"?

"I've been here since Monday." Since needs the present perfect.

Key takeaways

  • The present simple is for habits, facts, long situations and timetables.
  • After he, she, it or one name, the verb takes -s.
  • Negatives and questions use do or does with the base form.
  • The verb be needs no do. In a question it moves before the subject.
  • Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb and after be.
  • The present continuous is am, is or are with -ing. It is for now, around now and temporary situations.
  • State verbs like know, want and belong stay in the present simple.

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Stative verbs. The four groups of state verbs and verbs with two meanings.
  • British Council LearnEnglish Teens: Adverbs of frequency. The order of the adverbs and their position.
  • Cambridge Dictionary, English Grammar Today: Present simple. Spelling of the -s form and less common uses.
  • Cambridge Dictionary, English Grammar Today: Present, typical errors. The mistakes that learners make most often.

Past simple and past continuous

Stories, reports and status updates are about the past. The past simple gives the finished events. The past continuous shows what was in progress at that time.

  • Use was and were in statements, negatives and questions.
  • Form the past simple of regular verbs and of 80 irregular verbs.
  • Make negatives and questions with did and didn't.
  • Join the past simple and the past continuous with when and while.
  • Describe old habits with used to, and use time words like ago and last.

Three ways to talk about the past

Read this short text. It has three different past forms.

Yesterday I worked from home. At ten o'clock I was fixing a bug. I used to go to the office every day.

  • Worked is the past simple. The action is finished.
  • Was fixing is the past continuous. The action was in progress at ten o'clock.
  • Used to go describes an old habit. It is not true now.

Most of the time you need the past simple. It is the normal tense for finished events. The other two forms add extra information.

A time word like yesterday is not enough. The verb must change too. Many learners forget this when they speak fast.

Yesterday I go to the office.

Last week she start a new job.

Yesterday I went to the office.

Last week she started a new job.

Was and were

  • I was at home yesterday.
  • The servers were down for an hour.
  • It wasn't my fault.
  • Were you in the meeting?

Was and were are the past forms of be. Use was where the present has am or is. Use were where the present has are.

The past of be
SubjectPositiveNegativeQuestionShort answer
I, he, she, itshe wasshe wasn'tWas she late?Yes, she was. No, she wasn't.
you, we, theythey werethey weren'tWere they late?Yes, they were. No, they weren't.

Like in the present, be needs no helper verb. For a question, put was or were before the subject. For a negative, add not.

Two phrases with be are very common in the past.

  • There was a problem with the login. There were two problems.
  • I was born in 1995. Where were you born?

Do not say "you was" or "we was". Do not use did with was or were. And remember was in "was born".

You was right.

Did you was at home?

I didn't be tired.

I born in 1995.

You were right.

Were you at home?

I wasn't tired.

I was born in 1995.

Regular verbs: add -ed

  • I worked late yesterday.
  • She closed the ticket.
  • We deployed the fix.
  • They stopped the server.

A regular verb makes its past simple with -ed. The form is the same for every subject. There is no -s in the past. So "I worked" and "she worked" are both correct.

How to spell -ed
The verbWhat you doExamples
most verbsadd -edwork → worked, test → tested, open → opened
ends in -eadd -dclose → closed, use → used, agree → agreed
consonant + ychange y to -iedtry → tried, study → studied, copy → copied
vowel + yadd -edplay → played, enjoy → enjoyed, deploy → deployed
short verb: one vowel + one consonantdouble the consonantstop → stopped, plan → planned, drop → dropped
long verb, strong last partdouble the consonantprefer → preferred, admit → admitted
long verb, weak last partdo not doublevisit → visited, listen → listened, happen → happened
ends in -w, -x or -ydo not doubleshow → showed, fix → fixed, stay → stayed
ends in one vowel + l (British)double the ltravel → travelled, cancel → cancelled

These are the same doubling rules as for -ing. You can compare them in Present simple and present continuous. American English writes traveled and canceled with one l.

Three sounds for -ed

The letters -ed have three sounds. The last sound of the base verb decides.

How to say -ed
SoundWhenExamples
/t/after quiet sounds like k, p, s, sh, ch, fworked, stopped, fixed, pushed, watched
/d/after other soundscalled, opened, played, used, deployed
/ɪd/only after t or dwanted, needed, started, tested, loaded

Do not add a syllable to every past verb. Worked has one beat. It sounds like "workt". Only verbs that end in a t or d sound get the extra beat, like "wan-ted". The chapter Sounds and spelling has more practice.

Did and didn't

Kim: Did you see my message?

Leo: No, I didn't. I didn't check my phone.

Kim: Did Ana call you?

Leo: Yes, she did. She called at nine.

Negatives and questions in the past simple use the helper verb did. It is the past of do. It is the same for every subject.

She called at nine.

They went home.

She didn't call.

They didn't go home.

Did she call?

Did they go home?

Yes, she did. No, she didn't.

Yes, they did. No, they didn't.

Did already shows the past. So the main verb goes back to the base form. One past form is enough.

Questions with a question word

  • When did the error start?
  • What did you change?
  • Why did the test fail?
  • How long did it take?

When who or what is the subject, there is no did. The verb stays in the past form. "Who wrote this function?" "What happened?" You can read more in Questions and negatives.

After did and didn't, never use a past form. Do not use no to make the verb negative. Do not forget did in a question.

I didn't went to the meeting.

Did you saw the error?

She didn't called me.

I no finished the report.

What you did yesterday?

I didn't go to the meeting.

Did you see the error?

She didn't call me.

I didn't finish the report.

What did you do yesterday?

Irregular verbs in sound groups

  • go → I went home early.
  • write → She wrote the tests.
  • buy → We bought a new server.

An irregular verb does not take -ed. It has its own past form. Many of the most common verbs are irregular, so you need them every day.

There is no rule for these verbs. But there are sound patterns. Bought, thought and caught sound alike. So do knew, flew and threw. Verbs that sound alike are easier to learn together.

The lists below show three forms. The second form is the past simple. The third form is for the perfect tenses and the passive. Grammar books call it the past participle. You will use it in The perfect tenses. Learn the three forms together, like a small song: go, went, gone.

All three forms are the same. Only the time word shows the past: "I put it there yesterday."

The verb be is number 81. It is the only verb with two past forms: be, was or were, been.

Some verbs have two correct past forms. British English uses learnt, burnt, dreamt and spelt. The regular forms learned, burned, dreamed and spelled are correct too. American English uses gotten as the third form of get.

  1. Take one group a day. Start with the big groups.
  2. Read the three forms aloud. Listen to the rhyme.
  3. Cover the past forms. Say them from memory.
  4. Write three true sentences about your week with these verbs.
  5. Test the group again the next day, and again after one week.

Do not add -ed to an irregular verb. And like regular verbs, irregular verbs have one form for all subjects. "I went" and "she went" are both correct.

I buyed a new laptop.

He goed home.

The function throwed an error.

She teached me Rust.

I bought a new laptop.

He went home.

The function threw an error.

She taught me Rust.

Time words: ago, last, yesterday

  • The build failed ten minutes ago.
  • We released version 2 last week.
  • I called her yesterday morning.
  • I joined the company in 2019.

The past simple often comes with a finished time. The time word tells the listener when.

Time words for the past simple
WordPhrasesExample
yesterdayyesterday, yesterday morning, yesterday afternoonI sent the report yesterday.
lastlast night, last week, last month, last year, last FridayWe met last Friday.
agofive minutes ago, two days ago, a long time agoShe left an hour ago.
in, on, atin 2019, in March, on Monday, at six o'clockThe meeting started at six o'clock.
forfor an hour, for two yearsI lived in Seoul for two years.
whenwhen I was a child, when I was a studentI played chess when I was a child.
  • Ago counts back from now. It comes after the time. Say "two days ago".
  • Last and yesterday need no in, on or at. Say "last week", not "in last week".
  • Say last night, not "yesterday night".
  • For tells how long. Ago tells how far back. "I worked there for two years. I left three years ago."

The chapter Prepositions explains in, on and at for time.

With a finished time, use the past simple. Do not use the present perfect. This mistake is very common, so check it in every email.

I have seen him yesterday.

We have finished the project two days ago.

I started before two years.

I saw him yesterday.

We finished the project two days ago.

I started two years ago.

The chapter The perfect tenses compares the two tenses in detail.

Past continuous

  • At nine o'clock I was reading my email.
  • The tests were running all night.
  • She wasn't listening.
  • What were you doing at midnight?

The past continuous is was or were with the -ing form. It shows an action in progress at a past time. The action started before that time. It was not finished yet.

I was working.

They were working.

I wasn't working.

They weren't working.

Was she working?

What were they working on?

Yes, she was. No, she wasn't.

Yes, they were. No, they weren't.

Five uses of the past continuous
UseExample
An action in progress at a past timeAt nine I was reading my email.
The background of a storyIt was raining. People were leaving the office.
A long action when a short one happensI was writing code when the power went off.
Two long actions at the same timeWhile I was cooking, Tom was setting the table.
A slow change in the pastThe system was getting slower every week.

Compare two answers to the question "What did you do at nine?". "At nine I read my email" means I started at nine. "At nine I was reading my email" means I was in the middle of it.

Do not use the past continuous for a past habit. Use the past simple or used to. And do not use it with a state verb like know, want or need.

As a child I was playing football every day.

I was knowing the answer.

She was work when I called.

As a child I played football every day.

I knew the answer.

She was working when I called.

When and while

Stories often have a long action and a short action. The short action happens in the middle of the long one. Look at the same event in two ways.

I was writing code when the power went off.

While I was writing code, the power went off.

  • The long action is in the past continuous.
  • The short action is in the past simple.
  • When usually comes before the short action.
  • While comes before the long action.
  • If the when or while part comes first, put a comma after it.

One after another, or in the middle?

The tense after when changes the story. Compare these two sentences.

Two meanings with when
SentenceWhat happened
When Ana arrived, we started the meeting.First she arrived. Then we started.
When Ana arrived, we were having the meeting.The meeting was already in progress. She was late.
  1. Is it a finished action or a list of actions? Use the past simple.
  2. Was the action in progress when something else happened? Use the past continuous.
  3. Is it a state verb, like know or want? Use the past simple.

The background

It was Friday evening. It was raining. Most people were leaving the office.

The past continuous paints the scene. Nothing happens yet.

Something happens

Dana was checking the logs when she saw a strange error.

A long action, then a short action with when.

One after another

She opened the dashboard, found the broken service and called Omar.

Three finished actions in order. All are in the past simple.

At the same time

While Omar was restarting the service, Dana wrote a message to the users.

While comes before the long action.

A negative and a question

They didn't find the cause that night. Did they give up? No, they didn't.

After did and didn't, use the base form.

What changed

On Monday they found the cause. The team used to deploy on Fridays. They stopped after that week.

Used to shows an old habit that is finished.

Expert notes

When can also come before the long action

"When I was walking home, I met an old friend." This is correct too. While is clearer for a long action, so it is the safe choice.

As works like while

"As I was leaving, the phone rang." As is common in written stories. It often shows two things that happen at the same moment.

How writers build a story

The past continuous gives the background. The past simple moves the story forward. For an event before the story, writers use the past perfect. "Dana saw that someone had changed the settings." See Advanced tense and aspect.

Past forms that are not about the past

After if and wish, a past form can talk about now. "If I had more time, I would help." "I wish I knew the answer." The speaker imagines something that is not real. See Conditionals.

In the Cambridge B1 Preliminary exam, Writing Part 2 gives you a choice. You write an article or a story of about 100 words. A good story needs both past tenses. Use the continuous for the scene and the simple for the events.

Used to

  • I used to work at night. Now I work in the day.
  • We used to deploy on Fridays. We don't do that any more.
  • She didn't use to like coffee.
  • Did you use to live in Tokyo?

Used to with a base verb describes the past only. It is for a habit or a state that is finished. It tells the listener that things are different now.

The forms of used to
FormPatternExample
Positiveused to + base verbI used to play the guitar.
Negativedidn't use to + base verbI didn't use to read much.
QuestionDid + subject + use to + base verbDid you use to cycle to school?

After did and didn't, write use to without d. This follows the normal rule for did. In speech, used to sounds like "yoost to". The s is like the s in "bus".

Used to has no present form. For a present habit, use usually. And do not use used to for one single event. Use the past simple.

I use to get up at six.

I used to visit Rome in 2019.

Did you used to smoke?

I usually get up at six.

I visited Rome in 2019.

Did you use to smoke?

Expert notes

Would for old habits

In stories, would can replace used to for repeated actions. "Every summer we would visit my grandparents." It is a little more formal. It does not work for states. Say "I used to have a car", not "I would have a car".

Be used to is different

"I am used to working at night" means it is normal for me now. This phrase has be before it and -ing after it. It is not about the past. See Verb patterns: -ing and to.

The past simple can do the same job

"I played the guitar when I was young" is also correct. The past simple is neutral. Used to adds the idea that it is not true now.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the past
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + was or were + noun, adjective or placeDescribe a past stateThe servers were down for an hour.I, he, she, it take was. You, we, they take were.
Subject + verb-edGive a finished actionWe deployed the fix yesterday.One form for every subject. No -s.
Subject + irregular past formGive a finished actionShe wrote the tests last week.No -ed. Not "writed".
Subject + didn't + base verbSay what did not happenI didn't see your message.Not "didn't saw".
Did + subject + base verb + ?Ask a yes or no questionDid you restart the server?Not "Did you restarted".
Question word + did + subject + base verb + ?Ask for past informationWhen did the error start?No did when who is the subject: Who wrote this?
Past simple + time + agoSay how far backThe build failed ten minutes ago.Ago comes after the time.
Past simple + last or yesterdayGive a finished timeWe met last Friday.No in, on or at before last.
Subject + was or were + verb-ingShow an action in progress in the pastAt nine I was reading my email.Not with state verbs: I knew, not I was knowing.
Past continuous + when + past simpleA short action in the middle of a long oneI was writing code when the power went off.The short action takes the past simple.
While + past continuous, past simpleThe same idea, long action firstWhile I was writing code, the power went off.Put a comma after the while part.
When + past simple, past simpleOne action after anotherWhen the test passed, we merged the code.Two simple forms mean a sequence.
Subject + used to + base verbDescribe a finished habit or stateI used to work at night.Only for the past. Not "I use to".
Did + subject + use to + base verb + ?Ask about an old habitDid you use to live in Tokyo?Write use, not used, after did.

Practice

Choose the right answer

We ___ very busy last week.

  • was
  • were
  • did be

With we, the past of be is were.

I ___ the email, so I don't know the news.

  • didn't read
  • didn't readed
  • no read

After didn't we use the base form. Here it is read, with the long e sound.

Which verb has an extra syllable in the past?

  • worked
  • called
  • started

Start ends in a t sound, so -ed sounds like /ɪd/. The others have one beat.

I ___ lunch when you called.

  • had
  • was having
  • have

Lunch was in progress. The call was the short action in the middle.

She moved to Canada ___.

  • before three years
  • ago three years
  • three years ago

Ago comes after the time and counts back from now.

I ___ smoke, but I stopped in 2020.

  • use to
  • used to
  • was used to

Used to + base verb describes an old habit that is finished.

Write the past simple

Regular verbs. Check the spelling.

  • stop → ?
  • try → ?
  • play → ?
  • plan → ?

Irregular verbs. Think of the sound group.

  • buy → ?
  • write → ?
  • keep → ?
  • throw → ?
  • choose → ?
  • find → ?

Complete the sentences

Use the past simple or the past continuous.

We (release) the new version last Monday.

At eight o'clock this morning I (drive) to work.

When (you / start) your first job?

While the tests (run), I made a coffee.

She (not / come) to the meeting yesterday.

I (know) the answer, but I said nothing.

Think and write

  1. Find the mistake in each sentence and correct it. (a) Did you went to the party? (b) I have met her last year. (c) He was wanting a new phone. (d) They was late. (e) I didn't used to like tea.
    Answer

    (a) Did you go to the party? (b) I met her last year. (c) He wanted a new phone. (d) They were late. (e) I didn't use to like tea.

  2. Write a question for each answer. (a) I went to Osaka. (b) She called at nine. (c) Tom wrote this function.
    Answer

    (a) Where did you go? (b) When did she call? (c) Who wrote this function? In (c) who is the subject, so there is no did.

  3. Join the two sentences with when or while. "I was walking to work. I saw an accident."
    Answer

    I was walking to work when I saw an accident. Or: While I was walking to work, I saw an accident.

  4. Write three sentences about your life ten years ago. Use used to.
    Model answer

    I used to live with my parents. I used to play football every weekend. I didn't use to drink coffee.

  5. Write a short incident report with four sentences. Say what happened, what was in progress, what you did and the result.
    Model answer

    Yesterday at 14.05 the payment service stopped. The team was deploying a new version at that moment. Dana restarted the service at 14.20. We did not lose any data.

  6. Expert question. What is the difference? (a) When I got home, my sister cooked dinner. (b) When I got home, my sister was cooking dinner.
    Answer

    In (a) she started to cook after I arrived. The two actions happened one after another. In (b) she started before I arrived. The cooking was in progress when I came in.

go

went. "I went home at six."

think

thought. "I thought about the design."

run

ran. "The tests ran for an hour."

know

knew. "Nobody knew the password."

break

broke. "The update broke the login page."

take

took. "The build took ten minutes."

read

read, but say "red". "I read the logs."

send

sent. "She sent the invoice on Monday."

freeze

froze. "My screen froze twice."

catch

caught. "The test caught the bug."

Key takeaways

  • The past simple is the normal tense for finished events.
  • The past of be is was or were. It needs no did.
  • Regular verbs take -ed. It has three sounds: /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/.
  • Irregular verbs have their own forms. Learn them in sound groups.
  • After did and didn't, always use the base form.
  • With ago, last and yesterday, use the past simple, not the present perfect.
  • The past continuous shows an action in progress. Join it to a short action with when or while.
  • Used to describes a habit or state that is finished.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Past simple. Form, questions, negatives and uses.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Irregular verbs. The three forms of the most common irregular verbs.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Past continuous and past simple. How the two tenses work together with when and while.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Past habits. Used to, would and the past simple.
  • Cambridge Dictionary, English Grammar Today: Ago. Ago with the past simple, and ago or for.
  • Cambridge English: B1 Preliminary exam format. The parts of the Writing paper.

Talking about the future

English has no single future tense. It has several future forms. Each form tells the listener something extra: a plan, a fixed meeting, a timetable or a quick decision.

  • Use will for decisions, predictions, offers and promises.
  • Use be going to for plans and for predictions with evidence.
  • Talk about arrangements with the present continuous and timetables with the present simple.
  • Make offers and suggestions with Shall I and Shall we.
  • Use a present tense after when, as soon as and other time words.

Four ways to talk about the future

Read this short message. It talks about the future four times. Each time the form is different.

The release meeting starts at nine. I'm meeting the client after lunch.

Next month I'm going to learn Rust. Wait, the phone is ringing. I'll answer it.

  • Starts is the present simple. The meeting is on the timetable.
  • Am meeting is the present continuous. The meeting is fixed with another person.
  • Am going to learn is be going to. It is my plan. I decided it before now.
  • Will answer uses will. I decide at this moment.

All four forms talk about the same time: the future. The difference is the reason.

Did you decide now or before? Is it fixed with other people? Is it on a timetable?

Many learners use will for every future idea. It is often correct, but it can sound strange. A plan you made last week is not a decision at this moment.

I will visit my parents this weekend. I booked the train ticket yesterday.

I'm visiting my parents this weekend. I booked the train ticket yesterday.

Will

The form

  • I will call you tonight.
  • She'll be here at ten.
  • The fix won't take long.
  • Will you be at the meeting?

Will is a modal verb. It has one form for every subject. After it comes the base form of the main verb. There is no to and no -s.

I will help. She will help.

Short: I'll help. She'll help.

I will not help.

Short: I won't help.

Will she help?

When will it be ready?

Yes, she will.

No, she won't.

In speech and emails we usually use the contraction. Write I'll, you'll, it'll and won't. In a short answer, do not use the contraction for yes. Say "Yes, I will", not "Yes, I'll".

Won't rhymes with don't. Want has a different vowel. So "I won't go" and "I want to go" sound different. They also mean the opposite.

Do not put to after will. Do not add -s to will or to the main verb. Do not use do or does in a question with will.

I will to send the file.

She wills come tomorrow.

He will comes tomorrow.

Do you will be there?

I will send the file.

She will come tomorrow.

He will come tomorrow.

Will you be there?

What will means

Look at these sentences. Each one uses will for a different job.

Six jobs of will
JobExampleWords that help
A decision at the moment of speakingThe printer is empty. I'll get some paper.OK, then, in that case
A prediction from your opinionI think the new version will be faster.I think, I'm sure, probably
An offerYour bag looks heavy. I'll carry it.I'll ... for you
A promiseI'll send the report by Friday.I promise, definitely
A requestWill you check my code, please?please
A refusalMy laptop won't start.won't

The first job is very common in conversation. You do not have a plan. Something happens, and you decide now.

Ana: The tests are failing on the main branch.

Ben: Really? I'll have a look.

Ana: Thanks. I'll tell the team.

The last job is interesting. Won't can mean "refuses to".

"The door won't open" means it does not open, even when you try. People use it for machines and programs too. "The app won't load."

How sure are you?

Add a word to show how sure you are. Look at the order of the words.

  • It will definitely rain. It definitely won't rain.
  • It will probably rain. It probably won't rain.
  • I think it will rain. I don't think it will rain.

The words definitely and probably go after will. But they go before won't. For a negative opinion, put the negative on think. "I don't think it will rain" is more natural than "I think it won't rain".

Do not put probably after won't. And do not use will for a plan you made before. Will is for a decision now.

He won't probably come.

The phone is ringing. I answer it.

He probably won't come.

The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.

I think it won't work.

I don't think it will work.

Be going to

  • I'm going to learn Rust this year.
  • We're going to move the database next month.
  • She's not going to join the call.
  • What are you going to do after the course?

Be going to has three parts. First comes am, is or are. Then comes going to. The last part is the base form of the verb.

I'm going to call her.

They're going to call her.

I'm not going to call her.

He isn't going to call her.

Are you going to call her?

When is she going to call?

Yes, I am. No, I'm not.

Yes, she is. No, she isn't.

Two meanings

Two jobs of be going to
JobExampleWhy
A plan or intentionI'm going to ask for a pay rise.I decided before now.
A prediction with evidenceLook at those clouds. It's going to rain.I can see the reason now.

In the second meaning, the future is already starting. You can see it.

"The disk is 98% full. It's going to stop soon." "Watch out! You're going to drop your phone."

In fast speech, going to often sounds like "gonna". You will hear it in films, meetings and videos. It is fine in relaxed speech. Do not write "gonna" in an email, a report or an exam.

With the verb go, many people do not say "going to go". They use the present continuous of go. "I'm going to the gym tonight" is more common than "I'm going to go to the gym tonight". Both are correct.

Do not forget be. Do not forget to. After to, use the base form, never a past form or an -ing form.

I going to call her.

We're going finish today.

She's going to visited us.

Are you going to calling him?

I'm going to call her.

We're going to finish today.

She's going to visit us.

Are you going to call him?

Will or going to?

This is the most common question about the future. Look at two short scenes.

Scene 1

A: We have no milk.

B: Oh! I'll buy some.

B did not know. B decides now. Use will.

Scene 2

A: Why are you taking the car?

B: I'm going to buy some milk.

B decided before. It is a plan. Use going to.

There are two simple tests. One test is for decisions. The other test is for predictions.

Will or be going to
Questionwillbe going to
When did you decide?Now, while speaking. "I'll fix it."Before now. "I'm going to fix it this afternoon."
Why do you think it will happen?It is my opinion. "I think Ana will get the job."I can see evidence now. "Ana is smiling. She's going to get the job."

Often both forms are correct. The choice changes the message a little. "I think it'll rain" is an opinion. "It's going to rain" points to something you see, like dark clouds.

Will is a new idea. Going to is an old idea. Ask yourself: is this idea new in my head?

Do not use going to for a quick offer. When someone needs help now, use will.

A: This box is heavy. B: I'm going to help you.

A: This box is heavy. B: I'll help you.

Present continuous for arrangements

  • I'm meeting the client at two.
  • We're flying to Berlin on Monday.
  • She's starting her new job next week.
  • What are you doing on Saturday?

You know the present continuous from Present simple and present continuous. It can also talk about the future.

Use it for an arrangement. You agreed it with other people. You know the time and maybe the place. It is often in your calendar.

The future meaning needs a time word, or the situation must make it clear. Without a time word, the present continuous usually means now.

  • I'm working. (now)
  • I'm working on Sunday. (a future arrangement)

The present continuous and going to are very close. "I'm seeing the dentist tomorrow" and "I'm going to see the dentist tomorrow" are both fine. The first sentence sounds more fixed. Maybe you have a booking.

To ask about someone's plans in general, use going to. "What are you going to do after university?" To ask about one fixed day, both forms work. "What are you doing tonight?" is very common.

Do not use the present continuous for a prediction. Nobody can arrange the weather. And do not use it with state verbs, like know or need.

It's raining tomorrow.

I meet my manager at four today.

Next year I'm knowing more English.

It's going to rain tomorrow.

I'm meeting my manager at four today.

Next year I'll know more English.

Present simple for timetables

  • The train leaves at 9.15.
  • The sprint ends on Friday.
  • What time does the webinar start?
  • The shop doesn't open until ten on Sunday.

Use the present simple for future events on a timetable or a schedule. The person does not decide the time. A company, a school or a system decides it. Typical verbs are start, begin, finish, end, open, close, leave, arrive and depart.

This use is common at work. Teams talk about sprints, releases, deadlines and meetings in this way. "The conference starts on 3 March." "Support closes at six."

Do not use the present simple for your own plans and arrangements. A dinner with a friend is not on a timetable. Use the present continuous or going to.

I have dinner with Tom tonight.

What do you do this weekend?

I'm having dinner with Tom tonight.

What are you doing this weekend?

Note the second example. "What do you do?" asks about your job or your habits. "What are you doing this weekend?" asks about your plans.

Shall for offers and suggestions

Ana: It's hot in here.

Ben: Shall I open the window?

Ana: Yes, please. And shall we take a short break?

Ben: Good idea. Let's get a coffee, shall we?

Today shall lives mostly in questions with I and we. It has two jobs.

The two jobs of shall
PatternJobExample
Shall I + base verb?An offer. You ask if the person wants your help.Shall I send you the slides?
Shall we + base verb?A suggestion. You give an idea for the group.Shall we start the meeting?
Let's ..., shall we?A friendly suggestion with a question at the end.Let's take a break, shall we?
What / Where / When shall we ...?Ask for ideas or advice.Where shall we have lunch?

Shall is mainly British. American speakers use it less. They often say "Should I open the window?" or "Do you want me to open the window?". These forms are correct in British English too.

Do not use shall with you, he or they in normal speech. For an offer, do not ask "Will I ...?".

Will I help you with that?

Shall you come with us?

Shall I to call a taxi?

Shall I help you with that?

Will you come with us?

Shall I call a taxi?

You will also see shall in contracts, rules and technical standards. There it means "must". The rule book for internet standards, RFC 2119, says SHALL and MUST have the same meaning. The chapter Reading technical English explains these words.

Time clauses: when, as soon as, until

  • I'll call you when I arrive.
  • As soon as the build finishes, I'll deploy it.
  • Please wait here until the manager comes.
  • We'll check the logs before we restart the server.

Each sentence has two parts. The main clause has will. The time clause starts with a time word.

The time clause also talks about the future. But its verb is in the present simple.

Time words that start a time clause
WordMeaningExample
whenat the time thatWhen I finish, I'll send it.
as soon asright after, with no waitAs soon as I hear news, I'll tell you.
onceafter, and only afterOnce the tests pass, we'll merge.
beforeearlier thanSave your work before you leave.
afterlater thanAfter the meeting ends, I'll call you.
untilup to that time, then stopI'll wait until you're ready.
by the timenot later than that momentBy the time you arrive, I'll be at home.

The time clause can come first or second. If it comes first, put a comma after it. "When I arrive, I'll call you." If it comes second, you need no comma. "I'll call you when I arrive."

Present perfect in a time clause

Sometimes you want to show that the first action is complete. Then use the present perfect in the time clause. "I'll call you when I've finished the report." It means the report will be complete first. The chapter The perfect tenses explains this form.

The same rule is true after if and unless. "If it rains, we'll stay inside." See Conditionals.

Never put will in the time clause. This is one of the most common mistakes, even at B2 level.

When I will arrive, I will call you.

I'll wait until you will be ready.

As soon as I will know, I tell you.

When I arrive, I will call you.

I'll wait until you are ready.

As soon as I know, I'll tell you.

But "When will you arrive?" has will. Why?

That when is a question word, not a time word. The rule is only for time clauses. A question with when takes will as usual. "When will the fix be ready?"

The same is true in "I don't know when he will come". This part is not a time clause. It is the thing you do not know.

Which form should I choose?

Use this decision tree. Start at the top. Answer the questions in order.

  1. Is the verb after when, as soon as, until or if? Use the present simple.
  2. Is it on a timetable, like a train or a sprint? Use the present simple.
  3. Did you fix it with other people, with a time? Use the present continuous.
  4. Did you plan it before now? Use be going to.
  5. Are you deciding, offering or promising now? Use will. For an opinion about the future, use will too.

The timetable

The new sprint starts today. It ends on Friday at noon.

A sprint is on the team's timetable. Use the present simple.

Dana's plan

This sprint Dana is going to rewrite the login page.

She decided this last week. It is her plan.

An arrangement

She is meeting the designer on Tuesday at ten.

The meeting is in both calendars. Use the present continuous.

A quick decision

Omar: "The staging server is down!" Dana: "I'll restart it."

Dana decides at this moment. Use will.

An offer

Dana: "Shall I write the incident report too?"

She offers help with Shall I.

A prediction

The tests are slow again. "We're going to miss the deadline."

She can see the evidence. Use going to.

A time clause and a promise

"As soon as the tests pass, I'll send you the link. I promise."

Present simple after as soon as. Will for the promise.

Expert notes

These forms go beyond A2 level. You will meet them in meetings, news and technical writing.

Will be + -ing: the future continuous

Use it for an action in progress at a future time. "At ten tomorrow I'll be flying to Seoul."

It also asks about plans in a soft, polite way. "Will you be using the meeting room this afternoon?" This question is not a request. It only asks about the plan.

The chapter Advanced tense and aspect says more.

Will have + past participle: the future perfect

Stand at a future point and look back. "By Friday we'll have fixed all the bugs." See The perfect tenses.

Be about to: the very near future

The action will happen in a moment. "Hurry! The train is about to leave." "I'm about to start a call. Can I ring you back?"

Be due to and be due: the expected time

Something is expected at a time, often by a schedule. "The flight is due to land at 6.40." "The report is due on Friday." At work, due date means deadline.

Be likely to, may and might: less sure

"Prices are likely to rise." means a rise is probable. "The update might break old plugins." means it is possible, but not sure. See Modal verbs and Hedging and stance.

Be to: formal plans in the news

News reports use be to for official plans. "The minister is to visit Japan next month." You will read this. You do not need to say it.

Hope, plan, expect and other verbs

Some verbs carry a future meaning on their own. "I hope to finish today." "We plan to launch in May." "I expect the client will agree." After hope, the present simple is common for the future: "I hope the demo goes well."

In Part 3 of the IELTS Speaking test, the examiner asks about wider ideas. You give opinions and talk about what may happen. Show range with will probably, probably won't, is likely to and might. Grammatical Range and Accuracy is one of the four marking criteria.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the future
PatternPurposeModelNote
I'll + base verbMake a decision at the moment of speakingThe printer is empty. I'll get some paper.Not "I get". Not "I'm going to" for a new idea.
I think + subject + will + base verbGive a prediction from your opinionI think the new version will be faster.For a negative, "I don't think it will" is more natural.
Subject + will probably / probably won't + verbSay how sure you areIt probably won't take long.Probably goes after will but before won't.
I'll + verb + for youMake an offerI'll carry that for you.No to after will.
Will you + base verb + please?Ask someone to do somethingWill you check my code, please?Not "Do you will".
Subject + won't + verbSay that a person or thing refusesThe app won't load.Won't rhymes with don't.
Subject + am / is / are going to + base verbTalk about a plan made before nowI'm going to learn Rust this year.Do not drop be or to.
Evidence + it's going to + verbPredict from what you can see nowLook at those clouds. It's going to rain.Write going to, not gonna.
Subject + am / is / are + verb-ing + timeTalk about an arrangement with othersI'm meeting the client at two.Needs a time word or a clear situation.
Event + present simple + timeTalk about a timetable or scheduleThe sprint ends on Friday.Not for personal plans.
Shall I + base verb?Offer to helpShall I send you the slides?Only with I and we.
Shall we + base verb?Make a suggestionShall we take a short break?Let's ..., shall we? is also common.
Will + verb ... when / as soon as + present simpleJoin a future action to a future timeI'll call you when I arrive.Never will after when.
When + present perfect, will + verbShow the first action will be completeWhen I've finished the report, I'll send it.Put a comma after the time clause.

Practice

Choose the right answer

A: "Someone is at the door." B: "___ get it."

  • I'll
  • I'm going to
  • I get

B decides at this moment. A new decision takes will.

I've bought the paint. I ___ my kitchen this weekend.

  • will paint
  • am going to paint
  • paint

The plan was made before. Buying the paint shows that.

The flight to Madrid ___ at 7.30 tomorrow morning.

  • leaves
  • is going to leave
  • will leaving

A flight is on a timetable. Use the present simple.

___ I open the window?

  • Will
  • Shall
  • Do

An offer with I takes shall in British English.

I'll send you the file as soon as I ___ it.

  • will find
  • find
  • am going to find

After as soon as, use a present tense. Never will.

Which sentence is correct?

  • He won't probably come to the party.
  • He probably won't come to the party.
  • He will not probably come to the party.

Probably goes before won't.

Complete the sentences

Use the verb in brackets. Choose will, be going to, the present continuous or the present simple.

I can't come on Thursday. I (meet) a client at four.

The webinar (start) at 10.00, so please join five minutes early.

A: "I don't understand this error." B: "Don't worry. I (help) you."

Look at that car! It (hit) the wall!

When I (get) home, I'll call you.

We (move) to a bigger office next year. We decided last month.

I promise I (not / tell) anyone.

Please don't leave until the meeting (end).

Think and write

  1. Find the mistake in each sentence and correct it. (a) I will to call you later. (b) When I will finish, I'll tell you. (c) I meet my dentist tomorrow at nine. (d) She's going to visited her parents. (e) Will I carry your bag?
    Answer

    (a) I will call you later. (b) When I finish, I'll tell you. (c) I'm meeting my dentist tomorrow at nine. (d) She's going to visit her parents. (e) Shall I carry your bag?

  2. Write a reply with will for each situation. (a) A friend says, "I'm cold." (b) Your colleague says, "The build is broken." (c) Your manager says, "Can you finish the report today?"
    Model answer

    (a) I'll close the window. (b) I'll look at it now. (c) Yes, I'll send it by five o'clock.

  3. Write three sentences about your plans for next year. Use be going to.
    Model answer

    I'm going to take an English exam. I'm going to read one book every month. I'm not going to work at weekends.

  4. Write your calendar for tomorrow. Write three arrangements with the present continuous and one timetable fact with the present simple.
    Model answer

    I'm having a call with the design team at ten. I'm meeting Sara for lunch. I'm seeing the doctor at five. My train leaves at 8.20.

  5. Join each pair with the word in brackets. (a) The tests will finish. I will deploy. (as soon as) (b) You will be ready. I will wait. (until)
    Answer

    (a) As soon as the tests finish, I'll deploy. (b) I'll wait until you're ready. The time clause takes the present simple.

  6. Expert question. Explain the difference. (a) Will you come to the meeting? (b) Will you be coming to the meeting?
    Answer

    (a) can be a request or an invitation. The speaker may want you to come. (b) only asks about your plan. It is softer and more polite. It puts no pressure on you.

A decision at the moment of speaking

will. "I'll answer it."

A plan made before now

be going to. "I'm going to learn Rust."

A prediction with evidence you can see

be going to. "It's going to rain."

A prediction from your opinion

will. "I think it will work."

An arrangement with other people

Present continuous. "I'm meeting Ana at two."

A timetable or schedule

Present simple. "The train leaves at 9."

An offer with I

Shall I. "Shall I send the slides?"

The verb after when or as soon as

Present simple. "When I arrive, I'll call."

Key takeaways

  • English has several future forms. Each one adds a reason or a feeling.
  • Will is for decisions now, opinions, offers, promises and requests.
  • Be going to is for plans made before and for predictions with evidence.
  • The present continuous is for arrangements. The present simple is for timetables.
  • Shall I makes an offer. Shall we makes a suggestion.
  • After when, as soon as, until, before and after, use a present tense, never will.
  • Probably goes after will but before won't.

Sources
