  • British Council LearnEnglish: Future forms. Will, be going to and the present continuous compared.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: The future, degrees of certainty. Will probably, probably won't, likely to and might.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Verbs in time clauses and if clauses. Present forms after when, until and if.
  • RFC 2119: Key words for use in RFCs. Shows that SHALL and MUST have the same meaning in standards.
  • IELTS: Academic Speaking format. The three parts and the four marking criteria.

Adjectives and adverbs

Adjectives and adverbs add detail. They tell us what kind, how, when, where and how much. With them, a plain sentence becomes clear and exact.

  • Put adjectives in the right place and the right order.
  • Choose between -ed and -ing adjectives, like bored and boring.
  • Compare things with comparatives, superlatives and as ... as.
  • Form adverbs and put them in the right position in a sentence.
  • Use very, quite, too, enough, so and such correctly.

Adjective or adverb?

Read these two sentences. They have almost the same words.

  • Ana is a careful driver.
  • Ana drives carefully.

Careful is an adjective. It describes the noun driver.

Carefully is an adverb. It describes the verb drives. It says how Ana drives.

What each word type describes
Word typeIt describesIt answersExample
adjectivea noun or pronounWhat kind? Which one?a fast laptop, an old server
adverba verbHow? When? Where? How often?She types quickly. I'll call later.
adverban adjective or another adverbHow much?very fast, really quickly
adverbthe whole sentenceWhat do I think about it?Luckily, the backup worked.

Many adverbs are an adjective with -ly: quick and quickly, slow and slowly. So the ending often helps you. But be careful. Some words with -ly are adjectives, like friendly.

Do not use an adjective to describe a verb. This mistake is very common in fast speech.

She speaks English very good.

Please drive slow.

The app runs smooth now.

She speaks English very well.

Please drive slowly.

The app runs smoothly now.

Where adjectives go, and in what order

  • a new laptop. two new laptops.
  • The laptop is new.
  • The laptop looks expensive.

An adjective has two normal places. It comes before a noun: "a new laptop". Or it comes after a linking verb: "The laptop is new".

An adjective never changes. It has no plural and no -s.

The most common linking verbs are be, become, get, seem, look, feel, sound, smell and taste. After these verbs, use an adjective, not an adverb.

  • You look tired. (not tiredly)
  • This soup tastes good. (not well)
  • I feel bad about the mistake. (not badly)
  • Your plan sounds great.

Two or more adjectives

When you use two or three adjectives, they have a usual order. Opinion comes first. Facts come after it. The type of thing comes last, next to the noun.

Adjective order with real examples
OpinionFactType or useNoun
a beautifuloldhouse
a usefulsmalltool
a black leatherlaptopbag
an expensivenew Germansportscar
a comfortablegreyofficechair

Two or three adjectives are normal. More than three is very unusual. With adjectives from different groups, use no comma: "a big black dog". With two colours, use and: "a black and white photo".

Grammar books do not fully agree about size, shape and age. Some put age before shape.

The strong rules are simple. Opinion comes first. Type or use comes last. Colour, origin and material come near the end.

In English the adjective usually comes before the noun. Do not add -s to an adjective. And keep opinion before fact.

I bought a laptop new.

We have two olds servers.

She has a black big bag.

You look tiredly.

I bought a new laptop.

We have two old servers.

She has a big black bag.

You look tired.

-ed and -ing adjectives

The meeting was boring.

The meeting gave this feeling to people.

I was bored.

This is how I felt.

Many adjectives come in pairs. The -ing adjective describes the thing that causes a feeling. The -ed adjective describes how a person feels. "The film was interesting, so I was interested."

Common pairs
-ing: it gives the feeling-ed: you have the feeling
The news was surprising.Everybody was surprised.
This error message is confusing.I'm confused.
The project is exciting.The team is excited.
The long call was tiring.After the call I was tired.
The slow build is annoying.Developers are annoyed.
The results are disappointing.The client is disappointed.
Losing data is frightening.We were frightened.
The weekend was relaxing.I feel relaxed.
Your talk was interesting.I'm interested in AI.
The test was embarrassing.I was embarrassed.

A person can be both. "Tom is bored" means Tom has the feeling. "Tom is boring" means other people feel bored with Tom. Be careful with this one.

"I am boring" means people do not like talking to you. You probably want to say "I am bored". Also remember the preposition after interested: interested in. See Prepositions.

I'm very interesting in machine learning.

The lesson was bored.

I was very exciting about the trip.

I'm very interested in machine learning.

The lesson was boring.

I was very excited about the trip.

Comparatives and superlatives

  • Rust is faster than Python.
  • This laptop is more expensive than that one.
  • This is the fastest server in the data centre.
  • It was the most difficult bug of the year.

A comparative compares two things. It is often followed by than. A superlative puts one thing at the top or bottom of a group. It usually has the before it.

The form depends on the number of syllables in the adjective.

How to make comparatives and superlatives
AdjectiveRuleExamples
one syllableadd -er, -estfast, faster, the fastest. cheap, cheaper, the cheapest
one syllable, ends in -eadd -r, -stnice, nicer, the nicest. safe, safer, the safest
one syllable, one vowel + one consonantdouble the consonantbig, bigger, the biggest. hot, hotter, the hottest
ends in a consonant + ychange y to i, add -er, -esteasy, easier, the easiest. busy, busier, the busiest
two syllables, most othersmore, the mostmodern, more modern, the most modern. useful, more useful
three or more syllablesmore, the mostexpensive, more expensive, the most expensive
some two-syllable wordsboth forms are correctsimple, simpler or more simple. narrow, polite, gentle, common

A few common adjectives are irregular. Learn them by heart.

Irregular forms
AdjectiveComparativeSuperlative
goodbetterthe best
badworsethe worst
farfurther or fartherthe furthest or the farthest
much, manymorethe most
little (amount)lessthe least

Adverbs follow almost the same rules. Short adverbs take -er: faster, harder, earlier. Adverbs with -ly take more: more slowly, more carefully. Well becomes better, and badly becomes worse.

Make the difference big or small

  • Big difference: much faster, far faster, a lot faster.
  • Small difference: a bit faster, a little faster, slightly faster.
  • The other direction: less expensive, the least useful.

Useful superlative patterns

  • Use in with a place or a group: the best developer in the team, the tallest building in the world.
  • Use of with a time or a number: the busiest day of the week, the cheapest of the three.
  • One of the + superlative + plural noun: one of the best tools.
  • Superlative + present perfect: the best book I've ever read.

Use -er or more, never both. Use than after a comparative, not that or as. Do not forget the before a superlative.

This version is more faster.

Go is more simple that C++.

He is the most good engineer of the company.

It's one of the best tool.

This version is faster.

Go is simpler than C++.

He is the best engineer in the company.

It's one of the best tools.

As ... as and other comparisons

  • My laptop is as fast as yours.
  • The new design isn't as good as the old one.
  • This server is twice as fast as the old one.
  • Your error is the same as mine.

Use as + adjective or adverb + as when two things are equal. The negative not as ... as means less. "Python is not as fast as Rust" means Python is slower.

You can also say not so ... as. It is less common.

Comparison patterns
PatternMeaningExample
as + adjective + asequalThe test is as easy as last year's.
not as + adjective + aslessThe train isn't as fast as the plane.
twice / three times as ... asa multipleIt's three times as big as our office.
as much / many + noun + asan equal amountI don't have as much time as you.
the same + noun + asno differenceShe is the same age as me.
similar to, different fromalmost the same, not the sameMy job is similar to yours. Yours is different from mine.
as ... as possiblethe most you canPlease reply as soon as possible.

After than and as, people usually say me, him, her. "She is taller than me." In formal writing you can add the verb. "She is taller than I am."

Do not mix the two patterns. As goes with as. Than goes with a comparative. Say the same as, not "the same like".

My code is as fast than yours.

It's more cheap as the old plan.

My phone is the same like yours.

My code is as fast as yours.

It's cheaper than the old plan.

My phone is the same as yours.

Making adverbs

  • He closed the door quietly.
  • The tests ran successfully.
  • She works hard.
  • You did that well.

Most adverbs of manner are an adjective + -ly. An adverb of manner says how something happens. Some spelling changes are needed.

How to spell -ly adverbs
AdjectiveRuleExamples
most adjectivesadd -lyquick → quickly, careful → carefully, sudden → suddenly
consonant + ychange y to -ilyeasy → easily, happy → happily, lucky → luckily
consonant + lechange e to ysimple → simply, possible → possibly, gentle → gently
ends in -icadd -allybasic → basically, automatic → automatically
ends in -uedrop e, add -lytrue → truly
ends in -lladd -yfull → fully

Irregular adverbs

Some adverbs do not use -ly. The most important is good → well. "She is a good speaker. She speaks well." Other adverbs look the same as the adjective.

Same word, two jobs
WordAs an adjectiveAs an adverb
fasta fast networkIt loads fast.
harda hard problemWe worked hard.
latea late trainThe train arrived late.
earlyan early meetingI got up early.
dailya daily stand-upWe meet daily.

Be careful. Adding -ly to some of these words makes a new meaning.

  • hardly = almost not. "I hardly slept." (I slept very little.)
  • lately = recently. "Have you seen Tom lately?"
  • nearly = almost. "I'm nearly ready."
  • highly = very. "I highly recommend this book."

Some adjectives already end in -ly: friendly, lovely, lonely, silly, likely. They have no adverb. Use "in a ... way": "She answered in a friendly way."

Other kinds of adverb

Kinds of adverb
KindQuestionExamples
mannerHow?slowly, carefully, well, fast
timeWhen?now, today, soon, later, yesterday, already, still
placeWhere?here, there, outside, upstairs, abroad, everywhere
frequencyHow often?always, usually, often, sometimes, never
degreeHow much?very, really, quite, too, enough, almost
commentWhat do I think?luckily, unfortunately, honestly, clearly

The chapter Present simple and present continuous covers adverbs of frequency in detail. Linkers like however are in Linking words.

Do not say hardly when you mean hard. Do not add -ly to friendly. And remember that well is the adverb of good.

He works very hardly.

She smiled friendlily.

You did the job good.

The train arrived lately.

He works very hard.

She smiled in a friendly way.

You did the job well.

The train arrived late.

Where adverbs go

An adverb has three main positions. Look at the examples.

The three positions
PositionExampleTypical adverbs
front: at the startLuckily, we had a backup.comment adverbs, time words, linkers
middle: before the main verbI often work late.frequency, probably, almost, also, just, already
end: after the verb and objectShe checked the code carefully.manner, place, time

End position

Most adverbs of manner, place and time go at the end. If the verb has an object, the adverb goes after the object. Never put it between the verb and the object.

  • She speaks English well.
  • I like coffee very much.
  • We tested the app carefully.

With two or three end adverbs, the usual order is how, then where, then when. "She worked quietly in the library all afternoon." The order can change for emphasis. A time word can also go at the front: "Yesterday we released the fix."

Middle position

The middle position has three simple rules. They are the same rules as for adverbs of frequency.

  • Before the main verb: I usually start at nine. We almost missed the train.
  • After be: She is always on time. The report is already finished.
  • After the first helper verb: I have never seen this error. It will probably rain.

Degree adverbs

Degree adverbs like very, really and almost go right before the word they change. "a very long meeting", "almost ready". The exception is enough. It goes after an adjective or adverb: "fast enough".

Do not put an adverb between the verb and its object. This is the most common position mistake.

I like very much coffee.

She speaks very well English.

I always am tired on Mondays.

I go often to the gym.

I like coffee very much.

She speaks English very well.

I am always tired on Mondays.

I often go to the gym.

Expert note: only can change the meaning

The position of only changes what it describes. "Only Ana tested the app" means nobody else tested it.

"Ana only tested the app" means she did not do more, like fix it. In speech, people often put only before the verb. Stress then shows the meaning.

Very, quite and strong adjectives

  • It's a bit cold today.
  • It's very cold today.
  • It's absolutely freezing today.

Most adjectives can be weaker or stronger. They are gradable. Degree adverbs make them weaker or stronger. Here is a scale from weak to strong.

Strong adjectives

Some adjectives already contain the idea of "very". Freezing means very cold.

These are strong adjectives. Do not use very with them. Use absolutely or really.

Strong words help you sound natural. They also help in speaking exams. You can find more strong pairs in Register, collocation and idiom.

Normal and strong adjectives
Normal (very ...)Strong (absolutely ...)
very coldabsolutely freezing
very hotabsolutely boiling
very bigabsolutely huge, enormous
very smallabsolutely tiny
very tiredabsolutely exhausted
very goodabsolutely brilliant, amazing
very badabsolutely awful, terrible
very angryabsolutely furious
very hungryabsolutely starving

A few adjectives describe a yes or no state: finished, perfect, impossible, dead. They take completely, totally or absolutely. "The task is completely impossible." Really works with every group, so it is a safe choice.

Quite has two meanings

  • With a normal adjective, British quite means "fairly". "The film was quite good" means good, but not very good.
  • With a strong or yes-or-no adjective, quite means "completely". "You're quite right." "That's quite impossible."
  • In American English, quite good is often closer to "very good".

Note the word order with a noun. Quite goes before a: "It was quite a long meeting." Pretty means the same as British quite, but it is informal. "The demo went pretty well."

Do not use very with a strong adjective. And do not say "quite" to praise strongly in Britain. It can sound like a small complaint.

The office was very freezing.

Your idea is very perfect.

It was a quite long meeting.

The office was absolutely freezing.

Your idea is perfect.

It was quite a long meeting.

Too, enough, so and such

Too and enough

This laptop is very heavy, but I can carry it.

This laptop is too heavy. I can't carry it every day.

This laptop isn't light enough. I can't carry it every day.

Very only makes a word stronger. Too means more than is good or possible. It shows a problem. Enough means as much as you need.

Patterns with too and enough
PatternExample
too + adjectiveThe text is too small.
too + adjective + for + personThe exam was too difficult for me.
too + adjective + to + verbIt's too late to change the plan.
too much + uncountable nounThere is too much noise.
too many + plural nounWe have too many meetings.
adjective or adverb + enoughThe server isn't fast enough. You didn't speak loudly enough.
enough + nounWe don't have enough memory.
adjective + enough + to + verbShe is old enough to drive.

Enough goes after an adjective but before a noun. Compare "big enough" and "enough space".

So and such

  • The build is so slow!
  • It's such a slow build!
  • They are such nice people.
  • We had so many bugs this week.

So and such make a word stronger. They also show a feeling, like surprise. Use so before an adjective or adverb with no noun. Use such before a noun.

So or such
PatternExample
so + adjective or adverbThe meeting was so long. She types so fast.
such + a / an + adjective + singular nounIt was such a long meeting.
such + adjective + plural or uncountable nounsuch good ideas, such bad weather
so much / so many + nounso much work, so many emails
so ... that + resultThe meeting was so long that I missed lunch.
such ... that + resultIt was such a long meeting that I missed lunch.

Put enough after the adjective. Do not use too as a strong very. Use such, not so, before a + noun. And weather, advice and information are uncountable, so they take no a. See Nouns and articles.

The room isn't enough big.

Thank you! The gift is too beautiful.

It was so a nice day.

We had such a bad weather.

There are too much bugs.

The room isn't big enough.

Thank you! The gift is very beautiful.

It was such a nice day.

We had such bad weather.

There are too many bugs.

Start simple

We bought a chair.

Subject, verb and object. No detail yet.

Add adjectives

We bought a comfortable black office chair.

Opinion first, then colour, then type next to the noun.

Add a comparison

It is much cheaper than the old one.

Much makes the difference big. Than follows the comparative.

Add an adverb of manner

The delivery team carried it carefully up the stairs.

The adverb goes after the object, not between verb and object.

Add a comment adverb

Luckily, it was small enough for the lift.

A comment adverb goes at the front. Enough goes after the adjective.

Add so ... that

It is so comfortable that I work better now.

So + adjective + that + result.

Expert notes

These points go beyond A2 level. You will meet them in reading and in exams.

Adjectives that only come after a verb

Some adjectives do not go before a noun: asleep, awake, alive, alone and afraid. Say "The baby is asleep", not "an asleep baby". Before a noun, use another word: a sleeping baby, a frightened child, a living person.

Adjectives after the noun

After something, anything, nothing and somebody, the adjective comes after. "Let's try something new." Some adjectives also follow the noun in fixed uses: "the people involved", "the best solution possible".

The + adjective for a group of people

The rich, the poor, the young, the elderly, the unemployed. The phrase means all people of that kind. It takes a plural verb: "The young are often online." Do not add -s.

Compound adjectives

A compound adjective joins words with a hyphen: a two-hour meeting, a ten-minute break, a well-known library. The number word stays singular.

Say "a two-hour meeting", not "a two-hours meeting". Before a noun we write "open-source code". After a verb, "the code is open source" often has no hyphen.

Double comparatives

Two comparatives can show change. "The tests are getting slower and slower." "Cloud bills are getting more and more expensive." With the ... the, one change causes another. "The sooner we start, the sooner we finish." "The more tests we write, the fewer bugs we ship."

Elder, eldest and further

Elder and eldest are used for people in a family, before a noun: "my elder sister". Older is also correct. Further can mean "more" or "extra": "further information", "until further notice". Farther is only for distance.

Look carefully or look careful?

Some verbs can be a linking verb or an action verb. "She looked careful" describes her (adjective). "She looked carefully at the code" describes the action of looking (adverb). Ask: am I describing the person, or the action?

Too ... to with no object at the end

Say "The box is too heavy to lift." Do not add it at the end. The box is already the thing you lift. The same is true with enough: "The text is big enough to read."

The Cambridge B2 First Reading and Use of English paper has a word formation part. It is Part 3.

You change a word to fit a gap, often by adding a prefix or suffix. Many answers are adjectives and adverbs. Practise word families like care, careful, careless, carefully. See How to grow your vocabulary and Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for adjectives and adverbs
PatternPurposeModelNote
a / an + adjective + nounDescribe a thingWe need a fast server.Adjective before the noun. No plural -s.
Subject + linking verb + adjectiveDescribe a person or thingYou look tired.Adjective, not adverb, after look, feel, sound, taste.
Opinion + fact + type + nounUse two or three adjectivesa comfortable grey office chairOpinion first. Type or use next to the noun.
Thing + is + -ing adjectiveSay what causes a feelingThe error message is confusing.Not "confused" for the thing.
Person + is + -ed adjectiveSay how someone feelsI'm interested in AI."I'm boring" means people find you dull.
Comparative + thanCompare two thingsRust is faster than Python.Use -er or more, never both.
much / a bit + comparativeShow a big or small differenceThe new plan is much cheaper.Not "very cheaper".
the + superlative + in / ofPut one thing at the top of a groupShe is the best tester in the team.In for a place or group. Of for a time or number.
(not) as + adjective + asSay two things are equal or notMy laptop isn't as fast as yours.Not "as fast than".
Verb + object + adverbSay how something happensShe checked the code carefully.Never between verb and object.
Subject + mid adverb + main verbAdd frequency or certaintyI usually start at nine.After be: She is always on time.
absolutely + strong adjectiveMake a strong adjective strongerThe office was absolutely freezing.Not "very freezing".
too + adjective + to + verbShow a problemIt's too late to change the plan.Too is negative. Very is not.
adjective + enough / enough + nounSay you have what you needIt isn't fast enough. We don't have enough memory.After an adjective. Before a noun.
so + adjective / such + a + adjective + nounMake a word stronger, show feelingIt was such a long meeting.Not "so a long meeting".

Practice

Choose the right answer

She sings ___.

  • beautiful
  • beautifully
  • more beautiful

The word describes the verb sings. Use an adverb.

I was ___ because the video call lasted three hours.

  • exhausting
  • exhausted
  • exhaust

This is how the person feels. Use the -ed adjective.

Which is the right order?

  • a leather old brown bag
  • a nice old brown leather bag
  • a brown nice old leather bag

Opinion (nice), age (old), colour (brown), material (leather).

This is ___ restaurant in the city.

  • the more good
  • the better
  • the best

Good is irregular: good, better, best. Use the superlative for the top of a group.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I like very much this song.
  • I like this song very much.
  • I very much this song like.

The adverb goes after the object, not between the verb and the object.

It was ___ that we stayed at home.

  • such a cold day
  • so a cold day
  • such cold day

Before a + adjective + noun, use such.

Write the form

Write the comparative.

  • cheap → ?
  • big → ?
  • easy → ?
  • expensive → ?
  • bad → ?

Write the adverb.

  • careful → ?
  • happy → ?
  • simple → ?
  • good → ?
  • fast → ?

Complete the sentences

The new office is (big) the old one.

My English is not as (good) as my sister's.

This screen isn't (big / enough) for two windows.

The coffee is (too / enough) hot. I can't drink it yet.

The weather was absolutely (cold: use a strong adjective).

Think and write

  1. Find the mistake in each sentence and correct it. (a) He speaks French very good. (b) This is more cheaper. (c) I'm boring, let's go out. (d) She is the same age like me. (e) The room isn't enough big.
    Answer

    (a) He speaks French very well. Well describes the verb speaks.

    (b) This is cheaper. (c) I'm bored. Let's go out. (d) She is the same age as me. (e) The room isn't big enough.

  2. Write the adjectives in the right order. (a) a / Japanese / small / car (b) an / plastic / cheap / phone case (c) a / old / beautiful / stone / bridge
    Answer

    (a) a small Japanese car (b) a cheap plastic phone case (c) a beautiful old stone bridge

  3. Compare two programming languages, two phones or two cities. Write three sentences. Use a comparative, a superlative and as ... as.
    Model answer

    Python is easier to learn than C. C is one of the fastest languages in the world. Python is not as fast as C, but it is much more popular for AI.

  4. Put the adverb in the right place. (a) I check my email. (usually) (b) She is late. (never) (c) We have finished. (already) (d) He drives. (carefully)
    Answer

    (a) I usually check my email. (b) She is never late. (c) We have already finished. (d) He drives carefully.

  5. Rewrite each sentence with too or enough. Keep the meaning. (a) The bag is very small. My laptop doesn't fit. (b) He is only 16. He can't vote.
    Answer

    (a) The bag is too small for my laptop. Or: The bag isn't big enough for my laptop. (b) He is too young to vote. Or: He isn't old enough to vote.

  6. Expert question. Explain the difference in British English. (a) The talk was quite good. (b) You're quite right.
    Answer

    In (a) good is a normal adjective. Quite means fairly. The talk was good, but not very good.

    In (b) right is a yes-or-no adjective. Quite means completely. You are 100% right.

The adverb of good?

well. "You did that well."

The comparative of far?

further or farther.

What does hardly mean?

Almost not. "I hardly slept."

Bored or boring: how you feel?

bored. "I'm bored."

A strong adjective for very tired?

exhausted. "I'm absolutely exhausted."

Where does enough go with an adjective?

After it. "fast enough".

So or such before a + noun?

such. "such a good idea".

The adverb of friendly?

There is none. Say "in a friendly way".

Key takeaways

  • Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, other adverbs and sentences.
  • An adjective goes before a noun or after a linking verb. It never takes -s.
  • With two or three adjectives, opinion comes first and type comes last.
  • -ing adjectives give a feeling. -ed adjectives describe how you feel.
  • Short adjectives take -er and -est. Long adjectives take more and most.
  • Never put an adverb between a verb and its object.
  • Strong adjectives take absolutely or really, not very.
  • Too shows a problem. Enough goes after an adjective. Such goes before a noun.

Prepositions

Prepositions are small words like in, on, at, to and for. They are short, but they carry a lot of meaning. You use them in almost every sentence. This chapter gives you clear pictures, safe rules and the lists you need to learn.

  • Choose in, on or at for time and for place.
  • Describe movement with to, into, through, across and along.
  • Use by, with, for, from, of and about with their main meanings.
  • Learn verbs and adjectives together with their fixed prepositions.
  • Ask questions with a preposition at the end, like "Who are you waiting for?"

What a preposition does

Read these four sentences. Only one small word changes.

  • The keys are on the desk.
  • The keys are in the desk.
  • The keys are under the desk.
  • The keys are by the desk.

The keys and the desk stay the same. The small word changes the picture. That small word is a preposition. It shows how two things connect in place, in time or in meaning.

A preposition never stands alone. Something always comes after it. That partner is a noun, a pronoun or a verb with -ing. The preposition and its partner make a prepositional phrase.

What comes after a preposition
PartnerExamples
A noun or noun phraseat the station, for my team, in the config file
An object pronounwith me, for them, about it, between us
A verb with -ingbefore leaving, good at testing, thanks for helping

So the rule is simple. After a preposition, use an object pronoun. Use the -ing form for a verb. Never put to + verb or a bare verb after a preposition.

This gift is for you and I.

Thank you for help me.

I'm interested in to learn Rust.

After finish the review, I went home.

This gift is for you and me.

Thank you for helping me.

I'm interested in learning Rust.

After finishing the review, I went home.

"After I finished the review" is also correct. There, after joins two clauses. The chapter Linking words explains this second job.

A preposition is a small link word. It always has a partner after it. The partner is a thing, a person word like me, or a verb with -ing.

In, on and at for time

Read from top to bottom. The time gets more exact each line.

  1. I was born in 1992.
  2. I was born in May.
  3. I was born on 12 May.
  4. I was born at 6.30 in the morning.

Think of a pyramid. In is the wide base. It is for long periods. On is the middle. It is for days and dates. At is the small top. It is for an exact point in time. The same pyramid works for place too, as the next section shows.

In, on and at for time
WordUse it forExamples
atclock times, meal times, some fixed phrasesat 9.30, at noon, at midnight, at lunchtime, at night, at the weekend, at Christmas, at the moment
ondays, dates, special dayson Monday, on 3 June, on my birthday, on Christmas Day, on Friday morning
inparts of the day, months, seasons, years, long periodsin the morning, in June, in winter, in 2026, in the 1990s, in the past, in the future

Look at "on Friday morning". It has a day and a part of the day. The day wins, so use on. Compare "in the morning" and "on Friday morning".

No preposition at all

Some time words never take in, on or at. These are this, next, last, every, today, tonight, tomorrow and yesterday.

See you on next Monday.

We deploy at every Friday.

I'm busy in this week.

See you next Monday.

We deploy every Friday.

I'm busy this week.

Four useful details

  • Weekend. British English says at the weekend. American English says on the weekend. Both are correct.
  • Night. At night means during the night in general. In the night means at one moment of one night. "I woke up in the night."
  • On time and in time. On time means at the planned time, not late. In time means early enough. "The train left on time." "We fixed the bug in time for the release."
  • In + period. For the future, in means "after this much time from now". "The build will finish in ten minutes."

Do not say "I will call you after ten minutes" when you mean from now. Say "I will call you in ten minutes". Use after for an order of events: "After ten minutes, the build finished."

By or until? For or during?

These two pairs cause many mistakes at work. Compare them.

by = at the latest. One action happens before a deadline.

Please send the report by Friday.

until = up to that time. The action continues, then stops.

The office is open until six.

for + a length of time. It answers "how long?"

I worked on the bug for two hours.

during + an event or a period. It answers "when?"

My laptop crashed during the meeting.

Please finish the review until Friday.

I waited during two hours.

Please finish the review by Friday.

I waited for two hours.

For since and for with the present perfect, see The perfect tenses.

In, on and at for place

Imagine you are at a train station. Read the three sentences.

  • I'm at the station. (a point on the map)
  • I'm on platform 4. (a surface)
  • I'm in the waiting room. (a space with walls)

The pyramid works again. At is a point, or a place where an activity happens. On is a surface or a line. In is inside a space with sides, like a room, a box, a city or a country.

In, on and at for place
WordUse it forExamples
ata point, an address with a number, a place for an activityat the door, at the bus stop, at 15 Craig Street, at home, at work, at school, at the top of the page
ona surface, a line, a floor, a page, a street nameon the desk, on the wall, on the screen, on page 3, on the second floor, on the left, on King Street, on the river
ininside a space, an area, a city, a countryin the room, in the drawer, in the office, in Osaka, in Japan, in the photo, in the middle

Transport

Transport has its own rule. Big public transport takes on. You can stand up and walk inside it. Small private cars take in.

  • on the bus, on the train, on a plane, on a ship, on a bike
  • in a car, in a taxi, in my friend's van
  • by + transport, with no article: by bus, by train, by car, by plane
  • Walking is different: on foot.

Places in software

Software has its own places. These are the common choices.

Prepositions for software places
WordExamples
inin a file, in a folder, in the repo, in the code, in the logs, in the database, in an app
onon GitHub, on the website, on the screen, on the server, on Linux, on the main branch, on the internet
atat the top of the file, at the end of the function, at this address

For lines of code, you hear both on line 42 and in line 42. Both are fine. For a server, say "The app runs on the server." But say "The server is in the server room."

Arrive, reach and home

  • Arrive in a city or a country: "We arrived in Berlin."
  • Arrive at a building or a point: "We arrived at the airport."
  • Never arrive to. But get to is fine: "I get to the office at nine."
  • Reach takes no preposition: "We reached the hotel."
  • Home takes no to after go and come: "I go home at six." But "I'm at home."

I'm in the bus.

We arrived to Tokyo at noon.

I go to home after work.

She lives at Japan.

I'm on the bus.

We arrived in Tokyo at noon.

I go home after work.

She lives in Japan.

For a street name without a number, on is safe everywhere: "a café on King Street". British speakers also say "in King Street". With a house number, use at: "at 15 King Street".

Movement: to, into, through, across

Now the person moves. Follow the path.

  1. I walked to the station.
  2. I went into the station.
  3. I walked through the station.
  4. I came out of the station.
  5. I walked across the bridge and along the river.

In, on and at show where something is. Movement words show where something goes. The picture shows six common paths.

Common prepositions of movement
WordMeaningExample
totowards a goal, and you arriveI go to the gym on Mondays.
towardsin the direction of, maybe not arrivingThe storm is moving towards the coast.
from ... tothe start and the endWe flew from Osaka to Seoul.
into / out ofoutside to inside, inside to outsideShe went into the meeting room.
onto / offto a surface, away from a surfaceThe cat jumped onto the table.
throughin one side and out the other of a spaceThe train goes through a long tunnel.
acrossfrom one side to the other of a flat area or a lineWe swam across the river.
alongfollowing a lineI run along the river every morning.
overabove, and to the other sideThe ball flew over the wall.
pastgoing by something, not stoppingWalk past the bank and turn left.
up / downto a higher or lower placeHe ran up the stairs.

Through or across?

Use through for a space that is around you: a tunnel, a forest, a crowd, a door. Use across for a flat surface or a line: a road, a field, a river, a bridge. "We walked through the forest. Then we walked across a field."

In or into?

After verbs like go, walk, run, jump and move, use into for the change from outside to inside. After put, in and on are normal. "Put the file in the folder." "Put your bag on the chair."

Movement in software

Data moves too. Software English uses the same movement words.

  • Pass the value to the function.
  • Copy the images into the assets folder.
  • Move the data from staging to production.
  • Merge the feature branch into main.
  • Download the installer from the website. Upload the report to the shared drive.
  • Scroll through the logs. Go through the checklist.
  • Convert the string to a number. Split the text into lines.

The Microsoft Writing Style Guide uses sign in to and sign out of: "Sign in to the app." It says not to write "sign into". You will still see "log in to" and "log into" in many products.

He entered into the office.

She walked across the forest.

The cat jumped in the box from the floor.

He entered the office.

She walked through the forest.

The cat jumped into the box from the floor.

By, with, for, from, of and about

Read this short text. Six small words do six different jobs.

This app was built by a small team. They built it with Rust. It is for data engineers. The team is from Finland. It is one of the fastest tools. Their blog is about performance.

These six prepositions are very common. Each has a few main meanings. The tree shows them. Open a branch to see the meanings.

By or with?

Both can answer "how?". But they are different. By names the person who did it in a passive sentence. With names the tool.

  • The bug was found by a tester. (the person)
  • The bug was found with a debugger. (the tool)
  • You can improve by practising every day. (a method: by + -ing)

The chapter The passive explains by + agent in detail.

For a thing, to for a person's aim

Use for + noun or -ing to say what a thing is for. Use to + verb to say why a person does something.

  • This script is for testing. These tools are for beginners.
  • I came to London to study English. (not "for study")
  • She called to ask about the invoice. (not "for to ask")

Of, from and about

  • of shows a part or a link: "one of my colleagues", "the end of the file", "a list of users".
  • from shows a start or an origin: "a message from HR", "from Monday to Friday", "a friend from work".
  • about shows a topic: "a meeting about the budget". It can also mean roughly: "about 50 people came".

I came here for study English.

I go to work by my car.

This book was written from a famous engineer.

I go to school by foot.

I came here to study English.

I go to work by car. Or: I go to work in my car.

This book was written by a famous engineer.

I go to school on foot.

Verb + preposition

I'm waiting for the build. It depends on the network. Meanwhile, I'm listening to a podcast about Rust.

Many verbs need a fixed preposition before their object. We call this a dependent preposition. Often there is no logic. So learn the verb and its preposition together, as one chunk. Learn "depend on", not just "depend".

Common verbs with their prepositions
PrepositionVerbs
tolisten to, talk to, belong to, reply to, happen to, explain something to someone
forwait for, look for, ask for, pay for, apply for (a job), search for, apologise for
ondepend on, rely on, focus on, work on, comment on, insist on
abouttalk about, think about, worry about, care about, complain about, know about
atlook at, laugh at, point at, stare at
withagree with (a person), deal with, help someone with, cope with
ofconsist of, think of (an idea), hear of, approve of
inbelieve in, succeed in, specialise in, invest in, result in
fromsuffer from, recover from, benefit from, differ from, result from

Verbs with no preposition

Some verbs take their object directly. Learners often add a preposition by mistake. Learn this list well: discuss, contact, call, email, reach, enter, attend, answer, meet, marry, tell, lack.

Let's discuss about the plan.

Please contact with the vendor.

Can you explain me the error?

I'm waiting the build.

It depends of the network.

Let's discuss the plan.

Please contact the vendor.

Can you explain the error to me?

I'm waiting for the build.

It depends on the network.

Notice the noun twin. You discuss the plan, but you have a discussion about the plan. You contact someone, but you are in contact with them.

Verb + object + preposition

Some verbs have an object and then a preposition. Keep the order: verb, object, preposition, second object.

  • Thank someone for something: "Thank you for the review."
  • Remind someone about something: "Remind me about the call."
  • Spend money or time on something: "We spend a lot on cloud costs."
  • Protect something from something: "The firewall protects the network from attacks."
  • Add something to, remove something from: "Add the user to the group. Remove the item from the list."
  • Borrow from, lend to: "I borrowed a charger from Mia. She lent it to me."

A verb + preposition is not the same as a phrasal verb. In "look at the screen", at just links the verb to its object. In "give up", the small word changes the meaning. See Phrasal verbs. After a preposition, a verb takes -ing: "I'm thinking about changing jobs." See Verb patterns: -ing and to.

I'm waiting ___ the build.

for. Wait for something.

The price depends ___ the plan.

on. Depend on something.

Please listen ___ the recording.

to. Listen to something.

Who does this laptop belong ___?

to. Belong to someone.

I agree ___ you.

with. Agree with a person.

Let's discuss ___ the budget.

Nothing! Discuss the budget.

The team consists ___ five engineers.

of. Consist of something.

She is very good ___ testing.

at. Good at a skill.

I'm interested ___ security.

in. Interested in a topic.

Who is responsible ___ the API?

for. Responsible for a job.

Adjective + preposition

I'm good at Python. I'm interested in AI. I'm a little afraid of public speaking. And I'm responsible for the login page.

Adjectives also have dependent prepositions. There is no grammar rule for which one. But there are useful groups. The table groups the most common pairs.

Common adjectives with their prepositions
PrepositionTypical meaningAdjectives
atskillsgood at, bad at, great at, terrible at
aboutfeelings about a topicworried about, excited about, nervous about, sure about, angry about (a thing)
ofsome feelings, knowledge, contentafraid of, proud of, tired of, aware of, capable of, full of
toa link to people or thingssimilar to, kind to, polite to, married to, related to, close to
fora job, a reason, a benefitresponsible for, famous for, ready for, late for, good for (healthy)
ininterest and taking partinterested in, involved in, experienced in
withpeople, or things you use or acceptangry with (a person), happy with, familiar with, compatible with, busy with
fromdifference and distancedifferent from, far from, safe from

One adjective can take different prepositions with different meanings. Look at good.

  • She is good at maths. (a skill)
  • Walking is good for you. (a benefit)
  • He is good with customers. (he handles people well)

Different from is correct everywhere. British English also uses different to. American English also uses different than. If you are not sure, use different from.

Nouns have partners too

Many nouns also take a fixed preposition. These are common at work.

  • the reason for, the need for, demand for
  • a solution to, the answer to, access to
  • a problem with, an issue with
  • an increase in, a drop in, interest in
  • an effect on, an impact on
  • the difference between A and B

I'm interested about data science.

This version is similar with the old one.

She is married with a doctor.

We found the solution of the problem.

Who is responsible of the release?

I'm interested in data science.

This version is similar to the old one.

She is married to a doctor.

We found the solution to the problem.

Who is responsible for the release?

A day in prepositions

Read the story slide by slide. It follows one engineer from morning to evening. Every preposition is in bold. Say each slide aloud.

At home

I wake up at seven. I make coffee in the kitchen. I read the news on my phone.

On the train

I go to work by train. I get on the train at 8.15. I listen to a podcast about AI.

In the office

I arrive at the office at nine. My desk is on the fourth floor. I sit by the window.

At the stand-up

The stand-up is at 9.30. I talk about my tasks. I'm waiting for a review from Kenji.

In the code

I find a bug in the parser. The error is on line 42. I fix it with a small patch.

At lunch

I have lunch with my team. We talk about the weekend. Lunch is from one to two.

Release time

We merge the branch into main. We deploy the fix to production. It must be live by five.

Home again

I walk through the park and across the bridge. Then I go home. I relax for an hour.

Prepositions at the end of questions

Ana: Who are you working with this week?

Ben: With Kenji. We're working on the payment service.

Ana: What is the new service for?

Ben: For refunds. What are you looking at?

Ana: The error logs. I don't know what the problem is caused by.

Look at the end of each question. The preposition stays with its verb or adjective. The question word moves to the front. So the preposition ends up last. Watch it happen in three steps.

  1. Start with a statement: You are talking to Kenji.
  2. Replace the person with a question word: You are talking to who?
  3. Move the question word to the front and add the question order: Who are you talking to?

Here are common questions of this type. Learn them as whole chunks.

  • Where are you from?
  • What is this button for?
  • Who is this email from?
  • What are you thinking about?
  • What does the price depend on?
  • Which team do you work in?
  • What are you interested in?

The same thing happens in other sentences. "This is the team I work with." "There is nothing to worry about." "The issue has been dealt with." The chapter Relative clauses shows more.

The formal way

Very formal English can put the preposition at the front. Then use whom for people, not who.

Normal

Who should I send the invoice to?

Which version is it compatible with?

Formal

To whom should I send the invoice?

With which version is it compatible?

Some people learned a school rule: "Never end a sentence with a preposition." It is not a real rule of English grammar. A preposition at the end is normal in speech and in most writing.

Who are you waiting?

What are you looking?

In which file is the error in?

To who should I write?

Who are you waiting for?

What are you looking at?

Which file is the error in?

Who should I write to? Or: To whom should I write?

The third wrong line has the preposition twice. Use it once, at the front or at the end. More question types are in Questions and negatives.

Expert level: same word, new meaning

At a higher level, the hard part is meaning. One verb can take two or three prepositions. Each one gives a different meaning. Open each pair below.

agree with, agree on, agree to

Agree with a person or an opinion: "I agree with you." Agree on a decision you make together: "We agreed on a date." Agree to a request or terms: "She agreed to the new contract."

look at, look for, look after, look into

Look at means point your eyes: "Look at this graph." Look for means search: "I'm looking for my keys." Look after means take care of: "Who looks after the servers?" Look into means investigate: "I'll look into the bug."

at the end, in the end

At the end of something is the last part of it: "Ask questions at the end of the talk." In the end means finally, after a long time: "In the end, we chose PostgreSQL."

result in, result from

The arrow changes direction. "The bug resulted in data loss." The bug is the cause. "Data loss resulted from the bug." The data loss is the effect.

think of, think about

Think of often means have an idea or an opinion: "What do you think of the design?" Think about means consider for some time: "I'm thinking about the offer."

angry with, angry about

Angry with a person: "She was angry with me." Angry about a situation: "She was angry about the delay."

on the way, in the way

On the way means during the journey: "I'm on the way to the office." In the way means blocking: "The box is in the way. I can't open the door."

Preposition or linking word?

A preposition takes a noun. A linking word takes a full clause with a verb. Many pairs have the same meaning but different grammar.

Preposition + noun, or linker + clause
MeaningPreposition + nounLinker + clause
timeduring the meetingwhile we were meeting
reasonbecause of the rainbecause it was raining
contrastdespite the delayalthough there was a delay

So "despite it was late" is wrong. Say "despite the late hour" or "although it was late". The chapter Linking words shows these pairs in detail.

Prepositions with two or three words

Some prepositions have more than one word. They work as one unit. Common ones are because of, due to, according to, instead of, next to, in front of, in spite of and on behalf of. "I'm writing on behalf of my team." "According to the docs, this method is deprecated." The C1 chapter Advanced articles and prepositions adds formal ones like in terms of and with regard to.

British and American differences

A few prepositions change between British and American English. These are tendencies, not strict rules. British speakers also say "on the team", for example. Both sides understand both forms. Choose one style and keep it.

Small British and American differences
BritishAmerican
at the weekendon the weekend
in the teamon the team
Monday to FridayMonday through Friday
different from or different todifferent from or different than
write to mewrite me, or write to me

Gap-fill tasks in many exams test dependent prepositions, like interested in or depend on. Learn each new word with its preposition from the first day. Write "rely on" in your notebook, not just "rely".

Patterns to remember

Patterns for prepositions
PatternPurposeModelNote
at + clock timeGive an exact timeThe stand-up is at 9.30.Not "in 9.30" or "on 9.30".
on + day or dateName a dayWe release on Friday.A day wins: on Friday morning.
in + month, year or part of the dayName a longer periodThe course starts in April.No preposition before next, last, this or every.
at + point or addressSay where something happensI'm at the office.Use in for cities and countries.
on + surface, page, floor or lineName a surface or a lineThe table is on page 3.On the bus, but in a car.
in + space with sidesSay something is insideThe config is in the root folder.For movement inside, use into.
verb + to, into, through or across + placeDescribe a pathWe walked across the bridge.Go home, not go to home.
by + person or meansSay who did it or howThe bug was found by a tester.By + transport has no article: by train.
for + noun or -ingSay what a thing is forThis script is for testing.For a person's aim, use to + verb.
by + deadline, until + end pointGive a deadline or a durationSend it by Friday.Until means the action continues.
verb + fixed preposition + objectUse common verbs correctlyIt depends on the network.Discuss, contact, enter: no preposition.
adjective + fixed prepositionTalk about skills and feelingsI'm good at SQL.Learn the pair as one chunk.
preposition + -ingPut a verb after a prepositionThank you for helping me.Never preposition + to + verb.
question word ... preposition?Ask about the object of a prepositionWho are you waiting for?Do not drop the preposition.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the correct sentence

Which sentence is correct?

  • The meeting is in Monday.
  • The meeting is on Monday.
  • The meeting is at Monday.

Days take on.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I'll see you on next week.
  • I'll see you in next week.
  • I'll see you next week.

Next, last, this and every take no preposition.

Which sentence is correct?

  • We arrived to Tokyo at noon.
  • We arrived in Tokyo at noon.
  • We arrived at Tokyo in noon.

Arrive in a city. Clock times and noon take at.

Which sentence is correct?

  • Let's discuss about the budget.
  • Let's discuss on the budget.
  • Let's discuss the budget.

Discuss takes its object directly, with no preposition.

Which sentence is correct?

  • Please send the report until Friday.
  • Please send the report by Friday.
  • Please send the report during Friday.

A deadline for one action takes by.

Which question is correct?

  • Who are you waiting?
  • For who are you waiting for?
  • Who are you waiting for?

Wait needs for. Use the preposition once, at the end.

Fill the gap

The train leaves ? 7.45.

My birthday is ? 12 May.

I started this job ? 2023.

I go to work ? bus.

The build will finish ? ten minutes.

She is very good ? data analysis.

He is interested ? machine learning.

I'm responsible ? the login page.

This laptop is similar ? my old one.

Copy the images ? the assets folder.

The firewall protects the network ? attacks.

What is this button ??

Think and write

  1. Find and fix three mistakes. "I go to home at six. I arrive to the station in 6.20."
    Answer

    I go home at six. I arrive at the station at 6.20. Go home has no to. A station is a point, so arrive at. Clock times take at.

  2. Choose through or across. (a) We drove ___ a long tunnel. (b) She swam ___ the lake. (c) The data flows ___ three services.
    Answer

    (a) through, because a tunnel is around you. (b) across, from one side to the other. (c) through, because the data goes in and out of each service.

  3. Make a question with the preposition at the end. Ask about the bold words. (a) She is talking to the client. (b) This tool is for load testing. (c) The email is from HR.
    Answer

    (a) Who is she talking to? (b) What is this tool for? (c) Who is the email from?

  4. Explain the difference. "The bug was fixed by Ana." "The bug was fixed with a patch."
    Answer

    By names the person who fixed it. With names the tool or the thing she used.

  5. Make these sentences formal. Put the preposition first. (a) Who should I address the letter to? (b) Which database is this driver compatible with?
    Answer

    (a) To whom should I address the letter? (b) With which database is this driver compatible?

  6. Fill each gap with with, on or to. "I agree ___ you. We agreed ___ a launch date. The client agreed ___ our price."
    Answer

    with, on, to. Agree with a person. Agree on a decision. Agree to a request or terms.

  7. Correct the sentence twice: once with a preposition, once with a linking word. "Despite it was raining, we walked to the office."
    Answer

    Despite the rain, we walked to the office. Although it was raining, we walked to the office. Despite takes a noun. Although takes a clause.

  8. Write five sentences about your working day. Use at, on, in, by and for at least once each.
    Model answer

    I start work at nine. On Mondays I work from home. My team is in Singapore. I send my weekly report by Friday noon. I spend about an hour on code reviews every day.

Key takeaways

  • A preposition always has a partner: a noun, an object pronoun or a verb with -ing.
  • Use the pyramid. At is a point. On is a day, a surface or a line. In is a long period or a space with sides.
  • Next, last, this, every, today and tomorrow take no preposition.
  • Into, through, across and along describe a path, not a position. Go home has no to.
  • By names the person or the means. With names the tool. By also gives a deadline.
  • Learn verbs, adjectives and nouns with their fixed prepositions, as one chunk.
  • Discuss, contact, enter, reach and attend take no preposition.
  • In questions, the preposition goes to the end: "What is it for?" Never drop it.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Prepositions of time: at, in, on. Clock times, days, longer periods, at night and the weekend.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Prepositions of place: in, on, at. Spaces, surfaces, lines, transport and addresses.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Adjectives and prepositions. Groups of adjectives with at, about, of, to, for, in and with.
  • Purdue OWL: Prepositions. Time, place and verbs that need a preposition before their object.
  • Microsoft Writing Style Guide: sign in, sign out. Why the guide writes sign in to and avoids sign into.

Questions and negatives

At work you ask questions all day. You also say "no", "not yet" and "I don't think so" all day. One small machine builds all of these forms. Learn the machine once, and you can use it in every tense.

  • Make yes or no questions and wh- questions in any tense.
  • Tell subject questions from object questions: "Who called you?" and "Who did you call?"
  • Make negatives with not, never and no, and give short answers.
  • Use question tags and polite indirect questions.
  • Agree and disagree with so do I, neither do I, me too and me neither.

Yes or no questions: the helper moves

Look at each pair. What changes?

  • The build is green. → Is the build green?
  • You can join the call. → Can you join the call?
  • She has finished the review. → Has she finished the review?
  • You use Docker. → Do you use Docker?

In the first three pairs, one small verb jumps in front of the subject. This small verb is a helper verb. Grammar books call it an auxiliary. In the last pair, there is no helper verb. So English adds one: do.

So the rule has two steps.

  1. Find the first helper verb: be, have, will, can, should and the others. Move it in front of the subject.
  2. No helper verb? Add do, does or did in front. The main verb goes back to its base form.
The same machine in every tense
TenseStatementQuestion
beThe API is slow.Is the API slow?
present simpleShe works remotely.Does she work remotely?
past simpleThe deploy failed.Did the deploy fail?
present continuousThey are testing it.Are they testing it?
present perfectYou have pushed the fix.Have you pushed the fix?
willIt will rain.Will it rain?
modal verbWe should restart it.Should we restart it?
there isThere is a test for this.Is there a test for this?

Look at does and did. They carry the -s and the past. So the main verb has no -s and no -ed: "Does she work?" and "Did it fail?"

Does she works remotely?

Did the deploy failed?

You have pushed the fix?

Do you can help me?

Does the API be slow?

Does she work remotely?

Did the deploy fail?

Have you pushed the fix?

Can you help me?

Is the API slow?

The third wrong line can work in speech. Your voice goes up at the end, and it shows surprise. But it is not a normal question. In writing, move the helper verb.

Have as a main verb usually takes do: "Do you have a minute?" British English also says "Have you got a minute?" Both are correct. "Have you a minute?" sounds old.

Wh- questions

Mia: Where do you work?

Raj: At a fintech company in Osaka.

Mia: What do you do there?

Raj: I build the payment API.

Mia: How long have you worked there?

Raj: For about two years.

A wh- question asks for information, not yes or no. Take a yes or no question. Put a question word in front. That is all.

Question word + Auxiliary + Subject + Verb. Remember it as QASV.

  • Where + do + you + work?
  • Why + did + the test + fail?
  • When + will + the release + be ready?
  • How long + have + you + worked there?
Question words
WordAsks aboutExample
whata thing or an actionWhat does this function return?
whicha choice from a small, known groupWhich branch are you on?
whoa personWho did you ask?
whosethe ownerWhose laptop is this?
wherea placeWhere is the config file?
whena timeWhen does the sprint end?
whya reasonWhy is the page so slow?
howa way or a stateHow do I reset my password?
how longa length of timeHow long does the build take?
how oftena frequencyHow often do you deploy?
how much / how manyan amount (uncountable / countable)How much memory does it use? How many users do we have?
what timea clock timeWhat time does the meeting start?
what kind ofa typeWhat kind of database do you use?

What or which?

Use which when the choices are few and known. Use what when the choices are open. "Which option do you want, A or B?" "What do you want for lunch?"

What is it like?

"What is the new office like?" asks for a description. The answer is not "I like it". The answer is "It's big and bright." Compare: "What does the logo look like?" asks only about how it looks.

Where you work?

What means "idempotent"?

Why you didn't come?

How much users do we have?

Where do you work?

What does "idempotent" mean?

Why didn't you come?

How many users do we have?

Subject questions: who called you?

Read the two questions. They look similar. But they ask for opposite people.

Who called you?

Someone called you. I want to know that person. Who is the subject.

Who called you? Kenji called me.

Who did you call?

You called someone. I want to know that person. You is the subject.

Who did you call? I called Kenji.

In the first question, who is the subject. It takes the subject's place. So the word order stays like a statement. There is no do, does or did. This is a subject question.

In the second question, who is the object. So we need the normal question machine: did + you + call. This is an object question.

Subject questions and object questions
StatementAsk about the subjectAsk about the object
Ana broke the build.Who broke the build?What did Ana break?
The cache causes the delay.What causes the delay?What does the cache cause?
Three tests failed.How many tests failed?(no object)
Something happened.What happened?(no object)

Subject questions can also start with which + noun, whose + noun or how many + noun. "Which test failed?" "Whose code caused this?" "How many people came?" The question word and its noun are the subject.

Who did break the build?

What did happen yesterday?

Which test did fail?

Who does know the password?

Who broke the build?

What happened yesterday?

Which test failed?

Who knows the password?

"What did happen?" is possible with heavy stress on did. It shows strong emphasis, like "Tell me what really happened!" This is rare. For normal questions, leave out did.

A subject question in the present simple uses the -s form: "Who knows the answer?" Treat who and what like he or it.

Question words with prepositions

Many verbs and adjectives have a fixed preposition: wait for, talk to, interested in. In a question, the preposition usually goes to the end.

  • You are waiting for someone. → Who are you waiting for?
  • The meeting is about something. → What is the meeting about?
  • She comes from somewhere. → Where does she come from?
  • This tool is for something. → What is this tool for?

Very formal English moves the preposition to the front with whom or which: "To whom should I address the letter?" In daily speech and at work, the end position is normal. The chapter Prepositions explains this in more detail.

Short replies keep the preposition too. "I'm going to the shop." "What for?" "I'm meeting a client." "Who with?" These short forms are informal but very common.

Who are you talking?

What are you interested?

About what is the meeting about?

Who are you talking to?

What are you interested in?

What is the meeting about?

Negative forms

Now say "no" to the same sentences. Watch where not goes.

  • The build is green. → The build is not green. → The build isn't green.
  • You can join. → You cannot join. → You can't join.
  • You use Docker. → You do not use Docker. → You don't use Docker.

The machine works again. Put not after the first helper verb. No helper verb? Add do not, does not or did not. Then use the base form. In speech and most emails, we use the short form with n't. This short form is a contraction.

Common negative contractions
Full formShort formExample
is not, are notisn't, aren'tThe tests aren't ready.
am notI'm notI'm not sure.
do not, does not, did notdon't, doesn't, didn'tIt doesn't compile.
have not, has nothaven't, hasn'tShe hasn't replied yet.
will notwon'tIt won't take long.
cannotcan'tI can't access the server.
should not, must notshouldn't, mustn'tYou mustn't share your token.

There is no short form "amn't" in standard English. Say "I'm not". Note also that cannot is one word.

Other negative words

Not is the most common negative word. But there are others. Each one already contains "not".

  • never = not ever: "I never work on Sundays."
  • no + noun = not any: "There are no errors." = "There aren't any errors."
  • nobody, nothing, nowhere: "Nothing changed." "Nobody replied."
  • none = not one: "None of the tests failed."

Standard English uses one negative word in a clause. Two negatives make the sentence wrong, or they cancel each other.

I don't know nothing about it.

He doesn't never test his code.

I no like long meetings.

She not works here.

I don't know anything about it. Or: I know nothing about it.

He never tests his code.

I don't like long meetings.

She doesn't work here.

No or not?

No goes before a noun. Not goes with a verb, an adjective, an adverb, a or any.

  • No problem. / It's not a problem.
  • There's no time. / There isn't any time.
  • It's not ready. (not "It's no ready")

Three special negatives

  • Negative orders use don't + base form, even with be: "Don't push to main." "Don't be late." Never "Not be late."
  • Negative infinitive: put not before to. "Try not to break the build." "He asked me not to call." You will also hear "to not" in speech, but "not to" is the safe form.
  • I don't think: with think, believe, expect and suppose, English moves the "not" to the first verb. "I don't think it will rain" is more natural than "I think it won't rain." Both are correct.

"Ain't" is very informal and not standard. You hear it in films and songs. Do not use it at work or in exams. Say "isn't", "aren't", "hasn't" or "haven't".

Short answers

Lead: Is the hotfix ready?

Dev: Yes, it is.

Lead: Did QA test it?

Dev: No, they didn't. But they will test it this afternoon.

Lead: Can we release today?

Dev: I think so.

A plain "Yes" or "No" can sound short or rude. A short answer is more polite. It has three parts: yes or no, a subject pronoun and the helper verb from the question.

Short answers repeat the helper verb
QuestionYesNo
Do you use Linux?Yes, I do.No, I don't.
Does it work?Yes, it does.No, it doesn't.
Are you busy?Yes, I am.No, I'm not.
Has she replied?Yes, she has.No, she hasn't.
Can you hear me?Yes, I can.No, I can't.
Will it be ready?Yes, it will.No, it won't.

One detail: positive short answers never use a contraction. Say "Yes, I am" and "Yes, it is". Never say "Yes, I'm" or "Yes, it's". Negative short answers usually use one.

So and not

Sometimes you are not sure. Then use so and not after verbs like think, hope, guess and be afraid.

  • "Will the server be back soon?" "I think so." / "I don't think so."
  • "Will it rain at the picnic?" "I hope not."
  • "Is there any coffee left?" "I'm afraid not." (polite "no")

Do not say "I think yes" or "I don't think". They are not natural answers.

Answering a negative question

A negative question has not in it: "Don't you drink coffee?" How do you answer? In English, the answer is about the fact. It is not about the question.

  • You drink coffee: "Yes, I do." (yes = positive fact)
  • You don't drink coffee: "No, I don't." (no = negative fact)

Some languages work the other way. In Japanese and Korean, for example, "yes" can mean "your sentence is right". English does not work like that. Always add the short answer, so the meaning is clear.

"Didn't you get my email?" "Yes, I didn't." This mixes two systems. Say "No, I didn't" if you did not get it. Say "Yes, I did" if you got it.

Question tags

Sara: The demo is at three, isn't it?

Tom: Yes, it is. You've tested the new login, haven't you?

Sara: I have. It doesn't break on mobile, does it?

Tom: No, it doesn't. Let's do a last check, shall we?

A question tag is a mini question at the end of a statement. It checks a fact, or it asks the listener to agree. Tags are much more common in speech than in writing.

Make the tag with the same machine. Take the helper verb from the statement. Add a pronoun for the subject. Then flip it: a positive statement takes a negative tag. A negative statement takes a positive tag.

How to build a question tag
StatementHelper verbTag
The demo is at three,isisn't it?
You've tested it,havehaven't you?
She works remotely,(none, add does)doesn't she?
They fixed it,(none, add did)didn't they?
It doesn't break,doesdoes it?
We can't leave yet,cancan we?

Your voice changes the meaning

The tag can go up or go down. The picture shows both.

Special tags

  • I am → aren't I? "I'm on the call list, aren't I?"
  • Let's → shall we? "Let's start, shall we?"
  • An order → will you? or could you? "Close the door, will you?" This can sound direct, so be careful.
  • There is → isn't there? "There's a meeting today, isn't there?"
  • This and that → it. "That was easy, wasn't it?"
  • Nobody, somebody, everyone → they. "Everyone is here, aren't they?"
  • Never, nobody, nothing make the statement negative, so the tag is positive. "You never use tabs, do you?" "Nothing broke, did it?"

She works here, isn't it?

You never lose your keys, don't you?

I'm late, amn't I?

They fixed it, didn't it?

She works here, doesn't she?

You never lose your keys, do you?

I'm late, aren't I?

They fixed it, didn't they?

Some languages have one fixed tag for every sentence. English does not, except in informal speech. There, many people just say "right?": "You're coming tomorrow, right?" This is fine in chat. In an exam, show the full tag.

Indirect questions for politeness

A direct question can sound sudden with a stranger, a client or your boss. An indirect question sounds softer. It puts the question inside a polite opening. Swipe through the slides. Each one is a little more polite.

Direct

Where is the meeting room?

Fine with a friend or a close colleague.

Do you know ...?

Do you know where the meeting room is?

Friendly and polite. Good for most people at work.

Can you tell me ...?

Can you tell me where the meeting room is?

Polite. Good with a receptionist or a stranger.

Could you tell me ...?

Could you tell me where the meeting room is?

More polite. Could is softer than can.

Would you mind telling me ...?

Would you mind telling me where the meeting room is?

Very polite. Note the -ing after mind.

Now look at the word order. After the polite opening, the question becomes a statement. The helper verb does not move. There is no do, does or did.

Direct question

Where is the meeting room?

What time does the train leave?

Why did the job fail?

Indirect question

Do you know where the meeting room is?

Can you tell me what time the train leaves?

Do you know why the job failed?

For a yes or no question, add if or whether. Whether is a little more formal.

  • Is the build green? → Do you know if the build is green?
  • Did the client sign? → Could you check whether the client signed?

Polite openings

  • Do you know ...? / Do you happen to know ...?
  • Can you tell me ...? / Could you tell me ...?
  • Could you let me know ...? (common in emails)
  • I was wondering ... / I wonder ...
  • I'd like to know ... / Do you have any idea ...?

Check the end of the sentence. If the opening is a question, use a question mark: "Do you know where it is?" If the opening is a statement, use a full stop: "I wonder where it is."

Could you tell me where is the station?

Do you know what time does it start?

I wonder if is it ready.

Can you tell me did the client sign?

Could you tell me where the station is?

Do you know what time it starts?

I wonder if it is ready.

Can you tell me if the client signed?

Indirect questions are also common in technical writing, with no polite opening. "Check whether the service is running." "We don't know why the job fails." The same word order applies. Reported questions use it too: "She asked where I worked." See Reported speech.

So do I, neither do I

Ana: I love Rust.

Ben: So do I.

Ana: I can't stand long meetings.

Ben: Neither can I.

Ana: I'm a bit tired today.

Ben: Really? I'm not.

To agree with a positive sentence, use so + helper verb + subject. To agree with a negative sentence, use neither + helper verb + subject. The helper verb comes before the subject, like in a question. Take the helper verb from the first sentence. No helper verb? Use do, does or did.

Agreeing with so and neither
First speakerAgree (same for me)Informal
I love Rust.So do I.Me too.
I'm tired.So am I.Me too.
I went to the meetup.So did I.Me too.
I can't swim.Neither can I.Me neither.
I haven't finished.Neither have I. Or: Nor have I.Me neither.
I don't like tabs.Neither do I.Me neither.

You can also agree with a normal sentence: "I do too." "I don't either." These are neutral and very common.

Disagreeing

To disagree, give the opposite short form. Stress the subject.

  • "I love Rust." "Oh, I don't."
  • "I can't swim." "Really? I can."
  • "I'm not hungry." "I am."

"I love Rust." "So I do."

"I can't swim." "Neither I can."

"I don't like tabs." "Me too."

"I didn't go." "Neither didn't I."

"I'm tired." "So do I."

"I love Rust." "So do I."

"I can't swim." "Neither can I."

"I don't like tabs." "Me neither."

"I didn't go." "Neither did I."

"I'm tired." "So am I."

The last wrong line uses the wrong helper verb. "I'm tired" has am, so the answer is "So am I". The third wrong line is common. "Me too" agrees with a positive sentence only. You may hear "me either" in American speech. "Me neither" is the safe choice.

Expert level: questions that do more

Questions are not only for information. At a higher level, questions also suggest, complain, show surprise and soften requests. Open each one.

Negative questions for surprise or annoyance

"Don't you like sushi?" means "I expected you to like it." "Isn't it ready yet?" shows that the speaker is a little annoyed. "Haven't we met before?" means "I think we have met."

Negative questions for polite suggestions

"Why don't we take a break?" is a suggestion, not a real question about a reason. "Wouldn't it be better to cache the result?" is a soft way to say "I think we should cache it." Use this in code review to sound less direct.

Echo questions

You repeat part of what you heard, with a rising voice. "I moved to Berlin." "You moved where?" or "To Berlin?" It shows surprise, or that you did not hear well. The word order stays like a statement.

Same-way tags

A positive statement with a positive tag: "So you're the new engineer, are you?" It is not a real question. It shows interest or surprise at new information. The voice usually goes up. Use it carefully, because it can sound unfriendly.

So I do! So it is!

"So do I" means "me too". But "So I do!" or "So it is!" has a different meaning. It means "You're right, I see that now." "You've got paint on your shirt." "Oh, so I have!" The subject comes before the helper verb.

Rhetorical questions

A rhetorical question expects no answer. "Who doesn't want faster builds?" means "Everyone wants faster builds." It is good in talks and blog posts. In formal essays, use few of them.

Negative adverbs at the front

In formal writing, words like never, rarely and not only can start a sentence. Then the question order follows: "Never have I seen such a fast database." The C1 chapter Inversion and emphasis covers this.

In speaking tests, you often need to ask the examiner to repeat or explain. Use a polite indirect question: "Could you say that again, please?" "Could you explain what you mean by 'heritage'?" In writing tasks, question tags and "me too" are too informal. Use full sentences.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for questions and negatives
PatternPurposeModelNote
Helper verb + subject + verb?Ask a yes or no questionHave you pushed the fix?Move the first helper verb in front of the subject.
Do, does or did + subject + base verb?Ask when there is no helper verbDid the deploy fail?No -s and no -ed on the main verb.
Question word + helper + subject + verb?Ask for informationWhy did the test fail?Remember QASV.
Who or what + verb + object?Ask about the subjectWho broke the build?No do, does or did.
Question word ... preposition?Ask about the object of a prepositionWhat is this tool for?Keep the preposition at the end.
Subject + helper + not + verbMake a negativeIt doesn't compile.One negative word per clause.
No + nounSay there is zero of somethingThere are no errors.No before nouns, not before verbs and adjectives.
Don't + base verbGive a negative orderDon't be late.Never "Not be late".
Yes or no + pronoun + helperGive a short answerYes, it is. No, it isn't.No contraction in positive short answers.
I think so. I hope not.Answer when you are not sure"Will it work?" "I think so."Not "I think yes".
Statement, flipped helper + pronoun?Check a fact or invite agreementYou've tested it, haven't you?Falling voice: sure. Rising voice: asking.
Polite opening + question word + subject + verbAsk politelyCould you tell me where the room is?Statement order after the opening.
Polite opening + if or whether + clauseAsk a yes or no question politelyDo you know if the build is green?No do, does or did after if.
So or neither + helper + subjectSay "the same for me""I can't swim." "Neither can I."Match the helper verb of the first sentence.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the correct sentence

Which question is correct?

  • Does she works on Fridays?
  • Does she work on Fridays?
  • Do she work on Fridays?

She takes does. After does, use the base verb with no -s.

Which question asks for the person who sent the message?

  • Who sent you the message?
  • Who did you send the message?
  • Who did send you the message?

Who is the subject here, so there is no did.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I don't know nothing about Kafka.
  • I no know anything about Kafka.
  • I don't know anything about Kafka.

Use one negative word. Don't + anything is correct.

Choose the correct tag. "She works in sales, ___?"

  • isn't she
  • doesn't she
  • don't she

Works has no helper verb, so the tag uses does. Positive statement, negative tag.

Which indirect question is correct?

  • Could you tell me where is the lift?
  • Could you tell me where the lift is?
  • Could you tell me where does the lift is?

After the polite opening, use statement order: subject, then verb.

"I'm not ready yet." You agree. What do you say?

  • So am I.
  • Neither do I.
  • Neither am I.

The sentence is negative, so use neither. The helper verb is am.

Fill the gap

? you watch the keynote yesterday?

? there a test for this function?

What ? this error mean?

How ? users signed up last week?

"Can you hear me?" "Yes, I ?."

"Is it ready?" "Yes, it ?."

The demo went well, ??

Let's take a break, ??

Do you know ? the client replied?

"I went to the meetup." "So ? I."

Think and write

  1. Make yes or no questions. (a) The tests are running. (b) She speaks Korean. (c) They fixed the bug. (d) We should update the docs.
    Answer

    (a) Are the tests running? (b) Does she speak Korean? (c) Did they fix the bug? (d) Should we update the docs?

  2. Ask two questions about this sentence: one about the subject, one about the object. "The new intern found the bug."
    Answer

    Who found the bug? What did the new intern find?

  3. Make each sentence negative. (a) I have finished. (b) He likes meetings. (c) Be late. (d) Try to forget.
    Answer

    (a) I haven't finished. (b) He doesn't like meetings. (c) Don't be late. (d) Try not to forget.

  4. "Didn't you get the invite?" Give two answers: one if you got it, one if you did not.
    Answer

    If you got it: "Yes, I did." If you did not: "No, I didn't." The answer is about the fact.
