  5. Make these direct questions polite. Use the opening in brackets. (a) What time does the office close? (Could you tell me) (b) Is the API free? (Do you know) (c) Why did the payment fail? (I'd like to know)
    Answer

    (a) Could you tell me what time the office closes? (b) Do you know if the API is free? (c) I'd like to know why the payment failed. The last one ends with a full stop, because the opening is a statement.

  6. Add tags. (a) Nobody called, ___? (b) I'm on the list, ___? (c) You never work late, ___? (d) That was a good talk, ___?
    Answer

    (a) did they? (b) aren't I? (c) do you? (d) wasn't it? Nobody and never make the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

  7. Agree, then disagree. (a) "I can't read this font." (b) "I prefer tea." (c) "I've never used Go."
    Answer

    (a) Neither can I. / Oh, I can. (b) So do I. / Oh, I don't. (c) Neither have I. / Really? I have.

  8. Expert: rewrite this code review comment as a softer negative question. "You should use a constant here."
    Model answer

    Wouldn't it be clearer to use a constant here? Or: Shouldn't this be a constant? Both suggest the change without sounding like an order.

Key takeaways

  • Questions: move the first helper verb in front of the subject. No helper verb? Add do, does or did.
  • Wh- questions follow QASV: question word, auxiliary, subject, verb.
  • When who or what is the subject, there is no do, does or did: "Who broke the build?"
  • Negatives: not goes after the first helper verb. Use only one negative word in a clause.
  • Short answers repeat the helper verb: "Yes, I do." Never "Yes, I'm".
  • Question tags flip the helper verb. A falling voice checks, a rising voice asks.
  • Indirect questions use statement order: "Could you tell me where the room is?"
  • So do I agrees with a positive sentence. Neither do I agrees with a negative one.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Questions and negatives. Helper verbs, do in questions and negatives, wh- questions and indirect questions.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Question forms. Word order in questions and subject questions with who and what.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Question tags. How to form tags, aren't I, negative words and intonation.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Reported speech: questions. Statement word order after the question word, and if or whether.
  • Espresso English: So, neither, too: how to agree in English. So do I, neither can I and matching the helper verb.

Linking words

Linking words show how two ideas connect: addition, contrast, reason, result, time, condition or example. You already know 30 of them from your connector table. This chapter goes deeper. It shows the small differences, the grammar after each word and how to choose the right one.

  • Choose a linker by its meaning, its grammar and its level of formality.
  • Tell clause linkers from noun linkers: although or despite, because or because of.
  • Use time and condition linkers with the right tense: "When it finishes, I'll call you."
  • Give examples with for example, such as, e.g. and i.e.
  • Punctuate linkers correctly and avoid comma splices, fragments and linker overload.

Why linkers matter

Read three versions of one short report. Which one is easiest to follow?

The test failed. I checked the logs. The database was down. I restarted it. The test passed. The root cause is still unclear.

Firstly, the test failed. Moreover, I checked the logs. Furthermore, the database was down. Therefore, I restarted it. Consequently, the test passed. Nevertheless, the root cause is still unclear.

The test failed, so I checked the logs. The database was down. After I restarted it, the test passed. However, the root cause is still unclear.

The first version is a list of facts. You must guess the links. The second version has a linker on every sentence. Most of them are wrong or heavy. Moreover adds a strong new point, but checking logs is not a new point. The third version uses four linkers, and each one shows a real link.

A linker is a signal for the reader. It says "a reason comes next" or "now the opposite". Use a linker when the link is not obvious. Do not use one as decoration.

The IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023) say this too. At band 9, linking is so natural that the reader rarely notices it. At band 6, linking can be "mechanical" because of misuse, overuse or missing linkers. So more linkers do not mean a higher score.

Your favourite chapter, The 15 sentence patterns, has the full table of 30 connectors. It also has four grammar groups and four punctuation rules. This chapter builds on that table. Keep it open as you read.

Three kinds of linker: what comes after?

Look at these four sentences. They all show contrast. But the grammar after the linker is different each time.

  • The app is fast, but it uses a lot of memory.
  • Although the app is fast, it uses a lot of memory.
  • Despite its speed, the app uses a lot of memory.
  • The app is fast. However, it uses a lot of memory.

After but and although comes a clause: "it uses", "the app is". After despite comes a noun: "its speed". However starts a new sentence. So every linker belongs to one grammar type. This is the most useful fact in this chapter.

What comes after the linker
TypeWhat followsExamplesShape
Joinera clause, in the same sentenceand, but, or, so, yetClause, but clause.
Clause linkera clausebecause, although, even though, while, when, if, unlessAlthough clause, clause.
Noun linkera noun, a pronoun or -ingbecause of, due to, despite, in spite of, during, such asDespite noun, clause.
Sentence linkera full new sentencehowever, therefore, moreover, in addition, for exampleClause. However, clause.

Many meanings have one linker of each type. Learn them as families. Then you can change the grammar and keep the meaning.

Families: one meaning, four grammar types
MeaningJoiner+ clause+ nounNew sentence
contrastbut, yetalthough, even thoughdespite, in spite ofHowever, Nevertheless,
reason(for, formal)because, since, asbecause of, due to(The reason is that ...)
resultso(so that, for purpose)(hence + noun, formal)Therefore, As a result,
additionand(as well as + -ing)as well as, in addition toIn addition, Moreover,
timeand thenwhile, when, afterduring, afterMeanwhile, After that,

Despite it was raining, we went out.

Because of the server was down, we waited.

During we were in the meeting, the build failed.

Although it was raining, we went out. Or: Despite the rain, we went out.

Because the server was down, we waited. Or: Because of the outage, we waited.

While we were in the meeting, the build failed. Or: During the meeting, the build failed.

Before you use a linker, ask: what comes after it? A sentence with a verb, a noun, or a full new sentence? The answer tells you which linker fits.

And, but, or, so: the small joiners

These four words are the most common linkers in English. Your table gives the basics. Here are the details that learners miss.

And: one subject, no comma

  • I checked the logs, and Kenji restarted the server. (two subjects: comma)
  • I checked the logs and found the error. (one subject, two verbs: no comma)

When both verbs share one subject, do not add a comma before and. The second part is not a full clause.

In a list, put and before the last item: "Python, Rust and Go". Some style guides add a comma before and: "Python, Rust, and Go". This is called the serial comma. Both styles are correct. Choose one and keep it.

But and yet

Yet means "but, and this is surprising". It is a little more formal. "The fix was tiny, yet it saved the release." Do not confuse it with yet in questions: "Has she replied yet?"

Or in negatives

After a negative verb, use or, not and, for "not this, not that". "I don't drink tea or coffee." With no negative verb, use neither ... nor: "I drink neither tea nor coffee." Or can also give a warning: "Save your work, or you will lose it."

So and so that

So shows a result. So that shows a purpose. It often has can, could or will after it. Purpose has no comma.

  • The tests were slow, so we added a cache. (result)
  • We added a cache so that the tests run faster. (purpose)

The seven joiners

English has seven joiners. Some teachers remember them as FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. For as a joiner means "because". It sounds old and formal: "He left early, for he was tired." You will see it in books, but you do not need to use it.

The site was slow, we added a cache.

I checked the logs, and found the error.

I don't like tea and coffee.

The site was slow, so we added a cache.

I checked the logs and found the error.

I don't like tea or coffee.

The first wrong line is a comma splice. A comma alone cannot join two full sentences. Add a joiner, or use a full stop.

Can you start a sentence with And or But? Yes. Many modern style guides accept it, and it is common in emails and blogs. In a formal exam essay, a sentence linker like However or In addition usually sounds better.

Reason and result

Lead: Why was the release late?

Dev: Because the payment tests failed.

Lead: Why did they fail?

Dev: Because of a timeout in the test database. So we moved the tests to a faster machine.

Because or because of?

Because takes a clause. Because of takes a noun. Due to means the same as because of, but it is more formal.

  • The release was late because the tests failed. (clause)
  • The release was late because of the failed tests. (noun)
  • The delay was due to a timeout. (formal, noun)

Since and as

Since and as also give reasons. They often start the sentence, and the reason is already known. "Since you are here, can you review my PR?" But both words have other meanings. Since also means "from that time". As also means "while" or "in the same way". So because is the clearest choice. Use it when you are not sure.

Because alone: speech or writing?

In speech, "Because the tests failed." is a normal answer to "Why?" In writing, it is a fragment. A clause with because cannot stand alone. Join it to a main clause.

Result linkers by formality

Result linkers from informal to formal
LinkerLevelModel
that's whyspokenThe server was down. That's why the site was slow.
soneutralThe server was down, so the site was slow.
as a resultneutral to formalThe server was down. As a result, the site was slow.
thereforeformal, logicalThe input is invalid. Therefore, the function returns an error.
consequentlyformalThe road was closed. Consequently, traffic moved elsewhere.
thus, hencevery formalThe model overfits. Hence the poor test score.

Therefore can also move inside the sentence: "The result is therefore invalid." This sounds smooth in reports. Hence is often followed by a noun only: "hence the delay".

Because the price rose, so customers left.

Because of the server was down, we waited.

Due to it was late, we left.

Because the price rose, customers left. Or: The price rose, so customers left.

Because the server was down, we waited.

Because it was late, we left. Or: Due to the late hour, we left.

For "so ... that" and "such ... that", as in "The file was so large that Git rejected it", see Adjectives and adverbs.

Contrast: although, though, even though, however

Contrast has the most linkers. The tree groups them by the grammar after them. Open each branch.

Although, though, even though

  • Although the plan is costly, it may save time. (neutral)
  • Though the plan is costly, it may save time. (the same, a little less formal)
  • Even though I was tired, I finished the test. (stronger: the contrast is surprising)

Though has one extra job. It can go at the end of a sentence, after a comma. This is very common in speech. "The plan is costly. It may save time, though." Here it means "however".

Even though or even if?

These two look alike but mean different things. Even though talks about a fact. Even if talks about a possible situation.

Even though = this is true, but ...

Even though it is raining, I'll walk.

It is raining now.

Even if = this may be true, but it does not change the result

Even if it rains, I'll walk.

Maybe it will rain. Maybe not.

Despite and in spite of

Despite and in spite of take a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form. To add a full clause, use despite the fact that.

  • Despite the rain, we enjoyed the trip.
  • In spite of feeling ill, she gave the talk.
  • Despite the fact that the tests passed, the bug came back.

However: three positions

However can sit in three places. Each place needs its own commas.

  • Start: "The plan is costly. However, it may save time."
  • Middle: "The plan, however, may save time." (formal and smooth)
  • End: "The plan may save time, however." (less common)

The middle position lets you stress the topic first. It is very common in reports and academic writing.

Other contrast linkers

  • Nevertheless and nonetheless: "but still". Formal. "The risk is small. Nevertheless, we will test it."
  • While and whereas: compare two facts side by side. "Python is easy to read, whereas C gives more control."
  • On the other hand: the other side of the same question. Often after "On the one hand".
  • On the contrary: "No, the opposite is true." It corrects a wrong idea. "The test is not slow. On the contrary, it is the fastest one."

Although the app is fast, but it uses a lot of memory.

Despite of the rain, we went out.

The plan is costly, however it may save time.

The test is slow. On the contrary, the build is fast.

Although the app is fast, it uses a lot of memory.

Despite the rain, we went out. Or: In spite of the rain, we went out.

The plan is costly. However, it may save time.

The test is slow. On the other hand, the build is fast.

Adding ideas: also, moreover, as well as

The new tool is free. It also runs on Linux. In addition, it has good docs. Moreover, the community is very active.

Addition linkers say "here is another point". But they differ in strength, formality and position.

Addition linkers
LinkerPosition and grammarModel
alsobefore the main verb, after beIt also runs on Linux. It is also free.
too, as wellat the end, informalIt runs on Linux too.
as well as+ noun or -ingIt runs on Linux as well as macOS.
in additionnew sentence, neutral to formalIn addition, it has good docs.
in addition to+ noun or -ingIn addition to fixing bugs, she writes docs.
moreover, furthermorenew sentence, formal, a stronger pointMoreover, the community is very active.
besides, what's morenew sentence, spoken, often a final reasonBesides, it's free.

Use moreover for a point that makes your argument stronger. It is not just "and". In emails and chat, also is enough. Starting a sentence with Also, is common in speech. In formal writing, In addition, is better.

In addition to fix bugs, she writes docs.

It runs also on Linux.

The tool is cheap. Moreover, it is very expensive to host.

In addition to fixing bugs, she writes docs.

It also runs on Linux.

The tool is cheap. However, it is very expensive to host.

The last wrong line uses an addition linker for a contrast. Always check the meaning first.

Time: when, while, before, after, until

Time linkers put events in order. Read the steps of a release.

  1. Before you merge, run the tests.
  2. When the tests pass, open a pull request.
  3. While the reviewer reads it, update the changelog.
  4. As soon as it is approved, merge it.
  5. After the deploy finishes, check the dashboard.
  6. Watch the error rate until it is stable.

Present tense for the future

Look at step 4: "As soon as it is approved". The meaning is future, but the verb is present. After time linkers like when, before, after, until and as soon as, use a present tense for the future. Put will in the main clause only.

When the build will finish, I will deploy it.

I'll call you as soon as I will land.

When the build finishes, I will deploy it.

I'll call you as soon as I land.

The chapter Talking about the future explains time clauses in more detail.

When or while?

When often goes with a short action or a point in time. While goes with a longer action in progress. "My laptop crashed when I opened the file." "My laptop crashed while I was writing the report." See Past simple and past continuous for more.

Before, after and afterwards

Before and after can take a clause, a noun or an -ing form.

  • After I finished the draft, I checked it. (clause)
  • After lunch, I checked it. (noun)
  • After finishing the draft, I checked it. (-ing)

But after alone cannot start a sentence with no partner. Then use afterwards or after that. "I finished the draft. Afterwards, I checked it."

Until, not until and once

  • Until means "up to that time". The action continues, then stops. "Wait until the tests pass."
  • Not ... until means "only then, not before". "The bug didn't appear until we added more users."
  • Once means "after, and as soon as". "Once the PR is approved, merge it."

For a deadline, use by, not until: "Send it by Friday." See Prepositions.

Sequence words

For a process with many steps, use first, then, next, after that and finally. Finally means "as the last step". In the end means "after a long time or many problems". "In the end, we chose PostgreSQL."

Conditions: if, unless, in case

The job will fail if the disk is full. It will fail unless you clean the cache. Keep a backup in case the disk fails.

If gives a condition. Unless means "if not". It has a positive verb after it, because the "not" is already inside it.

if ... not

If you don't save, you'll lose your work.

unless + positive verb

Unless you save, you'll lose your work.

In case is different. It does not mean "if". It means "because this might happen". You act now, to be safe.

  • Take an umbrella if it rains. (Take it only when it rains.)
  • Take an umbrella in case it rains. (Take it now. Maybe it will rain.)

As long as and provided that mean "only if". "You can work from home as long as you join the stand-up." The chapter Conditionals covers all of these with each conditional type.

Unless you don't save, you'll lose your work.

If it will rain, we'll stay inside.

I'll bring a charger if my battery dies. (meaning: to be safe)

Unless you save, you'll lose your work.

If it rains, we'll stay inside.

I'll bring a charger in case my battery dies.

Examples: for example, such as, e.g.

Read the pair. Both give examples. The grammar is different.

  • Some tools are free. For example, Git costs nothing.
  • Free tools such as Git and Linux are very popular.

For example and for instance are sentence linkers. A full sentence can follow them. Such as is a noun linker. A noun or a short list follows it. Never put a full clause after such as.

Linkers for examples
LinkerWhat followsModel
for example, for instancea full sentence, or a noun in the middleSome languages, for example Rust, have no garbage collector.
such asa noun or a list of nounsWe use cloud services such as storage and queues.
likea noun, informalI like languages like Go.
includingpart of a longer listFive teams, including mine, joined.
especially, in particularthe most important exampleTest everything, especially the payment code.
e.g.short examples, often in bracketsUse a short name (e.g. api or web).
i.e.the exact meaning, said againUse the LTS version (i.e. version 22).

Do not mix up e.g. and i.e.. e.g. means "for example": there are more. i.e. means "that is": this is the only one. Both are common in notes and technical docs. In a formal essay, write the full words.

Many tools are free, such as we can use Git.

For example Git and Linux.

Use a modern browser (i.e. Chrome or Firefox).

Many tools are free. For example, we can use Git.

Free tools include Git and Linux.

Use a modern browser (e.g. Chrome or Firefox).

The second wrong line has no verb. It is a fragment. The third uses i.e., but Chrome and Firefox are only examples. There are other modern browsers.

Punctuation: the expert points

Your connector table already gives the four main rules. Here they are in one line each. Then come five details that even strong writers get wrong.

  • Joiner between two clauses: comma before it. "It is fast, but it is old."
  • Clause linker first: comma after the clause. "If it fails, call me."
  • Clause linker second: usually no comma. "Call me if it fails."
  • Sentence linker: full stop or semicolon before it, comma after it. "It failed. However, we fixed it."

See The 15 sentence patterns for these rules with more examples.

Five expert details

  1. Contrast clauses at the end keep the comma. "City life is fast, whereas rural life is quiet." "I finished, although I was tired." The comma marks the contrast.
  2. However in the middle needs two commas. "The plan, however, is costly." One comma is a mistake.
  3. A semicolon can replace the full stop. "Demand rose; therefore, prices rose." Use it when the two ideas are very close. A comma there is a comma splice.
  4. No comma after a short linker is fine. "Then we deployed." "So what now?" Short words like then, so and yet at the start often have no comma.
  5. However can also mean "in any way". "However you try, it won't compile." Here there is no comma after it. The meaning changes completely.

The plan, however is costly.

Demand rose, therefore prices rose.

Because it was late. We left.

The plan, however, is costly.

Demand rose; therefore, prices rose. Or: Demand rose. Therefore, prices rose.

Because it was late, we left.

Choosing the right linker

Ask three questions, in this order. First: what is the link between the ideas? Second: what comes after the linker? Third: how formal is the text?

The third question: how formal?

Linkers by formality
MeaningChat and speechNeutral emailsFormal reports and essays
additionalso, plus, tooalso, in additionmoreover, furthermore
contrastbut, though (at the end)but, howeverhowever, nevertheless, whereas
reasonbecause, 'causebecause, sincesince, as, due to, owing to
resultso, that's whyso, as a resulttherefore, consequently, thus
examplelikefor example, such asfor instance, such as, e.g. (in brackets)
summaryanyway, so basicallyoverall, in shortin conclusion, to sum up

Do not mix levels in one text. "Moreover, the API is kinda slow" sounds strange. A formal linker needs formal words around it.

Linker overload. Some learners put a linker on every sentence, often the same three: moreover, furthermore, in addition. This makes writing heavy and mechanical. Many sentences need no linker. The order of the sentences shows the link.

Expert level: linking a whole paragraph

Linkers join two ideas. But a good paragraph also links with reference words: this, these, it, such, the problem. This web of links is called cohesion. The IELTS descriptors call this "reference and substitution". Watch a paragraph grow, one step at a time.

Raw notes

Remote work saves travel time. Remote work can feel lonely. Many teams use video calls. Video calls help a little. Companies should allow some office days.

Find the links

Saves time / feels lonely: contrast. Video calls: an example of a fix. Office days: the result, or the conclusion.

Add the contrast

Remote work saves travel time. However, it can feel lonely.

Use reference words

Many teams try to solve this problem with video calls. These help a little.

Add the result

For this reason, companies should allow some office days.

Read it as one

Remote work saves travel time. However, it can feel lonely. Many teams try to solve this problem with video calls, but these only help a little. For this reason, companies should allow some office days.

Count the linkers in the final paragraph. There are three: However, but and For this reason. The other links come from it, this problem and these. That balance is what examiners mean by natural cohesion.

Three expert habits

  • Put the known idea first. Start a sentence with something the reader already knows. End it with the new idea. "This problem" points back. "office days" is new.
  • Use a noun after this. "This causes delays" can be unclear. "This timeout causes delays" is clear.
  • Vary the grammar, not just the word. Do not switch from however to nevertheless to nonetheless. Switch from a sentence linker to although or despite instead.

The chapter Writing sentences and paragraphs covers topic sentences and cohesion. For exam essays, see IELTS Writing.

In IELTS Writing, linkers count in Coherence and Cohesion. Accurate linkers with clear meaning help. Memorised strings like "Moreover, furthermore, in addition" do not. Before the exam, learn two or three linkers for each meaning and use them correctly.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for linking words
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + verb and verbAdd a second action by the same personI checked the logs and found the error.No comma when the subject is shared.
Clause so that + can or willGive a purposeWe added a cache so that pages load faster.Result is so. Purpose is so that, with no comma.
because of or due to + nounGive a reason as a nounThe release was late because of the tests.Because takes a clause. Because of takes a noun.
Despite + noun or -ing, clauseContrast with a nounDespite the rain, we went out.Never "despite of" or "despite it was".
Even though + fact, clauseStrong contrast with a true factEven though it is raining, I'll walk.For a possible situation, use even if.
Clause. Clause, though.Add a soft contrast in speechIt's expensive. It's fast, though.Though at the end means however.
Subject, however, verbContrast in formal writingThe plan, however, is costly.Two commas around however.
Subject also + verbAdd a point in neutral styleIt also runs on Linux.After be: It is also free.
In addition to + noun or -ingAdd a point as a nounIn addition to fixing bugs, she writes docs.Not "in addition to fix".
When or as soon as + present, willOrder future eventsWhen the build finishes, I'll deploy it.No will after the time linker.
Not ... until + time or clauseSay "only then, not before"The bug didn't appear until Monday.For a deadline, use by.
Unless + positive verbSay "if not"Unless you save, you'll lose it.Not "unless you don't".
Clause in case + clauseAct now to be safeKeep a backup in case the disk fails.In case is not if.
Noun such as + noun listGive examples inside the sentenceTools such as Git are free.For a full sentence, use for example.
(e.g. ...) and (i.e. ...)Short examples or the exact meaningUse a short name (e.g. api).e.g. = for example. i.e. = that is.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the correct sentence

Which sentence is correct?

  • Despite it was late, we kept working.
  • Despite the late hour, we kept working.
  • Despite of the late hour, we kept working.

Despite takes a noun, with no of.

Which sentence is correct?

  • Because of the API was slow, users left.
  • Because the API was slow, so users left.
  • Because the API was slow, users left.

Because takes a clause. Use only one linker for one link.

Which sentence is correct?

  • When the tests pass, I'll merge the branch.
  • When the tests will pass, I'll merge the branch.
  • When the tests will pass, I merge the branch.

After when, use the present for the future. Will goes in the main clause.

You are not sure it will rain. Which sentence fits?

  • Even though it rains, the match will go ahead.
  • Even if it rains, the match will go ahead.
  • Although it rains, the match will go ahead.

Even if is for a possible situation. Even though is for a fact.

Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

  • The design, however is too complex.
  • The design, however, is too complex.
  • The design however, is too complex.

However in the middle needs a comma on each side.

Which sentence uses the linker correctly?

  • Many tools are free, such as you can use Git.
  • Use the stable version (e.g. the only supported one).
  • Tools such as Git and Docker are free.

Such as takes a noun list. The second line needs i.e., because it gives the exact meaning.

Fill the gap

The flight was cancelled ? the storm.

We added logging ? we can find errors faster.

? the tool is old, it still works well.

It's a great laptop. It's heavy, ?.

The tool is fast. ?, it is free.

Don't deploy ? all the tests pass.

Take a power bank ? your battery runs out.

I'll text you as soon as I (arrive).

The bug didn't appear ? we added more users.

I finished the draft. ?, I checked it for errors.

Think and write

  1. Join the ideas in three ways: with but, with although and with however. "The course is cheap. It takes a lot of time."
    Answer

    The course is cheap, but it takes a lot of time. Although the course is cheap, it takes a lot of time. The course is cheap. However, it takes a lot of time.

  2. Rewrite with despite. Then rewrite with because of. (a) Although the network was slow, the upload finished. (b) We stopped because the battery was low.
    Answer

    (a) Despite the slow network, the upload finished. (b) We stopped because of the low battery.

  3. Find and fix three mistakes. "The tests failed, we checked the logs. In addition to check the logs, we restarted the server. Unless the server doesn't start, we will call support."
    Answer

    (1) The tests failed, so we checked the logs. A full stop also works. (2) In addition to checking the logs, we restarted the server. (3) If the server doesn't start, we will call support. Or: Unless the server starts, we will call support.

  4. Explain the difference in meaning. (a) Bring a jacket if it gets cold. (b) Bring a jacket in case it gets cold.
    Answer

    (a) Bring it only when it is cold. (b) Bring it now, because it might get cold later.

  5. Make this email more neutral. It mixes formal linkers with chat style. "Hi Tom! Moreover, the demo was kinda cool. Furthermore, the client liked it. Consequently, let's party!"
    Model answer

    Hi Tom, the demo went really well, and the client liked it. So let's celebrate! The neutral words and, so and really fit the friendly tone.

  6. This paragraph has a linker on every sentence. Remove or change at least two, and add one reference word. "Firstly, our app is slow. Moreover, users complain. Furthermore, the slow app costs money. Therefore, we must fix the slow app."
    Model answer

    Our app is slow, and users complain. This slowness also costs money. Therefore, we must fix it. Moreover was wrong, because complaints are a result, not a new point. This slowness and it replace the repeated words.

  7. Expert: write a short paragraph (four sentences) about a tool you use at work. Use one contrast linker, one example linker and one reference word. Underline them in your notes.
    Model answer

    Our team uses Docker for every service. It makes local setup fast and repeatable. However, it uses a lot of memory on older laptops. For example, a full stack with five containers can need 8 GB, so this is a real problem for new hires. (Linkers: However, For example, so. Reference words: It, this.)

Key takeaways

  • A linker shows a real link: addition, contrast, reason, result, time, condition or example. Never use it as decoration.
  • Check what comes after the linker: a clause (although, because), a noun (despite, because of) or a new sentence (however, therefore).
  • Use one linker for one link. Never "although ... but" or "because ... so".
  • Even though is for facts. Even if is for possible situations. In case is not the same as if.
  • After when, as soon as, until and if, use a present tense for the future.
  • Such as takes nouns. For example can start a full sentence. e.g. means for example, i.e. means that is.
  • Match the linker to the style: so in chat, as a result in emails, therefore in reports.
  • Good paragraphs link with reference words like this and these, not only with linkers.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Contrasting ideas. Although, even though, though at the end, despite and in spite of.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Verbs in time clauses and if clauses. Present forms for the future after when, after, until and if.
  • IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023). Coherence and cohesion, cohesive devices, reference and substitution.
  • Purdue OWL: Transitions and transitional devices. Choosing a transition by the real relationship between ideas.
  • Grammarly: Like vs. such as. Such as for examples, like for comparisons, and how people mix them.

The perfect tenses

A perfect tense looks back from one point in time. It joins an earlier action to that point. This chapter covers the present perfect, the past perfect and the future perfect.

  • Form the present perfect, the past perfect and the future perfect.
  • Choose between the present perfect and the past simple.
  • Put ever, never, just, already, yet, for and since in the right place.
  • Choose a simple form or a continuous form.
  • Read a timeline for each perfect tense.

One idea: look back from a point

Mina: Can you open the door, please?

Tom: I can't. I have lost my key.

Tom lost the key some time before now. We do not know when. The result matters now: the door stays closed. The form have lost joins the past action to the present.

Every perfect tense works like this. You stand at one point in time. You look back at an earlier action. That action still matters at your point.

Three points to look back from
You stand atFormExample
nowhave or has + past participleI have lost my key.
a moment in the pasthad + past participleI had lost my key, so I waited outside.
a moment in the futurewill have + past participleBy tonight I will have found it.

The past participle is the third form of a verb: do, did, done. All perfect forms use it.

Each perfect tense has a simple form and a continuous form. The tree shows all six.

The past simple tells a finished story. A perfect tense joins two times. It says: this earlier thing matters at that later point.

The present perfect: form

I have finished the report.

She has fixed the bug.

They have not replied.

Have you tested the new version? Yes, I have.

The rule is short. Use have or has, then the past participle. Here have is an auxiliary verb. It does not mean "own".

Present perfect forms
TypeFormExample
PositiveI, you, we, they + have + past participleWe have deployed the app.
Positivehe, she, it + has + past participleThe build has failed.
Negativehave not (haven't) or has not (hasn't)He hasn't answered my email.
QuestionHave or Has + subject + past participle?Has the server restarted?
Short answerYes or No + subject + have, has, haven't or hasn'tYes, it has. No, it hasn't.

In speech we use a contraction: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's, she's, it's. Be careful with 's. It can mean is or has. "She's tired" means she is tired. "She's finished" means she has finished.

Past participles

A regular verb adds -ed: worked, tested, deployed. An irregular verb has its own third form. You must learn these forms. The chapter Past simple and past continuous lists 80 irregular verbs.

Twelve irregular verbs you need every day
Base formPast simplePast participle
bewas, werebeen
dodiddone
gowentgone
seesawseen
writewrotewritten
taketooktaken
givegavegiven
knowknewknown
breakbrokebroken
choosechosechosen
runranrun
sendsentsent

I have saw the error.

She has went home.

He have finished.

I have seen the error.

She has gone home.

He has finished.

Do not put the past simple form after have. Use the third form: seen, gone, done, written.

Been or gone?

has gone to

Sara has gone to Berlin.

She is in Berlin now, or on the way. She is not here.

has been to

Sara has been to Berlin.

She went there and came back. The visit is finished.

Three uses of the present perfect

Use 1: life experience up to now

I have worked with three databases.

Have you ever been to Japan?

She has never missed a deadline.

An experience is part of your life story. The exact time is not important, so you do not say it. You can say how many times: once, twice, three times.

Use 2: a past action with a result now

I have lost my key. (I cannot open the door now.)

The team has fixed the bug. (The app works now.)

Someone has deleted the file. (The file is not there now.)

The action is finished. The result is here now. News and status updates at work often use this form.

Use 3: a situation that started before and is still true

I have lived here for three years. (I still live here.)

She has known Ali since 2019. (She still knows him.)

We have fixed ten bugs this week. (The week is not finished.)

The situation began in the past. It continues up to now. Many languages use a present tense here. English uses the present perfect.

I live here since 2022.

I am working here for two years.

I have lived here since 2022.

I have worked here for two years.

Do not use a present tense for time up to now. With for and since, use the present perfect.

Small time words: ever, never, just, already, yet, for, since

Ana: Have you finished the code review yet?

Ben: I have already read the first file. I haven't opened the second one yet.

Ana: Has Chris replied?

Ben: No, he still hasn't replied. Oh, wait. He has just sent a message.

These small words often come with the present perfect. Each one has its own place in the sentence.

Time words with the present perfect
WordMeaningPlaceExample
everat any time in your lifebefore the past participle, in questionsHave you ever used Linux?
neverat no timebetween have and the past participleI have never broken the build.
justa very short time agobetween have and the past participleShe has just left.
alreadybefore now, sooner than expectedbetween have and the past participle, or at the endWe have already tested it.
yetup to now, and we expect it soonat the end of a negative or a questionI haven't eaten yet. Have you eaten yet?
stillthe waiting continuesbefore haven't or hasn'tHe still hasn't replied.
forhow longbefore a length of timefor two years, for ten minutes
sincefrom whenbefore a starting pointsince Monday, since 2020, since I joined

For or since?

I have worked here for three years.

I have worked here since 2023.

Both sentences can be true together. For measures the whole period. Since names the point where the period starts. To ask, use How long: "How long have you worked here?"

After since you can also put a short sentence part. Its verb is in the past simple: "I have learned a lot since I joined the team."

I have worked here since three years.

I have ever been to Paris.

I haven't yet finished it. (too formal for daily speech)

I have worked here for three years.

I have been to Paris.

I haven't finished it yet.

Quick check. Write for or since.

We have used this server ? six months.

She has been in the meeting ? nine o'clock.

I have known my manager ? I was a student.

The tests have been red ? a long time.

Present perfect or past simple?

Present perfect

I have visited Tokyo.

No time is given. The visit is part of my life up to now.

Past simple

I visited Tokyo in 2023.

The time is given. That time is finished.

Ask one question: is the time finished? A finished time needs the past simple. Time up to now takes the present perfect.

Time words that decide the tense
Finished time: past simpleTime up to now: present perfect
yesterday, last night, last weektoday, this week, this year
in 2020, in March, on Mondayso far, up to now, recently
two days ago, a minute agoever, never, before
when I was a child, at nine o'clockjust, already, yet
When ...? What time ...?How long ...? How many times ...?

Four more points help you choose.

  • News first, details after. "I have found the bug. It was in the date parser." The news is present perfect. The details are past simple.
  • The clock matters. At 10 in the morning: "I have had two coffees this morning." At 3 in the afternoon: "I had two coffees this morning."
  • Experience, then the story. "Have you ever been to Korea?" "Yes, I have. I went there in 2022."
  • A finished life is a finished time. "My grandfather wrote three books." He is dead. "My sister has written three books." She can still write more.

I have finished the task yesterday.

When have you arrived?

We have released version 2 two weeks ago.

I finished the task yesterday.

When did you arrive?

We released version 2 two weeks ago.

British speakers often use the present perfect with just, already and yet: "Have you eaten yet?" American speakers often use the past simple here: "Did you eat yet?" Both are easy to understand. This book follows British use.

Mei (join) the company in March. She (lead) the data team since June.

  1. Find the time words. The first is in March. The second is since June.
  2. In March is a finished time. Use the past simple: joined.
  3. Since June runs up to now. Use the present perfect: has led.
  4. Check the third form. Lead, led, led. Correct.

Present perfect continuous

Lena: You look tired.

Omar: I am. I have been debugging since six o'clock.

Lena: How long has the server been failing?

Omar: It has been failing all morning.

The form is have or has + been + verb with -ing. The negative is haven't been working. The question is Have you been working?

This form puts the light on the activity. It has two main uses.

  • An activity started before now and still continues. "I have been learning English for two years."
  • A recent activity explains what we see now. "The ground is wet. It has been raining."

Simple or continuous?

Present perfect simple and continuous
QuestionSimple: have doneContinuous: have been doing
What is the focus?The result. "I have written the report." It is ready.The activity. "I have been writing the report." Maybe it is not ready.
What do you count?How many or how much. "She has sent six emails."How long. "She has been sending emails all morning."
What kind of verb?State verbs. "I have known Ali for years."Action verbs. "I have been working with Ali for years."

A state verb does not normally take a continuous form. Common state verbs are be, know, like, believe, understand and own. The chapter Present simple and present continuous has a longer list.

With live and work, both forms are correct. "I have lived here for a year" and "I have been living here for a year" mean the same. The continuous form can sound less permanent.

Some verbs describe one short moment: start, stop, finish, arrive. Use the simple form with them. Say "The meeting has started".

I am learning English for two years.

I have been knowing him since 2019.

She has been sending six emails.

I have been learning English for two years.

I have known him since 2019.

She has sent six emails.

Past perfect and past perfect continuous

Past perfect

When I arrived, the meeting had started.

The meeting started first. I was late.

Past simple

When I arrived, the meeting started.

I arrived first. Then the meeting started.

The past perfect is had + past participle. The form is the same for every subject. The short forms are I'd, she'd and hadn't. The question is Had you met her before?

Use it for the earlier of two past actions. You tell a story in the past simple. Then you step back to an earlier time. The past perfect marks that step.

These words often come with the past perfect: by the time, already, just, never, before, when, after.

By the time the fix was ready, the customer had left.

I had never seen a database that big before.

She said that she had already sent the file.

The last example is reported speech. The chapter Reported speech explains it. The past perfect also talks about an unreal past: "If I had known, I would have helped." See Conditionals.

One past action needs only the past simple. Say "I went to the bank yesterday", not "I had gone to the bank yesterday". With before and after the order is already clear. "After I finished the tests, I merged the branch" is correct.

Past perfect continuous

The server had been running for 300 days when it crashed.

Her eyes were red. She had been reading logs for six hours.

The form is had been + verb with -ing. An activity was in progress up to a past moment. The form shows how long, or it explains a past situation. With state verbs, use the simple form: "We had known each other for years."

Future perfect

Here is a plan for one week of work.

  1. Monday Design. We write the design document.
  2. Wednesday Code. We finish the code and the tests.
  3. Friday Release. We release version 2.

By Wednesday evening, we will have finished the code.

By Friday evening, we will have released version 2.

We won't have finished the code by Tuesday.

The future perfect is will have + past participle. It is the same for every subject. The negative is won't have. The question is Will you have finished by Friday?

Use it for an action that will be complete before a future point. You stand at that future point. You look back.

A deadline is a natural place for this tense. Three time expressions are common.

  • by + a time: by Friday, by 2030, by the end of the month.
  • by the time + present simple: "By the time you arrive, I will have cooked dinner."
  • in + a period: "In two years' time, I will have finished my degree."

By the time he will arrive, we will have left.

By the time he arrives, we will have left.

There is also a future perfect continuous. The form is will have been + verb with -ing. It shows how long at a future point: "In June, I will have been working here for ten years." It is not common. The chapter Advanced tense and aspect says more.

Will have can also show that you feel sure about the present. "It is ten o'clock. They will have landed by now." You do not know. But you feel sure.

Choose the form in five steps

Find your point in time

Where do you stand? At now, use have done. At a past moment, use had done. At a future moment, use will have done.

Check for a finished time

Do you see yesterday, last, ago or a past date? Then stop. Use the past simple.

We shipped it two days ago.

Result or activity?

For a result or a number, use the simple form. For an activity or its length, use the continuous form.

I have read 40 pages. I have been reading all day.

Check the verb

Is it a state verb, like know or be? Then use the simple form.

I have been here since nine.

Place the small words

Put just, already and never after have. Put yet at the end. Use for with a period and since with a start.

I have just started. I haven't finished yet.

Fine points for higher levels

This is the first time ...

After "This is the first time", use the present perfect. "This is the first time I have used Rust." After "It was the first time", use the past perfect. "It was the first time I had spoken in a meeting."

The best ... I have ever ...

In positive sentences, ever comes after words like best, worst and first. "This is the best editor I have ever used."

When I have finished ...

After when, after, until and as soon as, do not use will. Use the present perfect to show that one action is complete first. "I will call you when I have finished." The chapter Talking about the future explains these time clauses.

A news story changes tense

A news report often starts with the present perfect. Then it moves to the past simple for the details. "A fire has destroyed a factory in the north. It started at about two o'clock."

Perfect forms after other verbs

The perfect idea also works after modal verbs: "You should have checked the logs." See Modal verbs. It also works in the passive: "The bug has been fixed." See The passive.

The Cambridge B1 Preliminary handbook lists the present perfect simple in its grammar list. It names just, yet, already, never, ever, for and since. Higher exams expect the other perfect forms too. Check the official handbook before your exam, because lists can change.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the perfect tenses
PatternPurposeModelNote
have or has + past participleSay an experience up to nowI have worked with three databases.Do not add a finished time word.
have or has + just + past participleSay that something happened a moment agoShe has just pushed the fix.Put just after have or has.
have or has + already + past participleSay that something is done sooner than expectedWe have already tested it.Put already after have, or at the end.
haven't or hasn't + past participle + yetSay that something is not done up to nowI haven't replied yet.Put yet at the end.
Have or Has + subject + ever + past participle?Ask about life experienceHave you ever worked from another country?Give the details in the past simple.
have or has + past participle + for + periodSay how long up to nowI have worked here for two years.Do not use a present tense here.
have or has + past participle + since + startSay when a situation startedHe has lived here since 2021.Never say "since two years".
have or has + been + -ingShow an activity up to now, or its lengthI have been learning English for a year.Not with state verbs such as know.
Past simple + finished timeSay when a finished action happenedI finished the task yesterday.No present perfect with yesterday, last or ago.
had + past participleStep back from a past momentWhen I arrived, the meeting had started.One past action needs only the past simple.
had been + -ingShow an activity up to a past momentIt had been raining for hours when we left.Say had known, not had been knowing.
will have + past participle + by + timeSay that something will be complete before a future pointBy Friday, we will have released version 2.Use the present simple after by the time.
This is the first time + present perfectTalk about a first experienceThis is the first time I have used Rust.Not "the first time I use".

Practice

Choose the right answer

Which sentence is correct?

  • I have seen that film last week.
  • I saw that film last week.
  • I have saw that film last week.

"Last week" is a finished time. A finished time needs the past simple.

"Tom has gone to the bank." What does it mean?

  • Tom is at the bank now, or on the way.
  • Tom went to the bank and came back.
  • Tom has never visited the bank.

"Has gone" means he is not back. "Has been" means he went and came back.

Which sentence is NOT correct?

  • I have known Maria for ten years.
  • I have been knowing Maria for ten years.
  • I have been working with Maria for ten years.

Know is a state verb. State verbs do not normally take the continuous form.

"When Sam got to the station, the train had left." What happened first?

  • The train left.
  • Sam got to the station.
  • Both things happened at the same moment.

The past perfect marks the earlier action. Sam did not catch the train.

By the time you ___, we will have finished dinner.

  • will arrive
  • arrive
  • will have arrived

After "by the time" we use the present simple for the future.

She ___ six emails this morning, and it is only ten o'clock.

  • has been sending
  • sent
  • has sent

The morning is not finished, so we need the present perfect. A number needs the simple form.

Write the verb form

I (never / use) this tool before.

She (just / send) the email.

He (go) to Osaka in 2022.

How long (you / wait)?

When I opened the laptop, the battery (die).

By next June, I (finish) the course.

They (not / reply) yet.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "I am working at this company since 2021."
    Answer

    "I have worked at this company since 2021." You can also say "I have been working". Since needs a perfect form, not a present tense.

  2. Correct the mistake: "I have met him two years ago."
    Answer

    "I met him two years ago." Ago gives a finished time. Use the past simple.

  3. Explain the difference: "I have read the book." and "I have been reading the book."
    Answer

    The first sentence shows a result. The book is finished. The second sentence shows an activity. Maybe the book is not finished.

  4. Join the two facts in one sentence. Start with "When I arrived". Fact 1: The meeting started at 9:00. Fact 2: I arrived at 9:10.
    Answer

    "When I arrived, the meeting had started." You can add already: "had already started".

  5. Write the sentence again with the word FOR. Keep the meaning. "I started learning English two years ago."
    Answer

    "I have been learning English for two years." "I have learned English for two years" is also possible. The Cambridge exams have a task like this. See Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

  6. Put each verb in the right tense. "Last year our team (move) to a new office. We (be) here for eleven months now. Before the move, we (work) in one small room for five years. By next March, we (spend) a full year here."
    Answer

    moved, have been, had worked, will have spent. "Had been working" is also correct for the third verb. Each verb has its own point in time: a finished time, now, an earlier past, and a future point.

  7. Write three true sentences about your own life. Use one for each use of the present perfect.
    Sample answer

    Experience: "I have visited four countries." Result: "I have finished my work, so I am free now." Still true: "I have lived in this city since 2020."

What is the form of the present perfect?

have or has + past participle

For or since: "___ last Monday"?

Since. Last Monday is a starting point.

Where does yet go?

At the end of a negative or a question.

Which tense goes with yesterday?

The past simple. Yesterday is a finished time.

What does the past perfect mark?

The earlier of two past actions.

What is the form of the future perfect?

will have + past participle

Key takeaways

  • A perfect tense looks back from a point: now, a past moment or a future moment.
  • The present perfect has three uses: experience, a result now, and a situation that is still true.
  • A finished time word needs the past simple, not the present perfect.
  • For goes with a period. Since goes with a starting point.
  • The simple form shows a result or a number. The continuous form shows an activity or its length.
  • The past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions.
  • The future perfect shows what will be complete by a deadline.

  • Past perfect, British Council LearnEnglish. The B1-B2 lesson on the earlier of two past actions.
  • Future continuous and future perfect, British Council LearnEnglish. The form, by, by the time and in two years' time.
  • Past simple or present perfect?, Cambridge Dictionary. English Grammar Today on finished time, time up to now and American use.
  • B1 Preliminary handbook for teachers, Cambridge English. The exam owner's list of grammar for B1.

Modal verbs

Modal verbs are small helping verbs like can, must and might. They add your view to a sentence. They show ability, duty, advice, or how sure you are. People use them all the time, at work and at home.

  • Build positive sentences, negatives and questions with modal verbs.
  • Talk about ability, obligation, advice and permission.
  • Show how sure you are with must, might, may, could and can't.
  • Talk about the past with should have, could have and must have.
  • Make polite requests and offers, and answer them.

What a modal verb does

Ana: The deploy failed. Can you look at it?

Ben: Sure. It might be the config file.

Ana: You should ask Kim. She may know.

Ben: Good idea. But first I must check the logs.

Look at the small words: can, might, should, may, must. Each one adds a meaning to the main verb. Can asks for help. Might and may show a guess. Should gives advice. Must shows a strong duty.

These words are modal verbs. The main modal verbs are can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will and would. Ought to is a modal verb too.

The form of modal verbs
TypeFormExample
Positivesubject + modal + base formShe can speak Japanese.
Negativesubject + modal + not + base formYou must not share your password.
Questionmodal + subject + base form?Could you send me the file?
Short answerYes or No + subject + modalYes, I can. No, she shouldn't.

The base form is the verb with no ending: go, be, check. Three rules make modal verbs different from other verbs.

  • No -s for he, she and it. Say "He can swim", not "He cans swim".
  • No do in questions and negatives. Say "Can you help?", not "Do you can help?"
  • No to after the modal. Say "I must go", not "I must to go". Ought to is the one exception.

The negative short forms are can't, couldn't, mustn't, shouldn't, won't and wouldn't. Cannot is written as one word.

She cans drive.

Do you can come tomorrow?

I must to leave now.

He will can help us.

She can drive.

Can you come tomorrow?

I must leave now.

He will be able to help us.

Two modal verbs never stand together. "I will can" is wrong. For the second one, use a semi-modal: "I will be able to", "You will have to".

Semi-modals are phrases like be able to, have to and need to. They act like normal verbs. They take -s, do and to. So they can go after will, in the past, and after other verbs.

A modal verb and its semi-modal partner
ModalSemi-modalExample with the semi-modal
canbe able toShe has been able to swim since she was five.
musthave toWe will have to wait.
needn'tdon't need toHe doesn't need to come.

One modal verb can have more than one meaning. The tree groups them by meaning.

Ability: can, could, be able to

I can read Python, but I can't write it well.

When I was ten, I could swim very fast.

The server was down, but we were able to restore it.

I will be able to join the call after lunch.

An ability is a skill or a power. Use can for ability now. Use could for a general ability in the past. Use a form of be able to in all other places.

Ability in different times
TimePositiveNegativeExample
Presentcancan't, cannotShe can speak three languages.
Past, general skillcouldcouldn'tMy grandmother could sew very well.
Past, one eventwas able to, managed tocouldn't, wasn't able toWe managed to fix the bug at midnight.
Futurewill be able towon't be able toYou will be able to log in tomorrow.
Present perfecthave been able tohaven't been able toI haven't been able to sleep well.
After another verbto be able tonot to be able toI want to be able to code in Rust.

Could or was able to?

General skill: could

I could run fast when I was young.

It was a skill for a long time.

One success: was able to

The fire was big, but everyone was able to escape.

It happened one time, in one situation.

For one success in the past, do not use could. Use was able to or managed to. Managed to also shows that it was difficult. In the negative, couldn't is fine for one event: "I couldn't open the file."

The test was hard, but I could pass it.

The test was hard, but I managed to pass it.

With see, hear, smell, taste and feel, English often uses can. "I can hear you now." "I can smell smoke." This sounds more natural than "I hear you now" in a call.

Obligation: must, have to, need to

Lead: Everyone must lock the screen before they leave the desk.

Sam: Do we have to wear badges too?

Lead: Yes, you have to. It's company policy.

Sam: And a tie?

Lead: No, you don't have to wear a tie.

An obligation is a duty. Must, have to and need to all say that something is necessary. They are not exactly the same.

Four ways to say that something is necessary
FormUseExample
mustA strong duty from the speaker, or a written ruleI must call my mother tonight. Visitors must sign in.
have toA duty from outside: a law, a boss, a timetableI have to wear a badge at work.
have got toThe same as have to, in informal British speechSorry, I've got to go now.
need toSomething is necessary to get a resultYou need to restart the server.

In speech the difference between must and have to is small. Many speakers use have to most of the time. Must is common in signs, rules and instructions.

Past and future

Yesterday I had to work late.

Next year we will have to update the system.

Did you have to pay for the course?

Must has no past form. For the past, use had to. For the future, use will have to. Have to is a normal verb, so questions need do: "Do you have to work on Saturday?"

Mustn't or don't have to?

You mustn't share your password.

You don't have to come to the meeting.

You needn't bring a laptop.

The forms look similar. The meanings are far apart. A prohibition says that something is not allowed. Mustn't is a prohibition. Don't have to, don't need to and needn't mean no obligation. You are free to choose.

"You mustn't come" does not mean "You don't have to come". If a meeting is optional, say "You don't have to come." If it is secret, say "You mustn't come."

Needn't and don't need to

You needn't worry. = You don't need to worry.

Needn't is a modal verb. It is more common in British English. Don't need to is a normal verb, and it is common everywhere. Both mean no obligation. Need to also has a past: "I didn't need to wait."

Advice: should, ought to, had better

You should back up your files.

You ought to take a break.

You shouldn't drink coffee late at night.

You'd better leave now, or you'll miss the train.

Use should and ought to for advice and for the right thing to do. Ought to means the same as should. It is less common and a little more formal. The negative ought not to is rare. Most people say shouldn't.

Had better is stronger. It gives advice for one situation now. It is often a warning: if you do not do it, something bad will happen. The short form is 'd better. The negative is had better not.

We'd better not deploy on Friday evening.

From a soft idea to a strong duty
StrengthFormExample
1 an ideacould, mightYou could try a different browser.
2 adviceshould, ought toYou should update your laptop.
3 strong advice, a warninghad betterYou'd better save your work. The battery is low.
4 a dutymust, have toYou must change your password today.

You should to call him.

You'd better to hurry.

You don't should eat that.

You should call him.

You'd better hurry.

You shouldn't eat that.

Had better looks like a past form. But it talks about now or the future. Say "You'd better go now." Never say "You had better to go" or "You had better went".

Possibility: may, might, could

Take an umbrella. It might rain later.

The bug may be in the date parser.

That could be the problem.

I might not come to the party.

A possibility is something that can be true. Use may, might and could when you are not sure. The three words mean almost the same. May is a little more formal.

Be careful with the negatives. May not and might not mean "maybe not". But couldn't means "impossible".

might not

The story might not be true.

Maybe it is false. I am not sure.

couldn't

The story couldn't be true.

It is impossible. I am sure it is false.

Use can for a general possibility. This is something that sometimes happens: "Bugs can appear in any code." For one real situation now, use may, might or could.

Where is Ali? He can be in the kitchen.

Where is Ali? He may be in the kitchen.

Deduction: must be, can't be

Mia: The office lights are on, and it's midnight.

Raj: Someone must be there. Maybe it's Leo.

Mia: It can't be Leo. He's on holiday in Spain.

Raj: Then it might be the cleaner.

A deduction is a logical guess. You look at the facts. Then you decide what is true. The modal shows how sure you are.

  • must: you are sure it is true. "She has three monitors. She must be a developer."
  • should: you expect it. "The build started ten minutes ago. It should be ready."
  • may, might, could: it is possible. "He isn't answering. He might be in a meeting."
  • can't, couldn't: you are sure it is not true. "That can't be the price. It's too cheap."

For an action in progress now, use the continuous form after the modal. "He must be working from home." "She can't be sleeping. Her light is on."

For deduction, the opposite of must is can't. Say "It can't be Leo", not "It mustn't be Leo". Keep mustn't for rules.

The car is not in the drive, and the house is dark. They (be) at home.

  1. Find the facts. No car. No lights.
  2. Decide how sure you are. The facts point one way. You are sure.
  3. Decide true or not true. You think they are not at home.
  4. Sure and not true means can't. They can't be at home.

Past modals: modal + have + past participle

The street is wet. It must have rained.

Leo can't have seen the email. He was on a plane.

I can't find my phone. I might have left it in the taxi.

You should have told me. I could have helped.

To look back at the past, use modal + have + past participle. The form is the same for every subject. The past participle is the third verb form: done, seen, left. In speech, have is short and sounds like "of": should've, must've.

Past modals and their meanings
FormMeaningExample
must have doneI am sure it happened.She must have left early. Her coat is gone.
can't have done, couldn't have doneI am sure it did not happen.He can't have taken the train. There are no trains on Sundays.
may have done, might have doneMaybe it happened.I might have deleted the file by mistake.
could have doneIt was possible, but it did not happen.We could have won, but we made mistakes.
should have doneIt was a good idea, but nobody did it.I should have saved my work.
shouldn't have doneSomebody did it, and it was a mistake.I shouldn't have eaten so much.
needn't have doneSomebody did it, but it was not necessary.You needn't have brought food. We have plenty.
didn't need to doIt was not necessary. Maybe nobody did it.I didn't need to take a taxi. Ana drove me.

I should of called you.

He must had forgotten.

You could helped me.

I should have called you.

He must have forgotten.

You could have helped me.

Never write "should of", "could of" or "must of". They sound like the real forms. But the word is have.

Regret and criticism

I should have studied more. (I didn't. Now I am sorry.)

You shouldn't have shouted at him. (You did. It was wrong.)

A regret is a sad feeling about your own past action. With I, should have shows regret. With you, it is often a criticism. Be careful at work. "You should have tested it" can sound hard. "It might be good to test it next time" sounds softer.

Needn't have or didn't need to?

needn't have done

I needn't have printed the slides.

I printed them. Then nobody used them.

didn't need to do

I didn't need to print the slides.

It was not necessary. Usually I did not print them.

Needn't have is mostly British. Many speakers use didn't need to for both meanings. Then the context tells you what happened.

Requests, offers and permission

Guest: Excuse me. May I use the Wi-Fi?

Host: Of course. Can I get you a coffee?

Guest: Yes, please. Could you tell me the password?

Host: Sure. Shall I write it down for you?

Guest: That would be great. Thank you.

A request asks someone to do something. An offer says that you will do something. Permission means that someone allows you to do a thing. Modal verbs do all three jobs.

Requests, offers and permission
JobForms, from friendly to formalExampleTypical answer
Ask for permissionCan I ...? Could I ...? May I ...?Could I leave early today?Yes, of course. Sorry, I'm afraid not.
Give permissionYou can ... You may ...You can use my desk.Thanks!
Refuse permissionYou can't ... You may not ...You can't park here.Oh, sorry.
Ask someone to do somethingCan you ...? Could you ...? Would you ...?Could you check my code?Sure. No problem.
Ask very politelyWould you mind + -ing?Would you mind closing the window?Not at all.
OfferCan I ...? Shall I ...? I can ... I'll ...Shall I send you the slides?Yes, please. That's kind.
SuggestShall we ...? We could ...Shall we start the meeting?Good idea.

Could is more polite than can. May is the most formal. Use could and would with people you do not know well. Shall I and shall we are common in British English. American speakers often say "Should I ...?" or "Do you want me to ...?"

Could I? When you give permission, use can. "Could I sit here?" "Yes, you can." Do not say "Yes, you could." Would you mind? This question means "Is it a problem for you?" So the polite yes is "No, not at all." The verb after it takes -ing.

Would you mind to open the door?

Can you to help me?

Could I borrow your pen? Yes, you could.

Would you mind opening the door?

Can you help me?

Could I borrow your pen? Yes, of course.

Choose the right modal

What is the job?

Ability, duty, advice, a guess, or a request? Each job has its own words.

Now or past?

For the past, change the form. Use had to, could, was able to, or modal + have + past participle.

I had to wait. She must have forgotten.

How strong?

An idea is could. Advice is should. A warning is had better. A duty is must.

Not allowed or not necessary?

Not allowed is mustn't or can't. Not necessary is don't have to or needn't.

You mustn't smoke here. You don't have to stay.

How sure?

Sure and true is must. Expected is should. Possible is might. Sure and not true is can't.

Check the form

Base form after the modal. No to. No -s. No do.

He can swim. Can he swim?

Fine points for higher levels

May well, might well, could well

Add well to show that something is quite likely. "Prices may well rise next year." It is stronger than may alone.

Might as well

This means there is no better choice. "The bus is very late. We might as well walk."

Be supposed to

This shows a rule or a plan that people often break. "You're supposed to write tests before you merge." Often the rule was not followed.

Be allowed to

This states permission as a fact. "We aren't allowed to use personal laptops." For one past event, use was allowed to, not could: "I was allowed to leave early yesterday."

Will and would for a sure guess

Will can show a strong belief about now. Someone knocks at the door. "That will be the courier." The speaker feels sure, but has no proof.

Modals in reported speech

In reported speech, can often becomes could, will becomes would, and may becomes might. Must can stay, or it becomes had to. "You must leave." becomes "She said I had to leave." See Reported speech.

Modals in other chapters

Modals with the passive: "The form must be signed." See The passive. Would, could and might in unreal situations: see Conditionals. Modals to make writing softer: see Hedging and stance.

The Cambridge B1 Preliminary handbook lists these modals for B1: can, could, would, will, shall, should, may, might, have (got) to, ought to, must, mustn't, need, needn't and used to. Higher exams also test past modals and deduction. A common task asks you to rewrite a sentence with a given word. Check the official handbook before your exam, because lists can change.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for modal verbs
PatternPurposeModelNote
subject + can + base formSay what someone is able to do nowI can read Python.No -s and no to: never "she cans" or "can to".
was or were able to + base formSay that you succeeded one time in the pastWe were able to restore the data.Do not use could for one past success.
will be able to + base formSay what someone can do in the futureYou will be able to log in tomorrow.Never "will can".
have to or must + base formSay that something is necessaryI have to wear a badge at work.For the past, use had to.
mustn't + base formSay that something is not allowedYou mustn't share your password.It does not mean "not necessary".
don't have to or needn't + base formSay that something is not necessaryYou don't have to come.The person is free to choose.
should or ought to + base formGive adviceYou should back up your files.Say shouldn't, not "don't should".
'd better (not) + base formGive a strong warning about nowYou'd better save your work.No to after better, and no past form.
may, might or could + base formSay that something is possibleThe bug may be in the parser.Not can for one real situation.
must be or can't beMake a sure guess from factsIt can't be Leo. He's in Spain.Not "mustn't be" for a guess.
must, might or can't + have + past participleMake a guess about the pastShe must have left early.Write have, never "of".
should have + past participleShow regret or criticism about the pastI should have saved my work.It means you did not do it.
Could you + base form ...?Make a polite requestCould you check my code?Give permission with can, not could.
Would you mind + -ing ...?Make a very polite requestWould you mind closing the door?The polite yes is "Not at all".
Shall I or Shall we + base form ...?Make an offer or a suggestionShall I send you the slides?Mostly British. Also "Should I ...?"

Practice

Choose the right answer

Which sentence is correct?

  • She cans speak French.
  • She can to speak French.
  • She can speak French.

A modal has no -s and no to. The base form follows it.

The meeting is optional. You ___ go.

  • mustn't
  • don't have to
  • can't

Optional means not necessary. Mustn't and can't mean not allowed.

The car was stuck in the snow, but we ___ push it out.

  • could
  • managed to
  • can

This was one success in the past. Use managed to or was able to, not could.

He has a key and a desk here. He ___ work here.

  • must
  • mustn't
  • should to

The facts make you sure. Sure and true is must.

"You needn't have cooked." What happened?

  • The person cooked, but it was not necessary.
  • The person did not cook.
  • The person was not allowed to cook.

Needn't have + past participle: the action happened, but it was not needed.

"Would you mind waiting a moment?" You are happy to wait. What do you say?

  • Yes, I would.
  • No, not at all.
  • Yes, I mind.

The question asks if it is a problem. "Not at all" means it is no problem.

Write the modal form

Last year I (must) travel every month.

You look tired. You (advice) go to bed early.

It's late, and the last train leaves at 11. We (strong warning) leave now.

I can't find my keys. I (maybe / leave) them at work.

That (sure: not true / be) Sara. She is in Tokyo this week.

After the course, you (ability, future) write simple programs.

I failed the test. I (advice, past / study) harder.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "I will can finish the report tomorrow."
    Answer

    "I will be able to finish the report tomorrow." Two modals cannot stand together, so use be able to after will.

  2. Correct the mistake: "You mustn't pay. The museum is free on Sundays."
    Answer

    "You don't have to pay." It is not necessary. Mustn't would mean that paying is not allowed.

  3. Explain the difference: "He might be at home." and "He must be at home."
    Answer

    "Might" means it is possible, but the speaker is not sure. "Must" means the speaker is sure, because of some facts.

  4. Make each request more polite: "Give me the report." and "Close the door."
    Answer

    "Could you give me the report, please?" and "Would you mind closing the door?" "Would you give me the report?" is also possible.

  5. Write a past deduction for each fact. Fact 1: Tom's desk is empty and his bag is gone. Fact 2: Kim was in a meeting all day. People say she sent the email at noon.
    Answer

    1: "Tom must have gone home." 2: "Kim can't have sent the email at noon." You can also say "couldn't have sent".

  6. Rewrite with the word in capitals. Keep the meaning. "It wasn't necessary for me to wear a suit, but I wore one." NEEDN'T
    Answer

    "I needn't have worn a suit." The person wore a suit, and it was not necessary. Exams such as Cambridge B2 First have tasks like this.

  7. A colleague deleted a file without a backup. Write one sentence of criticism and one softer sentence for next time.
    Sample answer

    Criticism: "You should have made a backup first." Softer: "Next time, it might be a good idea to make a backup first."

What comes after a modal verb?

The base form, with no to: can go, must check.

What is the past of must (obligation)?

had to

Mustn't or don't have to: "It's free. You ___ pay."

don't have to. It is not necessary.

What is the opposite of "must be" for a guess?

can't be

Which form shows one past success?

was able to, or managed to. Not could.

What does "I should have called" mean?

I did not call. Now I am sorry.

"Would you mind helping?" What is the polite yes?

No, not at all.

Key takeaways

  • A modal verb takes the base form. It has no -s, no do and no to.
  • Use be able to and have to where a modal cannot go: after will, and in perfect forms.
  • Use could for a general past skill, and was able to or managed to for one past success.
  • Mustn't means not allowed. Don't have to and needn't mean not necessary.
  • Should gives advice. Had better gives a strong warning about now.
  • Must and can't are sure guesses. May, might and could are possible guesses.
  • For the past, use modal + have + past participle: must have, might have, should have.
  • Could and would make requests polite. Give permission with can.

Sources

  • 'can' and 'could', British Council LearnEnglish. Ability, possibility, permission, requests, offers and could have.
  • Past ability, British Council LearnEnglish. Could for a general skill, was able to and managed to for one event.
  • Modals: permission and obligation, British Council LearnEnglish. Can, could and may for permission, must and have to, mustn't and don't have to.
  • Modals: deductions about the present, British Council LearnEnglish. Must, might, may, could and can't for sure and possible guesses.
  • Modals: deductions about the past, British Council LearnEnglish. Must have, might have, may have and can't have.
  • B1 Preliminary handbook for teachers, Cambridge English. The exam owner's list of modal verbs and their uses at B1.

Conditionals

A conditional sentence joins a condition and a result. "If it rains, we stay inside." Conditionals let you talk about facts, plans, dreams and regrets. This chapter shows every type and helps you choose the right one.

  • Build zero, first, second, third and mixed conditionals.
  • Choose the right type with a simple decision tree.
  • Use unless, provided that, as long as and in case.
  • Talk about regrets and wishes with wish and if only.
  • Say what you prefer with would rather.

Two parts: the condition and the result

If you press this button, the machine stops.

The machine stops if you press this button.

Each sentence has two parts. A clause is a part with a subject and a verb. The if clause gives the condition. The main clause gives the result.

The order can change. The meaning stays the same. When the if clause comes first, put a comma after it. When the main clause comes first, do not use a comma.

If you are late you miss the bus.

You miss the bus, if you are late.

If you are late, you miss the bus.

You miss the bus if you are late.

Real and unreal

Some conditions are real. They are true, or they can easily happen. Other conditions are unreal. They are imagined, impossible or very unlikely.

Real

If I have time, I will call you.

Maybe I will have time. It is possible.

Unreal

If I had time, I would call you.

I do not have time. I am imagining.

Look at the verbs. For an unreal idea, English moves the verb one step back in time. Present becomes past. Past becomes past perfect. The step back in time is a step away from reality.

The five types at a glance
TypeIf clauseMain clauseUseExample
Zeropresent simplepresent simplefacts, rules, things that always happenIf you heat ice, it melts.
Firstpresent simplewill + base forma real or possible futureIf it rains, we will stay inside.
Secondpast simplewould + base forman unreal present or an unlikely futureIf I had a car, I would drive to work.
Thirdpast perfectwould have + past participlean unreal pastIf I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.
Mixedpast perfect, or past simplewould + base form, or would have + past participlean unreal past with a result now, or the oppositeIf I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
