Real: present in the if clause. Unreal: go one step back in time, and use would in the result.

Zero conditional: facts and rules

If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.

If the tests fail, the server sends an email.

When I drink coffee at night, I can't sleep.

If the light is red, stop.

The form is if + present simple, present simple. Use it for facts, science, rules and habits. The result always follows the condition. So you can often use when or whenever instead of if. The meaning does not change.

The main clause can also be an imperative. Instructions often use this form: "If the app freezes, restart it."

Code uses the same idea. In if x > 0: print("positive"), the condition comes first. The action follows only when the condition is true. The zero conditional says this in English: "If x is greater than zero, the program prints positive."

If you mix red and blue, you will get purple. (every time)

If you mix red and blue, you get purple.

The first sentence is not a big error. But for a fact that is always true, the present simple is clearer.

First conditional: a real future

Kim: Are we still going to the beach on Saturday?

Leo: If it doesn't rain, we'll go.

Kim: And if it rains?

Leo: If it rains, we'll watch a film at home.

The form is if + present simple, will + base form. Use it for a future situation that is real or possible. You think it may really happen.

The main clause can use other words too. Use may or might when the result is not sure. Use can for ability or permission. Use an imperative for an instruction.

  • If the price goes down, we might buy two.
  • If you finish early, you can go home.
  • If you see Ana, tell her to call me.

Do not use will in the if clause for a future condition. Say "If it rains tomorrow", not "If it will rain tomorrow". The if clause uses the present simple, even for the future.

If I will see him, I will tell him.

If you will need help, call me.

If I see him, I will tell him.

If you need help, call me.

If or when?

when

When I get home, I'll call you.

I am sure I will get home.

if

If I get the job, I'll call you.

Maybe I will get the job. Maybe not.

Time words like when, as soon as, before, after and until follow the same rule. Use the present simple after them for the future. The chapter Talking about the future explains these time clauses.

Second conditional: an unreal present or an unlikely future

If I had more time, I would learn Korean. (I don't have time.)

If I won the lottery, I would stop working. (It probably won't happen.)

If I were you, I would ask for a raise. (Advice.)

If we hired two more people, we could finish in May.

The form is if + past simple, would + base form. The past simple here does not mean past time. It means unreal. The sentence is about now or the future.

Use it for three things.

  • An unreal present. The situation is not true now. "If I lived near the office, I would walk."
  • An unlikely future. It probably will not happen. "If aliens landed here, what would you do?"
  • Advice. "If I were you, I'd take the job."

In the main clause, could means "would be able to". Might means "would perhaps".

Were or was?

After if, you can use were for every person: if I were, if she were, if it were. This form is correct in formal writing and in exams. In everyday speech, many people say "if I was" or "if he was". But always say "If I were you". It is a fixed phrase.

First or second?

First: I think it can happen

If I get the job, I will move to London.

I had a good interview. It is possible.

Second: I think it is unlikely

If I got the job, I would move to London.

There are 500 people for one job. It is a dream.

Both sentences are correct. The choice shows how you see the future. The second conditional can also sound more polite: "Would it be a problem if I left early?"

If I would have money, I would buy a house.

If I knew the answer, I will tell you.

If I had money, I would buy a house.

If I knew the answer, I would tell you.

Do not put would in the if clause. Would belongs in the result. "If I would know" is wrong. Say "If I knew".

Third conditional: an unreal past

If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.

The facts are different. I did not leave earlier. I missed the train. The sentence imagines another past.

The form is if + past perfect, would have + past participle. The past perfect is had + past participle. The chapter The perfect tenses explains it.

Use it to talk about a past that did not happen. It often shows a regret. It also explains why something went wrong, or right.

  • If we had tested the code, we wouldn't have lost the data.
  • If you had asked me, I could have helped. (I was able to help.)
  • If it hadn't rained, the match might have gone ahead. (Maybe.)

Short forms

In speech, both had and would become 'd. "If I'd known, I'd have come." The first 'd is had. The second 'd is would. Here is a trick. 'd have is always would have. 'd + past participle is had.

If I would have known, I would have come.

If I knew yesterday, I would have helped.

If I had known, I would have come.

If I had known yesterday, I would have helped.

Some native speakers say "If I would have known" in casual talk. It is not correct in exams or in writing. Use had in the if clause.

Mixed conditionals: two times in one sentence

Sometimes the condition and the result are at different times. Then you mix the forms. There are two common mixes.

Mix 1: an unreal past, a result now

If I had taken the job in Berlin, I would live in Germany now.

The facts: I did not take the job in the past. I do not live in Germany now. The form is if + past perfect, would + base form.

Mix 2: an unreal present, a result in the past

If I were better at maths, I would have passed the exam.

The facts: I am not good at maths. This is a general fact, now and always. So I failed the exam last week. The form is if + past simple, would have + past participle.

How to build a mixed conditional
MixCondition timeResult timeExample
1past: had donenow: would doIf she hadn't missed the flight, she would be here now.
2now, always: didpast: would have doneIf he weren't so shy, he would have spoken at the meeting.

Facts: I didn't sleep last night. I am very tired now.

  1. Find the time of the condition. "Didn't sleep" is in the past.
  2. Find the time of the result. "Am tired" is now.
  3. Change the facts to unreal. Past becomes past perfect: had slept. Now becomes would + base form.
  4. Turn the positives and negatives around. "If I had slept last night, I wouldn't be so tired now."

Other words for if: unless, provided that, as long as, in case

Unless

Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.

= If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.

Unless means "if not" or "except if". The verb after unless is positive. Do not add another not.

Unless you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.

Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.

Provided that, as long as, on condition that

You can borrow my car as long as you bring it back by six.

We will ship on Friday provided that all the tests pass.

These phrases mean "only if". They make the condition strong and clear. The other person must do this thing. Provided that and on condition that are more formal. Providing and so long as mean the same. Use the present simple after them for the future.

In case

in case

I'll take an umbrella in case it rains.

I take it now, before I know. It is a precaution.

if

I'll take a taxi if it rains.

I wait. I take a taxi only when it rains.

In case is not the same as if. With in case, you act first, because something might happen. Do not use will after in case. Say "in case it rains", not "in case it will rain".

On signs you see in case of + noun. "In case of fire, use the stairs." This is formal. It means "if there is a fire".

Words that replace if
WordMeaningExample
unlessif not, except ifI won't come unless you invite me.
as long as, so long asonly if (a clear condition)You can stay as long as you are quiet.
provided (that), providingonly if (more formal)The loan is free provided that you pay on time.
on condition thatonly if (formal, contracts)He got the job on condition that he moved.
in caseas a precaution, because it might happenSave a copy in case the laptop crashes.
even ifit does not matter ifI'll finish it even if it takes all night.
otherwiseif not (starts a new sentence)Hurry. Otherwise, you'll be late.

Wish and if only

Ola: I wish I spoke French. The client only speaks French.

Ben: I wish I had learned it at school.

Ola: And I wish the client would answer our emails.

A wish is about something you want to be different. After wish, the verb moves one step back in time, like in an unreal conditional.

Wish: four patterns
You want to changeFormExampleThe fact
the presentwish + past simpleI wish I spoke French.I don't speak French.
an ability nowwish + couldI wish I could drive.I can't drive.
the pastwish + past perfectI wish I had learned French.I didn't learn it.
another person's actionwish + someone + wouldI wish the client would reply.The client doesn't reply. I am annoyed.

If only works in the same way. It is stronger and more emotional. "If only I had saved the file!"

After wish, you can use were for every person: "I wish I were taller." In speech, "I wish I was taller" is also common.

Use hope for a real future that you want. "I hope you pass the exam." Do not say "I wish you will pass". Also, do not use wish ... would about yourself. Say "I wish I could stop", not "I wish I would stop".

I wish I have more free time.

I wish it will be sunny tomorrow.

I wish I didn't eat so much last night.

I wish I had more free time.

I hope it will be sunny tomorrow.

I wish I hadn't eaten so much last night.

Would rather

I'd rather walk. It's a nice day.

I'd rather stay at home than go to the party.

I'd rather not talk about it.

I'd rather you didn't share this email.

Would rather shows a preference. It means "would prefer". The short form is I'd rather.

  • Same person: would rather + base form. "I'd rather take the train." There is no to.
  • Two choices: would rather + base form + than + base form. "I'd rather work late than work at the weekend."
  • Negative: would rather not + base form. "I'd rather not say."
  • Another person, now or future: would rather + someone + past simple. "I'd rather you came tomorrow." The past form means unreal, not past.
  • Another person, past: would rather + someone + past perfect. "I'd rather you hadn't told him."

would rather

I'd rather stay here.

I'd rather you stayed here.

would prefer

I'd prefer to stay here.

I'd prefer you to stay here.

I'd rather to stay at home.

I'd rather you don't smoke here.

I'd rather stay at home.

I'd rather you didn't smoke here.

The chapter Subjunctive and unreal past shows more forms like this, such as it's time and as if.

Choose the type: a decision tree

Ask two questions. First: is the situation real or unreal? Second: what time is it about? The tree gives the answer.

The story below uses all five types. Each slide changes one thing.

A fact

The laptop battery is old.

If the battery is old, it dies fast.

A real future

Maybe Nina will forget her charger today.

If she forgets the charger, her laptop will die.

A dream now

Nina has no money for a new laptop.

If she had more money, she would buy a new laptop.

A regret

Yesterday she didn't save her work. She lost two hours.

If she had saved her work, she wouldn't have lost two hours.

Past to now

She lost the work yesterday. Now she is working late.

If she hadn't lost the work, she wouldn't be here so late.

A wish

Nina feels bad about it.

She wishes she had saved the file. If only she had a new laptop!

Fine points for higher levels

Inversion without if

Formal English can drop if and change the word order. "Had I known" means "If I had known". "Were I you" means "If I were you". "Should you need help" means "If you need help". See Inversion and emphasis.

If it weren't for, but for

"If it weren't for my team, I would quit." This means my team is the only reason I stay. For the past, say "If it hadn't been for". But for + noun is a formal short form: "But for the rain, we would have won."

If you should, if you happen to

These make the condition less likely. "If you should see Tom, tell him I called." "If you happen to pass a shop, buy some milk."

Will in the if clause

Sometimes will in the if clause is correct. It shows willingness, not the future. "If you will wait here, the doctor will see you soon." It is polite and formal.

Suppose, imagine, what if

These start an unreal idea. "Suppose you lost your job. What would you do?" "What if the server went down during the demo?"

If so, if not

These replace a whole clause. "Is the file ready? If so, send it. If not, tell me when."

The Cambridge B1 Preliminary handbook lists the zero, first and second conditionals. It also lists "If I were you". The British Council puts third and mixed conditionals at B1 to B2 level. In writing exams, a correct third or mixed conditional can show a wide range of grammar. Check the official handbook before your exam, because lists can change.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for conditionals
PatternPurposeModelNote
If + present, presentState a fact or a ruleIf you heat ice, it melts.You can use when instead of if.
If + present, will + base formTalk about a real futureIf it rains, we will stay inside.No will in the if clause.
If + present, imperativeGive an instructionIf the app freezes, restart it.Common in manuals and messages.
If + past, would + base formImagine an unreal presentIf I had a car, I would drive.No would in the if clause.
If I were you, I would + base formGive adviceIf I were you, I would ask for help.Always were in this phrase.
If + past perfect, would have + past participleImagine a different pastIf I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.Not "if I would have".
If + past perfect, would + base formShow a past cause with a result nowIf I had slept, I wouldn't be tired now.Check the time of each clause.
Unless + positive verbSay "if not"Unless you hurry, you'll be late.Never "unless you don't".
as long as or provided that + presentSet a clear conditionYou can go as long as you finish first.It means only if.
in case + presentDo something as a precautionTake a coat in case it gets cold.Not the same as if. No will after it.
wish + past simpleWant a different presentI wish I spoke French.Use hope for a real future.
wish + past perfectShow regret about the pastI wish I had saved the file.Not "I wish I saved" for the past.
wish + someone + wouldComplain about another person's actionI wish he would reply.Not about yourself.
would rather + base form (+ than)Say what you preferI'd rather walk than drive.No to after rather.
would rather + someone + past simpleSay what you want another person to doI'd rather you didn't call me late.The past form means unreal, not past.

Practice

Choose the right answer

If you ___ water to 0 degrees, it freezes.

  • cool
  • will cool
  • would cool

This is a fact. The zero conditional uses the present simple in both clauses.

If I ___ him tomorrow, I'll give him your message.

  • will see
  • see
  • saw

A real future condition takes the present simple, not will.

"If I had a dog, I would walk every day." What is true?

  • I have a dog.
  • I don't have a dog.
  • I had a dog in the past.

The second conditional is unreal. The past form means "not true now".

Which sentence is correct?

  • If she would have called, I would have answered.
  • If she had called, I would have answered.
  • If she called, I would have answered yesterday.

An unreal past needs had + past participle in the if clause.

Take your phone ___ you get lost.

  • in case
  • unless
  • as long as

You take the phone now, as a precaution. That is in case.

I wish I ___ to the party last night. It was great, people say.

  • went
  • would go
  • had gone

A regret about the past takes wish + past perfect.

Write the verb form

If it (not / rain) tomorrow, we will have a picnic.

If I (be) you, I would update the software.

If we had booked earlier, we (get) cheaper tickets.

You can use my laptop as long as you (be) careful.

I wish I (can) play the piano.

I'd rather you (not / tell) anyone about this.

If he hadn't missed the bus, he (be) here now.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "If I will have time, I will help you."
    Answer

    "If I have time, I will help you." The if clause takes the present simple, even for the future.

  2. Correct the mistake: "Unless you don't study, you will fail."
    Answer

    "Unless you study, you will fail." Unless already means "if not".

  3. Explain the difference: "If I win, I will buy a boat." and "If I won, I would buy a boat."
    Answer

    The first speaker thinks winning is possible. The second speaker thinks it is unlikely, or is only dreaming.

  4. Write a third conditional from these facts: "I didn't check the weather. I got wet."
    Answer

    "If I had checked the weather, I wouldn't have got wet." American English often says "gotten".

  5. Write a mixed conditional from these facts: "I didn't learn to code at school. I am not a developer now."
    Answer

    "If I had learned to code at school, I would be a developer now." The condition is past. The result is now.

  6. Rewrite with the word in capitals. Keep the meaning. "It's a pity I can't speak Spanish." WISH
    Answer

    "I wish I could speak Spanish." A present ability takes wish + could. "I wish I spoke Spanish" is also correct.

  7. Your colleague wants to deploy on Friday night. Write two sentences: one with "provided that" and one with "in case".
    Sample answer

    "We can deploy on Friday provided that all the tests pass." "Let's keep the old version ready in case something goes wrong."

Form of the first conditional?

if + present simple, will + base form

Form of the second conditional?

if + past simple, would + base form

Form of the third conditional?

if + past perfect, would have + past participle

What does "unless" mean?

if not, except if

"In case" or "if": you act now as a precaution?

in case

Regret about the past with wish?

wish + past perfect: I wish I had known.

"I'd rather you ___ (not / come) late."

didn't come

Key takeaways

  • A conditional has an if clause for the condition and a main clause for the result.
  • Real conditions use the present simple in the if clause, even for the future.
  • Unreal conditions move the verb one step back: past for now, past perfect for the past.
  • Would goes in the result clause, never in the if clause.
  • Mixed conditionals join a past condition and a present result, or the opposite.
  • Unless means if not. As long as and provided that mean only if. In case means as a precaution.
  • Wish uses the same step back. Use hope for a real future.
  • Would rather takes the base form, or a past form for another person.

Sources

  • Conditionals: zero, first and second, British Council LearnEnglish. Forms and uses, words like unless and in case, and were after if.
  • Conditionals: third and mixed, British Council LearnEnglish. The unreal past and the two kinds of mixed conditional.
  • Wishes: 'wish' and 'if only', British Council LearnEnglish. Wish with the past simple, the past perfect and would.
  • Unreal time, British Council LearnEnglish. The step back in tense, would rather, it's time and as if.
  • Conditionals, British Council LearnEnglish Teens. Unless as a negative if, and as long as for a clear condition.
  • B1 Preliminary handbook for teachers, Cambridge English. The exam owner's list of conditional types at B1.

The passive

The passive puts the focus on the thing that receives an action. "My bike was stolen." You care about the bike, not the thief. News, reports, science and software documents use the passive a lot.

  • Build the passive in every tense and with modal verbs.
  • Decide when the passive is better than the active.
  • Use by + agent only when it adds new information.
  • Use have something done, the get passive and "it is said that".
  • Use the passive well in reports and technical writing.

Active and passive: one event, two views

Someone stole my bike last night.

My bike was stolen last night.

Both sentences tell the same story. The first one is in the active voice. The subject someone does the action. The second is in the passive voice. The subject my bike receives the action.

The person or thing that does the action is the agent. In a passive sentence, you can name the agent with by. Very often, you leave it out.

To make a passive sentence, follow three steps.

  1. Move the object to the front. It becomes the new subject.
  2. Change the verb to be + past participle. Keep the tense in be.
  3. Put the old subject after by, or leave it out.

The past participle is the third verb form: fixed, written, sent. The chapter Past simple and past continuous lists irregular verbs.

Only verbs with an object

A transitive verb has an object: fix the bug, send an email. Only these verbs have a passive. Verbs like happen, arrive, die, sleep and seem have no object. So they have no passive form.

The accident was happened at night.

The parcel was arrived yesterday.

The accident happened at night.

The parcel arrived yesterday.

The form in every tense

The main verb is always the past participle. Only be changes. So to find the tense of a passive verb, look at be.

Active and passive in each tense
TenseActivePassive
Present simpleThey clean the office every day.The office is cleaned every day.
Present continuousThey are cleaning the office.The office is being cleaned.
Past simpleThey cleaned the office.The office was cleaned.
Past continuousThey were cleaning the office.The office was being cleaned.
Present perfectThey have cleaned the office.The office has been cleaned.
Past perfectThey had cleaned the office.The office had been cleaned.
Future with willThey will clean the office.The office will be cleaned.
Future with going toThey are going to clean the office.The office is going to be cleaned.
Future perfectThey will have cleaned the office.The office will have been cleaned.
Modal verbThey must clean the office.The office must be cleaned.
to-infinitiveThey want to clean the office.The office needs to be cleaned.
-ing formI hate people interrupting me.I hate being interrupted.

Negatives and questions work like the tense of be. Put not after the first helping verb. For a question, move the first helping verb to the front.

  • The email wasn't sent.
  • Has the bug been fixed?
  • Will the results be published online?
  • When was this house built?

The report written last week.

The bug has fixed.

The new office is build now.

The report was written last week.

The bug has been fixed.

The new office is being built now.

Do not forget be, and do not forget the past participle. "The bug has fixed" is active. It means the bug did the fixing. Say "The bug has been fixed."

When and why to use the passive

Read this short news item.

A rare painting was stolen from the city museum last night. The alarm was not switched on. Two men have been arrested. The painting has not been found yet.

Who stole the painting? We do not know. Who arrested the men? The police, of course. The story is about the painting, so the painting stays at the front. These are the main reasons to choose the passive.

  1. The agent is unknown. "My laptop was stolen."
  2. The agent is clear or not important. "He was arrested." (by the police) "Rice is grown in Asia." (by farmers)
  3. The result is the main news. "The new version was released today."
  4. You want to keep the topic at the start. "This is our new office. It was designed by a young architect."
  5. You want to sound formal or neutral. "Your application has been received."

Point 4 is important for good writing. English likes known information first and new information last. The passive can help you keep this order.

The passive can also hide who is responsible. "Mistakes were made." Who made them? The sentence does not say. Readers notice this. If you made the mistake, the active voice is more honest: "We made a mistake."

Do not use the passive everywhere. Too many passive sentences make a text slow and hard to follow. For most daily speech, the active voice is better.

By + agent

The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

This library was written by two students.

Add by + agent when the agent is new and important. It often comes at the end, the place for new information. Leave it out when it adds nothing.

My wallet was stolen by someone.

English is spoken by people in many countries.

My wallet was stolen.

English is spoken in many countries.

by: the agent

The door was opened by the manager.

A person or a force does the action.

with: the tool

The door was opened with a key.

A tool or material is used.

The passive with modal verbs

The form must be signed by both parties.

Passwords should not be shared.

The meeting can't be moved.

The file might have been deleted.

The data should have been backed up.

The form is modal + be + past participle. For the past, use modal + have been + past participle. Rules, signs and instructions use these forms a lot. The chapter Modal verbs explains the meaning of each modal.

Modal passives
TimeFormExample
Now or futuremodal + be + past participleThe tickets can be bought online.
Pastmodal + have been + past participleThe error must have been caused by the update.

The form must signed today.

It should be send to the manager.

The form must be signed today.

It should be sent to the manager.

Verbs with two objects

Active: The company gave Ana a prize.

Passive 1: Ana was given a prize.

Passive 2: A prize was given to Ana.

Some verbs have two objects: a person and a thing. Common ones are give, send, show, offer, tell, teach, lend, pay, promise and award. Either object can become the subject. The person is the more common subject. It sounds more natural in most cases.

  • I was sent the wrong file. (Someone sent me the wrong file.)
  • We were shown the new office. (Someone showed us the new office.)
  • She has been offered a job in Seoul.

Explain, describe, suggest and say do not work like this. They take to + person. Say "The plan was explained to us", not "We were explained the plan".

The get passive

My phone got broken on the train.

He got fired last month.

Did anyone get hurt?

In informal speech, get can replace be: get + past participle. It often describes something that happens suddenly, or something bad. Questions and negatives need do: "Did he get hurt?" "She didn't get paid."

Some get forms are fixed phrases: get married, get dressed, get lost, get started. They are very common.

Keep the get passive for speech and informal messages. In a report, use be. Write "Three servers were damaged", not "Three servers got damaged".

Have something done

I cut my hair.

I did it myself.

I had my hair cut.

Someone else did it for me. I asked and paid.

The form is have + object + past participle. It is called the causative. Use it for a service that someone does for you. Have takes any tense.

  • We're having the office painted this week.
  • I need to have my eyes tested.
  • Have you had the car repaired yet?
  • I'll get my laptop fixed tomorrow. (informal: get)

The same form can describe a bad experience. Nobody arranged it. "She had her phone stolen." This means her phone was stolen. It happened to her.

Two related forms name the worker.

  • have + person + base form: "I'll have my assistant call you." This is more common in American English.
  • get + person + to + base form: "I got my brother to fix the sink." This often means you persuaded the person.

I cut my hair at the hairdresser's yesterday.

I had repaired my car.

I got my brother fix it.

I had my hair cut at the hairdresser's yesterday.

I had my car repaired.

I got my brother to fix it.

Word order changes the meaning. "I had my car repaired" is the causative. "I had repaired my car" is the past perfect. It means I did the work myself, earlier.

It is said that ...: reporting with the passive

It is said that the castle is haunted.

The castle is said to be haunted.

News reports often use this form. It reports what people in general say or believe. The writer does not say who. The writer also does not say that the claim is true.

There are two patterns with the same meaning.

  • It + passive verb + that + clause: "It is believed that the fire started in the kitchen."
  • Subject + passive verb + to-infinitive: "The fire is believed to have started in the kitchen."

Common reporting verbs are say, think, believe, know, report, expect, consider, estimate, claim and allege.

In the second pattern, choose the infinitive by time.

The infinitive after "is said to"
Time of the actionInfinitiveExample
The same time, or a general factto + base formHe is said to be very rich.
In progress nowto be + -ingThe company is thought to be planning job cuts.
Earlierto have + past participleThe thief is believed to have left the country.

He is said that he is rich.

It is said him to be rich.

The thief is believed to leave the country last week.

It is said that he is rich.

He is said to be rich.

The thief is believed to have left the country last week.

Use this form to be careful in writing. "Prices are expected to rise" is softer than "Prices will rise". The chapter Hedging and stance has more ways to be careful.

The passive in reports and technical writing

The samples were heated to 80 degrees. The results were recorded every ten minutes.

Your settings are saved automatically. Old logs are deleted after 30 days.

The outage was caused by an expired certificate. The certificate was renewed at 14:05.

In these texts, the process and the result matter most. The person often does not matter. So the passive is common and natural.

But for instructions, most style guides prefer the active voice. The Google developer documentation style guide says this. It also allows the passive in three cases. Use it to put the result first, or to make the actor less important. Use it when the reader does not need to know the actor.

Unclear passive

The config file should be edited, and the server should be restarted.

Who does it? The reader is not sure.

Clear active

Edit the config file. Then restart the server.

The reader knows what to do.

Start: "The Save button must be clicked before the window is closed."

  1. Find the hidden agent. Who clicks? The reader.
  2. Make the reader the subject. For an instruction, use the imperative.
  3. Put the steps in time order.
  4. Result: "Click Save. Then close the window."

A small passive finder in Python

Some writing tools mark passive sentences. Here is a very small version. It looks for a form of be, then a past participle.

import re

# A form of "be", then maybe one adverb, then a past participle.
BE = r"\b(am|is|are|was|were|be|been|being)\b"
ADVERB = r"(\s+\w+ly)?"
IRREGULAR = "built|done|found|given|known|made|sent|shown|taken|written"
PARTICIPLE = r"\s+(\w+ed|" + IRREGULAR + r")\b"
PASSIVE = re.compile(BE + ADVERB + PARTICIPLE, re.IGNORECASE)

text = """The report was written by the data team.
The service is queried every minute.
We tested the new login page.
Errors are automatically sent to the log.
She is interested in Rust."""

for number, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), start=1):
    match = PASSIVE.search(line)
    if match:
        print(number, "passive?", repr(match.group(0)))
    else:
        print(number, "active")
1 passive? 'was written'
2 passive? 'is queried'
3 active
4 passive? 'are automatically sent'
5 passive? 'is interested'

Line 5 is a false alarm. In "She is interested", interested is an adjective, not a passive verb. A pattern can only guess. A human must check the meaning. The code ran with Python 3.14.

Active or passive? Decide in steps

Does the verb have an object?

No object means no passive. Happen, arrive and die stay active.

What is the topic?

Put the topic at the start of the sentence. If the topic receives the action, use the passive.

The bridge was built in 1890.

Is the agent important?

If yes, name it with by, or use the active. If no, leave it out.

Is it an instruction?

Use the imperative. Write "Restart the server", not "The server should be restarted".

Check the form

Be in the right tense, then the past participle.

has been fixed, is being tested, will be sent

Fine points for higher levels

Phrasal and prepositional verbs

Keep the small word after the verb. "They called off the meeting" becomes "The meeting was called off." "Nobody has looked into the problem" becomes "The problem hasn't been looked into." See Phrasal verbs.

Passive after other verbs

Use the passive infinitive or the passive -ing after other verbs. "Everyone wants to be listened to." "I don't like being told what to do."

Need + -ing

Need + -ing can have a passive meaning. "The car needs washing" means "The car needs to be washed." This form is more common in British English.

Be born

Born is almost always passive in this meaning. Say "I was born in 1995", not "I born in 1995".

State or action?

"The shop was closed" can be a state or an action. As a state, the door was not open. As an action, someone closed it. Context decides. "The shop was closed at six by the manager" is clearly an action.

There is said to be

With there, use "there is said to be" or "there are thought to be". "There are thought to be 200 species in the lake." This style is typical of news and science writing.

Passive and dense writing

Formal writing often joins the passive with nouns made from verbs. "The decision was made to close the office." The chapter Participle clauses and nominalisation explains this style.

The Cambridge B1 Preliminary handbook lists the present simple and past simple passive, the modal passive, and causative have and get. It also lists give, send, show and similar verbs with two objects. The British Council puts the "it is believed that" passive at C1 level. In exam rewrite tasks, check the tense of be first. Check the official handbook before your exam, because lists can change.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the passive
PatternPurposeModelNote
subject + am, is or are + past participleDescribe a general process or factThe office is cleaned every day.Only verbs with an object have a passive.
subject + was or were + past participleReport a finished past eventMy bike was stolen last night.Never "was happened".
subject + has or have been + past participleGive news or a result nowThe bug has been fixed.Not "has fixed": that is active.
subject + is or are being + past participleDescribe a passive action in progressThe office is being painted.Keep being before the participle.
subject + will be + past participleSay what will happen to somethingThe results will be published on Monday.Going to be + participle is also correct.
... + by + agentName a new and important agentThe song was written by two students.Do not write "by someone" or "by people".
modal + be + past participleState a rule or a possibilityThe form must be signed.Never "must signed".
modal + have been + past participleGuess or judge a past passive eventThe file might have been deleted.Have been, not "be been".
person + was given or sent + thingUse a verb with two objectsI was sent the wrong file.Not with explain: "was explained to me".
get + past participleTell an informal story about a sudden or bad eventHe got hurt playing football.Use be in formal writing.
have + object + past participleSay that someone did a service for youI had my laptop repaired.Not "I had repaired my laptop".
have + object + past participle (bad event)Describe a bad experienceShe had her phone stolen.Nobody arranged it.
It is said or believed that + clauseReport a general beliefIt is believed that prices will rise.Common in news and reports.
subject + is said or thought to + infinitiveReport a belief about a person or thingHe is thought to have left.Use to have + participle for an earlier action.

Practice

Choose the right answer

Which sentence is correct?

  • The letter sent yesterday.
  • The letter was sent yesterday.
  • The letter was send yesterday.

The passive needs be in the right tense and the past participle: was sent.

The road ___ at the moment, so take the other way.

  • is repaired
  • is being repaired
  • has repaired

"At the moment" shows an action in progress. Use is being + past participle.

Which verb has no passive form?

  • send
  • build
  • happen

Happen has no object, so it cannot be passive.

"I had my car washed." What does it mean?

  • I washed my car.
  • Someone washed my car for me.
  • I had washed my car before something else.

Have + object + past participle is the causative. Someone else did the work.

Which sentence is best for a user guide?

  • The password should be entered by the user.
  • Enter your password.
  • The password is entered.

Instructions are clearer in the active voice, with the imperative.

The painter is believed ___ in Paris in 1850.

  • to be born
  • to have been born
  • that he was born

The birth was earlier than the belief. Use to have + past participle.

Write the passive form

English (speak) in many countries.

The first iPhone (release) in 2007.

Your order (ship). It will arrive tomorrow.

The new bridge (open) next year.

This form must (sign) by your manager.

I am going to have my hair (cut) on Saturday.

It (say) that the old house is haunted.

Think and write

  1. Make it passive. Leave out the agent if it adds nothing. "Someone has taken my umbrella."
    Answer

    "My umbrella has been taken." "By someone" adds nothing, so leave it out.

  2. Correct the mistake: "The meeting was happened in Room 4."
    Answer

    "The meeting happened in Room 4." You can also say "The meeting was held in Room 4." Happen has no passive.

  3. Write two passive sentences from "The school gave every student a laptop."
    Answer

    "Every student was given a laptop." and "A laptop was given to every student." The first is more common.

  4. Explain the difference: "I repaired my bike." and "I had my bike repaired."
    Answer

    In the first sentence, I did the work. In the second, someone else did it for me. I arranged it.

  5. Rewrite in two ways with the reporting passive. "People think that the company is losing money."
    Answer

    "It is thought that the company is losing money." and "The company is thought to be losing money." The action is in progress, so use to be + -ing.

  6. Rewrite this instruction in the active voice: "The cable should be connected and the power should then be switched on."
    Answer

    "Connect the cable. Then switch on the power." The imperative tells the reader what to do.

  7. Write a short incident report of three sentences. Use one present perfect passive, one past simple passive and one modal passive.
    Sample answer

    "The login problem has been fixed. It was caused by an expired certificate. Certificates should be checked every month."

What is the basic form of the passive?

be + past participle

Where do you see the tense of a passive verb?

In be: is, was, has been, will be.

Present perfect passive of "fix"?

has been fixed, have been fixed

Modal passive of "must sign"?

must be signed

"I cut my hair" or "I had my hair cut": a hairdresser did it?

I had my hair cut.

Why can't you say "was happened"?

Happen has no object, so it has no passive.

"He is said ___ (leave) yesterday."

to have left

Key takeaways

  • The passive is be + past participle. The tense lives in be.
  • Only verbs with an object have a passive form.
  • Use the passive when the agent is unknown, clear or not important, or when the result is the topic.
  • Add by + agent only when the agent is new and important.
  • Modal passives are modal + be + past participle, or modal + have been + past participle.
  • Have something done means someone else does it for you.
  • "It is said that" and "is said to" report beliefs in news and formal writing.
  • Reports often use the passive. Instructions should use the active voice.

Sources

  • Active and passive voice, British Council LearnEnglish. The form in each tense, by + agent, two objects, the get passive and phrasal verbs.
  • Advanced passives review, British Council LearnEnglish. Modal passives and the impersonal passive with reporting verbs at C1.
  • Active voice, Google developer documentation style guide. Why instructions prefer the active, and when the passive is fine.
  • B1 Preliminary handbook for teachers, Cambridge English. The exam owner's list of passive forms, causative have and get, and verbs with two objects.

Reported speech

Every day you tell people what other people said. "The client said the deadline was Friday." This is reported speech. This chapter shows how the verbs, pronouns and time words change, and how to report questions, orders and promises.

  • Choose between say and tell.
  • Move the tense back one step, and know when not to.
  • Change pronouns, time words and place words in a report.
  • Report questions, commands and requests with the right word order.
  • Use reporting verbs like admit, suggest, promise and warn with their patterns.

Two ways to give someone's words

Ana (Monday): "I'm tired. I'm going home."

You (Tuesday): Ana said she was tired. She said she was going home.

There are two ways to give Ana's words. Direct speech uses her exact words. Reported speech uses your words. Reported speech is also called indirect speech.

A reporting verb starts the report. Said is the most common one. After it comes a clause with the content: "she was tired".

Direct speech

Ana said, "I'm tired."

Her exact words. Quotation marks.

Reported speech

Ana said (that) she was tired.

No quotation marks. I becomes she. Am becomes was.

Writing direct speech

Put the exact words inside quotation marks. British books often use single marks: 'Hello.' American English uses double marks: "Hello." Both are correct. Choose one style and keep it.

  • Put a comma before the words: Tom said, "Let's start."
  • Or put a comma inside the end mark: "Let's start," Tom said.
  • A question mark stays inside: "Are you ready?" she asked.

Stories sometimes put the verb first: "Wait," said Tom. This order works with a name or a noun. With a pronoun, keep the normal order: "Wait," he said.

Direct speech copies the words. Reported speech retells them. When you retell, the words change to fit your time and your point of view.

Say and tell

She said that the server was down.

She told me that the server was down.

She said to me that the server was down.

All three sentences mean the same. But the grammar is different. Tell needs a person right after it. Say does not take a person. If you name the person after say, use to.

Say and tell: the patterns
VerbPatternExample
saysay + (that) + clauseHe said (that) he was busy.
saysay + something + to + personHe said hello to everyone.
telltell + person + (that) + clauseHe told me (that) he was busy.
telltell + person + to + verbHe told me to wait.
telltell + person + about + nounHe told us about the new release.

Some phrases always use tell, even without a person: tell the truth, tell a lie, tell a story, tell a joke, tell the time, tell the difference. Some phrases always use say: say hello, say goodbye, say sorry, say yes, say no, say a word.

She said me that she was busy.

He told that the build was green.

Can you say me the time?

She told me that she was busy.

He said that the build was green.

Can you tell me the time?

"Say me" is never correct. Ask yourself: is there a person right after the verb? Then use tell.

Can you leave out that?

Yes, often. In speech, people usually drop that after say and tell. "She said she was busy." Keep that after verbs like reply, explain and complain. Keep it in long or formal sentences too.

Tense backshift: one step back

"I work in Berlin." → He said he worked in Berlin.

"I'm fixing the bug." → She said she was fixing the bug.

"We have finished." → They said they had finished.

"I will call you." → He said he would call me.

The reporting verb said is in the past. So the verb after it often moves one step back in time. This is called backshift. Present becomes past. Past becomes past perfect.

The full backshift table
Direct speechReported speechExample
present simplepast simple"I like it." → She said she liked it.
present continuouspast continuous"I'm working." → She said she was working.
present perfectpast perfect"I've seen it." → She said she had seen it.
present perfect continuouspast perfect continuous"I've been waiting." → She said she had been waiting.
past simplepast perfect (often optional)"I saw him." → She said she had seen him.
past continuouspast perfect continuous"I was sleeping." → She said she had been sleeping.
past perfectno change"I had left." → She said she had left.
am, is, are going towas, were going to"I'm going to quit." → She said she was going to quit.

Modal verbs

A modal verb changes too. But only some modals change.

Modal verbs in reported speech
DirectReportedExample
willwould"I'll help." → He said he would help.
cancould"I can swim." → He said he could swim.
maymight"It may rain." → He said it might rain.
must (rule)had to, or must"You must sign here." → He said I had to sign there.
shall (offer)offered to, asked if ... should"Shall I carry it?" → He offered to carry it.
would, could, should, might, ought tono change"You should rest." → He said I should rest.

The chapter Modal verbs explains each modal. The chapter The perfect tenses explains the past perfect.

He said he will call me yesterday.

She said she can't come to the party last week.

He said he would call me.

She said she couldn't come to the party.

When the tense does not change

The teacher said the Earth goes round the Sun.

Mia says she's on the train. (She just sent a message.)

Tom told me he lives in Leeds. (He still lives there.)

Backshift is common. But it is not a law. The tense rules in a report are the same as everywhere in English. You use the tense that fits the facts now. Here are the cases with no change.

  • The reporting verb is in the present. "The manager says we can leave early." Use says for news that is fresh, or for a text that still exists.
  • The fact is still true. "She said she works at Google." She still works there. Both "works" and "worked" are correct. "Worked" says nothing about now.
  • It is a general truth. "He said water boils at 100 degrees." Science and facts stay in the present.
  • The verb cannot move back. The past perfect, would, could, should and might stay the same.
  • The time order is clear. "She said she left at six." In speech, many people keep the past simple. In exams, the past perfect is safer.

Still true

Ben said he is 30.

Ben is 30 now. You report it the same day.

Not true now, or not sure

Ben said he was 30.

You do not know about now. Or it was a long time ago.

Do not keep the present when the fact is false now. Tom said last year, "I'm a student." Now he works. Say "Tom said he was a student." Do not say "Tom said he is a student."

Not sure? Use backshift. It is always correct after said. Keeping the present is a choice, not a rule.

Pronouns, time words and place words

Words like I, here and tomorrow point to the speaker's own place and time. They are called pointing words in this chapter. When you report later, or in another place, they change.

Monday, in the office, Tom says: "I'll fix this bug here tomorrow."

  1. Change the pronoun. I becomes he. "He'll fix this bug here tomorrow."
  2. Move the verb back. Will becomes would. "He would fix this bug here tomorrow."
  3. Change this. You are not near the bug now. "He would fix that bug here tomorrow."
  4. Change the place. You are at home now. "He would fix that bug there tomorrow."
  5. Change the time. Tomorrow is now in the past. "He would fix that bug there the next day."
  6. Add the reporting verb. "Tom said he would fix that bug there the next day."
Common changes to pointing words
DirectReported (later, or in another place)
nowthen, at that time
today, tonightthat day, that night
yesterdaythe day before, the previous day
tomorrowthe next day, the following day
last weekthe week before, the previous week
next weekthe week after, the following week
two days agotwo days before, two days earlier
this, thesethat, those (or the)
herethere
I, me, my, we, ourhe, she, they, his, her, their (the new point of view)

Use common sense. Change a word only when the time or place is really different. Tom speaks on Monday morning. You report it on Monday afternoon. Then say "Tom said he would fix it tomorrow". Tomorrow is still tomorrow.

(Reported a week later) She said she would send it tomorrow.

(Reported a week later) She said she would send it the next day.

Do not forget the pronouns. "My laptop is broken," said Ana. The report is "Ana said her laptop was broken". It is not "Ana said my laptop was broken". That means your laptop.

Reported questions

Interviewer: "Where do you live?"

Interviewer: "Have you used Kubernetes?"

You, later: She asked me where I lived. She asked if I had used Kubernetes.

A reported question is not a question anymore. It is a statement about a question. So it uses statement word order: subject, then verb. There is no do, does or did. There is no question mark.

Pattern 15 on the page The 15 sentence patterns builds a question with do or does. In a reported question, that do or does disappears. The order goes back to pattern 1: subject + verb.

Yes or no questions: if or whether

"Are you free?" → He asked if I was free.

"Does it work on Linux?" → She asked whether it worked on Linux.

Use if or whether. They mean the same here. If is more common in speech. Whether is a little more formal.

Wh- questions: keep the question word

"Why did you leave?" → They asked why I had left.

"How much does it cost?" → I asked how much it cost.

Keep the question word. Then use subject + verb.

Subject questions

"Who broke the build?" → The lead asked who had broken the build.

Here who is the subject. The order is already subject + verb. So only the tense changes.

She asked me where did I live.

He asked me was I free?

They asked what time was it.

She asked me where I lived.

He asked me if I was free.

They asked what time it was.

Other verbs for questions

  • ask: the most common. "She asked (me) if I was ready."
  • want to know: neutral. "He wanted to know when the meeting started."
  • wonder: a question in your head. "I wondered why nobody answered."
  • enquire: formal. "The customer enquired whether the item was in stock."

The same order works in polite questions with no backshift. "Could you tell me where the station is?" "Do you know if the shop is open?" The chapter Questions and negatives calls these indirect questions.

Do not use a question mark after a reported question. "She asked where I lived." It ends with a full stop. Only a polite question like "Do you know where she lives?" needs a question mark.

Reported commands and requests

"Wait here." → The guard told us to wait there.

"Don't touch the cable." → She told me not to touch the cable.

"Could you send me the file?" → He asked me to send him the file.

"Can I borrow your charger?" → She asked if she could borrow my charger.

A command uses the imperative. To report it, use tell + person + to + verb. For a negative command, put not before to. For a polite request, use ask + person + to + verb.

Reporting orders, requests and offers
DirectKindReported
"Close the door."orderShe told me to close the door.
"Don't be late."negative orderShe told us not to be late.
"Please call me back."requestHe asked me to call him back.
"Can I have a coffee, please?"request for a thingHe asked for a coffee.
"Can I go now?"asking permissionHe asked if he could go.
"Shall I help you?"offerShe offered to help me.
"Log out before you leave."instructionIT reminded us to log out before we left.

Stronger verbs show more force. Order and instruct come from a boss or a rule. Beg shows a very strong request. Remind means the person knew but might forget.

He told me don't touch it.

She said me to wait.

They asked to me to help.

He told me not to touch it.

She told me to wait.

They asked me to help.

In casual speech you hear "She said to wait here." It means "She told us to wait here". It is fine in speech. In writing and exams, use tell or ask with a person.

Reporting verbs and their patterns

"I broke the printer. Sorry." → He admitted breaking the printer.

"Let's order pizza." → She suggested ordering pizza.

"I'll finish it tonight. I promise." → He promised to finish it that night.

"Don't open that email. It's a scam." → She warned me not to open the email.

A good report gives the meaning, not every word. A said sentence can be long and flat. A precise reporting verb is short and clear. It also shows the speaker's purpose: a promise, a warning, an apology.

Each reporting verb has its own pattern. You must learn the verb and its pattern together. The tree shows the main groups. Some verbs belong to more than one group.

Four verbs to know well

admit

He admitted taking the money.

He admitted (that) he had taken it.

He admitted to taking it.

Say yes to something bad or embarrassing.

suggest

She suggested taking a break.

She suggested (that) we take a break.

She suggested (that) we should take a break.

Give an idea. Never "suggest someone to".

promise

He promised to call.

He promised (me) (that) he would call.

Say you will surely do something.

warn

She warned me not to click it.

She warned (me) that it was a scam.

She warned us about the risks.

Tell someone about a danger.

After suggest that, the verb is often the base form: "we take", "he take". This is a special formal form. The chapter Subjunctive and unreal past explains it. British English often adds should: "he should take".

More reporting verbs and their patterns
VerbPatternExample
agreeto + verb, or thatShe agreed to review my code.
offerto + verbHe offered to drive us.
refuseto + verbThe client refused to pay.
threatento + verbThey threatened to cancel the contract.
adviseperson + to + verbThe doctor advised me to rest.
remindperson + to + verbRemind me to send the invoice.
encourageperson + to + verbMy manager encouraged me to apply.
deny-ing, or thatHe denied deleting the file.
recommend-ing, or thatShe recommended using a password manager.
apologise(to person) for + -ingHe apologised for being late.
insiston + -ing, or thatShe insisted on paying.
accuseperson + of + -ingThey accused him of lying.
explain(to person) that, or wh-She explained to me how it worked.
complain(to person) about, or thatUsers complained that the app was slow.

He suggested me to take a break.

She denied to take the money.

He explained me the problem.

She apologised to be late.

He suggested (that) I take a break.

She denied taking the money.

He explained the problem to me.

She apologised for being late.

The chapter Verb patterns: -ing and to shows these patterns for many more verbs.

Verbs that show an opinion

Some reporting verbs are neutral. Others show your view of the speaker.

  • said, stated, explained: neutral. You only report.
  • claimed: maybe it is not true. "He claimed he had sent the email."
  • admitted: it was something bad. "She admitted she had forgotten."
  • insisted: the speaker was very firm. "He insisted he was right."
  • pointed out: a true and useful fact. "She pointed out that the test was flaky."

Do not use claim when you believe the speaker. "The vendor claimed the fix was ready" sounds like you doubt them. Use said or confirmed if you trust them.

Reporting at work: one stand-up, step by step

At work, you report speech all the time. You write meeting notes. You update people who missed a call. The slides follow one stand-up. Each slide shows the direct words and a good report.

A statement

Lena: "I've finished the login page."

Lena said she had finished the login page.

A plan

Lena: "I'm going to start the tests today."

She said she was going to start the tests that day.

A yes or no question

Omar: "Is the API ready?"

Omar asked if the API was ready.

A wh- question

Omar: "When can we deploy?"

He wanted to know when we could deploy.

An admission

Sam: "Sorry. I forgot to update the docs."

Sam admitted forgetting to update the docs.

A suggestion

Sam: "Let's move the demo to Friday."

Sam suggested moving the demo to Friday.

A request

Lead: "Please review Sam's pull request."

The lead asked us to review Sam's pull request.

A warning

Lead: "Don't merge anything before the release."

She warned us not to merge anything before the release.

Reporting texts and messages

Texts that still exist usually take a present reporting verb. "The docs say the flag is optional." "The error message says the file is missing." "Your email says you can start on Monday." The words are still there, so the present fits.

Live chat and meeting notes often use the present too, for fresh news. "Ana says the build is green." Use the past for a finished event: "In the meeting, Ana said the build was green."

Fine points for higher levels

It is said that, he is said to

News often reports without a speaker. "It is said that the company is for sale." "The company is said to be for sale." These are passive reports. See The passive.

Reporting with nouns

Formal writing turns a reporting verb into a noun. "He claimed that ..." becomes "his claim that ...". "The announcement that the office would close surprised everyone." Other nouns: promise, warning, suggestion, request, advice.

According to

Use according to + a source. "According to the report, sales fell by 10%." Do not use it with your own opinion. "According to me" is wrong. Say "In my opinion".

Whether or not, whether to

Whether can take or not: "She asked whether or not I agreed." Before a to verb, use whether, not if: "I asked whether to restart the server." Question words work the same way: "He asked me how to fix it."

Come and go, bring and take

The point of view can change these verbs. Ana in Paris says, "Come to Paris!" You report it in London: "Ana asked me to go to Paris." The place word changes with the speaker.

Free indirect speech

Novels sometimes mix the two styles. "She looked at the screen. Why was the test still failing? She had fixed it twice." The thoughts use past tenses but no reporting verb. You only need to recognise this style when you read.

Cambridge B2 First and C1 Advanced have a key word transformation task. You rewrite a sentence with a given word. Reporting verbs fit this task very well. For example, rewrite "Let's go by train," said Ann, with SUGGESTED: "Ann suggested going by train." Check the official handbook for the current format. See Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for reported speech
PatternPurposeModelNote
say + (that) + clauseReport a statementShe said the server was down.No person right after say.
tell + person + (that) + clauseReport a statement to someoneShe told me the server was down.Tell always needs the person.
said + past formReport words from the pastHe said he worked in Berlin.Move the verb one step back.
says + present formReport fresh news or a textThe docs say the flag is optional.No backshift after a present verb.
said + would, could, mightReport will, can, mayShe said she would help.Would, could, should, might never change.
ask + if or whether + subject + verbReport a yes or no questionHe asked if I was free.No do, no question mark.
ask + question word + subject + verbReport a wh- questionShe asked where I lived.Not "where did I live".
tell + person + (not) to + verbReport an orderHe told me not to touch it.Not "told me don't".
ask + person + to + verbReport a requestShe asked me to send the file.Not "asked to me".
admit or deny + -ingReport yes or no to a bad actHe denied deleting the file.Not "denied to delete".
suggest + -ing, or suggest that + subject + verbReport an ideaShe suggested taking a break.Never "suggest someone to".
promise or offer + to + verbReport a promise or an offerHe promised to call me.The to verb follows directly.
warn + person + (not) to + verbReport a warningShe warned me not to click it.Also warn someone that, or about.
apologise for + -ingReport an apologyHe apologised for being late.A preposition takes -ing.

Practice

Choose the right answer

She ___ me that the meeting was cancelled.

  • said
  • told
  • asked

A person (me) comes right after the verb. So use told.

"I am hungry," said Tom. → Tom said he ___ hungry.

  • is being
  • was
  • has been

After said, the present simple usually moves back to the past simple.

"Where do you work?" → She asked me ___.

  • where do I work
  • where did I work
  • where I worked

A reported question uses statement order and no do or did.

"Don't park here." → The guard told us ___ there.

  • don't park
  • not to park
  • to not parking

A negative order becomes tell + person + not to + verb.

Which sentence is correct?

  • He suggested me to try again.
  • He suggested trying again.
  • He suggested to try again.

Suggest takes -ing, or a that clause. It never takes a to verb.

Your colleague said yesterday, "The office closes at six." It still does. Which report is fine?

  • She said the office closed at six.
  • She said the office closes at six.
  • Both are fine.

The fact is still true. So you can keep the present or use backshift.

Write the missing words

"I can't come." → Ben said he (can't / come).

"I have lost my keys." → She said she (lose) her keys.

"Are you ready?" → He asked (I / be) ready.

"Please close the window." → She asked me (close) the window.

"I'll see you tomorrow." (reported a week later) → He said he would see me (tomorrow).

"Sorry I'm late." → He apologised (be) late.

"You stole my idea!" → She accused him (steal) her idea.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "He said me that he was tired."
    Answer

    "He told me that he was tired." Or "He said that he was tired." Say does not take a person directly.

  2. Correct the mistake: "She asked me what time did the train leave?"
    Answer

    "She asked me what time the train left." Use statement order, no did and no question mark.

  3. Report this, one month later: "I'm moving to Tokyo next week," Kenji said.
    Answer

    "Kenji said he was moving to Tokyo the following week." Or "the week after". The verb moves back and next week changes.

  4. Report with a verb from this chapter, not said: "I didn't take your charger!" said Leo.
    Answer

    "Leo denied taking my charger." Also correct: "Leo denied that he had taken my charger."

  5. Report with a verb from this chapter: "Don't use the old API. It will stop working in May," the architect said.
    Answer

    "The architect warned us not to use the old API. She said it would stop working in May." In a report the same week, "will stop" is also possible.

  6. Explain the difference: "He said he is ill." and "He said he was ill."
    Answer

    The first says he is still ill now. The second only reports his words. It says nothing about now.

  7. Write two lines of meeting notes from this: Client: "Can you add a dark mode? We'd like it before June."
    Sample answer

    "The client asked if we could add a dark mode. They said they would like it before June." Or shorter: "The client asked us to add a dark mode before June."

Say or tell: "___ me the truth."

Tell. Tell the truth, and a person comes next.

Backshift of "will"?

would

Backshift of the present perfect?

past perfect: has done becomes had done

Report: "Is it free?"

She asked if it was free.

Report: "Don't be late."

He told us not to be late.

Pattern after suggest?

suggest + -ing, or suggest that + subject + verb

"tomorrow", reported later?

the next day, or the following day

Key takeaways

  • Say takes no person. Tell needs a person: tell me, tell her.
  • After said, move the verb one step back: present to past, past to past perfect, will to would.
  • Keep the present when the fact is still true, or after a present verb like says.
  • Change pronouns, time words and place words only when the point of view really changes.
  • Reported questions use if, whether or a question word, then subject + verb. No question mark.
  • Report orders with tell + person + (not) to, and requests with ask + person + to.
  • Learn each reporting verb with its pattern: admit -ing, suggest -ing, promise to, warn someone not to.
