  • Reported speech: statements, British Council LearnEnglish. The backshift table and changes to pronouns, time and place words.
  • Reported speech: questions, British Council LearnEnglish. If and whether, word order and verbs like enquire and wonder.
  • Reported speech: reporting verbs, British Council LearnEnglish. Verbs with to, with person + to, with -ing and with a preposition.
  • Reported speech, British Council LearnEnglish Teens. Commands with to and not to, and common sense with time words.
  • say, Oxford Learner's Dictionaries. Say never takes a person as its object.

Relative clauses

A relative clause adds information about a noun. "The developer who wrote this code has left." It tells you which person or thing, or it adds an extra fact. Relative clauses join short sentences into one clear sentence.

  • Choose who, which, that, whose, where, when and what.
  • Tell defining and non-defining clauses apart, and use commas correctly.
  • Leave out the relative pronoun when it is allowed.
  • Put prepositions in the right place in formal and informal English.
  • Shorten relative clauses with -ing, past participles and to + verb.

What a relative clause does

I have a colleague. She speaks five languages.

→ I have a colleague who speaks five languages.

This is the laptop. I bought it last week.

→ This is the laptop that I bought last week.

Two short sentences become one. The second part now describes a noun in the first part. This part is a relative clause. It starts with a relative pronoun: who, which, that or whose.

The relative clause comes right after its noun. It works like a long adjective. "A red car" puts the adjective before the noun. "A car that uses no petrol" puts the clause after it.

You already know this shape. It is pattern 11 on the page The 15 sentence patterns: Noun + who, which, or that + information. The model there is "I need a course that fits my schedule." This chapter takes pattern 11 all the way to C1 level.

This is the laptop that I bought it last week.

The man who he called me was angry.

This is the laptop that I bought last week.

The man who called me was angry.

The relative pronoun replaces a word. Do not keep the old word too. That already means "the laptop". So "that I bought it" says the laptop twice. Many languages repeat it. English does not.

Where does the clause end?

A relative clause can sit in the middle of a sentence. Find the main verb to see the end.

The tests that failed last night are fixed now.

The subject is "the tests". The clause "that failed last night" describes it. The main verb is "are". It agrees with "tests", not with "night".

Who, which, that and whose

The engineer who fixed the bug is new.

The bug which crashed the app is fixed.

The bug that crashed the app is fixed.

The user whose account was locked called us.

Choose the word by the noun before it.

The main relative words
WordUse it forExample
whopeoplethe woman who lives next door
whichthings and animalsthe app which I use every day
thatpeople or things (defining clauses only)the app that I use every day
whosebelonging: his, her, its, theira company whose office is in Leeds
whompeople, as an object (formal)the person to whom I spoke
whereplacesthe city where I was born
whentimesthe day when we met
whyafter the reasonthe reason why he left

That

That is very common. It works for people and things. In everyday English, it is more common than who or which in defining clauses. But that has two limits. It cannot follow a comma. It cannot follow a preposition.

Whose

I met a developer. Her app has a million users.

→ I met a developer whose app has a million users.

Whose replaces his, her, its or their. A noun always follows it: whose app, whose car. It works for people and for things. "A library whose code is open" is correct.

Who or whom?

Whom is the object form of who. It is formal. In speech, people use who or that, or no pronoun. After a preposition, you must use whom: "the manager to whom I report". Never write "to who".

The man which lives here is a doctor.

I met a woman who's car was stolen.

The person to who I wrote never replied.

The man who lives here is a doctor.

I met a woman whose car was stolen.

The person to whom I wrote never replied.

Who's means "who is" or "who has". Whose shows belonging. They sound the same. "Who's ready?" but "Whose laptop is this?"

Where, when and why

This is the café where we first met.

I remember the day when the servers went down.

That's the reason why I left.

Where follows a place. When follows a time. Why follows the noun reason. These words are relative adverbs. They mean "in which", "at which" or "for which".

  • the café where we met = the café at which we met
  • the year when I started = the year in which I started
  • the reason why he left = the reason for which he left

You can often leave out when and why. You can also use that. "The day (that) we met." "The reason (that) he left."

Where or which?

where

This is the city where I work.

"I work in the city." The verb has no object. Where = in which.

which, that, or nothing

This is the city (that) I visited.

"I visited the city." The city is the object of visited.

Test it. Put the noun back into the clause. If you need in, at or to, use where. If the noun is a plain object, use which or that.

This is the city where I visited last year.

The reason because he left is a secret.

This is the city (that) I visited last year.

The reason (why) he left is a secret.

Defining and non-defining clauses

My brother who lives in Paris is a chef.

My brother, who lives in Paris, is a chef.

The words are the same. Only the commas change. But the meaning is different.

Defining

The students who passed got a certificate.

Only some students passed. The clause tells you which ones. Without it, the sentence changes meaning.

  • no commas
  • who, which, that
  • you can sometimes drop the pronoun

Non-defining

The students, who all passed, got a certificate.

All the students passed. The clause adds a fact. Without it, the sentence still works.

  • commas before and after
  • who, which, whose, where, when
  • never that, never drop the pronoun

A defining clause is needed to know which noun you mean. A non-defining clause adds extra information. It often follows a name, or a noun that is already clear. "Python, which is free, is popular." There is only one Python. So the clause cannot define it.

In speech, a non-defining clause has small pauses around it. In writing, the pauses become commas. Non-defining clauses are more common in writing than in speech.

Python, that is free, is popular.

My mother who lives in Rome is a teacher.

The office, which we use, is in the centre.

Python, which is free, is popular.

My mother, who lives in Rome, is a teacher.

The office that we use is in the centre.

You have only one mother. So "my mother who lives in Rome" sounds like you have two mothers. Add the commas.

A non-defining clause needs two commas: one before, and one after. Only the end of the sentence can replace the second comma. "My manager, who is from Spain, speaks four languages." Do not forget the second comma.

Which about a whole idea

The train was late, which meant I missed the meeting.

Here which does not describe a noun. It describes the whole first clause: the train was late. Always put a comma before this which. Do not use what or that here.

He passed the exam, what surprised everyone.

He passed the exam, which surprised everyone.

Leaving out the pronoun

The book (that) you lent me is great.

The people (who) we met were friendly.

The man who called you is here.

In a defining clause, you can leave out the pronoun when it is the object. It cannot go when it is the subject.

How do you know? Look at the next word. If a new subject follows the pronoun, it is the object. You can drop it. If a verb follows the pronoun, it is the subject. You must keep it.

Can you drop the pronoun?
SentenceNext wordDrop it?
the file that you sentyou (a subject)Yes: the file you sent
the file that broke the buildbroke (a verb)No
the woman who I work withI (a subject)Yes: the woman I work with
the woman who works with meworks (a verb)No
my car, which I love, ...non-definingNo, never

The man lives next door is a pilot.

My laptop, I bought in May, is broken.

The man who lives next door is a pilot.

My laptop, which I bought in May, is broken.

In speech, native speakers drop object pronouns most of the time. "The film I saw", "the guy I told you about". Learn to hear these clauses. There is no that to warn you.

Sentences: "We hired a designer. You recommended her."

  1. Find the shared person. "A designer" and "her" are the same person.
  2. Replace "her" with a relative pronoun. "You recommended who." A person, so who or that.
  3. Move the pronoun to the start of the clause. "who you recommended"
  4. Put the clause right after the noun. "We hired a designer who you recommended."
  5. Defining or non-defining? It tells you which designer. So no commas.
  6. Is the pronoun an object? Yes. "You" follows it. So you may drop it: "We hired the designer you recommended."

Prepositions in relative clauses

This is the colleague I told you about.

This is the colleague who I told you about.

This is the colleague about whom I told you.

All three are correct. The first one is the most common in speech. The last one is very formal.

  • Informal: the preposition goes at the end. "the team (that) I work for"
  • Formal: the preposition goes before whom or which. "the team for which I work"
  • After a preposition, use only whom or which. Never that, never who.

The project on that I worked was cancelled.

The client with who I spoke was happy.

The house in which I live in is old.

The project (that) I worked on was cancelled.

The client with whom I spoke was happy.

The house in which I live is old.

Use the preposition only once. If it moves to the front, it is not at the end too. "The house in which I live." Not "in which I live in".

A phrasal verb keeps its small word at the end. "The children (who) she looks after" is correct. "The children after whom she looks" sounds wrong. See Phrasal verbs.

Some of which, most of whom

We tested ten tools, three of which were free.

I have two brothers, both of whom live abroad.

In a non-defining clause, a number or a quantifier can come before of which or of whom. Common ones are some, many, most, all, none, both, neither, one, two. This is useful in reports.

We interviewed 20 people, most of them were developers.

We interviewed 20 people, most of who were developers.

We interviewed 20 people, most of whom were developers.

We interviewed 20 people. Most of them were developers.

"Most of them" needs a new sentence, or a word like and. "Most of whom" joins the clauses by itself.

Formal fixed phrases

Formal and academic writing uses some fixed phrases with which.

  • the way in which: "the way in which users log in"
  • the extent to which: "the extent to which the model is accurate"
  • in which case: "The test may fail, in which case we roll back."
  • by which time: "We arrive at nine, by which time the talk has started."
  • whereby: "a system whereby users vote" (= by which)

Reduced relative clauses

The people waiting outside are clients. (= who are waiting)

The files deleted last week are gone. (= that were deleted)

The book on the table is mine. (= that is on the table)

She was the first person to finish. (= who finished)

Many relative clauses can be shorter. You drop the pronoun and change or drop the verb. This is a reduced relative clause. It is common in news, reports and technical writing.

Four ways to reduce a relative clause
Full clauseReducedRule
the man who is sitting therethe man sitting thereactive verb → -ing
anyone who wants a ticketanyone wanting a ticketactive verb → -ing
the data that was collected in Maythe data collected in Maypassive → past participle
the keys that are in the drawerthe keys in the drawerdrop who, which, that + be
the only person who passedthe only person to passafter first, last, only, next: to + verb

The -ing form shows an active meaning. The past participle shows a passive meaning. Compare them.

-ing: active

a service sending emails

The service sends the emails.

past participle: passive

emails sent by the service

The emails are sent by the service.

Only a subject pronoun can be reduced this way. "The report that Ana wrote" cannot become "the report writing Ana". But you can drop that: "the report Ana wrote".

The man broke the window ran away.

The products making in China are cheap.

The man who broke the window ran away.

The products made in China are cheap.

The -ing form usually describes an action in progress or a general fact. It does not usually replace one finished action. "The man who broke the window" is one finished act. "The man breaking the window" means he is doing it now. Keep the full clause.

The chapter Participle clauses and nominalisation goes further with this style.

What clauses

What I need is a good night's sleep.

I didn't understand what she said.

Show me what you've built.

What means "the thing that" or "the things that". It has no noun before it. The noun is inside what. "What I need" = "the thing that I need". The what clause works like a noun. It can be a subject or an object.

The thing what I need is time.

Everything what he said was true.

This is the tool what I use.

The thing that I need is time. / What I need is time.

Everything (that) he said was true.

This is the tool (that) I use.

Never put what after a noun. After a noun, use that, which or who. After everything, something, anything, nothing and all, use that, or no pronoun.

What for emphasis

I need more tests. → What I need is more tests.

We called the client. → What we did was call the client.

A what clause + be puts the focus on the last part. It is common in speech and in presentations. "What I want to show you today is our new dashboard." The chapter Inversion and emphasis calls these cleft sentences.

Whoever, whatever, wherever

These words mean "any person who", "anything that", "any place where".

  • Whoever breaks the build buys coffee.
  • You can choose whatever framework you like.
  • We can meet wherever you like.

Relative clauses at work

Technical writing uses relative clauses all the time. They define things exactly. Look at these lines from imaginary docs.

  • Write a function that returns the total price.
  • Users whose password has expired must reset it.
  • Requests sent without a token are rejected.
  • The config file, which lives in the root folder, sets the port.
  • This is the step where most new users get stuck.

The slides build one sentence step by step. Each step adds a relative clause.

Start

We fixed the bug.

A simple sentence: subject, verb, object.

Define the bug

We fixed the bug that crashed the app.

A defining clause. It tells you which bug.

Add a person

We fixed the bug that crashed the app for users who logged in with Google.

A second defining clause, with who.

Shorten it

We fixed the bug that crashed the app for users logging in with Google.

A reduced clause. "who logged in" becomes "logging in".

Add an extra fact

We fixed the bug, which took two days, ...

A non-defining clause about the whole fix. Use commas.

Check and split

We fixed the bug that crashed the app for Google users. It took two days.

Too many clauses are hard to read. Two short sentences are often better.

British English uses both that and which in defining clauses. Many American style guides ask for that only. So "the bug which crashed the app" is fine in British English. In American company docs, write "the bug that crashed the app". With commas, always use which.

Fine points for higher levels

One of the people who ...

"She is one of the engineers who know Rust." Here who refers to "the engineers", a plural. So the verb is plural: know. Many speakers say knows. In exams and careful writing, use the plural.

Of which or whose for things

"A house whose roof is red" is correct. Very formal English can say "a house the roof of which is red". Most people prefer whose, or a different sentence: "a house with a red roof".

Two clauses on one noun

"The only course I know that teaches Rust is online." The first clause (I know) has no pronoun. The second one (that teaches Rust) does. This stacking is normal, but keep it short.

Sentence relative with a noun

Formal writing can use which + noun about a whole idea. "The vote may be delayed, in which case we will wait." "He said nothing, which fact surprised us" is old style. Use "which surprised us" today.

Where in abstract places

Where also works with "situations", "cases" and "points". "There are cases where the cache is empty." It means "in which". This is normal in technical English.

The British Council lists defining and non-defining relative clauses at B1 to B2 level. Writing exams like IELTS reward a range of complex sentences. One correct non-defining clause with which or whose shows that range. Check the official band descriptors before your exam: they can change. See IELTS Writing.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for relative clauses
PatternPurposeModelNote
Noun + who, which, or that + informationAdd defining detailI need a course that fits my schedule.Choose who for people and which or that for things.
Noun + who + verbSay which personThe engineer who fixed it is new.Keep who when a verb follows.
Noun + (that) + subject + verbSay which thing, short formThe file you sent is empty.Drop the pronoun only when it is the object.
Noun + whose + noun + verbShow belongingA user whose account was locked called.Not who's. A noun follows whose.
Place + where + subject + verbSay which placeThis is the café where we met.Use which or that if the place is an object.
Time + when + subject + verbSay which timeI remember the day when it crashed.You can drop when.
Name, who or which + information,Add an extra factPython, which is free, is popular.Two commas. Never that.
Clause, which + verbComment on a whole ideaThe train was late, which annoyed me.Not "what annoyed me".
Noun + (that) + subject + verb + prepositionInformal preposition at the endthe team I work forMost common in speech.
Noun + preposition + whom or whichFormal preposition at the frontthe team for which I workNever "for that" or "for who".
Number or quantifier + of whom or whichGive part of a groupten tools, three of which were freeNot "three of them" after a comma.
Noun + -ing or past participleShorten a relative clausefiles deleted last week-ing is active, past participle is passive.
the first, last or only + noun + to + verbShorten after first, last or onlyShe was the first to arrive.Not "the first who arrive".
What + subject + verbSay "the thing that"What I need is more time.Never after a noun or everything.

Practice

Choose the right answer

The woman ___ lives upstairs is a nurse.

  • who
  • which
  • whose

A person, and a verb follows. Use who (or that).

I met a man ___ dog had bitten my friend.

  • who
  • who's
  • whose

Whose shows belonging: his dog becomes whose dog.

Which sentence needs commas?

  • The car that I bought is red.
  • My father who is 70 still works.
  • People who smoke get ill more often.

You have only one father. The clause adds an extra fact. Write: My father, who is 70, still works.

In which sentence can you leave out the pronoun?

  • The man who called you is here.
  • The film that we watched was long.
  • The server which crashed is old.

"We" follows "that". So "that" is the object. You can drop it.

This is the town ___ I grew up.

  • which
  • where
  • what

"I grew up in the town." You need "in", so use where.

She failed the test, ___ upset her a lot.

  • what
  • that
  • which

The clause is about the whole idea. After a comma, use which.

Write the missing word

The developer ? wrote this module has left the company.

I can't find the email ? you sent me.

Is this the bag ? was on the train?

I don't understand ? you mean.

We invited 50 people, most of ? came.

The data (collect) last year is out of date.

He was the last person (leave) the office.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "The phone what I bought is broken."
    Answer

    "The phone (that) I bought is broken." Do not use what after a noun.

  2. Correct the mistake: "Linux, that is free, runs on most servers."
    Answer

    "Linux, which is free, runs on most servers." A non-defining clause never uses that.

  3. Join with a relative clause: "I work with a woman. Her husband is a pilot."
    Answer

    "I work with a woman whose husband is a pilot."

  4. Join with a non-defining clause: "Our CTO is from Brazil. She started the company in 2019."
    Answer

    "Our CTO, who is from Brazil, started the company in 2019." Or: "Our CTO, who started the company in 2019, is from Brazil."

  5. Make the sentence formal: "That's the manager I complained to."
    Answer

    "That is the manager to whom I complained." The preposition moves to the front, and who becomes whom.

  6. Reduce the relative clauses: "Developers who are working on the API should read the notes that were posted today."
    Answer

    "Developers working on the API should read the notes posted today."

  7. Explain the difference: "The employees who worked late got a bonus." and "The employees, who worked late, got a bonus."
    Answer

    In the first, only some employees worked late, and only they got a bonus. In the second, all the employees worked late, and all got a bonus.

Relative word for belonging?

whose: a user whose account was locked

Can you use that after a comma?

No. Use who or which in a non-defining clause.

When can you drop the relative pronoun?

In a defining clause, when it is the object: the file you sent.

Formal: "the person I spoke to"?

the person to whom I spoke

"What" means ...?

the thing that, or the things that

Reduce: "the emails that were sent today"

the emails sent today

"twenty people, most of ___ were new"

whom

Key takeaways

  • A relative clause comes right after its noun and describes it.
  • Use who for people, which for things, that for both, whose for belonging.
  • Use where for places, when for times, why after reason.
  • Defining clauses have no commas. Non-defining clauses have two commas and never use that.
  • Drop the pronoun only in a defining clause, and only when it is the object.
  • Prepositions go at the end in speech, and before whom or which in formal writing.
  • Shorten clauses with -ing (active), a past participle (passive) or to + verb after first, last, only.
  • What means the thing that. Never put what after a noun.

Sources

  • Relative clauses: defining relative clauses, British Council LearnEnglish. Who, which, that, when, where, whose, and when to drop the pronoun.
  • Relative clauses: non-defining relative clauses, British Council LearnEnglish. Commas, no that, and where or which with prepositions.
  • Relative pronouns and relative clauses, British Council LearnEnglish. Whom, the two places for a preposition, and some of whom.
  • Using reduced relative clauses to write concisely, George Mason University Writing Center. How to drop the pronoun and be, and use -ing.
  • Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion and auxiliaries, British Council LearnEnglish. What clauses with be for emphasis.

Verb patterns: -ing and to

When one verb follows another, the second verb takes a special form. "I enjoy coding." "I want to code." "She made me code." Each first verb chooses its form. This chapter shows the main groups, the verbs that change meaning, and the famous trap: used to, be used to and get used to.

  • Use verb + to, verb + -ing and verb + object + to with common verbs.
  • Explain the change in meaning with stop, remember, forget, try and regret.
  • Use the -ing form after prepositions and as a subject.
  • Use make, let and help with the base form.
  • Choose between used to, be used to and get used to.

Three forms after a verb

I enjoy working from home.

I want to work from home.

My boss lets me work from home.

The first verb (enjoy, want, let) decides the form of the second verb. There are three forms.

The three forms
FormShapeExample
to-infinitiveto + base verbI decided to leave.
-ing formbase verb + ingI finished writing the report.
base formthe verb with nothing addedShe made me laugh.

The to-infinitive is to + the base verb. The -ing form here works like a noun. Many books call it a gerund. The base form is the verb as it is in the dictionary.

Remember pattern 2 on the page The 15 sentence patterns: Subject + verb + object. The object can be a noun: "I enjoy music." It can also be an -ing form: "I enjoy coding." Or a to-infinitive: "I want to code." The shape of the sentence stays the same.

There is no single rule for every verb. You learn each verb with its pattern, like a word and its partner. This chapter gives you the most common partners in groups.

I enjoy to work from home.

I want working from home.

She made me to laugh.

I enjoy working from home.

I want to work from home.

She made me laugh.

Verb + to

We decided to rewrite the service in Rust.

I can't afford to buy a new laptop.

The tests seem to pass now.

She refused to sign the contract.

These verbs take to + base verb. Many of them look forward. They talk about plans, wishes, decisions and attempts. The action comes later.

Common verbs + to
MeaningVerbs
wishes and planswant, would like, hope, plan, intend, expect, decide, choose, mean
promises and answersagree, promise, refuse, offer, threaten
success and effortmanage, fail, try, attempt, afford, learn
how things lookseem, appear, tend, happen
needsneed, arrange, prepare

The negative is not to: "I decided not to go." Put not before to.

To for purpose

I went to the shop to buy milk.

The to-infinitive also gives a purpose. It answers "Why?". In formal English, say in order to or so as to. For a negative purpose, say "so as not to" or "in order not to".

I hope seeing you soon.

I came here for learn English.

I decided to not go.

I hope to see you soon.

I came here to learn English.

I decided not to go.

Do not use for + verb for a purpose. Say "to learn", not "for learn" or "for to learn". Use for + noun: "I came here for the course."

Adjective + to

This library is easy to use.

I'm happy to help.

It's too late to change the plan.

Many adjectives take to + verb: easy, hard, difficult, ready, happy, glad, sorry, surprised, likely. Too + adjective + to, and adjective + enough + to, use it as well. "He is old enough to drive."

Verb + -ing

I enjoy pair programming.

Please avoid pushing to main.

Have you finished testing?

Would you mind closing the door?

These verbs take the -ing form. There is no easy meaning rule. Learn them as a list. Many are about likes, ends, and avoiding things.

Common verbs + -ing
MeaningVerbs and phrases
likes and dislikesenjoy, don't mind, can't stand, dislike, miss, fancy (British)
start, continue, endfinish, keep, give up, carry on, quit
avoiding and delayingavoid, delay, postpone, put off, risk, resist
thinking and sayingconsider, imagine, suggest, recommend, admit, deny, mention
doing againpractise, keep
fixed phrasescan't help, it's worth, it's no use, feel like, look forward to

The negative is not + -ing: "I regret not asking." "Imagine not having internet."

I suggest to use a password manager.

Would you mind to wait a moment?

She keeps to forget her badge.

I suggest using a password manager.

Would you mind waiting a moment?

She keeps forgetting her badge.

Suggest, recommend, avoid and consider never take to. Learners often say "suggest to do". Say "suggest doing", or "suggest that we do". The chapter Reported speech shows more verbs like these.

Go + -ing for activities

Use go + -ing for many free-time activities: go swimming, go shopping, go running, go skiing, go fishing. "Let's go hiking on Saturday." Do not say "go to swimming".

Verb + object + to, and make, let, help

I want you to review this code.

My manager asked me to lead the project.

The app doesn't allow users to change their email.

Some verbs take a person (an object) and then to + verb. The person does the second action. The main ones are want, would like, ask, tell, allow, expect, invite, remind, encourage, advise, persuade, force, teach, enable.

I want that you review this code.

She wants I call her.

They don't allow to smoke here.

I want you to review this code.

She wants me to call her.

They don't allow people to smoke here.

Want never takes a that clause. "I want that you come" is wrong. Use an object + to: "I want you to come." The object is an object pronoun: me, you, him, her, us, them.

Make, let and help: no to

The film made me cry.

My parents let me stay up late.

Can you help me (to) move this desk?

Make and let take an object + the base form. There is no to. Make means force or cause. Let means allow. Help can take the base form or to. Both are correct. The base form is more common.

Make, let, allow and have
VerbActivePassive
makeThey made him work late.He was made to work late.
letThey let him leave early.(no passive) He was allowed to leave early.
allowThey allowed him to leave.He was allowed to leave.
haveI had the IT team check my laptop.I had my laptop checked.

In the passive, make gets its to back. Let has no passive. Use be allowed to. The chapter The passive explains have something done.

My boss made me to rewrite the report.

Let me to explain.

I was let to go home.

My boss made me rewrite the report.

Let me explain.

I was allowed to go home.

See, hear, watch: base form or -ing

object + base form

I saw her leave the office.

I saw the whole action, from start to end.

object + -ing

I saw her leaving the office.

I saw part of the action. It was in progress.

Verbs of the senses work like this: see, hear, watch, notice, feel. "I heard someone shout." "I heard someone shouting."

Both forms, same meaning

It started to rain. = It started raining.

I love to cook. = I love cooking.

Some verbs take both forms. The meaning hardly changes. These are begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer, can't bear.

  • After starting or beginning, use to. Two -ing forms together sound bad. Say "It's starting to rain", not "It's starting raining".
  • With know, understand and realise, use to. "I began to understand."
  • In British English, like + -ing often means "enjoy". Like + to can mean "think it is a good idea". "I like to see the dentist twice a year." I do not enjoy it. I think it is wise.

Would like, would love, would prefer

I'd like to book a table.

I'd prefer to work remotely.

With would, these verbs take to. They talk about one wish now or in the future. Compare: "I like swimming" (always, in general). "I'd like to swim" (now, a wish).

I would like going to the meeting.

It's beginning getting dark.

I would like to go to the meeting.

It's beginning to get dark.

Verbs that change meaning

I stopped drinking coffee. (I don't drink it now.)

I stopped to drink a coffee. (I stopped walking. Then I drank a coffee.)

A few verbs take both forms, but the meaning changes. Here is a useful idea. The -ing form often looks back, at an action that already exists. The to-infinitive often looks forward, at an action that comes next.

The slides show each verb. Read the two sentences on each slide and compare them.

stop

He stopped smoking. (He doesn't smoke now.)

He stopped to smoke. (He paused his work so that he could smoke.)

remember

I remember meeting her in 2020. (a memory of the past)

Remember to call her. (a job you must not forget)

forget

I'll never forget seeing the sea for the first time. (a memory)

I forgot to send the invoice. (I didn't do the job.)

try

I tried to open the file, but I couldn't. (an effort, maybe it failed)

Try restarting the server. (an experiment: does it help?)

regret

I regret saying that. (I said it. I feel bad now.)

We regret to inform you that the flight is cancelled. (formal: sorry, bad news comes now)

go on

She went on talking for an hour. (she continued the same thing)

She went on to become CEO. (the next step in her life)

mean

I didn't mean to delete it. (I didn't plan it.)

A new job means moving to Berlin. (it involves this)

"I stopped to smoke" does not mean you quit. It means you stopped something else so that you could smoke. To quit, say "I stopped smoking" or "I gave up smoking".

Try to or try -ing?

Mei: The page won't load. I've tried to fix it all morning.

Raj: Have you tried clearing the cache?

Mei: Yes. I've also tried using another browser. Nothing works.

Try to is about effort. The action is hard. Try + -ing is about an experiment. The action is easy, but you don't know if it will help. In tech support, you hear "try -ing" all the time.

Need + -ing

"The car needs washing" means "the car needs to be washed". Here need + -ing has a passive meaning. It is common in British English. "The code needs refactoring."

After prepositions, and as a subject

I'm interested in learning Go.

Thanks for helping me.

Check the logs before restarting the server.

She left without saying goodbye.

After a preposition, a verb takes the -ing form. This rule is very reliable. Use it after in, on, at, of, for, about, without, before, after, instead of, by.

  • adjective + preposition: good at cooking, tired of waiting, afraid of flying, keen on running
  • verb + preposition: think about leaving, succeed in passing, apologise for being late, insist on paying
  • by + -ing for method: "You can save time by using shortcuts."

When to is a preposition

I'm looking forward to meeting you.

Here to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive. So the -ing form follows. Common phrases: look forward to, be used to, get used to, object to, be committed to, when it comes to, in addition to.

Test it. Can you put a noun after to? "I look forward to the meeting." Yes. So to is a preposition. Use -ing.

I look forward to hear from you.

She is good at to explain things.

Before to leave, turn off the lights.

I look forward to hearing from you.

She is good at explaining things.

Before leaving, turn off the lights.

"I look forward to hear from you" is a very common error in emails. Always write "I look forward to hearing from you". The chapter Emails and messages uses this phrase.

The -ing form as a subject

Learning a language takes time.

Writing tests is part of the job.

An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence. It takes a singular verb: "Writing tests is". A to-infinitive as a subject is possible, but it sounds very formal. "To err is human." Instead, use it + be + adjective + to.

-ing subject

Learning Rust is hard.

it + adjective + to

It is hard to learn Rust.

Both sentences are natural. The second one is very common in speech.

Used to, be used to, get used to

Ola: I used to work in an office. Now I work from home.

Ben: Was it hard at first?

Ola: Yes. I wasn't used to working alone. But I got used to it after a month.

These three look alike. They are completely different.

Three different meanings
FormMeaningNext wordExample
used to + basea past habit or state, not true nowbase verbI used to smoke.
be used to + -ingit is normal for me, not strange-ing or nounI'm used to working late.
get used to + -ingit is becoming normal for me-ing or nounI'm getting used to the noise.

Used to + base form

Used to talks about the past only. It has no present form. For a present habit, use the present simple: "I usually walk to work". In questions and negatives, write use to after did.

  • Negative: "I didn't use to like coffee."
  • Question: "Did you use to live in Paris?"

The chapter Past simple and past continuous also shows would for past habits.

Be used to and get used to + -ing

In these phrases, to is a preposition. So a noun or an -ing form follows. Be used to is a state: it is normal now. Get used to is a change: it is becoming normal. Both work in any tense.

  • "You'll soon get used to the new keyboard." (future)
  • "I've got used to waking up early." (present perfect)
  • "At first, she wasn't used to the cold." (past)

I am used to work at night.

I use to go to the gym every day.

Did you used to play football?

I am used to working at night.

I usually go to the gym every day.

Did you use to play football?

A quick test. Is there a form of be or get before used to? Then use -ing. No be or get? Then it is a past habit. Use the base form.

Higher level: negative, passive and perfect forms

I hate being interrupted.

She expects to be promoted this year.

He denied having seen the email.

The server seems to have crashed.

The -ing form and the to-infinitive also have passive and perfect forms.

Full forms of -ing and to
Form-ingto
simpledoingto do
negativenot doingnot to do
passivebeing doneto be done
perfecthaving doneto have done
continuous(none)to be doing
  • Passive: the subject receives the action. "Nobody likes being ignored." "The bug needs to be fixed."
  • Perfect: the action came earlier. "He seems to have left." This means it seems now that he left before now.
  • Continuous: the action is in progress. "She seems to be working on it."

After remember, deny, admit and regret, the simple -ing form already looks back. So "He denied taking it" and "He denied having taken it" mean the same. The perfect form is more formal.

Fine points

My leaving or me leaving?

An -ing form can have its own subject. "Do you mind my opening the window?" is formal. "Do you mind me opening the window?" is normal in speech. Both are correct.

Help with or without to

"She helped me to fix it" and "She helped me fix it" are both correct. American English prefers the base form. You can also leave out the person: "This tool helps reduce errors."

Dare

Dare can work like a modal: "I daren't tell him" (British) or "How dare you!". It can also be a normal verb: "I didn't dare (to) ask." With do, to is optional.

Split infinitives

"To quickly check" puts a word between to and the verb. This is a split infinitive. Old style guides disliked it. Today it is normal English. Use it when it sounds clearer.

Sorry for or sorry to

"Sorry to bother you" is about now: I am bothering you now. "Sorry for being late" is about something you already did. For the past, formal English also says "Sorry to have kept you waiting".

But and except + base form

After nothing but, anything but and except, the base form is common. "He did nothing but complain." "I did everything except clean the kitchen." This is the one common case where a preposition takes the base form.

Cambridge key word transformation tasks are a good place to practise these patterns. Check verbs like suggest, stop, remember, used to and make in the passive. For example: "My teacher made me rewrite it." → "I was made to rewrite it." See Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for -ing and to
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + verb + to + baseTalk about plans and wishesWe decided to use Rust.Negative: decided not to.
Subject + verb + -ingTalk about likes, ends and avoidingI enjoy pair programming.Suggest, avoid, mind never take to.
Subject + verb + object + to + baseSay what you want someone to doI want you to review it.Never "want that you".
make or let + object + baseForce or allow someoneShe let me leave early.No to. Passive: was made to.
to + base for purposeSay whyI came here to learn English.Not "for learn".
stop + -ingSay an action endedHe stopped smoking.Stop + to = pause in order to.
remember + to + baseDo a job you must not forgetRemember to lock the door.Remember + -ing = a memory.
try + -ingSuggest an experimentTry restarting the app.Try + to = make an effort.
preposition + -ingUse a verb after in, for, withoutThanks for helping me.Not "for help" or "for to help".
look forward to + -ingSay you are happy about the futureI look forward to hearing from you.To is a preposition here.
-ing as subject + singular verbTalk about an activityWriting tests is part of the job.Or: It is hard to learn Rust.
used to + baseTalk about a past habitI used to work in an office.Did you use to (no d).
be used to + -ingSay something is normal for youI'm used to working late.Not "used to work".
get used to + -ingSay something is becoming normalI'm getting used to the noise.Works in every tense.

Practice

Choose the right answer

I really enjoy ___ new languages.

  • to learn
  • learning
  • learn

Enjoy takes the -ing form.

We can't afford ___ another developer this year.

  • to hire
  • hiring
  • hire

Afford takes to + base verb.

My manager made me ___ the slides again.

  • to do
  • doing
  • do

Make + object + base form, with no to.

"I stopped to check my phone." What does it mean?

  • I don't check my phone anymore.
  • I paused another action so that I could check my phone.
  • I tried to check my phone, but I couldn't.

Stop + to means you stop one thing in order to do another.

I'm looking forward to ___ you next week.

  • see
  • seeing
  • have seen

To is a preposition in look forward to. So use -ing.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I'm used to get up early.
  • I use to get up early.
  • I'm used to getting up early.

Be used to + -ing means it is normal for you.

Write the verb form

Would you mind (open) the window?

She promised (call) me after the meeting.

I want you (send) me the logs.

Did you remember (book) the meeting room? It isn't in the calendar.

I'll never forget (meet) my favourite author.

You can fix this by (update) the driver.

When I was a child, I (used to / be used to) live near the sea.

I hate (interrupt, passive) when I'm working.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "I suggest to restart the router."
    Answer

    "I suggest restarting the router." Or "I suggest (that) you restart the router."

  2. Correct the mistake: "My parents didn't let me to go out."
    Answer

    "My parents didn't let me go out." Let takes the base form, with no to.

  3. Explain the difference: "I tried to call him." and "I tried calling him."
    Answer

    The first is about effort. Maybe I could not call him. The second is about an experiment. I called him to see if it helped, for example to find him.

  4. Rewrite in the passive: "They made us wait for two hours."
    Answer

    "We were made to wait for two hours." In the passive, make takes to.

  5. Rewrite with "used to": "I lived in Tokyo before. I don't live there now."
    Answer

    "I used to live in Tokyo."

  6. Write about a change in your life with "be used to" and "get used to".
    Sample answer

    "When I moved to London, I wasn't used to driving on the left. It took me three months to get used to it. Now I'm used to it."

  7. Rewrite with a perfect infinitive: "It seems that the build failed last night."
    Answer

    "The build seems to have failed last night." The perfect form shows the earlier action.

enjoy + ?

-ing: I enjoy coding.

decide + ?

to + base: We decided to wait.

make + object + ?

base form: It made me laugh.

stop smoking or stop to smoke: which means you quit?

stop smoking

Verb form after a preposition?

always -ing: before leaving, without asking

Question form of used to?

Did you use to ...? (no d)

be used to + ?

-ing or a noun: I'm used to working late.

Key takeaways

  • The first verb decides the form of the second: to, -ing or the base form.
  • Plans and wishes often take to. Enjoy, avoid, finish, mind and suggest take -ing.
  • Want, ask, tell and allow take an object + to. Make and let take an object + base form.
  • Stop, remember, forget, try and regret change meaning. -ing looks back, to looks forward.
  • After a preposition, always use -ing. In look forward to, to is a preposition.
  • An -ing subject takes a singular verb. "It is hard to ..." is a common alternative.
  • Used to + base is a past habit. Be used to and get used to take -ing or a noun.

Sources

  • Verbs followed by the infinitive, British Council LearnEnglish. Verb + to, verb + object + to, make and let, and passives.
  • Verbs followed by -ing or infinitive to change meaning, British Council LearnEnglish. Stop, try, remember and forget.
  • -ing forms, British Council LearnEnglish. The -ing form as a noun, as a subject and after prepositions.
  • Different uses of used to, British Council LearnEnglish. Used to, be used to and get used to.

Phrasal verbs

A phrasal verb is a verb with a small word after it. "Turn off the light." "We set up a new server." English speakers use phrasal verbs all day, at home and at work. This chapter explains the four types, the meaning of each small word, and 120 common phrasal verbs.

  • Recognise a phrasal verb and its particle.
  • Put the object in the right place for the four types.
  • Guess meanings from the particles up, down, out, off, on and in.
  • Use 120 common phrasal verbs in your own sentences.
  • Choose a formal one-word verb when the text needs it.

What a phrasal verb is

I called my mother. (I phoned her.)

They called off the meeting. (They cancelled it.)

The car broke down. (It stopped working.)

A phrasal verb is a verb + one or two small words. The small word is a particle. The particle often changes the meaning. Call means phone. Call off means cancel.

Some phrasal verbs are easy. The meaning comes from the parts. "Sit down." "Come in." "Go out." Others are idiomatic. You cannot guess them from the parts. "Give up" means stop trying. "Put up with" means accept something bad.

Clear meaning

Please sit down.

She took off her coat.

Verb + direction. Easy to guess.

New meaning

Don't give up.

The plane took off.

The whole phrase has a new meaning. Learn it as one word.

One phrasal verb can have many meanings. Take off means remove clothes. It also means leave the ground, for a plane. It also means become popular fast: "The app took off." Read the whole sentence to find the meaning.

Treat a phrasal verb as one new word made of two parts. Learn the parts together, with an example sentence.

They called the meeting. (You mean: cancelled)

I'm looking my keys.

They called off the meeting.

I'm looking for my keys.

Do not drop the particle. Without it, you have a different verb. "Look" and "look for" are different. "I'm looking my keys" has no meaning.

Phrasal verbs and tense

Only the verb changes for tense. The particle never changes. "I give up." "She gave up." "They have given up." "He is giving up." Learn the irregular forms of the verb, and the phrasal verb follows.

The four types

The type tells you where the object goes. An object is the person or thing after the verb: "turn off the light". There are four types.

Type 1: no object

I get up at seven.

My laptop broke down.

These verbs have no object. Nothing comes after the particle, except a time or a place. This is pattern 1 on the page The 15 sentence patterns: Subject + verb. The verb is just two words long.

Type 2: separable

Turn off the light.

Turn the light off.

Turn it off.

A separable verb can split. A noun object can go after the particle, or in the middle. This is pattern 2, Subject + verb + object, with the object inside the verb. But a pronoun like it, them or me must go in the middle.

A long object usually goes after the particle. "Turn off all the lights in the building." This is easier to read than "Turn all the lights in the building off".

Type 3: inseparable

Who looks after the children?

Who looks after them?

An inseparable verb never splits. The object always goes after the particle, even a pronoun. Many of these verbs end in a preposition: look after, look for, rely on, get off (the bus).

Type 4: three-part

I can't put up with this noise.

We've run out of coffee.

A three-part verb has a verb and two particles. It never splits. The object goes at the end: "put up with it".

The four types and the object
TypeWith a nounWith a pronoun
1. no objectThe plane took off.(no object)
2. separablepick up the kids / pick the kids uppick them up
3. inseparablelook after the kidslook after them
4. three-partcatch up with the otherscatch up with them

I wrote down it.

Can you look the baby after?

I can't put up this with.

I wrote it down.

Can you look after the baby?

I can't put up with this.

"Turn off it" and "pick up them" are very common errors. With a separable verb, the pronoun always goes in the middle: turn it off, pick them up.

How do you know the type?

Use a learner dictionary. The entry shows where the object goes. For example, it shows "turn something off" for a separable verb. It shows "look after somebody" for an inseparable verb. Learn the type with the verb.

One phrasal verb can belong to two types. "The plane took off" has no object. "Take off your coat" is separable. "Wake up!" has no object. "Wake me up at six" is separable.

What the particles mean

Particles are not random. Each one has a few main meanings. If you know them, you can often guess a new phrasal verb. The graph shows the main meanings. Drag the words to see the links.

The six particles and their main ideas
ParticleMain ideasExamples
upmore, higher / finished completely / appearspeed up, turn up the music, eat up, use up, show up
downless, lower / on paper / stop workingslow down, cut down on, write down, break down
outoutside / find or solve / nothing left / loudgo out, find out, work out, run out of, read out
offaway, leave / stop, disconnect / cancelset off, take off, turn off, cut off, call off
oncontinue / start, connect / on the bodycarry on, keep on, turn on, log on, put on
ininside, enter / submit / take partcome in, log in, hand in, fill in, join in

The pairs are often opposites: turn on and turn off, log in and log out, speed up and slow down, put on and take off.

Do not learn phrasal verbs by verb (all the verbs with get). That is confusing. Learn them by particle, or by topic. This chapter groups them by particle.

120 common phrasal verbs

Here are 120 common phrasal verbs, 20 for each particle. The Type column uses short labels. no obj means no object. sep means separable. insep means inseparable. 3-part means three-part. Some verbs have two types. In the Meaning column, a slash (/) separates two different meanings.

Do not learn all 120 at once. Learn five a day. Write one sentence about your life with each one.

Some verbs differ between British and American English. British English says "fill in a form". American English often says "fill out a form". Both are understood everywhere.

Formal single-verb twins

We need to find out why the server crashed.

We need to determine why the server crashed.

Many phrasal verbs have a one-word twin. The twin is usually more formal. Many twins come from Latin or French. Phrasal verbs feel more relaxed and personal.

Phrasal verbs and their formal twins
Phrasal verbFormal twinFormal example
find outdiscover, determineThe team discovered the cause.
look intoinvestigateWe will investigate the issue.
put offpostponeThe launch was postponed.
call offcancelThe event has been cancelled.
set upestablishThe company was established in 2015.
carry outconduct, performWe conducted a survey.
go up, go downincrease, decreaseCosts increased by 5%.
cut down onreduceWe must reduce energy use.
come up withpropose, deviseThe team proposed a new method.
put up withtolerateThe system tolerates small errors.
leave outomitPersonal data was omitted.
turn downreject, declineThe offer was declined.
make upinvent, fabricateThe data was fabricated.
bring upraiseShe raised an important point.
point outnote, indicateThe report notes three risks.
hand insubmitApplications must be submitted by May.
work out, figure outcalculate, solveWe calculated the total cost.
get rid ofremove, eliminateThe update removes the bug.
go overreviewPlease review the contract.
keep oncontinuePrices continued to rise.

When do you use the twin? In academic essays, reports, contracts and formal letters. Phrasal verbs can sound informal there. Some also have many meanings, so a single verb is clearer.

When do you use the phrasal verb? In speech, chat, stand-ups and most work emails. Formal twins in speech can sound stiff. "Shall we postpone lunch?" sounds odd to a friend. "Shall we put off lunch?" sounds natural.

(Essay) Scientists have found out that the ice is going down fast.

(Essay) Scientists have discovered that the ice is decreasing rapidly.

A twin is not always a perfect match. Give up can mean "quit" or "surrender". Make up can mean "invent", but also "become friends again". Fabricate fits only the first meaning. Check the meaning in your sentence before you swap.

Phrasal verbs at work

Lead: Let's kick off. Priya, what are you working on?

Priya: I'm setting up the new staging server. I ran into a problem with the certificates. I'm looking into it.

Lead: OK. If you can't sort it out by noon, reach out to the platform team.

Tom: We rolled out the fix to 10% of users. If errors go up, we'll roll it back.

Lead: Great. Can you follow up with support? Let's move on.

Software teams use many phrasal verbs. Some are general. Some are special to tech.

Phrasal verbs in software work
VerbMeaning at workExample
spin upstart a new server or containerSpin up a test environment.
roll backgo back to an older versionWe rolled back the release.
run intomeet a problem by chanceI ran into a timeout error.
look intoinvestigateI'll look into the bug.
break downdivide a big task into small onesLet's break down this epic into tickets.
hand overgive work to another personI'll hand over the project before my holiday.
reach out (to)contactFeel free to reach out with questions.
check in (with)talk briefly to see how things areI'll check in with you on Friday.
sign off (on)approveThe client signed off on the design.
phase outstop using slowly, step by stepWe're phasing out the old API.

The story below is one working day. It uses phrasal verbs from this chapter in order.

Morning

Ana wakes up at seven. She gets up and puts on her clothes.

Start work

She logs in and checks out the new tickets. The stand-up kicks off at nine.

A problem

The test server goes down. Ana looks into it. She runs into a strange error.

The fix

She tracks down the bug and figures out the cause. A config line was left out.

Release

The team rolls out the fix. Ana follows up with support.

Evening

She logs off and turns off her laptop. Tonight she will stay in and relax.

Phrasal nouns: one word or two?

Log in to see your data. (verb: two words)

The login page is slow. (noun or adjective: one word)

Many phrasal verbs have a noun form. The verb is two words. The noun is usually one word, or has a hyphen.

  • back up your files → make a backup
  • set up the server → the setup (British also: set-up)
  • shut down the system → a shutdown
  • roll out the update → the rollout
  • work out at the gym → a workout
  • break down a task → a breakdown of the costs

Please login to your account.

Did you backup the database?

Please log in to your account.

Did you back up the database?

Some work phrasal verbs are popular but can sound like jargon. "Circle back" means "talk about it again later". "Reach out" means "contact". They are fine in many offices. In formal writing, "contact" is safer.

Fine points for higher levels

Phrasal verbs in the passive

The particle stays with the verb. "They called off the meeting" becomes "The meeting was called off." "Someone has looked into the problem" becomes "The problem has been looked into." See The passive.

Phrasal verbs in relative clauses

The particle stays at the end. "The children she looks after are five." "The problem we ran into is fixed." Do not move it to the front. See Relative clauses.

Phrasal verbs + -ing

A verb after a phrasal verb takes -ing. "I gave up smoking." "We put off deciding." "She carried on working." "I look forward to meeting you." See Verb patterns: -ing and to.

Object between verb and two particles

A few three-part verbs take an object in the middle. "She talked me out of leaving." "He put the delay down to bad weather." "Don't take it out on me." Learn these as fixed phrases.

Stress in speech

In speech, the particle is usually stressed. "Turn it OFF." "She gave UP." A preposition after a normal verb is usually not stressed: "Look at me." Stress helps listeners hear the phrasal verb. See Pronunciation and fluency.

Adverbs and particles

An adverb usually goes before the verb or at the end. "She quickly turned it off." "She turned it off quickly." Do not put the adverb inside a phrasal verb with a pronoun: "turned it quickly off" sounds wrong.

In speaking exams, natural phrasal verbs can show a wide vocabulary. In an academic essay, choose the formal twin when it fits. For IELTS, read the official band descriptors for Lexical Resource. They can change, so check the current version. See IELTS Speaking and IELTS Writing.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for phrasal verbs
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + verb + particleSay what happens, with no objectMy laptop broke down.Only a time or place can follow.
verb + particle + nounUse a separable verb with a nounTurn off the light.Best for long objects.
verb + noun + particleUse a separable verb with a nounTurn the light off.Fine with short objects.
verb + pronoun + particleUse a separable verb with it, them, meTurn it off.Never "turn off it".
verb + particle + object (inseparable)Use an inseparable verbWho looks after them?Never split it.
verb + particle + particle + objectUse a three-part verbI can't put up with it.The object goes at the end.
be + past participle + particleUse a phrasal verb in the passiveThe meeting was called off.Keep the particle.
phrasal verb + -ingAdd an action after the verbHe gave up smoking.Not "gave up to smoke".
log in (verb) / login (noun)Write tech words correctlyLog in on the login page.Verb: two words. Noun: one.
phrasal verb in speech, one-word twin in reportsChoose the right stylefind out / determineCheck that the meaning matches.
up = more or completeGuess a meaningSpeed up the build.Opposite: slow down.
off = stop or cancelGuess a meaningThey called off the trip.Opposite of on: turn on, turn off.

Practice

Choose the right answer

It's dark. Can you ___ the light?

  • turn on
  • turn off
  • turn down

Turn on starts a machine or a light.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I wrote down it.
  • I wrote it down.
  • I down wrote it.

Write down is separable. A pronoun goes in the middle.

We have no more printer paper. We have ___ paper.

  • run out
  • run out of
  • run off

Run out of is a three-part verb. It needs of before the noun.

The rain stopped, so the match wasn't ___.

  • called off
  • called up
  • called on

Call off means cancel. The passive keeps the particle.

Which is the best word for a formal report? "We ___ a survey of 500 users."

  • carried out
  • conducted
  • did out

Conducted is the formal twin of carried out. Carried out is also correct, but less formal.

Which sentence is correct?

  • Can you look the kids after?
  • Can you look after?
  • Can you look after the kids?

Look after is inseparable and needs an object.

Write the particle

Please fill ? this form before the meeting.

I can't figure ? why the test fails.

Don't give ?. You're nearly there.

Please log ? when you leave the office.

The CEO stepped ? after ten years.

We came up ? a great name for the product.

She turned ? the offer because the salary was too low.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "Can you pick up me at six?"
    Answer

    "Can you pick me up at six?" With a pronoun, a separable verb splits.

  2. Correct the mistake: "Did you backup the files?"
    Answer

    "Did you back up the files?" The verb is two words. "Backup" is the noun.

  3. Replace the phrasal verb with a formal twin: "The meeting was put off until May."
    Answer

    "The meeting was postponed until May."

  4. Replace the formal verb with a phrasal verb for a chat message: "We need to investigate this error."
    Answer

    "We need to look into this error."

  5. Explain the two meanings of "take off" with two sentences.
    Sample answer

    "Please take off your shoes." (remove) "The plane took off at noon." (leave the ground) A third meaning: "The app took off." (became popular fast)

  6. Write three lines for a stand-up. Use "work on", "run into" and "sort out".
    Sample answer

    "Yesterday I worked on the search page. I ran into a problem with the API. I'll sort it out this morning."

  7. Which particle means "more" in "speed up" and "turn up the music"? Give its opposite with the same verbs.
    Answer

    Up means more. The opposite is down: "slow down" and "turn down the music".

call off

cancel: They called off the meeting.

put up with

accept something bad: I can't put up with the noise.

turn off + it: word order?

turn it off

Formal twin of "find out"?

discover, or determine

run into (at work)

meet a problem by chance: I ran into an error.

Verb or noun: login or log in?

log in is the verb. login is the noun or adjective.

come up with

think of an idea: She came up with a plan.

Key takeaways

  • A phrasal verb is a verb + particle. Together they often have a new meaning.
  • There are four types: no object, separable, inseparable and three-part.
  • With a separable verb, a pronoun always goes in the middle: turn it off.
  • Inseparable and three-part verbs never split: look after them, put up with it.
  • Particles have main ideas: up for more, down for less, off for stop, on for continue.
  • Use phrasal verbs in speech and chat. Use one-word twins in formal reports.
  • Write the verb as two words (log in) and the noun as one (login).
