Advanced tense and aspect

You already know the main tenses. This chapter shows how good writers mix them. You will tell stories, talk about plans that changed, and choose the right tense for news, stories and academic papers.

  • Tell a story with four past forms working together.
  • Talk about the future from a point in the past.
  • Use the future continuous and the future perfect continuous with confidence.
  • Choose a state meaning or an action meaning for verbs like think, have and see.
  • Pick the right tense for headlines, news, stories, academic papers and subtle present perfect uses.

Tense and aspect: two different questions

She works in Berlin.

She is working in Berlin this month.

She has worked in Berlin since 2020.

All three sentences are about the present. The time is the same. But each sentence shows the action in a different way.

Tense answers the question "When?". Aspect answers a second question: "How do I see the action?". English has three common ways to see an action.

Three aspects
AspectFormHow you see the actionExample
Simpleverbas one whole fact or eventI wrote the report.
Continuousbe + -ingin progress, in the middle, temporaryI was writing the report.
Perfecthave + past participlelooking back from a later pointI had written the report.

You can join two aspects. "I had been writing" is perfect and continuous together. It looks back, and it shows an activity in progress.

Tense is the clock. Aspect is the camera. The camera can show the whole scene, a moment in the middle, or a look back.

Grammar books do not all use the same names. Some say "the future perfect tense". Others say this is not a true tense, because English builds it with helping verbs. The names matter less than the meaning. This chapter uses the common names.

Narrative tenses: four past forms together

Read this short story. Look at the verbs in bold.

Last Friday, Mia was fixing a bug in the payment code. She had been working on it since ten in the morning. At four o'clock, the power went off. Her screen went black. She had not saved her changes. She sat back and laughed. She was going to push the code at five.

Narrative tenses are the past forms we use to tell a story. Each form has a job.

Four narrative forms and their jobs
FormJob in the storyFrom the story
Past simplethe main events, one after anotherthe power went off, she sat back, she laughed
Past continuousthe background: what was in progressMia was fixing a bug
Past perfectan earlier event, before the main eventsshe had not saved her changes
Past perfect continuousa long activity up to a past momentshe had been working since ten

The picture shows the same story on one timeline.

How much past perfect?

Use the past perfect to go back once. Then return to the past simple. You do not need the past perfect for every earlier event. When before or after shows the order, the past simple is often enough.

Too much

She had opened the laptop. She had checked the logs. She had found the bug.

Better

She had already opened the laptop. She checked the logs and found the bug.

Do not use the past perfect only because an event is "far in the past". "I had been to Paris in 2010" is wrong when there is no later past moment. Say "I went to Paris in 2010."

The chapters Past simple and past continuous and The perfect tenses show each form alone. Here we use them together.

Future in the past: plans seen from the past

Sam: Did you call the client?

Ana: I was going to call her, but the meeting ran late.

Sam: She said she would send the contract on Monday.

Ana: I know. I was about to email her when you came in.

Sometimes we stand at a point in the past and look forward. This is the future in the past. Each future form has a past form.

Future forms and their past forms
Future from nowFuture from the pastExampleMeaning
willwouldI knew the test would fail.a prediction or a promise in the past
am going towas going toI was going to call, but I forgot.a plan, often one that did not happen
am about towas about toI was about to leave when it started raining.very near, then something stopped it
am meeting (arrangement)was meetingI was meeting Jo at six, so I left early.a fixed arrangement
is due towas due toThe train was due to leave at nine.an expected time
is to (formal)was toShe did not know it, but she was to become CEO.a future that really came, like fate

Was going to: the plan that changed

Was going to often means the plan did not happen. "We were going to launch in May" tells the listener: we did not launch in May. It is very useful at work. It explains changes without long sentences.

  • I was going to fix it today, but the server is down.
  • We were going to use Postgres. Then we chose a simpler option.
  • Sorry, I was going to reply yesterday. I forgot.

Was to have done: very formal

In formal writing, was to have + past participle shows a plan that failed. "The bridge was to have opened in 2024." It means "It was planned for 2024. It did not open then." You will see this in news and history books. In speech, say "was going to".

In a past story, do not use will for a future idea. "He said he will come" is common in speech. But in a past story or a formal report, say "He said he would come." The chapter Reported speech explains this step back.

In 2019 I didn't know that I will move to Tokyo.

I was going to called you.

In 2019 I didn't know that I would move to Tokyo.

I was going to call you.

Future continuous and future perfect continuous

This time tomorrow, I'll be flying to Seoul.

By June, I'll have been working here for ten years.

These two forms are rare in textbooks but common in real life. Both stand at a point in the future.

Future continuous: will be + -ing

The form is will be + -ing. It has four uses.

  1. In progress at a future time. "At ten tomorrow, I'll be giving my talk. Don't call then."
  2. A polite question about plans. "Will you be using the meeting room at three?" This asks about the plan. It does not push the person to decide.
  3. A future event that will happen anyway. "I'll be passing the post office. Shall I post your letter?" I am not going there for you. It is already part of my day.
  4. A guess about now. "Don't call Tom. He'll be sleeping." I think he is sleeping now. This is a guess.

Will you come?

Will you come to the party?

A request or an invitation. You ask the person to decide.

Will you be coming?

Will you be coming to the party?

A neutral question. You only want to know the plan.

Future perfect continuous: will have been + -ing

The form is will have been + -ing. Stand at a future point. Look back. Say how long an activity has continued. The activity may continue after that point.

  • By Friday, the tests will have been running for 48 hours.
  • In May, we will have been living here for three years.
  • When the flight lands, I'll have been travelling for 20 hours. I'll be tired.
Four future forms side by side
FormPictureExample
will + verba future fact or decisionI'll finish the report.
will be + -ingin progress at a future pointAt noon, I'll be writing the report.
will have + past participlefinished before a future pointBy noon, I'll have finished the report.
will have been + -inghow long, up to a future pointBy noon, I'll have been writing for four hours.

The future perfect continuous needs been. "I will have working" and "I will have being working" are both wrong. Say "I will have been working". Also, do not use it with state verbs. Say "By June, I'll have known her for ten years", not "I'll have been knowing her".

State meaning and action meaning

State

I think it's a good idea.

This is an opinion.

Action

I'm thinking about your idea.

My brain is working on it now.

A state verb describes a situation that does not change much. An action verb describes something that happens. State verbs are usually not used in the continuous forms. We say "I know", not "I am knowing".

One verb, two meanings

Many verbs have a state meaning and an action meaning. The meaning decides the form, not the verb.

Verbs with two meanings
VerbState meaningAction meaning
thinkI think you're right. (opinion)I'm thinking about it. (using my brain)
haveShe has two laptops. (owns)She's having lunch. (eating)
seeI see what you mean. (understand)I'm seeing the doctor at five. (meeting)
beHe is rude. (his nature)He is being rude. (only today, on purpose)
tasteThe soup tastes salty. (a quality)The chef is tasting the soup. (trying it)
weighThe box weighs 5 kilos. (a fact)They're weighing the box. (measuring it)
lookYou look tired. (seem)I'm looking at the logs. (using my eyes)
appearIt appears to be broken. (seems)She's appearing in a new film. (acting)

State verbs in the continuous: special effects

Good speakers sometimes break the rule on purpose. The continuous form adds a special meaning.

  • Politeness. "I was wondering if you could review my code." "I was hoping to talk to you." The past continuous makes a request softer. It is very common in work emails.
  • A change in progress. "I'm understanding the code better every day." "He's resembling his father more and more."
  • A temporary feeling. "I'm loving this new job." This is informal. Do not write it in an exam essay.

I am knowing the answer.

This bag is belonging to me.

By June, I'll have been owning this car for a year.

I know the answer.

This bag belongs to me.

By June, I'll have owned this car for a year.

See Present simple and present continuous for the basic rule.

Tense in news

Headlines

A headline has its own grammar. It must be short. So it drops small words and uses special tenses.

How to read a headline
HeadlineFull sentenceRule
Storm hits south coastA storm has hit the south coast.present simple for a recent past event
Minister to visit JapanThe minister is going to visit Japan.to + verb for the future
Two arrested after fightTwo people have been arrested after a fight.past participle alone for the passive
Prices rising, says bankPrices are rising, the bank says.-ing alone for a change in progress
Tech firm cuts 500 jobsA tech firm has cut 500 jobs.no articles (a, the)

A past form in a headline is usually a passive. "Man held after robbery" means "A man has been held by the police." It does not mean the man held something. Short headlines can be ambiguous. Read the first sentence of the story to check.

The news story

The story under the headline uses normal grammar. It often follows the same order:

  1. Announce the news with the present perfect. "A storm has hit the south coast."
  2. Give the details with the past simple. "It arrived at 3 a.m. Winds reached 120 km per hour."
  3. Add earlier background with the past perfect. "Experts had warned of the danger on Sunday."
  4. Report words with past reporting verbs. "The mayor said the clean-up would take weeks."

Why the change? The present perfect says "this is new and important now". Once you give a time, like 3 a.m., the past simple is needed. American news often starts with the past simple too: "A storm hit the coast early Monday."

Tense in stories

Stories do not always use the past. The type of story decides the tense.

Tense by type of story
TypeUsual tenseExample
Novels and written storiesnarrative past formsShe opened the door. Someone had been there.
Spoken stories and jokespresent simple and present continuousSo I'm standing at the bus stop, and this man comes up to me.
Summary of a film or bookpresent simpleIn the film, a robot falls in love with a human.
Sports commentarypresent simpleShe passes, she shoots, she scores!
Instructions and recipesimperative or present simpleAdd the eggs. Then you mix everything.

The present tense in a spoken story is called the historical present. It makes the story feel alive. The listener feels "inside" the moment. Speakers often switch to it at the exciting part.

Leo: You won't believe my morning. I was waiting for the train. It was late, as usual.

Leo: Then this guy walks up to me. He looks at my laptop bag and says, "Are you the new developer?"

Kim: No way. Who was he?

Leo: My new boss!

Use the present simple to summarise a document, a ticket or a meeting decision. "The report shows three problems." "In this ticket, the user cannot log in." The text still exists now, so the present is natural.

Do not switch tense by accident in the middle of a written story. Choose past or present. Keep it. A switch must have a reason, like a new time or a flashback.

Tense in academic writing

Read this short paragraph from an imagined paper. Look at how the tense changes.

  1. Many studies have examined code review. (present perfect: research up to now)
  2. Few have looked at review in small teams. (present perfect: a gap in the research)
  3. Lee (2021) found that short reviews catch more bugs. (past simple: one past study)
  4. In our study, we interviewed 40 developers. (past simple: what we did)
  5. The results suggest that review size matters. (present simple: what it means now)

Research guides agree on one main idea. Three tenses do most of the work in academic writing: present simple, past simple and present perfect.

Tenses in a research paper
TenseUseExample
Present simplegeneral facts, what this paper does, tables and figures, what results meanThis paper describes a new method. Table 2 shows the results.
Past simpleyour method, your results, one named past studyWe tested 12 models. Accuracy rose by 4%.
Present perfectresearch up to now in general, and gapsSeveral studies have used this data set.

The literature review mixes all three. Many style guides allow the present simple for a writer's ideas: "Lee (2021) argues that..." Use the past simple for one finished study: "Lee (2021) found...". Check the style guide of your journal or university. Guides differ here.

Do not use the present perfect with a year. "Lee has found this in 2021" is wrong. Say "Lee found this in 2021", or "Lee (2021) has shown this" with no time word in the sentence.

In IELTS Writing Task 1, a chart about the past needs the past simple. "Sales rose in 2020." A chart with future numbers needs future forms: "Sales are expected to rise" or "will have doubled by 2030". Check the years on the chart before you write.

Subtle uses of the present perfect

You know the three main uses from The perfect tenses. Here are finer points that C1 and C2 speakers use.

A time period that is not finished

"I've had three coffees this morning." It is still morning. "I had three coffees this morning." Now it is afternoon. The same words, this morning, take a different tense. The question is: is the period still open?

A repeated action up to now

"The build has failed four times today." The day is not over. It may fail again. Compare "The build failed four times yesterday." Yesterday is closed.

Alive or not alive

"My aunt has written three books." She is alive. She may write more. "My grandfather wrote three books." He is dead. His list is closed. The present perfect keeps the door open.

It's the first time ...

"It's the third time this week the server has crashed." After it's the first, second, third time, use the present perfect. For a past story, move back: "It was the first time I had flown."

It's been ages since ...

"It's been two years since we met." This means "We met two years ago." After since, the verb is usually past simple. "I haven't seen her since she left."

Have you seen ...? about something new

"Have you seen the new design?" This is not about your whole life. It asks about something that exists now. The present perfect connects the question to now.

After when, after, as soon as

"I'll call you when I've finished." The present perfect shows the action will be complete first. It refers to the future. "When I finish" is also fine. The perfect makes the order clearer.

British and American English

British English likes the present perfect with just, already and yet: "Have you eaten yet?" American English often uses the past simple here: "Did you eat yet?" Both are correct in their own country. In British exams, use the present perfect.

I have seen him yesterday.

It's the first time I see snow.

Shakespeare has written many plays.

I saw him yesterday.

It's the first time I've seen snow.

Shakespeare wrote many plays.

One event, many tenses

Each slide tells part of one project story. Each slide uses a different form from this chapter.

Past perfect continuous

The team had been preparing the release for six weeks.

A long activity up to a past moment.

Past continuous

On launch day, everyone was watching the dashboards.

The background scene.

Past simple

At noon, the error rate jumped.

The main event.

Past perfect

Someone had changed a setting the night before.

An earlier event, before the main event.

Future in the past

They were going to announce the release at two. They waited.

A plan that did not happen.

Present perfect

The team has fixed the problem. The service is stable.

News with a result now.

Future continuous

Next week, we'll be testing the new setting.

In progress at a future time.

Future perfect continuous

By then, we'll have been running the new version for a month.

How long, up to a future point.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for advanced tense and aspect
PatternPurposeModelNote
was + -ing, when + past simpleSet a background and a main eventI was cooking when the phone rang.The short event takes the past simple.
had + past participleGo back to an earlier past eventShe had not saved her work.Use it once, then return to the past simple.
had been + -ing (+ for, since)Say how long, up to a past momentHe had been waiting for an hour.Not with state verbs like know.
was going to + base formTalk about a past plan that changedI was going to call, but I forgot.It often means the plan failed.
knew, said, thought + wouldGive a future from the pastI knew it would rain.Not will in a past story.
was about to + base form, whenShow something very near, then stoppedI was about to leave when she arrived.Often followed by when.
will be + -ingShow a future action in progressAt ten, I'll be giving my talk.Also for polite questions about plans.
Will you be + -ing?Ask about plans politelyWill you be using the room at three?Softer than "Will you use".
will have been + -ing (+ for)Say how long, up to a future pointBy May, I'll have been working here for a year.Do not forget been.
I was wondering if + couldMake a polite requestI was wondering if you could help me.The past here is polite, not past time.
Headline: noun + present simpleReport a recent event in a titleStorm hits coast.It means "has hit".
Headline: noun + to + verbReport a future event in a titleMinister to visit Japan.It means "is going to visit".
Many studies have + past participleSum up research up to nowMany studies have examined this.No year in the same sentence.
It's the first time + present perfectTalk about a new experienceIt's the first time I've used Rust.Not "It's the first time I use".

Practice

Choose the right answer

When I arrived at the office, the meeting ___. I was ten minutes late.

  • already started
  • had already started
  • has already started

The meeting started before I arrived. An earlier past event takes the past perfect.

I ___ you last night, but my phone died.

  • will call
  • was going to call
  • have called

A past plan that did not happen takes was going to.

Which question about plans is the most polite and neutral?

  • Will you use the car tonight?
  • Will you be using the car tonight?
  • Do you use the car tonight?

Will you be + -ing asks about the plan. It does not push for a decision.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I am owning two bikes.
  • I'm having a quick break.
  • She is knowing the answer.

Have means "take" or "eat" here. That is an action, so the continuous is fine.

What does the headline "CEO to step down" mean?

  • The CEO stepped down last year.
  • The CEO is going to leave the job.
  • The CEO wants to come down the stairs.

To + verb in a headline means the future.

In a research paper, which sentence fits the methods section best?

  • We have interviewed 40 developers in 2025.
  • We interviewed 40 developers.
  • We will interview 40 developers.

Methods describe finished steps. Use the past simple.

Write the verb form

She was tired because she (work) all night.

Don't phone at eight. We (have) dinner then.

By next March, I (study) English for five years.

I knew the demo (go) well. I had practised a lot.

It's the second time this month the site (go) down.

I (wonder) if you could check my report.

Why are you so rude today? You (be) very unkind.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "I have finished the project last week."
    Answer

    "I finished the project last week." Last week is a finished time. Use the past simple.

  2. Explain the difference: "I've drunk two coffees this morning." and "I drank two coffees this morning."
    Answer

    In the first, it is still morning, and I may drink more. In the second, the morning is over.

  3. Write the full sentence for the headline "Bank boss quits after scandal".
    Answer

    "The boss of a bank has quit after a scandal." The present simple in a headline means a recent past event.

  4. Join these facts in one story sentence with two narrative forms: "I walked home. It started to rain."
    Sample answer

    "I was walking home when it started to rain." The long action takes the past continuous. The short event takes the past simple.

  5. Rewrite in a formal style with "was to have": "The new office was planned to open in April, but it didn't."
    Answer

    "The new office was to have opened in April." The form means the plan did not happen.

  6. Write three sentences for a short literature review on remote work. Use the present perfect, the past simple and the present simple.
    Sample answer

    "Many studies have looked at remote work. Chen (2022) found that remote teams wrote longer messages. These findings suggest that written skills matter more in remote teams."

  7. Tell a four-sentence story about a problem at work. Use the past simple, past continuous, past perfect and was going to.
    Sample answer

    "I was preparing a demo for a client. Suddenly, the app crashed. Someone had deleted the test data. I was going to show the new search feature, so I showed the slides instead."

Tense or aspect: which one answers "How do I see the action?"

Aspect: simple, continuous or perfect.

Which narrative form gives the background?

The past continuous: "Mia was fixing a bug."

"Was going to" often means ...?

A past plan that did not happen.

Form of the future perfect continuous?

will have been + -ing

"He is rude" or "He is being rude": which is only today?

"He is being rude": a temporary behaviour.

Headline "Two arrested": full form?

Two people have been arrested.

Tense for your methods in a paper?

The past simple: "We tested 12 models."

Key takeaways

  • Tense shows time. Aspect shows how you see the action: whole, in progress, or looking back.
  • In a story, the past simple carries the main events. The past continuous gives the background.
  • The past perfect goes back once. Then return to the past simple.
  • Would, was going to and was about to give a future seen from the past.
  • Will be + -ing shows a future in progress and asks about plans politely.
  • Will have been + -ing says how long, up to a future point.
  • The meaning, not the verb, decides between state and action forms.
  • Headlines use the present for the past and to + verb for the future.
  • Academic papers use the present perfect for research so far and the past simple for one study.
  • The present perfect needs an open time period. A finished time takes the past simple.

  • Stative verbs, British Council LearnEnglish. Groups of state verbs and verbs with two meanings.
  • Present perfect, British Council LearnEnglish. Unfinished time periods, time clauses and other uses.
  • The three common tenses used in academic writing, George Mason University Writing Center. Present simple, past simple and present perfect in research writing.

Inversion and emphasis

Sometimes one part of a sentence matters most. English can move words, add words or change the word order to make that part stand out. This chapter shows the main tools: inversion, cleft sentences, fronting and emphatic do.

  • Use inversion after never, rarely, not only, no sooner, hardly and similar words.
  • Write formal conditionals without if: had I known, were I, should you.
  • Build cleft sentences with it is ... that and what ... is.
  • Move a phrase to the front of a sentence for effect.
  • Use do, does and did to add emphasis or to correct someone.

Normal order and changed order

I have never seen such a mess.

Never have I seen such a mess.

Both sentences are correct. They mean the same thing. But the second one sounds stronger and more formal. The word never comes first. Then the helping verb have comes before the subject I.

The normal order of an English sentence is subject, then verb. See The 15 sentence patterns. Inversion changes this order. The auxiliary moves in front of the subject. It is the same order as in a question.

Why change the order? The start and the end of a sentence are strong places. The reader notices them. When you move a word to the front, you give it emphasis.

Inversion after negative words

Rarely do we deploy on a Friday.

Not only did she find the bug, but she also fixed it.

Under no circumstances should you share your password.

An adverbial with a negative or limiting meaning can start a sentence. Then the next part takes question order. This is formal. You see it in speeches, reports, news and good essays.

Start: "We have seldom seen such fast growth."

  1. Move the negative word to the front. "Seldom ..."
  2. Find the auxiliary. Here it is have.
  3. Put the auxiliary before the subject. "Seldom have we ..."
  4. Add the rest. "Seldom have we seen such fast growth."

What if there is no auxiliary? Then add do, does or did, as in a question. "She rarely complains" becomes "Rarely does she complain." The main verb goes back to its base form.

Negative and limiting words that cause inversion
WordsMeaningExample
never, rarely, seldomnot ever, not oftenSeldom has the team worked so hard.
littlenot at all (did not know or understand)Little did I know that I would get the job.
not only ... but (also)this, and that tooNot only is it fast, but it is also cheap.
no sooner ... thanone thing happened right after anotherNo sooner had I sat down than the phone rang.
hardly, scarcely, barely ... whenone thing happened right after anotherHardly had the meeting started when the power failed.
under no circumstances, on no accountnever, for any reasonOn no account should you restart the server.
at no time, in no waynever, not at allAt no time did the company warn us.
only then, only later, only after ..., only when ..., only if ...not before this pointOnly when I read the logs did I understand.
not until ...not before this timeNot until Monday will we know the results.
nowherein no placeNowhere is this problem clearer than in our tests.

No sooner and hardly

These two show a fast order of events in the past. They usually take the past perfect. Learn their partner words: no sooner ... than and hardly ... when. Do not mix them.

no sooner ... than

No sooner had we launched than the first bug report arrived.

hardly ... when

Hardly had we launched when the first bug report arrived.

Only and not until: inversion in the main clause

With only when, only after, only if and not until, there are two clauses. Do not invert the first clause. Invert the second one, the main clause.

Only when did I read the logs, I understood.

Not until did she call, we knew.

Only when I read the logs did I understand.

Not until she called did we know.

When there is no inversion

Inversion only happens when the negative word changes the whole sentence. Some phrases look negative but are not.

  • In no time means "very quickly". It is not negative. "In no time, she had fixed it." There is no inversion.
  • Not long ago means "recently". "Not long ago, I moved to Seoul." There is no inversion.
  • Only + subject has no inversion. "Only Ana knows the password." Here only belongs to the subject.

Do not forget the auxiliary. "Never I have seen this" is wrong. "Not only he speaks French" is wrong. Say "Never have I seen this" and "Not only does he speak French".

Do not use inversion in every paragraph. One or two in an essay sound strong. Five sound strange. In chat and normal speech, people rarely use it. Common spoken phrases like "Little did I know" are the exception.

Inversion in conditionals: had I known, were I, should you

Had I known about the meeting, I would have come.

= If I had known about the meeting, I would have come.

In formal English, you can drop if and use inversion. Only three words can start the sentence this way: had, were and should. The chapter Conditionals explains the normal forms.

Conditionals without if
Normal formInversionUse
If I had known, I would have helped.Had I known, I would have helped.third conditional: an unreal past
If I were you, I would wait.Were I you, I would wait.second conditional with be
If prices rose, sales would fall.Were prices to rise, sales would fall.second conditional with other verbs: were + to
If you need help, please call me.Should you need help, please call me.first conditional: a possible but less likely future

Should you ...: very common in business

You will see should you at the end of many formal emails and letters. It sounds polite and a little less direct.

  • Should you have any questions, please contact me.
  • Should the problem continue, restart the device.
  • Please call us should you need more information. (The clause can come last.)

Negatives: not after the subject

In negative inversions, put not after the subject. Do not use short forms like hadn't.

Hadn't I seen the error, we would have lost data.

Weren't it for your help, I would fail.

Had I not seen the error, we would have lost data.

Were it not for your help, I would fail.

Only had, were and should work this way. "Did I know, I would tell you" is wrong. "Would I have time, I would help" is wrong. Use if: "If I knew, I would tell you."

"Were it not for" means "without". "Were it not for the rain, we would go." "Had it not been for" is the past form. "Had it not been for her, the project would have failed."

So, such and neither

So strong was the wind that the trees fell.

Such was the noise that nobody could sleep.

I can't swim, and neither can my brother.

These words also cause inversion. They are less common than the negative words, but they are useful.

  • So + adjective + be + subject + that. "So popular was the app that the servers crashed." The normal form is "The app was so popular that the servers crashed."
  • Such + be + noun + that. "Such was the demand that we hired ten people." This means "The demand was so big that ...".
  • So, neither, nor + auxiliary + subject. "I love tea. So does my wife." "He didn't come, nor did he call." This is normal in speech too.

Do not use normal order after so and neither in short answers. "So I do" means something different. It means "Yes, it is true, I do". To agree, say "So do I".

Cleft sentences: it is ... that

Ana fixed the bug on Friday.

It was Ana who fixed the bug on Friday.

It was on Friday that Ana fixed the bug.

A cleft sentence splits one sentence into two parts. This puts one part in focus. The focus is the new or important information. The other part is usually known already.

The form is It + be + focus + that / who + the rest. Use who or that for people. Use that for things, times and places.

Correcting someone

The it-cleft is perfect for a correction. It shows a contrast.

Ben: So you broke the build yesterday?

Ola: No, it wasn't me who broke it. It was the new script.

Ben: And it was the database that failed?

Ola: No. It was the network that failed, not the database.

Focus on a reason or a time

  • It was because of the rain that we stayed in. (focus on the reason)
  • It was only last year that I started coding. (focus on the time)
  • It is in the details that most bugs hide. (focus on the place)

Use that, not when or where, after a time or place in an it-cleft. "It was in 2020 when I moved" is common in speech. But "It was in 2020 that I moved" is better in writing.

"It was me who called" is normal English. "It was I who called" is very formal. Both are correct. In an exam essay, avoid the problem. Write about a noun: "It was the manager who called."

Cleft sentences: what ... is

I need a long holiday.

What I need is a long holiday.

A wh-cleft starts with a what clause. Then comes is or was. The focus comes at the end, the strong place. This is very common in speech and in presentations.

Kinds of wh-cleft
StartFocus onExample
What I want is ...a thingWhat I want is a clear plan.
What happened was ...a whole eventWhat happened was the server ran out of memory.
What we did was (to) ...an actionWhat we did was restart every service.
All I want is ...only this, nothing moreAll I want is a quiet room.
The thing is ...a problem or a key pointThe thing is, we don't have time.
The reason (why) ... is that ...a reasonThe reason I left is that the pay was low.
The person who ... is ...a personThe person who helped me most was my mentor.
The place where ... is ...a placeThe place where we met was a small café.

The reversed form

You can also put the focus first. "A long holiday is what I need." "That's what I meant." "That's why I called." These short forms are very common in speech.

Focus on an action: what ... do

To focus on an action, use a form of do in the what clause. Then use the base form, with or without to.

  • What you should do is ask your manager.
  • What I did was (to) write a small test first.
  • What the update does is make the app faster.

What I need it is a break.

What I did was I called the client.

All I want are a coffee.

What I need is a break.

What I did was call the client.

All I want is a coffee.

Do not add a second subject after the what clause. The what clause is already the subject. "What I need it is" has two subjects. Say "What I need is".

Fronting: put it first

This plan I like. That one I don't.

Into the room walked a tall man in a black coat.

Here comes the bus!

Fronting means you move a part of the sentence to the front. It is not the subject. It can be an object, an adjective or a place.

Fronting an object for contrast

"Most of the report I understood. The last part I didn't." The objects come first. They show a contrast. This is common in speech. In writing, use it only for a clear contrast.

Place and movement: full inversion

After a phrase of place or movement, the main verb can come before the subject. This is common in stories and descriptions.

  • On the hill stood an old castle.
  • Down came the rain.
  • Off went the alarm.
  • Here comes the bus. There goes my last chance.

This works only when the subject is a noun. When the subject is a pronoun, keep the normal order.

Noun subject: inversion

Here comes the bus.

Off ran the dog.

Pronoun subject: normal order

Here it comes.

Off it ran.

Strange as it may seem

This form fronts an adjective with as or though. It means "although".

  • Strange as it may seem, the old code was faster. (= Although it may seem strange ...)
  • Tired as she was, she finished the report. (= Although she was tired ...)
  • Try as I might, I couldn't fix it. (= Although I tried hard ...)

Fronting to link sentences

Good writers often put known information first. New information comes at the end. Fronting helps with this order.

We tested three models. Of these, the smallest was the fastest.

The team found two problems. More serious was the memory leak.

In stories, the verb can come before a noun after direct speech. "'Stop!' shouted the guard." With a pronoun, use normal order: "'Stop!' he shouted." The form "said he" is old-fashioned.

Do, does and did for emphasis

Kim: You never read my messages.

Leo: That's not true. I do read them. I just reply late.

Kim: You didn't call the client.

Leo: I did call her. Check the call log.

In a positive sentence, we do not normally use do. But we can add it for emphasis. The form is do / does / did + base form. In speech, the do is stressed.

Use emphatic do for four things.

  1. To correct someone. "I did send the email. It's in your spam folder."
  2. To make a contrast. "I don't speak Spanish, but I do understand it."
  3. To agree strongly. "That does make sense, actually."
  4. To be warm and polite. "Do come in." "Do have another biscuit." This is British and a little formal.

When a sentence already has an auxiliary, just stress it in speech. "I AM listening!" "She HAS finished." In writing, you can use bold or italic for this stress, but not in formal texts.

I did called you.

She does works hard.

I did call you.

She does work hard.

After do, does and did, use the base form. Never add -s or -ed. The do already shows the tense and the person.

One sentence, many kinds of emphasis

Here is one plain sentence: "Ana found the bug on Friday." Each slide puts the focus on a different part. Read them aloud.

It-cleft on the person

It was Ana who found the bug.

Not Ben. Not Ola. Ana.

It-cleft on the time

It was on Friday that Ana found the bug.

Not on Monday.

Wh-cleft on the action

What Ana did was find the bug.

The action is new information.

Not until

Not until Friday did Ana find the bug.

It took a long time.

Not only

Not only did Ana find the bug, but she also fixed it.

Two good things.

No sooner

No sooner had Ana found the bug than another one appeared.

One event right after another.

Emphatic did

Ana did find the bug. She just didn't tell anyone.

A correction.

Which tool when?

Emphasis tools and their style
ToolStyleBest for
Negative inversionformal, written, speechesstrong statements, essays, rules
Had I, were I, should youformalbusiness letters, contracts, polite emails
It-cleftall stylescorrections and contrast
Wh-cleftall styles, very common in speechpresentations, explaining, building to a point
Fronting a placestories, descriptionsscenes and drama
Emphatic doall styles, very common in speechcorrections, contrast, strong agreement

Practice books for Cambridge C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency often test these forms in key word transformations. A common task gives the word NEVER or ONLY and asks for an inversion. In IELTS and other writing exams, one correct inversion or cleft can show a range of grammar. Accuracy matters more than variety. Check the official handbook of your exam.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for inversion and emphasis
PatternPurposeModelNote
Never / Rarely / Seldom + auxiliary + subject + verbMake a strong formal statementRarely have I seen such clean code.Add do, does or did if there is no auxiliary.
Not only + auxiliary + subject ..., but ... alsoAdd a second, surprising pointNot only is it fast, but it is also free.Only the first clause is inverted.
No sooner had + subject + past participle + thanShow that one event came right after anotherNo sooner had I left than it rained.Than, not when.
Hardly had + subject + past participle + whenShow that one event came right after anotherHardly had we started when the power failed.When, not than.
Only when / Not until + clause + auxiliary + subjectShow the moment something finally happenedOnly when I read it did I understand.Invert the main clause, not the first clause.
Under no circumstances + should + subject + verbGive a strong ruleUnder no circumstances should you share it.Common in rules and warnings.
Had + subject + past participle, would have ...Write a formal third conditionalHad I known, I would have called.Negative: had I not, never hadn't I.
Should + subject + base form, ...Offer help politely in formal writingShould you need help, please call.Very common at the end of emails.
Were + subject + to + verb, would ...Write a formal second conditionalWere prices to rise, sales would fall.With be: Were I you.
It + be + focus + that / who ...Correct or contrast one partIt was Ana who found it.Use that after a time, not when.
What + subject + verb + is ...Build up to the key pointWhat I need is more time.No second subject after the what clause.
All + subject + verb + is ...Say "only this"All I want is a quiet room.Usually is, not are.
Place phrase + verb + noun subjectDescribe a scene with dramaInto the room walked a tall man.Not with pronouns: Here it comes.
do / does / did + base formCorrect someone or stress a contrastI did send it. Check your spam.Base form after did: not "did sent".

Practice

Choose the right answer

Never ___ such a fast laptop.

  • I have used
  • have I used
  • I used

After never at the start, use question order: auxiliary + subject.

No sooner had we arrived ___ the meeting began.

  • when
  • than
  • that

No sooner goes with than. Hardly goes with when.

Which sentence is correct?

  • Only when did I see the error, I stopped.
  • Only when I saw the error did I stop.
  • Only when I saw the error I did stop.

With only when, invert the main clause, not the first clause.

___ you need more information, please contact us.

  • Would
  • Should
  • Had

Should + subject + base form replaces if in a formal first conditional.

Which sentence needs no inversion?

  • Rarely ___ she late.
  • In no time, she ___ the task.
  • At no time ___ we told.

In no time means "very quickly". It is not negative, so the order is normal.

Which cleft sentence is correct?

  • What I want it is a new job.
  • What I did was I called the team.
  • What I did was call the team.

The what clause is the subject. After was, use the base form for an action.

Complete the sentence

Not only (he / speak) Japanese, but he also writes it.

Little (I / know) that the company would close.

? I known about the delay, I would have taken a taxi.

Were it ? for my mentor, I would have quit.

It was the manager ? approved the change.

I don't play the guitar well, but I ? enjoy it.

Here (it / come)!

Think and write

  1. Rewrite with inversion: "I have rarely heard such a good talk."
    Answer

    "Rarely have I heard such a good talk."

  2. Rewrite with "Should": "If you have any problems, call the help desk."
    Answer

    "Should you have any problems, call the help desk."

  3. Correct the mistake: "Hadn't she warned us, we would have lost everything."
    Answer

    "Had she not warned us, we would have lost everything." Put not after the subject. Do not use a short form.

  4. Make two it-clefts from "Tom deleted the file on Monday." Focus on Tom, then on Monday.
    Answer

    "It was Tom who deleted the file on Monday." "It was on Monday that Tom deleted the file."

  5. Your colleague says you forgot to test the code. You did test it. Reply with emphatic do and a cleft.
    Sample answer

    "I did test it. What I didn't test was the old browser version."

  6. Rewrite with "Not until": "We only understood the problem when we read the logs."
    Answer

    "Not until we read the logs did we understand the problem." Invert the main clause.

  7. Write the opening of a formal report about a security incident. Use one negative inversion and one wh-cleft.
    Sample answer

    "At no time was customer data at risk. What the attacker reached was a test server with no real data."

What is inversion?

The auxiliary goes before the subject, as in a question.

No sooner ... ? Hardly ... ?

No sooner ... than. Hardly ... when.

With "only when", which clause is inverted?

The main clause, the second one.

Three words that replace if with inversion?

had, were, should

Negative of "Had I known"?

Had I not known.

"Here comes the bus." With a pronoun?

Here it comes.

Emphatic do: "I ___ (send) it yesterday."

did send

Key takeaways

  • Inversion puts the auxiliary before the subject, like in a question.
  • Negative and limiting words at the front cause inversion: never, rarely, little, not only, no sooner, hardly.
  • With only when and not until, invert the main clause.
  • Some phrases look negative but are not, like in no time. They take normal order.
  • Had, were and should can replace if in formal conditionals. The negative is had I not.
  • It-clefts focus on one part and are great for corrections.
  • What-clefts build up to the key point at the end.
  • After a place phrase, a noun subject can follow the verb. A pronoun cannot.
  • Do, does and did + base form add emphasis to a positive sentence.
  • Use these tools a little. Too many make writing sound unnatural.

Sources

  • Inversion after negative adverbials, British Council LearnEnglish. The list of negative words, the word order and the formal style.
  • Inversion and conditionals, British Council LearnEnglish. Should, were and had without if, and the negative forms.
  • Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion and auxiliaries, British Council LearnEnglish. It-clefts, what-clefts and emphatic do.
  • Cleft sentence, Wikipedia. The main types of cleft and the idea of focus.
  • Subject–verb inversion in English, Wikipedia. Inversion after place phrases and after direct speech.

Subjunctive and unreal past

English has special verb forms for wishes, demands and imagined situations. Some look like the present but break the rules. Others look like the past but are not about the past. This chapter shows both, from "I suggest he leave" to "It's time we went".

  • Use the subjunctive after suggest, insist, demand and it is vital that.
  • Choose between the subjunctive, should and the normal form.
  • Use were in formal unreal sentences.
  • Use the unreal past after it's time, would rather, would sooner, as if and as though.
  • Understand and use formal fixed phrases like be that as it may and come what may.

Two strange families of verb forms

The doctor suggested that he rest for a week.

It's time we went home.

Look at the first sentence. The subject is he, but the verb is rest, not rests. Look at the second sentence. The verb is went, but it is about now, not the past.

These are two different families. Both are about ideas that are not real facts yet.

Two families
FamilyWhat it looks likeMeaningExample
The subjunctivethe base form for every person: be, go, restsomething someone wants or demandsWe insist that she be on time.
The unreal pasta past form: went, had, weresomething imagined, wished or not trueI wish I had more time.

Subjunctive: "This must happen." Unreal past: "This is not real. I am imagining it."

The subjunctive after suggest, insist and demand

The manager insisted that every developer write tests.

They demanded that the company pay them for overtime.

I recommend that she take the senior role.

After some verbs, a that clause takes the base form of the verb. This is the subjunctive. It has the same form for every person. There is no -s for he, she or it.

The verbs all show that someone wants something to happen. They are verbs of demand and advice.

The form in four cases

The subjunctive form
CaseFormExample
Positivebase formI suggest that he call the client.
With bebe (not is, are, am)They asked that we be quiet.
Negativenot + base form (no do)She insisted that he not tell anyone.
Passivebe + past participleThe law requires that all data be encrypted.

The past does not change it

The subjunctive does not show time. When the main verb is in the past, the subjunctive stays the same.

  • The teacher suggests that he study more.
  • The teacher suggested that he study more.

This is different from normal reported speech. There, the verb moves back in time. Here, it does not.

Do not use to after suggest. "He suggested me to rest" is wrong. Say "He suggested that I rest", "He suggested that I should rest" or "He suggested resting". The same is true for recommend and insist.

She suggested me to take a break.

They insisted that he doesn't leave.

I recommend that he is promoted.

She suggested that I take a break.

They insisted that he not leave.

I recommend that he be promoted.

It is vital that ...: adjectives and nouns

It is vital that the patient receive treatment today.

It is essential that every user change their password.

Our main requirement is that the system be available all day.

Some adjectives also take the subjunctive. The pattern is It is + adjective + that + subject + base form. The adjectives show that something is very important or necessary.

Common adjectives: vital, essential, important, necessary, crucial, imperative. The word imperative here means "very important, must happen".

Some nouns work the same way: suggestion, demand, requirement, recommendation, insistence, proposal. "The committee made the recommendation that the project be stopped."

You will see the subjunctive in contracts, policies, rules and formal reports. "The tenant requests that the deposit be returned." "It is a condition of entry that all bags be checked." It sounds clear and serious.

Not every adjective takes the subjunctive. "It is true that he is late" is a fact. It needs the normal form. The subjunctive follows adjectives of need and importance, not adjectives of fact or feeling.

Subjunctive, should or the normal form?

You can say the same idea in three ways. They differ in style and in region.

Three ways to say one idea
FormExampleStyle and region
SubjunctiveI suggest that he leave early.formal. Normal in American English. Common in formal British English.
should + base formI suggest that he should leave early.more common in British English
Normal present or pastI suggest that he leaves early.informal British English. Avoid it in formal writing.

Studies of large collections of real texts show a pattern. American English mostly uses the subjunctive here. British English uses should more often than American English. But a 2020 study found that the British subjunctive is still alive. The choice also depends on the verb, like suggest or insist. See Modal verbs for other uses of should.

In an exam, use the subjunctive or should. Both are safe. The normal form, "I suggest that he leaves", is common in British speech. But some examiners may count it as an error, so avoid it.

A fact

He insisted that he was innocent.

He said strongly: "I am innocent." This is a claim.

A demand

He insisted that she be present.

He said strongly: "She must be there." This is a demand.

The verb insist can have two meanings. The form shows which one you mean. The same is true for suggest: "The data suggests that the plan works" is a fact. It takes the normal form.

Were in formal style

If I were you, I would accept the offer.

I wish she were here.

He talks as if he were the boss.

In unreal sentences, formal English uses were for every person: I, he, she and it. Grammar books call this the were-subjunctive. In everyday speech, many people say was. Both are common. Were is the safe choice in writing and exams.

Where to use were
AfterExampleNote
if (unreal)If it were cheaper, I would buy it.See Conditionals.
wish, if onlyI wish it were Friday.was is common in speech
as if, as thoughShe acts as if she were in charge.unreal comparison
if ... were toIf the server were to fail, we would lose data.an unlikely future, formal
inversionWere I in your place, I would wait.very formal

Were to: an unlikely future

If + subject + were to + base form makes a future event sound unlikely. It is common in formal writing and polite requests.

  • If the price were to double, we would lose customers.
  • If you were to move the meeting, I could join.
  • Were the bank to raise rates, house prices would fall.

The last example uses inversion. See Inversion and emphasis.

Use were only for unreal ideas. For a real past fact, use was. "If he was at the office yesterday, he saw the email." This is a real possibility, not an imagined one. "If he were at the office yesterday" is wrong here.

It's time, it's high time, it's about time

It's time we left. The last train goes at eleven.

It's high time you updated your CV.

It's about time the company fixed the website.

After it's time + subject, use a past form. The meaning is present: we should do this now. High and about make it stronger. They often show that you are annoyed. The action is late already.

Two patterns after it's time
PatternExampleMeaning
it's time + to + base formIt's time to go.a neutral fact: now is the right moment
it's time + subject + past simpleIt's time we went.we should do it, and maybe we are late
it's time + for + person + to + base formIt's time for us to go.neutral, with a person

It's time we go home.

It's high time you have a holiday.

It's time we went home.

It's high time you had a holiday.

Do not use the past perfect after it's time. "It's time we had left" is wrong. The idea is about now, so use the past simple.

Would rather and would sooner

I'd rather work from home today.

I'd rather you didn't call me after nine.

I'd sooner walk than wait an hour for the bus.

Would rather and would sooner show a preference. They mean the same. Would sooner is less common. The chapter Conditionals introduced would rather. Here are all the forms.

Would rather and would sooner: the forms
Who and whenFormExample
Same personwould rather + base formI'd rather stay here.
Same person, two choiceswould rather + base form + than + base formI'd sooner cook than order food.
Same person, the pastwould rather + have + past participleI'd rather have stayed at home. (I didn't.)
Another person, now or futurewould rather + subject + past simpleI'd rather you came tomorrow.
Another person, the pastwould rather + subject + past perfectI'd rather you hadn't told him.

The phrase "I'd rather you didn't" is a polite way to say no. "Can I share your slides?" "I'd rather you didn't. They aren't finished."

With another person, do not use the present. "I'd rather you don't smoke" is common in speech but wrong in careful English. Say "I'd rather you didn't smoke". And never use to: "I'd rather to stay" is wrong.

As if and as though

It looks as if it's going to rain.

He talks as if he knew everything.

She looked at me as though I had said something terrible.

As if and as though compare a situation with another idea. They mean the same. As if is more common. The verb form shows what the speaker thinks.

Maybe true: normal tense

It looks as if the build is broken.

I think it may really be broken.

Not true: unreal past

He acts as if he owned the company.

He doesn't own it. I am sure.

As if: choose the form
Time of the ideaReal or possibleUnreal
Same time as the main verbShe sounds as if she has a cold.She talks as if she were the CEO.
Before the main verbYou look as if you've been running.He looked as if he had seen a ghost.

In informal speech, many people say like instead of as if. "It looks like it's going to rain." This is very common, especially in American English. In formal writing, use as if.

The phrase "As if!" alone is informal. It means "That will never happen" or "I don't believe it."

The unreal past: one idea behind many forms

You have now seen many forms with a past verb that does not mean past time. They all follow one idea. A past form moves the idea away from reality. A past perfect moves an unreal idea into the past.

Words that take the unreal past
WordsAbout now (past simple)About the past (past perfect)
if (unreal)If I knew, I would tell you.If I had known, I would have told you.
wish, if onlyI wish I knew.If only I had known.
would rather, would soonerI'd rather you stayed.I'd rather you had stayed.
as if, as thoughHe acts as if he knew.He acted as if he had known.
suppose, supposing, imagine, what ifSuppose you lost your job.Suppose you had lost your job.
it's timeIt's time we left.(not used)

The same idea of distance explains polite past forms. "I wondered if you could help" is softer than "I wonder if you can help". The past puts some distance between you and the request. See Advanced tense and aspect.

The carousel shows one office problem. Each slide uses a different form from this chapter.

The fact

Tom is late to every meeting. Today he is late again.

Wish + would

I wish Tom would come on time.

It's high time

It's high time Tom started on time.

Would rather

I'd rather he told us when he is late.

As if

He walks in as if nothing were wrong.

Suggest + subjunctive

The manager suggests that Tom set an alarm.

It is vital that

It is vital that everyone be present at nine.

If only (past)

If only we had started without him!

Formal fixed phrases

Some old subjunctive forms survive in fixed phrases. You cannot change their words. They are formal or old-fashioned. Learn them as whole units.

Be that as it may

It means "even so" or "that may be true, but". "The plan is expensive. Be that as it may, we need it."

Come what may

It means "whatever happens". "Come what may, we will ship on Friday."

So be it

It means "I accept this, even if I don't like it". "If they want to cancel the project, so be it."

Suffice it to say

It means "I will only say this much". "Suffice it to say, the demo did not go well."

If need be

It means "if necessary". "We can work at the weekend if need be."

Far be it from me to ...

It means "I don't want to criticise, but ...". It often comes before a criticism. "Far be it from me to complain, but the coffee is cold."

Heaven forbid

It means "I really hope this never happens". "If, heaven forbid, the server fails, call me at once."

Truth be told

It means "to be honest". "Truth be told, I never liked the old design."

As it were

It means "in a way" or "so to speak". It shows that a word is not exact. "She is the heart of the team, as it were."

Long live ..., God save the King

These are wishes for a person or an idea. "Long live the open web!" "God save the King" is the British national anthem.

Be it ... or ...

It means "whether it is ... or ...". "Be it a small team or a large company, the rules are the same." This is very formal.

Lest

It means "so that ... not". It is very formal. "We keep a backup lest the data be lost." In normal English, say "in case the data is lost".

Do not change the words in these phrases. "Be this as it may" and "Comes what may" are wrong. Also, do not use too many of them. One in a formal email is enough. In chat, they can sound strange or funny.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the subjunctive and the unreal past
PatternPurposeModelNote
suggest / recommend + that + subject + base formGive formal adviceI suggest that he rest.No -s. Never "suggest him to".
insist / demand + that + subject + base formMake a strong demandThey insisted that she be paid.Use be, not is.
... that + subject + not + base formMake a negative demandHe asked that we not wait.No do or don't.
It is vital / essential that + subject + base formSay something must happenIt is vital that he call today.Only after words of need and importance.
... that + subject + should + base formGive advice in British styleI suggest that he should rest.Safe in exams too.
... that + data + be + past participleWrite a formal passive demandWe require that all files be checked.Common in rules and contracts.
If + subject + were (to) ...Imagine something formal or unlikelyIf the system were to fail, we would lose data.Were for every person in formal style.
It's time + subject + past simpleSay something should happen nowIt's time we went home.Past form, present meaning.
It's high time + subject + past simpleSay something is late alreadyIt's high time you updated it.Shows annoyance.
would rather / would sooner + base formSay what you preferI'd sooner walk than wait.No to after rather or sooner.
would rather + subject + past simpleSay what you want another person to doI'd rather you didn't share it.Not "you don't".
would rather + subject + past perfectWish another person had acted differentlyI'd rather you hadn't told him.About the past.
as if / as though + normal tenseDescribe what seems likelyIt looks as if it's going to rain.Maybe true.
as if / as though + past or past perfectCompare with something not trueHe talks as if he were the boss.Not true, in the speaker's view.
Be that as it may, ...Accept a point, then go onBe that as it may, we need a decision.Fixed phrase. Do not change it.

Practice

Choose the right answer

The doctor recommended that she ___ more water.

  • drinks
  • drink
  • to drink

After recommend + that, use the base form for every person.

It's time we ___ the meeting. It's already six.

  • finish
  • finished
  • had finished

It's time + subject takes the past simple. The meaning is now.

I'd rather you ___ my laptop without asking.

  • don't use
  • not use
  • didn't use

With another person, would rather takes the past simple.

Which sentence says that the speaker thinks it is NOT true?

  • He looks as if he is tired.
  • He behaves as if he were the manager.
  • It looks as if the train is late.

The unreal past after as if shows that the idea is not true.

Which sentence is correct?

  • She suggested me to apply for the job.
  • She suggested that I apply for the job.
  • She suggested that I applied for the job next year.

Suggest takes that + subject + base form, or an -ing form. Never object + to.

"We can stay late if need be." What does "if need be" mean?

  • if necessary
  • if we want
  • if the manager is there

If need be is a fixed phrase. It means "if necessary".

Write the verb form

It is essential that every employee (complete) the training.

The law requires that all passwords (store) safely.

She insisted that he (not / drive) home.

If I (be) in your position, I would ask for help.

It's high time you (get) a new phone.

I'd rather you (not / tell) the client yesterday.

He looked as though he (not / sleep) for days.

Think and write

  1. Correct the mistake: "The manager demanded that he finishes the report today."
    Answer

    "The manager demanded that he finish the report today." Or, in British style: "that he should finish". Use the base form, with no -s.

  2. Explain the difference: "She insisted that he was honest." and "She insisted that he be honest."
    Answer

    The first is a claim: she said strongly that he was an honest person. The second is a demand: she wanted him to tell the truth.

  3. Rewrite with "It's time": "We should start the project now. We are late."
    Answer

    "It's (high) time we started the project."

  4. Rewrite with "would rather": "Please don't call me during the weekend."
    Answer

    "I'd rather you didn't call me during the weekend."

  5. Rewrite in formal style with "were to": "If we lose this client, we will have problems."
    Answer

    "If we were to lose this client, we would have problems." Or with inversion: "Were we to lose this client, we would have problems." The form makes the event sound unlikely.

  6. Write a formal rule for a server room. Use "It is essential that" and a passive subjunctive.
    Sample answer

    "It is essential that the door be locked at all times. Visitors must sign in."

  7. Write a short formal email reply. You do not agree with a plan, but you accept it. Use two fixed phrases.
    Sample answer

    "Thank you for the update. Far be it from me to question the board, but the deadline is very short. Be that as it may, the team will do its best. If need be, we can add extra hours."

"I suggest that he ___ (be) on time."

be

Negative subjunctive: "We asked that they ___ (not / wait)."

not wait

British alternative to the subjunctive?

should + base form: "that he should leave".

"It's time we ___ (go)."

went

"I'd rather you ___ (not / smoke) here."

didn't smoke

As if + normal tense or past: which one means "not true"?

The past: "as if he were the boss".

What does "come what may" mean?

Whatever happens.

Key takeaways

  • The subjunctive uses the base form for every person: that he go, that she be.
  • It follows verbs, adjectives and nouns of demand and need: suggest, insist, vital, requirement.
  • The negative is not + base form. The passive is be + past participle.
  • The subjunctive does not change when the main verb is past.
  • British English often uses should + base form instead. Both are safe in exams.
  • Formal English uses were for every person in unreal sentences.
  • It's time, would rather, would sooner, as if and wish use a past form for an unreal idea now.
  • For an unreal idea about the past, move one more step back to the past perfect.
  • As if + normal tense means maybe true. As if + past means not true.
  • Fixed phrases like be that as it may and if need be never change their words.

Sources

  • Unreal time, British Council LearnEnglish. It's time, would rather, as if, as though, wish and if only.
  • Everyday Grammar: We suggest that you learn the subjunctive, VOA Learning English. Trigger verbs and adjectives and the base form.
  • English subjunctive, Wikipedia. The forms, the negative, should in British English, the were-subjunctive and fixed phrases.
  • Inversion and conditionals, British Council LearnEnglish. Were and were to in formal conditionals.
  • Mandative subjunctive versus should in world Englishes, Deshors and Gries, Corpora (2020). A corpus study of the subjunctive and should in many kinds of English.

Hedging and stance

Good writers show how sure they are. A small word like may, probably or suggest makes a claim softer. A word like clearly makes it stronger. This chapter shows you how to choose the right strength in research, reports and work messages.

  • Explain what hedges, boosters and stance are, and why writers use them.
  • Soften a claim with modal verbs, adverbs, verbs, nouns and approximate numbers.
  • Make a claim stronger with boosters, but only when the evidence is strong.
  • Use polite stance in emails, code reviews and incident reports.
  • Find the right amount of hedging: not too much and not too little.

What hedging and stance are

Read three versions of one sentence from a test report. Which one would you trust?

The new cache fixes all slow pages.

It might perhaps be possible that the new cache could help with some pages.

The new cache seems to fix most slow pages.

The first version is too sure. If one slow page is still slow, the writer is wrong. The second version is too unsure. The reader cannot find the result. The third version is honest. It gives the result and the right amount of doubt.

A hedge makes a claim softer. In the third version, seems to and most are hedges. A booster does the opposite. Clearly, definitely and always are boosters. A claim is any sentence that says "this is true".

Hedges and boosters are part of your stance. Stance answers three questions about the writer.

The three parts of stance
PartQuestionExamples
CertaintyHow sure am I?may, probably, seem, clearly, show
AttitudeWhat do I feel about it?unfortunately, surprisingly, importantly
PresenceDo I show myself?I think, we found, in my view

The linguist Ken Hyland described stance in academic writing in a well-known 2005 model. Its four parts are hedges, boosters, attitude markers and self-mention. Self-mention means words like I and we. This chapter uses the same names.

You already know the grammar of may, might and must from Modal verbs. This chapter does not repeat it. Here, these words become a style tool.

A hedge is not the same as vague language. "Most pages" is a clear hedge. It gives exact information about your doubt. "Some stuff kind of works" is just vague. The reader learns nothing.

Why writers hedge

Compare two sentences about one small study.

Remote work makes people more productive.

Our data suggest that remote work may make some people more productive.

The study had 200 people from one company. It cannot speak for every worker in the world. So the second sentence is more accurate. It is not weaker. It is more honest.

Five reasons to hedge

  1. Accuracy. Your evidence has limits. A hedge shows them. "In our two-week test, errors fell by half."
  2. Safety. New data can prove you wrong. A hedged claim survives. "The patch should fix the issue."
  3. Politeness. A soft request or opinion protects the other person's feelings. "Could we rename this variable?"
  4. Room for discussion. Other experts will read your work. A hedge invites them to check it.
  5. Respect for the reader. A strong claim says "trust me". A hedge says "here is the evidence, you decide".

Research writers hedge most when they explain their results. They hedge least when they describe their method. You know for sure what you did. You can only guess what the results mean.

A fact you measured: no hedge

The test took 4.2 seconds.

Disk usage was 99% at 02:00.

A reason you guess: hedge

This may be because of a cold cache.

The backup job probably filled the disk.

Hedge what you think. Do not hedge what you know.

The server maybe has 16 GB of memory.

The meeting possibly starts at ten.

The server has 16 GB of memory. (You checked it.)

I think the meeting starts at ten. I'll check. (You will find out.)

If you can check a fact, check it. Then write it as a plain fact. Hedging a fact you could check looks lazy.

Hedging with modal verbs

  • The bug may be in the date parser.
  • This might explain the slow start.
  • A bad config could cause the same error.
  • Large files can slow down the build.
  • I would suggest a smaller first release.
  • The update should take about ten minutes.

Modal verbs are the most common hedges in English. Each one has its own job.

Modal verbs as hedges
ModalHedging jobModel
maya real possibility, neutral or formalThe results may change with more data.
mighta weaker possibilityThis might be a network problem.
couldone possible explanation among othersLow memory could explain the crash.
cansomething that sometimes happens, in generalRetries can hide real errors.
woulda soft opinion or a careful guessI would argue that the risk is small.
shouldwhat you expect, if all goes wellThe fix should be live by noon.

Can or may?

Can talks about a general fact. It sometimes happens. May talks about this case. It is possible here and now.

  • Retries can hide real errors. (true in general)
  • Here, the retry may hide a real error. (this situation)

Would: the softest opinion

Would makes an opinion sound careful. "I would say", "I would argue" and "I would suggest" are common in meetings. Academic writers also use "This would seem to show ..." It is very formal. Use it rarely.

Hedges about the past

For a guess about the past, use modal + have + past participle. "The power cut may have caused the data loss." "The test might have failed because of the timeout." The full rules are in Modal verbs.

Negative hedges

May not means "maybe not". "This may not be the only cause." Cannot is not a hedge. It means you are sure. "This cannot be the cause."

The fix may can solve the problem.

It may possibly could be the cache.

This maybe is the cause.

The fix may solve the problem.

It may be the cache.

This may be the cause. Or: Maybe this is the cause.

Maybe (one word) is an adverb. It means "perhaps". May be (two words) is a modal verb + be. "Maybe it is the cache" means "It may be the cache". Maybe is informal. In formal writing, use perhaps or may.

Adverbs, adjectives and approximate numbers

The outage was probably caused by a bad deploy. It affected approximately 12% of users. Arguably, our alerts were too slow.

Adverbs like probably show how likely something is. You can line them up by strength.

Probability adverbs from strong to weak
StrengthAdverbModel
very strongalmost certainlyThe job will almost certainly fail again.
strongvery probably, most likelyIt is most likely a DNS problem.
mediumprobablyThe vendor probably changed the API.
weakpossibly, perhaps, maybePerhaps the token expired.
very weakconceivablyThe bug could conceivably be in the compiler.

Where the adverb goes

  • After be: "It is probably the cache."
  • After the first helping verb: "It will probably work." "It has probably finished."
  • Before a negative helping verb: "It probably won't work." Not "It won't probably work."
  • Perhaps and maybe often start the sentence: "Perhaps the config is wrong."

Likely and unlikely

Likely is mostly an adjective. It has two patterns. Do not mix them.

  • Subject + is likely to + verb: "The release is likely to slip."
  • It is likely that + clause: "It is likely that the release will slip."

American English also uses likely as an adverb: "The release will likely slip." British writers more often say "will probably" or "is likely to".

Arguably, apparently, presumably

  • Arguably means "I can give good reasons for this". It hedges, but it still takes a position. "Rust is arguably the safest choice here." Give the reason next.
  • Apparently means "from what I heard or read". It keeps you at a distance. "Apparently, the vendor changed the API."
  • Presumably means "I think so, from what I know". "The job presumably ran at midnight, as usual."

Approximate numbers

An approximator hedges a number: about, around, roughly, approximately, nearly, almost, just under, just over. Formal writing also uses some: "some 40 customers". "Roughly a third of users left." "Just under half of the tests passed."

Quantity and frequency hedges

Words like most, many and some limit a claim to part of a group. Words like often, usually, generally and in most cases limit it in time. Compare: "Users hate pop-ups." and "Many users dislike pop-ups." The second claim is much easier to defend.

It won't probably work.

The release is likely that it will slip.

Approximately 12.37% of users left.

It probably won't work.

The release is likely to slip.

Approximately 12% of users left. Or: Exactly 12.37% of users left.

The last wrong line mixes an approximator with an exact number. Choose one. Give a round number with an approximator, or the exact number without one.

Verbs and nouns that hedge

The logs suggest a memory leak. The service appears to restart every night. Users tend to log in at 9 a.m.

Some verbs are hedges too. They let you report what you see without saying it is a fact. These verbs are very common in reports and research.

Seem, appear and tend to

  • Subject + seems to / appears to + verb: "The service appears to restart every night."
  • Subject + seems to have / appears to have + past participle: "The deploy appears to have failed." Use this for the past.
  • It seems / It appears that + clause: "It appears that the token expired."
  • Subject + tends to + verb, for a general habit: "Large teams tend to ship more slowly."

Appear is more formal than seem. "It seems like a bug" is informal and spoken. In writing, say "It seems to be a bug" or "This appears to be a bug".

Reporting verbs: from strong to soft

When you report results, the verb shows how strong your evidence is.

  • prove: no doubt at all. This is rare in research. Use it for maths and logic.
  • show, demonstrate: strong evidence. "The benchmark shows a 40% speed-up."
  • indicate: good evidence, but not complete. "The logs indicate a timeout."
  • suggest: some evidence. Other explanations are possible. "The pattern suggests a memory leak."

The passive also helps you hedge. It hides who believes the claim. "It is thought that ...", "The bug is believed to be in the parser." See The passive.

Nouns that hedge

Nouns like possibility, likelihood, chance, assumption, estimate, tendency and evidence can carry the doubt. They sound formal and fit reports.

  • There is a possibility that + clause: "There is a possibility that some data was lost."
  • There is a strong likelihood that + clause: "There is a strong likelihood that prices will rise."
  • The likelihood of + noun is low or high: "The likelihood of a second outage is low."
  • In all likelihood means "very probably": "In all likelihood, the vendor will fix it."
  • One possible explanation is that + clause.
  • There is some evidence that + clause.

Turning verbs into nouns is called nominalisation. The chapter Participle clauses and nominalisation explains when it helps.

Phrases and if-clauses

A short phrase can limit a whole claim: to our knowledge, as far as we know, in my view, from the data we have. An if-clause limits it to a condition: "If these results hold, we can drop the old service." "Under normal load, the queue stays short."

It is seemed that the token expired.

The deploy appears to fail yesterday.

This one test proves that the design is better.

It seems that the token expired.

The deploy appears to have failed yesterday.

This test suggests that the design is better.

Seem and appear have no passive form. For the past, use the perfect form: to have + past participle.

Boosters and attitude markers

The results clearly show a drop in errors. In fact, errors fell by 80%. Surprisingly, the fix was only three lines.

Boosters make a claim stronger. Use them when your evidence is strong, or when you correct a wrong belief.

  • Adverbs: clearly, certainly, definitely, undoubtedly, of course
  • Phrases: in fact, indeed, it is clear that, there is no doubt that
  • Verbs: show, demonstrate, prove, confirm
  • Absolute words: always, never, all, none

Hedge the claim, boost the evidence

Expert writers often use a booster and a hedge in neighbouring sentences. The booster sits on the evidence. The hedge sits on the meaning.

We clearly measured a 40% drop in latency. This may be due to the new index.

The measurement is certain. The reason is a guess. So each sentence gets the right strength.

Be careful with obviously

"Obviously, you should test first." This can sound rude. It tells the reader they missed something easy. Use clearly, or no booster at all.

Attitude markers

An attitude marker shows feeling, not certainty: unfortunately, fortunately, surprisingly, interestingly, importantly, it is worth noting that. They guide the reader to what matters. One or two in a paragraph is plenty.

I and we

Self-mention shows who is responsible. Many research papers use we: "We found ..." In business, "I recommend ..." shows that you own the advice. Some school essays avoid I. Check the style your reader expects.

This obviously proves that users love the new design.

Undoubtedly, the results may show a small effect.

Very importantly and surprisingly, the test passed.

The survey shows that 70% of users prefer the new design.

The results may show a small effect.

Surprisingly, the test passed.

The second wrong line sends two signals. Undoubtedly says "sure". May says "not sure". Choose one strength for each claim.

Stance at work

At work, hedges do a second job. They make you polite. Read the same message in two styles.

This function is wrong. Rewrite it with a map.

I wonder if a map would work better here. Lookups might be faster. What do you think?

Both versions give the same advice. The second one leaves room for the author's view. People accept advice more easily in this form.

Softening messages at work
SituationToo directSoftened
RequestSend me the report today.Could you send me the report today, if possible?
DisagreementThat's wrong.I'm not sure that's right. The logs seem to show something different.
Code reviewRename this.Could we rename this to make it clearer?
Bad newsWe will miss the deadline.I'm afraid we may miss the deadline.
EstimateIt will be done on Friday.It should be done by Friday, assuming the API is ready.
OpinionOption B is better.I'd suggest option B. It seems easier to maintain.

Tools for a softer tone

  • Would, could, might: "I'd suggest ...", "Could we ...?", "It might be worth adding a test."
