  • Soft starters: "I wonder if ...", "I'm not sure ...", "It looks like ..."
  • Small words: "a bit late", "slightly slower".
  • Not very + a good word: "not very clear" sounds kinder than "unclear".
  • Past tense for distance: "I was wondering if you could help." This is very polite.
  • I'm afraid before bad news: "I'm afraid the demo is cancelled."

Soften the tone, not the facts. "We may miss the deadline" is fine only if it is still uncertain. If you know you will miss it, say so: "We will miss Friday. The new date is Tuesday." A clear message is kinder than a foggy one.

Hedges in incident reports

Many teams write a postmortem after an outage. Good postmortems are blameless. They hedge open questions and state confirmed facts plainly.

Timeline (facts): At 14:02 the deploy started. At 14:05 the error rate rose to 30%. At 14:11 we rolled back.

Cause (still open): The new connection pool appears to have run out of connections. We have not yet confirmed this.

Impact (estimate): Roughly 8,000 requests failed.

Next step: We will add a limit test before the next deploy.

When the team confirms the cause, the report changes. "The new connection pool ran out of connections." The hedge goes away because the doubt went away.

For estimates in meetings, see Meetings and stand-ups. For review comments, see Writing at work.

Academic and business writing hedge different things. Research hedges claims about the world: "This may explain ..." Business hedges claims about people and plans: "Could you ...?" In chat, people hedge less and use short words: "prob", "maybe", "looks like".

Too much and too little hedging

Hedging is a dial, not a switch. Turn it too low and you overclaim. Turn it too high and nobody can find your point.

Too little hedging

Remote work always improves productivity. This proves that offices are useless.

Signs: always, never, all, prove. One example becomes a rule. No limits on the claim.

Too much hedging

It may possibly be that remote work could perhaps help some people somewhat.

Signs: two or more hedges on one claim. Hedges on facts. The main point is hard to see.

Too little hedging makes you look careless. Too much makes you look unsure, or as if you are hiding something. The goal is calibration. One hedge per claim is usually enough. The evidence decides how strong it is.

Match the strength to the evidence
Your evidenceStrengthModel
measured, repeated many timesplain fact or boosterThe new index cuts query time by 40%.
strong but from one settingplain fact + scopeIn our tests, the new index cut query time by 40%.
some evidencesoft hedgeThe index seems to help most queries.
a guess from experiencestronger hedgeThe index might also help the reports.
no evidence yetsay soWe have not tested the reports yet.

Write the bare claim

Remote work increases productivity.

Name your evidence

A survey of 300 developers at our company. They rated their own productivity.

Limit the scope

For developers at our company, remote work increases productivity.

Choose one hedge

The data are self-ratings, so use a soft reporting verb: suggest.

Remove extra hedges

Not "may possibly suggest". One hedge is enough: "Our survey suggests ..."

Read the final claim

Our survey of 300 developers suggests that remote work increases their productivity. The point is clear, and the limits are honest.

A rough stance counter in Python

You can count hedges and boosters in a draft with a few lines of code. This gives a rough signal, not a grade.

import re

# Small word lists. Real research tools use lists of 100+ items.
HEDGES = {"may", "might", "could", "perhaps", "possibly", "probably",
          "likely", "seem", "seems", "appear", "appears", "suggest",
          "suggests", "tend", "tends", "approximately", "roughly"}
BOOSTERS = {"clearly", "obviously", "certainly", "definitely",
            "always", "never", "prove", "proves", "undoubtedly"}

def stance(text):
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower())
    hedges = [w for w in words if w in HEDGES]
    boosters = [w for w in words if w in BOOSTERS]
    rate = lambda found: round(100 * len(found) / len(words), 1)
    return len(words), rate(hedges), rate(boosters), hedges + boosters

drafts = {
    "overclaim": "This clearly proves that caching always makes the API "
                 "faster. Users will definitely notice.",
    "balanced": "The results suggest that caching makes most API calls "
                "faster. Users will probably notice the change.",
    "overhedged": "It may possibly seem that caching could perhaps make "
                  "some calls slightly faster in some cases.",
}

for name, text in drafts.items():
    n, h, b, found = stance(text)
    print(f"{name:<10} words={n}  hedges/100={h}  boosters/100={b}  {found}")
overclaim  words=14  hedges/100=0.0  boosters/100=28.6  ['clearly', 'proves', 'always', 'definitely']
balanced   words=16  hedges/100=12.5  boosters/100=0.0  ['suggest', 'probably']
overhedged words=16  hedges/100=31.2  boosters/100=0.0  ['may', 'possibly', 'seem', 'could', 'perhaps']

The balanced draft has two hedges in two sentences. The other drafts have four or five. But a word counter does not understand meaning. It counts "May" the month as a hedge. It misses "slightly" and "some". So use it to find problem paragraphs, then read them yourself.

The IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023) ask for a clear position in Task 2 at band 7 and above. At band 7, they also mention "a tendency to over-generalise". So hedge your examples and generalisations, but never hedge your main position. In Task 1, use approximators for data: "just under half", "roughly a third".

Expert level: calibrated language

Words like likely mean different things to different people. One reader hears 60%. Another hears 90%. For a big decision, this gap is dangerous.

The IPCC solves this with calibrated language. In its reports, each likelihood word has a fixed range. The words are printed in italics, so readers know they are special. The table shows the main terms from its Sixth Assessment Report.

IPCC likelihood terms (Sixth Assessment Report)
TermProbability
virtually certain99–100%
very likely90–100%
likely66–100%
about as likely as not33–66%
unlikely0–33%
very unlikely0–10%
exceptionally unlikely0–1%

The IPCC also uses a second scale for confidence: very low, low, medium, high and very high. Confidence depends on the amount and quality of evidence, and on how much experts agree. So a report can say a result is likely, with medium confidence. Two separate questions get two separate answers.

Use it in your own work

  • Give a number when you have one. "A 70% chance" is clearer than "likely".
  • Define your words. In a risk document, add one line: "In this document, likely means more than 66%."
  • Hedge with scope, not only with modals. "In staging", "for files under 1 GB" and "in our survey" are precise hedges.
  • Put the hedge where the doubt is. "The fix should reduce errors" doubts the effect. "The fix reduced errors in staging" limits the place.
  • Search long documents for stacks. Look for "may possibly", "could potentially" and "might perhaps". Keep one word.

Before you send an important message, mark each claim. Is it a fact, an estimate or a guess? Facts get no hedge. Estimates get a number or an approximator. Guesses get one hedge.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for hedging and stance
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + may / might / could + verbSoften a possible claimThe bug may be in the parser.Never "may can" or "may possibly could".
Subject + may have + past participleHedge a guess about the pastThe update may have caused the crash.Not "may caused".
Subject + appears to / seems to + verbReport what you see, softlyThe service appears to restart at night."Seems like" is informal.
Subject + appears to have + past participleSoft claim about a past eventThe deploy appears to have failed.No passive: never "it is seemed".
Subject + tends to + verbDescribe a habit, not a ruleLarge teams tend to ship more slowly.Use it instead of always.
The data suggest / indicate that + clauseReport results with careThe data suggest a memory leak.Prove is too strong for most results.
Subject + is likely to + verbSay something is probableThe release is likely to slip.Or: It is likely that the release will slip.
There is a possibility that + clauseA formal hedge with a nounThere is a possibility that data was lost.Fits reports better than chat.
Subject + will probably / probably won'tTalk about a probable futureIt probably won't rain.Probably goes before won't.
about / roughly / approximately + numberGive an approximate numberRoughly a third of users left.Round the number too.
Arguably, + claimTake a position that people can debateArguably, Rust is the safer choice.Give your reason next.
In our tests / For X, + claimLimit the scope of a claimIn our tests, the cache halved latency.Scope is often better than may.
The results clearly show + nounBoost a strong, measured resultThe results clearly show a 40% drop.Boost the evidence, hedge the reasons.
Could we + verb ...?Soften a request or review commentCould we add a test for this?Soften the tone, not the facts.
I'm afraid + clauseGive bad news politelyI'm afraid we may miss Friday.Still give the news clearly.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

Which sentence is a fact that needs no hedge?

  • The cache probably caused the delay.
  • The test took 4.2 seconds.
  • Users seem to prefer dark mode.

You measured the time. A measured fact needs no hedge.

Which sentence is correct?

  • It may can be the cache.
  • It maybe the cache.
  • It may be the cache.

Use one modal verb. Maybe is one word and an adverb: "Maybe it is the cache."

Which sentence has the adverb in the right place?

  • The update probably won't fix it.
  • The update won't probably fix it.
  • The update won't fix probably it.

Probably goes before a negative helping verb like won't.

Which reporting verb is the softest?

  • prove
  • show
  • suggest

Suggest means there is some evidence, but other explanations are possible.

Which sentence is over-hedged?

  • The new index seems to help most queries.
  • The new index might possibly perhaps help some queries a little.
  • In our tests, the new index cut query time by 40%.

Might, possibly, perhaps, some and a little: five hedges on one claim. The point is lost.

Which code review comment is clear and polite?

  • This is wrong. Fix it.
  • Could we use a map here? Lookups would be faster.
  • Maybe it could perhaps be possible to think about a map, possibly.

One soft request and one clear reason. The third comment hides the advice.

In an IPCC report, what does very likely mean?

  • 66–100%
  • 90–100%
  • 99–100%

Very likely is 90–100%. Likely is 66–100%. Virtually certain is 99–100%.

Fill the gap

The update (cause) the crash. We are not sure yet.

The service appears ? restarted twice last night.

Large teams tend ? ship more slowly.

The release is likely ? slip by two days.

There is a strong ? that the data is incomplete.

? a third of users left after the change.

The benchmark (clear) shows a 40% drop in errors.

? we add a test for this case?

Think and write

  1. Hedge this overclaim in two different ways: "Remote work makes developers more productive."
    Answer

    Remote work may make developers more productive. Remote work tends to make many developers more productive. Our survey suggests that remote work makes developers more productive. Each version uses one hedge only.

  2. Remove the extra hedges. Keep one. "It might possibly be the case that the cache could perhaps be causing some of the errors."
    Answer

    The cache may be causing some of the errors. "Some" is fine here. It is a quantity, and it limits the claim.

  3. Fact or guess? Decide which sentences need a hedge. (a) The job failed at 02:14. (b) The disk was full. (c) Disk usage was 99%. (d) The backup job filled the disk.
    Answer

    (a) and (c) are facts from the logs. No hedge. (b) is almost a fact: 99% is nearly full, so "The disk was almost full" is more exact. (d) is a guess until you confirm it: "The backup job probably filled the disk."

  4. Soften this code review comment, but keep the advice clear: "This is wrong. Use a map, not a list."
    Model answer

    I think a map might work better here than a list. Lookups would be faster with large inputs. What do you think?

  5. Write a two-sentence status update. The release will probably slip by two days because of a failing test. Use one hedge and one clear fact.
    Model answer

    The payment tests are failing on the new build. I'm afraid the release will probably slip by two days. The first sentence is a fact. The second has one hedge.

  6. Find the hedges and boosters. Is each one a good choice? "The logs clearly show 500 errors after 14:05. This obviously proves that the deploy caused the outage."
    Model answer

    Clearly is fine: the logs are hard evidence. Obviously and proves are too strong. The timing is only a clue. Better: "This suggests that the deploy caused the outage." Also, drop obviously. It can sound rude.

  7. Expert: rewrite this sentence for a risk report with calibrated language. Use a number and a scope. "The new region will likely cut latency."
    Model answer

    Based on tests from three cities, we estimate a 70–80% chance that the new region cuts median latency by at least 30 ms for users in Asia. The number replaces likely. The scope says where and for whom.

Key takeaways

  • A hedge makes a claim softer. A booster makes it stronger. Together they show your stance.
  • Hedge what you think. Do not hedge facts that you measured or can check.
  • Hedges come in families: modal verbs, adverbs, adjectives, verbs, nouns, approximators and phrases.
  • Use one hedge per claim. "May possibly could" is too much.
  • Choose the reporting verb by your evidence: prove, show, indicate, suggest.
  • Boost the evidence and hedge the explanation: "We clearly measured X. This may be due to Y."
  • At work, soften the tone, not the facts. Bad news still needs a clear date or number.
  • For big decisions, use numbers or calibrated words, like the IPCC scale.

Sources

  • UEfAP: Writing features, hedging. Kinds of hedges in academic writing: verbs, modals, adverbs, adjectives, nouns and clauses.
  • EAP Foundation: Hedging, using cautious language. Reasons to hedge, word lists, and boosters.
  • George Mason University Writing Center: Hedges, softening claims. Why hedged claims are harder to refute, and when to use boosters.
  • IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023). Clear position and over-generalising in Task 2.
  • Carbon Brief: How the AR6 WG1 summary compares to its predecessor. The IPCC likelihood scale with probability ranges, and italics for calibrated terms.

Participle clauses and nominalisation

These are two tools for dense, formal English. Participle clauses join two ideas with fewer words. Nominalisation turns actions into nouns. Both make writing shorter, but they can also make it hard to read. This chapter shows how to use them and when to stop.

  • Build present, past and perfect participle clauses and know what each one means.
  • Find and fix dangling participles.
  • Shorten clauses after when, while, after, once and if.
  • Turn verbs into nouns and build long noun phrases that stay clear.
  • Decide when a dense style helps the reader and when it hurts.

What a participle clause is

Read each pair. The meaning is the same. The second sentence in each pair is shorter.

  • When I opened the log, I saw the error. → Opening the log, I saw the error.
  • Because it is written in Rust, the tool is very fast. → Written in Rust, the tool is very fast.
  • After she had fixed the bug, she merged the branch. → Having fixed the bug, she merged the branch.

The short part is a participle clause. It has a verb form but no subject and no tense. The subject comes from the main clause. The time comes from the main verb.

The three kinds of participle clause
KindShapeMeaningModel
present participleverb + -ingactive, often at the same timeWalking to work, I listened to a podcast.
past participlethird form: tested, writtenpassiveBuilt in 2019, the app needs updates.
perfect participlehaving + past participleactive, finished beforeHaving read the docs, I tried again.
perfect passivehaving been + past participlepassive, finished beforeHaving been tested, the code was deployed.

Participle clauses are most common in writing: reports, news, research and stories. In speech, people usually say the full clause.

A participle clause can also follow a noun: "the people waiting outside". This is a reduced relative clause, and you met it in Relative clauses. This chapter looks at participle clauses that work like adverbs. They say when, why, how, or with what result.

Do not add a subject or a tense. "I opening the log, I saw the error" is wrong. So is "Opened the log, I saw the error." Use the -ing form with no subject: "Opening the log, I saw the error."

Present participle clauses: -ing

An -ing clause has an active meaning. The subject of the main clause does the action. But the clause can mean several things.

What an -ing clause can mean
MeaningParticiple clauseFull clause
same timeWaiting for the build, I answered emails.While I was waiting ...
just beforeOpening the file, she found the bug.When she opened the file ...
reasonFeeling tired, he went home early.Because he felt tired ...
resultThe server crashed, taking the database with it.... and so it took the database with it.
extra informationThe report, covering three years, shows steady growth.The report, which covers three years ...

The result clause at the end

Technical writers use this pattern a lot. The -ing clause comes after a comma at the end. It gives the result of the whole main clause.

  • The cache expired, causing a spike in database load.
  • The patch removed two locks, making the service 30% faster.
  • Prices rose sharply, forcing many users to cancel.

Negatives and being

Put not before the -ing form. "Not knowing the password, I called IT." For a reason with an adjective or noun, use being. "Being new to the team, she asked a lot of questions."

Not for a much earlier action

A simple -ing clause means "at the same time" or "just before". For an action that finished long before, use the perfect form.

Feeling tired, so he went home.

Knowing not the password, I called IT.

Finishing the course in 2020, she got a job in 2023.

Feeling tired, he went home.

Not knowing the password, I called IT.

Having finished the course in 2020, she got a job in 2023.

The first wrong line has two links: the clause and so. A participle clause already links the ideas. Do not add a second linker.

Past participle clauses: passive meaning

  • Written in Rust, the tool uses little memory. (because it is written)
  • Used carefully, AI tools save a lot of time. (if they are used carefully)
  • Asked about the delay, the manager blamed the vendor. (when she was asked)
  • The library, first released in 2015, is still popular. (which was first released)

A past participle clause has a passive meaning. The subject of the main clause receives the action. In the first line, someone wrote the tool. The tool did not write anything.

It can show a reason, a condition, a time or extra information. The meaning comes from the context.

-ing: the subject acts

Testing the app, we found three bugs.

We tested the app.

Past participle: the subject receives

Tested on 50 phones, the app worked well.

Someone tested the app.

Learn the irregular past participles well: written, built, given, taken, chosen, known, shown, sent. A wrong form breaks the whole clause.

Writing in Rust, the tool is very fast.

Tested the app, we found three bugs.

Builded in 2019, the app needs updates.

Written in Rust, the tool is very fast.

Testing the app, we found three bugs. Or: Having tested the app, we wrote a report.

Built in 2019, the app needs updates.

Perfect participle clauses: having + past participle

Having finished the review, Ana merged the pull request.

First Ana finished the review. Then she merged. The perfect participle shows that the first action was complete before the main action. It often adds a reason too.

  • Having lived in Tokyo for five years, he speaks good Japanese. (earlier time and reason)
  • Having been warned twice, the team added monitoring. (passive: someone warned them)
  • Not having seen the email, I missed the meeting. (negative: not goes first)

You do not always need the perfect form. For two quick actions in a row, a simple -ing clause is fine. "Taking off her coat, she sat down." Use having when the first action takes time, or when you want to stress that it finished first.

Having finish the tests, we deployed.

Having been fixed the bug, we closed the ticket.

Having finished the tests, we deployed.

Having fixed the bug, we closed the ticket. Or: The bug having been fixed, we closed the ticket.

"After having finished" is common, but it says "after" twice. "After finishing" or "Having finished" is shorter and enough.

Dangling participles

Walking into the office, the coffee smelled great.

Who is walking? Grammar says the coffee is walking. The writer means "I", but "I" is not in the sentence. This mistake is a dangling participle.

The rule is simple. The hidden subject of the participle clause must be the subject of the main clause.

Dangling participles at work, and how to fix them
DanglingProblemFixed
After running the tests, the build passed.The build did not run the tests.After I ran the tests, the build passed.
Once installed, you can open the app from the menu.You are not installed.Once installed, the app appears in the menu.
Being a holiday, the office was closed.The office is not a holiday.Because it was a holiday, the office was closed.
Having been delayed for two hours, the airline gave us vouchers.The airline was not delayed.Our flight was delayed for two hours, so the airline gave us vouchers.

Use these four steps to check your own writing.

  1. Find the participle clause.
  2. Ask: who does this action, or who receives it?
  3. Look at the subject of the main clause.
  4. If they are different, change the main subject, or write a full clause with its own subject.

Usually the reader understands a dangling participle. But it sounds careless, and sometimes funny. In specs and contracts, it can make the meaning unclear. Examiners count it as a grammar error.

Words that are allowed to dangle

Some -ing and -ed words now work like prepositions or linkers. They do not need the same subject.

  • Considering the cost, the result is good.
  • Given the deadline, a smaller scope makes sense.
  • Generally speaking, Rust programs are fast.
  • Judging by the logs, the job never started.
  • Also: regarding, concerning, assuming, provided that, including, following, strictly speaking.

Based on is a special case. "Based on the data, we chose option B" is very common. But some careful editors still object, because "we" are not based on the data. "On the basis of the data, we chose option B" is always safe.

Absolute clauses: a participle with its own subject

A participle clause can have its own subject. Then it does not dangle. This is an absolute clause. It is formal and fairly rare.

  • The work done, we went home.
  • Weather permitting, the event will be outdoors.
  • All things considered, the launch went well.
  • With all tests passing, we can deploy. (with + noun + participle)

Reduced adverbial clauses

  • While waiting for the build, I wrote the docs.
  • Once deployed, the service scales automatically.
  • If needed, add more memory.
  • When in doubt, ask the team.

An adverbial clause starts with a linker like when, if or although. You can often shorten it. Keep the linker and drop the subject and be. Or use an -ing form. This works only when both clauses have the same subject.

Linkers that allow a short clause
LinkerShapeModelFull clause
when, while+ -ingWhile waiting, I read the docs.While I was waiting
before, after, since+ -ingAfter merging, delete the branch.After you merge
once, if, unless, until, when+ past participleOnce installed, the plugin starts itself.Once it is installed
although, though+ adjective or past participleAlthough tired, she finished the talk.Although she was tired
if, when+ adjectiveIf possible, reply today.If it is possible
on, upon+ -ing, means "as soon as"On arriving, call me.As soon as you arrive
by+ -ing, means "how"By caching results, we cut costs.(the method)

Before, after and since are also prepositions. That is why an -ing form follows them. The same is true for despite, instead of and without: "Despite testing everything, we missed a bug."

Fixed short clauses in formal writing

Learn these as chunks. They are very common in documentation: if necessary, if possible, if so, if not, when needed, as shown in Figure 2, as discussed above, unless stated otherwise, where applicable, as expected.

While I waiting for the build, I wrote the docs.

Because being tired, I went home.

Once installing, the app runs at startup.

If needing help, please call us.

While waiting for the build, I wrote the docs.

Being tired, I went home. Or: Because I was tired, I went home.

Once installed, the app runs at startup.

If you need help, please call us.

Because cannot start a short clause. Use a participle clause alone, or a full clause. And keep the active and passive meaning right. The app does not install. Someone installs it. So the form is installed.

Nominalisation: from verb to noun

Read each pair. The second version uses nouns for the actions.

  • We analysed the logs, and we found that the cache failed. → Analysis of the logs revealed a cache failure.
  • The price increased sharply. → There was a sharp increase in price.
  • Users complained often, so we changed the design. → Frequent user complaints led to a design change.

Nominalisation turns a verb or an adjective into a noun. The action becomes a thing. Now you can describe it, count it, or make it the subject of a new sentence. The linguist Michael Halliday called this a grammatical metaphor.

Common ways to make a noun
EndingFromNoun
-tion, -siondecide, install, migratedecision, installation, migration
-mentdeploy, improve, requiredeployment, improvement, requirement
-ance, -enceperform, depend, preferperformance, dependence, preference
-alapprove, remove, arriveapproval, removal, arrival
-urefail, close, exposefailure, closure, exposure
-ity, -nessavailable, complex, readyavailability, complexity, readiness
no changeincrease, delay, release, review, usean increase, a delay, a release, a review, use

What changes when you nominalise

  1. The adverb becomes an adjective. "increased sharply" → "a sharp increase".
  2. The subject becomes an of-phrase, a possessive or a noun in front. "the server failed" → "the failure of the server", "the server's failure", "server failure".
  3. The object becomes an of-phrase. "we analysed the data" → "analysis of the data", or "data analysis".
  4. A new verb carries the logic. Linkers like because and so become verbs: led to, resulted in, caused, was due to.
  5. The preposition can change. depend on → dependence on, respond to → response to, discuss the plan → discussion of the plan, rise → a rise in.

Prices rose. Because of this, demand fell. → The rise in prices caused a fall in demand.

Look at the second version. The two events are now nouns: the rise and a fall. The verb caused shows the link between them.

Why writers nominalise

  • To pack ideas. Titles and abstracts must be short. "Reduction of cold-start time in serverless functions".
  • To point back. "The team moved the database to a new server. This migration took six weeks." The noun sums up the whole earlier sentence.
  • To put the known idea first. The old information becomes the subject. The new information comes at the end.
  • To sound neutral. No person is named. This fits reports and research.
  • To add judgement. You can add an adjective: "a careful analysis", "a significant improvement".

Light verbs

Nominalisations often need a weak verb in front: make a decision, carry out a test, conduct a review, give an explanation, take action, reach an agreement. These pairs are normal in formal English. But do not use them when one verb is enough.

We conducted an analysis of the logs and made a decision to carry out a rollback.

We analysed the logs and decided to roll back.

US government plain language guidance calls these "hidden verbs". The real verb hides inside a noun. Its advice is to find the verb and use it.

Building complex noun phrases

A noun phrase can grow on both sides of its main noun. Watch one grow, step by step.

The head noun

a cache

Add an adjective

a fast cache

Add a compound adjective

a fast in-memory cache

Add a noun in front

a fast in-memory session cache

Add a phrase after

a fast in-memory session cache for the payment service

Add a participle clause

a fast in-memory session cache for the payment service, built by the platform team

Use it with a clear verb

The platform team built a fast in-memory session cache for the payment service. One long noun phrase is fine. Give it a clear subject and verb.

The main noun is the head. Words before it are short: a determiner, adjectives and other nouns. Longer parts go after it: a prepositional phrase, a participle clause, a relative clause or a to-infinitive.

Four rules for long noun phrases

  1. The verb agrees with the head. "The list of failing tests is long." The head is list, not tests.
  2. A noun in front is usually singular. "a password manager", "a three-day course", "a 64-bit system". A few fixed words keep -s: "a sales report", "a systems engineer".
  3. Compound adjectives before a noun take hyphens. "a well-known library", "a long-running job", "an open-source project". After the verb, there is often no hyphen: "The library is well known."
  4. Keep noun stacks short. Three nouns in a row is usually the limit. Move the rest after the head with a preposition.

We use a passwords manager.

It is a three-days course.

The list of failing tests are long.

Update the user account password reset email template.

We use a password manager.

It is a three-day course.

The list of failing tests is long.

Update the email template for password resets.

Corpus research by Douglas Biber and Bethany Gray (2010) shows something surprising. Academic writing does not have more long clauses than speech. Its complexity is mostly inside noun phrases: adjectives, nouns in front, and phrases after the head. They call this style "compressed". It is short, but it can be less clear, because the links between ideas are hidden.

When dense style helps and when it hurts

Dense style helps in

titles and headings, abstracts and summaries, slide bullets and changelogs. It also helps when you point back to an idea: "This decision ..." And it fits specs, where the action matters more than the person.

Dense style hurts in

instructions, where readers need verbs: "Click Save". It also hurts in emails, in texts for second-language readers, and anywhere people need to know who did what.

The writing teacher Helen Sword called bad nominalisations "zombie nouns" in a 2012 New York Times essay. They eat the verbs and remove the people. Look at this example.

The implementation of the optimisation resulted in a reduction in the duration of the execution.

We optimised the query, so it now runs in half the time.

The dense version has five abstract nouns and no person. The plain version has a person (we), a real verb (optimised) and a number (half). But dense style is not always wrong. Here is the same idea in an abstract, where space is short.

We tested three ways to cache data. The one that uses Redis cut response times the most.

A comparison of three caching methods showed the largest reduction in response time for Redis-based caching.

The "who does what" test

Read each sentence and ask: who does what? If you cannot answer, rewrite it with a person and a verb. Watch for sentences that hide responsibility: "A decision was taken to cancel the project." Who decided? A reader may need to know.

One or two nominalisations in a sentence are fine. Three or more, check the sentence. Always keep at least one strong verb.

A rough nominalisation finder in Python

A short script can mark sentences with many abstract nouns. It only looks at word endings, so it gives a rough signal.

import re

# Common endings of nouns made from verbs and adjectives.
ENDINGS = ("tion", "sion", "ment", "ance", "ence", "ity", "ness")

def nominalisations(sentence):
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z]+", sentence.lower())
    # Skip short words like "mention" or "city" to cut false hits.
    return [w for w in words if len(w) > 7 and w.endswith(ENDINGS)]

text = ("The implementation of the optimisation resulted in a reduction "
        "in the duration of the execution. We optimised the query, "
        "so it now runs in half the time.")

for sentence in re.split(r"(?<=\.)\s+", text):
    found = nominalisations(sentence)
    print(len(found), found)
5 ['implementation', 'optimisation', 'reduction', 'duration', 'execution']
0 []

The first sentence has five hits. The plain sentence has none. The script misses nouns with no ending, like increase or delay. It also catches words that are not nominalisations. So use it to find sentences to read again, not to judge them.

In the IELTS Writing band descriptors, band 7 grammar needs "a variety of complex structures" with some accuracy. At band 6, complex structures are less accurate than simple ones. So use a few participle clauses and nominalisations to show range. But a dangling participle is an error. Check every one before you finish.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for participle clauses and nominalisation
PatternPurposeModelNote
-ing clause, main clauseTwo actions at the same time, or a reasonWaiting for the build, I answered emails.Same subject in both parts.
Main clause, -ing clauseGive the result of an actionThe cache expired, causing a spike in load.Put a comma before the -ing.
Past participle clause, main clausePassive reason or conditionWritten in Rust, the tool is fast.The subject receives the action.
Having + past participle, main clauseOne action finished before anotherHaving read the docs, I tried again.Not "having read" for the same time.
Not + -ing, main clauseA negative reasonNot knowing the password, I called IT.Not goes first.
While / after / before + -ingA short time clauseAfter merging, delete the branch.Only with the same subject.
Once / if / unless + past participleA short passive conditionOnce installed, the app starts itself."Once installed, you ..." dangles.
If / when + adjectiveA very short conditionIf possible, reply today.Fixed chunks: if necessary, when ready.
Given / Considering + noun, clauseAccepted openers with any subjectGiven the deadline, a smaller scope makes sense.These words may dangle.
a + adjective + noun from a verbTurn an action and its adverb into a nounThere was a sharp increase in price.Adverb becomes adjective.
Noun + led to / resulted in + nounShow cause with two nounsThe rise in prices led to a fall in demand.The verb carries the logic.
This + nounPoint back to a whole ideaThis migration took six weeks.Better than "This took six weeks".
number-noun + nounDescribe size or time in fronta three-day courseNo -s on the front noun.
The + head + of + plural + singular verbKeep agreement in long subjectsThe list of failing tests is long.The verb follows the head.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

Which sentence is correct?

  • Writing in Python, the script is easy to read.
  • Written in Python, the script is easy to read.
  • Wrote in Python, the script is easy to read.

Someone wrote the script. The meaning is passive, so use the past participle: written.

Which sentence shows that one action finished before the other?

  • Reading the report, she called the client.
  • Having read the report, she called the client.
  • Read the report, she called the client.

Having + past participle shows the first action was complete.

Which sentence has a dangling participle?

  • Checking the logs, I found the error.
  • Checking the logs, the error was easy to find.
  • Given the logs, the error was easy to find.

The error did not check the logs. Given is an accepted opener, so the third line is fine.

Which short clause is correct?

  • Because being late, he took a taxi.
  • Once installing, the tool updates itself.
  • Once installed, the tool updates itself.

The tool is installed by someone, so use the past participle. Because cannot start a short clause.

Which is the best nominalisation of "The number of users grew quickly"?

  • There was a quickly growth in users.
  • There was rapid growth in the number of users.
  • The users made a growing quickly.

The verb grew becomes the noun growth. The adverb quickly becomes the adjective rapid.

Which sentence is correct?

  • The results of the new tests is promising.
  • The results of the new test are promising.
  • The result of the new tests are promising.

The verb agrees with the head noun: results are, result is.

Fill the gap

(feel) unwell, she left the meeting early.

The storm cut the power, (leave) thousands of homes in the dark.

(build) in 1890, the bridge is now a museum.

(finish) the migration, the team took a week off.

(not know) the answer, I asked a colleague.

While (wait) for the reply, I updated the docs.

If ?, restart the service.

The company decided to expand. This (decide) surprised the market.

The team analysed the data. → An ? of the data showed a clear trend.

Think and write

  1. Join each pair with a participle clause. (a) She opened the dashboard. She saw the alert. (b) The app was designed for children. It has large buttons. (c) He had worked there for ten years. He knew everyone.
    Answer

    (a) Opening the dashboard, she saw the alert. (b) Designed for children, the app has large buttons. (c) Having worked there for ten years, he knew everyone.

  2. Fix the dangling participles. (a) Looking out of the window, the mountains were beautiful. (b) Once logged in, the dashboard shows your projects. Is this one dangling? (c) After reading the reviews, the hotel seemed perfect.
    Answer

    (a) Looking out of the window, I saw the beautiful mountains. (b) This one is grammatically dangling: the dashboard does not log in. Better: Once you log in, the dashboard shows your projects. (c) After reading the reviews, we thought the hotel was perfect.

  3. Make these sentences more formal with nominalisation. (a) The network failed, so the team could not deploy. (b) Users strongly prefer dark mode.
    Answer

    (a) The network failure prevented deployment. Or: Network failure meant that the team could not deploy. (b) There is a strong user preference for dark mode.

  4. Rewrite this in plain English. Find the hidden verbs. "We are responsible for the management of the servers and the provision of support to users."
    Answer

    We manage the servers and support users. The hidden verbs were manage (management) and support (provision of support).

  5. Make this noun stack clear. Move words after the head. "the customer data export job failure alert"
    Model answer

    the alert for failures of the customer data export job. Or, even clearer as a sentence: the alert that fires when the customer data export job fails.

  6. Expert: write a one-sentence abstract (about 25 words) from these notes. Use at least two nominalisations. "We moved our API from VMs to containers. Deploys got faster. Costs went down by 20%."
    Model answer

    The migration of our API from virtual machines to containers led to faster deployments and a 20% reduction in infrastructure costs. Nominalisations: migration, deployments, reduction.

  7. Expert: decide which version fits each reader, and say why. (a) "Restart the service." (b) "A restart of the service is required." Reader 1: a new user following a guide. Reader 2: an audit report.
    Model answer

    The new user needs (a). It is a direct instruction with a verb. The audit report can use (b). It describes a requirement and does not need a person. Even there, "The service must be restarted" is clearer.

Key takeaways

  • A participle clause has no subject and no tense. It takes both from the main clause.
  • -ing is active. The past participle is passive. Having + past participle means "finished before".
  • The hidden subject of the participle clause must be the subject of the main clause. Otherwise, it dangles.
  • Given, considering, generally speaking and similar openers may dangle. Based on is debated.
  • After when, while, after, before and since, you can use -ing. After once, if and unless, use a past participle or an adjective.
  • Nominalisation turns actions into nouns. The adverb becomes an adjective, and a new verb carries the logic.
  • In noun phrases, short parts go before the head and long parts go after it. The verb agrees with the head.
  • Dense style suits titles, abstracts and summaries. Plain verbs suit instructions, emails and anything about who did what.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Participle clauses (C1). Present, past and perfect participle clauses, their meanings and the same-subject rule.
  • Purdue OWL: Dangling modifiers and how to correct them. What a dangling modifier is and ways to repair it.
  • Digital.gov plain language guide: Writing. US federal advice to avoid hidden verbs, also called nominalisations.
  • Biber and Gray (2010): Challenging stereotypes about academic writing. Academic prose is compressed, with complexity inside noun phrases.
  • IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023). Range and accuracy of complex structures at bands 6 to 9.

Advanced articles and prepositions

Articles and prepositions are small words, but they stay hard even at C1. This chapter covers what the basic chapters left out: names, institutions, general statements and the formal prepositions of reports and emails. It ends with fixed expressions that examiners love to test.

  • Choose the right article with names of places, organisations and institutions.
  • Make general statements with a, the or no article, and know what each one means.
  • Solve zero-article puzzles with meals, illnesses, roles, transport and fixed pairs.
  • Use C1 dependent prepositions after nouns, verbs and adjectives.
  • Use formal prepositional phrases and fixed expressions correctly.

The basics are in Nouns and articles and Prepositions. This chapter does not repeat them. Keep them open if you need a reminder.

Articles with place names

Last summer I flew from Japan to the United States. I hiked in the Rockies and swam in Lake Tahoe. Then I flew over the Pacific to the Philippines.

Look at the names. Japan and Lake Tahoe have no article. The United States, the Rockies, the Pacific and the Philippines have the. Why?

Most names have no article. A name already tells you which one. But the comes back in four cases.

  • The name is plural: the Netherlands, the Alps, the Maldives.
  • The name has a common noun like republic, kingdom, states or union: the Czech Republic, the UK, the USA.
  • The name has of: the Gulf of Mexico, the Bay of Bengal, the Isle of Wight.
  • The name is water, a desert or a region (but not a lake): the Nile, the Pacific, the Sahara, the Middle East.
Place names: no article or the
No articleThe
most countries: Japan, Brazil, Kenyaplural or "union" names: the Netherlands, the Philippines, the UK, the UAE
continents: Asia, Africa, Europethe Arctic, the Antarctic, the Americas
cities and towns: Tokyo, BerlinThe Hague, the Vatican
lakes: Lake Baikal, Lake Genevarivers, seas, oceans, canals: the Thames, the Red Sea, the Atlantic, the Suez Canal
single mountains: Mount Fuji, Everestmountain ranges: the Alps, the Himalayas, the Andes
single islands: Sicily, Baliisland groups: the Canary Islands, the Bahamas
streets, parks, squares: Oxford Street, Hyde Park, Times Squaredeserts and regions: the Sahara, the Gobi, the Midwest
airports and stations: Heathrow, Shinjuku Stationsome UK roads: the High Street, the M25

Three expert details

  • A phrase can add the. A name gets the when a phrase picks one version of the place. "the Tokyo of the 1980s", "the London I knew as a child".
  • An adjective alone does not add the. "modern Japan", "ancient Rome", "northern Italy". But "the north of Italy" has of, so it takes the.
  • Some names changed. Most style guides now write Ukraine, not "the Ukraine". The Gambia and the Bahamas keep the.

She lives in the Japan.

We sailed across Atlantic.

He works in Netherlands.

We climbed the Mount Fuji.

She lives in Japan.

We sailed across the Atlantic.

He works in the Netherlands.

We climbed Mount Fuji.

Articles with organisations and institutions

She studied at the University of Tokyo, then worked at Google. Now she writes for The Guardian about NASA and the BBC.

Organisations follow some clear patterns. Learn the patterns, then learn the exceptions one by one.

Organisations and their articles
TypeArticleExamples
companiesnoneGoogle, Microsoft, Toyota, IBM
names with of or a common nounthethe United Nations, the World Bank, the Bank of England
letters read one by onethethe BBC, the EU, the UN, the FBI
letters read as a wordnoneNASA, NATO, UNESCO
X UniversitynoneStanford University, Harvard University
the University of Xthethe University of Tokyo, the University of Cambridge
museums, galleries, theatres, hotelsthethe British Museum, the Louvre, the Hilton
many newspapersthe (often part of the name)The Guardian, The New York Times

Letters read one by one are called an initialism. They keep the when the full name has it: the British Broadcasting Corporation, so the BBC. Letters read as one word are an acronym. They usually drop the. Company initialisms also drop it: IBM, BMW. Usage decides in the end, so check new names.

Names used like adjectives

When a name stands before a normal noun, the article belongs to that noun. This is very common in software.

  • Python is popular. → the Python interpreter, the Python docs
  • Linux is free. → the Linux kernel
  • NASA has no article. → a NASA mission, the NASA budget
  • GitHub is a website. → the GitHub API, a GitHub account

Choose a or an by the first sound: an FBI agent (eff), a NASA project (na), an HTTP request (aitch), a URL (you). With SQL, both happen. People who say "es-queue-el" write an SQL query. People who say "sequel" write a SQL query.

Institutions: the building or the purpose?

You know "go to school" and "in hospital" from the basic chapter. The same idea works for more places. No article means the normal purpose of the place. The means one building or one visit.

  • He went to prison for fraud. (as a prisoner) / She went to the prison to visit him.
  • The case went to court. (a legal process) / The court is next to the station.
  • They go to church on Sundays. (to pray) / The church has a new roof.
  • The party has been in office for ten years. (in power) / I'm in the office today.
  • Let's meet in town. (the local centre) / The town is small.

She works at the Google.

He works for BBC.

She studied at the Stanford University.

Update Python interpreter.

She works at Google.

He works for the BBC.

She studied at Stanford University.

Update the Python interpreter.

Use these five questions to choose an article for any name.

Is it a person or a company?

Then no article: Ana, Dr Lee, Google, Toyota.

Is it plural, or does it have of?

Then use the: the Alps, the Philippines, the University of Tokyo, the Bank of England.

Does it end in a common noun?

Republic, kingdom, union, museum, hotel: use the. The Czech Republic, the British Museum.

Is it water, a desert or a region?

Use the: the Nile, the Pacific, the Sahara. But lakes have no article: Lake Geneva.

Is it short letters?

Read one by one: usually the (the BBC). Read as a word: no article (NASA). If you are still unsure, search a news site.

General statements: four ways

All four sentences talk about a whole kind of thing. But they are not the same.

  • Tigers are big cats. (plural, no article)
  • The tiger is endangered. (the + singular)
  • A tiger has stripes. (a + singular)
  • Water boils at 100 °C. (uncountable, no article)

Talking about a whole kind is called generic reference. The basic chapter showed the forms. Here is what each form can do, and what it cannot do.

Generic reference: what works and what fails
FormMeaningWorksFails
no article + pluralmembers in generalDevelopers like good docs.Almost never. This is the safest form.
a / an + singularany typical memberA compiler translates code. A good test checks one thing.Facts about the whole group: not "A tiger is endangered".
the + singularthe kind as one ideaThe tiger is endangered. Who invented the telephone?Everyday groups: "The developer likes coffee" sounds like one person.
the + plurala whole known groupThe Dutch are tall, on average.Most general groups: not "The cats like milk".

Why "a tiger is endangered" fails

A + singular means "any one member". So the sentence says each tiger is endangered on its own. But being endangered is a fact about the whole species. Use "Tigers are endangered" or "The tiger is endangered". In the same way, say "Dinosaurs died out", not "A dinosaur died out".

The + singular in science and software

Formal texts use the + singular for a class. It is common for species, inventions, instruments and body parts: "The heart pumps blood", "play the piano". Requirements and user stories use it for roles.

The user enters a password. The system checks it and shows the dashboard.

Here "the user" means any user in this role. It is a generic the, not one real person.

Nationalities

Nationality words ending in -sh, -ch, -ese or -ss have no plural -s. With the, they mean the whole nation and take a plural verb: the British, the French, the Chinese, the Swiss. Other nationalities use a normal plural noun: (the) Germans, (the) Brazilians, (the) Kenyans.

For one person, say a Chinese person or a French woman. "A Chinese" can sound rude. For groups like "the poor" and "the young", see Nouns and articles.

Older texts use "man" or "mankind" for all people: "Man has walked on the Moon." Modern style prefers "people", "humans" or "humanity". These words include everyone.

A tiger is endangered.

The Chinese is the largest group.

The computers have changed our lives. (meaning all computers)

Tigers are endangered. Or: The tiger is endangered.

The Chinese are the largest group.

Computers have changed our lives. Or: The computer has changed our lives.

Zero article puzzles

No article at all is called the zero article. These cases confuse even strong learners. Open each puzzle. Each one has a rule and a contrast.

Meals: lunch, a quick lunch, the lunch

Meals have no article: "We had lunch at one." Add an adjective and the meal becomes one example, so use a: "We had a quick lunch." Use the for a specific meal: "The lunch at the conference was great."

Illnesses: flu, a cold, a headache

Many illnesses have no article: cancer, diabetes, measles. Small, countable problems take a: a cold, a headache, a sore throat. With flu, British English says "flu" or "the flu". American English usually says "the flu".

Roles: a developer, but president

Jobs need a: "She is a developer." But a role that only one person can have often has no article after be, become, elect, appoint and as: "She was elected president." "He works as head of IT." A title before a name has no article: President Lincoln, Dr Lee, Professor Kim.

Transport: by car, but in my car

By + transport has no article: by car, by train, by email, by phone. Add a word like my or a time, and the article returns: "in my car", "on the 8:15 train". "On the phone" means "talking on the phone now".

Fixed pairs: step by step, face to face

Pairs of repeated or linked nouns have no article: step by step, face to face, day after day, side by side, hand in hand, from start to finish, from top to bottom. Learn them as chunks.

Abstract nouns: history, the history of Rome

General abstract nouns have no article: "History repeats itself." "Society changes slowly." A phrase that limits them brings the back: "the history of Rome", "the society we live in". Note that "the nature of the problem" uses nature with a different meaning: its basic character.

Most or the most?

Most with no article means "the majority": "Most developers use Git." The most is a superlative: "Python is the most popular language in this survey."

Kind of, sort of, type of

After kind of, sort of and type of, a singular countable noun usually has no article: "What kind of database is it?" Not "a database".

The doctor, the bank, the radio

Some familiar places and services take the, even when you do not mean one special place: go to the doctor, the dentist, the bank, the gym, the cinema. "Listen to the radio" takes the, but "watch TV" and "on television" do not.

A second chance

"A second" can mean "another one", not a place in order: "Can I have a second look?" "We need a second opinion." "The second" means number two in a known order: "The second test failed."

Short texts like headlines, labels and commit messages drop articles: "Fix typo in README". This is normal only in those texts. See Nouns and articles.

Dependent prepositions at C1: nouns

We need a solution to this problem. There is no alternative to a rewrite. The team showed a strong commitment to quality, and the results gave us real insight into user behaviour.

A dependent preposition is fixed by the word before it. You met common ones in Prepositions. At C1, you need the formal nouns of reports and meetings.

C1 nouns and their prepositions
PrepositionNouns
toaccess to, an alternative to, an approach to, a commitment to, a contribution to, an exception to, an obstacle to, a threat to
fordemand for, a need for, a preference for, respect for, responsibility for, capacity for
inan increase in, a decline in, a change in, confidence in, a delay in, a role in
onan effect on, an impact on, a ban on, emphasis on, pressure on, a limit on
ofa lack of, awareness of, the cause of, the risk of, a sign of
intoinsight into, research into, an investigation into
towardsan attitude towards, a tendency towards, a step towards
overcontrol over, an advantage over, a dispute over
betweena balance between, a link between, a trade-off between

An increase in or an increase of?

Both are correct, but they mean different things. In says what changed. Of says how much.

  • an increase in sales (sales went up)
  • an increase of 20% (the size of the change)
  • an increase of 20% in sales (both)

The same works for rise, fall, drop and decline. This is very useful in IELTS Writing Task 1.

Word families: the preposition can change

A verb, its noun and its adjective do not always share a preposition. Learn them as a family.

Word families with different prepositions
VerbNounAdjective
emphasise the risk (no preposition)emphasis on the risk-
discuss the plan (no preposition)a discussion of / about the plan-
depend ondependence ondependent on, but independent of
prefer A to Ba preference for Apreferable to
lack time (no preposition)a lack of timelacking in experience
be able tothe ability to, the capacity forcapable of
attend the meeting (no preposition)attendance at the meeting-

There is no alternative for a rewrite.

The report emphasises on security.

We lack of time.

There was an increase of sales last year.

There is no alternative to a rewrite.

The report emphasises security. Or: The report puts emphasis on security.

We lack time. Or: We have a lack of time.

There was an increase in sales last year.

Dependent prepositions at C1: verbs and adjectives

All services must comply with the new policy. The delay stems from a config error. An open office is not always conducive to deep work.

Verbs

C1 verbs and their prepositions
PrepositionVerbs
toadhere to, attribute X to Y, conform to, contribute to, object to, resort to, subscribe to
withcomply with, cope with, interfere with, tamper with, provide someone with something
fromrefrain from, stem from, derive X from Y, deter someone from, distinguish X from Y
oncapitalise on, elaborate on, embark on, impose X on Y, reflect on
foraccount for, allow for, compensate for, opt for, qualify for, cater for (British)
ofdispose of, accuse someone of, deprive someone of, convince someone of
inengage in, persist in, culminate in, result in
againstdiscriminate against, guard against, warn someone against

Account for has two meanings. It means "explain": "How do you account for the drop?" It also means "be a part of": "Mobile accounts for 60% of traffic."

Adjectives

C1 adjectives and their prepositions
PrepositionAdjectives
toaccustomed to, averse to, conducive to, integral to, prone to, subject to, susceptible to, akin to, detrimental to
ofdevoid of, indicative of, representative of, tolerant of, wary of, characteristic of
withcompatible with, consistent with, fraught with, synonymous with, preoccupied with
oncontingent on, reliant on, intent on
foreligible for, liable for, renowned for, accountable for (a thing)
ininherent in, rooted in, instrumental in, implicated in
fromexempt from, distinct from, absent from

Some words take two prepositions, for two partners. "The team is accountable to the CTO for uptime." To a person, for a task.

The to + -ing trap

In many of these phrases, to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive. So the verb after it takes -ing.

  • I look forward to hearing from you.
  • We are committed to improving quality.
  • She objected to working late.
  • I'm not used to writing in English.
  • When it comes to testing, we use pytest.
  • They changed the plan with a view to reducing costs.

Test it: can a noun follow to? "I look forward to the meeting." Yes. So to is a preposition, and a verb after it needs -ing. Compare: "I want to the meeting" is impossible, so "want to" takes the infinitive. See Verb patterns: -ing and to.

I look forward to hear from you.

We must comply to the rules.

The plan is depending of the budget.

Please refrain to smoke.

I look forward to hearing from you.

We must comply with the rules.

The plan depends on the budget. Or: The plan is contingent on the budget.

Please refrain from smoking.

Formal prepositional phrases

With regard to your question, the API is stable. In terms of speed, the new version is twice as fast. In the light of these results, we will change the plan.

Some prepositions have two, three or four words. They work as one unit. Most are formal. They are common in reports, legal texts and formal emails.

Formal prepositional phrases
PhrasePlain meaningModel
with regard to, regarding, as regardsabout this topicWith regard to pricing, we offer three plans.
in terms ofmeasured by, from this point of viewIn terms of cost, option A is cheaper.
with respect to, in relation toabout, compared withCosts rose in relation to revenue.
in (the) light ofbecause of new informationIn the light of the test results, we delayed the launch.
in view ofbecause of a fact you considerIn view of the risk, we added a manual check.
on behalf offor, representingI'm writing on behalf of the whole team.
in accordance with, in line withfollowing a rule or planWe deleted the data in accordance with the policy.
owing to, due tobecause ofThe delay was due to a bug.
in the event ofif this (bad) thing happensIn the event of an outage, call the on-call engineer.
prior tobeforePrior to deployment, run the full test suite.
with a view towith the aim ofWe split the service with a view to scaling it.
in favour ofchoosing this insteadWe dropped MySQL in favour of PostgreSQL.
regardless of, irrespective ofnot caring aboutRegardless of the cost, we must fix this.
at the expense ofcausing a loss toThey gained speed at the expense of safety.
in the absence ofwhen this is missingIn the absence of tests, review the code twice.
with the exception ofexceptAll tests passed, with the exception of two.

Use them with care

  • With regard to has no s. "With regards to" is common, but most guides call it a mistake. "Kind regards" at the end of an email is fine.
  • In terms of is overused. Use it for a measure or a point of view: "in terms of cost". Do not use it to mean "about".
  • In the light of is more common in British English. American writers often say in light of.
  • Due to after be is always fine: "The delay was due to a bug." At the start of a sentence, some careful writers prefer owing to or because of.
  • In the event of takes a noun. For a clause, use in the event that or just if.
  • Prior to and with a view to take a noun or -ing. In everyday writing, "before" is better than "prior to".

With regards to your email, the date is fine.

In terms of the meeting, it starts at three.

In the event of it rains, the match moves inside.

Prior to we deploy, we run the tests.

With regard to your email, the date is fine.

The meeting starts at three.

In the event of rain, the match moves inside. Or: If it rains, ...

Before we deploy, we run the tests. Or: Prior to deploying, ...

Formal phrases are like a suit. Wear one for a report. Do not wear five at once. In chat, say about, because of, before and using.

Fixed expressions with prepositions

A fixed expression never changes. You cannot change the preposition or add an article. Learn each one as a chunk, with a model sentence.

Fixed expressions for work and study
ExpressionMeaningModel
at riskin dangerCustomer data is at risk.
at stakethat you can win or loseA big contract is at stake.
at short noticewith little warningThe meeting moved at short notice.
at randomwith no plan or orderPick ten users at random.
at odds within disagreement withThe data is at odds with our theory.
by defaultwhen nobody choosesLogging is off by default.
by designon purpose, as plannedThe API is read-only by design.
by farby a big amountThis is by far the fastest option.
by and largemostly, in generalBy and large, the launch went well.
for goodfor everWe turned off the old server for good.
for the time beingfor now, not for everUse the old API for the time being.
in advancebefore the eventThanks in advance for your help.
in hindsightlooking back nowIn hindsight, we should have tested it.
in practice / in theoryin real life / on paperIn theory it scales. In practice it doesn't.
in the long runafter a long timeTests save time in the long run.
on averageas a typical amountOn average, a build takes six minutes.
on holdstopped for a whileThe project is on hold.
on trackgoing as plannedWe are on track for Friday.
on callready to answer alertsWho is on call this weekend?
out of scopenot part of this workMobile support is out of scope.
out of dateold, no longer correctThese docs are out of date.
under wayalready startedThe migration is under way.
under reviewbeing checkedYour request is under review.
beyond our controlwe cannot change itThe outage was beyond our control.
without failalways, every timeBack up the data daily, without fail.

On time or in time?

On time means at the planned time: "The train arrived on time." In time means early enough, before it is too late: "We fixed the bug in time for the demo."

He deleted the file by purpose.

In the hindsight, it was a mistake.

At the long run, it saves money.

The docs are out of the date.

He deleted the file on purpose. Or: by mistake / by accident.

In hindsight, it was a mistake.

In the long run, it saves money.

The docs are out of date.

Expert level: small changes, big meaning

At C2, the hard part is meaning. One noun or verb can take two prepositions with two meanings. Open each pair.

an advantage of, an advantage over

An advantage of X is a good feature of X: "One advantage of Rust is memory safety." An advantage over Y means "better than Y": "Rust has an advantage over C in safety."

responsibility for, responsibility to

Responsibility for a task or result: "She has responsibility for the release." Responsibility to a person or group: "We have a responsibility to our users."

consist of, consist in

Consist of lists the parts: "The team consists of five engineers." Consist in is formal and names the main idea: "Good design consists in removing what is not needed."

comprise, consist of, be composed of

Comprise means "consist of", with no preposition: "The suite comprises 400 tests." "Comprise of" is wrong. "Is comprised of" is common, but many editors object. "Consists of" or "is made up of" is always safe.

compare to, compare with

Traditionally, compare to shows that two things are alike: "She compared the codebase to a maze." Compare with looks at differences in detail: "We compared the new version with the old one." Many writers now use both freely. The traditional choice is safe in exams.

concern about, concern for

Concern about or over a problem: "There is concern about the cost." Concern for a person's safety or well-being: "We have real concern for our users' privacy."

between, among

Use between for two things, or for separate items you name: "a trade-off between speed and safety", "talks between Japan, Korea and China". Use among for a group with no separate members: "The idea is popular among developers."

on, upon

Upon means the same as on, but it is more formal: "upon request", "upon arrival". It fits contracts and formal emails. In daily writing, on is better.

Cambridge C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency often test these small words in the Reading and Use of English paper. Open cloze tasks leave out articles and prepositions. Key word transformations often need a fixed phrase, like "in spite of" or "on behalf of". See Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for advanced articles and prepositions
PatternPurposeModelNote
the + plural or "of" place nameName plural places and places with ofShe lives in the Netherlands.Most countries have no article: Japan.
the + river / sea / ocean / rangeName water and mountain rangesWe crossed the Atlantic.Lakes and single peaks: no article.
the + initialism, acronym aloneName organisations by lettersShe works for the BBC, not NASA.Companies drop the: IBM.
the + name + common nounUse a name like an adjectiveUpdate the Python interpreter.The article goes with the common noun.
Plural noun + verbMake a safe general statementDevelopers like good docs.The safest generic form.
The + singular + verbTalk about a whole kind as one ideaThe tiger is endangered.Not "A tiger is endangered".
The + -sh / -ch / -ese word + plural verbTalk about a whole nationThe French are proud of their food.One person: a French woman.

an increase in + thing, of + amountDescribe changes in dataan increase of 20% in salesIn = what changed. Of = how much.
