Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

Which sentence is correct?

  • We sailed down Nile and crossed the Lake Victoria.
  • We sailed down the Nile and crossed Lake Victoria.
  • We sailed down the Nile and crossed the Lake Victoria.

Rivers take the. Lakes have no article.

Which sentence is correct?

  • She works for NASA, and he works for BBC.
  • She works for the NASA, and he works for the BBC.
  • She works for NASA, and he works for the BBC.

NASA is read as a word, so no article. BBC is read letter by letter, so the.

Which general statement is correct?

  • A dinosaur died out 66 million years ago.
  • Dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago.
  • Dinosaur died out 66 million years ago.

Dying out is a fact about the whole group. A + singular means one typical member, so it fails here. A singular countable noun also needs an article.

Which sentence is correct?

  • I look forward to meet you.
  • I look forward to meeting you.
  • I look forward meeting you.

To is a preposition here, so the verb takes -ing.

Which sentence shows the size of a change?

  • Prices rose, with an increase of 8%.
  • There was an increase of prices.
  • There was an increase in 8%.

Of + amount shows how much. For the thing that changed, use in: an increase in prices.

Which phrase is correct in a formal email?

  • With regards to your request, ...
  • With regard to your request, ...
  • In terms of your request, ...

With regard to has no s. In terms of is for a measure, not for "about".

Fill the gap

She studied at ? University of Cambridge, then joined ? Microsoft. (write - for no article)

We went to the Alps and climbed ? Mont Blanc. (write - for no article)

He was elected ? chair of the committee. (write - for no article)

There is no alternative ? a full rewrite.

The new office is not conducive ? deep work.

All suppliers must comply ? the new rules.

The bug stems ? a missing null check.

Mobile users account ? 60% of our traffic.

We are committed to (improve) our response times.

We dropped the old tool in ? of a faster one.

Logging is turned off ? default.

We fixed it just ? time for the demo.

Think and write

  1. Add the where it is needed: "Last year I visited Netherlands, United Kingdom and Japan. I saw Thames, climbed Ben Nevis and swam in Lake Windermere."
    Answer

    Last year I visited the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Japan. I saw the Thames, climbed Ben Nevis and swam in Lake Windermere. Plural and "kingdom" names take the. Rivers take the. Single mountains and lakes do not.

  2. Explain the difference. (a) He went to prison. (b) He went to the prison.
    Answer

    (a) He became a prisoner. (b) He visited the building, perhaps to see someone or to work there.

  3. Correct the four preposition mistakes. "Regarding to your email, the delay was due of a bug. We will compensate you of the lost time, and we look forward to work with you again."
    Answer

    Regarding your email (or: With regard to your email), the delay was due to a bug. We will compensate you for the lost time, and we look forward to working with you again.

  4. Rewrite these chat messages in formal style. Use one formal prepositional phrase in each. (a) About the budget, we need more time. (b) Because of the new data, we changed the plan. (c) Before the launch, please test everything.
    Model answer

    (a) With regard to the budget, we need more time. (b) In the light of the new data, we changed the plan. (c) Prior to the launch, please test everything.

  5. Describe this data in one sentence with increase in and of: sales were 200 units in 2024 and 250 units in 2025.
    Model answer

    There was an increase of 25% in sales between 2024 and 2025, from 200 to 250 units.

  6. Expert: explain the difference and write one sentence for each. advantage of / advantage over.
    Model answer

    An advantage of X is a good feature of X: "One advantage of containers is fast start-up." An advantage over Y compares two things: "Containers have an advantage over virtual machines in start-up time."

  7. Expert: write a short incident note (three sentences) with at least three fixed expressions from this chapter.
    Model answer

    The payment service went down at short notice on Monday. A fix is now under way, and we are on track to finish by Friday. In hindsight, our alerts were too slow, so we will improve them for good. (Fixed expressions: at short notice, under way, on track, in hindsight, for good.)

Key takeaways

  • Most names have no article. Plural names, names with of or republic, water, ranges and island groups take the.
  • Initialisms read letter by letter usually keep the (the BBC). Acronyms read as a word usually drop it (NASA). Companies never take it.
  • When a name stands before a normal noun, the article belongs to that noun: the Python interpreter.
  • Plural with no article is the safest general statement. A + singular cannot carry facts about a whole group.
  • Meals, illnesses, unique roles, by + transport and fixed pairs often have no article, until a word makes them specific.
  • Learn C1 words with their prepositions, and learn word families: emphasise X, but emphasis on X.
  • When to is a preposition, use -ing after it: look forward to hearing.
  • Formal phrases like with regard to and in the light of fit reports. Use them one at a time, and say about or because of in chat.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: The definite article. The with unique things, names, countries, instruments and groups.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Articles, the or no article. Which place names and universities take the.
  • Grammaring: The zero article with geographical names. Countries, lakes, peaks, cities and streets, with exceptions.
  • The Editor's Manual: Use of the before an abbreviation. Acronyms, initialisms and convention.
  • Grammar Monster: With regard to or with regards to. The standard form and simpler alternatives.

Register, collocation and idiom

Good English is not only correct. It also fits the reader and the moment. This chapter shows you how to choose the right style, the right word partners and the right fixed phrases. These skills move you from B2 to C1 and beyond.

  • Choose a formal, neutral or informal style for a reader and a channel.
  • Swap everyday and formal words to move up or down in formality.
  • Use strong C1 word partners like "pose a risk" and "highly unlikely".
  • Understand 60 useful idioms and know when not to use them.
  • Spot connotation, euphemism, clichés and British or American forms.

What register is

Read three messages. They give the same news. Who is each one for?

Hi all! Bad news: the release will be a few days late. Some tests are still failing. I'll let you know when it's fixed.

Hello everyone,

The release will be two days late because some tests are still failing. I will send an update when they pass.

Thanks, Mia

Dear Ms Lee,

I am writing to inform you that the release has been postponed until 20 November. This delay is due to unresolved test failures. We apologise for any inconvenience.

Yours sincerely,
Mia Chen

The first message is for the team chat. The second is an email to colleagues. The third is a letter to a client. The facts are the same. The style changes.

This style is called register. Every text has one. A formal register is for clients, strangers, official letters and reports. An informal register is for friends and team chat. A neutral register sits in the middle.

Three questions choose the register

  1. Who is the reader? A friend, a colleague, a manager, a client, a stranger?
  2. What is the purpose? A quick question, a request, a complaint, a legal record?
  3. What is the channel? A chat, an email, a report, a contract, a talk?

When you are not sure, choose neutral. It is never rude and never too stiff. Most work emails are neutral.

What changes between registers

Features of each register
FeatureInformalNeutralFormal
GreetingHey Sam!Hi Sam,Dear Mr Lee,
Short formscan't, gonna, thxcan't, I'llcannot, I will
Verbsget, find outget, find outobtain, discover
Who does itwe, youwe, youoften passive: "It was decided"
Linkersso, butso, howevertherefore, nevertheless
RequestsCan you ...?Could you ...?I would be grateful if you could ...
Emoji and slangcommonrarenever

Formal writing also uses more nouns and longer phrases. See Participle clauses and nominalisation. Formal writers also soften claims. See Hedging and stance. For full model emails, see Emails and messages.

Five steps from informal to formal

The informal message

"Hey! Can't get the report. Can u send it again? Thx"

This is fine for a friend. It is wrong for a client.

Fix the greeting and the close

"Dear Mr Lee, ... Kind regards, Mia"

Use the family name. Add a closing line and your name.

Write full words

u becomes you. Thx becomes thank you. Can't becomes cannot.

Write full sentences

"Can't get the report" has no subject. Write "I cannot get the report."

Choose more formal verbs

get becomes access. send it again becomes resend it.

Soften the request

"Can you send it?" becomes "I would be grateful if you could resend it."

The formal message

"Dear Mr Lee, I have not been able to access the report. I would be grateful if you could resend it. Thank you. Kind regards, Mia"

Do not mix registers in one text. A formal opening and a slang ending sound strange. The reader feels the change.

Dear Mr Lee, I am writing to inform you that the build is kinda broken lol. Will fix ASAP!!

Dear Mr Lee, I am writing to let you know that the build is currently failing. We expect to fix it today.

Germanic and Latinate words

We need to find out why the build broke.

We need to determine why the build failed.

Both sentences are correct. The first one sounds like a person talking. The second one sounds like a report. The difference comes from the history of English words.

Where English words come from

Old English was a Germanic language. In 1066, French-speaking Normans took control of England. For about 300 years, French was the language of the court and the law. Later, scholars took many words straight from Latin. Words from Latin or French are called Latinate.

Look at the chart. More than half of all dictionary words are Latinate. But the words people use most are mostly Germanic: the, and, be, have, go, get, house, water. So daily speech feels Germanic. Reports and laws feel Latinate.

Pairs and triplets

English often has two or three words for one idea. A famous example is kingly (Old English), royal (French) and regal (Latin). Another is ask, question and interrogate. The Germanic word is everyday. The Latin word is the most formal.

Everyday and formal pairs
Everyday (Germanic)Formal (Latinate)Formal example
askenquire (UK), inquireI am writing to enquire about prices.
helpassistOur staff will assist you.
buypurchaseTickets can be purchased online.
begin, startcommenceWork will commence in May.
endterminateThe contract was terminated.
needrequireAll users require a password.
getobtainYou must obtain permission first.
showdemonstrateThe data demonstrates a clear trend.
giveprovideWe provide free support.
enoughsufficientThe memory is not sufficient.
keepretainWe retain logs for 30 days.
tellinformPlease inform us of any changes.
answerrespondWe will respond within 24 hours.
hideconcealThe report concealed the real cost.
deepprofoundThe change had a profound effect.

Many phrasal verbs also have a formal one-word twin: look into and investigate, put off and postpone. See Phrasal verbs for that list.

Plain English is usually better

Latinate words are not wrong. They are often precise. But too many of them make a text slow and cold. The GOV.UK style guide asks writers to use "buy", not "purchase", and "help", not "assist". It also says "use", not "utilise".

Use the short everyday word first. Use the formal word when the reader expects it, like in a contract, or when it is more exact. In software, "terminate a process" is a normal technical phrase.

Do not make every word formal. "We will endeavour to ascertain the cause" sounds stiff. "We will try to find the cause" is clear and polite.

Strong collocations at C1

There was strong rain last night.

There was heavy rain last night.

Both words mean "a lot". But English speakers say heavy rain and strong coffee. Nobody says "heavy coffee". There is no logic here. You must learn the pairs.

A collocation is a pair or group of words that often go together. Some collocations are fixed, like utter disaster. Few other words fit with "utter". Others are free, like make a cake. You can also make a plan, a list or a call.

At A2 you learned collocations with make, do, have, take and get. See Everyday vocabulary. At C1 the pairs are more precise and more formal.

Collocations for work and study

Strong collocations at C1
CollocationNotExample
meet a deadlinecatch a deadlineWe met the deadline with a day to spare.
raise a concernrise a concernThe tester raised a concern about security.
address an issueaddress to an issueThe patch addresses two issues.
pose a riskmake a riskOld libraries pose a security risk.
draw a conclusionpull a conclusionIt is too early to draw conclusions.
reach an agreementarrive an agreementThe teams reached an agreement on the API.
do research, conduct researchmake researchWe conducted research with 40 users.
make progressdo progressWe made good progress this sprint.
take precautionsdo precautionsTake precautions before you migrate the data.
heavy trafficbig trafficThe site had heavy traffic on launch day.
a sharp rise, a slight dropa strong riseThe chart shows a sharp rise in errors.
a tight deadlinea narrow deadlineWe are working to a tight deadline.

How to check a collocation

  1. Look up the noun in a learner's dictionary. Many entries have a collocation box.
  2. Search the exact phrase in quotation marks. Compare "heavy rain" and "strong rain".
  3. Prefer results from news sites, books and official pages.
  4. Write the whole phrase in your notebook, not the single word.

Learn more about chunks in How to grow your vocabulary. Strong adjectives like "absolutely freezing" are in Adjectives and adverbs.

Do not translate collocations word by word from your language. "Do a mistake", "make a photo" and "say a lie" are translations. English says make a mistake, take a photo and tell a lie.

The IELTS Speaking band descriptors mention collocation at band 7 and band 8. Cambridge Use of English tasks often test collocations too. See Cambridge exams.

Idioms: 60 useful ones

Lead: I sent the client our offer on Monday.

Dev: Did they reply?

Lead: Not yet. The ball is in their court now.

Nobody is playing tennis. "The ball is in their court" means "now it is their turn to act". This is an idiom. You cannot guess the meaning from the single words.

Four rules for idioms

  1. The form is fixed. Say "a piece of cake", not "a slice of cake". Say "in their court", not "on their court".
  2. Most idioms are informal or neutral. Use them in speech and chat. Avoid most of them in essays, reports and contracts.
  3. Use few, and use them well. One good idiom helps. Five in one minute sound forced.
  4. Learn the grammar too. "I bit off more than I could chew." The verbs change tense.

In IELTS Speaking, band 7 needs "some ability to use less common and idiomatic items". Band 8 needs "skilful use" of them. Examiners reward the right idiom in the right place. A wrong or forced idiom does not help.

Here are 60 useful idioms in six groups. Each has a plain meaning, an example and a style note. "Neutral" means safe at work. "Informal" means speech and chat only.

Do not learn all 60 at once. Choose five that fit your life. Use each one once this week, in speech or chat. Then choose five more.

Do not change the words or mix two idioms. "We'll burn that bridge when we come to it" mixes two idioms and means nothing. Keep the exact form.

Connotation and euphemism

She is slim.

She is thin.

She is skinny.

All three describe the same body. "Slim" sounds positive. "Thin" is neutral. "Skinny" often sounds negative. The dictionary meaning is the same, but the feeling is different.

This feeling is called connotation. Choose the word with the right feeling, especially when you talk about people.

Positive, neutral and negative words
PositiveNeutralNegative
slimthinskinny
confidentsure of herselfarrogant
careful with moneyeconomicalstingy, cheap
curiousinterestednosy
determinedfirmstubborn
assertivedirectpushy
affordable, good valuelow-costcheap (can mean low quality)
mature, provenolderoutdated

"Our product is cheap" can sound like "our product is low quality". In sales and on websites, say "affordable" or "good value".

Euphemism: soft words for hard facts

The company let 20 people go.

"Let go" is softer than "fired". It is a euphemism. People use euphemisms to be kind or polite. They also use them to hide bad news.

Common euphemisms
EuphemismDirect meaningWhen it is fine
pass awaydieAlways kind when you talk to a family.
be between jobshave no job nowPolite small talk.
let someone gofire someoneFine in speech. Contracts need the exact term.
restructuring, downsizingcutting jobsCommon in company news. Often hides numbers.
a service disruptionan outage, the service was downFine in a status page if you give details.
sunset a productstop selling or supporting itCommon in tech. Give the end date.
a learning opportunitya mistakeKind in a team review. Do not overuse it.

The rule: be kind about people and clear about facts. An incident report must say what broke, for how long and for how many users. A vague euphemism there damages trust. See Writing at work for incident reports.

Soft words for feelings are good. Soft words for numbers and facts are bad.

Clichés and buzzwords

Going forward, we will leverage our synergies to drive key improvements.

From now on, we will use each team's strengths to make the product faster.

The first sentence sounds busy, but it says almost nothing. It is full of clichés and buzzwords. The second sentence is shorter and says what will happen.

The UK government's GOV.UK style guide has a list of words to avoid. It says plain English is required on GOV.UK. Here are some of its suggestions.

Words to avoid and plain choices (from the GOV.UK style guide)
AvoidUse insteadNote
going forwardfrom now on, in the future
leverageuse, influenceFine in the money sense.
utiliseuse
deliver (an idea)make, create, provideYou can deliver pizzas, post and services.
drive (a change)create, cause, encourageYou drive vehicles.
robustwell thought out, comprehensiveFine for a strong object.
streamlinesimplify
key (as in key issue)important, or nothingFine for a key that opens a lock.
impact (as a verb)have an effect on, influenceFine for a collision.
tacklestop, solve, deal withFine in sport.

Office talk adds more clichés: "at the end of the day", "think outside the box", "low-hanging fruit", "circle back", "a game changer". An idiom becomes a cliché when people use it too often. Use one only when it is the clearest way to say the idea.

GOV.UK says "deploy" is fine for software and the military. So "we deployed the fix" is good plain English at work.

Learners sometimes collect buzzwords to sound fluent. Native readers often feel the opposite. Clear, specific words sound more expert.

British and American English

British

I've already had lunch.

My team are working on it.

See you at the weekend.

American

I already had lunch.

My team is working on it.

See you on the weekend.

Both columns are correct. They are two varieties of English. The differences are small. Speakers understand each other easily. But a good writer keeps one variety in one text.

Main differences
AreaBritishAmerican
-our / -orcolour, behaviourcolor, behavior
-re / -ercentre, metrecenter, meter
-ise / -izeorganise, realise (Oxford style uses -ize)organize, realize
-yse / -yzeanalyseanalyze
double ltravelled, cancelledtraveled, canceled
-ce / -sedefence, licence (noun), license (verb)defense, license (noun and verb)
programmea TV programme, but a computer programprogram for both
Wordsflat, lift, holiday, CV, mobile phoneapartment, elevator, vacation, résumé, cell phone
More wordsautumn, rubbish, queue, maths, postcodefall, trash, line, math, zip code
Floorsground floor, first floorfirst floor, second floor
Present perfectHave you eaten yet?Did you eat yet? (also correct: Have you eaten yet?)
getIt has got worse.It has gotten worse.
Group nounsThe team is / are ready.The team is ready.
have / takehave or take a breaktake a break
shallShall I open the window?Should I / Can I open the window?

Dates: a real risk at work

In the UK, 04/12/2026 means 4 December. In the US, it means 12 April. This can break a deadline. Write the month as a word: "4 December 2026". In data and file names, use the ISO 8601 form: 2026-12-04. It means the same thing everywhere.

This book uses British spelling. Code usually uses American spelling. CSS has color, not colour. So many engineers write British text and American code. That is normal.

Do not mix "colour" and "color" in one document. Choose one variety. Set your spell checker to it.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for register, collocation and idiom
PatternPurposeModelNote
I am writing to + verbOpen a formal emailI am writing to enquire about your prices.Too stiff for team chat.
I would be grateful if you could + verbMake a formal requestI would be grateful if you could resend the file.Not "if you would could".
Could you + verb, please?Make a neutral requestCould you review my pull request, please?Safe for most work messages.
everyday verb → formal verbRaise the formalityneed → require, get → obtainDo not change every word.
meet / miss + a deadlineTalk about deadlinesWe met the deadline.Not "catch a deadline".
raise / address / pose + nounTalk about problems formallyThe audit raised two concerns.Raise (give) is not rise (go up).
highly / fully / deeply + adjectiveGive strong, precise meaningA second failure is highly unlikely.Not "highly sure".
heavy / sharp / tight + nounDescribe size and strengthWe had heavy traffic and a tight deadline.Heavy rain, but strong coffee.
The ball is in your / their courtSay it is someone else's turnI sent the quote. The ball is in their court.Fixed form. Not "on your court".
In the long run, + clauseGive a long-term viewIn the long run, tests save time.Safe in essays and emails.
As a rule of thumb, + clauseGive a practical ruleAs a rule of thumb, keep pull requests small.It is not an exact rule.
let + person + goSay "fire" kindlyThey let three people go.Facts in reports must stay exact.
cliché → plain wordWrite clear textgoing forward → from now onSay what you actually do.
at the weekend (UK) / on the weekend (US)Keep one varietySee you at the weekend.Do not mix varieties in one text.

Practice

1. You write to a new client for the first time. Which opening is best?

  • Hey there!
  • Dear Ms Novak,
  • Yo Ms Novak,

A new client needs a formal opening. Use Dear + title + family name.

2. Which word is the most formal?

  • get
  • receive
  • obtain

Get is informal and neutral. Receive is neutral. Obtain is formal and Latinate.

3. There was very ___ traffic on the motorway.

  • big
  • heavy
  • strong

The collocation is heavy traffic, like heavy rain.

4. We worked late to ? the deadline.

5. A second outage is ? unlikely.

6. Old, unpatched libraries ? a serious security risk.

7. In the review, Ana ? a concern about privacy.

8. Your manager says: "We'll cross that bridge when we come to it." What does she mean?

  • We will travel next week.
  • We will deal with that problem only if it happens.
  • We will finish the project soon.

The idiom means: do not worry about a future problem now.

9. Which form of the idiom is correct?

  • The test was a slice of cake.
  • The test was a piece of cake.
  • The test was a cake piece.

Idioms have a fixed form. Only "a piece of cake" means "very easy".

10. Which word has a negative connotation?

  • economical
  • careful with money
  • stingy

Stingy means "not willing to spend or share". It criticises the person.

11. Which sentence is typical of American English?

  • Shall I send the file?
  • The bug has gotten worse.
  • See you at the weekend.

Gotten is American. British English says "has got worse".

keep someone in the loop

Keep someone informed.

the elephant in the room

A big problem that nobody talks about.

a ballpark figure

A rough number, an estimate.

cut corners

Do a job badly to save time or money.

once in a blue moon

Very rarely.

play devil's advocate

Argue the other side to test an idea.

  1. Make this chat message formal for a client: "Hi! Can't open the invoice u sent. Can u send it again? Thx"
    Answer

    Dear Mr Lee, I am unable to open the invoice you sent. I would be grateful if you could send it again. Thank you. Kind regards, Mia. Other formal versions are also correct.

  2. Rewrite in plain English: "Going forward, we will leverage the new tool to streamline onboarding."
    Answer

    From now on, we will use the new tool to make onboarding simpler. Even better, say exactly how: "to cut onboarding from five days to two".

  3. Find the register problem and fix it: "Dear Professor Kim, thanks a ton for the feedback, it was awesome!!"
    Answer

    The opening is formal, but the rest is slang. Better: "Dear Professor Kim, Thank you very much for your feedback. It was very helpful."

  4. An incident report says: "There was a minor service disruption." In fact, the site was down for four hours for all users. What is wrong? Rewrite it.
    Answer

    The euphemism hides the facts. Better: "The website was unavailable for all users for four hours, from 09:00 to 13:00 UTC."

  5. Choose the best words for a research paper and say why: "The results (show / demonstrate) a (big / substantial) increase."
    Answer

    "The results demonstrate a substantial increase." A paper uses a formal register, so the Latinate words fit. In a team chat, "The results show a big increase" is better.

  6. Correct the collocations: "We did a big progress, but we must do more research and do less mistakes."
    Answer

    "We made a lot of progress (or great progress), but we must do more research and make fewer mistakes." Progress is uncountable, so not "a big progress". Do research is correct.

  7. A colleague writes 04/05/2026 in a plan for a team in London and New York. What is the risk? How do you fix it?
    Answer

    London reads 4 May. New York reads 5 April. Write "4 May 2026" or use the ISO form 2026-05-04.

Key takeaways

  • Register is the style for one situation. Choose it by reader, purpose and channel. When unsure, choose neutral.
  • Germanic words are short and everyday. Latinate words are longer and more formal. Use the plain word first.
  • Collocations are natural word partners: heavy rain, meet a deadline, highly unlikely. Learn them as whole phrases.
  • Idioms have a fixed form. Use a few of them well in speech. Avoid most of them in formal writing.
  • Connotation is the feeling of a word. Slim, thin and skinny are not the same.
  • Euphemisms are kind for feelings, but bad for facts. Reports must stay exact.
  • Replace clichés and buzzwords with plain, specific words.
  • British and American English differ a little. Keep one variety in one text, and write dates without confusion.

Sources

  • GOV.UK A to Z style guide. The "words to avoid" list and the rule that plain English is required.
  • GOV.UK writing guidelines: clear language. Short words like buy and help instead of purchase and assist.
  • British Council TeachingEnglish: Collocation. Fixed and free collocations, with utter disaster and make a cake.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: British English and American English. Present perfect, got and gotten, group nouns, have and take, shall.
  • IELTS Speaking band descriptors. Idiomatic language and collocation at bands 7, 8 and 9.
  • Wikipedia: Foreign language influences in English. The Finkenstaedt and Wolff word-origin study and the Germanic core of common words.

The error clinic

Most learners make the same small mistakes again and again. This chapter collects 60 of the most common ones in eight groups. Each one shows the wrong form, the right form, the reason and the chapter that teaches the rule. Then you get a method to find your own mistakes.

  • Find and fix 60 common mistakes with articles, nouns, verbs, word order, prepositions, word form, false friends and punctuation.
  • Explain each correction with one short rule.
  • Check your own writing with a five-step self-check method.
  • Edit any text with a short checklist before you send it.
  • Keep an error log and search your writing for your top mistakes.

How the clinic works

Read this short email. It has five mistakes. Can you find them before you open the second tab?

Hi Tom, thanks for the informations. I am working here since 2022, so I know old system. Can we discuss about the design on Monday? I look forward to hear from you.

Hi Tom, thanks for the information. I have worked here since 2022, so I know the old system. Can we discuss the design on Monday? I look forward to hearing from you.

  1. informations → information (uncountable noun)
  2. I am working → I have worked (since + up to now)
  3. old system → the old system (missing article)
  4. discuss about → discuss (no preposition)
  5. to hear → to hearing (to is a preposition here)

The reader understands the first version. But each small mistake costs a little trust. Five mistakes in four lines look careless, even when the ideas are good.

Errors and mistakes

The linguist S. Pit Corder made a useful split in 1967. An error comes from a gap in your knowledge. A mistake is a slip. You know the rule, but you were tired or fast. You fix mistakes by checking. You fix errors by learning the rule.

Some errors stay for years, even at C1. The linguist Larry Selinker called this fossilisation. The cure is to notice the error, learn the rule and practise the right form many times.

Your first language matters

The language research team at Cambridge University Press publishes lists of common errors. There is one list for each of several first languages. The lists look similar in many ways. Wrong prepositions, missing articles, wrong verbs in fixed phrases, tense confusion and spelling appear again and again.

The details depend on your first language. Speakers of languages without a word like "the" often forget articles. Speakers of French or German often use false friends. So read all 60 items, but mark the ones you make.

Each table below has five columns. "Wrong" and "Right" show the form. "Why" gives the rule in a few words. The last column links to the chapter with the full lesson.

Articles and countable nouns (1 to 15)

I am software engineer at the Google. I have a MBA. I need an advice about the new equipments.

I am a software engineer at Google. I have an MBA. I need some advice about the new equipment.

An article goes before a noun. A singular countable noun almost always needs a word before it: a, an, the, my or this. Names of most companies and countries need no article. Uncountable nouns have no plural and no "a".

Articles
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
1I am engineer.I am an engineer.A singular job needs a or an.Nouns and articles
2She has a MBA.She has an MBA.Choose by the first sound. MBA starts with "em".Nouns and articles
3The life is hard.Life is hard.An idea in general takes no article.Nouns and articles
4The developers love coffee. (all developers)Developers love coffee.A plural in general takes no article.Nouns and articles
5I found a bug. A bug is in the login code.I found a bug. The bug is in the login code.First mention a. Second mention the.Nouns and articles
6Please send me report.Please send me the report.Both people know which report: the.Nouns and articles
7He works at the Microsoft in the Germany.He works at Microsoft in Germany.Most company and country names: no article. But: the UK, the USA.Advanced articles
8I go to the bed at midnight.I go to bed at midnight.Fixed phrases: go to bed, at work, at home, by train.Nouns and articles
Countable and uncountable nouns
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
9Thanks for the informations.Thanks for the information.Information is uncountable: no -s. Say "a piece of information".Nouns and articles
10Can I give you an advice?Can I give you some advice?Advice is uncountable: no a. Or "a piece of advice".Nouns and articles
11We bought new equipments.We bought new equipment.Equipment is uncountable.Nouns and articles
12Thanks for all your feedbacks.Thanks for all your feedback.Feedback is uncountable.Nouns and articles
13I installed a software. Push your codes.I installed some software. Push your code.Software and code (program text) are uncountable. But "error codes" is fine.Nouns and articles
14We have less bugs this month.We have fewer bugs this month.Fewer + plural. Less + uncountable (less time).Nouns and articles
15How much tickets are left?How many tickets are left?Many + plural. Much + uncountable.Nouns and articles

Not sure if a noun is countable? Look it up in a learner's dictionary. Countable nouns are marked [C]. Uncountable nouns are marked [U].

In casual speech, many native speakers say "less bugs". In exams and formal writing, use "fewer".

Verbs and tenses (16 to 25)

She work from home since March. Did you saw her message? When she will finish, she will call you.

She has worked from home since March. Did you see her message? When she finishes, she will call you.

Most verb mistakes come from four rules. Add -s with he, she and it. Use the base verb after did. Use the present perfect for a time up to now. Use a present tense after when and if, even for the future.

Verbs and tenses
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
16She work from home on Fridays.She works from home on Fridays.Present simple with he, she, it: add -s.Present tenses
17I am knowing the answer.I know the answer.State verbs (know, want, need) are rarely continuous.Present tenses
18Did you saw my message?Did you see my message?After did and didn't: the base verb.Past tenses
19I have finished it yesterday.I finished it yesterday.Finished time (yesterday, ago, last week): past simple.Perfect tenses
20I live here since 2021.I have lived here since 2021.Since or for, up to now: present perfect.Perfect tenses
21I will call you when I will arrive.I will call you when I arrive.After when, if, as soon as: present for future.Future forms
22If I would know, I would tell you.If I knew, I would tell you.No would in the if-clause.Conditionals
23I am agree with you.I agree with you.Agree is a verb. Do not add am.Present tenses
24I look forward to meet you.I look forward to meeting you.Here to is a preposition: add -ing.Verb patterns
25The error was happened at 3 a.m.The error happened at 3 a.m.Happen has no object, so no passive.The passive

"Since" does not choose the tense alone. "I have lived here since 2021" talks about now. "I lived there from 2015 to 2019" is finished, so it is past simple.

Word order (26 to 33)

I check always the logs. Can you tell me where is the meeting room? I met yesterday the client.

I always check the logs. Can you tell me where the meeting room is? I met the client yesterday.

The basic English order is subject, verb, object. Keep the verb and its object together. Short adverbs like always and also go before the main verb. Time words usually go at the end. Questions have their own order, but indirect questions do not.

Word order
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
26I like very much this tool.I like this tool very much.Keep the verb and the object together.Adjectives and adverbs
27I check always the logs.I always check the logs.Frequency adverbs go before the main verb, after be.Adjectives and adverbs
28Can you tell me where is the room?Can you tell me where the room is?Indirect questions use statement order.Questions and negatives
29Why you didn't come?Why didn't you come?Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb.Questions and negatives
30Who did write this code?Who wrote this code?When who is the subject: no do or did.Questions and negatives
31a plastic small black boxa small black plastic boxOrder: opinion, size, age, colour, origin, material.Adjectives and adverbs
32The server is not enough fast.The server is not fast enough.Enough goes after an adjective, before a noun.Adjectives and adverbs
33I met yesterday the client.I met the client yesterday.Time usually goes at the end.The 15 sentence patterns

"Also" follows the same rule as "always". Say "We also have a Linux version", not "We have also a Linux version". After be, it comes after the verb: "It is also free."

Prepositions (34 to 41)

I'm interested about the new role. It depends of the team. Can we discuss about it in Monday?

I'm interested in the new role. It depends on the team. Can we discuss it on Monday?

A preposition often belongs to the word before it. Interested takes in. Depend takes on. There is often no logic. Learn the verb or adjective together with its preposition. Some verbs take no preposition at all.

Prepositions
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
34I'm interested about machine learning.I'm interested in machine learning.Interested in.Prepositions
35It depends of the data.It depends on the data.Depend on.Prepositions
36We discussed about the design.We discussed the design.Discuss takes no preposition. Talk about is fine.Prepositions
37See you in Monday at the morning.See you on Monday morning.On for days. In the morning, but on Monday morning.Prepositions
38We arrived to Berlin at night.We arrived in Berlin at night.Arrive in a city or country. Arrive at a building. Never arrive to.Prepositions
39Can you explain me the problem?Can you explain the problem to me?Explain something to someone.Prepositions
40I have used Rust since two years.I have used Rust for two years.For + a period. Since + a start point.Perfect tenses
41Please finish the review until Friday.Please finish the review by Friday.By = a deadline. Until = all the time up to then.Linking words

Mistake 41 can cause real problems at work. "Work until Friday" means "keep working, then stop on Friday". "Finish by Friday" means "Friday is the last day".

Word form, word choice and false friends (42 to 54)

I am very interesting in this role. The launch was very success. Actually I work for a bank, but eventually I will change jobs.

I am very interested in this role. The launch was very successful. Currently I work for a bank, but I might change jobs.

One word can have many forms: success, succeed, successful, successfully. These forms are a word family. Choose the form the sentence needs: a noun, a verb, an adjective or an adverb.

Word form and word choice
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
42I am very interesting in this role.I am very interested in this role.-ed = how you feel. -ing = what makes you feel it.Adjectives and adverbs
43He codes very good.He codes very well.Well is the adverb of good.Adjectives and adverbs
44The launch was very success.The launch was very successful.After very, use an adjective.Vocabulary system
45We need to analysis the logs.We need to analyse the logs.Analysis is the noun. Analyse (US analyze) is the verb.Vocabulary system
46I did a mistake in the config.I made a mistake in the config.Make a mistake, make a decision. Do a task.Everyday vocabulary
47The price is too expensive.The price is too high.Prices are high or low. Things are expensive or cheap.Register and collocation
48Me and Ana fixed the bug.Ana and I fixed the bug.Subject form: I, not me. Put yourself last.Pronouns

False friends

A false friend looks like a word in your language. But the meaning is different. False friends are dangerous because they feel safe.

False friends
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
49Actually I work for a bank. (meaning "now")Currently I work for a bank.Actually = in fact. Spanish actualmente means "now". German aktuell means "current".Technical English
50Eventually I will join the call. (meaning "maybe")I might join the call.Eventually = in the end, after a long time. German eventuell means "possibly".Technical English
51Please control the numbers before you send them.Please check the numbers before you send them.Control = have power over. In several European languages, the similar word means "check".Technical English

53I bought milk in the magazine.I bought milk in the shop.A magazine is a paper with articles. Russian magazin means "shop".Vocabulary system

Many English loanwords in other languages have new meanings. Japanese has many of these. Here are a few more. Check any loanword in an English dictionary before you use it.

WordMeaning in the other languageEnglish meaningSay instead
mansionJapanese manshon: a flat in a modern blocka very large, expensive houseflat, apartment
