If an English word looks exactly like a word in your language, stop. Check it once in a dictionary. It might be a false friend.

Punctuation and spelling (55 to 60)

The tests passed, we merged the branch. The app lost it's settings. I think, that the new version is faster then the old one.

The tests passed, so we merged the branch. The app lost its settings. I think that the new version is faster than the old one.

A comma cannot join two full sentences. Two full sentences joined by only a comma make a comma splice. Use a full stop, or add a linker like so, and or but. Apostrophes show missing letters or owners. They never make a plural.

Punctuation and spelling
#WrongRightWhyLearn the rule
55The tests passed, we merged the branch.The tests passed, so we merged the branch.A comma cannot join two sentences. Add so, or use a full stop.Linking words
56The app lost it's settings.The app lost its settings.It's = it is or it has. Its = of it.Pronouns
57We updated all the API's.We updated all the APIs.No apostrophe for plurals, also after short forms like API and PDF.Nouns and articles
58I think, that it works. The bug, that you found, is fixed.I think that it works. The bug that you found is fixed.No comma before that.Relative clauses
59I study english every monday.I study English every Monday.Capitals for languages, nationalities, days and months.Writing paragraphs
60Don't loose the file. It's bigger then the old one.Don't lose the file. It's bigger than the old one.Lose = not keep. Loose = not tight. Than compares. Then = next.Sounds and spelling

Cambridge lists some words that many learners misspell. Check these: accommodation, recommend, definitely, environment, government, which, because, beginning.

Do not put a space before a question mark or an exclamation mark. Write "Really?" and "Done!", not "Really ?" and "Done !". This space is normal in French, but not in English.

A self-check method

Watch one email get better in five passes. Each pass looks for one kind of mistake only.

The first draft

"Thanks for the informations. I am working on the API since Monday. I have still some problems. Can you explain me the login flow? Let's discuss about it on Friday, the tests are failing."

Verbs and tenses

"I am working ... since Monday" becomes "I have been working ... since Monday". Since + up to now needs the present perfect.

Nouns and articles

"informations" becomes "information". It is uncountable.

Word order

"I have still some problems" becomes "I still have some problems". Still goes before the main verb.

Prepositions

"explain me the login flow" becomes "explain the login flow to me". "discuss about it" becomes "discuss it".

Punctuation

"on Friday, the tests are failing" is a comma splice. Write "on Friday. The tests are failing."

The final email

"Thanks for the information. I have been working on the API since Monday. I still have some problems. Can you explain the login flow to me? Let's discuss it on Friday. The tests are failing."

The five steps

  1. Rest first. Wait at least ten minutes before you check. For a long text, wait a day. Fresh eyes see more.
  2. Read it aloud, slowly. Your ear hears missing words and strange order.
  3. Do one pass for each problem. Verbs, then nouns and articles, then word order, then prepositions, then punctuation.
  4. Search for your top mistakes. Use Ctrl + F, or grep. Search for "since", "discuss about", "it's".
  5. Log every new mistake. Write it in your error log. Read the log once a week.

Your error log

An error log turns random mistakes into a short list. After a month, you will see your top five. Those five are your real study plan.

An example error log
DateI wroteCorrectGroupRule in one lineSeen again
3 Novdiscuss about the plandiscuss the planPrepositionsDiscuss takes no preposition.2
5 Novsince two yearsfor two yearsPrepositionsFor + a period.1
8 Novthe informationsthe informationCountable nounsInformation has no plural.3
12 NovI am working here since MayI have worked here since MayTensesSince + up to now: present perfect.1

Search your writing like code

You already search code for bugs. You can search your writing the same way. Put your top mistakes in a pattern file, one per line. Then run grep on your draft.

Hi Tom,
Thanks for the informations about the new API.
I am working here since 2022, so I know the old system.
Can we discuss about the design on Monday?
The app lost it's settings after the update.
I look forward to hear from you.
informations|advices|feedbacks|equipments
discuss about
depends? of
interested about
since [0-9]+ (years|months)
it's (own|settings|data|name)
look forward to (hear|meet|see|work)
# -n line numbers, -i ignore case, -E extended patterns, -f read patterns from a file
grep -n -i -E -f my-errors.txt draft.txt
2:Thanks for the informations about the new API.
4:Can we discuss about the design on Monday?
5:The app lost it's settings after the update.
6:I look forward to hear from you.

The draft had five mistakes. Grep found four. Line 3 said "I am working here since 2022". That is a tense mistake, and no simple pattern finds it. So a search helps, but you still need to read.

Do not trust spell checkers and grammar tools alone. They miss real words in the wrong place, like then for than or loose for lose. They can also suggest wrong changes. Use them, then read again yourself.

An editing checklist

Use this list for the last check before you send an important text. It takes five minutes. Go from big things to small things.

  1. Purpose. Is the main point in the first two lines? Does the reader know what to do?
  2. Register. Does the style fit the reader? See Register, collocation and idiom.
  3. Sentences. Is every sentence short and complete? Does every sentence have a subject and a verb?
  4. Verbs. Check -s with he, she and it. Check the tense with since, for, yesterday and ago.
  5. Nouns. Does every singular countable noun have a, an, the or my? Are uncountable nouns without -s?
  6. Order. Are verb and object together? Are indirect questions in statement order?
  7. Prepositions. Check words like depend, interested, discuss, arrive, explain, by and until.
  8. Words. Check false friends, collocations and word forms (success or successful).
  9. Punctuation. No comma between two full sentences. Check its and it's. Capitals for days and languages.
  10. Facts. Check names, numbers, dates, links and attachments. Write dates like "4 December 2026".

In IELTS Writing, grammar is one of four criteria. Vocabulary is another, and it includes spelling and word form. So small mistakes can lower two of your four scores. Leave three minutes at the end to run this checklist. See IELTS Writing.

For more on editing sentences and paragraphs, see Writing sentences and paragraphs. For commit messages and pull requests, see Writing at work.

Patterns to remember

Correct patterns that fix the most common mistakes
PatternPurposeModelNote
I am + a / an + jobSay your jobI am an engineer.Never "I am engineer".
uncountable noun, no -sTalk about information, advice, feedbackThanks for the feedback.To count: a piece of advice.
fewer + plural, less + uncountableCompare amountsFewer bugs, less time.Many + plural, much + uncountable.
have + past participle + since / forTalk about time up to nowI have lived here since 2021.For a period, since a start point.
Did + subject + base verb?Ask about the pastDid you see my message?Not "Did you saw".
When / if + present, will + verbTalk about a future eventWhen I arrive, I'll call you.No will after when.
If + past, would + verbImagine an unreal situationIf I knew, I would tell you.No would in the if-clause.
Can you tell me + wh- word + subject + verb?Ask politelyCan you tell me where the room is?Statement order, no do or did.
subject + always / also + verb + objectPlace short adverbsI always check the logs.After be: It is also free.
adjective + prepositionUse fixed partnersinterested in, good at, depend onLearn them as one unit.
discuss + objectTalk about a topicLet's discuss the plan.No about after discuss.
explain + thing + to + personAsk for an explanationCan you explain it to me?Not "explain me".
by + deadlineGive the last possible timePlease finish it by Friday.Until means "up to then".
look forward to + -ingEnd a letter politelyI look forward to hearing from you.To is a preposition here.
Sentence, so sentence. / Sentence. Sentence.Join two full sentencesThe tests passed, so we merged.A comma alone is a comma splice.

Practice

1. Which sentence is correct?

  • I am engineer at a bank.
  • I am an engineer at a bank.
  • I am a engineer at a bank.

A singular job needs a or an. Engineer starts with a vowel sound, so use an.

2. Which sentence is correct?

  • Thank you for the useful informations.
  • Thank you for an useful information.
  • Thank you for the useful information.

Information is uncountable. It has no plural and no a or an.

3. I have lived in this city ? 2021.

4. I have lived in this city ? five years.

5. Please send me the slides ? Thursday at noon.

6. Whether we hire depends ? the budget.

7. The service restarted, but it lost ? cache.

8. Python is faster to write ? C.

9. Which question is correct?

  • Do you know where is the server room?
  • Do you know where the server room is?
  • Do you know where does the server room is?

An indirect question uses statement order: subject, then verb.

10. A colleague writes: "Actually I work on the payments team." What does she probably mean, if her first language is Spanish?

  • In fact, I work on payments, not search.
  • At the moment, I work on payments.
  • In the end, I will work on payments.

Spanish actualmente means "now". In English, say "currently" or "at the moment".

11. Which sentence has a comma splice?

  • The build failed, so I checked the logs.
  • The build failed, I checked the logs.
  • When the build failed, I checked the logs.

Two full sentences are joined by only a comma. Add so, or use a full stop.

  1. Find and fix three mistakes: "She work in Tokyo. She is very interesting in robots. Who did build this robot?"
    Answer

    (1) She works in Tokyo. (2) She is very interested in robots. (3) Who built this robot? Who is the subject, so there is no did.

  2. Find and fix four mistakes: "We discussed about the bug yesterday. I have fixed it yesterday evening, the tests pass now. Please review it until Friday."
    Answer

    (1) We discussed the bug yesterday. (2) I fixed it yesterday evening. (3) A full stop or "and" after evening: "... evening. The tests pass now." (4) Please review it by Friday.

  3. What is the difference between an error and a mistake? Give one example of each from your own English.
    Answer

    An error comes from not knowing the rule, so you make it every time. A mistake is a slip. You know the rule, and you can fix it when you check. Your examples will be personal. For example, an error: always writing "informations". A mistake: writing "he work" once when you were in a hurry.

  4. Write one grep pattern that finds "less bugs", "less users" and "less errors" in your draft.
    Answer

    One answer: less (bugs|users|errors). Put it on a new line in your pattern file. It finds the mistake, but you must still choose "fewer" yourself.

  5. Edit this paragraph. It has ten mistakes. "I am working as developer since 2020. Last year I have moved to Berlin, and I am agree that it is a interesting city. My manager give me many advices. Can you tell me what time does the meeting start? I look forward to see you on monday."
    Answer

    "I have worked (or have been working) as a developer since 2020. Last year I moved to Berlin, and I agree that it is an interesting city. My manager gives me a lot of advice. Can you tell me what time the meeting starts? I look forward to seeing you on Monday." The ten fixes: (1) have worked, (2) a developer, (3) moved, (4) agree, (5) an interesting, (6) gives, (7) a lot of advice, (8) what time the meeting starts, (9) seeing, (10) Monday with a capital.

Key takeaways

  • Most mistakes fall into eight groups: articles, countable nouns, verbs, word order, prepositions, word form, false friends and punctuation.
  • An error is a gap in knowledge. A mistake is a slip. Learn rules for errors. Check carefully for mistakes.
  • Singular countable nouns need a word before them. Uncountable nouns like information, advice and feedback have no plural.
  • Since and for with a time up to now take the present perfect. After when and if, use a present tense for the future.
  • Keep the verb and the object together. Indirect questions use statement order.
  • Learn prepositions with their words: interested in, depend on, discuss with no preposition, finish by Friday.
  • Check any word that looks like a word in your language. It may be a false friend.
  • Rest, read aloud, do one pass per problem, search for your top mistakes and keep an error log.

Sources

  • Cambridge University Press: Common English errors by first language. Typical errors for learners with different first languages: prepositions, determiners, verbs, nouns and spelling.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Nouns, countable and uncountable. Information, advice and equipment, and "a piece of".
  • Purdue OWL: Run-ons, comma splices and fused sentences. Why a comma cannot join two full sentences.
  • UNC Writing Center: Editing and proofreading. Reading aloud, one error type per pass, and knowing your patterns of error.
  • Wikipedia: False friend. Definition and examples such as actualmente and Gift.
  • Wikipedia: List of gairaigo and wasei-eigo terms. Japanese meanings of mansion, claim, smart, tension and cunning.

How to grow your vocabulary

Words carry most of the meaning in English. Grammar helps, but a missing word stops a conversation. This chapter gives you a system: which words to learn, how to learn them and how to keep them for years.

  • Tell the difference between words you understand and words you can use.
  • Explain how many words each CEFR level needs, and why the numbers are estimates.
  • Build new words from word families, prefixes and suffixes.
  • Learn words with their partners: collocations and chunks.
  • Run a spaced repetition schedule with a five-step word card.

Active and passive words

Read this sentence from a security report.

The new patch mitigates the risk of a data leak.

You probably understand mitigates. It means "makes the risk smaller". Now imagine a meeting. Would you say "mitigate"? Many learners say "make the risk smaller" instead. So for them, mitigate is a word they know, but cannot use yet.

Words you understand when you read or hear them are your passive vocabulary. Words you can say and write are your active vocabulary. Teachers also call them receptive and productive vocabulary. Your passive vocabulary is always bigger than your active one.

What "knowing a word" means

Knowing a word is not one thing. It has many parts. The researcher Paul Nation groups them into three areas.

Three areas of word knowledge, with the word "deploy"
AreaQuestionsExample
FormHow do I say it? How do I spell it? What are its parts?de-PLOY, /dɪˈplɔɪ/. Parts: de + ploy.
MeaningWhat does it mean? What other words are close?To put software on a server so people can use it. Close: release, ship.
UseWhat grammar does it need? What words go with it? Is it formal?deploy something to production. A neutral word at work.

A word moves step by step. First you recognise its shape. Then you know its meaning. Then you know its partners and grammar. At the end you can use it fast, in speech, without thinking.

"I know this word" often means "I recognise it". Test yourself. Can you say it with the right stress? Can you spell it? Can you use it in a sentence with a correct partner, in three seconds? If not, it is still a passive word.

Passive words help you read and listen. Active words help you speak and write. You need both. But you must work on purpose to move a word from passive to active.

How many words do you need?

Here is a common question. "How many words do I need for B2?" Researchers give different answers. The answers depend on what they count and how they test.

What counts as one word?

Look at these forms: use, uses, used, using, useful, user. Is that one word or six?

  • A lemma is a base word with its grammar endings: use, uses, used, using.
  • A word family is bigger. It adds close forms with prefixes and suffixes: useful, user, reuse.

So "3,000 words" can mean very different things. Always ask: lemmas or word families?

Estimates for each CEFR level

In 2009, James Milton and Thomaï Alexiou linked vocabulary size to the CEFR levels. They used a test called X-Lex. It checks how many of the 5,000 most common words a learner knows. Their numbers for English are below. The authors say clearly that these figures are a guide, not a fixed rule.

Estimated vocabulary size for each CEFR level (Milton and Alexiou, 2009)
LevelWords known from the 5,000 most common
A1under 1,500
A21,500 to 2,500
B12,750 to 3,250
B23,250 to 3,750
C13,750 to 4,500
C24,500 to 5,000

Look at the steps. From A1 to B1, the number about doubles. After B1, each level adds only about 500 to 750 common words. But you also start to learn rarer words outside the top 5,000.

Coverage: how many words in a text do you know?

A second way to think about size is coverage. Take a text of 100 words. If you know 98 of them, your coverage is 98%. That is one unknown word in every 50.

What coverage feels like
CoverageUnknown wordsHow it feels
98%1 in 50You can read alone and enjoy it.
95%1 in 20You understand, but it is work.
90%1 in 10Hard. You lose the meaning often.

Paul Nation studied this in 2006. He used 98% coverage as the target for reading without help. With that target, he estimated 8,000 to 9,000 word families for written English. For spoken English, he estimated 6,000 to 7,000. Later studies suggest that 95% may be enough for listening. That needs fewer words, perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 word families.

All these numbers are estimates. They come from different tests, different word units and different learners. Use them to plan, not to judge yourself. The clear message is simple: the first few thousand common words give you the most value.

Use a list to find the common words. The Oxford 3000 lists core words for A1 to B2. The Oxford 5000 adds 2,000 more words for B2 and C1. The English Vocabulary Profile from Cambridge shows a CEFR level for each meaning of a word. Check the official sites: access rules can change.

Word families, prefixes and suffixes

Read these sentences from one project.

  • Our service depends on the database.
  • The database is a dependency.
  • The two modules are independent.
  • The old server was not very dependable.

Four words, one family. If you know depend, you can guess the others. That is the power of word families. One family can give you five or more words for the price of one.

Words are built from parts. The main part is the root. A prefix goes at the start. It usually changes the meaning. A suffix goes at the end. It usually changes the word class, for example from verb to noun.

Prefixes: they change the meaning

Common prefixes with work examples
PrefixMeaningExamples
un-not, or reverseunclear, unstable, undo, unlock
in-, im-, il-, ir-notinvalid, impossible, illegal, irregular
dis-not, oppositedisable, disconnect, disagree
non-notnon-blocking, non-zero, non-profit
re-againrestart, rewrite, redeploy
mis-wronglymisread, misunderstand, misconfigure
pre-beforepreview, preinstalled, preprocess
de-remove, reversedecode, decrypt, deactivate
over-, under-too much, too littleoverload, underestimate
sub-under, a smaller partsubfolder, subtask, subclass
inter-betweeninterface, interact, international
multi-, co-, anti-many; together; againstmultithreaded, co-author, antivirus

Use im- before m and p (impossible), il- before l (illegal), and ir- before r (irregular). This rule works for most common words.

Suffixes: they change the word class

Common suffixes and the word class they make
SuffixMakes aExamples
-er, -ornoun: a person or a tooldeveloper, compiler, editor
-tion, -sionnouncreate, creation. decide, decision.
-mentnoundeploy, deployment. require, requirement.
-ness, -itynoun from an adjectiveaware, awareness. secure, security.
-ise, -ify, -enverboptimise, simplify, shorten
-able, -ibleadjective: can be donereadable, scalable, visible
-ful, -lessadjective: with, withoutuseful, useless, stateless
-al, -ive, -ousadjectivefunctional, interactive, dangerous
-lyadverb, usuallyquick, quickly. clear, clearly.

Suffixes can move the stress: Analyse, aNAlysis, anaLYtical. The chapter Pronunciation and fluency gives the stress rules for these endings.

This tool is very depend.

We need more secure for the API.

The code is not readability.

This tool is very dependable.

We need more security for the API.

The code is not readable.

Learners often know the family but choose the wrong member. Ask one question: what does the sentence need here, a noun, a verb, an adjective or an adverb? Then pick the suffix. After "very" you need an adjective. After "more" before a full stop, you often need a noun.

Cambridge B2 First and C1 Advanced have a word formation task. You change a word to fit a gap. Learning whole families is the best preparation. See Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

The Academic Word List idea

Read a research paper or a long design document. You meet words like analyse, approach, data, method, process, require and significant. They are not everyday words. They are not technical words for one field either. They appear in serious writing about every subject.

In 2000, Averil Coxhead made the Academic Word List, or AWL. She studied about 3.5 million words of university texts. The list has 570 word families in 10 sublists. Sublist 1 has the most frequent families. The list leaves out the 2,000 most common general words, because learners need those anyway.

Here is the idea. High-frequency words cover about 80% of words in written texts. The AWL covers about 10% of words in academic texts. Together they give about 90% coverage of a typical academic text. That is a big gain from a short list.

How to use the idea today

  • Learn sublists 1 to 3 first. They give the most coverage.
  • Learn each word as a family: analyse, analysis, analyst, analytical.
  • Make your own list for your job too. Technical words like latency and throughput are frequent in your texts.
  • The AWL is old now. Newer lists exist, for example the Academic Vocabulary List (2014). The idea stays the same.

Do not learn the AWL from A to Z. Alphabetical order gives you rare and common words mixed together. Follow the sublists, and learn words in sentences from your own reading. See also Reading technical English.

Collocations and chunks

We did a decision to fix the error yesterday.

There was strong rain, so I made my homework at home.

We made a decision to fix the bug yesterday.

There was heavy rain, so I did my homework at home.

The wrong sentences have correct grammar. Every word is a real word. But native speakers do not put these words together. English says make a decision, heavy rain and do homework.

A collocation is a pair or group of words that often go together. A chunk is a longer group that you can use as one piece, like "as far as I know". Fluent speakers do not build every sentence word by word. They join chunks.

Kinds of collocation, with work examples
KindExamples
Verb + nounfix a bug, run a test, raise an issue, meet a deadline
Adjective + nouna tight deadline, a breaking change, high availability, heavy traffic
Adverb + adjectivewidely used, fully tested, highly available
Noun + nounerror message, code review, release notes
Verb + prepositiondepend on, consist of, apply for
Fixed chunksas far as I know, it depends on, let me check, on the other hand

How to find the right partner

  1. Look at the example sentences in a learner dictionary. Copy the partners you see.
  2. Use a collocation dictionary for common words like problem or risk.
  3. When you read, mark the partner, not only the new word. Write "raise an issue", not "issue".
  4. Not sure? Search both phrases in quotes, like "make a decision" and "do a decision". The common one is usually right. This is only a rough check.

Do not translate partners from your own language word by word. Some languages say "open the light" or "learn knowledge". English says turn on the light and gain knowledge. When a partner feels strange, check it.

The basic partners with make, do, have, take and get are in Everyday vocabulary. Strong C1 collocations are in Register, collocation and idiom.

Spaced repetition: the schedule

Ana and Ben want to learn 20 new words. Ana studies for one hour on Monday. Ben studies for ten minutes on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and the next Monday. Each of them spends about one hour in total. One month later, Ben remembers many more words. Why?

Memory fades fast after you learn something. In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus showed this with his own memory. We call the line of this loss the forgetting curve. Each review makes the memory stronger. After a good review, the memory fades more slowly.

Two research ideas explain Ben's success.

  • The spacing effect. The same study time works better when you spread it over days.
  • Retrieval practice. Trying to remember a word builds memory more than reading it again. So hide the answer and try first.

How long should the gaps be?

In 2008, Cepeda and his team tested more than 1,350 people. They found that the best gap depends on how long you want to remember. To remember for a few weeks, the best gap was about 20% of that time. To remember for a year, it was about 5 to 10% of a year. That is roughly three weeks to a month.

So start with short gaps and let them grow. Here is a simple starter schedule. It is a common rule of thumb, not an exact law from research.

A starter schedule for one new word
ReviewWhenIf you fail
LearnDay 0Try again in 10 minutes
Review 1Day 1Start again from day 0
Review 2Day 3Go back to a 1-day gap
Review 3Day 7Go back to a 1-day gap
Review 4About day 16Go back to a 3-day gap
Review 5About day 35Go back to a 7-day gap
After thatEvery 2 to 4 monthsGo back to a shorter gap

A paper version is the box system in Everyday vocabulary. Apps do the maths for you. Anki is a popular free flashcard app. Its older scheduler is based on the SM-2 algorithm. Since version 23.10, Anki also offers FSRS, a newer scheduler. FSRS learns from your own review history.

In FSRS you choose a desired retention. The default is 90%. A higher number means shorter gaps and more reviews each day. The Anki manual warns that the work grows very fast above 90%. It advises staying below 97%. Check the manual for your version: settings change.

Three mistakes kill a review habit. First, adding 50 new cards in one day. Each new card brings many reviews later. Start with 5 to 10 new cards a day. Second, reading the answer before you try. Third, pressing "Good" when you were not sure. Be honest. The schedule only works with honest answers.

The five-step word card

A card with only "word = translation" is weak. It gives you meaning, but not form or use. The card below adds the missing parts. It works on paper or in an app. Each slide is one step.

Sound and stress

Write the word, the IPA and the stress. mitigate, /ˈmɪtɪɡeɪt/, MI-ti-gate. Add the word class: verb. Say it aloud three times.

Simple meaning

Write the meaning in easy English: "to make something bad less serious". Add a word from your own language only if it helps.

Partners

Write two or three collocations: mitigate a risk, mitigate the impact, mitigate an attack. Add the grammar: mitigate + noun. No preposition.

Your own sentence

Write a true sentence from your life: "We added rate limits to mitigate the attack." Real sentences are easier to remember.

Family and style

Add family members: mitigation (noun). Add the style: formal, mostly written. In casual speech people often say "reduce the risk".

Now turn the card into questions. Use different card types for passive and active words.

Front: mitigate

Back: to make something bad less serious. mitigate a risk.

Use it for passive words. You see English and recall the meaning.

Front: to make a risk less serious (formal verb, starts with m)

Back: mitigate a risk

Use it for active words. You see the meaning and must produce the English.

Front: We added rate limits to ______ the attack.

Back: mitigate

The best type for most words. It trains the word with its partner and grammar.

A gap card is often called a cloze card. It is the strongest card for moving words to your active vocabulary.

Add audio when you can. Many apps can attach the sound from a dictionary or a text-to-speech voice. Then you train your ear and your mouth together.

Do not put ten facts on one card. One card asks one question. If a word has two meanings, make two cards, each with its own sentence.

Learning words from reading

You read a blog post of 500 words. Ten words are new. Your coverage is 98%. You can read happily and guess most new words. Another post has 50 new words. That is 90% coverage. You stop every few lines. The first post teaches you more.

Reading a lot of easy, interesting text is called extensive reading. You meet common words again and again in new sentences. Each meeting adds a little knowledge: a new partner, a new meaning, a new grammar pattern. Cards cannot give you all of this. Reading can.

What to do with an unknown word

  1. Keep reading to the end of the sentence. The meaning often becomes clear.
  2. Guess. What word class is it? What do the other words tell you?
  3. Use the dictionary only if the word is important or you meet it again.
  4. Save the whole sentence, not only the word. Mark the partner.
  5. Later, make a card from the saved sentence.

The chapter Reading skills shows how to guess words from context. The chapter Listening skills shows how to learn from podcasts and videos.

Balance your time

Paul Nation describes four strands of a good course. Each strand gets about a quarter of your time.

The four strands, for vocabulary
StrandWhat you doExample
Meaning-focused inputRead and listen for meaningAn easy tech blog, a podcast
Meaning-focused outputSpeak and write to share ideasA pull request description, a stand-up
Language-focused learningStudy words on purposeWord cards, word families
Fluency developmentUse known words fasterRead an easy text quickly, timed talk

Many engineers only read hard documentation. Every page has 30 unknown words. They look up each word and forget it the next day. Mix in easy texts. Easy reading builds speed and makes common words automatic.

Expert view: build your own word system

Think of your vocabulary like a small software pipeline. Words come in. A filter decides what to keep. A scheduler brings words back. Use turns them into active words.

The filter: three questions

  • Is the word frequent? Check the Oxford 3000 or 5000, or the AWL.
  • Did I meet it two or more times this month?
  • Will I need to say or write it at work?

Two "yes" answers: make a gap card. One "yes": make a recognition card or let it go. Rare words come back if they matter.

How a modern scheduler thinks

FSRS gives each card a stability. Stability is the number of days until your chance of remembering falls to 90%. The short script below uses the forgetting curve from FSRS version 4.5. Newer versions change the details, but the idea is the same.

# FSRS-4.5 forgetting curve (from the FSRS wiki)
DECAY = -0.5
FACTOR = 19 / 81

def recall(days, stability):
    # chance (0 to 1) that you still remember the word
    return (1 + FACTOR * days / stability) ** DECAY

stability = 10  # this card is "stable" for 10 days
for days in [1, 5, 10, 20, 40]:
    print(f"day {days:>2}: {recall(days, stability):.0%}")
day  1: 99%
day  5: 95%
day 10: 90%
day 20: 83%
day 40: 72%

On day 10 the chance is exactly 90%. That is why a 90% desired retention sends the card back after about one stability period. Each good review raises the stability, so the next gap grows.

You can measure your size with a free online vocabulary size test. Treat the result as a rough number, plus or minus a few hundred words. Measure again after six months. Growth matters more than the exact number.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for growing your vocabulary
PatternPurposeModelNote
What does X mean?Ask for a meaningWhat does "mitigate" mean?Not "What means mitigate?"
What do you call X?Find a missing wordWhat do you call the slow part of a system?Answer: a bottleneck. Use "call", not "say".
What's the difference between X and Y?Compare two close wordsWhat's the difference between "lend" and "borrow"?Use "between", not "among", for two words.
Is X formal or informal?Check the styleIs "mitigate" formal?Formal words are fine in writing. In speech they can sound stiff.
I came across X in ...Say where you met a wordI came across "idempotent" in the API docs."Came across" means met by chance.
un-, in-, dis- + adjectiveMake the oppositeclear, unclear. valid, invalid.Check which prefix the word takes. Not "unvalid".
Verb + -ment or -tionMake a noun from a verbdeploy, deployment. create, creation.Stress the syllable before -tion: inforMAtion.
Adjective + -ity or -nessMake a noun from an adjectivesecure, security. aware, awareness.After "more", check: noun or adjective?
Verb + noun collocationUse the right partnermake a decision. fix a bug.Not "do a decision". Learn the pair.
Day 1, 3, 7, 16, 35Plan reviewsReview "mitigate" on day 1, then day 3.A rule of thumb. Apps adjust it for each card.
Sentence with a gapMake a cloze cardWe added rate limits to ___ the attack.Use your own true sentence.

Practice

Quick quiz

You understand "throughput" in a report, but you never say it. For you, "throughput" is...

  • a passive word
  • an active word
  • a collocation

You understand it but cannot use it yet. That is passive, or receptive, vocabulary.

Which group is one lemma?

  • test, tests, tested, testing
  • test, tester, testable, retest
  • test, exam, quiz, check

A lemma is a base word with its grammar endings. The second group is a word family. The third group is synonyms.

You know 95 words in a text of 100 words. What is your coverage?

  • 98%, one unknown word in 50
  • 95%, one unknown word in 20
  • 90%, one unknown word in 10

5 unknown words in 100 is 1 in 20.

Which collocation is correct?

  • do a decision
  • strong rain
  • raise an issue

English says make a decision and heavy rain. Raise an issue is correct.

Which card type best moves a word into your active vocabulary?

  • English word on the front, translation on the back
  • Your own sentence with a gap
  • A list of 20 words on one card

A gap card makes you produce the word with its partner and grammar.

Choose the right family member

The service is not very (depend). It fails every week.

We need more (secure) for the login page.

The (deploy) took ten minutes.

This password is (valid, opposite). Try again.

Please (simple, verb) this function. It is too long.

The two teams work (depend, adverb).

Think and write

  1. Write the word family for create: a noun for the thing, a noun for the person, an adjective and an adverb.
    Answer

    creation (thing), creator (person), creative (adjective), creatively (adverb). Also creativity (noun for the skill).

  2. Fix the collocations: "I did a mistake in the config. Can you make a check before we make the deploy?"
    Answer

    I made a mistake in the config. Can you do a check (or check it) before we deploy? "Make the deploy" is wrong. Use the verb "deploy", or "do the deployment".

  3. Make a five-step word card for bottleneck.
    Answer

    1. bottleneck, /ˈbɒtlnek/, BOT-tle-neck, noun. 2. The slow part that limits the whole system. 3. a performance bottleneck, find the bottleneck, remove a bottleneck. 4. "The database was the bottleneck in our checkout flow." 5. Family: none common. Style: neutral, used in speech and writing.

  4. You learn a new word today. Using the starter schedule, on which days do you review it in the first month?
    Answer

    Day 1, day 3, day 7 and about day 16. The next review is about day 35, so it falls in the second month.

  5. An article has 400 words. You do not know 20 of them. What is your coverage? Is this a good text for extensive reading?
    Answer

    380 of 400 is 95%. It is possible, but it is work. For extensive reading, choose easier texts, close to 98%: about 8 unknown words in 400.

  6. Write a production card and a gap card for deprecate (to mark a feature as old, so people stop using it).
    Answer

    Production: Front: "to mark an old feature so people stop using it (verb, starts with d)". Back: "deprecate. This function is deprecated." Gap: Front: "Version 3 will ______ the old login API." Back: "deprecate".

  7. Expert. Your friend says: "C2 means 5,000 words." Explain what is wrong with this sentence.
    Answer

    The 4,500 to 5,000 figure is an estimate from one study. The X-Lex test only checks the 5,000 most common words, so it cannot count higher. Real C2 users know many more words in total. Also, studies count lemmas or word families in different ways.

  8. Expert. With the FSRS-4.5 curve, a card has a stability of 10 days. Why does a desired retention of 90% give a gap of about 10 days?
    Answer

    Stability is defined as the time until recall falls to 90%. So the chance of recall reaches 90% on day 10. A 90% target therefore schedules the review at about day 10. A higher target, like 95%, gives a shorter gap.

re- (redeploy, rewrite)

again

mis- (misread, misconfigure)

wrongly

sub- (subfolder, subtask)

under, or a smaller part

-less (stateless, useless)

without. It makes an adjective.

-able (scalable, readable)

can be done. It makes an adjective.

-ment (deployment, requirement)

It makes a noun from a verb.

Key takeaways

  • Passive words you understand. Active words you can use. Move words from passive to active on purpose.
  • Knowing a word means form, meaning and use, not only a translation.
  • Vocabulary sizes per CEFR level are estimates. One study gives about 2,750 to 3,250 common words for B1 and 3,250 to 3,750 for B2.
  • Learn word families. Prefixes change the meaning. Suffixes change the word class.
  • High-frequency words first, then academic words like the AWL, then your technical words.
  • Learn words with their partners. Collocations and chunks make you sound natural.
  • Spread reviews over growing gaps, and test yourself before you look.
  • Use a five-step card and gap cards. Read a lot of easy text, too.

Sources

  • Milton and Alexiou: Developing a vocabulary size test (GALA). Contains the table of vocabulary size and CEFR levels from their 2009 study.
  • Paul Nation (2006): How large a vocabulary is needed for reading and listening?. The 98% coverage target and the 8,000 to 9,000 word family estimate.
  • Schmitt and others (2015): How much vocabulary is needed to use English?. A replication study, with the 95% listening finding.
  • EAP Foundation: The Academic Word List. The 570 families, the sublists and the coverage figures.
  • Cepeda and others (2008): Spacing effects in learning. How the best review gap depends on how long you want to remember.
  • Anki Manual: Deck options. FSRS, desired retention and the legacy SM-2 scheduler.

Pronunciation and fluency

People understand you because of stress, rhythm and melody, not only because of single sounds. This chapter goes beyond single words. It shows how English sounds in real sentences and how to practise for ten minutes a day.

  • Place word stress with suffix rules, phrasal verbs, numbers and short forms.
  • Stress the right words in a sentence and keep an English rhythm.
  • Use weak forms, linking and other features of fast speech.
  • Choose a falling or rising tone for questions, tags and lists.
  • Practise with minimal pairs and shadowing in a daily 10-minute plan.

Word stress: the next level

Say these words: deVELop, deVELoper, deVELopment. The stress stays on the same syllable. Now say comPUTE, compuTAtion. The stress moves. Why?

The chapter Sounds and spelling gives the basics: syllables, the stress mark ˈ and five stress tendencies. This section adds the rules for longer words. The key is the suffix. Some suffixes leave the stress alone. Others pull it to a new place.

How suffixes act on word stress
GroupSuffixesExamples
Leave the stress alone-ment, -er, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly, -ing, -ed, usually -ableemPLOY, emPLOYment, emPLOYer. HAPpy, HAPpiness.
Stress the syllable just before-tion, -sion, -ic, -ical, -ity, -ian, -ial, -ious, -logy, -graphytechNOLogy, phoTOGraphy, techNIcian, esSENtial, inDUStrial
Stress the third syllable from the end-ate, -ise or -ize, -ify (in longer words)comMUnicate, OPtimise, CUStomise, iDENtify
Take the stress themselves-ee, -eer, -ese, -iquetrainEE, engiNEER, JapaNESE, techNIQUE

Three more groups for work English

Phrasal verb or noun? A phrasal verb stresses the small word at the end. The noun made from it stresses the first part.

Phrasal verb stress and noun stress
Verb (stress the end)Noun (stress the start)
Please log IN.Your LOGin failed.
Let's set UP the server.The SETup takes ten minutes.
Back UP the database.We have a daily BACKup.
We need to roll BACK.The ROLLback worked.

Numbers. The -teen numbers stress the end: thirTEEN, fourTEEN, fifTEEN. The -ty numbers stress the start: THIRty, FORty, FIFty. Make the difference clear. A wrong price or time can cost money.

Letters. Short forms said letter by letter stress the last letter: A-P-I, U-R-L, S-Q-L, H-T-M-L. Short forms said as one word follow normal rules: JSON, NASA.

Compound adjectives often stress the second part: well-KNOWN, user-FRIENDly, hard-WORKing. But before a noun the stress often moves forward: "a WELL-known tool". English does this to keep two strong beats apart.

Many learners put the stress where it is in their own language, or on the first syllable of every word. Then develOPment or DEvelopment sounds strange. Remember: -ment never moves the stress. So development keeps the stress of develop: deVELopment.

Sentence stress and rhythm

Read this message aloud. Say the capital words strongly.

I NEED to FINish the REport by FRIday.

The strong words carry the message. If you only hear "NEED, FINish, REport, FRIday", you still understand. The small words, like "to", "the" and "by", only join the big words.

Words that carry meaning are content words. They are usually stressed. Words that build grammar are function words. They are usually weak.

Usually stressed and usually weak
Usually stressedUsually weak
Nouns: server, report, FridayArticles: a, an, the
Main verbs: finish, deployHelping verbs: is, are, was, have, can
Adjectives: slow, readyPrepositions: to, for, of, at, from
Adverbs: quickly, neverPronouns: I, you, it, them
Negatives and question words: not, can't, where, whyJoining words: and, but, that

The beat of English

English likes a regular beat on stressed syllables. The weak syllables between beats get shorter and faster. Look at the picture.

Teachers call this a stress-timed rhythm. Researchers say the timing is not exact. Still, the tendency is real, and it is why weak forms exist. Many languages give every syllable about the same length. Speakers of those languages often sound "flat" or "too careful" in English.

Moving the stress to change the meaning

You can stress any word to show focus. The words are the same, but the message changes.

One sentence, four meanings
You sayYou mean
ANA sent the report on Monday.Ana did it, not Ben.
Ana SENT the report on Monday.She sent it. She did not only write it.
Ana sent the REport on Monday.The report, not the slides.
Ana sent the report on MONday.Monday, not Tuesday.

With no special focus, the main stress goes on the last content word: "I work in a BANK." When a word is old information, the stress moves away from it: "Did you fix the bug?" "I FOUND the bug. I haven't FIXED it yet."

Do not stress every word. "I. NEED. TO. FIN-ISH. THE. RE-PORT." sounds angry or robotic. Listeners cannot find the important words. Make content words strong and let the rest go weak.

Weak forms and the schwa

Listen to a friend order a drink: "a cup of tea". You hear /ə kʌp əv tiː/. The words "a" and "of" are tiny. They both use the sound /ə/, the schwa. In fast speech "of" can even become just /ə/: "a cuppa tea".

Many function words have two pronunciations. The strong form is the full sound. The weak form is short and usually has schwa. In normal speech, you use the weak form most of the time.

Common weak forms in British English
WordStrongWeakExample
a, an/eɪ/, /æn//ə/, /ən/a bug, an error
the/ðiː//ðə/, /ði/ before a vowelthe code, the API
and, but/ænd/, /bʌt//ən/ or /n/, /bət/fish and chips
to, for, of/tuː/, /fɔː/, /ɒv//tə/, /fə/, /əv/time to go, one of them
at, from/æt/, /frɒm//ət/, /frəm/at home, from Osaka
can, could/kæn/, /kʊd//kən/, /kəd/I can help.
was, were/wɒz/, /wɜː//wəz/, /wə/It was late.
have, has/hæv/, /hæz//əv/, /əz/They've gone. It has failed.
do, does/duː/, /dʌz//də/, /dəz/What do you think?
you, them, us/juː/, /ðem/, /ʌs//jə/, /ðəm/, /əs/Tell them. Call us.
than, that/ðæn/, /ðæt//ðən/, /ðət/faster than before. I think that it works.

When to use the strong form

  • At the end of a sentence, for prepositions and helping verbs: "Where are you from?" /frɒm/. "Yes, I can." /kæn/.
  • For contrast or emphasis: "It's not for you. It's from you."
  • When you say the word alone, as a word: "The word 'the' is an article."

I can come. /aɪ kən ˈkʌm/

Weak vowel. The stress is on come.

I can't come. /aɪ ˈkɑːnt ˈkʌm/

Full long vowel and stress. Can't has no weak form.

This pair matters a lot. Listeners often miss the final t of "can't". They hear the difference in the vowel and the stress. So make "can" weak and "can't" strong.

Weak forms cause a famous writing mistake. "Could have" and "could of" both sound like /kʊd əv/. So people write "I could of finished". The correct form is could have, or could've.

Linking and connected speech

What are you going to do?

Do you want to get a coffee?

I don't know.

Whatcha gonna do? /ˈwɒtʃə ˈɡʌnə ˈduː/

D'you wanna get a coffee?

I dunno.

In real speech, words do not stand alone. They join, change and lose sounds. This is called connected speech. You do not need to speak this fast. But you must understand it, and a little linking makes you sound smooth.

Linking

Consonant to vowel. A final consonant moves to the next word when it starts with a vowel. "Check it out" sounds like "che-ki-tout". "Turn it off" sounds like "tur-ni-toff".

Vowel to vowel. English adds a small glide. After /iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/ or /ɔɪ/, you hear a light y: "I agree" /aɪ jəˈɡriː/, "the end" /ði jend/. After /uː/, /əʊ/ or /aʊ/, you hear a light w: "go on" /ɡəʊ wɒn/, "do it" /duː wɪt/.

Linking r. In British English, a final r is silent: "far" is /fɑː/. But before a vowel the r comes back: "far away" /fɑːr əˈweɪ/, "for example" /fər ɪɡˈzɑːmpl/. Many speakers even add an r where there is no letter: "the idea of it" /ði aɪˈdɪər əv ɪt/. You need to recognise this extra r. You do not need to copy it.

Lost sounds

When /t/ or /d/ is between two consonants, speakers often drop it. This is called elision. "Next week" sounds like "neks week". "Last time" sounds like "las time". The /h/ in weak he, him, her and his often disappears too: "tell him" sounds like "tellim".

Changed sounds

A sound can change to become more like the next sound. This is called assimilation.

  • /n/ becomes /m/ before /p/, /b/ or /m/: "ten people" /tem ˈpiːpl/.
  • /t/ + /j/ becomes /tʃ/: "meet you" /ˈmiːtʃuː/, "don't you" /ˈdəʊntʃuː/.
  • /d/ + /j/ becomes /dʒ/: "did you" /ˈdɪdʒuː/, "would you" /ˈwʊdʒuː/.

Start with two habits only. Link consonants to vowels. Use weak forms for a, the, to, of, and and can. These two habits change your rhythm more than anything else.

Do not write "gonna", "wanna" or "dunno" in emails or reports. They show how people speak. In writing use "going to", "want to" and "don't know".

Intonation in questions and lists

Say "Really." as a fact, with your voice going down. Now say "Really?" with surprise, with your voice going up. Same word, different message. The melody of your voice is called intonation.

Common tone choices
TypeToneExample
StatementFallThe build is green. ↘
Wh- questionFallWhen is the release? ↘
Yes or no questionUsually riseIs it ready? ↗
ListRise on each item, fall on the lastTests ↗, docs ↗ and a demo ↘.
Choice questionRise, then fallTea ↗ or coffee ↘? (choose one)
Open offerRise at the endTea or coffee ↗? (any drink?)

Question tags

A question tag can fall or rise. The tone shows how sure you are.

  • "It's ready, isn't it? ↘" You are almost sure. You want agreement.
  • "It's ready, isn't it? ↗" You are not sure. It is a real question.

The fall-rise: "but..."

A fall and then a rise on one word means "there is more" or "but". "The code is fine ↘↗" suggests "...but the tests are not". This tone is common in polite disagreement.

A flat voice can sound bored or rude in English, even when your words are polite. "Could you check this" with no movement can sound like an order. Let your voice move on the main stressed word.

The phonetician John Wells describes English intonation as three choices. Tonality: where you split speech into chunks. Tonicity: which syllable gets the main stress. Tone: fall, rise or fall-rise on that syllable. These are tendencies, not strict laws. Real speakers vary.

Minimal pairs: hear and say the difference

I found a bag in the code.

Ana meant "bug" /bʌɡ/. She said "bag" /bæɡ/. One sound changed, and the meaning changed. Two words that differ in only one sound are a minimal pair. They show you which sounds you must keep apart.

Minimal pairs that cause problems for many learners
SoundsPairsTip
/ɪ/ and /iː/ship, sheep. fill, feel. list, least./iː/ is long, with a smile.
/æ/ and /ʌ/bag, bug. cap, cup. match, much./æ/: open your mouth wide.
/e/ and /æ/pen, pan. men, man. said, sad./æ/ is lower and longer.
/ɜː/ and /ɔː/work, walk. bird, board./ɜː/: lips relaxed, not round.
/ʊ/ and /uː/full, fool. pull, pool./uː/ is long, with round lips.
/l/ and /r/light, right. load, road. collect, correct./l/: tongue touches the top. /r/: it does not.
/b/ and /v/base, vase. best, vest./v/: top teeth on the bottom lip.
/θ/ and /s/think, sink. path, pass./θ/: tongue between the teeth.
/s/ and /ʃ/seat, sheet. save, shave. sort, short./ʃ/: round lips, tongue back.

How to practise a pair

  1. Listen. Find a recording of the two words, in a learner dictionary. Hear the difference.
  2. Test your ear. Ask a friend or a recording to say one word at random. Choose which one.
  3. Say each word slowly. Watch your mouth in a mirror. Use the tip in the table.
  4. Put the words in sentences: "I found a bug. I left my bag."
  5. Check yourself with your phone's voice typing. Say the word. See which word it writes.

Voice typing is forgiving. It guesses from the whole sentence. So say single words for the test, and do not trust it fully. A human listener is better.

A vowel is longer before a voiced consonant. The vowel in bed is longer than in bet. The vowel in cab is longer than in cap. Listeners use this length to hear the last sound. So if your final /d/ is weak, a longer vowel still helps them hear "bed".

Fluency and the shadowing method

Ben knows a lot of English. But he speaks like this: "I... think... we... should... er... restart... the... the server." Every word is correct. Still, listening to him is tiring. Ben has a fluency problem, not a grammar problem.

Researchers often split fluency into three parts.

  • Speed: how many words or syllables per minute.
  • Pauses: how often you stop, and where.
  • Repairs: how often you repeat or correct yourself.

Where you pause matters more than how often. Pause between chunks: "I think | we should restart the server | before lunch." Do not pause inside a chunk: "we should re- | start the". Learn phrases as chunks, and they come out in one breath.

What is shadowing?

In shadowing, you play a recording and speak along with it. You stay just behind the speaker, like a shadow behind a person. This is different from repetition. In repetition, you wait for the speaker to stop, then you speak.

The researcher Yo Hamada explains why it works. While you shadow, almost all your attention goes to sounds. You copy stress, linking and melody without thinking about meaning. Research reports gains in listening for students, and gains in pronunciation and fluency for advanced learners.

  1. Choose 1 to 2 minutes of clear speech with a transcript. A short talk or a podcast clip is good.
  2. Listen two or three times. Understand the content first. Read the transcript and check new words.
  3. Mark the transcript. Underline stressed words. Draw links between words. Mark ↗ and ↘.
  4. Mumble. Shadow quietly without the transcript. Only follow the rhythm.
  5. Shadow clearly. Copy the stress, the linking and the melody.
  6. Record yourself with your phone. Compare it with the original. Choose one thing to fix.
  7. Stop after five or six rounds with one clip. Then choose a new clip.

Hamada advises short, intense periods. He reports clear change from two 10 to 15 minute sessions a week for about a month. Shadow without the text when you can. Reading while shadowing turns it into a different task.

Do not shadow clips that are too hard. If you cannot catch the sounds, shadowing turns into noise. First use it to train your ear. When you can catch most sounds, use it to train your mouth.

A daily 10-minute plan

Ten minutes every day work better than one hour on Sunday. Follow the five steps on the slides. Use a timer.

Warm up with a minimal pair

Choose one pair from the table, for example bag and bug. Say each word five times. Then say five sentences with both.

Stress three new words

Take three new words from your work this week. Check the stress mark in a dictionary. Say each word in a short sentence.

Shadow one clip

Shadow your 1-minute clip two times. Copy the beat of the stressed words. Link consonants to vowels.

Record yourself

Read the same transcript aloud once, alone. Record it with your phone.

Compare and note

Listen to the original, then to yourself. Write one thing to fix tomorrow, for example "weak to and of".

One focus for each day of the week
DayFocusExample task
MondayWord stressStress five suffix words: technology, communicate, deployment
TuesdaySentence stressMark the content words in your stand-up notes
WednesdayWeak formsSay ten phrases with to, of, and, can
ThursdayLinkingLink "check it out", "turn it off", "log in again"
FridayIntonationRead three lists and three question tags aloud
SaturdayMinimal pairsTest yourself on your two hardest pairs
SundayReviewCompare this week's recording with last week's

Self-recording also helps your speaking. The chapter Speaking skills shows a full method. The chapter Listening skills shows how to choose good clips.

Expert view: clear, not native

Do you need a British or an American accent? No. Researchers separate three ideas.

  • Accent: how different your speech sounds from a local speaker.
  • Intelligibility: how much a listener actually understands.
  • Comprehensibility: how much effort the listener needs.

In 1995, Murray Munro and Tracey Derwing showed that these are not the same. A speaker with a strong accent can be fully intelligible. They also found that problems with intonation were more closely linked to listener effort than other features. So melody and stress deserve your time.

What matters most for international listeners?

Many English conversations at work are between non-native speakers. In 2000, Jennifer Jenkins proposed a Lingua Franca Core. It lists the features that matter most when non-native speakers talk to each other.

Core: work on these

  • Most consonant sounds
  • A puff of air after p, t, k at the start of a word
  • Not dropping consonants at the start of a word
  • Long and short vowels (ship and sheep)
  • The main stress in each chunk

Less important for being understood

  • The th sounds
  • The exact vowel quality
  • Weak forms
  • Some features of connected speech

This list is still debated. For example, some researchers argue that word stress also belongs in the core. And if you want to understand native speakers, you still need to know weak forms and connected speech.

IELTS Speaking has a Pronunciation criterion. The public band descriptors say that at band 8, accent has minimal effect on intelligibility. At band 9, accent has no effect on it. They also talk about chunking, rhythm, stress and intonation. See IELTS Speaking.

A good plan for an engineer: first fix the sounds that change meaning, like bug and bag. Then fix word stress for your work words. Then work on sentence stress and intonation. Polish weak forms and linking last.

Practice

Quick quiz

Where is the stress in employment?

  • EMployment
  • emPLOYment
  • employMENT

-ment does not move the stress. Employ has stress on PLOY, so employment does too.

Where is the stress in technology?

  • TECHnology
  • techNOLogy
  • technoLOgy

-logy stresses the syllable just before it.

"The SETup is easy." Here "setup" is...

  • a noun
  • a phrasal verb

The noun stresses the first part. The verb is "set UP".

Which sentence means "not Ben"?

  • ANA sent the report.
  • Ana SENT the report.
  • Ana sent the REport.

Stress shows focus. Stress on ANA contrasts her with another person.

"You're coming to the meeting, aren't you? ↘" The speaker is...

  • almost sure and wants agreement
  • not sure and asks a real question

A falling tag checks something you believe. A rising tag asks.

Which pair is a minimal pair?

  • work and walk
  • work and worked
  • walk and talk and chalk

Work /wɜːk/ and walk /wɔːk/ differ in one sound only.

Fill in the stress or the sound

The verb "log in" has the main stress on the word ?.

The noun "a backup" has the main stress on ?.

"Investigate" has the stress on syllable number ?.

The number 15 has the stress on the syllable ?.

Write the correct form: "I could (of / have) finished earlier."

Think and say

  1. Mark the content words with capitals: "We need to fix the login bug before the demo on Thursday."
    Answer

    We NEED to FIX the LOGin BUG before the DEmo on THURSday. The main stress is on the last content word, THURSday.

  2. Say how the words in bold sound in fast speech: "Did you see the email? I want to ask her about it."
    Answer

    "Did you" often sounds like /ˈdɪdʒuː/. "want to" can be /ˈwɒnə/ or /ˈwɒntə/. "ask her" loses the h: /ˈɑːsk ə/. "about it" links and sounds like "abou-tit".

  3. Mark the tones for this list and question: "We need a laptop, a monitor and a keyboard. Do you have them?"
    Answer

    laptop ↗, monitor ↗, keyboard ↘. "Do you have them?" usually ↗, because it is a yes or no question.

  4. Your colleague hears "thirty" when you say "thirteen". Give two things you can do.
    Answer

    Stress the end strongly and make it long: thir-TEEN. Then confirm: "thirteen, one three". In writing, add the digits: 13.

  5. Plan a 10-minute session for a learner who says "sink" for "think" and stresses "development" on the first syllable.
    Answer

    Minutes 0 to 2: the pair think and sink, tongue between the teeth. Minutes 2 to 4: develop, developer, development, all with stress on VEL. Minutes 4 to 8: shadow a clip about software. Minutes 8 to 10: record and compare, with focus on th.

  6. Explain the difference between shadowing and repetition in two sentences.
    Answer

    In shadowing you speak at the same time as the recording, just behind it. In repetition you wait until the speaker stops, then you say the words.

  7. Expert. A learner says: "I must remove my accent to be understood." Answer with research.
    Answer

    Munro and Derwing (1995) showed that accent and intelligibility are different. A strong accent can still be fully intelligible. Focus on sounds that change meaning, word stress and intonation. The IELTS band descriptors also talk about intelligibility, not about a native accent.

  8. Expert. Why might a teacher of international engineers spend little time on the th sounds?
    Answer

    In Jenkins's Lingua Franca Core, th sounds are not core. Replacing them rarely stops understanding between non-native speakers. Other features, like vowel length and the main stress in a chunk, matter more. The idea is debated, so th is still useful for listening to native speakers.

Stress: photography

phoTOGraphy. -graphy stresses the syllable before it.

Stress: communicate

comMUnicate. -ate: third syllable from the end.

Weak form of "for" in "a gift for you"

/fə/

Fast speech: "would you"

/ˈwʊdʒuː/: d + you becomes "ju".

Stress: API

A-P-I, with stress on the last letter.

Tone: "Tea or coffee?" when you want one of the two

Tea ↗ or coffee ↘?

Key takeaways

  • Suffixes decide stress in long words. -ment keeps it. -tion, -ic and -logy pull it to the syllable before.
  • Phrasal verbs stress the small word. The matching noun stresses the first part.
  • Stress content words and keep a regular beat. Function words go weak.
  • Weak forms with schwa are normal. Use strong forms at the end, for contrast and alone.
  • Connected speech links, drops and changes sounds. Learn to hear it. Link consonants to vowels yourself.
  • Falls finish and show certainty. Rises ask and keep lists open.
  • Practise minimal pairs for sounds that change meaning. Shadow short clips five or six times.
  • The goal is clear speech, not a native accent. Ten minutes a day is enough to improve.

Sources

  • Yo Hamada (2018): Shadowing for language teaching. What shadowing is, how to use it, and the research on it.
  • David Deterding, NIE Singapore: Weak forms and reduced vowels. University course notes with strong and weak forms.
  • John Wells: English Intonation, chapter 1 (Cambridge University Press excerpt). Tonality, tonicity and tone: the three Ts.
  • Munro and Derwing: Foreign accent, comprehensibility and intelligibility, redux. The authors look back at their 1995 study.
  • McCrocklin (2011): The role of word stress in English as a lingua franca. The Lingua Franca Core and the debate about word stress.
  • IELTS Speaking band descriptors. The public Pronunciation descriptors for each band.

Listening skills

Listening is the skill you use most and practise least. You cannot stop a speaker, and spoken English has no spaces between words. This chapter gives you strategies for meetings, calls, podcasts and exams, and a practice method that really trains your ear.

  • Listen for the main idea first and for details second.
  • Predict content and use signpost words to follow a talk.
  • Take fast notes and catch numbers, names and spellings.
  • Understand the main accents of English better.
  • Train with dictation, transcription, podcasts and subtitles.

How listening works

Your manager says: "We'll have to push the release." You know every word. But you hear "we la to push"... and you miss it. Then you see the calendar change, and you understand. You used two kinds of help.

  • Bottom-up processing: you build meaning from the sounds. Sounds make words. Words make sentences.
  • Top-down processing: you use what you already know. The topic, the speaker and the situation help you guess.

Learners often depend too much on top-down guessing. They catch a few words and guess the rest. This works in easy situations. But it fails with new topics, numbers and names. So you need strategies for top-down listening, and training for bottom-up listening. This chapter gives you both.

Strategies help you understand today. Ear training helps you understand more next month. Do both.

Listening for gist and for detail

A colleague leaves you a one-minute voice message. Ask two different questions.

Gist question

Is it good news or bad news? Is the project on time?

Detail question

What is the new date? Which room? How many tests fail?

The gist is the main idea. When you listen for gist, you do not stop at unknown words. You follow the stressed words and the general direction. When you listen for detail, you wait for one exact fact. You know what you want, and you catch it.

Do not try to do both on the first listen. Use a plan with several listens. The steps below follow the ideas of the researchers Larry Vandergrift and Christine Goh. They teach learners to plan, check and review their own listening.

Plan and predict

Read the title and the questions. Write five words you expect to hear. Guess what the speaker wants.

Listen for gist

Do not write much. Check your guesses. Answer one question: what is the main message?

Find the gaps

Write what you understood. Mark the parts you missed. Decide what to focus on next.

Listen for detail

Focus on the parts you missed. Write numbers, names and key words.

Check with the transcript

Listen again with the transcript, if there is one. Find every place where you heard something different.

Reflect

Why did you miss those parts? A new word? A weak form? A fast speaker? Choose one thing to practise.

Many learners stop at the first unknown word. While they think about it, the speaker says three more sentences. Let the unknown word go. Keep following the stressed words. The meaning often comes back later.

Predicting before you listen

Look at this meeting invitation: "Q3 budget review. Agenda: cloud costs, new hires, travel." Before the meeting, you can already guess many words: cost, increase, reduce, headcount, approve, per month. When you hear them, your brain is ready.

Prediction is the strongest top-down strategy. Use every clue you have before you listen.

  • Topic: the title, the agenda, the slide.
  • Speakers: who they are, and what they usually say.
  • Questions: in an exam, read the questions first. They tell you what to listen for.
  • Grammar: a gap after "on" might be a day. A gap after "a" needs a noun that starts with a consonant sound.
  1. Read the gap: "Meeting room: ______ (floor 3)". You need a room name or number.
  2. Predict the form: maybe a number and a letter, like 3A or 305.
  3. Predict a trap: the speaker may say one room, then correct it.
  4. Listen and write. Then check the spelling and the word limit.

The recording rarely uses the exact words of the question. It uses a paraphrase. The question says "cheap". The speaker says "it doesn't cost much". So predict synonyms too. See IELTS Listening and Reading.

Signpost words

Listen to the start of a talk: "Today I want to cover three things. First, our costs. Then, the new tools. Finally, the plan for next year." These small phrases are like road signs. They tell you where the talk goes next.

A signpost word helps you follow the structure. Speakers often stress signposts and pause after them. So they are easy to catch, even when the rest is hard.

Signposts and what to do when you hear them
JobSignpostsWhat you do
Orderfirst of all, then, next, finallyNumber your notes.
Addingalso, in addition, another point isAdd an item at the same level.
Contrastbut, however, on the other handExpect the opposite idea.
Examplefor example, for instance, such asNote one example, not all.
Reason and resultbecause, so, as a result, that's whyDraw an arrow.
Important pointthe key point is, what really matters isPut a star in your notes.
New topicmoving on to, let's turn to, nowStart a new heading.
Correctionsorry, I mean; actually; no, waitChange what you wrote.
Summaryto sum up, so overall, in shortCheck your gist.

Do not write the first answer you hear and stop listening. Speakers often correct themselves: "The meeting is on Tuesday. Oh, actually, no. It's Wednesday." Exams use this trap a lot. Wait for the end of the idea.

The same signposts help you speak and present. See Linking words and Presentations and remote work.

Taking notes

You cannot write every word. People speak much faster than anyone can write by hand. So notes are not a copy. They are a short map of the ideas.

What to write

  • Content words only: nouns, verbs, numbers, names. Leave out "the", "is", "of".
  • Symbols and short forms instead of full words.
  • One idea per line. Indent the details under the main point.
  • Space. Leave empty lines to add things later.
Symbols and short forms for fast notes
WriteMeaningWriteMeaning
→leads to, causes, thenb/cbecause
↑ ↓increase, decreasew/ , w/owith, without
= , ≠is, is not the samee.g.for example
+ , −and, more; minus, lessapprox. or ~about
✓ , ✗done or yes; failed or noinfo, dept, mgrinformation, department, manager
?not sure, check later★important

The Cornell page

Walter Pauk, a professor at Cornell University, developed a popular page layout for notes. You divide the page into three areas.

Here are notes from a short team update. The full update is in the practice section.

1. Release: Thu → Mon (+2 working days)
   b/c 15 payment tests ✗
2. Room 3 closed (repairs) → book 5B
3. New designer starts Tue: Siobhan (spelling!)

Review your notes within a few minutes after the talk. Add the missing words while your memory is fresh. Mark every ? and ask about it.

Note-taking is a key skill in TOEFL iBT. See TOEFL iBT.

Numbers, names and spellings

A wrong number is worse than a missed word. "Fifty" and "fifteen" can change a price, a date or a server count. The basic rules for saying numbers, dates and money are in Everyday vocabulary. This section is about hearing them correctly.

Number traps in listening
TrapWhat you hearHow to check
-teen or -tythirTEEN or THIRtyListen for the stress and the long "teen". Ask: "One three or three zero?"
Zero"oh", "zero", "nought"British speakers often say "oh" in phone numbers: "oh two oh".
Double"double five", "triple seven"Write 55 and 777.
Years"twenty twenty-six", "two thousand and six"Both ways are common.
Decimals"three point five", "point two""Point" is the dot. 0.2 is often "point two" or "nought point two".
Prices"fourteen fifty"Usually £14.50, not 1,450. Check the context.
Big numbers"two point four million"Write 2.4m first, then the full number.

Names and spellings

Names are hard because you cannot predict them. Many names do not follow spelling rules either. The Irish name Siobhan sounds like "shi-VAWN". So always ask for the spelling of a new name.

Some letters sound alike, especially on a bad line: B, D, P, T and V. M and N. F and S. To avoid mistakes, many people use a spelling alphabet. The international one is often called the NATO alphabet.

The NATO spelling alphabet
A-GH-NO-UV-Z
Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, GolfHotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, NovemberOscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, UniformVictor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu

Ben: Can I have the booking code, please?

Desk: Yes, it's P M V 7 3.

Ben: Sorry, was that P for Papa or B for Bravo?

Desk: P for Papa. Then M for Mike, V for Victor, seven, three.

Ben: Great. Let me read it back: P, M, V, seven, three.

The official spellings are "Alfa" and "Juliett". They are spelled this way so that speakers of other languages say them correctly. In normal business calls, people also use simple words: "B for book, D for dog".

In IELTS Listening, names and numbers often come in Part 1, in a form. A spelling mistake makes the answer wrong. Write exactly what you hear, letter by letter, and check capital letters at the end.

Understanding accents

Say "water". A London speaker may say "waw-tuh". A New York speaker may say "wah-der". Both are standard English. The word is the same, but the sounds are different.

An accent is a way of pronouncing a language. Everyone has one. At work you hear many accents: British, American, Australian, Indian, and the accents of colleagues who learned English like you.

Five differences between British and American speech
FeatureExampleSouthern BritishGeneral American
r after a vowelcar, serverNot said: "cah", "ser-vuh"Said: "car", "ser-ver"
t between vowelswater, better, dataA clear tA quick d-like sound: "wadder", "bedder"
t at the end of a word, before a vowelget it, a lot ofOften a stop in the throat: "ge' i'"A quick d-like sound: "geddit", "a lodda"
Vowel in bath wordscan't, last, askLong "ah": "cahn't"Short /æ/, as in cat
Vowel in hot wordshot, stop, jobShort, round /ɒ/Open "ah": "haht"

These are tendencies. Accents vary inside every country. Scottish and Irish speakers say the r, like Americans. Many people in the north of England say "bath" with a short vowel, like Americans. Australian and New Zealand English drop the r after a vowel, like southern British English.

How to get used to a new accent

  1. Choose one accent for a week. Find three or four clips with clear speech.
  2. Watch with English captions first. Notice the sounds that surprise you.
  3. Watch again without captions. Then check the hard parts.
  4. Make a small list of "sound rules" for that accent, like "t sounds like d".

Research supports step 2. In 2009, Mitterer and McQueen tested Dutch students with unfamiliar Scottish and Australian English. Students who watched with English subtitles got better at the new accent. Students who watched with Dutch subtitles got worse at new parts. Subtitles in the language of the speech show you which words you hear. So your ear learns.

IELTS Listening uses a range of accents, including British, Australian, New Zealand and North American. You hear each recording once only. Practise with all of these accents before the test.

Do not train with only one accent, for example only American films. Then a British or Indian colleague sounds "unclear". It is not their speech. It is your training. Mix accents in your listening plan.

Dictation and transcription

A learner listened to this sentence and wrote what she heard.

I like to ask if you question about it.

I'd like to ask a few questions about it.

She knew every word in the real sentence. But "I'd" lost its d. And "ask a few" ran together into "as-ka-few". She heard the sounds, but put the word edges in the wrong places. This is a bottom-up problem. Strategies cannot fix it. Only ear training can.

Dictation is the best test for this. You write exactly what you hear. A transcript then shows you exactly where your ear failed.

A micro-dictation routine

  1. Choose 20 to 30 seconds of audio with a transcript.
  2. Play one sentence. Pause. Write every word.
  3. Replay the sentence up to three times. Fill the gaps.
  4. Compare with the transcript. Mark every difference.
  5. Sort each mistake: unknown word, weak form, linking, a lost sound, or speed.
  6. Shadow the hard sentences five or six times.

Most learners find a surprise in step 5. Many mistakes are not unknown words. They are known words in fast speech. The chapter Pronunciation and fluency explains weak forms and linking. Shadowing is also explained there.

A second method: rebuild the text

In a dictogloss, you hear a short text two times at normal speed. You write only key words. Then you rebuild the full text with correct grammar. This trains listening for meaning and your grammar at the same time.

In 1987, Anne Cutler and David Carter studied a large set of everyday British conversation. About 90% of the content words began with a strong syllable. So a good guess is: a strong syllable starts a new word. Native listeners use this trick without knowing it. Train your ear to hear strong syllables, and word edges become easier to find.

Podcasts and subtitles

You listen to a 40-minute tech podcast on the train. You understand the general idea. Is that useful practice? Yes, but only for one kind of listening.

  • Extensive listening: long, easy material for meaning and pleasure. It builds speed and vocabulary.
  • Intensive listening: short clips studied in detail, like dictation and shadowing. It trains the ear.

You need both. A good balance is long, easy podcasts every day, plus 10 minutes of intensive work on a short clip.

Choosing podcasts

  • Choose topics you love. Interest keeps you listening for months.
  • Choose your level. You should follow the main ideas without subtitles.
  • Choose shows with transcripts. Use them for intensive work.
  • Stay with one show or one speaker for a while. Teachers call this narrow listening. The voice and the words become familiar.

Using subtitles well

Text in the same language as the speech is often called captions. Text in your own language is a translation. In 2013, Montero Perez and colleagues combined the results of many studies. They found a large positive effect of captions on listening and on vocabulary learning.

Which subtitles, and when
OptionUse it forWatch out
Your own languageRelaxing, or very hard contentYour brain reads and stops listening.
English captionsLearning new words and new accentsDo not only read. Listen to the sounds.
No subtitlesTesting yourself, extensive listeningGo back to captions for parts you miss.

A good order is: watch a clip with English captions, then watch it again without them. Finally, check the hard parts with captions on.

Use speed controls carefully. For hard clips, 0.75x speed helps you catch sounds. Yo Hamada suggests another trick: shadow a clip at 1.5x, then play it at normal speed. The normal speed now feels slower.

Automatic captions on video sites are made by a computer. They often get names, numbers and technical words wrong. Trust human-made captions and official transcripts more.

A sample listening week
DayExtensive (20 to 40 min)Intensive (10 min)
MondayTech podcast episodeMicro-dictation: 30 seconds
TuesdaySame podcast, next episodeShadow two hard sentences
WednesdayA talk with a new accent, English captionsWrite five "sound rules" for the accent
ThursdayPodcast episodeNumbers and names: write every number you hear
FridayA recorded meeting or webinarCornell notes and a summary
WeekendA film or series with English captionsDictogloss of one short scene

Practice

Listen to the update

Read this team update aloud, or ask a friend or a text-to-speech app to read it. Then answer the questions.

Maya: Hi everyone. A quick update before the weekend. First of all, the release. We planned it for Thursday, but we need two more working days. So the new date is Monday. The main reason is the payment tests. Fifteen of them still fail.

Maya: Moving on to the office. From next week, the meeting room on floor three is closed for repairs. Please book room 5B instead. That's five, B for Bravo.

Maya: Oh, and one more thing. Our new designer starts on Tuesday. Her name is Siobhan. That's S, I, O, B, H, A, N. To sum up: the release is on Monday, use room 5B, and say hello to Siobhan.

Gist: what is the main purpose of the update?

  • To give three pieces of team news
  • To explain how the payment tests work
  • To book a meeting room for Monday

The update covers the release, the room and the new designer. The summary at the end confirms it.

Detail: how many payment tests still fail?

  • 15
  • 50
  • 5

She says "fifteen". Listen for the stressed "teen".

Which signpost starts a new topic?

  • First of all
  • Moving on to
  • To sum up

"Moving on to" changes the topic. "First of all" starts a list. "To sum up" gives a summary.

The new release day is ?.

The new meeting room is ?.

The new designer's name is spelled ?.

Quick quiz

You use the topic and the situation to guess the meaning. This is...

  • top-down processing
  • bottom-up processing

Top-down help comes from what you already know. Bottom-up help comes from the sounds.
