A speaker says "The deadline is the 3rd. Sorry, I mean the 13th." What do you write?

  • 3rd
  • 13th
  • both

"Sorry, I mean" is a correction signpost. The last version is the answer.

According to Mitterer and McQueen (2009), which subtitles helped students learn a new English accent?

  • English subtitles
  • Subtitles in their own language
  • No subtitles at all

English subtitles helped. Subtitles in Dutch, the students' own language, made them worse at new parts.

Think and write

  1. Write notes for this sentence with symbols: "Costs went up by about ten percent because of the new servers, but they will go down next year."
    Answer

    Costs ↑ ~10% b/c new servers. Next yr ↓. (Many good answers are possible. Keep content words and symbols.)

  2. Before a call about a laptop repair, predict six words or phrases you may hear.
    Answer

    Possible answers: serial number, warranty, screen, battery, replace, cost, collection date, back up your data, a few days.

  3. A learner wrote "We need to test it more." The speaker said "We needed to test it more." What happened, and why?
    Answer

    She missed the -ed. In "needed to", the /ɪd/ is short and joins the weak "to". It is a bottom-up problem with fast speech, not with vocabulary.

  4. Write how you would check this booking code on a bad phone line: B D 9 9 T.
    Answer

    "Let me read it back: B for Bravo, D for Delta, double nine, T for Tango." You can also say "nine, nine" instead of "double nine".

  5. Your friend watches series with subtitles in her own language every night, but her listening does not improve. Give her a plan in three steps.
    Answer

    1. Switch to English captions for learning. 2. Rewatch short scenes without captions. 3. Add 10 minutes of micro-dictation or shadowing on one hard scene. Keep own-language subtitles only for relaxing.

  6. Expert. Why does a strong syllable help you find the start of a word in English?
    Answer

    Cutler and Carter (1987) found that about 90% of content words in everyday British conversation begin with a strong syllable. So guessing "a new word starts at a strong syllable" is usually right. Weak syllables are usually function words or word endings.

  7. Expert. Design a 20-minute session to get used to Scottish English for a work call next week.
    Answer

    Minutes 0 to 8: watch a clear Scottish speaker with English captions, and note surprising sounds, for example a strong r. Minutes 8 to 13: rewatch one minute without captions. Minutes 13 to 18: micro-dictation of three sentences, then compare with the captions. Minutes 18 to 20: write your sound rules and two phrases to check meaning on the call.

"On the other hand..."

A contrast. Expect the opposite idea.

"Moving on to..."

A new topic. Start a new heading in your notes.

"The key point is..."

The most important idea. Put a star next to it.

"As a result..."

A result. Draw an arrow →.

"Actually, no..."

A correction. Change what you wrote.

"To sum up..."

A summary. Check your gist.

Key takeaways

  • Good listeners use bottom-up help from sounds and top-down help from what they know.
  • Listen for gist first and details second. Plan several listens.
  • Predict words, types of answer and paraphrases before you listen.
  • Signposts show the structure. Corrections like "actually, no" change the answer.
  • Notes are a map, not a copy. Use content words, symbols and a Cornell page.
  • Check numbers, names and codes. Read them back and use a spelling alphabet.
  • Accents differ in a few regular ways. English captions help you adapt.
  • Dictation shows where your ear fails. Mix extensive and intensive listening every week.

Sources

  • TESL Canada Journal: review of Vandergrift and Goh, Teaching and Learning Second Language Listening. The metacognitive approach: planning, monitoring, problem-solving, evaluation.
  • Mitterer and McQueen (2009): Foreign subtitles help but native-language subtitles harm foreign speech perception. The study with Scottish and Australian English.
  • Yo Hamada (2018): Shadowing for language teaching. Bottom-up and top-down listening, shadowing and speed tips.
  • IELTS Academic format: Listening. The four parts, one listen only and the range of accents.
  • Cornell University Learning Strategies Center: The Cornell note-taking system. The note system developed by Walter Pauk.
  • Cutler and Carter (1987): The predominance of strong initial syllables in the English vocabulary. Strong syllables and word edges.

Speaking skills

Good speaking is more than good grammar. It is a set of small skills. You give a full answer, buy time, agree, ask, interrupt and tell a story. This chapter teaches these skills for daily life and for work first. Exams come second.

  • Give full answers with the frame answer + reason + example.
  • Buy time, ask for clarification and interrupt without sounding rude.
  • Agree and disagree at the right strength for the situation.
  • Tell a story with past tenses and describe a picture or a process.
  • Make small talk and improve every week with self-recording.

Give a full answer: answer + reason + example

A colleague asks you a simple question at lunch. Read three possible answers.

Sara: Do you like working from home?

Yes.

Well, two years ago my company changed its rules. At first we had three office days. Then my manager left, and the new manager had different ideas. And my flat is quite small, and my partner also works...

Yes, I do. Mainly because I save an hour of travel every day. For example, yesterday I used that hour for a run. How about you?

The short answer stops the talk. Sara must think of a new question. The long answer never says yes or no. The third answer works. It has three parts, and then it passes the turn back to Sara.

The three parts of a full answer
PartIts jobStarters
AnswerSay yes, no or your choice. One short sentence.Yes, I do. / Not really. / I'd choose the train.
ReasonSay why. One main reason is enough.Mainly because ... / The main reason is ... / It's ...
ExampleMake it real with one detail.For example, ... / Last week, ... / Once, ...

This simple shape is a frame. It works for almost any question about you. It also helps you think. You do not need to plan the whole answer. You only need the next part.

At work: answer first

In meetings, people want the answer before the story. Look at this short exchange.

Lead: Can we release on Friday?

Dev: No, not on Friday. Two payment tests are still failing. For example, one failed twice this morning. So Monday is more realistic.

The developer says the answer, the reason and an example. Then he says the answer again as a plan. Some speaking trainers call this shape PREP: point, reason, example, point. Use it for status updates, decisions and opinions.

How long should an answer be?

  • Small talk: two to four sentences. Then pass the turn back.
  • A question in a meeting: three to five sentences. Answer first.
  • A job interview question: one to two minutes. Use a story. See Job interviews in English for the STAR method.

"Yes, I like." is wrong. Like needs an object. Say "Yes, I do." or "Yes, I like it." Also, do not start with "Because ..." before you give the answer. The listener does not know yet what the reason is for.

In IELTS Speaking Part 1, the same frame is called A-R-E. See IELTS Speaking for exam answers and timing. This chapter uses the frame for real conversations.

Buying time without silence

Your manager asks you a hard question in a meeting.

Manager: How many users will the new search feature bring?

You: Hmm, good question. How many users? I'd say a few hundred in the first month. But I don't have the data here. Let me check and get back to you today.

You did not know the answer at once. But you did not stay silent. You used three tools. You used a short sound ("Hmm"). You repeated the question. And you promised a clear next step. Every speaker needs thinking time. The skill is to fill it with useful words.

Thinking time in four sizes
You needSayNote
one or two secondsWell, ... / So, ... / Hmm, let me see.Very natural. Use them at the start of an answer.
five secondsThat's a good question. / Let me think about that for a moment.Use one per conversation, not one per answer.
time to understandWhat would I change? Hmm ... / You mean in my team, or in the company?Repeating the question also checks that you heard it.
a dayI'm not sure. Let me check and get back to you. / Can I send you the numbers after the meeting?Fine at work. Then really send the answer.

"I don't know" is an honest answer. At work, it is fine if you add a next step: "I don't know yet, but I can find out by Thursday." Without the next step, it sounds like the end of the topic.

Native speakers also say small fillers: um, uh, you know, like. A few are normal. Too many make you hard to follow. In the last section of this chapter you will count your own fillers.

Learn each phrase as one chunk, like one long word. "Let-me-check-and-get-back-to-you" comes out fast when you do not build it word by word. For words you cannot remember, the chapter IELTS Speaking shows four ways to describe a missing word.

Ehhh ... ehhh ... (five seconds of silence) ... I don't know.

That's a good question. (next answer) That's a good question. (next answer) That's a good question.

Hmm, let me see. I'd say about two weeks. But I need to check with the design team.

Good question. I'm not sure yet, but I can find out by Thursday.

Agreeing and disagreeing

Three engineers choose a database for a new project.

Ana: I think we should use PostgreSQL for this.

Ben: I agree. The whole team knows it.

Kim: I see your point, but I'm not sure it's the best fit. The data has no fixed shape.

Ana: That's true. But Postgres has a JSON type, so it could still work.

Kim: Fair enough. Why don't we test both for a day?

Kim disagrees, but nobody feels attacked. Kim starts with a soft phrase, gives a reason and then offers a next step. Ana agrees with part of Kim's idea before she adds her own. This is how most work discussions sound in English.

Phrases for each strength

  • Agree: I agree. / That's true. / Good point. / Exactly. / I think so too.
  • Agree in part: I agree up to a point, but ... / That's true, but ... / Maybe, but have we thought about ...?
  • Disagree softly: I see your point, but ... / I'm not sure about that. / I see it a bit differently.
  • Disagree strongly: I don't agree at all. / I really don't think that's a good idea. Use these only when the topic is serious.

A soft disagreement has three parts. First comes a softener: "I see your point, but". Then comes the reason. Then comes a way forward: a test, a question or a compromise. Disagree with the idea, not with the person. "This plan may be too slow" is fine. "Your plan is bad" is not.

The grammar of agree

Agree is a verb. It does not need am. Also learn its three prepositions.

  • agree with a person or an idea: "I agree with Kim." "I agree with that."
  • agree on a shared decision: "We agreed on a date."
  • agree to a request or a plan: "She agreed to help us."

"I don't agree" and "I disagree" are both polite. The British Council's teachers say "I disagree" is a little more formal. In normal talk, "I don't agree" is the safe choice.

I am agree with you.

I'm not agree.

You are wrong. Your plan is bad.

I agree with you.

I don't agree. Or: I'm not sure I agree.

I see your point, but I think the plan is a bit risky. Could we test it first?

For "So do I" and "Neither do I", see Questions and negatives. For softer opinions with may, might and seem, see Hedging and stance. For disagreeing in meetings, see Meetings and stand-ups.

Clarifying: when you do not understand

You are on a video call with a client. The sound is not good, and she speaks fast.

Client: We need it ASAP, and the SLA is very tight.

You: Sorry, I didn't catch the last part. Could you say it again?

Client: The SLA is very tight.

You: Sorry, what does SLA stand for?

Client: Service level agreement. The promise about uptime.

You: Ah, I see. So, just to check: you need it soon, and the service must almost never go down?

Client: Exactly.

To clarify is to make the meaning clear. You did it in three steps. First you asked her to repeat one part. Then you asked about one word. Then you said her idea back in your own words. That last step is the strongest. It finds a misunderstanding before it becomes a problem.

Start with "Sorry". Here it is not a real apology. It is a soft signal: "I need help". Then name the exact part: "the last part", "the date", "the word after tight". A narrow question gets a fast answer.

To catch means "to hear" in "I didn't catch that". It is very common and very polite.

On video calls

  • "Sorry, you're breaking up." To break up means the sound keeps cutting out.
  • "I think you're on mute." The person is talking, but you hear nothing.
  • "Sorry, we lost you for a second. Could you repeat the last point?"

What?

Repeat, please.

Can you repeat again?

(You nod and say "OK" but you did not understand.)

Sorry, what was that?

Sorry, could you say that again?

Could you repeat that, please?

Sorry, I'm not sure I follow. Do you mean the test server or production?

"Repeat again" is wrong because repeat already means "say again". The worst mistake is the last one: pretending to understand. In software work, a hidden misunderstanding can become a bug. For more about understanding speech, see Listening skills.

Interrupting politely

In a planning meeting, a colleague is talking about the release. You notice a problem.

Tom: ... so we release on the 25th, and then on the 26th we start the next sprint, and ...

You: Sorry to interrupt, but isn't the 25th a public holiday?

Tom: Oh! Good catch. Let's say the 24th, then.

You: Thanks. Sorry, go on.

To interrupt is sometimes necessary. The fact was important, and it could not wait. You did it in five small steps.

  1. Wait for a small pause. The end of a sentence or a breath is enough.
  2. Give a signal. Raise a hand a little, or lean in. On a call, use the raise-hand button.
  3. Say a soft opener. "Sorry to interrupt, but ..." or "Can I just jump in here?"
  4. Make your point short. One or two sentences.
  5. Give the turn back. "Sorry, go on." or "Anyway, please continue."
Openers by purpose
PurposePhrase
ask a questionSorry, can I ask a quick question?
add a pointCan I add something here? / Just to add to that, ...
correct a factSorry, just a quick correction: it's version 3, not 2.
check understandingSorry for interrupting, but I want to make sure I understand.
urgent newsExcuse me, sorry. The client is on the phone for you.
leave earlyI'm sorry to cut this short, but I have another meeting.

When someone interrupts you

You can keep your turn politely. "Can I just finish this point?" "One second, I'm almost done." "Let me finish, and then I'd love to hear your view." A good team habit is to help quiet people too: "I think Mei wanted to say something."

British speakers often start an interruption with "Sorry", even when they did nothing wrong. "Excuse me" is common for strangers and for getting attention. Customs about interrupting differ between cultures. In international teams, short clear pauses help everyone take a turn.

Wait, wait, wait. No.

Stop. The 25th is a holiday.

(You interrupt and then talk for three minutes.)

Sorry, can I just jump in here?

Sorry to interrupt, but I think the 25th is a holiday.

That's all from me. Sorry, Tom, go ahead.

Telling a story with past tenses

People tell stories all the time: at lunch, in interviews, in incident reviews. Read this short work story. Look at the verbs.

Last Friday I was working from home. It was raining, and I was finishing a small task. Suddenly my phone rang. It was my manager. The website had stopped an hour before, and nobody had noticed. I opened the logs and found the problem in ten minutes. A disk was full. I cleaned it, and the site came back. In the end, I finished work at nine. But I felt quite proud.

The story uses three past tenses. Each tense has its own job. Together they are called narrative tenses.

Three tenses, three jobs
TenseJob in the storyFrom the story
past continuousthe background: what was going onI was working. It was raining.
past simplethe main events, in orderMy phone rang. I opened the logs.
past perfectan event before the story timeThe website had stopped an hour before.

The hook

One sentence that makes people want to listen. "Let me tell you about my worst Friday at work."

Set the scene

When, where, what was going on. Use the past continuous. "I was working from home. It was raining."

The turning point

Something changes. Use "Suddenly" or "Then" with the past simple. "Suddenly my phone rang."

Go back in time

Explain what happened earlier. Use the past perfect. "The website had stopped an hour before."

The main events

Two to four short actions in order. Past simple. "I opened the logs. I found the problem. I cleaned the disk."

The ending and the lesson

How it ended and how you felt. "In the end, I finished at nine. Now I check the disk space every week."

Story words

These words guide the listener: one day, at first, suddenly, then, after that, meanwhile, luckily, unfortunately, in the end. In the end means "after a long time or many problems". It is the natural way to start the last part.

The listener's job

A story is a conversation too. Listeners react: "Really?", "Oh no!", "What happened next?", "That must have been stressful." These short reactions tell the speaker to continue.

In jokes and very casual stories, native speakers sometimes switch to the present: "So I'm sitting there, and my phone rings." This makes the story feel live. It is fine to understand it. But in your own stories, stay in the past. It is clearer and safer.

Yesterday I go to the office and I was see my manager.

When I arrived, the meeting already started.

I opened the logs, I am finding the problem, I clean it.

Yesterday I went to the office and saw my manager.

When I arrived, the meeting had already started.

I opened the logs, found the problem and cleaned it.

The forms are in Past simple and past continuous and The perfect tenses. For longer stories with more tenses, see Advanced tense and aspect.

Describing pictures and processes

Describing a picture

Imagine a photo of an office. Here is a one-minute description.

This photo shows a busy office. In the foreground, a woman is sitting at a desk. She's looking at two screens, and she's smiling. In the background, three people are standing near a whiteboard. They might be in a meeting. On the left, there's a big window. It looks like a modern tech company. I think it's afternoon, because the light is soft. It reminds me of my first office.

The speaker follows a clear order. First comes the big picture: "a busy office". Then come the details, place by place. Actions use the present continuous: "is sitting", "are standing". Guesses use soft words: might, probably, it looks like, I think. The end links the photo to the speaker's own life.

The foreground is the front of the picture. The background is the back. Other useful words are behind, next to, in front of and between.

In Cambridge B1 Preliminary Speaking Part 2, each candidate talks for about one minute about one photograph. Describe the people, what they are doing and the place. The order above works well. For the higher Cambridge exams, see Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency.

Describing a process

A new teammate asks how code goes to production. You explain the steps.

First, you create a branch. Then you write the code and the tests. After that, you open a pull request. Next, a teammate reviews it. Once it's approved, you merge it. Finally, the pipeline deploys it. If a test fails, the deploy stops.

First, a branch is created. Then the code and the tests are written. After that, a pull request is opened and reviewed. Once it's approved, it's merged. Finally, the change is deployed automatically. If a test fails, the deploy is stopped.

Use you or the imperative when the listener will do the steps. Use the passive when you explain how a system works and the doer is not important. Put one step in each sentence. Use sequence words: first, then, next, after that, once, finally. Also say what happens when something goes wrong. Listeners often need that most.

On the picture, there is a man who sit at a desk.

After, you open a pull request.

At the end, the change deployed.

In the picture, a man is sitting at a desk.

After that, you open a pull request.

Finally, the change is deployed.

For the passive forms, see The passive. For sequence words, see Linking words.

Small talk

It is Monday morning. Two colleagues meet at the coffee machine.

Leo: Morning! How was your weekend?

Mia: Good, thanks. I went hiking with some friends. How about you?

Leo: Oh, nice. Where did you go?

Mia: Up in the hills near the lake. It was beautiful, but my legs hurt today!

Leo: I bet! I just stayed home and watched the football.

Mia: Did your team win?

Leo: No, sadly. Anyway, I'd better get back to my desk. Enjoy your coffee!

Mia: Thanks, you too. See you at stand-up.

Small talk is not about information. It builds a friendly feeling. It also opens the door for real work talk later. The dialogue has three moves: open, keep going and close.

Open, keep going, close

  • Open with the shared situation or a light question: "Busy day?" "How was your weekend?" "How do you know the host?"
  • Keep going. Answer with one extra detail. Mia says "hiking with some friends", so Leo has something to ask about. Then pass the turn back: "How about you?" Ask follow-up wh- questions: "Where did you go?" "What was it like?"
  • React with short words: "Oh, nice!" "Really?" "That sounds fun." "Oh no."
  • Close with a reason and a kind wish: "Anyway, I should get back to work. Nice talking to you." "Enjoy the rest of your day."
Topics for small talk with people you do not know well
Usually safeUsually avoid
the weather, the weekend, planspolitics, religion
travel, food, hobbies, sportmoney and salary
films, TV series, bookshealth and medical problems
the event, the office, the local areaage, weight, personal beliefs

Customs differ by country. In the UK, the weather is a very common opener. In other places, it can sound empty. When you are not sure, ask about the shared situation.

Expert level: show that you are listening

Good listeners make small sounds and short words while the other person talks: "Mm-hm", "Right", "Yeah", "I see", "Really?" These are called backchannels. They tell the speaker "go on, I'm with you". On calls, people often cannot see you nod. So a short "right" or "I see" matters even more.

A: How was your weekend? B: Fine. (silence)

A: How are you? B: Not great. My back hurts, and I slept badly, and my doctor says ...

How old are you? How much do you earn?

A: How was your weekend? B: Fine, thanks. Quite quiet. I tried a new ramen place. How about yours?

A: How are you? B: Good, thanks. A bit tired. You?

What do you do in your free time?

"How are you?" in small talk wants a short answer, not a full report. British English says "at the weekend". American English says "on the weekend". Both are correct.

The self-recording method

You cannot hear your own mistakes while you speak. Your brain is busy. A recording lets you listen like another person. Cambridge English also tells learners to record themselves and listen back.

The chapter IELTS Speaking has a five-step method for exam answers. Here is a weekly loop for real life. It takes 10 to 15 minutes a day.

A weekly self-recording loop
DayTask
MondayRecord one minute on a real topic: "What did I work on last week?"
TuesdayWrite a transcript of the recording, word by word.
WednesdayMark three problems: one grammar, one word, one fluency problem.
ThursdayPractise only the fixed sentences. Say each one five times.
FridayRecord the same topic again. Compare it with Monday.

What to listen for

  • Did I answer first, then give a reason and an example?
  • Are my past tenses correct in stories?
  • How many fillers do I use? Do I repeat the same word?
  • Do I pause between ideas (good) or in the middle of a phrase (less good)?
  • Can I hear the stress on the key words?
  • Did I end clearly, or did my voice just stop?

A speech-to-text tool can make the transcript fast. But check it by ear. The tool may write the word it expected, not the word you said. So it can hide your errors.

Measure it

You are an engineer, so measure. This small script counts words, words per minute and fillers in your transcript. It also shows long words you repeat.

# speech_stats.py: simple numbers from a transcript of your own speech
import re
from collections import Counter

FILLERS = {"um", "uh", "er", "erm", "basically", "actually"}

def stats(text: str, seconds: float) -> dict:
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower())
    counts = Counter(words)
    fillers = sum(counts[f] for f in FILLERS)
    # long words you repeat a lot: maybe you need a synonym
    top = [w for w, n in counts.most_common() if len(w) > 4 and n > 1]
    return {
        "words": len(words),
        "words_per_minute": round(len(words) / seconds * 60),
        "fillers": fillers,
        "fillers_per_100_words": round(fillers / len(words) * 100, 1),
        "repeated": top[:3],
    }

transcript = """Um, last week I, uh, fixed a bug in our payment service.
Basically the bug was a timeout. Actually the timeout was too short,
so I, um, changed the timeout and I added a test for the timeout."""

print(stats(transcript, seconds=20))
{'words': 38, 'words_per_minute': 114, 'fillers': 5, 'fillers_per_100_words': 13.2, 'repeated': ['timeout']}

Read the result. Five of 38 words are fillers. That is a lot. The word "timeout" comes four times. "It" could replace two of them. Run the script every Friday and watch the numbers fall. Compare yourself with last month, not with native speakers. Clear and steady is better than fast.

Recording once and never listening is the most common mistake. The listening and the second recording are where you learn. Also, record only yourself. Ask before you record other people.

For stress, rhythm and the shadowing method, see Pronunciation and fluency.

Should I learn whole phrases by heart?

Yes, short ones. Phrases like "Sorry, I didn't catch that" are chunks. Learn them whole. But do not learn whole answers by heart. They sound like a speech, and they break when the question changes.

What if I make a grammar mistake while I speak?

If the meaning is clear, keep going. If the meaning is wrong, fix it fast: "Sorry, I mean he went, not he goes." Small mistakes rarely stop a conversation. Silence does.

Is it rude to say I don't understand?

No. "Sorry, I'm not sure I follow" is polite and professional. Pretending to understand is the real risk, at work and in life.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for speaking skills
PatternPurposeModelNote
Answer. Because + reason. For example, + detail.Give a full answerYes, I do. Mainly because it saves time. For example, I use that hour for a run.Answer first. Then stop or pass the turn.
Hmm, let me see. + answerBuy a few secondsHmm, let me see. I'd say two weeks.Use different phrases. Do not repeat one.
I'm not sure. Let me check and get back to you.Buy time until laterI'm not sure. Let me check and get back to you today.Then really send the answer.
I see your point, but + reasonDisagree softlyI see your point, but it may be too slow.Never "I am not agree".
I agree up to a point, but + ideaAgree in partI agree up to a point, but the cost is high.Agree with a person, on a decision, to a request.
Sorry, I didn't catch + partAsk someone to repeatSorry, I didn't catch the date.Not "Can you repeat again?"
What does + word + mean?Ask about a wordWhat does "rollback" mean?For short forms: What does SLA stand for?
So, just to check: + your words?Check that you understoodSo, just to check: you need it by Friday?Say it in your own words, not theirs.
Sorry to interrupt, but + short pointInterrupt politelySorry to interrupt, but the 25th is a holiday.Then give the turn back: "Sorry, go on."
Can I just finish this point?Keep your turnCan I just finish this point? Then I'd love to hear your view.Say it calmly, with a smile.
I was + -ing when + past simpleSet the scene in a storyI was making coffee when the alarm went off.Background: continuous. Event: simple.
When + past simple, subject had + past participleShow an earlier eventWhen I arrived, the meeting had already started.Not "the meeting already started".
In the foreground or background, subject + is + -ingDescribe a pictureIn the background, two people are talking.In the picture, not on the picture.
First, ... Then ... After that ... Finally, ...Describe a processFirst, you create a branch. Then you write the tests."After that", not "After" alone.
Answer and detail. How about you?Keep small talk goingGood, thanks. I went hiking. How about you?One extra detail gives the other person a topic.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

A colleague asks: "Do you like your new laptop?" Which answer is best?

  • Yes.
  • Yes, I like.
  • Yes, I do. It's really fast. For example, my builds take half the time now.

It has an answer, a reason and an example. "Yes, I like" has no object.

Which is a polite way to disagree at work?

  • You are wrong.
  • I am not agree with this.
  • I see your point, but I'm worried about the cost.

A softener, then a reason. Agree is a verb, so there is no "am".

On a call, you did not hear the date. What do you say?

  • What?
  • Sorry, I didn't catch the date. Could you say it again?
  • Can you repeat again the date?

Start with "Sorry" and name the exact part. "Repeat again" says "again" twice.

Which sentence is correct in a story?

  • When I arrived, the meeting already started.
  • When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
  • When I arrived, the meeting has already started.

The meeting started before you arrived. Use the past perfect for the earlier event.

Which sentence describes a picture correctly?

  • On the picture, there is a man who sit at a desk.
  • In the picture, a man is sitting at a desk.
  • In the picture, a man sit at a desk.

Use "in the picture" and the present continuous for actions.

Which is the best way to end small talk?

  • OK. Bye.
  • Anyway, I'd better get back to work. Nice talking to you!
  • Stop. I go now.

A closing word, a reason and a kind wish sound friendly.

Fill the gap

I agree ? you about the deadline.

We finally agreed ? a date for the launch.

Sorry to ?, but the client is here.

Sorry, I didn't ? that. Could you say it again?

What does API ??

I (walk) to the station when it started to rain.

By the time we found the bug, many users (leave).

First, you open the app. ?, you choose a language.

Good, thanks. I went to the beach. How ? you?

Think and speak

Say your answers aloud first. Then read the model.

  1. Answer with answer + reason + example: "Do you prefer mornings or evenings?"
    Model answer

    I prefer mornings. Mainly because my head is clear before lunch. For example, I write my hardest code between eight and ten. How about you?

  2. Make this softer, with a softener, a reason and a way forward: "Your plan is bad. We need more time."
    Model answer

    I see your point, but I'm not sure the plan gives us enough time. The tests alone take three days. Could we move the date by one week?

  3. Find and fix three mistakes: "Can you repeat again? I am not understand the word rollback. I am agree with the plan."
    Answer

    (1) Could you repeat that, please? Or: Could you say that again? (2) I don't understand the word "rollback". Or: What does "rollback" mean? (3) I agree with the plan.

  4. Tell a story from these notes. Use the past continuous, the past simple and the past perfect. Notes: work late / office quiet / lights go off / someone forget to pay the bill / use phone light / finish report.
    Model answer

    Last winter I was working late. The office was very quiet. Suddenly the lights went off. Someone had forgotten to pay the electricity bill! I used the light on my phone and finished the report. In the end, I left at ten, but the report was done.

  5. Describe a process you know in five steps, with first, then, after that, next and finally. Then change two steps into the passive.
    Model answer

    First, you boil the water. Then you put a tea bag in a cup. After that, you pour the hot water on it. Next, you wait three minutes. Finally, you take out the bag and add milk. Passive: The water is boiled. The tea bag is taken out after three minutes.

  6. Expert: a learner ran the script and got: words 120, words per minute 72, fillers 18, repeated: "basically", "problem". What should the learner work on first, and how?
    Model answer

    Fillers come first: 18 of 120 words is 15 per 100 words, which is very high. Replace "um" with a short pause, and "basically" with nothing. "Basically" also appears in the repeated list, so it is a habit. Next, find other words for "problem": "issue", "bug", or "it". The speed of 72 words a minute is slow, but it will rise when the fillers fall. Record again on Friday and compare.

  7. Expert: write a six-line small talk dialogue with a colleague after a holiday. Include an open, an answer with a detail, a pass back, a follow-up question, a reaction and a close.
    Model answer

    A: Hi! Welcome back. How was your holiday? B: Great, thanks. We went to Portugal for a week. How about you? Busy here? A: Quite busy, yes. What was the best part of the trip? B: The food, I think. The fish was amazing. A: Oh, nice! Anyway, I'd better get back to my code. Good to have you back!

Key takeaways

  • Answer first. Then add a reason and one example. Then stop, or pass the turn back.
  • Fill thinking time with short phrases. At work, "Let me check and get back to you" is a full answer.
  • Agreement is a scale. At work, use the middle: "I agree up to a point", "I see your point, but".
  • Agree is a verb: I agree, I don't agree. Agree with a person, on a decision, to a request.
  • Clarify with "Sorry" plus the exact part. Then say the idea back in your own words.
  • Interrupt in five steps: pause, signal, soft opener, short point, give the turn back.
  • Stories need three tenses: continuous for the scene, simple for events, perfect for earlier events.
  • Describe a picture from the big picture to the details. Describe a process one step per sentence.
  • Small talk has three moves: open, keep going with details and questions, close kindly.
  • Record yourself every week, listen, fix three problems and record again.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Agreeing and disagreeing. A B1 video lesson with softened disagreement at work.
  • British Council LearnEnglish: Keeping a conversation going. Phrases to buy time, change topic and pass the turn back.
  • VOA Learning English: How to interrupt someone in a nice way. Openers for questions, added points, urgent news and leaving.
  • British Council English Online: Small talk topics, phrases and openers. Safe topics, topics to avoid, and how to open and close.
  • Cambridge English: B1 Preliminary information for candidates. The one-minute photograph task and the advice to record yourself.
  • British Council English Online: Telling a story with narrative tenses. Why stories need background and more than one past tense.

Reading skills

Good readers do not read every text the same way. They choose a speed and a method for each purpose. This chapter teaches those methods for daily life and work first: emails, articles, docs and papers. They also help in every reading exam.

  • Choose the right way to read: skim, scan, read for detail or read for pleasure.
  • Find the main idea of a paragraph from its topic sentence.
  • Guess unknown words from context and follow reference words like this and it.
  • Make inferences and tell facts from opinions.
  • Read technical texts and papers in passes, and track your progress in a reading log.

Four ways to read

Think about your last working day. You probably read in four different ways.

  • An email from HR about holidays. You only wanted one date. You found it in five seconds.
  • A news article. You read the headline and the first lines. Then you knew the story.
  • A contract for a new job. You read every line, slowly, twice.
  • A novel on the train. You read for fun. You did not stop for every new word.

Each way has a name. Choose the way by your purpose, not by the text.

Four ways to read
WayPurposeSpeedExample
Skimget the main ideavery fasta news article, a long email
Scanfind one detailvery fast, then stopa date, a price, an error code
Read for detailunderstand everythingslow, often twicea contract, an exam question, a bug report
Extensive readingenjoy, learn naturallynormal, smootha novel, a blog you like

How to skim

  1. Read the title and any subtitle.
  2. Look at headings, pictures, bold words and lists.
  3. Read the first paragraph. It often says what the text is about.
  4. Read the first sentence of each other paragraph.
  5. Read the last paragraph. It often sums up.
  6. Stop and say the main idea in one sentence.

How to scan

First, know exactly what you are looking for. Then guess its shape. A date has numbers. A name has a capital letter. A price has a symbol like £ or $. Move your eyes fast down the page and look only for that shape. When you find it, stop. Read the sentence around it to check.

On a screen, Ctrl + F is a scanner. But it finds only the exact word. The text may say "cost" when you search for "price". So also search for one or two other words with the same meaning.

Reading every text word by word at the same slow speed. It wastes time on easy texts. The opposite mistake is just as bad: skimming a contract or an exam question. Skim to decide. Read for detail when the details matter.

For reading strategies inside the IELTS test, with timing, see IELTS Listening and Reading.

Topic sentences: find the main idea

Read this paragraph. Which sentence gives the main idea?

Remote work has changed how teams write. Many teams now use chat instead of meetings. Decisions often live in documents, not in people's heads. New team members read old threads to learn the history. For this reason, clear writing has become a key skill for engineers.

The first sentence is the main idea. Every other sentence supports it with details and a result. This first sentence is the topic sentence. In English articles, reports and essays, it usually comes first.

So you can read a text fast by reading only its topic sentences. Together they form a short outline of the whole text. This is the heart of skimming.

When the first sentence is not the main idea

Writers do not always follow the rule. Watch for three cases.

  • A question first. "Why do so many projects finish late?" The main idea is the answer, in the next sentence.
  • A popular idea, then a turn. "Many people think open offices help teamwork. However, studies show the opposite." The main idea comes after However.
  • The main idea at the end. Some paragraphs give examples first and the point last, often after "So" or "In short".

Taking the first sentence of every paragraph as the writer's view. In the "popular idea" case, the first sentence is the idea the writer argues against. Always check for a turn word: but, however, yet, in fact.

To write your own topic sentences, see Writing sentences and paragraphs.

Guessing words from context

Read this sentence. The word in bold does not exist. It is a made-up word.

After the outage, the team was so flendered that they went home early and slept for twelve hours.

You do not know flendered. But you can guess it: very tired. The context told you. Work stopped, they went home early, and they slept a long time. This skill saves you from the dictionary many times a day.

A five-step method

The researchers Clarke and Nation described a guessing method in 1980. Here it is in simple steps.

  1. What kind of word is it? Noun, verb, adjective or adverb? "So flendered that" shows an adjective.
  2. Look at the sentence. What does the word go with? Here: "the team was so ...".
  3. Look at the wider context. Read the sentences around it. Find links like because, but and so.
  4. Guess. Say a simple meaning: "very tired".
  5. Check. Put your guess in the sentence. Does it make sense? Sometimes, check a learner's dictionary too.

Clues writers give you

  • Definition: "Latency, that is, the delay before a response, went up after the update."
  • Same meaning: "At first, the managers were sceptical: they doubted the plan could work."
  • Opposite: "The old tool was clunky, but the new one is smooth and easy."
  • Example: "Use a linter, such as Ruff or ESLint, to find style problems."
  • Cause or result: "The file was corrupted, so nobody could open it."

Look it up or keep reading?

Not every new word needs a dictionary. Look a word up when it appears many times, when it is in a title or a question, or when you cannot follow the text without it. Skip it when you understand the main idea anyway.

Guessing has limits. You can only guess well when you understand most of the other words. A 2022 article in the NYS TESOL Journal also warns that guesses can be wrong. It suggests checking guesses in a learner's dictionary some of the time, for example one guess in three. For how many words you need to read with ease, see How to grow your vocabulary.

Guessing from word parts alone. "Pre-" often means "before", but not every word that starts with "pre" means "before" something. Use word parts to check a guess, not to make it.

Reference words: who is "it"?

Read this short text from a team update.

We moved the cache to a new server last week. It is twice as fast as the old one. This change cut page load time by 40%. The mobile and web teams both noticed. The former asked us to do the same for their API.

Five words in bold point back to something earlier. They are reference words. To understand the text, you must know what each one points to.

Common reference words
WordPoints toExample
it, they, thema noun said beforeThe tests passed. They took ten minutes.
this, that, these, thosea noun or a whole ideaSales fell. This worried the board.
this + nounan idea, with a summary wordThis problem took a week to fix.
one, onesa noun, to avoid repeating itI need a new laptop. A light one.
sucha kind of thing said beforeSuch errors are rare.
the former, the latterthe first or second of twoPython and Rust are both good. The latter is faster.
do so, here, therean action, a placeWe asked them to test it, and they did so.

When you meet this or it, stop for one second. Ask: "This what?" Find the answer before you read on. In hard texts, draw a small arrow in your notes.

Thinking it always means the nearest noun. Often it means the main topic of the last sentence. In "The app sent the report to the server, and it crashed", it could be the app or the server. Good writers avoid this. As a reader, use the meaning to decide.

Inference: reading between the lines

Your manager sends you this email after you share a report.

Email: Thanks for the report. I've added a few comments on page 3. Could we have a quick call tomorrow at nine, before the client meeting?

The email does not say "There is a problem". But you can guess it. The manager made comments, wants to talk, and wants to do it before the client sees the report. So something on page 3 probably needs to change. This is an inference.

The writer implies something. This means the writer suggests it without saying it. The reader infers it. This means the reader works it out. A good inference has two parts: clues in the text and your general knowledge.

A good inference

Something on page 3 needs to change.

Clues: comments, a call, "before the client meeting".

Too far

My manager is angry, and I will lose my job.

No word in the email supports this.

After every inference, ask: "Which words tell me this?" If you cannot point to words, it is a fear or a wish, not an inference.

Clues that carry hidden meaning

  • Word choice: "The demo was interesting" can be polite for "not good". Compare "The demo was excellent".
  • What is missing: a review that praises the design but never mentions speed.
  • Hedging: "This may help" is weaker than "This will help". See Hedging and stance.
  • Tone: "As I said in my last email ..." often shows a little impatience.

Exams test inference with questions like "What does the writer suggest?" or "What can we infer?" The right answer is never written word for word. But it is always supported by the text. If an answer needs outside knowledge only, it is wrong.

Fact or opinion?

Read four sentences from a blog about programming languages.

  1. Rust 1.0 was released in 2015.
  2. Rust is clearly the best language for systems work.
  3. Many developers say Rust is hard to learn.
  4. Rust may become more popular in embedded devices.

Sentence 1 is a fact. You can check it. Sentence 2 is an opinion. "Best" is a judgment, and "clearly" tries to make it sound like a fact. Sentence 3 is a fact about opinions: people really say this, but it is not proof that Rust is hard. Sentence 4 is a prediction. It is hedged with "may".

Signals of fact and opinion
Usually factUsually opinion
dates, numbers, names, placesI think, I believe, in my view
a source: according to the 2024 reportbest, worst, amazing, terrible
neutral verbs: released, measured, increasedshould, must, ought to
results you can repeatclearly, obviously, of course

Expert level: fact, claim and opinion

A statement that sounds like a fact can still be false. "Our app is used by 10 million people" is a claim. It is checkable, but you have not checked it. So ask two questions. Can it be checked? Has it been checked, and by whom? Watch for "studies show" with no study named. Watch for numbers with no source.

Believing words like clearly, obviously and everyone knows. They do not add proof. They add pressure. A strong argument shows the evidence instead.

Reading speed

How fast do people read? In 2019, the psychologist Marc Brysbaert combined 190 studies with more than 18,000 adults. His average for English is in the chart.

The same review found that most adults read non-fiction at 175 to 300 words per minute. It also found that people reading in a second language read more slowly. So do not compare yourself with native speakers. Compare yourself with your own speed last month.

Measure your speed

Choose an easy text of known length. Time yourself. Then divide the words by the minutes. A 600-word article in 4 minutes is 150 words per minute. Answer two or three questions after it. Speed without understanding is not reading.

Speed reading: the truth

Many apps promise to double or triple your speed. In 2016, Keith Rayner and four other reading scientists reviewed the research. They found a trade-off: faster reading means less understanding. Big jumps in speed with full understanding are very unlikely. Their advice was simple. The best way to read faster is to know the language better.

For a second-language reader, that means three honest habits.

  • Read a lot of easy text. Common words become instant. This is extensive reading.
  • Do not stop at every unknown word. Guess, mark it and go on.
  • Read in groups of words. "In the end", "as a result", "on the other hand" are one unit each, not three words.

You cannot train your eyes to read faster in a magic way. You can train your English. Better English makes reading faster by itself.

Reading technical and academic texts

Technical texts are dense. One page of docs can take longer than ten pages of a novel. So read them with a plan.

Documentation

  • Start with a question. "How do I set a timeout?" A question turns reading into scanning.
  • Read the example first. Code examples often explain faster than the text around them.
  • Know the parts. Most docs have a quick start, guides and a reference. Use the quick start to begin. Use the reference to check one detail.
  • Read warnings for detail. Words like "must", "never" and "deprecated" need slow reading.

Research papers: three passes

In 2007, the computer scientist S. Keshav described a three-pass method for papers. Do not read a paper from the first word to the last. Read it in up to three passes, and stop when you have enough.

The quick look (5 to 10 minutes)

Read the title, the abstract and the introduction. Read the section headings only. Read the conclusions. Glance at the references. Then decide: do I need more?

Five questions after pass 1

What kind of paper is it? What other work is it related to? Do the assumptions look right? What are the main contributions? Is it clearly written?

The careful read (up to an hour)

Read with care, but skip the proofs. Look closely at figures and graphs. Write the key points in the margin. After this pass, you can explain the paper to a colleague.

The deep read (hours)

Try to rebuild the work in your head with the same assumptions. Question every step. Keshav says this can take four or five hours for a beginner.

Most of the time, pass 1 is enough. This is skimming with a clear goal.

Dense sentences: find the core

Academic sentences can be long. Look at this one.

The proposed caching strategy, which was evaluated on three large production workloads over a period of six months, significantly reduces the median response time of read-heavy services.

Find the main subject and the main verb first. Ignore the extra parts in commas.

The strategy reduces the response time.

Now add the details back, one by one: which strategy, how much, for which services. The core sentence is your map. For dense noun phrases, see Participle clauses and nominalisation. For the language of docs, standards, error messages and paper abstracts, see Reading technical English.

Keep a reading log

A reading log is a small table. You add one line for each text. After a month, it shows your progress.

A reading log with three example lines
DateTextMinutesWords per minuteLevelNew wordsOne-line summary
3 NovBlog post on code review6150easynitpick, gatekeeperReview the design first, style last.
5 NovGraded reader, chapter 420170easynoneThe detective finds the missing key.
7 NovDocs: database indexes2590hardselectivity, compositeIndexes speed up reads but slow down writes.

The one-line summary is the most important column. If you cannot write it, you did not really understand the text. Then read the topic sentences again.

What to read

The Extensive Reading Foundation describes extensive reading as reading a large amount of easy text. You should understand it without a dictionary. You choose texts you like. Graded readers are good for this. Blogs on topics you know are good too.

  • Most of your reading should be easy. If you stop on every line, choose an easier text.
  • Some reading should be hard. Read one work text slowly each week for detail and new words.
  • Review the log every Sunday. Look at the words per minute and the level. Are easy texts getting faster?

Reading only hard texts with a dictionary open. It feels like serious study. But you read little, and you read slowly. Easy reading in large amounts builds speed and vocabulary faster.

Patterns to remember

Signal patterns for readers
PatternPurposeModelNote
X, that is, YGives a definitionLatency, that is, the delay before a response, went up.The meaning of X is between the commas.
X: meaningExplains after a colonThe managers were sceptical: they doubted the plan.After the colon comes the explanation.
X, such as A and BGives examplesUse a linter, such as Ruff, to find problems.The examples tell you the kind of thing X is.
X, but YShows the oppositeThe old tool was clunky, but the new one is smooth.X means the opposite of Y.
Many people think X. However, Y.Introduces the writer's viewMany think open offices help. However, studies disagree.The main idea comes after however.
This + nounPoints back and sums upThis change cut load time by 40%.Ask: this what?
the former ... the latterPicks one of two thingsPython and Rust are both good. The latter is faster.Former is first. Latter is second.
In short, / In summary,Sums up the textIn short, the trial was a success.Read this part first when you skim.
As a result, / Therefore,Gives a resultSick days fell. As a result, the company kept the plan.The result is often the key point.
clearly / obviously + claimMakes an opinion sound like a factRust is clearly the best language.These words add pressure, not proof.
Studies show that + claimReports researchStudies show that short weeks reduce stress.Which studies? Look for a source.
may / might / suggests + claimShows the writer is not sureThe results suggest the plan may work.A hedged claim is weaker than "shows".
The writer implies X. I infer X.Talks about hidden meaningThe email implies a problem on page 3.Writers imply. Readers infer.

Practice

Read the text below first. The tasks get harder. The company and the numbers are invented for this book.

A shorter week at Brightline

Last year, Brightline, a small software company with 60 staff, tried a four-day week for six months. Staff worked 32 hours instead of 40, with the same pay. At first, the managers were sceptical: they doubted that people could do five days of work in four.

The results were mostly positive. The number of finished tasks stayed about the same, and sick days fell by a third. In a survey, 85% of staff said they felt less tired. These results were the main reason the company kept the new system.

However, not everything went well. The support team found it hard to answer customers on all five weekdays. They solved this by working in two groups. One group took Mondays off, and the other took Fridays.

Some experts think every company should copy Brightline. That may be too fast. A small software team is not a hospital or a shop. Still, the trial shows one thing clearly: hours and results are not the same.

Quick questions

Skim the text. What is it mainly about?

  • Why software companies pay too little
  • A company's trial of a four-day week and its results
  • How support teams answer customers

The title and the topic sentences all talk about the four-day week trial.

Scan the text. By how much did sick days fall?

  • By 85%
  • By a third
  • By eight hours

Paragraph 2 says sick days fell by a third. 85% is the survey result.

What does "sceptical" mean in paragraph 1?

  • doubtful, not sure the plan would work
  • excited and happy
  • angry with the staff

The colon gives the meaning: they doubted the plan could work.

In paragraph 3, what does "this" in "They solved this" refer to?

  • the four-day week
  • the problem of answering customers on all five weekdays
  • the survey

"This" sums up the problem in the sentence before.

Which sentence is the writer's opinion?

  • Staff worked 32 hours instead of 40.
  • Some experts think every company should copy Brightline.
  • That may be too fast.

The first is a fact. The second is a fact about other people's opinions. The third is the writer's own hedged view.

What can we infer about Brightline's customers?

  • They did not like the new system.
  • They expect help on all five weekdays.
  • They also moved to a four-day week.

The support team had to cover five weekdays, so customers need help on each of them. The text says nothing about their feelings.

Fill the gap

To find one date in a long email, you ? it.

To get the main idea of an article fast, you ? it.

The sentence that gives the main idea of a paragraph is the ?.

Python and Rust are both popular. The ? has no garbage collector.

The writer does not say it directly, but she ? that the plan failed.

From the clues, the reader can ? that the plan failed.

A 900-word article read in 6 minutes is ? words per minute.

Think and write

  1. Write the topic sentence of each paragraph of the Brightline text in five words or fewer.
    Model answer

    (1) Brightline tried a four-day week. (2) The results were mostly positive. (3) Not everything went well. (4) Do not copy it too fast. Together these lines are an outline of the text.

  2. Guess the meaning of the made-up word and name the clue: "Unlike the old laptop, which was slow and heavy, the new one is very trimble."
    Answer

    Trimble probably means fast and light. The clue is the opposite clue "Unlike ...". The new laptop is the opposite of slow and heavy.

  3. Find the core subject and verb: "The new onboarding guide, written by two senior engineers after many complaints from new hires, explains the build process in clear steps."
    Answer

    The guide explains the build process. The part between the commas tells you who wrote it and why.

  4. Is this a good inference? Text: "The meeting room was booked until 3, but the team was still there at 4." Inference: "The meeting went on longer than planned." Explain.
    Answer

    Yes. The room was booked until 3, and the team was still there at 4. Both clues support it. "The meeting was a failure" would go too far.

  5. Label each sentence as fact, opinion or claim to check: (a) The office opened in 2019. (b) It is the nicest office in the city. (c) Our product is used by half of all banks in Europe.
    Answer

    (a) Fact: a date you can check. (b) Opinion: "nicest" is a judgment. (c) A claim to check: it can be checked, but it needs a source.

  6. Expert: you have 15 minutes before a meeting to understand a 12-page research paper. Make a plan.
    Model answer

    Do only pass 1 of the three-pass method. Read the title, abstract and introduction carefully (about 6 minutes). Read the section headings (1 minute). Read the conclusions (3 minutes). Look at the main figure (2 minutes). Then write one line for each of the five questions: kind of paper, related work, assumptions, contributions, clarity. Bring these notes to the meeting.

  7. Expert: start your own reading log. Read one easy text and one hard text this week. Fill in all seven columns for both.
    What a good log line looks like

    8 Nov, "Blog: why tests are flaky", 7 minutes, about 160 words per minute, easy, new words "flaky" and "race condition", summary: "Most flaky tests come from timing and shared state." Your speed on the hard text should be lower. That is normal.

Key takeaways

  • Choose the way to read by your purpose: skim for the main idea, scan for one detail, read slowly for detail, read a lot for pleasure.
  • Topic sentences usually come first. Read them alone to get an outline. Watch for a turn after however.
  • Guess new words in five steps: word type, sentence, wider context, guess, check.
  • Writers give clues: definitions, same meanings, opposites, examples, causes.
  • For every reference word, ask: this what? it what?
  • A good inference rests on words in the text. If you cannot point to them, it is not an inference.
  • Facts can be checked. Opinions are judgments. Claims need a source before you trust them.
  • Average adult silent reading in English is about 238 words per minute for non-fiction. Better English, not tricks, makes you faster.
  • Read papers in passes. Most of the time, the first pass is enough.
  • Keep a reading log with a one-line summary for every text.

Sources

  • British Council TeachingEnglish: Scanning. Scanning for details, skimming for gist, and choosing a way to read by purpose.
  • Hall (2022): A renewed case for Clarke and Nation (1980). The five-step guessing strategy and the advice to check guesses in a learner's dictionary.
  • Brysbaert (2019): How many words do we read per minute?. Meta-analysis of 190 studies: 238 and 260 words per minute for silent reading, 183 for reading aloud.
  • Association for Psychological Science: Speed reading promises are too good to be true. Summary of Rayner and others (2016) on the speed and understanding trade-off.
  • S. Keshav (2007): How to Read a Paper. The three-pass method and the five questions after the first pass.
  • Extensive Reading Foundation: What is extensive reading?. Large amounts of easy, self-chosen reading with little dictionary use.

Writing sentences and paragraphs

Every email, report and essay is built from two units: the sentence and the paragraph. This chapter shows how to build both well. You will learn sentence types, variety, paragraph shape, cohesion, the key punctuation marks and a simple editing routine.

  • Write simple, compound and complex sentences, and mix them for variety.
  • Build a paragraph with a topic sentence, support, an example and a closing sentence.
  • Connect sentences with this, these, such and summary nouns.
  • Use the comma, full stop, colon and apostrophe correctly in British style.
  • Find and fix run-ons and fragments, and edit a paragraph in clear steps.

Three kinds of sentence

Here is one idea, written in four ways.

The build failed on Monday night.

The build failed, so we stayed late.

Because the build failed, we stayed late.

Because the build failed, we stayed late, but we fixed it before midnight.

Each sentence is built from clauses. A main clause can stand alone: "we stayed late". A dependent clause cannot: "because the build failed". The kind of sentence depends on how many clauses it has, and of which kind.

The four kinds of sentence
KindClausesJoining wordsExample
Simpleone main clausenoneThe build failed.
Compoundtwo main clausesand, but, or, so, yet (comma before)The build failed, so we stayed late.
Complexone main + one or more dependentbecause, although, when, if, who, which, thatBecause the build failed, we stayed late.
Compound-complextwo main + one or more dependentboth kindsWhen it failed, we stayed late, but we fixed it.

The chapter The 15 sentence patterns calls compound sentences "joined" sentences. It shows the patterns inside each family. This chapter uses the names you will meet in writing guides and exams.

Long is not the same as complex. "The new build server in our London office with 64 cores failed on Monday night" is long. But it has one subject and one verb, so it is a simple sentence.

Because the build failed.

Although the build failed, but we released on time.

Because the build failed, we stayed late.

Although the build failed, we released on time.

The first wrong line has only a dependent clause. It needs a main clause. The second has two joining words for one link. Use only one. See Linking words for more.

Sentence variety

Read three versions of one short paragraph about Git.

I use Git every day. It is a version control tool. It saves every change. It helps teams. It is hard at first.

I use Git every day because it is a version control tool which saves every change and helps teams work together, although it is hard at first, and many new people find the commands confusing, so they need some time.

I use Git every day, and I could not work without it. It saves every change, so nobody loses work, even when a laptop breaks. It also helps teams work on the same code at the same time. It is hard at first. But after a month, most people find it simple.

The choppy version sounds like a list. Every sentence starts with "It", and every sentence is short. The long version is one 40-word sentence. The reader gets lost. The varied version mixes long and short. The short sentence, "It is hard at first", stands out. That is where the writer wants your attention.

Five tools for variety

  1. Mix the lengths. Use longer sentences to explain. Use a short one for a key point.
  2. Vary the start. Do not start every sentence with "I", "It" or "The". Start some with a time phrase, a linker or a dependent clause: "After the meeting, ...", "If it fails, ...".
  3. Combine related short sentences. Use and, but, so, because, which or who. "It saves every change. It helps teams." becomes "It saves every change and helps teams."
  4. Split very long sentences. The UK government's style guide asks writers to review any sentence over 25 words. Split it if that makes it clearer.
  5. Put the news at the end. The end of a sentence carries the most weight. "In the end, the cause was a full disk." The new fact comes last.

Expert level: parallel structure

In a list, every item should have the same grammar. This is called parallel structure. It makes long sentences easy to read.

The new tool is fast, cheap and it is easy to use.

Our job is to plan, building and the testing of features.

The new tool is fast, cheap and easy to use.

Our job is to plan, build and test features.

Making sentences longer to look advanced. Examiners and readers want range and control, not length. A clear short sentence is better than a long broken one. Also avoid "Firstly ... Secondly ... Thirdly ..." on every sentence. That is a list, not variety.

The shape of a paragraph

Read this paragraph from a team proposal. Each sentence has a job.

Topic sentence: Automated tests save our team time in two ways.

Support 1: First, they find bugs before our users do.

Example: Last month, a test caught a wrong tax rate one hour before the release.

Support 2: Second, they make changes safer, so we can clean up old code without fear.

Closing sentence: For these reasons, every new feature should come with tests.

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. The first sentence gives the idea. The middle sentences support it with reasons and an example. The last sentence sums up. The picture shows this shape.

A good topic sentence

A topic sentence has two parts: the topic and a controlling idea. In "Automated tests save our team time in two ways", the topic is "automated tests". The controlling idea is "save time in two ways". It tells the reader what comes next.

Three topic sentences
Topic sentenceProblem
Technology is important.Too broad. It could start a whole book.
Our team reviewed 40 pull requests last week.Too narrow. It is a fact, not an idea to support.
Code review helps our team in two main ways.Just right. A clear topic and a clear plan.

One paragraph, one idea

Every sentence must support the topic sentence. This is called unity. Imagine this line in the middle of the test paragraph: "Our office also has a new coffee machine." It may be true. But it is not about tests, so cut it. If a second idea is important, give it its own paragraph.

When to start a new paragraph

  • When you start a new idea or point.
  • When you turn to the other side of an argument.
  • When a block of text is long and the reader needs a pause.
  • When you move from the introduction to the body, or from the body to the conclusion.

How long should a paragraph be? In essays and reports, Purdue OWL warns that two or three sentences are often not enough to develop an idea. In emails and chat, short paragraphs of one to three sentences are normal, because people read fast on screens.

Choose one idea

Notes: written stand-ups, time zones, a record, fewer meetings. The one idea: written stand-ups work well for our team.

Write the topic sentence

Topic + controlling idea: "Written stand-ups work better for our team than video calls."

Add two supports

"First, people in different time zones can post when it suits them. Second, the updates stay in the channel as a record."

Add one example

"For example, last week a new teammate read a month of updates on her first day."

Add the closing sentence

"For these reasons, I suggest we keep video calls for Mondays only."

Read it as one

Written stand-ups work better for our team than video calls. First, people in different time zones can post when it suits them. Second, the updates stay in the channel as a record. For example, last week a new teammate read a month of updates on her first day. For these reasons, I suggest we keep video calls for Mondays only.

(No topic sentence) People post when it suits them. The updates stay as a record. A new teammate read them all.

(Two ideas) Written stand-ups help us. Also, our office needs better chairs.

(New idea at the end) ... So written stand-ups are good. We should also use a new chat app.

Start with the main idea, then support it.

Move the chairs to their own paragraph, or cut them.

End with the main idea again: "For these reasons, we should keep written stand-ups."

Cohesion: this, these, such

Read three versions of a short update.

We moved the tests to a faster machine. Moving the tests to a faster machine cut the build time by half. Cutting the build time by half means developers wait less.

We moved the tests to a faster machine and changed the cache. This cut the build time by half. It means developers wait less.

We moved the tests to a faster machine. This change cut the build time by half. As a result, developers wait less, and such small gains add up over a year.

The first version repeats whole phrases. The second uses "This" alone after two actions. Which one cut the time: the machine or the cache? The third version is clear. "This change" points back to one action and names it. "Such small gains" points back to the faster build.

The way sentences connect is called cohesion. Linkers are one tool. Reference words are another. Linking words covers linkers. This section covers reference words.

Reference tools for cohesion
ToolUseExample
this or that + singular nounpoint back and name the ideaThis change cut the time by half.
these or those + plural nounpoint back to several thingsThese tests now run in parallel.
such + plural or uncountable noun"of this kind"Such errors are rare.
such a + singular noun"of this kind", one thingSuch a change needs a review.
the + summary nounrefer to a known eventThe delay cost us a day.
the same key wordkeep a technical term stablethe cache ... the cache ... the cache

Summary nouns

A summary noun sums up a whole sentence in one word. After "this" or "these", it makes the link clear. Useful summary nouns: approach, change, decision, problem, issue, result, increase, drop, step, trend, method.

  • Sales fell for three months. This trend worried the board.
  • We decided to rewrite the service in Rust. This decision took a year to pay off.

Expert level: keep your terms stable

At school, many learners hear "do not repeat words". In technical writing, the opposite is often true. If you write "cache", then "buffer", then "store", the reader thinks there are three things. Choose one term and keep it, like a variable name in code. Use reference words to avoid boring repetition, not new synonyms.

Mixing singular and plural: "this changes" or "these change". Write "this change" or "these changes". Also, the article goes after such: "such a problem", never "a such problem". And never "such a errors": errors is plural, so write "such errors".

Punctuation that matters most

Four marks do most of the work: the full stop, the comma, the colon and the apostrophe. This section gives the rules in British style. For the short list of punctuation errors, see The error clinic.

Full stop and capital letters

A full stop ends a statement. Put one idea in each sentence. Then start the next sentence with a capital letter.

  • Capitals for: the first word of a sentence, I, names, places, days, months, languages and nationalities.
  • On Monday, I met Anna in London. She speaks English and Polish.
  • UK style uses no full stops in short forms: BBC, UK, NHS.

The comma: five jobs

Five jobs of the comma
JobExample
after an opening phrase or clauseAfter the meeting, we deployed. If it fails, call me.
before and, but, so, or, yet between two main clausesThe test failed, so we checked the logs.
around extra informationOur CTO, who started the company, will speak first.
between items in a listWe use Python, Rust and Go.
after a sentence linkerHowever, the cost is high.

A comma before the last "and" in a list is called the serial comma. British writers often leave it out. The University of Cambridge style guide uses it only when it prevents confusion. Whatever you choose, be consistent.

Never put a comma between a subject and its verb: "The new version of the app, is faster" is wrong. Never join two full sentences with a comma alone. That error is in the run-ons section below. For commas with who and which, see Relative clauses.

The colon

A colon says "here it is". It comes after a complete sentence. After it comes a list, an explanation or an example.

  • List: We need three things: time, money and people.
  • Explanation: The cause was simple: the disk was full.
  • Example or quote: The error said one thing: "permission denied".

In British style, the word after a colon starts with a small letter, unless it is a name. The University of Cambridge style guide gives this rule.

The main tools are: Git, Docker and Python.

We use tools such as: Git and Docker.

The main tools are Git, Docker and Python.

We use three main tools: Git, Docker and Python.

"The main tools are" is not a complete sentence. So it cannot stand before a colon. The same is true after such as, include and for example.

The apostrophe: two jobs

An apostrophe has only two jobs. It shows missing letters, and it shows who owns something.

The apostrophe
JobRuleExample
missing lettersshort formsdon't, it's (it is), we're, I've
owner, singularadd 'sthe team's plan, my manager's email
owner, singular ending in sadd 'sJames's laptop, the bus's door
owner, plural ending in sadd ' onlythe teams' plans, the users' data
owner, plural without sadd 'sthe children's room, people's ideas
pluralsno apostropheAPIs, PDFs, the 1990s

The most common apostrophe mistake is its and it's. Use a test: can you say "it is" or "it has"? Then write it's. If not, write its. "It's late." "The app lost its settings." The same test works for who's (who is) and whose, and for you're (you are) and your.

Short forms like don't and it's are normal in emails and chat. In formal essays and reports, many writers use the full forms: do not, it is.

What about the semicolon? It is correct between two closely linked sentences: "Demand rose; prices followed." But the UK government's style guide and the University of Cambridge style guide both advise avoiding it, because readers often misread it. A full stop is always safe.

Run-ons and fragments

Look at three broken sentences.

  • The server crashed we lost an hour of data.
  • The server crashed, we lost an hour of data.
  • Because the server crashed.

The first is a run-on sentence. Two full sentences run into each other with nothing between them. The second is a comma splice. Two full sentences are joined by a comma alone. The third is a fragment. It looks like a sentence, but it cannot stand alone. Use the four questions in the picture to check any sentence.

Four ways to fix a run-on or comma splice

  1. Full stop: The server crashed. We lost an hour of data.
  2. Comma + joiner: The server crashed, and we lost an hour of data.
  3. Dependent clause: When the server crashed, we lost an hour of data.
  4. Semicolon (formal): The server crashed; we lost an hour of data.

The full stop is the simplest fix, and it is always correct. The third fix is often the best, because it shows the link: time, reason or contrast.

Five kinds of fragment

Fragments and their fixes
FragmentWhat is missingFixed
Because the API was down.a main clauseBecause the API was down, we waited.
Such as Python and Go.the sentence it belongs toWe use fast languages, such as Python and Go.
Waiting for the review.a subject and a full verbI am waiting for the review.
A new feature for our users.a verbWe built a new feature for our users.
Fixed the bug and deployed it.a subjectWe fixed the bug and deployed it.

Fragments are fine in some places: headings, notes, slides and short chat replies like "Sounds good." Journalists sometimes use them for effect. In essays, reports and formal emails, write full sentences.

The "and then" chain. "We met and then we talked and then we decided and then we started." It is grammatical, but it is tiring to read. Split it, and use time words: "We met and talked. After that, we made a decision. Work started the next day."

Editing your paragraphs

Here is a first draft of a paragraph about remote work. Find the problems before you read the edited version.

remote work has good and bad sides. People save time on travel, they also spend less money on lunch. Because the office is far from the city centre. Our team tried it last year. My manager has a new car. some people felt lonely and they missed there colleagues and they wanted more meetings. We should also give everyone a new laptop.

Remote work has good and bad sides. On the plus side, people save time on travel, because our office is far from the city centre. They also spend less money on lunch. However, when our team tried it last year, some people felt lonely. They missed their colleagues and wanted more meetings. For this reason, a mix of home days and office days may work best.

The editor fixed seven problems. Two capital letters were missing. "People save time on travel, they also spend ..." was a comma splice. "Because the office is far ..." was a fragment. "My manager has a new car" broke the unity. "There" should be "their", and the "and ... and" chain was split. Finally, the laptop sentence added a new idea at the end. A real closing sentence replaced it.

Edit from big to small

  1. Rest, then read for the point. Wait at least ten minutes. Who is the reader? What is the main point?
  2. Make a reverse outline. List the topic sentence of each paragraph. Do they make a clear plan in a good order?
  3. Check unity. One idea per paragraph. Cut or move sentences that do not fit.
  4. Check cohesion. Put a noun after this and these. Keep key terms stable. Add a linker only where the link is not clear.
  5. Check sentences. Mix the lengths. Fix run-ons and fragments. Split sentences over 25 words.
  6. Check punctuation and spelling. Commas, colons, apostrophes, capitals. Then use the checklist in The error clinic.
  7. Read it aloud once. Your ear finds missing words and strange rhythm.

A reverse outline is an outline you make after you write, not before. It shows the real plan of your text. If a topic sentence is missing or out of order, you see it at once.

Let a script do the counting

This small script makes a reverse outline. It prints the first sentence of each paragraph and the words in each sentence. It also flags sentences over 25 words and paragraphs where three sentences start with the same word.

# paragraph_check.py: a reverse outline and a sentence check for a draft
import re

LIMIT = 25  # GOV.UK style: review any sentence longer than 25 words

def check(text: str) -> None:
    paragraphs = [p.strip() for p in text.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]
    for i, para in enumerate(paragraphs, 1):
        # split after . ! or ? when a space follows
        sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", para)
        lengths = [len(s.split()) for s in sentences]
        print(f"P{i} topic: {sentences[0]}")
        print(f"   words per sentence: {lengths}")
        for s, n in zip(sentences, lengths):
            if n > LIMIT:
                print(f"   long ({n} words): {s[:30]}...")
        starts = [s.split()[0].lower() for s in sentences]
        for word in sorted(set(starts)):
            if starts.count(word) >= 3:
                print(f"   {starts.count(word)} sentences start with '{word}'")

draft = """Our team should write more automated tests. The tests catch bugs early. The tests also make changes safer. The tests run in two minutes.
