Last month we had a bug in the payment service and it took three days to find because nobody had written a test for the refund code and the logs did not help us at all."""

check(draft)
P1 topic: Our team should write more automated tests.
   words per sentence: [7, 5, 6, 6]
   3 sentences start with 'the'
P2 topic: Last month we had a bug in the payment service and it took three days to find because nobody had written a test for the refund code and the logs did not help us at all.
   words per sentence: [36]
   long (36 words): Last month we had a bug in the...

Read the output. Paragraph 1 starts three sentences with "The tests". Use "They" once, and join two sentences. Paragraph 2 is one 36-word sentence. Its "topic sentence" is a story, not an idea. Split it, and add a topic sentence like "Missing tests cost us time last month." The script counts. You still decide.

The IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023) name paragraphing in Coherence and Cohesion. At band 6, paragraphing "may not always be logical", or the main topic may be unclear. At band 5, it may be missing. So a clear topic sentence in every body paragraph helps your score. See IELTS Writing.

Editing while you write the first draft. You stop after every sentence, and the ideas never flow. Write the whole draft first. Then edit in a separate step, from big to small. Also, grammar tools check sentences, not structure. They cannot tell you that a paragraph has two ideas.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for sentences and paragraphs
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + verb + (object)Write a simple sentenceThe build failed on Monday night.Long can still be simple: one subject, one verb.
Main clause, and or but or so + main clauseWrite a compound sentenceThe build failed, so we stayed late.Comma before the joiner.
Because or When + clause, main clauseWrite a complex sentenceBecause the build failed, we stayed late.The because part cannot stand alone.
Long sentence. Short sentence.Make a key point stand outIt saves every change, so nobody loses work. It is hard at first.Use the short one for your main point.
A, B and C in the same formWrite a parallel listOur job is to plan, build and test features.Not "to plan, building and tests".
Topic + controlling ideaWrite a topic sentenceCode review helps our team in two main ways.Not too broad, not a bare fact.
For example, + one real detailSupport with an exampleFor example, a test caught a wrong tax rate.One concrete detail beats three general ones.
For these reasons, + main ideaClose a paragraphFor these reasons, every feature needs tests.No new idea in the last sentence.
This or These + summary nounLink back with a clear nameThis change cut the build time by half.This + singular. These + plural.
Such + plural noun, such a + singular nounRefer to a kind of thingSuch errors are rare. Such a change needs review.Never "a such" or "such a errors".
Complete sentence: list or explanationUse a colonThe cause was simple: the disk was full.Small letter after the colon in British style.
noun's, nouns'Show the ownerthe team's plan, the teams' plansNever for plurals: APIs, not API's.
it's = it is, its = of itChoose the right formIt's late. The app lost its settings.Test: can you say "it is"?
Sentence. Sentence.Fix a comma spliceThe test failed. We checked the logs.A comma alone cannot join two sentences.
Fragment, main clauseFix a fragmentBecause the API was down, we waited.Join it to a main clause, or add a subject and verb.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the correct answer

Which is a compound sentence?

  • Because it rained, we stayed in.
  • It rained, so we stayed in.
  • The heavy rain in the north of the city on Monday.

Two main clauses joined by so. The first is complex. The third has no verb, so it is a fragment.

Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about code review?

  • Code is important.
  • Our team reviewed 40 pull requests last week.
  • Code review helps our team in two main ways.

It has a topic and a controlling idea. The first is too broad. The second is a bare fact.

Which sentence is a comma splice?

  • The test failed, so we checked the logs.
  • The test failed, we checked the logs.
  • When the test failed, we checked the logs.

Two full sentences are joined by a comma alone.

Which uses the colon correctly?

  • The main tools are: Git and Docker.
  • We need two things: time and people.
  • We use tools such as: Git and Docker.

A colon needs a complete sentence before it. "The main tools are" is not complete.

Which uses the apostrophe correctly?

  • We updated all the API's.
  • The team's plan is ready.
  • The app lost it's data.

One team owns the plan: team's. Plurals take no apostrophe. "It's" means "it is".

Which second sentence links back best?

  • We changed the cache and the database. This made it faster.
  • We changed the cache. This change made the app faster.
  • We changed the cache. This changes made the app faster.

"This change" names one clear action. The first is unclear. The third mixes singular and plural.

Fill the gap

We changed three settings. These ? made the app twice as fast.

Data loss is rare. But ? errors are very serious.

The (team) plan is ready, but the two other teams are late.

All the (users) data is stored in Europe.

The app lost ? settings after the update.

? raining again, so I'll work from home.

Our CTO, ? started the company, will speak first.

The test failed, ? we checked the logs.

Think and write

  1. Join these two sentences in two ways: once as a compound sentence and once as a complex sentence. "The laptop was old. It was still fast."
    Answer

    Compound: The laptop was old, but it was still fast. Complex: Although the laptop was old, it was still fast.

  2. Fix this run-on in three different ways: "The deploy finished the site was still slow."
    Answer

    (1) The deploy finished. The site was still slow. (2) The deploy finished, but the site was still slow. (3) Although the deploy finished, the site was still slow.

  3. Make each fragment a full sentence: (a) Because the API was down. (b) Such as Python and Go. (c) Waiting for the review.
    Model answer

    (a) Because the API was down, the app showed an error. (b) We hire people who know languages such as Python and Go. (c) I am waiting for the review.

  4. Add capitals and punctuation: "on monday our team met in london we discussed three things the budget the hiring plan and the new office its a big week for the companys future"
    Answer

    On Monday, our team met in London. We discussed three things: the budget, the hiring plan and the new office. It's a big week for the company's future.

  5. Make this list parallel and this text less repetitive: "The new process is faster, cheaper and it makes fewer errors. The new process starts in May. The new process needs training."
    Model answer

    The new process is faster, cheaper and less error-prone. It starts in May, but it needs some training first. ("Less error-prone" keeps the adjective form. "It" replaces two repeats.)

  6. Expert: write a five-sentence paragraph on "Should junior developers work from home?" Use the shape topic, support, example, support, close. Include one "this + summary noun" and one colon.
    Model answer

    Junior developers learn faster when they spend some days in the office. First, they can ask quick questions and get answers at once. For example, a new hire can solve a setup problem in five minutes with a colleague next to her. Second, they see how seniors work: how they plan, debug and review. This learning is hard to get on video calls, so two or three office days a week make sense for juniors.

  7. Expert: here is a reverse outline of a short report. Which topic sentence is in the wrong place, and which does not belong? (1) Our app has become slow for many users. (2) We suggest moving to a faster database next quarter. (3) The main cause is the old database. (4) Our office party is on 12 December.
    Answer

    Line 2 is a conclusion, so it should come last: problem, cause, then suggestion. Line 4 does not belong. It has nothing to do with the app, so cut it or put it in a different message.

Key takeaways

  • A simple sentence has one main clause. Compound sentences join two with and, but or so. Complex sentences add a dependent clause.
  • Variety means mixing lengths and starts. Put your key point in a short sentence or at the end.
  • Use the same grammar for each item in a list.
  • A paragraph has one idea: topic sentence, support, an example, and a closing sentence.
  • A good topic sentence has a topic and a controlling idea.
  • Link with this or these + a summary noun. Keep technical terms stable.
  • A colon follows a complete sentence. An apostrophe shows missing letters or an owner, never a plural.
  • Fix comma splices and run-ons with a full stop, a joiner or a dependent clause. Fix fragments by adding what is missing.
  • Edit from big to small: point, outline, unity, cohesion, sentences, punctuation, then read aloud.

Sources

  • Purdue OWL: On paragraphs. Unity, coherence, topic sentences, development and when to start a new paragraph.
  • Purdue OWL: Run-ons, comma splices and fused sentences. What they are and the ways to fix them.
  • Purdue OWL: Sentence fragments. Common fragment types and how to reattach or complete them.
  • University of Cambridge: Style guide. British rules for colons, apostrophes, list commas, semicolons and dates.
  • GOV.UK: A to Z style guide. Review sentences over 25 words, avoid semicolons, no full stops in abbreviations.
  • IELTS Writing band descriptors (updated May 2023). Paragraphing and reference in Coherence and Cohesion.

Emails and messages

Most work in English happens in writing. You ask, remind, complain, say sorry and invite people by email and chat. This chapter gives you clear shapes for each job, eight model emails and the rules for chat at work.

  • Build an email from seven parts: subject line, greeting, purpose, details, action, closing and signature.
  • Choose a formal, neutral or informal style and keep it from start to end.
  • Write requests, follow-ups, complaints, apologies and invitations with ready phrases.
  • Write short, complete chat messages that work across time zones.
  • Put the main point first so busy readers can act quickly.

What makes a good email

Read this email from a developer to a colleague in another team.

Subject: Read access to the billing repo by Tuesday?

Hi Priya,

Could you give me read access to the billing repository? I need it for ticket 482.

I start the fix on Wednesday, so Tuesday would be perfect. My GitHub name is dan-kim.

Thanks a lot,
Daniel

Priya can act in ten seconds. She knows what Daniel wants, why he wants it and by when. She does not need to write back with a question. That is the test of a good email.

Each part has one job.

  1. Subject line: tells the reader what the email is about before they open it.
  2. Greeting: says hello in the right style.
  3. Purpose: says why you write, in the first one or two lines.
  4. Details: give only the facts the reader needs: dates, numbers, names, links.
  5. Action: says exactly what you want the reader to do, and by when.
  6. Closing: says goodbye in the same style as the greeting.
  7. Signature: your name, and at work your role and team.

Think of the reader

Who is it? A friend, a colleague, a client, a stranger? This decides the style.

Say your goal in one sentence

"I want Priya to give me access by Tuesday." If you cannot say it, you are not ready to write.

Write the subject line

Put the topic and, if needed, the action or date: "Read access to the billing repo by Tuesday?"

Write the first two lines

Purpose and action come first. A reader who stops here still knows what to do.

Add the details

Short paragraphs or a list. One idea per paragraph. Cut anything the reader does not need.

Check before you send

Names spelled right? Dates correct? File attached? Right people in the To line? Same style from start to end?

Many learners hide the request at the end, after a long story. The reader must read everything to find it. Put the request near the top. Explain after it.

Formal, neutral and informal style

Here is one message in three styles. The facts are the same. The words change.

Dear Mr Hughes,

I am writing to inform you that the meeting on 4 December has been postponed. I apologise for any inconvenience. I will send you a new date as soon as possible.

Yours sincerely,
Anna Kowalski

Hi David,

I'm afraid we need to move the meeting on 4 December. Sorry about that. I'll send a new date by Friday.

Kind regards,
Anna

Hi Dave,

Bad news, Thursday's meeting is off. Sorry! New date coming soon.

Cheers,
Anna

Register means how formal your language is. Choose it from your reader and your situation. The chapter Register, collocation and idiom explains register in depth. Here are the signs in emails.

Signs of each style in an email
SignFormalNeutralInformal
Readera stranger, a company, a senior person outside your teammost colleagues and clientsfriends and close teammates
GreetingDear Ms Lee, / Dear Sir or Madam,Hi Ms Lee, / Hello Sam, / Dear Sam,Hi Sam, / Hey Sam,
Short formsnone: I am, we willsome: I'm, we'llmany: I'm, can't, it's
Verbsreceive, inform, requireget, tell, needget, let you know
ClosingYours sincerely, / Yours faithfully,Kind regards, / Best regards, / Best wishes,Cheers, / Thanks, / See you soon,

Not sure? Choose neutral. Neutral is polite to everyone. Then copy the style of the reply you get.

Formal does not mean long. A formal email can have four short sentences. Formal means polite words, full forms and no jokes.

Dear Sir or Madam, my laptop is broken lol. Fix it ASAP pls. Cheers!

Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing about a laptop that stopped working after two weeks. I would be grateful if you could repair or replace it. Yours faithfully, ...

The wrong version mixes styles. It starts formal, then sounds like a chat. Keep one style from the greeting to the closing.

Subject lines, openings and closings

Subject lines

Weak

Question

Meeting

Urgent!!!

(no subject)

Strong

Can you review PR 219 by Friday?

Design review moved to Thu 4 Dec, 14:00

Payments down for EU users since 09:10

Enquiry about your evening IELTS course

A strong subject line is specific. It names the topic. It often has a date, a number or an action. The reader can sort the email without opening it.

  • Keep it short: about three to eight words.
  • Put the action or date in it when there is one: "by Friday", "moved to 4 Dec".
  • Change the subject when a reply starts a new topic.
  • Use "urgent" only for real emergencies. If every email is urgent, none is.

Email programs add short labels. Re: means this is a reply. Fwd: means someone forwarded the email. Some teams also start the subject with a tag, like [Action needed] or [FYI]. FYI means "for your information", so no action is needed.

Greetings

How to start an email
SituationGreeting
You do not know the nameDear Sir or Madam, / Dear Customer Service Team, / Dear Hiring Manager,
Formal, you know the nameDear Ms Lee, / Dear Dr Rossi, / Dear Mr Hughes,
Formal, you do not know if the person is a man or a womanDear Alex Morgan,
Neutral, a colleague or clientHi Sam, / Hello Sam, / Dear Sam,
A groupHi everyone, / Hi team, / Dear all,
A friendHi Sam, / Hey Sam,

Use a title with the family name: Ms Lee, Mr Hughes. Use a first name alone: Sam. Ms is the safe title for a woman when you do not know what she prefers. In British English, Mr, Ms and Dr have no full stop. In American English they do: Mr., Ms., Dr. Formal American letters often use a colon: "Dear Ms. Lee:".

First lines

  • To start a new topic, formal: "I am writing to ask about ..." / "I am writing regarding ..."
  • To reply: "Thank you for your email." / "Thanks for getting back to me."
  • To link to an earlier event: "Following our call this morning, ..." / "As we discussed on Monday, ..."
  • To a stranger: introduce yourself first. "My name is Kenji Sato. I am a developer at Brightline."

"I hope you are well" is friendly, but you can skip it. Going straight to the point is also polite in English.

Closing lines and sign-offs

Before the sign-off, add one line that looks forward: "Please let me know if you have any questions." "I look forward to hearing from you." (formal) "Speak soon." (informal)

British English has a classic rule for formal letters. Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully. Dear Ms Lee, with a name, goes with Yours sincerely. American writers usually write Sincerely. In most work emails, Kind regards or Best regards is fine for both.

Hi Mr John,

Dear Sir, (to a woman, or to a person you do not know)

Waiting for your reply.

Dear Sir or Madam, ... Yours sincerely,

Hi John, / Dear Mr Smith,

Dear Sir or Madam, / Dear Hiring Manager,

I look forward to hearing from you.

Dear Sir or Madam, ... Yours faithfully,

"Waiting for your reply" sounds impatient, like an order. "I look forward to hearing from you" says the same thing politely.

Requests and follow-ups

Subject: Can you review the API docs by Thursday?

Hi Marta,

Could you review the new API docs for the search service? They are short, about six pages. Here is the link: docs/search-api-v2.

We publish them on Friday morning. So Thursday at the latest would be great. I am most worried about the section on error codes. Is it clear for people outside our team?

If you don't have time this week, just let me know. I can ask someone else.

Thanks a lot,
Omar

  • The request is in the first line.
  • The deadline comes with a reason, so it does not sound bossy.
  • Omar says exactly what to check. A narrow request is easier to say yes to.
  • He gives an easy way to say no. This is polite and saves time.

The politeness ladder

English requests get softer as they get longer. Choose the step that fits the size of the favour and the person.

  1. Can you send me the file? (direct, fine with close teammates)
  2. Could you send me the file, please? (neutral, the safe choice)
  3. Would you mind sending me the file? (polite, for a bigger favour)
  4. I was wondering if you could send me the file. (very soft)
  5. I would be grateful if you could send me the file. (formal)

"I was wondering" uses the past tense, but it is about now. The past tense adds distance, and distance sounds polite. The grammar of could and would is in Modal verbs. How to soften without losing the point is in Hedging and stance.

"Would you mind to send ..." is wrong. After "would you mind", use the -ing form: "Would you mind sending ...?" Also, "Kindly do the needful" sounds strange to most British and American readers. Write the action: "Could you approve the invoice?"

Follow-ups

A follow-up is a second email about the same thing. You send it when nobody replied, or after a meeting.

Subject: Re: Quote for 20 laptops

Hi Mark,

I'm just following up on my email from last Tuesday about the laptop quote. I've copied it below.

We need to place the order by 30 November. Could you send the quote by this Friday? If someone else handles quotes now, could you forward this to them?

Best regards,
Sara Novak
Office Manager, Brightline Studio

  • She replies in the same thread, so Mark sees the first email.
  • She does not blame. People are busy, and emails get lost.
  • She adds a new reason to act: the order deadline.
  • She offers a way forward if Mark is the wrong person.

Follow-ups can get firmer each time. Start soft. Get clearer, but stay polite.

Three follow-ups, from soft to firm
WhenModel
First reminderJust a quick reminder about the quote. Is Friday still possible?
Second reminderI'm following up again on the quote. We need it by Friday to place the order in time.
Last reminderIf I don't receive the quote by Friday, I'm afraid we will order from another supplier.

"Why didn't you answer my email?" sounds angry. "Did you get my email?" can sound like an accusation too. Use "Just following up on ..." or "I wanted to check if you had a chance to look at ..."

Complaints and apologies

Subject: Complaint: repeated outages, account 7731-204

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about repeated internet outages at my home. My account number is 7731-204.

Since 3 November, the connection has failed six times. Each outage lasted between two and five hours. I work from home, so I have lost almost two full working days.

I reported the problem by phone on 5 and 10 November. The reference numbers are R-5521 and R-5589. However, nothing has changed.

I would be grateful if you could send a technician this week. I would also like a refund for the days without service.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Tomas Berger

Tomas is angry, but his email is calm. The facts do the work. A good complaint follows six steps.

  1. Purpose: say that you are complaining and about what.
  2. Facts: dates, times, numbers, order or account numbers.
  3. Effect: how the problem hurt you.
  4. History: what you have already done.
  5. Request: exactly what you want: a repair, a refund, a visit.
  6. Close: a polite closing line. A deadline if needed.

Your service is a joke. This is the WORST company ever. I demand my money back NOW.

The service has failed six times this month. I would like a refund for the days without service by 30 November.

Capital letters look like shouting. Insults make the reader defensive. Facts and a clear request get results.

Apologies

Subject: Yesterday's outage: what happened and what we are doing

Dear Ms Okafor,

I am sorry for the outage that affected your team yesterday. Our booking system was down for 47 minutes, from 14:05 to 14:52.

The cause was a faulty update on our side. We removed the update and restored the service. No customer data was lost.

To stop this from happening again, we now test every update on a copy of the live system first. We have also added one free month to your account.

Please accept our apologies again. If you have any questions, just reply to this email or call me on the number below.

Kind regards,
Leo Martins
Customer Success Manager

A good apology has five parts. Leo uses all five.

  1. Say sorry at the start, for a specific thing.
  2. Say what happened in one or two plain sentences.
  3. Take responsibility. "On our side" means "our fault".
  4. Fix it now, and offer something if it is fair.
  5. Prevent it. Say what will be different next time.

Small mistakes need small apologies. For a late reply, one line is enough: "Sorry for the slow reply. Here is the file." "Thanks for your patience" is a friendly option.

Sorry for to reply late.

We apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused, if any.

Sorry, but the server was old, and the other team didn't tell us, and ...

Sorry for replying late. / Sorry for the late reply.

We are sorry that your team could not use the system for 47 minutes.

Sorry. The update had a bug. We have fixed it, and we now test updates first.

"Any inconvenience this may have caused" sounds empty. It does not name the problem. A long list of excuses sounds like blame. Name the problem, own it, fix it.

Invitations, replies, enquiries and introductions

Subject: Farewell lunch for Mei, Friday 12:30

Hi everyone,

As you know, Friday is Mei's last day with us. Let's say goodbye properly!

We're having lunch at Green Bowl on King Street at 12:30. Everyone pays for their own meal, and the team pays for Mei's.

Can you let me know by Wednesday if you're coming? I need to book a table.

Cheers,
Jon

P.S. Please don't tell Mei about the cake!

An invitation answers four questions: what, when, where and how to reply. The P.S. adds a small extra point after the signature. It is fine in informal emails.

Subject: Re: Farewell lunch for Mei, Friday 12:30

Hi Jon,

Thanks for organising this! I'm afraid I can't make it. I'm at a client's office all day on Friday.

Could I give you some money for the cake? I'd also love to sign a card if there is one.

Have a great time!
Ana

A good "no" has three parts. Thank the person. Say no with a short reason. Offer something else if you can. To say yes, write "Count me in!" (informal) or "I'd be happy to come." (neutral).

Subject: Enquiry about your evening IELTS course

Dear Admissions Team,

I am writing to ask about your evening IELTS preparation course. I saw it on your website.

I would be grateful if you could tell me:

  • the start date of the next course
  • the class times and the largest class size
  • the total fee, and whether it includes the textbook

I work full time, so evening classes suit me best. My current level is about B1.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Kenji Sato

An enquiry asks for information. Lists make questions easy to answer one by one. In American English, the word is usually spelled inquiry.

Subject: Hello from your new backend engineer

Hi team,

I'm Elena, and I joined the platform team today as a backend engineer. I'm really happy to be here.

Before this, I worked for four years on payment systems in Rust and Go. I enjoy hard bugs and clear documentation.

I live in Lisbon, so I'm usually online from 9:00 to 17:30 UK time.

Over the next two weeks, I'd love to have a short call with each of you. I'll send some invites soon.

Looking forward to working with you all,
Elena Petrova

An introduction says who you are, what you did before and how people can work with you. Your working hours are useful when the team lives in different time zones.

Many exams test emails and letters. See IELTS General Training Task 1 in IELTS Writing, Write an Email in TOEFL iBT, and Writing Part 2 in Cambridge exams. Examiners check that you cover every point in the task and keep one style all the way.

Chat messages at work

Chat tools like Slack and Microsoft Teams are faster than email. But fast does not mean careless. Compare two ways to ask one question.

Slow

Ravi (10:02): Hi

Ravi (10:15): Are you there?

Lena (10:31): Hi, yes?

Ravi (10:32): Is staging down?

Fast

Ravi (10:02): Hi Lena, quick question. Is the staging database down? My tests can't connect since 10:00. No rush if you're busy.

Lena (10:31): Yes, we're upgrading it. Back by 11:00.

In the slow version, Lena waits for the question. In the fast version, she can answer as soon as she sees it. The website nohello.net makes this point: say hello and ask the question in the same message.

Rules for chat at work

  • One complete message. Greeting, question and context together. Each message sends a notification.
  • Add context. Give the error, the link and what you tried. "It doesn't work" is not enough.
  • Say how urgent it is. "No rush", "by end of day" or "blocking me now".
  • Use threads. A thread keeps a discussion in one place.
  • Prefer team channels to private messages. Other people can learn from the answer.
  • Use @mentions with care. Mention a person when you need them. Mention the whole channel only for something important.
  • Use emoji reactions for small replies. A thumbs-up can mean "seen" or "OK".

Short forms in chat

Common short forms at work
Short formMeaningModel
FYIfor your informationFYI, the release moved to Monday.
EODend of the working dayI'll send it by EOD.
ASAPas soon as possibleCan you check this ASAP? (can sound pushy)
OOOout of office, on leaveI'm OOO until Tuesday.
WFHworking from homeWFH today, online as usual.
PTALplease take a lookPTAL at PR 219 when you can.

Use these with your own team. In emails to clients or strangers, write the full words.

Do not use chat for bad news or angry feedback. Short words look colder in text than they sound in person. Call the person, or write a careful email. For more on remote work, see Presentations and remote work. For pull requests and status updates, see Writing at work.

Expert level: emails that busy people act on

Senior people get hundreds of messages a day. They read the subject and the first two lines. Then they decide. These habits help your email survive that test.

Bottom line up front

BLUF means "bottom line up front". The idea comes from US military writing. The first sentence gives the main point and the action. The reasons come after.

Hi Chris, last week we started testing the new database. At first, the results were good. Then on Thursday we saw slow queries. We looked at the logs and found ... So we think we should delay the launch by one week. Is that OK?

Hi Chris, can we delay the database launch by one week, to 12 December? Please decide by Wednesday.

Reason: on Thursday, some queries became ten times slower under load. We know the cause and need five days to fix and retest it.

A 2016 Harvard Business Review article by Kabir Sehgal described this military style. It also suggested keywords at the start of the subject line, like ACTION, INFO, REQUEST and DECISION. Many teams use similar tags.

Write for people who skim

  • One email, one topic. Two topics? Send two emails with two subject lines.
  • Short paragraphs. Two to four lines each.
  • Lists for questions, options and steps. Number them, so people can answer "1: yes, 2: no".
  • Clear dates. Write "3 December 2026", not "3/12". British readers read 3/12 as 3 December. American readers read it as March 12.
  • Time zones. Write the zone: "15:00 CET (14:00 UTC)".

To, CC, BCC and Reply all

Who gets the email
FieldMeaningUse it for
Tothe main readerspeople who must act or answer
CCcarbon copypeople who should know, but need not act
BCCblind carbon copylarge groups, so people cannot see each other's addresses

Before you click Reply all, ask: does everyone need my answer? "Thanks!" to forty people wastes forty minutes of attention. When you move someone to BCC, say so: "Moving Sam to BCC to save his inbox."

Clear English for an international team

  • Avoid idioms and jokes. "Let's touch base" or "it's a ballpark figure" can confuse readers. Write "Let's talk" and "a rough estimate".
  • Use one word for one thing. If you say "ticket", do not switch to "issue" and "card".
  • Never write in capital letters for emphasis. Use bold once, for the date or the action.
  • Never send passwords, card numbers or private data by email. Email is not secret by default.

Before you send an important email, read only the subject and the first two lines. Does the reader know what to do? If not, move the action up.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for emails and messages
PatternPurposeModelNote
I am writing to + verbGive the purpose of a formal emailI am writing to ask about your evening course.Not "I am writing for asking".
Could you + verb ..., please?Make a neutral, polite requestCould you send me the logs, please?Add a reason or a deadline.
Would you mind + -ing ...?Ask for a bigger favour politelyWould you mind checking my draft?Never "would you mind to check".
I was wondering if you could + verbMake a very soft requestI was wondering if you could join the call.The past tense is about now.
I would be grateful if you could + verbMake a formal requestI would be grateful if you could refund the fee.Good in complaints and enquiries.
I'm just following up on + nounRemind someone politelyI'm just following up on my email from Tuesday.Reply in the same thread.
I would like to complain about + nounOpen a formal complaintI would like to complain about repeated outages.Facts, not insults.
I am sorry for + noun / -ingApologise for something specificI am sorry for the late reply.Not "sorry for to reply".
Please accept our apologies for + nounApologise formally for a companyPlease accept our apologies for the delay.Then say what you will fix.
Would you like to + verb ...?Invite someoneWould you like to join us for lunch on Friday?Say when, where and how to reply.
Thanks for + -ing, but I'm afraid I can't + verbSay no politelyThanks for inviting me, but I'm afraid I can't come.Add a short reason.
I have attached + nounPoint to an attachmentI have attached the signed contract.Check that the file is really there.
Please let me know if + clauseInvite questions or a replyPlease let me know if you have any questions.Not "Let me know if any questions".
I look forward to + -ingClose a formal emailI look forward to hearing from you.Not "look forward to hear".
Hi + name, quick question: + questionStart a chat messageHi Lena, quick question: is staging down?Never "Hi" alone, then wait.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

You write to a company. You do not know the name of the reader. Which greeting is best?

  • Hi there,
  • Dear Sir or Madam,
  • Dear Sir,

"Dear Sir or Madam" works for any reader. "Dear Sir" assumes a man.

Your email starts "Dear Sir or Madam". Which closing matches it in British English?

  • Yours sincerely,
  • Yours faithfully,
  • Cheers,

No name in the greeting: Yours faithfully. A name in the greeting: Yours sincerely.

Which subject line is best?

  • Question
  • URGENT!!! PLEASE READ
  • Can you approve the March invoice by Friday?

It names the topic, the action and the deadline.

Which request is correct?

  • Would you mind to send me the file?
  • Would you mind sending me the file?
  • Would you mind send me the file?

After "would you mind", use the -ing form.

Which chat message is best?

  • Hi
  • Are you free?
  • Hi Tom, could you check why build 812 failed? The log is in the thread. Not urgent.

One message with the question, the context and the urgency.

You write to forty parents about a school event. You do not want them to see each other's addresses. Where do you put their addresses?

  • To
  • CC
  • BCC

BCC hides the list of readers from each other.

Fill the gap

I am writing ? ask about your evening course.

I look forward to (hear) from you.

I'm just following ? on my email from Monday.

I am sorry ? the late reply.

I would be ? if you could send me a refund.

Thanks for the invitation, but I'm ? I can't come.

Please find ? the signed contract.

Think and write

  1. Make this request more polite in two ways: "Send me the report."
    Answer

    Could you send me the report, please? Would you mind sending me the report? Also good: I was wondering if you could send me the report by Thursday.

  2. Fix the mixed style: "Dear Mr Lopez, hey, thanks a ton for the quote. We wanna go ahead. Yours faithfully, Ana."
    Model answer

    Dear Mr Lopez, Thank you for the quote. We would like to go ahead with the order. Yours sincerely, Ana Ruiz. (A name in the greeting means Yours sincerely. Kind regards is also fine.)

  3. Rewrite this follow-up so it is polite: "Why haven't you answered? I sent this a week ago."
    Model answer

    Hi Sam, I'm just following up on my email from last Monday about the test plan. Could you let me know by Thursday if it looks OK? Thanks, ...

  4. Your package came two weeks late, and the box was damaged. Write the first two sentences of a formal complaint. Include the order number 66120.
    Model answer

    Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to complain about order 66120. It arrived on 14 November, two weeks late, and the box was badly damaged.

  5. You missed a code review deadline. Write a three-sentence apology to your teammate. Say sorry, give the new time and offer something.
    Model answer

    Hi Priya, sorry I didn't finish your review yesterday. I'll send my comments by 11:00 today. If you want, we can also go through them together on a short call.

  6. Expert: rewrite this email with BLUF. Put the request first and keep it under 50 words. "Hi Chris, as you know we have been testing the new search service. The tests went well at first, but on Friday we saw some errors under heavy load. We think we need more time, maybe one week. Would that be OK?"
    Model answer

    Subject: Can we move the search launch to 12 Dec? Hi Chris, can we delay the search launch by one week, to 12 December? Please decide by Wednesday. Reason: on Friday we saw errors under heavy load. We need five days to fix and retest. Thanks, ...

Key takeaways

  • An email has seven parts. The subject, the purpose and the action carry the message.
  • Choose formal, neutral or informal from your reader. Keep one style from start to end. Neutral is the safe choice.
  • A good subject line is specific. Add the action or date when there is one.
  • Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully. Dear + name goes with Yours sincerely. Kind regards fits most work emails.
  • Requests get softer as they get longer: can you, could you, would you mind, I was wondering if.
  • A complaint uses calm facts and a clear request. An apology names the problem, owns it, fixes it and prevents it.
  • In chat, send one complete message. Never "Hi" alone, then wait.
  • Put the bottom line up front. Busy readers decide after two lines.

Sources

  • British Council LearnEnglish: Starting and finishing emails. Formal, informal and shared greetings and sign-offs.
  • Purdue OWL: Email etiquette. Subject lines, greetings, short paragraphs, signatures, Reply all and privacy.
  • Harvard Business Review: How to write email with military precision (Kabir Sehgal, 2016). Bottom line up front and subject line keywords.
  • Slack blog: Etiquette tips in Slack. Threads, channels over private messages, careful mentions and emoji reactions.
  • nohello.net. Why you should ask your question in the same chat message as your hello.

Essays, reports and summaries

Essays argue. Reports inform and recommend. Summaries make a long text short. These three are the main kinds of longer writing at university and at work. This chapter shows how to plan, build and check each one, with model texts written for this book.

  • Recognise the four common essay types and plan each one.
  • Write an introduction with a clear thesis, body paragraphs and a conclusion.
  • Paraphrase a sentence and summarise a text in your own words.
  • Organise a report and a proposal with clear headings.
  • Use academic style: precise, formal, objective and careful.

Three kinds of writing, three jobs

Here is one topic, a pair-programming trial, written in three ways.

I believe that every software team should try pair programming. It improves quality and spreads knowledge, and these benefits are worth the small loss of speed.

2. Findings. During the six-week trial, bugs after release fell from 14 to 6. The team finished 41 tickets, compared with 45 before the trial.

The report describes a six-week pair-programming trial. It found fewer bugs and slightly slower delivery, and it recommends pairing for complex work only.

The essay gives an opinion and defends it. The report gives facts under a heading. The summary repeats the main points of another text in fewer words. Each one has a different reader and a different shape.

Essay, report and summary compared
EssayReportSummary
Main jobargue a positioninform, evaluate, recommendshorten another text
Readera teacher or examinera manager or decision makersomeone with no time to read the original
Headingsnoyesno
Your opinionyes, all the wayonly in the recommendationsno
Listsrarelyoftenno

Do not write a report like an essay. A manager wants to find the findings and the recommendations in seconds. Use headings and put facts under them. Save your opinion for the recommendations.

Four essay types

Read four questions on one topic. Each one asks for a different essay.

  1. Opinion: AI writing tools should be banned in schools. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
  2. Discussion: Some people say AI tools help students learn. Others say they stop students thinking. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
  3. Problem and solution: Many students now copy homework answers from AI tools. Why is this a problem, and what can schools do?
  4. Advantages and disadvantages: Do the advantages of AI tools for homework outweigh the disadvantages?

The last sentence of the question tells you the type. Every type needs a thesis. A thesis is your answer to the question in one sentence. Its shape depends on the type.

The thesis for each essay type
TypeThesis shapeModel thesis
OpinionI agree / disagree / partly agree, because ...I disagree, because a ban is impossible to enforce and wastes a chance to teach good use.
DiscussionBoth views have merit, but I believe ...Both views have merit, but I believe AI tools help students who already know the basics.
Problem and solutionThis causes X and Y, which schools can reduce by ...Copying weakens learning and makes grades unfair, but schools can reduce it by changing how they test.
Advantages and disadvantagesThe advantages / disadvantages outweigh ..., because ...The disadvantages outweigh the advantages, because students skip the thinking that homework is for.

Exam versions of these types, with timing and a two-part question type, are in IELTS Writing. This chapter looks at the same shapes for any essay.

Answering a different question. "To what extent do you agree?" needs your position, not a list of advantages and disadvantages. Underline the instruction words before you plan.

Planning: from question to outline

Good essays are planned before they are written. A plan of five minutes saves twenty minutes of rewriting. Watch one question become an outline.

Take the question apart

Find three things. The topic: programming courses. The focus: for every university student. The instruction: to what extent do you agree?

Collect ideas fast

Write every idea for and against in two minutes. Do not judge them yet. Jobs use data. Logical thinking. Full timetables. Some students will never code.

Choose your position

Pick the side with the best ideas, not the side you feel first. "I largely agree, if the course is practical."

Pick two or three main ideas

Choose ideas you can explain well. Two developed ideas beat five short ones.

Add one example to each

A biology student who sorts data with a script. A student who learns to test ideas by debugging.

Write the outline

One line per paragraph. Now you can write without stopping to think about structure.

Intro   computers in every job -> question in new words -> thesis: largely agree, if practical
Body 1  coding is useful in many careers -> data, automation -> biology student, sorting data
Body 2  coding teaches a way of thinking -> small steps, testing, evidence -> useful in law, medicine
Body 3  other view: timetables are full -> reply: one short course, linked to each subject
End     restate position -> recommendation: design courses around each subject

Instruction words

What the instruction word asks you to do
WordWhat to do
discusslook at different sides, then usually give your view
to what extentsay how much you agree: fully, largely, partly or not at all
evaluatejudge how good or useful something is, with evidence
compareshow how two things are similar and different
contrastshow how two things are different
analysebreak something into parts and explain how they work
outlinegive the main points only, without detail

Starting to write without a position. Your view then changes halfway through, and the conclusion does not match the introduction. Decide your thesis first. Then every paragraph supports it.

Introduction, body and conclusion

Here is an introduction to the programming question. It has three sentences.

Computers now shape almost every area of work and study. For this reason, some people argue that all university students should complete at least one programming course, whatever they study. I largely agree with this view, provided that the course is practical and connected to each student's subject.

The first sentence gives background. The second gives the question in new words. The third is the thesis. The introduction moves from general to specific, like a funnel.

The introduction

  • Background: one sentence about the topic. Make it about this topic, not about the whole world.
  • The question in new words: show the reader what the essay is about. Paraphrase it. Do not copy it.
  • Thesis: your answer. Some writers add a map: "This essay will first ... and then ..."

The body

Each body paragraph has one main idea. It opens with a topic sentence. Then it explains the idea, gives an example or evidence and links back to the thesis. The chapter Writing sentences and paragraphs shows this shape in detail. Words that join the paragraphs are in Linking words.

A strong opinion essay often has one paragraph for the other side. It states the opposite view fairly. Then it answers it. This is called a concession and a rebuttal. It shows the reader that you thought about both sides.

The conclusion

  • Restate your thesis in new words.
  • Join the main points into one idea. Do not list every point again.
  • End with the wider meaning, a recommendation or a look at the future.

Nowadays, technology is very important in our lives. (too general, could start any essay)

In conclusion, coding helps students. Another advantage is that it is fun. (a new idea in the conclusion)

Computers now shape almost every area of work and study. (about this topic)

In conclusion, a short, practical course would benefit most students. (the thesis in new words)

"In conclusion" is fine in exams. Some university teachers find it too mechanical in longer essays. There, a sentence like "Overall, the evidence shows ..." can start the conclusion instead.

Two model essays

Here are two essays of about 300 words, written for this book. Read the plan, then the essay, then the comments.

Model essay 1: an opinion essay

Question: Some people think that every university student should take at least one programming course, whatever their main subject. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

  • Thesis: largely agree, if the course is practical and linked to each subject.
  • Body 1: coding is useful in many careers. Example: a biology student sorts data with a script.
  • Body 2: coding teaches a way of thinking: small steps, testing, evidence.
  • Body 3: other view, full timetables. Reply: one short course, linked to the subject.
  • Conclusion: restate, and advise universities how to design the course.

Computers now shape almost every area of work and study. For this reason, some people argue that all university students should complete at least one programming course, whatever they study. I largely agree with this view, provided that the course is practical and connected to each student's subject.

The main argument for such a course is that coding is now useful in many careers, not only in technology. Researchers, accountants and journalists all work with large amounts of data. Even a little programming allows them to automate boring tasks and check their results. For example, a biology student who can write a short script can sort thousands of measurements in seconds, instead of copying them by hand. This saves time and reduces mistakes.

A second benefit is the way of thinking that programming teaches. To write a working program, students must break a large problem into small steps and test each one. When the code fails, they have to find the cause from evidence rather than guess. These habits are valuable in any field, from law to medicine.

Critics point out that university timetables are already full, and that many students will never write code again. This is a fair concern. However, the course does not need to be long or highly technical. A single term focused on the student's field, such as data analysis for economics or text tools for history, would take little time. It would also give students more confidence with the digital tools they already use every day.

In conclusion, I believe that a short, practical programming course would benefit most university students. Universities should design these courses around each subject, so that every student can see how code might help in their own future work.

  • Introduction: background, then the question in new words ("whatever they study"), then a thesis with a condition ("provided that").
  • Body 1 and 2: each starts with a clear topic sentence. Each idea is explained, and the first has a concrete example.
  • Body 3: a fair concession ("This is a fair concern") and a rebuttal ("However, the course does not need to be long").
  • Conclusion: the thesis in new words and a recommendation. No new arguments.
  • Stance: "largely agree" and "would" show a careful, honest position. See Hedging and stance.
  • Length: about 300 words.

Model essay 2: a problem and solution essay

Question: Electronic waste, such as old phones and laptops, is growing quickly around the world. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them?

  • Introduction: background with one real figure, then a map of the essay.
  • Problems: (1) harm to health and the environment, (2) loss of valuable materials.
  • Solutions: (1) producers collect old devices, (2) a right to repair, (3) careful buying.
  • Conclusion: problems in one sentence, solutions in one sentence.

People now replace their phones, laptops and other devices more often than ever. According to a United Nations report, the Global E-waste Monitor 2024, the world produced a record 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022. This essay will explain the main problems that this waste causes and suggest some practical solutions.

The first problem is harm to health and the environment. Electronic devices contain dangerous substances, such as lead and mercury. When they are dumped or burned in the open, these substances can enter the soil, water and air. The people most at risk are informal workers, sometimes including children, who take devices apart by hand without protection. A second problem is the loss of valuable materials. Old devices contain metals such as gold and copper. However, the same report found that less than a quarter of the e-waste from 2022 was documented as properly collected and recycled. As a result, most of these materials are lost, and new ones must be mined.

Several measures could reduce these problems. Firstly, governments could make producers responsible for collecting and recycling the devices they sell. Free collection points in shops would make recycling as easy as throwing things away. Secondly, devices should be easier to repair. Laws that require spare parts and repair guides would help people keep their phones and laptops for longer. Finally, individuals also have a part to play. Before buying a new device, people can repair their old one, sell it or give it to someone who needs it.

In conclusion, electronic waste harms people and the environment, and it wastes valuable materials. Clear rules for producers, a right to repair and more careful buying could together turn this growing problem into a source of reusable materials.

  • Evidence: two real figures, and the source is named in the text. Precise numbers make the argument stronger than "a lot of waste".
  • Match: each solution answers a problem. Collection and repair reduce both harm and loss.
  • Modal verbs: "could" and "should" present solutions as suggestions, which fits this essay type.
  • Cause and effect: "When they are dumped ...", "As a result ..." show how one thing leads to another.
  • Map: "This essay will explain ... and suggest ..." tells the reader the order of the essay.
  • Length: about 300 words.

The figures in essay 2 come from the Global E-waste Monitor 2024, by the UN agencies ITU and UNITAR. It found 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022. It also found that only 22.3% was documented as properly collected and recycled. The health points about lead and child workers match the World Health Organization's fact sheet on e-waste. In an exam you cannot check sources, so do not invent numbers. In a university essay, always name the source of a number.

Paraphrasing

Read a sentence from a source and two attempts to paraphrase it.

Remote teams that write down their decisions spend less time in meetings, because people can find answers on their own.

Remote teams that record their decisions spend less time in meetings, since people can find answers by themselves.

When a distributed team keeps a written record of its decisions, its members can look up answers without asking. As a result, the team needs fewer meetings (Lee, 2024).

The first attempt only swaps four words. The order and structure are the same. This is called patchwriting. It still counts as copying. The second attempt keeps the meaning, but the words and the structure are new. It also names the source.

To paraphrase means to say the same meaning in your own words. A paraphrase is about as long as the original. A summary is much shorter. Copying someone's words or ideas without naming them is plagiarism.

Four techniques, used together

Paraphrasing techniques
TechniqueOriginalParaphrase
Change wordsspend less time in meetingsneed fewer meetings
Change word formsthey decidedtheir decision
Change the orderA, because BBecause B, A. Or: B. As a result, A.
Change the voiceThe team tested the app.The app was tested by the team.

One technique alone is not enough. Mix two or three. Keep technical words that have no real synonym, like "API", "database" or "climate change".

  1. Read the passage until you understand all of it.
  2. Cover the original, so you cannot copy it.
  3. Write the idea from memory, in your own sentence.
  4. Compare with the original. Is the meaning the same? Is anything missing or added?
  5. Put quotation marks around any special phrase you kept.
  6. Add the source: the author and the year.

Replacing every word with a thesaurus. "Big data" becomes "large facts", and "run a test" becomes "sprint a trial". The meaning breaks. Change the structure more than the words.

In IELTS and Cambridge writing, start the introduction by paraphrasing the question. Copied words from the question do not show your vocabulary. "Every university student should take a programming course" can become "all students should study coding, whatever their main subject".

Writing a summary

Read this short blog post, written for this book. Then read a summary of it.

Many teams treat code review as a final check for bugs. This is useful, but it is only part of the value. When a colleague reads your code, they also learn how that part of the system works. Over time, knowledge spreads across the team, so no single person becomes the only expert. Reviews also keep the style of the code consistent, which makes it easier for everyone to read later. However, reviews can slow a team down if they are too large. A change of two thousand lines is hard to read carefully, so reviewers often approve it without real checks. For this reason, the most effective teams keep changes small and review them within a day. In short, code review is not only about finding bugs. It is a way to share knowledge and keep code readable, as long as changes stay small.

The writer argues that code review does more than find bugs. It spreads knowledge across a team and keeps code consistent. However, large reviews are often checked badly, so the writer recommends small changes that are reviewed quickly.

The summary keeps the main idea and the key points. It drops the example of two thousand lines. It uses new words and a new order. It adds no opinion.

Five steps to a summary

  1. Read for the main idea. What is the writer's one big point? Write it in one sentence.
  2. Find the key points. Usually one per paragraph. Mark them.
  3. Cross out details. Examples, numbers, stories and repeated points usually go.
  4. Write from your notes, not from the text. Start with the writer and a reporting verb.
  5. Check. Is the meaning right? Is it short enough? Is there no opinion of yours?

Summaries use reporting verbs in the present simple: the writer argues, explains, describes, claims, concludes, recommends. Choose the verb carefully. "Claims" suggests that you are not sure the writer is right.

The executive summary

A long report often starts with an executive summary. It gives the purpose, the main findings and the recommendations in a few lines. It comes first, but you write it last, when you know what the report says. Many busy readers read only this part.

Copying the first sentence of every paragraph and calling it a summary. The words are still the writer's, and the result does not flow. Another mistake is adding your opinion: "The writer is right that ..." A summary reports. It does not judge.

Reports and proposals

Here is a short report, written for this book. The numbers are made up for practice.

Report on the six-week pair-programming trial

1. Introduction

The aim of this report is to present the results of the pair-programming trial in the mobile team and to make recommendations. The trial ran from 1 September to 10 October, and eight developers took part. The findings are based on a survey of all eight developers and on data from our bug tracker.

2. Findings

2.1 Quality. The number of bugs found after release fell from 14 in the six weeks before the trial to 6 during it.

2.2 Speed. The team finished slightly fewer tickets: 41, compared with 45 before the trial.

2.3 Experience. Six of the eight developers said they had learned new skills. However, five found full days of pairing tiring.

3. Conclusion

Pair programming clearly improved quality and helped people learn. It slowed delivery a little, and full days of pairing were too tiring.

4. Recommendations

It is recommended that the team:

  • pair on complex or risky tickets only
  • limit pairing to about three hours a day
  • review the results again after three months

A report has a title and clear headings. Each section has one job. Numbered headings, like 2.1 and 2.2, help in longer reports. The facts come first. The writer's view appears only in the conclusion and recommendations.

Common report sections
SectionWhat it contains
Executive summarythe whole report in a few lines (long reports only)
Introductionaim, background and where the information comes from
Findings or discussionthe facts, under sub-headings
Conclusionwhat the findings mean
Recommendationsactions to take, often as a list
Appendicesextra data and details that would slow the reader down

Proposals

A report looks at the past and the present. It is mostly factual. A proposal looks at the future. It suggests a plan and tries to persuade the reader to accept it.

Proposal for a weekly English practice hour

Introduction

The purpose of this proposal is to suggest a weekly English practice hour for our engineering team. It also explains the benefits and the costs.

Current situation

Our team has 24 engineers in five countries, and all meetings are in English. In our last team survey, nine people said they find it hard to speak in meetings.

The plan

I propose a one-hour online session every Thursday at 12:00 UTC. Each week, one volunteer would lead a short activity, such as a small demo or practice stand-ups. Attendance would be optional.

Benefits

The sessions would give people a safe place to practise. This could make meetings more balanced, because more people would share ideas. It would also help new colleagues get to know the team.

Costs

The only cost is time: one hour a week for each person who attends. No new tools are needed.

Recommendation

I recommend that we try the practice hour for eight weeks from January. At the end, we can ask the attendees whether it helped.

A proposal describes the situation briefly. Then it spends most of its words on the plan, the benefits and the costs. It uses would and could for the future plan. It ends with a clear request.

Report language

The aim of this report is to ...

The findings are based on ...

It was found that ...

The majority of users ...

It is recommended that the team pair on risky tickets.

Proposal language

The purpose of this proposal is to ...

At present, ...

I propose that we ...

This would allow ...

I recommend that we try it for eight weeks.

After "recommend that", formal English uses the base verb: "that the team pair", not "pairs". The chapter Subjunctive and unreal past explains this form.

Cambridge B2 First can ask for a report in Writing Part 2. C1 Advanced can ask for a report or a proposal. Use a title and headings in both. Details are in Cambridge exams. Design documents at work are in Writing at work.

Expert level: academic style

Compare two versions of the same paragraph.

Lots of people think AI is gonna take loads of jobs. I think that's kind of true, but it's not the whole story. Stuff like customer service will change a lot, but new jobs will come too, I guess.

Many people expect artificial intelligence (AI) to replace a large number of jobs. This view is partly correct, but it is incomplete. Roles such as customer service are likely to change significantly. At the same time, new types of work are likely to appear.

The academic version is not longer or harder. It is more exact and more careful. These are the main features of academic style.

Features of academic style
FeatureMeaningInstead ofWrite
Formalno slang, no short formscan't, gonna, kidscannot, going to, children
Preciseexact facts and numbersa lot of people, stuff62% of users, these tools
Objectivefocus on evidence, not feelingsI feel that ...The data suggest that ...
Explicitlinks between ideas are clearAlso, ...A second reason is that ...
Carefulclaims match the evidenceAI will destroy jobs.AI is likely to change many jobs.
Responsiblesources are namedStudies show ...According to a 2024 UN report, ...

Word choices

  • Phrasal verbs to single verbs: find out to discover, go up to increase, look into to investigate. See Phrasal verbs.
  • Vague words to exact words: thing, stuff and nice become a specific noun or adjective.
  • Questions to statements: "So why does this happen?" becomes "There are two main reasons for this."
  • Etc. to a full list or "such as" with two or three examples.
  • Verbs to nouns, sometimes: "when prices rose" becomes "the rise in prices". This is called nominalisation. Use it with care. See Participle clauses and nominalisation.

I, we and the passive

Some teachers ask you to avoid "I" in essays. Many fields accept it, especially in the thesis: "I argue that ..." Research papers often use "we". The passive hides the person and puts the focus on the action: "The data were collected in March." Check what your teacher or journal expects. More on the passive is in The passive.

Academic does not mean difficult. "The utilisation of the aforementioned methodology facilitated the ascertainment of results" is bad academic writing. "This method helped us find the results" is good. Use the simplest exact word.

An editing checklist

  1. The question: does the essay answer every part of it?
  2. The thesis: is it clear in the introduction, and the same in the conclusion?
  3. Paragraphs: does each one have one main idea and a topic sentence?
  4. Evidence: does each claim have a reason, an example or a source?
  5. Style: no short forms, no slang, no vague words?
  6. Your own errors: check articles, verb endings and plurals last, one at a time.

The Academic Phrasebank from the University of Manchester lists useful phrases for each part of an academic text. Use it to learn the shapes. Then fill them with your own ideas.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for essays, reports and summaries
PatternPurposeModelNote
I (largely) agree that + clause, provided that + clauseGive a thesis with a conditionI largely agree, provided that the course is practical.Say how much you agree.
This essay will + verb ... and + verb ...Map the essayThis essay will explain the problems and suggest solutions.Not "I will talk about".
One major advantage of + noun is that + clauseOpen a body paragraphOne major advantage of coding is that it saves time.One main idea per paragraph.
Critics argue that + clause. However, + clauseAdmit the other view, then answer itCritics argue that timetables are full. However, the course can be short.Be fair to the other side.
As a result, + clauseShow an effectAs a result, most of these materials are lost.Comma after "As a result".
Subject + could + verbSuggest a solutionGovernments could make producers collect old devices.Match each solution to a problem.
In conclusion, + thesis in new wordsStart the conclusionIn conclusion, a short course would benefit most students.No new ideas here.
According to + source, + clauseName the source of a factAccording to a UN report, e-waste reached 62 million tonnes in 2022.Never invent a number.
The writer argues / explains that + clauseStart a summaryThe writer argues that code review spreads knowledge.Present simple, no opinion.
The aim of this report is to + verbOpen a reportThe aim of this report is to present the trial results.Then say where the data come from.
It was found that + clauseReport a finding objectivelyIt was found that bugs fell by more than half.Put numbers in the findings.
It is recommended that + subject + base verbMake a formal recommendationIt is recommended that the team pair on risky tickets."the team pair", not "pairs".
I propose that we + verbSuggest a plan in a proposalI propose that we start a weekly practice hour.Then give benefits and costs.
This would + verbDescribe the effect of a planThis would help new colleagues settle in.Would, not will: it is a plan.
a large number of / a significant proportion of + nounGive a quantity formallyA significant proportion of users left.Better still: give the number.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

"Discuss both views and give your own opinion." Which essay type is this?

  • Problem and solution
  • Discussion
  • Advantages and disadvantages

Two views plus your opinion is a discussion essay.

Which sentence is the best thesis for an opinion essay?

  • Technology is very important nowadays.
  • This essay is about online learning.
  • I partly agree, because online courses suit adults but not young children.

A thesis answers the question and gives the reason in one sentence.

What should a conclusion NOT contain?

  • The thesis in new words
  • A new argument
  • A recommendation

New arguments belong in the body. The conclusion joins what you already said.

Original: "The city built new cycle lanes, so more people now cycle to work." Which is the best paraphrase?

  • The city built new bike lanes, so more people now cycle to work.
  • Since new cycle lanes were added, cycling to work has become more common in the city.
  • The city built cycle lanes.

The second one keeps the meaning but changes the structure. The first only swaps one word. The third loses half the meaning.

Which text suggests a future plan and tries to persuade?

  • A report
  • A proposal
  • A summary

A report is mostly about the past and present. A proposal is about what should happen.

Which sentence fits academic style best?

  • Loads of students can't afford books.
  • Many students cannot afford textbooks.
  • Students, like, really can't buy books.

No slang, no short forms, and an exact noun: textbooks.

Fill the gap

The ? of this report is to present the results of the trial.

It is recommended that the team (pair) on complex tickets only.

I propose ? we try the practice hour for eight weeks.

The writer (argue) that code review spreads knowledge.

? to a UN report, e-waste reached 62 million tonnes in 2022.

Critics argue that timetables are full. ?, the course could be short.

Think and write

  1. Underline the topic, the focus and the instruction: "To what extent do you agree that cities should ban cars from their centres?"
    Answer

    Topic: banning cars. Focus: in city centres. Instruction: to what extent do you agree. You must say how much you agree, for example "largely agree".

  2. Paraphrase this sentence. Use at least two techniques: "Students who sleep well get better marks in exams."
    Model answer

    Good exam results are more common among students who get enough sleep. (Changes: new order, "marks" to "results", "sleep well" to "get enough sleep".)

  3. Rewrite in academic style: "Loads of companies are getting into AI, and stuff is changing really fast."
    Model answer

    A large number of companies are adopting artificial intelligence, and their work is changing rapidly. Even better, give a number with a source.

  4. Write an introduction of three sentences for this question: "Some people think that public transport should be free. To what extent do you agree?"
    Model answer

    Many cities struggle with traffic and air pollution. One proposed answer is to make buses and trains free for everyone. I partly agree, because free transport would help people on low incomes, but it would need careful funding.

  5. Summarise the code review blog post from this chapter in one sentence of under 25 words.
    Model answer

    The writer argues that small, quick code reviews spread knowledge and keep code consistent, not only catch bugs.

  6. You ran a two-week trial of a new chat tool. Write the headings of the report and one sentence for each heading.
    Model answer

    1. Introduction: The aim of this report is to present the results of the two-week trial of the new chat tool. 2. Findings: Most of the 15 users found it faster, but three had problems with notifications. 3. Conclusion: The tool works well for most users. 4. Recommendations: It is recommended that the company adopt the tool and fix the notification settings first.

  7. Expert: plan a discussion essay for this question. Write the thesis and one line per paragraph. "Some people think that young people should be free to choose any job. Others think they should follow their parents' advice. Discuss both views and give your opinion."
    Model answer

    Thesis: Both views have merit, but young people should make the final choice, after listening to advice. Body 1: why free choice matters: motivation, a changing job market, an example. Body 2: why parents' advice helps: experience, money, knowledge of the child. Body 3, or inside body 2: my view, choose freely but use advice. Conclusion: restate, advise families to talk early.

Key takeaways

  • Essays argue, reports inform and recommend, and summaries shorten. Each has its own shape.
  • The question tells you the essay type. Your thesis answers it in one sentence.
  • Plan before you write: take the question apart, choose a position, pick two or three ideas with examples.
  • The introduction moves from background to thesis. The conclusion restates the thesis and adds no new ideas.
  • A good paraphrase changes the structure and the words, keeps the meaning and names the source.
  • A summary keeps the main idea and key points, drops details and adds no opinion.
  • Reports have headings and facts first. Proposals persuade with a plan, benefits and costs.
  • Academic style is formal, precise, objective, careful and responsible. It is not difficult.

Sources

  • EAP Foundation: Paraphrasing. Changing words, word forms and word order, and how a paraphrase differs from a summary.
  • Purdue OWL: Paraphrasing. Steps to an effective paraphrase, and why paraphrase is often better than quotation.
  • ANU Academic Skills: Report structure. The sections of a report and what each one contains.
  • Cambridge English: C1 Advanced Writing Part 2 lesson plan (2022). The different purposes of a report and a proposal, and the use of titles and sub-headings.
  • UEfAP: Writing features. The features of academic writing: formality, precision, objectivity, explicitness, hedging and responsibility.
  • UNITAR: Global E-waste Monitor 2024. The 62 million tonnes and 22.3% figures used in model essay 2.

CEFR and the exam map

Many English exams exist. Each one has its own format and its own score scale. The CEFR is the common ladder behind them. This chapter shows the ladder, the main exams and how their scores line up.

  • Describe the six CEFR levels with simple can-do statements.
  • Name the main English exams, their owners, their length and their score scales.
  • Read the owners' own tables that link exam scores to CEFR levels.
  • Choose the right exam for a goal: study, work or a visa.
  • Talk about exam requirements in clear, correct English.

The CEFR: one ladder with six steps

Lena: What is your English level?

Omar: I think I am B1. I can follow a stand-up meeting. I still find long documents hard.

Lena: I am B2 in reading but B1 in speaking.

Omar and Lena use the CEFR. The CEFR is a framework. It describes language ability in six levels. The Council of Europe made it. It works for any language, not only English.

Each level is described with can-do statements. "I can order food in a restaurant" is a can-do statement. The six levels form three groups.

The six CEFR levels in simple words
LevelGroupOld nameWhat a learner can do (our summary)Example at work
A1Basic userBreakthroughUse very common phrases. Say who you are. Ask simple questions."Hello, I am Omar. I work in the data team."
A2Basic userWaystageTalk about daily life, shopping and your job in short sentences."I fixed the bug yesterday. Now the test passes."
B1Independent userThresholdUnderstand the main points of clear talk on familiar topics. Give simple reasons.Follow a stand-up. Explain why a task is late.
B2Independent userVantageUnderstand complex texts in your field. Argue for and against a choice.Discuss two database designs and defend one.
C1Proficient userEffective Operational ProficiencyUnderstand long, hard texts and hidden meaning. Speak with few pauses.Lead a design review. Write a clear proposal.
C2Proficient userMasteryUnderstand almost everything with ease. Show fine differences in meaning.Negotiate a contract. Edit other people's writing.

The CEFR also has plus levels: A2+, B1+ and B2+. The 2020 update of the CEFR, called the Companion Volume, also describes a Pre-A1 level. You do not need these for most exams.

"I passed the CEFR" is wrong. The CEFR is not a test. You cannot take it or pass it. You take an exam. The exam owner then says which CEFR level your score matches.

C2 is called "Mastery". The Council of Europe says it does not mean native-speaker level. Many native speakers would not pass a C2 exam without study.

Can-do statements: check yourself

Your level is often different in each skill. This is normal. Teachers call it an uneven profile. Engineers often read at B2 or C1 but speak at B1.

Read the statements below. Mark each one you can really do today. The highest level with most marks is your level for that skill. The statements are written for this book. They follow the CEFR ideas but use our own words.

  • B1 I can follow a slow stand-up meeting about my own project.
  • B2 I can follow a fast team discussion and a conference talk in my field.
  • C1 I can follow a long lecture with jokes, side stories and unclear structure.
  • B1 I can read a short email or a simple README and get the main points.
  • B2 I can read a technical article and find the writer's opinion.
  • C1 I can read a research paper and see what the writer only suggests.
  • B1 I can describe what I did yesterday and why.
  • B2 I can give my view in a meeting, with reasons and examples.
  • C1 I can explain a complex system to a client without long pauses.
  • B1 I can write a short, clear message about a problem.
  • B2 I can write a design document with pros and cons.
  • C1 I can write a well-organised report and change my style for the reader.

Be honest. Mark a statement only if you can do it on a bad day too. Exams test your normal level, not your best day.
