LinguaskillCambridge University Press & AssessmentSeparate modules. Reading about 40 min, Listening about 40 min, Writing 55 min, Speaking about 16 min.Cambridge English Scale. The results page shows 140 (B1) to 210 (C2).Online, on demand, often set up by a university or company. Reading and Listening are adaptive.

Two exams changed a lot this year. IELTS stopped paper tests in most countries from mid-2026. Some countries keep an option to write the Writing part on paper. TOEFL iBT got new tasks and a new 1 to 6 scale on 21 January 2026.

Do not mix up the versions. IELTS Academic and IELTS General Training are different tests. PTE Academic UKVI and IELTS for UKVI are versions for UK visas. A university may reject the wrong version.

Scores side by side

Look at this case first. Mei has IELTS 7.0. Ravi has TOEFL 5. Ana has a DET score of 130. Are they at the same level? All three scores match C1 in the owners' tables.

Each owner publishes a table that links its scores to the CEFR. These tables are guides. They do not say two scores are exactly equal. The table below puts the owners' tables next to each other.

CEFR levels and exam scores (from each owner's own table)
CEFRIELTS overallTOEFL iBT (1 to 6)Cambridge English ScalePTE AcademicDETTOEIC L&R total (minimum)
C28.5 to 9 (8 is borderline)6200 to 23085 to 90155 to 160not mapped
C17 to 8 (6.5 is borderline)5 to 5.5180 to 19976 to 84130 to 150945
B25.5 to 6.54 to 4.5160 to 17959 to 75100 to 125785
B14 to 5 (5 is borderline)3 to 3.5140 to 15943 to 5860 to 95550
A2not mapped2 to 2.5not reported by these exams30 to 4210 to 55 (A1 to A2)225
A1not mapped1 to 1.5not reported by these exams10 to 29 (A1 or below)see A2 row120

Some notes on the table:

  • IELTS says 8.5 and above is C2. It says the C1 threshold falls between 6.5 and 7. If an organisation needs to be sure of C1, IELTS suggests asking for 7.
  • TOEFL uses the same number for a level in every section. A 4 is B2 in Reading, Listening, Writing and Speaking.
  • Cambridge uses one scale for all its exams. A 175 on B2 First and a 175 on C1 Advanced mean the same level.
  • TOEIC gives minimum scores, not ranges. ETS also gives separate minimums for Listening and Reading. It says to use them separately when you can.
  • DET numbers come from Duolingo's 2026 scoring guide.

Do not convert scores with your own maths. "IELTS 7 is 7/9, so 78% of TOEFL" is wrong. The scales are not straight lines. Always use the owner's table.

Most requirements have two parts: an overall score and a minimum in each skill. "IELTS 6.5 overall, with no band below 6.0" is typical. Your weakest skill decides if you pass the requirement.

How the overall score is made

Most exams give four skill scores and one overall score. The overall score is an average. But each owner rounds in its own way.

  1. Mei's scores: Listening 6.5, Reading 6.5, Writing 5.0, Speaking 7.0.
  2. Add them. 6.5 + 6.5 + 5.0 + 7.0 = 25.0.
  3. Divide by 4. 25.0 ÷ 4 = 6.25.
  4. IELTS rule: an average that ends in .25 goes up to the next half band.
  5. Overall band: 6.5.

IELTS rounds to the nearest half band. An average ending in .25 goes up to .5. An average ending in .75 goes up to the next whole band. An average of 6.125 becomes 6.0.

  1. Scores: Listening 90, Speaking 100, Reading 110, Writing 120.
  2. Average: (90 + 100 + 110 + 120) ÷ 4 = 105.
  3. DET rounds up to the nearest 5. 105 is already a step of 5.
  4. Overall score: 105.

TOEFL averages the four section scores and rounds to the nearest half band. ETS gives this example: an average of 5.25 becomes 5.5. For two years after January 2026, the TOEFL report also shows a comparable total on the old 0 to 120 scale.

Who accepts which exam

Every organisation chooses its own list. The same exam can be fine for one university and wrong for a visa. So the first step is always the same. Read the page of the organisation you apply to.

Study at a university

IELTS Academic is for study at degree level. TOEFL iBT is mostly for universities. PTE Academic says over 4,000 universities and colleges accept it. Many universities also accept Cambridge C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency, and many accept the DET. Check the exact list and the minimum scores on each course page.

Move to another country

IELTS says General Training is for migration and for training below degree level. Pearson says Australia and New Zealand accept PTE Academic for work and migration visas. Some UK visas need a special secure version: IELTS for UKVI or PTE Academic UKVI. Government lists change, so check the official visa page.

Get or change a job

TOEIC is built for workplace English. Employers often use it to hire or promote. Linguaskill and Linguaskill Business are often set up by companies and universities for their own staff and students.

Join a professional body

Some bodies for doctors, nurses or engineers name one exam and a high score. IELTS says its Academic test is the one for professional registration. Check the body's own rules.

Results also have a life span. IELTS recommends that organisations accept results for two years. ETS reports TOEFL scores for two years. Pearson says PTE scores are valid for two years. TOEIC scores older than two years cannot be reported. Cambridge says its certificates do not expire. But an organisation can still ask for a recent result.

"My friend used TOEFL for this visa, so I can too." Rules change often. Your friend's rule may be old. Read the official page on the day you book.

How to choose: a decision path

Follow the arrows. Start with your goal. End with an exam to check on the organisation's page.

Read the requirement

Open the page of the university, employer or visa office. Write down the exam names they accept.

Note the exact numbers

Write the overall score and the minimum for each skill. Note how old a result can be.

Match the format to you

Do you type fast? Do you like a human examiner? Do you want to test at home? Pick the format that suits you.

Try a free practice test

Every owner has free sample tasks. Do one under time pressure. See where you lose points.

Check dates and cost

Look at test dates and the fee in your country. Leave time for results and for one retake.

Book and plan

Book the date. Make a study plan backwards from that date. See Study plans and mock tests.

Here is how the format can help a choice. Ken is a software engineer. He types quickly. He gets nervous with a human examiner. Both TOEFL and IELTS are on his university's list. TOEFL Speaking is recorded on a computer, so it may suit him. Sara likes to talk with a real person. IELTS Speaking is a live interview, so it may suit her.

"Exam X is the easiest." People say this about every exam. The owners link their scores to the same CEFR levels. A B2 learner gets a B2 result on any good exam. Choose by the requirement and by format, not by rumour.

Fees, results and retakes

This book gives a fee only when the owner publishes one world price. Most owners set the fee by country. Only one owner shows a single world price.

  • DET: Duolingo's own guide says the test costs US$70 (updated October 2026).
  • IELTS, TOEFL, PTE, Cambridge and TOEIC: the fee depends on your country and test centre. Check the booking page for your city.
  • Linguaskill: usually bought by an organisation for its people.
When results arrive (owners' pages, November 2026)

The chapter IELTS Listening and Reading explains One Skill Retake in detail. The chapters TOEFL iBT, Cambridge exams and PTE, Duolingo and TOEIC cover the other exams task by task.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for talking about exams and levels
PatternPurposeModelNote

Score + is roughly equal to + level + on the CEFR.Compare a score with a levelTOEFL 4 is roughly equal to B2 on the CEFR.Use "roughly". Tables are guides, not exact matches.

Practice

1. Which sentence is correct?

  • I passed the CEFR B2 last year.
  • I took IELTS last year. My score matches B2.
  • The CEFR gave me 6.5.

The CEFR is a framework, not a test. You take an exam. The owner links your score to a level.

2. What is the TOEFL iBT score scale since 21 January 2026?

  • 0 to 120
  • 0 to 9
  • 1 to 6, in half bands

ETS introduced a 1 to 6 scale. For two years the report also shows a comparable 0 to 120 total.

3. Which exam can you take only at a test centre, never at home?

  • Duolingo English Test
  • PTE Academic
  • TOEFL iBT

Pearson says PTE Academic cannot be taken at home. DET is online at home. TOEFL has a home option.

4. Cambridge exams report results on the Cambridge English ?.

5. DET overall scores go up in steps of ?.

6. In IELTS, an average of 6.75 becomes an overall band of ?.

  1. Work out the IELTS overall band: Listening 7.0, Reading 6.5, Writing 6.0, Speaking 6.0.
    Answer

    Total 25.5. Average 25.5 ÷ 4 = 6.375. This is closer to 6.5 than to 6.0, so the overall band is 6.5.

  2. A university asks for "C1 Advanced, 180 overall, 176 in each paper". Is a score of 185 overall with Writing 172 enough? Why?
    Answer

    No. The overall score is fine, but Writing is below 176. Both parts of the rule must be true.

  3. Use the owners' tables. What CEFR level do these scores match: PTE 62, DET 115, TOEFL 4.5?
    Answer

    All three match B2. PTE 59 to 75 is B2. DET 100 to 125 is B2. TOEFL 4 to 4.5 is B2.

  4. Write two sentences about your own goal. Use "I need ... for ..." and "I am aiming for ... by ...".
    Answer

    Model: I need band 7 in IELTS Academic for a master's in data science. I am aiming for band 7 by next September.

  5. Your friend says: "IELTS 6.5 is B2, so it is never C1." Is your friend right? Explain with the IELTS statement.
    Answer

    Not fully. IELTS says the C1 threshold falls between 6.5 and 7. Many people with 6.5 are at C1, but some are a little below. That is why some organisations ask for 7 when they need to be sure of C1.

  6. Hard: a company wants to test 300 staff online and get results fast. Some staff are B1, some are C1. Which Cambridge product fits, and why?
    Answer

    Linguaskill. It is online and on demand. It has separate modules, so the company can test only the skills it needs. Its Reading and Listening are adaptive, so one test works for B1 and C1 staff.

Key takeaways

  • The CEFR is a framework with six levels, A1 to C2. It is not a test.
  • Each exam has its own scale: IELTS 0 to 9, TOEFL 1 to 6, Cambridge English Scale, PTE 10 to 90, DET 10 to 160, TOEIC 10 to 990.
  • Use only the owner's own table to compare a score with a CEFR level.
  • Most requirements have an overall score and a minimum for each skill.
  • IELTS went computer-only in most places from mid-2026. TOEFL changed its tasks and scale in January 2026.
  • Choose an exam by the organisation's list first, then by format. Ignore rumours about "easy" exams.

  • Cambridge English: results for qualifications. Scale ranges and grades for B2 First, C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency.
  • Pearson: PTE Academic score guide (July 2025). PTE scores and CEFR levels.
  • Duolingo: how to prepare for the DET. Price, length and results time, updated October 2026.

IELTS Listening and Reading

IELTS Listening and Reading are the two papers with right or wrong answers. Each one has 40 questions. With good strategies you can win many marks fast. This chapter shows the 2026 format, every question type and a strategy for each.

  • Describe the current format and timing of IELTS Listening and Reading.
  • Explain how correct answers become a band score.
  • Recognise every question type and use a strategy for each.
  • Tell the difference between Academic and General Training Reading.
  • Solve original practice tasks and check your answers.

The two papers at a glance

Here is a normal IELTS test day at a test centre. You sit at a computer. The three written papers come one after another, with no break.

  1. Part 1 Listening. About 30 minutes of recordings, plus time to check. On computer the paper takes 30 to 34 minutes.
  2. Part 2 Reading. 60 minutes. Three sections, 40 questions.
  3. Part 3 Writing. 60 minutes. Two tasks. See IELTS Writing.
  4. Same week Speaking. 11 to 14 minutes with an examiner, on the same day or up to a week before or after. See IELTS Speaking.
Listening and Reading in numbers (ielts.org, November 2026)
ListeningReading
TimeAbout 30 minutes. On computer: 30 to 34 minutes, with 2 minutes at the end to check.60 minutes. No extra time to copy answers.
Parts4 parts, 10 questions each3 sections
Questions4040
Marks1 mark for each correct answer1 mark for each correct answer
Academic or General Training?The same test for bothDifferent texts for each
Special ruleYou hear each recording once onlyAll answers come from the texts

In 2026 IELTS moved away from paper. The IELTS partners said in March 2026 that paper tests stop from mid-2026. Exact dates depend on the country. Some countries offer IELTS on computer (Writing on Paper). There you do Listening and Reading on screen and write the Writing tasks by hand.

IELTS Online lets you take IELTS Academic at home. The format is the same as at a centre. Results take longer: 6 to 8 days, not 1 to 5 days.

Many old books say "you get 10 minutes to transfer your Listening answers". That was for paper. On computer you type answers as you listen. At the end you get only 2 minutes to check.

One Skill Retake

Imagine your result is Listening 7.5, Reading 7.0, Writing 6.0 and Speaking 7.0. You need 6.5 in every skill. You do not have to take the whole test again. With One Skill Retake, you repeat Writing only.

  • You must sit the retake within 60 days of your full test.
  • You can retake one skill only, one time, for each full test.
  • Your full test must be IELTS on computer, at a centre that offers the option.
  • It works for Academic and General Training.
  • You get a new Test Report Form. You choose which form to use: the old one or the new one.
  • Not every organisation accepts it. IELTS says to check with the organisation first.

How marks become bands

Each correct answer gives you one mark. Your total out of 40 is your raw score. IELTS then turns it into a band from 1 to 9, in whole and half bands.

IELTS does not publish one fixed table. The number of marks for a band changes a little from one test version to another. But ielts.org gives the average marks for four bands.

Average marks out of 40 for some bands (ielts.org)
BandListeningAcademic ReadingGeneral Training Reading
4not givennot given15
5161523
6232330
7303035
83535not given

Look at the numbers. For band 7 in Listening you need about 30 of 40. That is 75 percent. You can lose 10 marks and still get 7.

Rules that cost marks

  • Word limits. An instruction like "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER" is strict. Three words lose the mark, even if the idea is right.
  • Spelling. A wrong spelling is a wrong answer. British and American spelling are both accepted. Choose one and keep it.
  • Hyphens. A word like "check-in" counts as one word.
  • No penalty for wrong answers. A wrong answer gets zero, the same as a gap. So never leave a gap. Guess.

The answer is "a large kitchen". The limit is two words. You write "a large kitchen". That is three words, so it is wrong. Write "large kitchen".

Listening: the four parts

The recordings get harder from Part 1 to Part 4. The topics move from daily life to study.

The four Listening parts
PartSpeakersSettingInvented example
1Two peopleEveryday lifeA caller books a room at a coworking space.
2One main speakerEveryday lifeA guide talks about a new sports centre.
3Two main speakers, sometimes a tutor tooStudy or trainingTwo students plan a project on solar panels.
4One speakerAn academic subjectA short lecture on how bees find flowers.

Part 4 is a monologue with no break in the middle. It is usually the hardest part. You hear accents from Britain, Australia, New Zealand and North America. The questions follow the order of the recording.

Three listening skills that win marks

1. Predict. Read the questions before the recording starts. Guess the kind of answer: a number, a name, a place, a noun.

2. Hear the signposts. A signpost tells you that the speaker moves on. Examples: "Now, moving on to...", "The second thing is...", "Finally...". Signposts help you find your place.

3. Watch for corrections. A distractor is a trap. Speakers often say one thing and then change it.

Caller: Can I start on the 12th of May?

Manager: The 12th is a Sunday, so we're closed. Let's say the 13th.

The first date, the 12th, is a distractor. The answer is the 13th. Words like "actually", "sorry, I mean", "no, wait" and "let's say" often come before the real answer.

Listening question types and strategies

IELTS lists six question types for Listening. Each slide gives one type, what you do, and one strategy.

Multiple choice

You choose one answer, or sometimes two or three, from a list.

Strategy: Underline the key words in each option. The speaker often mentions all options. Listen for which one is chosen.

Matching

You match items you hear to a list of options, such as people to opinions.

Strategy: Learn the list of options first. The items come in order. The options do not.

Plan, map or diagram labelling

You label places on a map, rooms on a plan or parts of a machine.

Strategy: Find the starting point. Know your direction words: opposite, next to, on your left, at the far end.

Form, note, table or flow chart completion

You fill gaps in notes about the recording.

Strategy: Check the word limit. Predict the word class: noun, number, adjective. Copy words as you hear them.

Sentence completion

You complete a sentence that sums up part of the recording.

Strategy: The sentence uses other words than the speaker. Listen for the same meaning, not the same words.

Short-answer questions

You answer a question in a few words. Answers are often facts: a place, a price, a time.

Strategy: Look at the question word. "When" needs a time. "How much" needs a price.

Train your ear for numbers and letters. In Part 1 people spell names and give phone numbers. Practise "double six", "oh" for zero, and the letters A, E, I, G and J.

An original Part 1 task

This script was written for this book. Ask a friend to read it aloud once. Or cover the script and read it fast once only. Then fill the form. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

Manager: Good morning, Hub Seven Coworking. How can I help?

Daniel: Hi. I'd like to join. My name is Daniel Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.

Manager: Thanks, Daniel. Do you want a fixed desk or a flexible desk?

Daniel: A fixed desk sounds good. Oh, wait. How much is that?

Manager: A fixed desk is 240 pounds a month. A flexible desk is 165.

Daniel: Hmm. I work from home two days a week. I'll take the flexible one.

Manager: Fine. When would you like to start?

Daniel: The first of June?

Manager: We're closed that day for repairs. Let's say the third.

Daniel: Perfect. Is there anywhere to leave my bike?

Manager: Yes, in the basement. And you'll get a locker. It's number 48.

Hub Seven membership form
FieldYour answer
1. Surname?
2. Type of desk?
3. Price per month: £?
4. Start date: June?
5. Bike parking: in the?
6. Locker number?
Why are these the answers?

Question 2 has a distractor: Daniel first says "fixed", then changes to "flexible". Question 3 follows from that: 165, not 240. Question 4 has a correction: the 1st becomes the 3rd. For question 1, the spelling must be exact.

Reading: Academic and General Training

Both Reading papers have 3 sections, 40 questions and 60 minutes. The texts are different.

Academic Reading

  • Three long texts, one in each section.
  • 2,150 to 2,750 words in total.
  • From books, journals, magazines, newspapers and online sources.
  • Written for a general reader, at university level.
  • Texts can include diagrams, graphs or pictures.

General Training Reading

  • Section 1: two or three short texts, or several very short ones, about daily life. Example: notices, timetables.
  • Section 2: two texts about work. Example: a job description, training material.
  • Section 3: one longer text on a topic of general interest.
  • Texts get harder from Section 1 to Section 3.

"General Training is easy, so I will get a high band." Not quite. Its texts are easier, but you need more correct answers for the same band. Look at the chart above.

Two reading speeds

To skim is to read fast for the main idea. You read titles, first sentences and last sentences. To scan is to look fast for one detail, like a name, a date or a number. Use both. Skim the text once in 2 or 3 minutes. Then scan for each answer.

The questions rarely use the words of the text. They use a paraphrase. The text says "sales doubled". The question says "twice as many were sold". Your job is to see the same meaning.

Reading question types and strategies

IELTS lists eleven question types for Academic Reading. General Training uses the same types. Any type can appear in any section.

The eleven Reading question types
Question typeWhat you doStrategy
Multiple choiceChoose the right option.Find the part of the text first. Then cut wrong options one by one.
Identifying information (True / False / Not Given)Say if a statement agrees with the facts in the text.See the flowchart below. "Not Given" means the text says nothing about it.
Identifying writer's views (Yes / No / Not Given)Say if a statement agrees with the writer's opinion.Look for opinion words: should, I believe, unfortunately, it is clear that.
Matching informationFind which paragraph contains a piece of information.Some paragraphs may be used twice, some never. Scan for details.
Matching headingsChoose a heading for each paragraph.Read the whole paragraph. The heading fits the main idea, not one detail.
Matching featuresMatch statements to a list, such as researchers or dates.Scan for the names in the list first. Mark them in the text.
Matching sentence endingsJoin the first half of a sentence to the right ending.Check grammar and meaning. Some endings fit the grammar but not the facts.
Sentence completionComplete sentences with words from the text.Respect the word limit. Copy the spelling from the text.
Summary, note, table or flow chart completionFill gaps in a summary of part of the text.Find where the summary starts in the text. Answers usually come in order.
Diagram label completionLabel parts of a diagram from the text.Find the paragraph that describes the object or process.
Short-answer questionsAnswer questions in a few words from the text.Answers come in text order. Use the question word to predict.

True, False or Not Given

This type causes the most lost marks. Follow the same three questions every time.

"The bridge opened in 2019. It cost less than planned, and about 9,000 people cross it each day."

a) The bridge was cheaper than expected. TRUE ("cost less than planned").

b) Fewer than 5,000 people use it daily. FALSE (the text says about 9,000).

c) The bridge won a design prize. NOT GIVEN (the text says nothing about prizes).

Do not use your own knowledge. You may know that the bridge won a prize. If the text does not say it, the answer is NOT GIVEN.

True / False / Not Given is about facts. Yes / No / Not Given is about the writer's views. The method is the same. Only the words change.

A time plan for the hour

Reading has no extra time. Plan your hour like a sprint plan.

  1. Section 1: 17 minutes. It is usually the easiest. Bank the marks.
  2. Section 2: 20 minutes.
  3. Section 3: 23 minutes. It is usually the hardest and longest.
  4. Inside each section: skim for 2 minutes, then answer the questions.
  5. Stuck for more than 90 seconds? Guess, flag it and move on.
  6. Use the last minute to fill every empty box with a guess.

On computer you can highlight words in the text. IDP's guides also describe making notes on screen. Try these tools in the free official practice tests before test day.

Do the question types you are fast at first, inside each section. For many people, completion tasks are quick and matching headings is slow.

An original Reading passage

This passage was written for this book. The town and the numbers are invented. It is shorter than a real IELTS passage, but the tasks work the same way.

A. Most libraries lend books. In the town of Westerby, the library also lends drills, tents and sewing machines. The idea started in 2021, when a group of residents noticed how rarely they used their own tools. A survey found that the average drill in the town was used for less than fifteen minutes a year.

B. The project began with forty donated items in a single room. Members pay a small yearly fee and can borrow up to three things for one week. By 2024 the collection had grown to more than six hundred items. The most popular item is not a tool at all. It is a carpet cleaner.

C. Not everyone was positive at first. Local shop owners worried that fewer people would buy new products. However, a later study by the town council found the opposite effect on one shop. The hardware store sold more spare parts, because borrowed tools still needed blades and batteries.

D. The organisers say the main benefit is not money. Volunteers repair broken items every Saturday, and residents come to learn these skills. Many members say they now speak to neighbours they had never met. In their view, the library has become a meeting place as much as a store.

E. The model has limits. Expensive items get damaged, and the library depends on unpaid helpers. Some members also return things late, so popular items are often unavailable. The organisers believe that a booking app would solve this problem, and they plan to test one next year.

Questions 1 to 4: True, False or Not Given

  1. The Library of Things started with tools that people gave away.
    Answer

    TRUE. Paragraph B: "forty donated items". Donated means given away.

  2. Members can keep an item for as long as they want.
    Answer

    FALSE. Paragraph B says they borrow things "for one week".

  3. The carpet cleaner is borrowed more often than any other item.
    Answer

    TRUE. Paragraph B: "The most popular item ... is a carpet cleaner."

  4. The town council gives money to the library every year.
    Answer

    NOT GIVEN. The council did a study (paragraph C). The text says nothing about money from the council.

Questions 5 to 7: matching headings

Choose the best heading for paragraphs C, D and E from this list: i. A meeting place for the community. ii. Problems that remain. iii. A fear that proved wrong. iv. How the collection grew.

  1. Paragraph C
    Answer

    iii. Shop owners feared lower sales, but the hardware store sold more. The fear proved wrong.

  2. Paragraph D
    Answer

    i. The paragraph is about skills, neighbours and "a meeting place". Money is mentioned only to say it is not the main benefit.

  3. Paragraph E
    Answer

    ii. Damage, unpaid helpers and late returns are problems. Heading iv fits paragraph B, which is not asked.

Questions 8 to 10: summary completion

Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

Some members return items late, so popular items are often ?. The organisers think a ? could solve this. On Saturdays, ? fix broken items.

Patterns to remember

The questions paraphrase the text. These patterns show the common kinds of paraphrase. Learn to see them, in Reading and in Listening.

Paraphrase patterns in IELTS Listening and Reading
PatternPurposeModelNote
Word to synonymSame meaning, new wordText: "donated". Question: "given away".Learn word groups, not single words.
Verb to nounChange the word classText: "prices rose". Question: "a rise in prices".The answer may be a different form of the word.
Active to passiveChange the sentence shapeText: "The council ran a study". Question: "A study was carried out by the council".Find who did what. Ignore the word order.
Not + oppositeSay the same with a negativeText: "cheaper than planned". Question: "did not cost as much as expected".Read negatives slowly. They often decide True or False.
Number in wordsShow a number another wayText: "half of the members". Question: "50 percent of members".Also: a quarter, a third, double, a dozen.
Specific to generalUse a wider wordText: "drills, tents and sewing machines". Question: "equipment".Headings often use the general word.
Time in other wordsChange a time phraseText: "not until 2021". Question: "only in 2021"."Not until" means "only then".
Speaker correctionSignal the real answer in Listening"The 12th... sorry, I mean the 13th."The answer comes after "sorry", "actually", "let's say".
Signpost + new pointShow a new part of a talk"Moving on to the second problem..."If you are lost, wait for the next signpost.
Contrast word + real viewShow the writer's true opinion"Some say it is cheap. However, the real cost is higher."The view after "however" is usually the answer.

Practice

1. How many times do you hear each Listening recording?

  • Once
  • Twice
  • As many times as you want on computer

IELTS plays each recording once only, on paper and on computer.

2. The form says "Item to collect: a wooden ______". The limit is ONE WORD ONLY. The speaker says "It's a wooden table." Which answer is correct?

  • wooden table
  • a table
  • table

Only one word is allowed. "Wooden" is already on the form, so the missing word is "table".

3. Text: "Most visitors arrive by train, but about a third come by car." Statement: "All visitors use public transport." What is the answer?

  • TRUE
  • FALSE
  • NOT GIVEN

A third of visitors come by car, so not all use public transport. The text goes against the statement. So it is FALSE. Without the part about cars, the answer would be NOT GIVEN.

4. Which Reading paper has three sections with everyday, work and general texts?

  • Academic
  • General Training
  • Both

General Training moves from daily life (Section 1) to work (Section 2) to a longer general text (Section 3).

5. On computer, you get ? minutes at the end of Listening to check your answers.

6. You must sit a One Skill Retake within ? days of the full test.

  1. Your Academic Reading raw score is 30. About what band is that, according to ielts.org averages? And for General Training?
    Answer

    About band 7 in Academic Reading. About band 6 in General Training Reading. The exact number changes a little between test versions.

  2. Write a paraphrase of "Visitor numbers fell sharply in 2023" with a noun instead of a verb.
    Answer

    Model: "There was a sharp fall in visitor numbers in 2023." Also good: "2023 saw a steep drop in the number of visitors."

  3. Text: "The writer argues that cities should ban cars from the centre." Statement: "The writer supports a ban on cars in city centres." Yes, No or Not Given?
    Answer

    YES. "Argues that cities should ban" shows the writer's opinion. It agrees with the statement.

  4. Hard: you have 4 minutes left and 6 questions unanswered in Section 3. What do you do?
    Answer

    Answer the quick ones first, like completion tasks. Guess every other question. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so leave no gaps.

  5. Hard: write your own Listening distractor. Write two lines where a speaker gives a wrong time and then corrects it.
    Answer

    Model: "The bus leaves at half past eight. Oh no, sorry. In summer it's a quarter to nine." The answer is 8.45.

Key takeaways

  • Listening: 4 parts, 40 questions, about 30 minutes, each recording once. On computer you get 2 minutes at the end to check.
  • Reading: 3 sections, 40 questions, 60 minutes, no extra transfer time.
  • Each correct answer is one mark. About 30 of 40 gives band 7 in Listening and Academic Reading.
  • Word limits and spelling are strict. Wrong answers lose nothing, so always guess.
  • Questions paraphrase the text. Train yourself to see the same meaning in new words.
  • From mid-2026 IELTS is on computer in most countries. One Skill Retake lets you repeat one skill within 60 days.

Sources

  • IELTS Academic format: Listening. Parts, question types and answer rules.
  • IELTS Academic format: Reading. Text length and the eleven question types.
  • IELTS General Training format: Reading. The three General Training sections.
  • IELTS scoring in detail. Average marks for each band and the rounding rule.
  • IELTS One Skill Retake. The 60-day rule and who can use it.
  • Updates to IELTS test delivery (March 2026). The move from paper to computer.

IELTS Writing

IELTS Writing has two tasks in 60 minutes. Examiners mark it with four public criteria. If you know the criteria, you know what to write. This chapter gives plans, frames and original model answers at band 6 and band 8.

  • Describe both Writing tasks for Academic and General Training.
  • Explain the four marking criteria in simple words.
  • Plan and write an Academic Task 1 report, a General Training letter and a Task 2 essay.
  • See the difference between a band 6 answer and a band 8 answer.
  • Find and fix the most common band 5 mistakes.

The Writing paper at a glance

Ali spends 35 minutes on Task 1. It is a beautiful report. Then he has 25 minutes for Task 2 and writes only 180 words. His Writing band goes down. Why? Task 2 counts twice as much as Task 1, and it is too short.

The two Writing tasks (ielts.org, November 2026)
Task 1Task 2
AcademicDescribe a graph, table, chart, diagram, process or map in your own words.An essay about a point of view, an argument or a problem.
General TrainingA letter about an everyday situation. The style can be personal, semi-formal or formal.An essay about a point of view, an argument or a problem. Topics are of general interest.
Minimum length150 words250 words
Suggested timeAbout 20 minutesAbout 40 minutes
WeightOne partTwo parts: counts twice as much as Task 1

The rules are short but strict.

  • Write full, connected sentences. Notes and bullet points are not allowed.
  • Writing off the topic is penalised.
  • Copied text, called plagiarism, is severely penalised. An answer that is fully memorised can get band 0.
  • A very short answer cannot show enough language for a high band. An answer of 20 words or fewer gets band 1.
  • Writing more than the minimum is not penalised. But long answers leave less time to check.

Most people now type their answers on a computer. The computer counts your words. In some countries you can choose Writing on Paper and write by hand. On computer there is a note tool for planning. The examiner does not see your notes.

Do not copy whole sentences from the question. Copied words do not show your English. Say the same idea in your own words.

The four criteria in simple words

Examiners give each task a band for four criteria. The four are equal. The task band is their average.

Task Achievement (Task 1) and Task Response (Task 2).

Did you do what the task asked? In Academic Task 1: did you choose the key features, give an overview and use correct numbers? In a letter: did you cover all three bullet points with the right tone? In Task 2: did you answer every part of the question and give a clear position?

Coherence and Cohesion.

Coherence means your ideas come in a logical order. Cohesion means you join sentences well with linking words and words like "this" and "they". Paragraphs matter here.

Lexical Resource.

Do you use a range of words? Are they exact and natural? Do you know which words go together, like "make a decision" and "heavy traffic"? Spelling and word forms count here too.

Grammatical Range and Accuracy.

Do you use simple and complex sentences? How many sentences have no errors? Punctuation counts here.

The public band descriptors explain each band. Here is the step from 6 to 7 for Task 2, in our own words.

Band 6 and band 7 in Task 2 (our summary of the public descriptors)
CriterionBand 6Band 7
Task ResponseCovers the main parts, some less well. Position is clear, but the conclusion may repeat or be unclear. Some ideas are not developed.Covers the main parts well. Position is clear and developed. Ideas are supported, but some may be too general.
Coherence and CohesionClear overall order. Linking words help, but some feel mechanical or wrong.Logical order all the way. Uses a range of linking words and words like "this" with only small slips.
Lexical ResourceWords are adequate. Meaning is clear, but the range is narrow. Some spelling errors.Enough range to be flexible and exact. Some less common words. Good feel for word partners.
GrammarA mix of simple and complex sentences. Complex ones have more errors.A variety of complex sentences. Many sentences have no errors.

Band 6: clear, but simple and a little repetitive. Band 7: clear, developed and mostly correct. Band 8: easy to read, exact words, very few errors.

Your lowest criterion pulls your band down. A writer with great vocabulary but no clear position often stays at band 6. Fix the weakest criterion first.

Academic Task 1: describe the data

Task 1 is a report about facts. You describe what the picture shows. You do not explain why, and you do not give your opinion.

Here is an original task, made for this book. The cities and the numbers are invented.

Task: The chart shows the average number of bicycle trips per day, in thousands, in three cities from 2016 to 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

A four-paragraph plan

  1. Introduction: one sentence. Say what the chart shows, in your own words.
  2. Overview: two sentences. Give the two or three biggest patterns, with no numbers. Examiners look for this.
  3. Body 1: one group of data with numbers. For example, the cities that grew.
  4. Body 2: the other group, with numbers and a comparison.

An overview is the most important paragraph. The band 7 descriptor asks for a clear overview. Without one, Task Achievement usually stays low.

The line graph show the number of bicycle trips per day in three cities, Norburg, Calden and Rivet Bay, between 2016 and 2024. The numbers are in thousands.

In 2016, Norburg had 20 thousand trips. In 2018 it was 24 thousand and in 2020 it was 35 thousand. Then it went up to 41 thousand in 2022 and 46 thousand in 2024. This was the highest number in the graph.

Calden had 32 thousand trips in 2016, which was more than the other two cities. After that it decreased to 31, 28, 27 and finally 25 thousand in 2024.

Rivet Bay started with only 6 thousand trips. In 2016 it was the lowest of the three cities. It increased a lot in 2020 to 21 thousand. After that it continued to increase and reached 30 thousand in 2024, so it was more than Calden at the end. But it was always lower than Norburg.

Overall, Norburg and Rivet Bay increased and Calden decreased.

  • Task Achievement: the numbers are correct and the key change in Rivet Bay is there. But the overview comes only at the end and is very short. Most of the report lists every number one by one.
  • Coherence and Cohesion: clear order, but "In 2016... In 2018... in 2020" is mechanical.
  • Lexical Resource: "increased" and "decreased" repeat. "Increased a lot" is vague.
  • Grammar: mostly simple sentences. One error: "The line graph show" should be "shows".
  • Our estimate: about band 6. It has about 160 words. Only an examiner can give an official band.

The line graph compares the average number of daily bicycle journeys in three cities, Norburg, Calden and Rivet Bay, over an eight-year period from 2016.

Overall, cycling became much more common in Norburg and Rivet Bay, while it slowly declined in Calden. Norburg recorded the most trips from 2020 onwards, and by 2024 Rivet Bay had also overtaken Calden.

Norburg saw the strongest growth. Its figure rose gradually from 20,000 trips a day in 2016 to 24,000 in 2018, before jumping to 35,000 in 2020. It then kept climbing steadily and reached a peak of 46,000 in the final year, more than double its starting level. Rivet Bay began from a much lower base of only 6,000 trips, but it followed a similar pattern. After a sharp rise to 21,000 in 2020, its total continued to grow and stood at 30,000 by 2024.

Calden was the only city where cycling fell. Although it had the highest figure in 2016, at 32,000 trips, the number dropped slightly in every period shown and ended at 25,000. As a result, it moved from first place to last.

  • Task Achievement: a clear overview in paragraph 2 with the main trends and the two changes of rank. Key numbers support each point. No explanation or opinion is added.
  • Coherence and Cohesion: the data is grouped by pattern (growth, then decline), not by year. "Its figure", "It then", "As a result" link ideas naturally.
  • Lexical Resource: exact trend words: rose gradually, jumping, kept climbing, reached a peak, dropped slightly. "From a much lower base" is a natural collocation.
  • Grammar: a range of structures: "before jumping", "Although it had...", "more than double its starting level". No errors.
  • Our estimate: about band 8. It has about 185 words.

Do not explain causes. "Calden fell because people bought cars" is not in the chart. Task 1 reports only what you can see.

Other Task 1 pictures

The same plan works for every picture. Only the language changes.

Bar charts and tables

Compare more than you describe. Use "the highest", "twice as many as", "a similar number". Group the categories, for example "the three largest" and "the rest".

Pie charts

Talk about shares: "a quarter", "just over half", "the largest proportion". The parts add up to 100 percent, so compare them.

A process diagram

Use the passive and sequence words. "First, the beans are washed. Next, they are dried in the sun. Finally, they are packed." The overview gives the number of stages and the start and end.

Maps

Describe changes with place words. "The car park was replaced by a library." "A new road was built to the north of the river." The overview says how much the place changed in general.

General Training Task 1: the letter

The task gives a situation and three bullet points. You must cover all three. The person you write to decides the tone.

Three tones for a letter
ToneWhenOpeningClosing
FormalA company or a person you do not know by nameDear Sir or Madam,Yours faithfully,
Semi-formalA person you know by name but not well: a manager, a landlordDear Mr Patel,Yours sincerely, or Kind regards,
InformalA friend or a relativeHi Sam, or Dear Sam,Best wishes, or See you soon,

Start with the purpose. The first or second sentence should say why you write. You do not need addresses.

An original task: You bought a laptop from an online shop. It stopped working after two weeks. Write a letter to the shop. In your letter: describe the problem; explain what you have already tried; say what you want the shop to do.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about a laptop that I ordered from your website on 2 October. The order number is 58214. Unfortunately, the computer stopped working after only two weeks, and I would like the problem solved as soon as possible.

Since last Monday, the laptop has refused to turn on. When I press the power button, a small light flashes three times, but the screen stays black. It is fully charged, and I have not dropped it or spilled anything on it.

Before contacting you, I followed every step in the troubleshooting guide on your support page. I tried a different charger and held down the power button for thirty seconds to reset it. I also spoke to your online chat assistant, who suggested the same steps. None of these solved the problem.

As the laptop is still well within the guarantee period, I would be grateful if you could send me a replacement. Alternatively, I would accept a full refund. Please let me know how I should return the faulty item.

Yours faithfully,

Maria Lopez

Why it works: the purpose is clear in the first paragraph. Each bullet point has its own paragraph with details. The tone is formal and polite all the way. It has about 180 words.

Mixed tone loses marks. "Dear Sir or Madam ... Anyway, hope you're OK, cheers!" starts formal and ends like a chat. Keep one tone from start to end.

Task 2: essay types and plans

Read the question twice. The last sentence tells you the essay type. Each type needs a slightly different plan.

Five common Task 2 essay types
TypeQuestion wordsPlan for the body
OpinionTo what extent do you agree or disagree?Two paragraphs with reasons for your view. You may admit one point on the other side.
DiscussionDiscuss both views and give your own opinion.Paragraph 1: view A. Paragraph 2: view B. Your opinion in the introduction and conclusion.
Advantages and disadvantagesDo the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?Paragraph 1: the weaker side. Paragraph 2: the stronger side, which is your answer.
Problem and solutionWhat problems does this cause? What can be done?Paragraph 1: problems or causes. Paragraph 2: solutions that match them.
Two-part questionWhy is this happening? Is it positive or negative?One paragraph for each question. Answer both directly.

Plan

Find the type. Underline every part of the question. Write your position in one line. Note two main ideas with one example each.

Introduction

Two or three sentences. Paraphrase the topic. Give your position clearly. Do not start with a memorised phrase.

Two body paragraphs

Each one: a topic sentence, an explanation, an example, and a link back to the question.

Conclusion

Two sentences. Repeat your position in new words. Add no new ideas.

Check

Look for your own common errors: verb endings, articles, plurals. Check the word count.

A good body paragraph has a clear shape. Here is a frame you can reuse. The chapter Writing sentences and paragraphs explains topic sentences in more detail.

  1. Topic sentence: One major benefit of remote work is that it saves time.
  2. Explain: Without a daily commute, employees gain one or two hours.
  3. Example: A developer who travelled 50 minutes each way now uses that time for exercise.
  4. Link back: This shows that working from home can improve well-being.

Task 2 model answers: band 6 and band 8

An original task: Many companies now let staff work from home. Some people think this is good for both workers and employers. Others believe that working in an office is better. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.

Nowadays many companies let their workers to work from home. Some people think it is good for workers and companies, but other people think office is better. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, working from home has many advantages. Firstly, workers do not need to travel to the office, so they save time and money. This is very important for people who live far from the city. Secondly, they can work in a quiet place and they are more productive. For example, my friend works from home and she says she finishes her tasks faster. Moreover, companies can save money because they do not need a big office.

On the other hand, some people think office is better. Firstly, in the office people can talk face to face and this is good for teamwork. Secondly, some workers feel lonely at home. For example, new workers cannot ask questions easily when they are at home. Furthermore, it is difficult for managers to check the work of their staff. Also, at home there are many distractions such as family and television.

In my opinion, I think working from home is better for most workers. It saves time and money and people can be more productive. Also, workers are happier when they can choose. However, companies should also have meetings in the office sometimes.

In conclusion, both working from home and in the office have advantages and disadvantages. I believe that working from home is better, but companies should find a balance because every company is different.

  • Task Response: both views and an opinion are there, so the main parts are covered. But ideas are listed, not developed. Only one short example. The opinion paragraph and the conclusion repeat each other.
  • Coherence and Cohesion: clear paragraphs. But "Firstly, Secondly, Moreover, Furthermore, Also" is mechanical. Each linker starts a new point without explanation.
  • Lexical Resource: adequate but simple. "Good", "better" and "save time and money" repeat. "In my opinion, I think" says the same thing twice.
  • Grammar: some complex sentences. Errors: "let their workers to work" (no "to" after let), "office is better" (needs "the office").
  • Our estimate: about band 6. It has about 265 words, so it is long enough.

Since remote work became widespread, opinions have been divided. Some argue that working from home benefits both staff and employers, while others insist that an office environment is more effective. In my view, a hybrid model, with most work done at home, offers the best of both.

Supporters of home working point first to the time it saves. Without a daily commute, employees often gain an hour or more, which they can spend resting, exercising or with their families. This tends to make them healthier and more motivated. Employers also benefit financially. A company whose staff work remotely needs far less office space and can hire talented people who live too far away to travel each day.

Those who prefer the office, however, raise valid concerns. Spontaneous conversations by the coffee machine often lead to new ideas, and these are hard to recreate on a video call. New employees in particular learn much faster when they can watch experienced colleagues and ask quick questions. In addition, some people find it difficult to separate work from home life, and this can lead to isolation or long, unhealthy working hours.

Having weighed both sides, I believe that neither extreme is ideal. Focused tasks, such as writing code or reports, are usually done better at home. Teamwork, training and planning, on the other hand, benefit from being in the same room. For this reason, companies should let staff work remotely most of the week but bring teams together regularly.

In conclusion, home working saves time and money, but offices still support learning and creativity. A balanced hybrid approach is therefore the most sensible choice for most organisations.

  • Task Response: both views are fully discussed. The position is clear in the introduction, developed in paragraph 4 and repeated in new words at the end. Each idea is explained with a reason or an effect.
  • Coherence and Cohesion: each paragraph has one clear purpose. Linking is natural: "Those who prefer the office, however", "For this reason", and reference words like "This" and "these".
  • Lexical Resource: exact and natural: "remote work became widespread", "raise valid concerns", "hard to recreate", "neither extreme is ideal".
  • Grammar: a wide range: relative clauses ("whose staff work remotely"), participle phrases ("Having weighed both sides"), no errors.
  • Our estimate: about band 8. It has about 275 words.

The band 8 essay does not use rare or fancy words. It uses common words in exact, natural pairs. Examiners reward precise words more than long words.

Common band 5 mistakes

These mistakes keep many writers at band 5 or 5.5. Each one has a wrong and a right version.

Task 1 with no overview, only a list of numbers.

This is a controversial issue that has many sides in today's modern world.

Moreover, Furthermore, Additionally, Also, Besides...

Technology is very important. It helps people. It is useful.

In conclusion, also governments should build more parks.

Companies should let workers to choose.

Task 1 with a two-sentence overview before the details.

Whether cities should ban cars from their centres is a question many councils now face.

Use a linker only when it shows a real link. Explain each idea before you add the next.

Technology helps doctors find diseases earlier, which saves lives.

In conclusion, both views have merit, but the benefits are greater.

Companies should let workers choose.

  • Under length. Count before you finish. Short answers cannot show enough language.
  • Not answering every part. "Discuss both views and give your opinion" has three parts. Missing one limits Task Response.
  • Memorised phrases. The descriptors name memorised and formulaic language as a problem. Examiners know these phrases.
  • No paragraphs. One big block of text hurts Coherence and Cohesion.
  • New ideas in the conclusion. The conclusion only sums up.
  • Small grammar slips. Articles, plural -s and verb endings. Make a list of your own top five errors. Check for them in the last five minutes.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for IELTS Writing
PatternPurposeModelNote
The + chart + compares / shows + what + where + when.Task 1 introductionThe line graph compares daily bicycle trips in three cities from 2016 to 2024.Do not copy the question. Change the words.
Overall, + main trend, while + contrast.Task 1 overviewOverall, cycling grew in two cities, while it declined in Calden.No numbers in the overview.
Noun + rose / fell + adverb + from X to Y.Describe a trendTrips rose sharply from 9,000 to 21,000."Rose", not "was risen". The verb has no object.
There was a + adjective + rise / fall + in + noun.Describe a trend with a nounThere was a steady fall in trips in Calden.Use "in" after the noun: "a fall in trips".
X + was + twice / three times + as high as + Y.Compare numbersNorburg's figure was almost twice as high as Calden's."As high as", not "as higher than".
First, ... is / are + past participle. Next, ...Describe a processFirst, the beans are washed. Next, they are dried.Use the present passive for processes.
I am writing to + verb + about + topic.Letter purposeI am writing to complain about a faulty laptop.Say the purpose in the first lines.
I would be grateful if you could + verb.Polite formal requestI would be grateful if you could send a replacement."Could", not "can", after "grateful if".
Some argue that + view A, while others + view B.Task 2 introductionSome argue that remote work helps everyone, while others prefer offices.Then give your own position.
In my view, + clear position.State your positionIn my view, a hybrid model works best.Not "In my opinion, I think". That says it twice.
Although + point against, + your point.Admit the other sideAlthough offices help teamwork, most tasks can be done at home.Do not add "but" after an "although" clause.
For example, + specific case.Support an ideaFor example, a developer can use her commute time to exercise.Make examples specific, not "many people".
In conclusion, + position in new words.End the essayIn conclusion, a balanced hybrid approach is the most sensible choice.No new ideas here.

Practice

1. How long should you spend on Task 2?

  • About 20 minutes
  • About 40 minutes
  • About 60 minutes

Task 2 counts twice as much and needs 250 words. IELTS suggests about 40 minutes.

2. Which sentence belongs in an Academic Task 1 report?

  • I think Calden should build more bike lanes.
  • Cycling fell in Calden because the weather was bad.
  • Cycling fell slightly in Calden, from 32,000 to 25,000 trips.

Task 1 reports the data. It gives no opinion and no causes.

3. You write to a company. You do not know a name. Which closing is right?

  • Yours faithfully,
  • Best wishes,
  • See you soon,

"Dear Sir or Madam" goes with "Yours faithfully" in British English.

4. In Task 1, the paragraph with the main trends and no numbers is the ?.

5. Task 2 needs at least ? words.

6. Correct the verb: Trips in Norburg (was risen) steadily.

  1. Name the essay type: "Some people say university should be free. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?"
    Answer

    Advantages and disadvantages. Discuss the weaker side first, then the stronger side, and say clearly which one is greater.

  2. Write an overview for the bicycle chart in two sentences. Use no numbers.
    Answer

    Model: Overall, cycling increased strongly in Norburg and Rivet Bay, but it fell gradually in Calden. By the end of the period, Calden had moved from first place to last.

  3. Correct the three errors: "Nowadays, many people is using bicycle because it is more cheaper than car."
    Answer

    "Nowadays, many people use bicycles because they are cheaper than cars." Errors: "people is" (people are or people use), "bicycle" (plural), "more cheaper" (just "cheaper"). "Car" also needs a plural.

  4. Make this body paragraph stronger: "Public transport is good. It is cheap. It helps the environment. Also it is fast."
    Answer

    Model: "One strong argument for public transport is its effect on the environment. A full bus can replace dozens of cars, which cuts both traffic and air pollution. In cities such as Seoul, fast bus lanes have made travel quicker as well. Investing in public transport therefore helps people and the planet at the same time." It now has one main idea, an explanation, an example and a link.

  5. Hard: write a semi-formal letter opening and purpose line to your landlord, Ms Green, about a broken heater.
    Answer

    Model: "Dear Ms Green, I am writing to let you know that the heater in my flat has stopped working, and I would like to ask you to arrange a repair."

  6. Hard: write an introduction for this question: "Some people believe that children should learn to code at primary school. To what extent do you agree or disagree?"
    Answer

    Model: "Coding is now a basic skill in many jobs, so some people want it taught from the first years of school. I largely agree, as long as it does not replace reading, maths and play." The position is clear and limited.

Key takeaways

  • Two tasks in 60 minutes. Task 1: 150 words, about 20 minutes. Task 2: 250 words, about 40 minutes, and it counts double.
  • Four equal criteria: task, organisation, vocabulary and grammar. Your weakest one pulls your band down.
  • Academic Task 1 needs a clear overview and grouped data. No causes, no opinion.
  • A letter needs a clear purpose, all three bullet points and one steady tone.
  • Task 2 needs a clear position, developed ideas and specific examples.
  • Avoid memorised phrases, bullet points, under-length answers and new ideas in the conclusion.

Sources

  • IELTS General Training format: Writing. The letter task and its styles.

IELTS Speaking

IELTS Speaking is a short, live conversation with a trained examiner. It has three parts and takes 11 to 14 minutes. You cannot memorise it, but you can train for it. This chapter gives the format, the four criteria, answer frames, model answers and a 14-day plan.

  • Describe the three parts of IELTS Speaking and their timing.
  • Explain the four criteria in simple words.
  • Use answer frames for Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3.
  • Keep talking when you do not know a word.
  • Follow a 14-day speaking plan with self-recording.

The test at a glance

Examiner: Do you work or are you a student?

Weak answer: I work.

Strong answer: I work. I'm a backend developer at a logistics company. I mostly build services that track parcels, so my day is a mix of coding and meetings.

Both answers are correct English. But the first gives the examiner nothing to assess. The second shows vocabulary, grammar and fluency in three sentences. That is the whole secret of IELTS Speaking: give the examiner enough language to judge.

The three parts (ielts.org, November 2026)
PartTimeWhat happens
1. Introduction and interview4 to 5 minutesThe examiner checks your identity. Then you answer questions about familiar topics: home, family, work, studies, interests.
2. Long turn3 to 4 minutesYou get a task card. You have 1 minute to prepare, with a pencil and paper. Then you talk for up to 2 minutes. The examiner may ask one or two short questions after.
3. Discussion4 to 5 minutesThe examiner asks more general and abstract questions linked to the Part 2 topic.
  • The test is with a human examiner, face to face or by video call. With IELTS Online it is always by video call.
  • It may be on the same day as the other papers, or up to a week before or after.
  • The test is recorded.
  • In Part 2 the examiner stops you when the time is up. This is normal. It is not a bad sign.

Do not learn long answers by heart. The questions are designed so that you cannot rehearse set answers. Examiners notice a sudden change to perfect, fast, "written" English. Learn frames and phrases, not whole answers.

The four criteria in simple words

The examiner judges your speaking on four criteria. Each one has equal weight. Your Speaking band is the average of the four.

What the examiner listens for
CriterionThe question in simple wordsBand 5Band 7
Fluency and CoherenceDo you keep going? Are your ideas easy to follow?Keeps going, but with many repeats, restarts or slow speech. Pauses to find basic words.Long turns without much effort. Some pauses to find language, but the message stays clear.
Lexical ResourceDo you have the words for many topics? Can you explain a word you do not know?Enough words for familiar topics, with little flexibility. Paraphrase sometimes fails.Flexible words on many topics. Some less common words and natural word partners.
Grammatical Range and AccuracyDo you use different sentence types? How many errors do you make?Simple sentences are mostly correct. Complex sentences nearly always have errors.A range of structures. Error-free sentences are frequent.
PronunciationIs it easy to understand you? Do you use stress and rhythm?Some good features, but control is limited. The listener needs some effort.Easy to understand, with good use of stress, rhythm and intonation most of the time.

This table is our summary of the public band descriptors. Read the official PDF for the full wording. Note two words. Fluency is speaking smoothly, at a normal speed. Paraphrase is saying a word or idea in other words.

Accent is not a problem in itself. The descriptors talk about how easy you are to understand. You do not need a British or American accent for band 8.

Fluency is not speed. Speaking very fast with many errors does not help. A steady, clear pace with short natural pauses is better.

Part 1: short personal answers

Part 1 questions are easy on purpose. They help you relax. Your goal is two to four sentences per answer. Use the A-R-E frame: Answer, Reason, Example. The chapter Speaking skills uses the same frame for daily life.

  1. Answer: Yes, I really enjoy cooking.
  2. Reason: It helps me switch off after a day of screens.
  3. Example: Last weekend I made dumplings from scratch with my sister.

Q: Do you like where you live? A: Yes. It is nice.

Q: How often do you use public transport? A: Every day.

Q: Did you like music as a child? A: Yes, I liked. Very much like.

Q: Do you like where you live? A: Yes, mostly. I live in a quiet area near a big park, so I can run before work. The only problem is that the shops close quite early.

Q: How often do you use public transport? A: Almost every day. I take the metro to the office because it's faster than driving. On weekends I usually cycle instead.

Q: Did you like music as a child? A: I did, actually. My parents made me take piano lessons, and I complained at first. Now I'm grateful, because I still play to relax.

Look at the tenses in the last strong answer. The question is in the past, so the answer starts in the past: "made", "complained". Then it moves to now: "I still play". Match the tense of the question first.

"Yes, I do like" and "Yes, I liked" are not complete. Use a full short answer, "Yes, I do", or add the object: "Yes, I liked it a lot."

Part 2: the long turn

Part 2 is a short talk of up to two minutes. The card gives a topic and some points. Here is an original card, written for this book.

Describe a piece of technology you use every day.

You should say: what it is; when you started using it; what you use it for; and explain why it is important to you.

One minute of notes

Do not write sentences. Write five or six key words, one line for each point. Add one story or detail you can describe. Here are notes for card 1.

noise-cancelling headphones
2 yrs ago, birthday, sister
open office, focus, calls, podcasts on metro
story: first day, heard nothing, missed my stop!
why: quiet = deep work, less tired

A five-step talk

Open

Say the topic in one sentence. "I'd like to talk about my noise-cancelling headphones."

Background

When and how it started. Use past tenses. "I got them about two years ago, as a birthday present."

Details

What you do with it, where and how often. Use the present simple.

A short story

One real moment, with feelings. A story makes the talk longer and more natural.

Why it matters

Answer the "explain" point clearly. It is often the most important point on the card.

I'd like to talk about my noise-cancelling headphones, which I honestly use every single day.

I got them about two years ago. My sister gave them to me for my birthday, because she was tired of hearing me complain about my noisy office. At first I thought they were a bit of a luxury, but I changed my mind very quickly.

I work in an open-plan office with about forty people, so there's always someone talking or on a call. When I need to concentrate on a difficult piece of code, I put them on, and the noise just disappears. I also use them for video calls, and on the metro I listen to podcasts about software design.

I remember the first morning I wore them on the train. The silence was so complete that I got lost in a podcast and missed my stop. I was ten minutes late for work, but I couldn't stop smiling.

The main reason they're important to me is focus. In my job, an hour of deep, uninterrupted work is worth more than a whole afternoon of small distractions. And because my brain isn't fighting the noise all day, I'm much less tired in the evening. So for me, they're not really a gadget. They're a tool for doing my job well.

  • Fluency and Coherence: it follows the card in order. Signposts guide the listener: "At first", "I remember", "The main reason".
  • Lexical Resource: topic words and natural partners: open-plan office, deep work, uninterrupted, a bit of a luxury.
  • Grammar: past simple for the story, present simple for habits, a relative clause ("which I honestly use"), a cause clause ("because my brain isn't fighting the noise").
  • Length: about 220 words. Spoken at a calm pace, that fills about two minutes.

Two more cards to practise

Cue card 2: Describe a time when you helped someone solve a problem.

You should say: who the person was; what the problem was; how you helped; and explain how you felt afterwards. Notes idea: new colleague, could not set up the dev environment, screen share for an hour, wrote a setup guide, felt useful, guide still used today.

Cue card 3: Describe a place in your city where you like to spend free time.

You should say: where it is; how often you go there; what you do there; and explain why you like it. Notes idea: riverside path, every Sunday, walk and coffee, watch boats, quiet after a busy week.

If you finish early, do not stop. Add another detail or a comparison: "Before I had them, I used to work in the meeting rooms just to get some quiet." Keep talking until the examiner stops you.

Part 3: discuss bigger ideas

Part 3 moves from you to people in general. The questions ask you to give opinions, compare, explain causes and imagine the future. The answers should be longer than in Part 1: four to six sentences.

Use the O-R-E-O frame: Opinion, Reason, Example, Other side. The "other side" shows that you can think in a balanced way.

  1. Opinion: To some extent, yes, especially young people.
  2. Reason: Phones are designed to keep our attention, with constant notifications.
  3. Example: In restaurants you often see whole families looking at screens instead of talking.
  4. Other side: That said, phones also make life much easier. Banking, maps and messages are all in one place, so it's natural to use them a lot.
Common Part 3 question types and useful language
The question asks you toExample questionUseful language
Give an opinionShould schools teach coding?I'd say that... / On balance, I think...
Compare past and presentHow has communication changed?In the past, people used to... Nowadays, ...
Explain causesWhy do people change jobs more often now?One reason is that... This is partly because...
Imagine the futureWhat technology will be common in 20 years?I imagine that... It's likely that... might...
EvaluateIs working from home good for society?The main advantage is... The downside is...

These forms need hedging: words like "probably", "tend to" and "I'd say". They sound natural in a discussion. The chapter Hedging and stance explains them in depth.

Part 3 is not about you. The question "Why do people change jobs?" needs answers about people in general. One short personal example is fine, but then go back to the general idea.

Fluency fixes and unknown words

Everyone pauses. The skill is to pause in a natural way. Silence and "ehh..." sound like a problem. A short phrase sounds like thinking.

To buy a few seconds

  • That's an interesting question.
  • Let me think about that for a second.
  • I've never really thought about that, but...
  • Well, it depends on what you mean by...

To fix a mistake

  • Sorry, I mean...
  • Or rather...
  • What I'm trying to say is...
  • Let me put that another way.

Use each phrase only once or twice in a test. The band 5 descriptor mentions overusing the same linking words. Variety matters.

When you do not know a word

You want to say "tripod", but the word does not come. Do not stop. Describe it. This is the paraphrase skill from the Lexical Resource criterion.

"I used a... it's a kind of stand with three legs that holds your camera still."

You can also ask the examiner to repeat a question: "Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?" This is fine once or twice. It is much better than answering a question you did not understand.

The examiner cannot score silence. A simple description of a missing word gives the examiner language to score.

A 14-day speaking plan

This plan needs 30 to 40 minutes a day. You need a phone to record yourself. Recording is the key. You hear your own errors only when you listen back.

The self-recording method

  1. Record one answer, for example a full Part 2 talk.
  2. Listen once. Do not stop the recording. Note your general feeling.
  3. Write down the first minute word by word. This is a transcript.
  4. Mark errors, repeated words and long pauses in the transcript.
  5. Record the same answer again. Fix the three biggest problems.
Fourteen days of practice
DayFocusTask
1Starting pointRecord a mini test: 4 Part 1 questions, one cue card, 2 Part 3 questions. Keep it to compare later.
2Part 1 framesAnswer 12 Part 1 questions with A-R-E. Record them all.
3Natural pausesLearn 6 phrases to buy time. Use them in 10 new answers.
4Part 2 notesFive cue cards: 1 minute of notes, 2 minutes of talk each.
5Past tensesTell 3 short stories about real events. Check past forms in the transcript.
6ParaphraseDescribe 10 objects in your room without saying their names.
7Mock test 1A full timed test with a friend, a teacher or a recording. Transcribe one minute.
8Part 3 framesAnswer 10 Part 3 questions with O-R-E-O.
9Compare and predictAnswer questions about past, present and future: "used to", "nowadays", "it's likely that".
10Topic wordsBuild word lists for 4 common topics: technology, work, environment, education.
11PronunciationShadow a model answer: play it and speak at the same time. Focus on stress and chunks.
12Your top errorsCollect your 3 most common errors from all transcripts. Practise only those.
13Mock test 2A new full test. Compare it with Day 1 and Day 7.
14Rest and routineLight review. Plan the test day. Speak English for 10 minutes before the test to warm up.

Shadowing trains rhythm and stress. The chapter Pronunciation and fluency shows the method step by step.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for IELTS Speaking
PatternPurposeModelNote
Short answer + reason + exampleA full Part 1 answerYes, I do. It helps me relax. Last week I cooked for friends.Two to four sentences. Not one word, not one minute.
I'd like to talk about + topic.Open the Part 2 talkI'd like to talk about my headphones.Not "I will talk about the topic of...".
I remember the time when + past simple.Start a short storyI remember the time when I missed my stop.Use the past simple for the events.
The main reason + is that + clause.Answer the "explain" pointThe main reason is that it helps me focus.Not "The main reason is because".
To some extent, yes, but + limit.A balanced opinionTo some extent, yes, but it depends on age.Good start for Part 3.
In the past, people used to + verb. Nowadays, ...Compare past and presentIn the past, people used to write letters. Nowadays, they send messages."Used to" + base verb, not "used to writing".
It's likely that + future.Predict with careIt's likely that most cars will be electric.Softer than "will definitely".
That said, + other side.Show the other sideThat said, phones also make life easier.Use it after your main view.
It's a kind of + general noun + that + verb.Describe a missing wordIt's a kind of stand that holds a camera.Use "that" or "which" for the job it does.
Let me think about that for a second.Buy time naturallyThat's a hard one. Let me think about that for a second.Use once or twice. Not before every answer.
Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?Ask for a repeatSorry, could you repeat the question, please?Better than guessing the question.
Sorry, I mean + correction.Fix your own errorShe go... sorry, I mean she went home.Correct quickly and continue.

Practice

1. How long do you have to prepare in Part 2?

  • No time
  • 1 minute
  • 2 minutes

You get one minute with a pencil and paper. Then you speak for up to two minutes.

2. Which Part 1 answer is best?

  • Yes.
  • Yes, I like reading. Reading is good. I like it very much.
  • Yes, mostly on my phone. I read tech blogs on the train, and at night I read novels to relax.

It answers, adds details and uses different words. The second answer repeats "like" and "reading" and adds nothing.

3. The examiner stops you in the middle of a sentence in Part 2. What does it mean?

  • Your answer was wrong.
  • The time is up. It is normal.
  • You spoke too fast.

The examiner stops you when the time is up. It is not a judgement on your answer.

4. The four criteria are Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and ?.

5. In the past, people used to (write) more letters.

6. The main reason is ? it saves time.

  1. Make this Part 1 answer stronger with A-R-E. Q: "Do you like weekends?" A: "Yes."
    Answer

    Model: "Yes, of course. Weekends are the only time I can sleep late and see my friends. Last Saturday, for example, we went hiking outside the city."

  2. You forget the word "ladder". Describe it in one sentence.
    Answer

    Model: "It's a kind of tool with steps that you climb to reach something high, like a shelf or a roof."

  3. Write one-minute notes for cue card 3 (a place where you spend free time). Use five lines.
    Answer

    Model notes: "city library, 10 min walk / Saturday mornings / read, work on side project / story: met an old classmate there / why: quiet, free, feels like a second home".

  4. Answer this Part 3 question with O-R-E-O in four sentences: "Should children have smartphones?"
    Answer

    Model: "I'd say not before the age of about twelve. Young children find it very hard to control their screen time. For example, many teachers say pupils come to school tired after late-night gaming. That said, an older child may need a phone for safety and to stay in touch with parents."

  5. Hard: correct the errors in this Part 2 opening. "I want talk about my laptop. I am using it since three years. It's very useful for me because many reasons."
    Answer

    "I'd like to talk about my laptop. I've been using it for three years. It's very useful to me for many reasons." Errors: "want talk" needs "to", the present perfect continuous with "for", and "because" needs a clause, so use "for many reasons".

  6. Hard: record yourself answering cue card 2 for two minutes. Transcribe the first minute. Count your repeated words and your errors. What will you fix first?
    Answer

    Answers vary. A good self-check looks like this: "I said 'and then' nine times. I made four past tense errors. I will use 'after that' and 'later' and check past forms." Fix the error that happens most often first.

Key takeaways

  • Three parts in 11 to 14 minutes: personal questions, a two-minute talk, then a discussion of general ideas.
  • Four equal criteria: fluency and coherence, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation.
  • Give the examiner enough language: A-R-E in Part 1, five steps in Part 2, O-R-E-O in Part 3.
  • Use one minute of notes in Part 2 for key words and one story, not full sentences.
  • When a word is missing, describe it. Never fall silent.
  • Record, transcribe and fix your top errors. Two mock tests in 14 days show your progress.
