  • IELTS scoring in detail. Equal weighting of the four criteria.
  • IELTS guide for test takers. Face to face or video call, and test-day timing.

TOEFL iBT

TOEFL iBT is an English test from ETS. Universities in many countries accept it. The test changed a lot on 21 January 2026. This chapter explains the new format, every task type and the new 1 to 6 scores.

  • Describe the four sections, their order, their tasks and their timing.
  • Explain what changed in 2023 and in January 2026.
  • Use a clear strategy for each of the twelve task types.
  • Take short, useful notes while you listen and read.
  • Read a score report on the 1 to 6 scale and link it to the CEFR.

The test at a glance

Meet Ken. He books a TOEFL test at home for a Saturday morning. He starts at 9:00. At about 11:00 he is finished. There is no break. Three days later his scores are in his ETS account.

That is a normal TOEFL day. The test has four sections. They always come in the same order: Reading, Listening, Writing, Speaking. Each section uses short task types.

The four sections (ETS pages, checked November 2026)
SectionTask typesItemsTime (about)
ReadingComplete the Words. Read in Daily Life. Read an Academic Passage.5030 minutes
ListeningListen and Choose a Response. Listen to a Conversation. Listen to an Announcement. Listen to an Academic Talk.4729 minutes
WritingBuild a Sentence. Write an Email. Write for an Academic Discussion.1223 minutes
SpeakingListen and Repeat. Take an Interview.118 minutes

The times do not include instructions. ETS says to allow about two hours in total. Reading and Listening times change a little, because these sections adapt to you.

  • Where: at a test centre, or at home with the Home Edition. At home a live human proctor watches you.
  • Breaks: there are no scheduled breaks.
  • Every section counts: answer at least one question in each section. If you skip a whole section, ETS scores no section at all.
  • Not allowed: phones and writing help software.
  • Results: in your ETS account three days after the test. Scores are valid for two years.

"I will skip Speaking. I only need Reading." This does not work. A test with an empty section gets no scores. Answer something in every section.

How the test changed in 2023 and 2026

Many free videos and old books still show the "old TOEFL". If you practise old tasks, you practise the wrong test. Always check the date of a book or a video.

  1. Before July 2023 The long test. ETS says it took about three hours. Writing had an Independent essay and an Integrated task.
  2. 26 July 2023 A shorter test. It took under two hours. Write for an Academic Discussion replaced the Independent essay. Reading became shorter. ETS removed all unscored questions.
  3. 2023 to 2025 Four long sections. Reading had two long passages. Speaking had four tasks, and three were integrated. Each section scored 0 to 30, and the total was 0 to 120.
  4. 21 January 2026 The new test. Short new tasks in every section. Reading and Listening became adaptive. A new 1 to 6 scale. Computer scoring for Writing and Speaking.
The 2023 format and the 2026 format side by side
Part2023 to January 2026Since 21 January 2026
ReadingTwo long academic passages, about 700 words eachWord gaps, short daily-life texts and short academic passages of about 200 words
ListeningLong conversations and lecturesShort clips: one-line replies, conversations, announcements and short talks
WritingIntegrated task (read, listen, write) and Academic DiscussionBuild a Sentence, Write an Email and Academic Discussion
SpeakingOne independent task and three integrated tasks, with time to prepareListen and Repeat, and a four-question interview with no time to prepare
Scores0 to 30 per section, 0 to 120 in total1 to 6 per section and overall, in half bands

The 2026 test checks two things. It checks foundational skills, like spelling and word order. It also checks real communication, like an email or an interview.

"Integrated Writing is the hardest task, so I practise it every day." That task left the test in January 2026. The skills behind it still help you. But do not plan your study around it.

Adaptive design: two stages

Ana and Ben start the same Reading section. Ana gets most of the first questions right. Ben makes many mistakes. In the second part, Ana gets harder questions. Ben gets easier ones. Both get a fair score.

Reading and Listening are multistage adaptive. Everybody starts with the same kind of first stage. ETS calls it the router. Your result there picks your second module: an easier one or a harder one.

  • You cannot go back from stage 2 to stage 1. You cannot skip a stage.
  • Your score uses your correct answers in both stages. It also uses how hard the questions were.
  • Hard questions in stage 2 are a good sign. Do not panic.
  • Some questions are pretest questions. ETS uses them to try new items. Every test taker gets some, in Reading or in Listening. You cannot see which ones they are.
  • The time changes with the module. In the ETS plan, the harder Listening module takes about 11 minutes. The easier one takes about 7.

Writing and Speaking are not adaptive. Everybody with the same test form gets the same tasks.

"I will go slowly in the first part and save my energy." This is a bad plan. Stage 1 decides how high you can go. Give the first questions your full attention.

Reading: three task types

Complete the Words

Here is an original example. Try it before you read the rule.

Many cities now build special lanes for bicycles. These la___ protect rid___ from fa__ cars a__ buses. I_ several cit___, the num___ of cycl____ grew qui____ after t__ lanes opened. Shops near the lanes often report more customers, not fewer.

Answer

lanes, riders, fast, and, In, cities, number, cyclists, quickly, the.

This task is a C-test. ETS uses a short academic text of about 70 to 100 words. The first sentence is complete. After that, every second word loses its second half. Ten words have missing letters. You type the missing letters.

  1. Read the full first sentence. It gives you the topic.
  2. Read the whole text once before you type.
  3. For each gap, ask: what kind of word fits here? A noun after "the"? A verb after "they"?
  4. Count the spaces. In the ETS sample, each missing letter has its own space.
  5. Check endings: plural -s, past -ed, -ly for adverbs.

Spelling counts. "quikly" is wrong, even if the meaning is clear. Learn the spelling of common academic words, not only their meaning.

Read in Daily Life

North Campus Library. From 3 March, the second floor closes at 6 p.m. on weekdays for repairs. Group study rooms move to the first floor. Book a room in the library app. If you are not there 15 minutes after your booking time, the room goes to the next person.

Question 1. Where will the group study rooms be after 3 March?

Question 2. What will probably happen to a student who arrives 20 minutes late?

Answer

1. On the first floor. 2. The student will probably lose the room. The notice gives a 15-minute limit. This is an inference question.

These are short texts from everyday life: notices, emails, menus, text messages, schedules, forms, receipts and social media posts. ETS says they have about 15 to 150 words. Two or three multiple-choice questions follow each text.

  • Read the question first. Then scan for the answer.
  • Use headings, times, prices and numbers. They show you where to look.
  • For "probably" questions, apply the rule in the text to the new person.

Do not choose an answer only because it has the same words as the text. Test writers often use the same words with a different meaning. Check the meaning, not the words.

Read an Academic Passage

Urban heat islands. Cities are often warmer than the countryside around them. Scientists call this an urban heat island. During the day, roads and buildings absorb heat from the sun. At night, they release it slowly, so the city stays warm. Cities also have fewer trees. Trees cool the air because water evaporates from their leaves. Cars and air conditioners add extra heat too. Some cities now paint roofs white. A light roof reflects more sunlight, so the rooms below stay cooler. Other cities plant trees along busy streets.

Question 1. Why does the writer mention white roofs?

Question 2. The word "release" is closest in meaning to: hold, give out, measure, reduce.

Question 3. What can you infer about a city with many trees?

Answer

1. To show one way to make a city cooler. 2. Give out. 3. It is probably cooler than a similar city with few trees.

ETS uses passages of about 200 words from subjects like history, art, business and science. Five questions follow. They ask about facts, words in context, inferences, links between ideas and the purpose of a part of the text. You do not need to know the topic before.

  • Read the first sentence of each paragraph first. Together they give the main idea.
  • For a word question, put each option into the sentence. Keep the one that keeps the meaning.
  • For "why does the writer mention X", think about the job of X: an example, a contrast, a cause or a solution.

Listening: four task types

You hear: "Could you send me the slides from this morning's lecture?"

A. Sure, I'll email them after lunch. B. The lecture was in Room 4. C. Yes, I slid on the ice this morning. D. No, I didn't see the morning news.

Answer

A. B is about the lecture but does not answer the request. C and D repeat sounds from the question ("slid", "morning"). This is the sound trap.

You hear each recording once. The questions and options come after the audio. ETS uses accents from North America, the UK, Australia and New Zealand.

The four Listening task types (ETS overview, 2026)
Task typeWhat you hearWhat you do
Listen and Choose a ResponseOne short question or statement. It is not written on the screen.Choose the best reply from four.
Listen to a ConversationA short talk between two people, often about campus or daily life.Answer two questions.
Listen to an AnnouncementA classroom or campus message of about 40 to 85 words.Answer questions on purpose, details and next steps.
Listen to an Academic TalkA short talk by a teacher or expert, about 100 to 250 words.Answer four questions.

Original transcript. "Good morning, everyone. A quick change for Chemistry 101. Tomorrow's lab moves from Room B12 to Room C3, because the air system in B12 is broken. The lab will start ten minutes late, at 2:10. Please bring your own safety glasses. We won't have spare pairs."

Question: What must students do? Answer: bring their own safety glasses.

Original transcript. "Today, let's talk about memory. In the 1880s, the German researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory. He learned lists of nonsense syllables. Then he checked how much he still knew later. He found that we forget very fast at first. After that, forgetting slows down. We call this the forgetting curve. So what can students do? Well, think about a path across a field. If you walk on it once, the grass grows back. If you walk on it every few days, the path stays clear. Memory works in a similar way. Each review makes the memory stronger. This method is called spaced repetition."

Question: Why does the speaker talk about a path across a field? Answer: to explain how regular reviews make a memory stronger.

  • For a one-line prompt, think about its job. A request needs a yes or a no. A complaint needs an apology or a solution.
  • Listen for signal words: "so", "but", "the main reason", "for example", "think about".
  • A "why does the speaker mention" question asks about purpose. Typical answers start with "To explain", "To compare" or "To give an example".
  • The speaker's next action is often at the end: "I'll go to the office after class."

Do not pick an option because it repeats a word you heard. In the example, "slid" sounds like "slides". The right answer usually uses different words with the same meaning.

Note-taking and integrated skills

Look at two sets of notes on the memory talk. Which one helps more?

In the 1880s a German researcher called Ebbinghaus tested his own memory with lists of syllables that had no meaning and he found that

★ memory → forgetting curve
1880s Ebbinghaus, own memory
forget fast ↑ first, then slow ↓
ex: path in field = review
review every few days → stronger
= spaced repetition

The first notes stop in the middle. The writer missed the next point. The second notes keep only keywords, arrows and the example.

ETS allows notes in every section. At a test centre you get paper and pencils. You cannot bring your own paper. At home you use a small whiteboard, or paper inside a clear plastic sleeve. You write on it with an erasable marker.

A small note-taking code
SymbolMeaningExample note
→leads to, causestrees → cooler air
↑ and ↓goes up, goes downriders ↑ after new lanes

≠is different fromonline class ≠ live class
b/cbecauseroom change b/c air broken

★main idea★ cities hotter

What happened to integrated tasks?

An integrated task joins skills. In the old test you read a short text, heard a lecture, then spoke or wrote about both. Those tasks left the test in January 2026.

But the new test still mixes skills in smaller ways:

  • Listen and Repeat joins listening and speaking.
  • Academic Discussion joins reading three posts and writing a reply.
  • Write an Email joins reading a situation and writing a response.
  • Listening questions join listening and reading the options.

So the old integrated skill still matters. You must hold an idea from one source and use it in another. The drill below trains it. It is a practice drill for this book, not a 2026 task type.

Read: "Some companies now give staff a four-day week. They say people work better when they rest more."

Listen (transcript): "We tried a four-day week for six months. Most teams did the same work in less time. But our support team had a problem. Customers still called on Fridays, so we had to make a rota."

Task: In two sentences, say how the talk connects to the reading.

Model answer

The reading says that a four-day week helps people work better. The speaker partly agrees, because most teams did the same work in less time, but the support team needed a rota for Friday calls.

Writing every word is the most common note-taking mistake. While you write, you miss the next idea. Write keywords. Mark the main idea with a star.

Writing: three task types

Build a Sentence

Speaker A: "I need a quiet place to study."

Speaker B: put these in order: are / do you know / the new / where / study rooms ?

Answer

Do you know where the new study rooms are? Inside "do you know", the question uses statement order: "the new study rooms are".

You see one sentence from speaker A. Then you see a reply with words and phrases in the wrong order. You move them into the right order. The reply must be correct grammar and must fit the situation. There are ten items. Each one is right or wrong.

  1. Find the subject and the main verb first.
  2. Look at the end mark. A question mark means a question.
  3. Put small words next to their partners: "the new" before its noun, "next to" before a place.
  4. Read the full reply to yourself. Does it answer speaker A?

Do you know where are the study rooms?

Do you know where the study rooms are?

An indirect question uses statement order. See Questions and negatives. Relative clauses like "the engineer who sits next to me" also appear often. See Relative clauses.

Write an Email

You get a situation in an academic or social setting and three things to do. You have 7 minutes. ETS asks you to write as much as you can, in complete sentences.

You are a member of a weekend coding club at your college. Last Saturday the room was locked, and nobody came to open it. Write an email to the club organiser, Ms Ortiz. In your email: say what you enjoy about the club; describe what happened; suggest a solution.

Subject: Locked room last Saturday

Dear Ms Ortiz,

I really enjoy the weekend coding club. The projects are practical, and I have learned a lot about testing from the other members.

However, there was a problem last Saturday. When we arrived at 10 a.m., Room 214 was locked. We waited for thirty minutes, but nobody came with a key, so most of us went home.

Could we find a way to avoid this in future? One idea is to give a spare key to a student volunteer each month. Another option is to post a message in the group chat if a session is cancelled.

Thank you for organising the club. I look forward to your reply.

Best regards,
Daniel

Why is this strong? It covers all three points, in three short paragraphs. The request is polite: "Could we find a way...". Linking words like "However" and "so" join the ideas. The tone fits a teacher.

Read and number

Read the situation. Number the three tasks 1, 2, 3. Decide who the reader is: a teacher, a friend, a company.

One paragraph per task

Write a greeting. Then write two or three sentences for each task. Add one detail to each: a time, a place, a reason.

Close politely

Thank the reader. Add a closing line: "I look forward to your reply." Sign your name.

Check

Check verb forms, plural -s, capital letters and full stops. Fix the errors you can see quickly.

Copying the task sentences into your email. ETS says that language borrowed from the task is a sign of a low score. Say the same ideas in your own words.

Write for an Academic Discussion

A professor posts a question in an online class forum. Two students reply with different views. You add your own post. You have 10 minutes. ETS says an effective answer has at least 100 words.

Dr Rahman: Many universities now record every lecture and put the videos online. Some people say this helps students learn. Others say students stop coming to class. Should universities record all lectures? Why or why not?

Maya: Yes. Recordings help students who are sick or who work part-time. They can also pause and replay the hard parts.

Tom: No. If every lecture is online, many students will stay at home. They lose the chance to ask questions and meet classmates.

I understand Tom's worry about empty classrooms, but I still think universities should record lectures. My main reason is that recordings help students review. In a live lecture, I often miss a key definition while I am taking notes. With a video, I can go back and check that one point in a minute. This is especially useful for students who study in a second language. To keep people coming to class, universities could publish each recording a few days later. They could also keep some activities live, such as group problem-solving. In my statistics course last year, attendance stayed high because the weekly quizzes happened only in the room. So recording lectures and valuable class time can work together.

  1. Minute 1: read the question and the two posts. Choose your side.
  2. Write one sentence that reacts to one student by name.
  3. Give your main reason and a personal example.
  4. Add one new idea that neither student gave.
  5. Finish with a short closing sentence. Check for two minutes.

Repeating Maya's or Tom's post in other words. The task asks for a contribution in your own words. Add something new: a different reason, a solution or an example.

The Writing scores in simple words (our summary of the ETS scoring guides)
ScoreEmailAcademic Discussion
5Fully successful. Every goal is done and well developed. Varied sentences. The right tone. Almost no errors.A relevant, very clear post. Well-developed reasons and examples. Varied sentences. Almost no errors.
4Mostly effective and easy to understand. Few errors.Relevant and easy to understand. Enough support. Few errors.
3The task is generally done. Some parts are unclear. Some clear errors.Mostly relevant. Part of a reason or example is missing or unclear.
2An attempt, but mostly not effective. Many errors.Ideas are weak or only partly on topic. Hard to follow.
1Very little, in short broken phrases. Mostly copied words.A few words on the topic but almost no clear ideas.
0Blank, not in English, fully copied, off the topic or random keys.

Speaking: two task types

Listen and Repeat

You are a new helper at a university library. Listen to the librarian and repeat each sentence.

  1. Welcome to the main library.
  2. Quiet study rooms are on the second floor.
  3. You can borrow up to ten books at a time.
  4. Please return laptops to the front desk before the library closes.
  5. If you need help with an article, ask anyone with a blue badge.

You hear a sentence. There is a short pause. Then you repeat it exactly. The real task has seven sentences in one situation. A picture of the place is on the screen. The sentences get longer and harder. You have 8 to 12 seconds to answer each one.

  • Hear the sentence in chunks: "You can borrow / up to ten books / at a time."
  • Copy the stress and the rhythm, not only the words.
  • Keep the small words: "the", "a", "to", plural -s and past -ed.
  • If you lose the middle, still say a full sentence with the same meaning.

The score is 0 to 5 for each sentence. A 5 is an exact copy that is easy to understand. A 4 keeps the meaning, with a small change like a missing "the". A 3 has most content words but changes the meaning. A 2 or below leaves out a large part.

She says that we can borrow ten books.

You can borrow up to ten books at a time.

Do not report the sentence. Repeat it, word for word, as if you are the speaker.

Take an Interview

A recorded interviewer asks you four questions about one situation, for example a research study. You have 45 seconds for each answer. There is no time to prepare. The first questions ask about facts and your experience. The later ones ask for your opinion on a bigger issue.

  1. Tell me about an online course you took. What was it about?
  2. What was difficult about learning online?
  3. Some people say online courses will replace classroom teaching. Do you agree? Why or why not?
  4. Should companies pay for their staff to take online courses? Why or why not?
  1. Answer in one clear sentence: "I don't fully agree."
  2. Reason: "Online courses are great for skills you practise alone."
  3. Example: "Last year I took an online course on data analysis."
  4. Close: "That's why I think..." Stop when the time ends.

I don't fully agree. Online courses are great for skills you can practise alone, like coding. Last year I took an online course on data analysis, and I studied at night after work. But a classroom does something that is hard online. Students can ask a quick question, hear how others think and get pushed by a teacher. So I think the future is a mix. People will learn the basics online and use class time for discussion and projects. That's why I don't think classrooms will disappear.

At a calm speed, 45 seconds is about 80 to 110 words. This is our estimate, not an ETS rule. The ETS scoring guide looks for four things: a full, on-topic answer, a good speaking speed, clear pronunciation and a range of correct grammar and words. In an ETS sample, natural "um" and "uh" still got a 5, because they did not block the meaning.

Stopping after 15 seconds. A short answer cannot show your range. Add a reason and an example. Another mistake is a memorised answer that does not fit the question. It gets a low score.

Scores and the score report

  1. Section scores: Reading 4.5, Listening 5, Writing 4, Speaking 4.
  2. Add them: 4.5 + 5 + 4 + 4 = 17.5.
  3. Divide by 4: 17.5 ÷ 4 = 4.375.
  4. Round to the nearest half band. 4.375 is closer to 4.5 than to 4.
  5. Overall score: 4.5. That is B2.

Each section gets a score from 1 to 6, in half bands. The overall score is the average of the four, rounded to the nearest half band. ETS gives two examples: 5.25 becomes 5.5, and 5.125 becomes 5.

TOEFL scores and the CEFR (ETS mapping, 2026)
TOEFL scoreCEFR level
6C2
5 or 5.5C1
4 or 4.5B2
3 or 3.5B1
2 or 2.5A2
1 or 1.5A1

The same numbers work for every section. A 4 in Speaking and a 4 in Reading are both B2. This matches CEFR and the exam map.

The old 0 to 120 scale

Many universities still list the old 0 to 120 scale. So for two years after January 2026, your report also shows a comparable total on that scale. ETS publishes a table that links the two scales.

How ETS scores each section

  • Reading and Listening: one point for each correct answer. ETS then changes the points to the 1 to 6 scale with a statistical method called equating. It adjusts for the difficulty of your stage 2 module.
  • Writing and Speaking: an ETS AI scoring engine scores the answers. It learns from human ratings, and humans check its work. Raw points are 0 to 20 in Writing and 0 to 55 in Speaking. ETS converts them with a weighted method, so do not try to count exact weights.
  • MyBest scores: your report also shows your best score in each section from all tests in the last two years.

ETS has no pass or fail score. Each university sets its own rule. Many ask for an overall score and a minimum in each section.

"My overall score is 5, so I am fine." Check the section rule too. A university may ask for 5 overall with no section below 4.5. One weak section can stop you.

All four sections count the same. Look at this case: Reading 5, Listening 5, Writing 4.5, Speaking 4. The average is 4.625, so the overall score is 4.5 (B2). If Speaking rises to 5, the average is 4.875, so the overall score is 5 (C1). Find your weakest section in a practice test and work on it first.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for TOEFL Writing and Speaking
PatternPurposeModelNote
I am writing to + verbOpen a formal email with its purposeI am writing to report a problem with the room.Use "to + verb", not "for + -ing".
Could we / you + verb ...?Make a polite requestCould you check if my form arrived?Use statement order after "if": "if my form arrived".
One idea is to + verb.Suggest a solutionOne idea is to give a spare key to a volunteer.Not "One idea is giving to".
I understand + name's + point, but I think ...React to a classmateI understand Tom's point, but I think recordings help.Name one student. Then add your own idea.
My main reason is that + clause.Give your main reasonMy main reason is that videos help students review.Not "My main reason is because".
In my experience, + clause.Bring in a personal exampleIn my experience, weekly quizzes keep people coming.Put a comma after "experience".
Do you know / Could you tell me + wh- + subject + verb?Ask an indirect questionCould you tell me where the lab is?Not "where is the lab".
The + noun + who + verb + main verbBuild a sentence with a relative clauseThe engineer who sits next to me fixed it.The main verb comes after the whole "who" part.
I don't fully agree. + reasonGive a balanced opinion in the interviewI don't fully agree. Online courses suit some skills.Give the reason at once. Do not stop after "agree".
That's why I think + clause.Close a spoken answerThat's why I think classrooms will stay.Use it as your last sentence.
So the main point is + noun / clause.Sum up what a speaker saidSo the main point is that reviews make memory stronger.Use it to check your notes after a talk.

Practice

1. In what order do the sections come?

  • Listening, Reading, Speaking, Writing
  • Reading, Listening, Writing, Speaking
  • Speaking, Writing, Reading, Listening

ETS always gives Reading first, then Listening, Writing and Speaking.

2. How long do you have for each answer in Take an Interview?

  • 15 seconds, after 30 seconds to prepare
  • 45 seconds, with no time to prepare
  • 2 minutes, after 1 minute to prepare

The interview has four questions. You have 45 seconds for each one and no preparation time.

3. You hear: "I can't find my student card anywhere." Choose the best response.

  • Yes, the card shop is near the station.
  • Did you check the pocket of your other jacket?
  • I found the answer in the book.

The speaker has a problem. A helpful reply offers a solution. The other options repeat the words "card" and "find".

4. Complete the Words: "The city planted new tr? along the main road."

5. Build a Sentence: "Could you tell me when the next bus ??"

6. Section scores 3.5, 4, 4 and 4.5 give an overall score of ?.

  1. Put the words in order as a reply. Speaker A: "Why were you late?" Words: because / I / it / missed / the train / was / full.
    Answer

    I missed the train because it was full.

  2. Work out the overall score and the CEFR level: Reading 5.5, Listening 5, Writing 4.5, Speaking 4.5.
    Answer

    Total 19.5. Average 19.5 ÷ 4 = 4.875. The nearest half band is 5. A 5 is C1.

  3. Write notes with symbols for this sentence: "Prices went up because fuel became more expensive, for example in shipping."
    Answer

    Model: prices ↑ b/c fuel ↑. ex: shipping.

  4. Write an email in 7 minutes. Your classmate lent you a book, and you spilled coffee on it. Write to your classmate: say sorry, describe the damage, offer a solution.
    Answer

    Model: Hi Sam, I am really sorry, but I had an accident with your book. Yesterday I spilled coffee on it, and about ten pages are now stained. You can still read them, but they look bad. I would like to buy you a new copy. I can order it today, and it should arrive by Friday. If you prefer, I can pay you the price instead. Again, I am very sorry. Best wishes, Lee.

  5. Use the Academic Discussion task above. Write a reply that agrees with Tom. Start by reacting to Maya.
    Answer

    Model: Maya makes a good point about students who are sick, but I agree with Tom. When every lecture is online, it is easy to say "I will watch it later" and then never do it. In my first year, I watched recorded lectures at double speed the night before the exam, and I remembered very little. Live classes give a fixed time to learn and a chance to ask questions. Universities could record lectures only for students with a good reason, such as illness. This would help those students without emptying the room.

  6. Answer interview question 4 in about 45 seconds: "Should companies pay for their staff to take online courses?"
    Answer

    Model: Yes, I think they should. When staff learn new skills, the company gets better work. For example, my team took a short cloud course last spring, and we now set up servers much faster. Courses also show staff that the company cares about them, so people stay longer. Of course, the course should be connected to the job. A company does not need to pay for every hobby. But for useful skills, it is a smart investment.

  7. Hard: your friend says "I did badly in Reading because the second part was so hard." Explain why this may be good news.
    Answer

    Reading is multistage adaptive. Harder stage 2 questions usually mean you did well in stage 1. ETS scoring also uses the difficulty of the questions, so a harder module can still lead to a high score.

Key takeaways

  • Since 21 January 2026, TOEFL iBT has four short sections: Reading, Listening, Writing, Speaking, in that order. Allow about two hours.
  • Reading and Listening are two-stage adaptive. Give stage 1 your full attention.
  • The long integrated tasks are gone. Skills still mix in Listen and Repeat, the email and the discussion post.
  • Write an Email: 7 minutes. Academic Discussion: 10 minutes and at least 100 words. Interview: four answers of 45 seconds.
  • Scores are 1 to 6 in half bands. 4 is B2, 5 is C1, 6 is C2. A comparable 0 to 120 total appears for two years.
  • Take keyword notes with symbols. Never write full sentences while you listen.

Sources

  • ETS: Updated TOEFL iBT Test Overview (PDF, 2026). Each task type, task timing, the scoring guides and the score tables.
  • ETS: TOEFL iBT 2026 test blueprint and specifications. Item counts, module timing and the two-stage adaptive design.
  • ETS: Understanding TOEFL scores. The 1 to 6 scale, rounding, the comparison with the 0 to 120 scale and score validity.
  • ETS: TOEFL iBT enhancements, July 2023. The 2023 changes: shorter test, Academic Discussion task, shorter Reading.
  • Ren et al. (2026): Comparing new TOEFL 2026 with former TOEFL 2023 and IELTS. A research report that describes the 2023 format in detail.

Cambridge B2 First, C1 Advanced, C2 Proficiency

Cambridge University Press & Assessment makes three famous exams for upper levels: B2 First, C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency. They have the same family design. This chapter shows the papers, the four Use of English tasks with original examples, the writing and speaking tasks and the Cambridge English Scale.

  • Compare the papers and timing of B2 First, C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency.
  • Solve the four Use of English task types: multiple-choice cloze, open cloze, word formation and key word transformation.
  • Plan the writing tasks for each exam.
  • Describe the four or three parts of the paired Speaking test.
  • Read a result on the Cambridge English Scale and know your grade.

Three exams, one family

Sofia is a developer in Madrid. She takes C1 Advanced and gets 185. Her friend Paulo takes B2 First and gets 185 too. Do they have the same level? Yes. Both results are C1 on the same scale.

The three exams belong to the Cambridge English Qualifications. Each exam aims at one CEFR level. It also reports the level just above or just below. All results use one shared scale, the Cambridge English Scale.

  • B2 First aims at B2. It can show B1 or C1.
  • C1 Advanced aims at C1. It can show B2 or C2.
  • C2 Proficiency aims at C2. It can show C1.

You take the exams at an exam centre. Most centres offer a digital version on computer and a paper version. Cambridge says the format is the same for both. Digital results arrive in 5 to 10 working days. Paper results take 4 to 6 weeks.

Choose the exam for the level you want to prove. If you are a little better than that level, the exam can still show it. If you are a little weaker, you get the level below.

"I failed B2 First, so I have nothing." Not true. A score of 140 to 159 gives a certificate at B1. Only scores below 140 get no certificate. They still appear on your Statement of Results.

Papers and timing

Each exam has four papers. Cambridge calls them components. Reading and Use of English are on one paper.

The three exams side by side (Cambridge pages and 2026 handbooks)
PaperB2 FirstC1 AdvancedC2 Proficiency
Reading and Use of English1 h 15 min. 7 parts, 52 questions.1 h 30 min. 8 parts, 56 questions.1 h 30 min. 7 parts, 53 questions.
Writing1 h 20 min. 2 tasks, 140 to 190 words each.1 h 30 min. 2 tasks, 220 to 260 words each.1 h 30 min. Part 1: 240 to 280 words. Part 2: 280 to 320 words.
ListeningAbout 40 min. 4 parts, 30 questions.About 40 min. 4 parts, 30 questions.About 40 min. 4 parts, 30 questions.
Speaking (per pair)14 min. 4 parts.15 min. 4 parts.16 min. 3 parts.
Total (handbook)About 3 h 29 minAbout 3 h 55 minAbout 3 h 56 min

You get five scores: Reading, Use of English, Writing, Listening and Speaking. Each one counts the same, 20%. Your overall score is the average of the five.

In every exam, Parts 1 to 4 of the first paper are Use of English. The other parts are Reading. The Reading parts test detail, opinion, text structure and finding information.

Reading parts after Use of English

B2 First: Part 5 multiple choice, Part 6 gapped text (missing sentences), Part 7 multiple matching. C1 Advanced: Part 5 multiple choice, Part 6 cross-text matching (compare opinions in four short texts), Part 7 gapped text (missing paragraphs), Part 8 multiple matching. C2 Proficiency: Part 5 multiple choice, Part 6 gapped text (missing paragraphs), Part 7 multiple matching.

Listening parts

You hear every recording twice. All three exams mix short extracts, a monologue with sentence completion, a longer conversation with multiple choice, and five short speakers to match. In B2 First digital, Listening Part 3 became drag and drop on 1 November 2025. The task itself did not change.

How the papers are marked

Reading, Use of English and Listening answers are marked against an answer key. For Writing, Cambridge uses hybrid marking in the digital B2 First and C1 Advanced exams: a trained computer marker plus human examiners who check. C2 Proficiency and all paper exams are marked only by humans. Two examiners mark Speaking.

Use of English is a full fifth of your result. It is also very trainable, because the same patterns come back again and again. Learn the patterns at the end of this chapter.

Use of English 1: multiple-choice cloze

Try this original example first. Choose A, B, C or D for each gap.

Last year our team decided to (1) ___ a new rule: no meetings on Fridays. At first, some managers were worried that projects would (2) ___ behind. In fact, the opposite happened. People finally had time to (3) ___ on difficult tasks, and the number of bugs went (4) ___.

GapABCD
1introduceproduceinventraise
2falllosemissleave
3focuspayattendgive
4lowdownunderless
Answer

1 A (introduce a rule). 2 A (fall behind). 3 A (focus on). 4 B (go down).

A cloze is a text with gaps. In Part 1 the real exam has eight gaps. Each gap has four options. The options often have similar meanings. Only one fits the words around the gap.

So Part 1 tests collocations, phrasal verbs, fixed phrases and dependent prepositions. At C1 and C2 it also tests idioms and fine differences in meaning.

  1. Read the whole text once for the main idea.
  2. Look at the words after the gap, not only before it. "___ on" needs a verb that takes "on".
  3. Say each option inside the sentence. Which one sounds like a fixed partner?
  4. Check the grammar after the gap too: "to + verb", "-ing" or a noun?

Choosing by meaning only. "Pay", "attend" and "focus" all relate to attention. But only "focus" goes with "on" here. Learn words with their partners: "focus on", "pay attention to", "attend to".

Use of English 2: open cloze

Many people believe (1) ___ learning a language takes a special talent. Research suggests otherwise. What matters most is (2) ___ often you practise. Ten minutes every day is better (3) ___ two hours once a week. If you keep going, you will be surprised (4) ___ how much you improve.

Answer

1 that. 2 how. 3 than. 4 at (also by).

Part 2 also has eight gaps, but there are no options. You think of one word for each gap. The missing words are mostly grammar words: articles, auxiliaries, prepositions, pronouns, linkers and words inside fixed phrases.

  • The answer is always one word.
  • Do not use a contraction like "didn't". It counts as two words. "Can't" is the one exception.
  • Spelling must be correct.
  • Sometimes two answers are possible. The mark scheme accepts both.
What to ask yourself at each gap
Words around the gapLikely wordExample
Comparative before itthanbetter ___ two hours
Adjective + ___ + noun phrasea prepositionsurprised ___ the result
Verb of thinking + ___ + clausethatbelieve ___ it works
___ + adjective or adverb, in a question ideahow___ often you practise
Two opposite ideasalthough, but, despite___ it rained, we went
A singular countable noun with no articlea, an, theshe is ___ engineer

Writing two words in one gap, like "so that" or "in order". Only one word fits. If two words seem right, the answer is a different single word.

Use of English 3: word formation

The new app was a great (1 SUCCEED) ___. Users said it was (2 EXTREME) ___ easy to use. But some critics pointed out its (3 ABLE) ___ to work offline. The company promised to fix this (4 WEAK) ___ in the next update.

Answer

1 success. 2 extremely. 3 inability. 4 weakness.

In Part 3 each gap has a stem word in capital letters. You change it to fit the gap. You always have to change it. You may add a prefix, a suffix, or change letters inside the word.

  1. Decide the part of speech. After "a great" you need a noun. Before "easy" you need an adverb.
  2. Check the meaning. Is it positive or negative? "Pointed out its ___ to work offline" is a problem, so the word is negative: inability.
  3. Check the number. Does the noun need -s?
  4. Watch internal changes: long → length, strong → strength, deep → depth.
Common endings and prefixes
JobEndings or prefixesExamples
Make a noun-tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance, -erreduction, agreement, weakness, ability, performance, developer
Make an adjective-ful, -less, -ive, -able, -al, -oushelpful, useless, effective, reliable, digital, dangerous
Make an adverb-lyextremely, carefully, surprisingly
Make a verb-en, -ise, -ifywiden, modernise, simplify
Make it negativeun-, in-, im-, ir-, il-, dis-, mis-unexpected, inability, impossible, irregular, illegal, dislike, misunderstand

Forgetting the negative. "Its ability to work offline" makes no sense after "critics pointed out". Always read the whole sentence. Then ask: positive or negative?

Use of English 4: key word transformation

I haven't seen Maria for three years.

LAST

The ___ Maria was three years ago.

Answer

last time I saw (4 words). One mark for "last time" and one mark for "I saw".

In Part 4 you get a sentence, a key word and a second sentence with a gap. You complete the second sentence so it means the same as the first. You must use the key word, and you must not change it.

The word limits (Cambridge pages and handbooks)
ExamItemsWords in the gap, with the key word
B2 First62 to 5
C1 Advanced63 to 6
C2 Proficiency63 to 8

Each item has two marks. The mark scheme splits the answer into two parts. So half an answer can still earn one mark. A contraction counts as two words: "didn't" is "did not". "Can't" is the one exception.

  1. Sentence: "It wasn't necessary for you to bring food." Key word: NEED.
  2. Gap: "You ___ food."
  3. Answer A: "didn't need to bring". "Didn't" counts as two words. Total: 5. This fits the limits of all three exams.
  4. Answer B: "needn't have brought". "Needn't" counts as two. Total: 4.
  5. Answer A keeps the meaning exactly. Answer B adds a new idea: you brought the food anyway. Choose A, unless the first sentence shows that the food was brought.

People say the company is planning a new product. SAID

The company ___ planning a new product.

Answer: is said to be (4 words).

I regret not taking the job in Berlin. WISH

I ___ the job in Berlin.

Answer: wish I had taken (4 words).

As soon as she arrived, the meeting began. SOONER

No ___ the meeting began.

Answer: sooner had she arrived than (5 words).

  1. Read the first sentence. Underline the key idea.
  2. Look at the key word. Which structure uses it? "SAID" often means "is said to".
  3. Look at the words after the gap. They often fix the tense or the preposition.
  4. Write the answer. Count the words, with contractions as two.
  5. Read the full second sentence. Does it mean the same?

Changing the key word. If the key word is "LAST", writing "lastly" gets zero marks. Another mistake is writing the whole second sentence. Write only the words for the gap.

Writing tasks

All three exams have two writing tasks. Part 1 is a compulsory essay. In Part 2 you choose one task from three. Examiners use four subscales, each from 0 to 5. So each task has 20 marks.

The four writing subscales in simple words
SubscaleThe question it asks
ContentDid you do everything the task asked? Is the reader fully informed?
Communicative AchievementIs the style right for this text type and this reader?
OrganisationIs the text logical, with paragraphs and good linking?
LanguageIs the vocabulary and grammar varied and correct?

Part 1: an essay. You get a question, two ideas to use and space for your own third idea. 140 to 190 words.

Part 2: choose one of three tasks: article, email or letter, report, or review. 140 to 190 words.

Original task: In class you talked about technology and free time. Essay question: Do smartphones make our free time better or worse? Write about: 1. keeping in touch with friends, 2. sleep, 3. your own idea.

Part 1: an essay after an academic activity, like a panel or a documentary. You get notes with three points and three short opinions. You choose two of the points. You say which one is more important and why. 220 to 260 words.

Part 2: choose one of three: letter or email, proposal, report, or review. 220 to 260 words.

Original task: Your class watched a documentary on city traffic. Notes: cheaper public transport, more cycle lanes, charges for driving in the centre. Write an essay on two of these. Which one would reduce traffic more?

Part 1: you read two short texts of about 100 words each. You write an essay that summarises and evaluates their key ideas and adds your own view. 240 to 280 words.

Part 2: choose one of three: article, letter, report, or review. 280 to 320 words.

Original task idea: Text 1 says remote work makes teams more productive. Text 2 says it weakens trust between new staff and their teams. Summarise both views, evaluate them and give your own opinion.

Smartphones are now part of almost everyone's free time. But do they make it better or worse? In my view, the answer depends on how we use them.

On the positive side, phones make it easy to keep in touch with friends. We can share photos, plan a weekend trip in a group chat or call a friend who lives abroad. For many people, this makes free time more social, not less.

However, phones can also harm our sleep. Many people check messages in bed, and the bright screen keeps them awake. As a result, they feel tired the next day and enjoy their free time less.

Another problem is that phones can replace hobbies. It is easy to spend an hour scrolling instead of reading, playing sport or learning an instrument.

To sum up, smartphones improve our free time when we use them to connect with people. The key is to set limits, for example no phones after ten at night.

  • Content: both given ideas and an own idea (hobbies). A clear opinion.
  • Communicative Achievement: a neutral essay style. A question in the introduction pulls the reader in.
  • Organisation: five short paragraphs. Linkers: "On the positive side", "However", "As a result", "To sum up".
  • Language: collocations like "keep in touch" and "set limits". Varied sentences.

At C1, discussing all three points in Part 1. The handbook says to choose two. Three points make every paragraph thin. Choose two, develop them, and say clearly which matters more.

The Speaking test

You take the Speaking test with one other candidate, or sometimes in a group of three. Two examiners are there. The interlocutor asks the questions. The assessor listens and gives marks. Cambridge says the interlocutor may sometimes join online.

Interview, 2 minutes

The interlocutor asks each of you simple questions: your work, studies and interests. Give full answers with a reason.

Long turn, 1 minute each

You get three pictures and talk about two of them for one minute. Then your partner comments for about 30 seconds. Then you swap.

Collaborative task, 3 minutes

You and your partner discuss a question with written prompts for 2 minutes. Then you have 1 minute to make a decision together.

Discussion, 5 minutes

The interlocutor asks wider questions on the Part 3 topic. Answer, then invite your partner: "What do you think?"

The Speaking parts in each exam
PartB2 First (14 min)C1 Advanced (15 min)C2 Proficiency (16 min)
1Interview, 2 minInterview, 2 minInterview, 2 min
2Long turn: compare two photos for 1 min. Partner answers a short question.Long turn: talk about two of three pictures for 1 min. Partner comments for 30 s.Collaborative task, 4 min: react to pictures, then decide together.
3Collaborative task: 2 min discussion, 1 min decisionCollaborative task: 2 min discussion, 1 min decisionLong turn about 2 min each from a card, then a discussion. 10 min in total.
4Discussion, 4 minDiscussion, 5 min(no Part 4)

The assessor gives marks for grammar, vocabulary, discourse management, pronunciation and interactive communication. At B2, grammar and vocabulary share one scale. At C1 and C2, they are two separate scales. The interlocutor also gives one overall mark.

Ana: Shall we start with cycle lanes? I think they help most in the city centre.

Leo: Maybe, but they don't help in winter. What do you think about cheaper buses?

Ana: Good point. Cheaper buses would help people who live far away.

Leo: So, are we agreed that cheaper buses would make the biggest difference?

Talking for the whole Part 3 and never asking your partner. Interactive communication is a separate mark. Ask questions, react to your partner's ideas and help the talk move towards a decision.

The Cambridge English Scale

  1. Scores: Reading 170, Use of English 168, Writing 165, Listening 178, Speaking 184.
  2. Add them: 170 + 168 + 165 + 178 + 184 = 865.
  3. Divide by 5: 865 ÷ 5 = 173.
  4. 173 is in the 173 to 179 band: Grade B, level B2.

Each exam reports on the same scale. The table shows the score bands from Cambridge's results page.

Score bands, grades and certificates (cambridgeenglish.org, November 2026)
ExamGrade AGrade BGrade CLevel belowReported, no certificate
B2 First180 to 190 (C1)173 to 179 (B2)160 to 172 (B2)140 to 159 (B1)122 to 139
C1 Advanced200 to 210 (C2)193 to 199 (C1)180 to 192 (C1)160 to 179 (B2)142 to 159
C2 Proficiency220 to 230 (C2)213 to 219 (C2)200 to 212 (C2)180 to 199 (C1)162 to 179
  • The full scale goes from about 80 (A2 Key) to 230 (C2 Proficiency).
  • The same number means the same level on every exam.
  • You also get a score for each of the five parts. A university may ask for a minimum in each.
  • Cambridge certificates do not expire. But a university can still ask for a recent result.

"185 on B2 First is worse than 185 on C1 Advanced." No. The scale is shared, so both are C1. The difference is the certificate. B2 First Grade A says "Level C1" on a B2 First certificate.

Patterns to remember

Key word transformation patterns that come up again and again
PatternPurposeModelNote
It's the first time + present perfectRewrite "never ... before"It's the first time I have used this tool.Not "It's the first time I use".
The last time + past simple + wasRewrite "haven't ... for"The last time I saw her was in May.Past simple after "last time".
be said / thought + to + verbReport what people sayThe firm is said to be hiring.Past idea: "is said to have hired".
wish + past perfectExpress regret about the pastI wish I had taken the job.Not "I wish I took" for the past.
needn't have + past participleSay an action was not necessary but happenedYou needn't have brought food."Needn't" counts as two words.
too + adjective + toRewrite "not ... enough"The box was too heavy to lift.No object at the end: not "to lift it".
no longer + verbRewrite "used to" or "not any more"She no longer works here."No longer" goes before the main verb.
in spite of / despite + -ingRewrite "although"Despite feeling ill, he came.Not "despite of".
succeed in + -ingRewrite "manage to"We succeeded in fixing the bug."In" plus -ing, not "to".
unless + positive verbRewrite "if ... not"Unless you hurry, you'll miss it.Not "unless you don't hurry".
It's not worth + -ingSay something has no valueIt's not worth waiting for him."Worth" plus -ing, not "to".
No sooner had + subject + past participle + thanEmphasise "as soon as" (C1 and C2)No sooner had she arrived than it began.Inversion: "had she", and "than", not "when".

Practice

1. Multiple-choice cloze. "The meeting was ___ off because the manager was ill."

  • called
  • taken
  • made

"Call off" means cancel. It is a phrasal verb, a typical Part 1 item.

2. How many words can you write in a C1 Advanced key word transformation?

  • 2 to 5
  • 3 to 6
  • 3 to 8

B2 First uses 2 to 5, C1 Advanced 3 to 6, C2 Proficiency 3 to 8. The key word is included.

3. Which C2 Proficiency paper has no Part 4?

  • Listening
  • Speaking
  • Reading and Use of English

C2 Speaking has three parts. B2 and C1 Speaking have four.

4. Open cloze: "She has worked here ? 2021."

5. Open cloze: "It was ? a long meeting that I missed lunch."

6. Word formation (EXPECT): "The results were completely ?."

7. Word formation (RELY): "We need a more ? server."

  1. Key word transformation (B2). "I started learning Python two years ago." BEEN. "I ___ Python for two years."
    Answer

    have been learning (3 words). "Have been studying" is also fine.

  2. Key word transformation (B2). "The film was so boring that we left early." SUCH. "It was ___ that we left early."
    Answer

    such a boring film (4 words).

  3. Key word transformation (C1). "He didn't study, so he failed the test." IF. "He would not have failed the test ___ studied."
    Answer

    if he had (3 words). Third conditional: "if he had studied".

  4. Key word transformation (C2). "We only understood the problem after reading the logs." UNTIL. "It was ___ the logs that we understood the problem."
    Answer

    not until we had read (5 words). "Not until we read" (4 words) also keeps the meaning.

  5. Work out the overall score and grade for C1 Advanced: Reading 190, Use of English 186, Writing 178, Listening 195, Speaking 186.
    Answer

    Total 935. Average 935 ÷ 5 = 187. That is Grade C, level C1 (180 to 192).

  6. Write a plan for the C1 traffic essay in the Writing section. Choose two points and say which is more important.
    Answer

    Model plan. Introduction: traffic is a growing problem; I will compare cheaper public transport and driving charges. Paragraph 2: cheaper transport gives people a real choice, but only if buses are reliable. Paragraph 3: driving charges cut traffic fast, but they can hurt people on low incomes, so the money should fund buses. Conclusion: charges are more effective, because they change behaviour at once, especially when the money improves public transport.

  7. Hard: write three sentences for B2 Speaking Part 2. Compare two photos: people working in an office and people working from a café.
    Answer

    Model: Both photos show people working on laptops, but the places are very different. In the first photo, the office looks quiet and organised, so it is probably easier to focus. The people in the café look more relaxed, but I imagine the noise might make it hard to join a video call.

Key takeaways

  • B2 First, C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency share one design: Reading and Use of English, Writing, Listening and a paired Speaking test.
  • Five scores count equally: Reading, Use of English, Writing, Listening and Speaking.
  • Use of English has four tasks: multiple-choice cloze, open cloze, word formation and key word transformation.
  • Key word transformation: 2 to 5 words at B2, 3 to 6 at C1, 3 to 8 at C2. Contractions count as two words.
  • Writing has a compulsory essay and a choice of three tasks. Marks come from four subscales.
  • The Cambridge English Scale is shared. 160 to 179 is B2, 180 to 199 is C1, 200 and above is C2.

Sources

  • Cambridge English: B2 First exam format. Papers, parts, questions and timing for B2 First.
  • Cambridge English: C1 Advanced exam format. Papers, parts, word counts and Speaking parts for C1 Advanced.
  • Cambridge English: C2 Proficiency exam format. Papers, parts and the 3 to 8 word limit for C2.
  • Cambridge English: results for qualifications. Score bands, grades and result times.
  • Cambridge English: B2 First handbook for teachers (2026). Marking rules for Use of English, writing subscales and Speaking criteria.
  • Cambridge English: a guide to hybrid marking of Writing. How digital B2 and C1 writing is marked, and why C2 stays human-marked.

PTE Academic, Duolingo English Test and TOEIC

These three exams look very different. PTE Academic is a fast computer test at a centre. The Duolingo English Test is a one-hour test at home. TOEIC measures English for work. This chapter explains the format, tasks and scores of each, with original practice items.

  • Describe the format, timing and score scale of PTE Academic, the DET and TOEIC.
  • Choose the exam that suits your goal: study, a visa or a job.
  • Use clear strategies for the special tasks: Read Aloud, Repeat Sentence and the interactive tasks.
  • Avoid the traps of word limits and minus marking.
  • Compare scores on the three exams with the CEFR.

Three exams, three jobs

Ravi wants to study in Australia. Mina wants a quick result for a university in the US. Jun needs a promotion at a company in Seoul. They need three different exams.

The three exams at a glance (owners' pages, checked November 2026)
PTE AcademicDuolingo English Test (DET)TOEIC
OwnerPearsonDuolingoETS
WhereOnly at a test centreOnline at homeUsually at a centre or arranged by an employer
LengthAbout 2 hoursAbout 1 hourListening and Reading: 2 hours. Speaking: about 20 min. Writing: about 60 min.
Scores10 to 9010 to 160, in steps of 5Listening and Reading: 10 to 990. Speaking and Writing: 0 to 200 each.
ResultsUsually within 2 business daysWithin 2 daysDepends on the centre
Main useUniversity study, and visas in Australia and New ZealandUniversity admissionJobs and promotion

Pearson has versions for visas. PTE Academic UKVI is for some UK visas. PTE Core is for Canadian permanent residence and citizenship. The DET is mostly used for university admission. Before you use any exam for a visa, read the government's own list.

"The DET is cheap and easy, so I will use it for everything." A university may accept it, but a visa office may not. Check the exact exam name on the official list first.

PTE Academic: the format

PTE Academic has three parts. You take them in one sitting on a computer. Pearson says the test takes about two hours. Its section pages give these times:

PTE Academic parts (pearsonpte.com, November 2026)
PartTimeQuestion types
1. Speaking and Writing76 to 84 minRead Aloud, Repeat Sentence, Describe Image, Retell Lecture, Answer Short Question, Summarize Group Discussion, Respond to a Situation, Summarize Written Text, Write Essay
2. Reading23 to 30 minReading and Writing Fill in the Blanks, Multiple Choice (multiple answers), Reorder Paragraphs, Fill in the Blanks (drag and drop), Multiple Choice (single answer)
3. Listening31 to 39 minSummarize Spoken Text, Multiple Choice (multiple answers), Fill in the Blanks, Highlight Correct Summary, Multiple Choice (single answer), Select Missing Word, Highlight Incorrect Words, Write from Dictation

That makes 22 question types and 65 to 75 questions. The test starts with a short Personal Introduction. It does not count. It only helps you test the microphone.

PTE uses integrated skills scoring. One task can count for two skills. For example, Repeat Sentence counts for listening and speaking. So the overall score is not a simple average of the four skill scores.

  • Scale: overall and each skill from 10 to 90.
  • Scoring: AI scores most traits. For the longer tasks, like Describe Image, Retell Lecture and Write Essay, a human expert also reviews the content before the score is final.
  • Notes: you get an erasable noteboard.
  • Recording: you can record each answer only once. You hear each audio once.

Waiting too long to start speaking. Pearson warns that if you wait more than three seconds, the recording can stop. Start as soon as you see "Recording".

PTE speaking tasks: read aloud, repeat and retell

Read Aloud

Many companies now let staff choose / where they work. / Some people work at home / on Mondays and Fridays / and meet their team / in the office / in the middle of the week. / Managers say / this mix keeps people happy, / but they also worry / that new staff / learn more slowly.

A text of up to 60 words appears. You have 30 to 40 seconds to prepare. Then you read it aloud. Pearson scores three things: content (every word, and only those words), pronunciation and oral fluency, which means a smooth, steady speed.

Find the chunks

Use commas and full stops. Mark small groups of words that belong together. You will pause only between chunks.

Find the stress

Pick the words that carry meaning: names, numbers, contrast words. Say them a little louder.

Check hard words

Say long words quietly to yourself: "development", "particularly". Decide on one pronunciation.

Start at the tone, keep going

Start right after the tone. If you make a mistake, do not go back. Repeating words hurts fluency more than one small error.

Repeat Sentence

1. "The library will close early on Friday because of the holiday."

2. "Please send your final report to the department office before the end of the month."

You hear a sentence of 3 to 9 seconds. You have 15 seconds to repeat it. Pearson gives partial credit for correct word groups in the right order. So a part of the sentence is still worth points.

  • Listen for three chunks: "Please send your final report / to the department office / before the end of the month."
  • Copy the rhythm and the stress, as in an echo.
  • If you lose the middle, say the beginning and the end clearly. Do not stop.

Tasks that need a frame

Four tasks ask you to talk with your own words. A frame helps you start fast.

PTE speaking tasks with a frame
TaskTimingA simple frame
Describe Image25 s to study, 40 s to speakTopic. Biggest or main point. Smallest or contrast. One comparison. Conclusion.
Retell LectureLecture up to 90 s. 10 s to prepare, 40 s to speakThe speaker talked about X. First, ... Then, ... One example was ... In conclusion, ...
Summarize Group DiscussionThree speakers, up to 3 min. 10 s to prepare, 2 min to speakThe group discussed X. Speaker A thought ... B disagreed because ... C suggested ... In the end, ...
Respond to a SituationText up to 60 words. 10 s to prepare, 40 s to speakGreeting. The problem. An apology or reason. A solution. A polite close.

This bar chart shows the average daily screen time for four age groups. People aged 18 to 34 spend the most time on screens, about seven hours a day. Young people under 18 are close behind, with six hours. Screen time then falls with age. People aged 35 to 54 use screens for about five hours, and people over 55 for only three. Overall, younger adults spend more than twice as much time on screens as the oldest group.

Situation: You borrowed a classmate's lecture notes, but you lost one page. Your classmate asks for the notes back today. What do you say?

Model: Hi Sara, thanks again for lending me your notes. I'm really sorry, but I have a problem. I lost one page, the one about the second experiment. I've looked everywhere, but I can't find it. Here are the other pages. Could I ask our lecturer for the slides and write that page again for you tonight? I can bring it tomorrow morning. Again, I'm very sorry.

Memorised templates with empty words, like "This is a very interesting image with many colours". The content score checks your real description. Name real numbers and real comparisons.

PTE writing and listening: word limits and minus marks

Some PTE tasks have strict rules. Break them and you can get zero.

The strict rules (Pearson's task pages)
TaskRuleWhat happens if you break it
Summarize Written TextOne sentence, 5 to 75 words, in 10 minutes. Text up to 300 words.Fewer than 5 or more than 75 words: zero.
Write Essay200 to 300 words in 20 minutes.Outside 200 to 300: lower score. Under 120 or over 380 words: zero.
Summarize Spoken Text50 to 70 words in 10 minutes, after a 60 to 90 second recording.Under 40 or over 100 words: zero. Wrong topic: zero.
Multiple Choice, multiple answers (Reading and Listening)Choose more than one answer.Each wrong choice takes away one point.
Highlight Incorrect WordsClick the words that differ from the audio.Each wrong click takes away one point.

Minus marking is called negative marking. In these three task types, never click everything. Choose only what you are sure of.

Text: Many cities are planting trees on busy streets. Trees give shade, so the air near the ground stays cooler on hot days. They also take in some rain, which reduces flooding after storms. Studies of house prices suggest that people will pay more to live on green streets. But trees need water and care for several years, and city budgets are often small. Some cities now ask local people to help water young trees in summer.

Model one-sentence summary (44 words): City trees keep streets cooler, reduce flooding and may raise house prices, but because young trees need years of water and care while budgets are small, some cities now ask residents to help look after them.

  1. Find the main idea and the key supporting ideas. Note keywords.
  2. Join them with linkers: "and", "but", "because", "while", "which".
  3. Check: one capital letter at the start, one full stop at the end.
  4. Check the word count on the screen.

Write from Dictation is the last task. You hear a short sentence of 3 to 5 seconds and type it. You get a point for each correct word. Example: "Students must register for the course before the end of September."

Write from Dictation and Repeat Sentence both count for listening. They are short, but there are many of them. Daily dictation practice helps both.

The Duolingo English Test: the format

You take the DET on your own computer at home. It takes about an hour. A setup comes first: rules, an ID check and a camera check. Then comes the main adaptive part. A Writing Sample and a Speaking Sample come last.

DET question types (Duolingo scoring guide for teachers, 2026)
Question typeWhat you doTimeAdaptive?

Fill in the BlanksFinish one word in a sentence20 s eachYes
Read and CompleteFinish half-words in a paragraph3 min eachYes
Listen and TypeType a sentence you hear, up to 3 plays1 min eachYes
Interactive ReadingFive tasks on one passage7 or 8 min per passageYes
Interactive ListeningComplete notes, choose replies in a conversation, then summarise it6 min 30 s, plus 75 s to summarisePartly
Write About the PhotoDescribe a photo in writing1 min, three timesNo
Interactive WritingAnswer a question, then a follow-up question5 min, then 3 minNo
Speak About the PhotoDescribe a photo aloudUp to 90 sNo
