Interactive SpeakingAnswer 6 to 8 spoken questions on two topicsUp to 35 s eachYes
Writing SampleWrite on a topic5 minNo
Speaking SampleSpeak on a topicUp to 3 minNo

DET scores

You get four main subscores: Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing. You also get four combined subscores. Each combined subscore is the average of two skills.

  • Comprehension: reading and listening.
  • Conversation: speaking and listening.
  • Literacy: reading and writing.
  • Production: speaking and writing.

The overall score is the average of the four main subscores, rounded up to the nearest 5. AI scores speaking and writing with clear criteria. Writing uses four: content, discourse coherence, grammar and lexis. Speaking adds fluency and pronunciation.

Duolingo's 2026 scoring guide says the Writing Sample and Speaking Sample count towards your Writing and Speaking subscores. Schools you send results to can also read your Writing Sample and watch your Speaking Sample video. Some older Duolingo pages still call these parts "ungraded". Check the official site before your test.

Duolingo's own guide gives the price as US$70 (updated October 2026). Results arrive within two days, after proctors check the recording. You can send results to as many schools as you want for free.

Looking away from the screen while you think. Duolingo lists this as one of the most broken rules. Proctors cannot see if you are reading notes. Keep your eyes on the screen. You may look at the keyboard to type. Duolingo also needs a second camera, usually a phone, that shows your screen and keyboard.

DET special tasks: quick and interactive

Read and Select

window, plenk, although, slombard, decision, mestion, nervous, trovely

Answer

Real: window, although, decision, nervous. Fake: plenk, slombard, mestion, trovely.

You have only 5 seconds for each word. A wrong click and no click both count as wrong. Fake words often look possible. They follow English spelling but have no meaning.

  • Trust your first reaction. You cannot "work it out" in 5 seconds.
  • Grow your reading vocabulary. Many real words in this task are less common, like "notion" or "vivid".

Fill in the Blanks and Read and Complete

1. The meeting was can______ because the manager was ill.

2. Our team us__ a new tool for tes____. It hel__ us find bu__ much ear____.

Answer

1. cancelled (also canceled, the US spelling). 2. uses, testing, helps, bugs, earlier.

Both tasks need exact spelling. Read and Complete is a C-test, like TOEFL Complete the Words. The first and last sentences are complete. Each half-word is scored on its own.

Interactive Listening

You are a student. Your professor says: "Did you get a chance to look at the reading for Thursday?"

A. Yes, I read it last night, but I had a question about the second chapter. B. Thursday is the fourth day of the week. C. No, I can't see the board very well.

Answer

A. It answers the question and keeps the conversation going. B and C use words from the question but do not answer it.

One scenario has three tasks. First you hear a short scenario and complete three or four sentences. Then you take part in a conversation and choose the best reply each time. Finally, you have 75 seconds to type a summary of the conversation.

Interactive Writing

Step 1 (5 minutes): Should all children learn to code at school? Why or why not?

Model: I think all children should learn some basic coding at school. Coding teaches them to break a big problem into small steps, and this skill helps in every subject. It also shows them how the apps they use every day really work. However, coding does not have to be a long, serious course. Short projects, like making a simple game, are enough to build interest. Children who enjoy it can then choose more advanced classes later.

Step 2 (3 minutes): Some people say that AI will write most code in the future, so children do not need to learn it. What do you think?

Model: I understand this view, but I still disagree. Even if AI writes code, people need to check it and explain what they want. Basic coding helps children understand what the AI produces. So coding skills will change, but they will not disappear.

Step 2 always connects to Step 1. Duolingo says a Step 2 answer that changes the topic may get a lower score. So link back: "I still think...", "This connects to my first point...".

Interactive Speaking and the photo tasks

In Interactive Speaking, a Duolingo character asks a question aloud. You click to record and speak for up to 35 seconds. The next question depends on what you said. This is the only adaptive speaking task.

  1. Answer the question in your first sentence.
  2. Add one reason.
  3. Add one short example from your life.
  4. Stop when the idea is complete. Do not wait in silence.

For Write About the Photo and Speak About the Photo, describe from big to small. Say what the scene is, then the people and actions, then the details and your guess about the situation.

Copying a memorised answer. Duolingo says your writing must be your own, written during the test. A prepared text is against the rules and can cancel your result.

TOEIC: the format

TOEIC is English for the workplace. There are two separate tests. Many people take only Listening and Reading. Speaking and Writing is a second test, taken together or alone.

TOEIC Listening and Reading: 200 questions, 2 hours
PartTaskQuestions
1Photographs6
2Question-Response25
3Conversations (13, with 3 questions each)39
4Talks (10, with 3 questions each)30
5Incomplete Sentences30
6Text Completion16
7Single passages (29) and multiple passages (25)54

Listening (Parts 1 to 4) takes about 45 minutes. Reading (Parts 5 to 7) takes 75 minutes. All questions are multiple choice.

TOEIC Speaking (about 20 minutes) and Writing (about 60 minutes)
QuestionsTaskTiming
Speaking 1 to 2Read a text aloud45 s to prepare, 45 s to read
Speaking 3 to 4Describe a picture45 s to prepare, 30 s to speak
Speaking 5 to 7Respond to questions3 s to prepare. 15, 15 and 30 s to answer.
Speaking 8 to 10Respond using information provided, such as a schedule45 s to read. 15, 15 and 30 s to answer.
Speaking 11Express an opinion45 s to prepare, 60 s to speak
Writing 1 to 5Write a sentence about a picture, using two given words8 min for all five
Writing 6 to 7Respond to a written request (an email)10 min each
Writing 8Write an opinion essay30 min
  • Listening and Reading scores: each section 5 to 495, total 10 to 990, in steps of 5. There is no penalty for wrong answers.
  • Speaking and Writing scores: each 0 to 200, in steps of 10. There is no total score.
  • No pass or fail: the employer or school sets the score it needs.

Some countries offer other TOEIC versions, like a shorter four-skills test. In 2026, centres in France announced a new version of it. ETS had not published the details when we checked. This chapter covers the standard tests above.

TOEIC strategies with original examples

Listening Part 1 and Part 2

Photo: a woman stands at a whiteboard and writes. Two men sit at a table with laptops.

A. She's writing on a board. B. The men are standing in line. C. The table is being carried. D. She's turning off the lights.

Answer

A. Describe only what you can see. B, C and D describe actions that are not in the photo.

You hear: "When does the training session start?"

A. At ten o'clock. B. In the training room. C. Yes, it started.

Answer

A. A "when" question needs a time. B answers "where". C answers with "yes", which never fits a wh- question.

  • Hear the first word of the question: who, what, when, where, why, how.
  • A "yes" or "no" answer cannot fit a wh- question.
  • Be careful with sound-alike words: "training" and "raining", "copy" and "coffee".

Reading Part 5

1. The new software is ___ easier to use than the old version. (A) very (B) much (C) more (D) many

2. Please send the signed contract to Ms Lee ___ Friday. (A) until (B) by (C) since (D) during

3. All visitors must ___ at the front desk. (A) registration (B) registered (C) register (D) registering

Answer

1 (B) much: use "much" before a comparative. 2 (B) by: a deadline. 3 (C) register: base verb after "must".

Part 5 has 30 short sentences. Many test grammar you can see quickly: the form after a modal, a comparative, a preposition of time. Do Part 5 fast. Then you have more time for the long passages in Part 7.

In the Reading section you have 75 minutes for 100 questions. That is 45 seconds per question on average. Many test takers run out of time in Part 7. Give Part 5 about 10 minutes, and never leave an answer blank. There is no penalty for guessing.

Speaking 8 to 10: use the information

Cloud Skills Day, Room 3, Saturday. 9:00 Welcome. 9:30 Talk: Saving money on cloud servers (Dana Park). 11:00 Workshop: Setting up alerts. 12:30 Lunch. 13:30 Talk: Security basics (Omar Ali).

Caller: What time does the first talk start, and who gives it?

Model: The first talk starts at nine thirty. It's given by Dana Park, and it's about saving money on cloud servers.

Caller: I can only come in the afternoon. What will I miss?

Model: In the morning there is a welcome at nine, Dana Park's talk at nine thirty and a workshop on setting up alerts at eleven. In the afternoon, you can still join Omar Ali's talk on security basics at one thirty.

Answer like a helpful colleague. Use full sentences. Give the exact time, name and place from the schedule.

Writing 1 to 5: one picture, two words

Example: the picture shows a man at a desk. The words are "coffee / while". A good answer: "The man drinks coffee while he reads an email." You may change the form of the words, but use both in one sentence.

Writing a long, clever sentence with an error. The scorers check grammar and relevance. A short, correct sentence that matches the picture is better.

Scores side by side

Each owner links its scores to the CEFR. These are the owners' own tables, as in CEFR and the exam map.

CEFR levels and scores (owners' published tables)
CEFRPTE AcademicDETTOEIC L&R total (minimum)TOEIC Speaking / Writing (minimum)
C285 to 90155 to 160not mappednot mapped
C176 to 84130 to 150945180 / 180
B259 to 75100 to 125785160 / 150
B143 to 5860 to 95550120 / 120
A230 to 4210 to 55 (A1 to A2)22590 / 70
  1. Subscores: Listening 115, Speaking 105, Reading 125, Writing 110.
  2. Average: (115 + 105 + 125 + 110) ÷ 4 = 113.75.
  3. Round up to the nearest 5: 115.
  4. 115 is B2 in Duolingo's table.

PTE does not work this way. Its overall score comes from all the questions, and integrated tasks count for two skills. So you cannot work out a PTE overall score from the four skill scores.

"TOEIC 800 means I am B2 in speaking." No. Listening and Reading say nothing about speaking or writing. If an employer needs speaking, take TOEIC Speaking too.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the special tasks
PatternPurposeModelNote
This + chart type + shows + topic.Start Describe ImageThis bar chart shows daily screen time by age.Say the topic in the first five seconds.
X + verb + the most / the least, + number.Give the key featurePeople aged 18 to 34 spend the most time, about seven hours.Always add a number.
Overall, + comparison.Close a descriptionOverall, younger adults spend twice as much time.Use "Overall", not "In overall".
The speaker talked about + noun.Start Retell LectureThe speaker talked about city trees.Past tense: you are reporting.
Speaker A thought ..., but B disagreed because ...Summarise a group discussionThe first speaker liked the plan, but the second disagreed because of the cost.Name each view and the reason.
I'm really sorry, but + problem.Open a polite apologyI'm really sorry, but I lost one page.Give the problem at once.
Could I + solution + ?Offer a solution politelyCould I write that page again for you tonight?"Could I" offers. "Could you" asks.
Main idea + linker + second idea, + which / while + detail.Write a one-sentence summaryTrees cool streets and reduce floods, while costs are a problem.One capital, one full stop.
I understand this view, but I still + verb.Answer the DET follow-up questionI understand this view, but I still disagree.Link Step 2 back to Step 1.
It starts at + time, and it's given by + name.Answer from a scheduleIt starts at nine thirty, and it's given by Dana Park.Give time and name in one sentence.
Subject + verb + word 1 + while / because + word 2.TOEIC sentence from a pictureThe man drinks coffee while he reads an email.Use both words, in one sentence.

Practice

1. Where can you take PTE Academic?

  • At home, with a live proctor
  • Only at a test centre
  • At home or at a centre

Pearson says PTE Academic cannot be taken at home.

2. In which PTE task can a wrong click take away a point?

  • Write from Dictation
  • Highlight Incorrect Words
  • Read Aloud

Highlight Incorrect Words and both Multiple Choice, multiple answers tasks use negative marking.

3. TOEIC Part 2. You hear: "Why was the flight delayed?" Choose the best response.

  • Yes, it was delayed.
  • Because of bad weather in Chicago.
  • At gate twelve.

A "why" question needs a reason. "Yes" never fits a wh- question. "At gate twelve" answers "where".

4. A PTE Summarize Written Text answer must be one sentence of no more than ? words.

5. DET overall scores go up in steps of ?.

6. TOEIC Part 5: "The report must be finished ? Monday morning."

7. DET Read and Complete: "Please che? your email for the link."

  1. Mark the chunks and two stressed words in this Read Aloud text: "Before you start the test, make sure your microphone works and your room is quiet."
    Answer

    Before you start the test, / make sure / your microphone works / and your room is quiet.

  2. Work out the DET overall score: Listening 95, Speaking 90, Reading 110, Writing 100.
    Answer

    Average (95 + 90 + 110 + 100) ÷ 4 = 98.75. Round up to the nearest 5: 100. That is B2 in Duolingo's table.

  3. Respond to a Situation (40 seconds). Your neighbour's music is very loud late at night. You meet them the next morning. What do you say?
    Answer

    Model: Hi, good morning. Sorry to bother you, but I wanted to mention something. Last night the music was quite loud until about one o'clock, and I have to get up early for work. I'm sure you didn't realise. Could you turn it down a bit after eleven on weekdays? Thanks a lot, I really appreciate it.

  4. Write a one-sentence summary (5 to 75 words): "Remote work saves travel time and lets people live outside big cities. But it can make new staff feel alone, and some managers find it harder to give feedback. Many firms now use a mix of home and office days."
    Answer

    Model (39 words): Remote work saves travel time and lets people live outside cities, but because it can isolate new staff and make feedback harder, many firms now combine home and office days.

  5. DET Interactive Speaking (35 seconds): "What is one skill you want to learn this year, and why?"
    Answer

    Model: This year I want to get better at public speaking. In my job I often explain technical ideas to clients, and I get nervous in front of big groups. Last month I gave a short demo and I spoke too fast. So I plan to join a speaking club and practise one short talk every week.

  6. TOEIC Writing 6 to 7. A customer writes: "I ordered a laptop stand two weeks ago, but it has not arrived." Write a reply: apologise, give a reason, offer a solution.
    Answer

    Model: Dear Mr Brown, thank you for your email, and I am sorry that your laptop stand has not arrived. We had a problem with our delivery partner last week, and some orders were delayed. I have sent your stand again today by express delivery, so it should arrive within two days. I have also refunded your delivery fee. Please contact me if there is anything else I can do. Kind regards, Anna Ruiz, Customer Service.

  7. Hard: Lena types fast, gets nervous with people, needs a result in one week and wants to study in Canada. Her university accepts PTE Academic, the DET and IELTS. Which exam would you suggest, and what must she check first?
    Answer

    The DET or PTE Academic could suit her. Both are on computer, so she does not speak to a person, and results usually come within two days. The DET is at home and shorter. She must first check that her university page names the exam and the score, and that her study permit or visa rules do not need a different test.

Key takeaways

  • PTE Academic: about 2 hours at a centre, 22 question types in three parts, scores 10 to 90. Integrated tasks count for two skills.
  • PTE has strict rules: one-sentence summaries of 5 to 75 words, and minus marks in three task types.
  • The DET: about 1 hour at home, adaptive, scores 10 to 160 in steps of 5. Keep your eyes on the screen.
  • DET Interactive Writing and Speaking build on your own answers. Link each new answer to the last one.
  • TOEIC is for work. Listening and Reading: 200 questions, 10 to 990. Speaking and Writing: 0 to 200 each.
  • Choose by the official list first. Then choose the format that suits you.

Sources

  • Pearson: PTE Academic test format, Speaking and Writing. Timing, task rules and scoring for each speaking and writing task. The Reading and Listening pages are linked from it.
  • Pearson: PTE Academic. Test length, results time, test centres and the visa versions.
  • Pearson: PTE Academic score guide (July 2025). The 10 to 90 scale, integrated scoring and the CEFR table.
  • Duolingo: DET scoring guide for teachers (2026). Every question type, its timing and how the subscores are made.
  • ETS: TOEIC Listening and Reading test. Parts, timing and the 10 to 990 scale.
  • ETS: TOEIC Speaking and Writing tests. The eleven speaking and eight writing questions.

Study plans and mock tests

A good plan turns "I want to improve" into small daily steps. This chapter gives three 12-week plans, a weekly routine and a can-do checklist. It ends with four original mini mock tests, a scoring guide and an exam-day checklist.

  • Estimate how many hours you need to reach your next level.
  • Find your level in each skill with a can-do checklist.
  • Follow a 12-week plan for A2 to B1, B1 to B2 or B2 to C1.
  • Take a mini mock test in each skill and score it.
  • Prepare for exam day with a clear checklist.

How long does one level take?

Tom is B1. His exam is in 12 weeks. He needs B2. He studies 4 hours a week. Is that enough? Let us do the maths.

Cambridge gives a guide in guided learning hours. It says one CEFR level takes about 200 hours. The numbers below are cumulative: they count from zero.

Cambridge guided learning hours, from beginner (Cambridge support site, updated December 2025)
CEFR levelHours from zero (about)
A2180 to 200
B1350 to 400
B2500 to 600
C1700 to 800
C21,000 to 1,200
  1. B1 to B2 is about 150 to 200 hours.
  2. Tom has 12 weeks × 4 hours = 48 hours.
  3. 48 hours is about a quarter of what he needs.
  4. With 12 hours a week he gets 144 hours. That is most of a level.

Cambridge says these hours are only a guide. Your past learning, your age and how much English you hear outside class all change the number. The plans in this chapter use about 12 hours a week. If you start at the top of a level, 12 weeks can be enough. If you start at the bottom, plan for more weeks.

"I will study 10 hours on Sunday and nothing in the week." Long, rare sessions work badly. The research below shows that short, regular sessions help memory much more.

Find your starting point: a can-do checklist

Read each statement. Mark it only if you can do it on a normal day, not your best day. Your level in a skill is the highest level where you can do almost every statement. These statements are our own. They follow the CEFR idea of can-do descriptions.

  • A2 I can understand a slow, clear message about times, prices and places.
  • A2 I can follow a short video if people speak slowly about daily life.
  • B1 I can follow the main points of a stand-up meeting about my own project.
  • B1 I can understand a podcast for learners at normal speed.
  • B2 I can follow a conference talk in my field and a fast team discussion.
  • B2 I can understand most films without subtitles if the speech is clear.
  • C1 I can follow a long talk with jokes, side stories and unclear structure.
  • C1 I can understand what a speaker means but does not say directly.
  • A2 I can read a short email or notice and find a time or a price.
  • A2 I can follow simple instructions, like installing an app.
  • B1 I can read a README or a short news article and get the main points.
  • B1 I can guess some new words from the sentence around them.
  • B2 I can read a technical article and find the writer's opinion.
  • B2 I can read quickly to find one detail in a long document.
  • C1 I can read a research paper and see what the writer only suggests.
  • C1 I can notice tone, like irony or careful politeness.
  • A2 I can talk about my job and my day in short sentences.
  • A2 I can ask simple questions in a shop or at a hotel.
  • B1 I can describe what I did yesterday and explain why.
  • B1 I can say what blocks my work in a stand-up meeting.
  • B2 I can give my view in a meeting with reasons and examples.
  • B2 I can talk for two minutes on a familiar topic without long pauses.
  • C1 I can explain a complex system to a client and answer hard questions.
  • C1 I can change my style for a friend, a manager or a customer.
  • A2 I can write a short message to say I am late or ill.
  • A2 I can fill in a form with my details and my work history.
  • B1 I can write a clear email about a problem and ask for help.
  • B1 I can write a short paragraph that gives my opinion with one reason.
  • B2 I can write a design document with pros and cons.
  • B2 I can write a 250-word essay with clear paragraphs.
  • C1 I can write a well-organised report for a reader who knows little.
  • C1 I can edit my own writing and make it shorter and clearer.

Most people have an uneven profile. Engineers often read at B2 or C1 but speak at B1. That is useful to know. Your weakest skill should get the most time in your plan.

Do the checklist again in week 6 and week 12. Write the date and your marks in a notebook. Seeing progress keeps you going.

What the research says about study methods

Ana rereads her notes for an hour. Ben closes the book and tests himself for 20 minutes. Who remembers more a week later? Usually Ben.

In 2013, a team of psychologists led by John Dunlosky compared ten popular study methods. Two methods got their highest rating:

  • Practice testing: quizzes, flashcards, past papers and mock tests.
  • Distributed practice: short sessions spread over days and weeks.

Rereading and highlighting got a low rating. They feel easy, but they do not help much. Here is how we use these findings in the plans:

From research to routine
FindingWhat you do
Testing yourself helps memoryStart each day with 10 minutes of flashcards. Do one mini mock test every week.
Spacing helps memoryReview new words after 1 day, 3 days, 1 week and 1 month. An app with spaced repetition does this for you.
Rereading helps littleAfter reading, close the text. Write three key points from memory.
Feedback fixes errorsEvery week, check one piece of writing or one recording against a scoring guide.

Only doing what feels comfortable. Many engineers read a lot, because reading is easy for them. Speaking feels hard, so they skip it. The hard skill is the one that raises your score.

The weekly routine

This is a model week of about 12 hours. Change the days to fit your life. Keep the mix of input and output.

A model study week (about 12 hours)
DayMain work (about 90 minutes)Every day (15 minutes)
MondayGrammar chapter from this book, then a reading text with questionsFlashcards and one short listening
TuesdayListening practice, then shadowing for 15 minutesFlashcards and one short listening
WednesdayNew vocabulary in context, then one writing taskFlashcards and one short listening
ThursdayReading for detail, then a 2-minute recorded talk on the same topicFlashcards and one short listening
FridayCorrect Wednesday's writing with the scoring guide. Rewrite it.Flashcards and one short listening
SaturdayOne mini mock test, timed. Then review every error.Flashcards
SundayRest, or something fun: a film, a podcast, a game in EnglishNothing, or a few flashcards

Warm up: 10 minutes

Do your flashcards. Say each word aloud in a short sentence.

Input: 30 minutes

Read or listen to one text at your level. Answer questions about it. Note five useful phrases.

Output: 30 minutes

Use the five phrases. Write a paragraph or record a talk on the same topic.

Feedback: 15 minutes

Check your output with a scoring guide, a teacher or a language tool. Write your three biggest errors in an error log.

Log: 5 minutes

Write the date, the time you studied and one thing you can do now. Small notes show big progress over 12 weeks.

An error log is the most useful notebook you can keep. After four weeks you will see the same five or six errors again and again. Those are your personal grammar plan. The chapter The error clinic helps you fix them.

Three 12-week plans

Each plan has three blocks of four weeks. Every block has a grammar focus, a vocabulary goal, a skills goal and a check at the end. The links go to chapters in this book.

  1. Week 1 Start. Do the can-do checklist and one mini mock test. Write down your scores.
  2. Week 4 First check. Repeat one mini mock test. Look at your error log.
  3. Week 8 Second check. Do a full official sample test from the exam owner, timed.
  4. Week 12 Final check. Do the checklist and all four mini mocks again. Decide: book the exam, or add four weeks.
A2 to B1 in 12 weeks
Weeks 1 to 4Weeks 5 to 8Weeks 9 to 12
GrammarPresent tenses, past tenses, questionsFuture forms, present perfect, can, must, shouldLinking words, first conditional, comparatives
Vocabulary15 new words a day: work, travel, health15 a day: feelings, plans, problems15 a day: opinions and reasons
SkillsShort emails. Describe your day aloud.Tell a story in the past. Follow learner podcasts.Give an opinion with one reason. Read short news.
Weekly outputOne 80-word emailOne 100-word story, one 1-minute recordingOne 120-word opinion, one 2-minute recording
CheckCan you write about your week with no tense errors?Can you tell a story for 1 minute?Can you give and support an opinion?
B1 to B2 in 12 weeks
Weeks 1 to 4Weeks 5 to 8Weeks 9 to 12
GrammarPerfect tenses, modal verbsConditionals, the passive, reported speechRelative clauses, -ing and to, phrasal verbs
Vocabulary20 a day: collocations for work and study20 a day: academic words, word families20 a day: phrasal verbs, linkers for essays

CheckCan you explain a technical choice with reasons?Can you write a polite complaint with no big errors?Can you argue both sides of a question?
B2 to C1 in 12 weeks
Weeks 1 to 4Weeks 5 to 8Weeks 9 to 12
GrammarAdvanced tense and aspect, hedgingParticiple clauses and nominalisation, inversionRegister and collocation, your error log
VocabularyPrecise verbs: "rise" or "soar", "claim" or "argue"Academic collocations and word formationIdioms you really hear at work, register changes

CheckCan you summarise a long article without copying?Can you hedge a claim in three different ways?Can you hit C1 in an official sample test?

From week 9, practise the exact tasks of your exam. Use the exam chapters: IELTS Writing, TOEFL iBT, Cambridge exams and PTE, Duolingo and TOEIC. Every exam owner offers free sample tests. ETS, for example, has a free 40-minute TOEFL sample test.

Mini mock tests: Reading and Listening

These mini mocks are written for this book. They are not real exam papers. They aim at the B1 to B2 border, so they work for all three plans. Time yourself. Do not use a dictionary.

Reading (12 minutes, 6 questions)

Last spring, Brightline, a small software company with forty staff, had a problem. Its team chat never stopped. Developers received about two hundred messages a day. Many said they could not concentrate for more than twenty minutes at a time.

The managers decided to try an experiment. From 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., the chat became "quiet". People could still read messages, but notifications were turned off, and nobody expected a reply before lunch. Urgent problems went to a single phone number.

At first, not everyone was happy. The support team worried that customers would wait longer for answers. Some new employees said they felt lonely without the constant conversation. To solve the first problem, the support team kept its own channel open all morning. For new staff, managers started a short video call at 12:15 every day, where people could ask anything.

After three months, the company asked staff to complete a survey. Seventy per cent said they finished difficult tasks faster. The number of messages fell by almost half. However, a few people admitted that they now checked email more often instead of chat. As one developer said, this "is just the same problem in a different place".

Brightline has kept quiet hours, but it is now looking at email too.

  1. Why did Brightline start quiet hours? A. Customers complained. B. Staff could not concentrate. C. The chat software was expensive. D. Managers wanted fewer meetings.
  2. During quiet hours, staff could: A. not open the chat at all. B. read messages without notifications. C. only use the phone. D. send messages only to managers.
  3. True, False or Not Given: urgent problems went to one phone number.
  4. True, False or Not Given: Brightline plans to hire more support staff.
  5. What did managers start for new employees? (Up to five words.)
  6. What does the developer mean by "the same problem in a different place"?
Answers: Reading

1 B. 2 B. 3 True. 4 Not Given: the text never mentions hiring. 5 A daily video call (at 12:15). 6 The constant interruptions did not stop. They moved from chat to email.

Listening (about 8 minutes, 6 questions)

You need someone to read the transcript to you. Or use a computer voice. On a Mac, save the transcript as listening.txt and run this script. It reads the woman's lines with one voice and the man's lines with another.

#!/bin/bash
# Read the dialogue in listening.txt aloud with two voices.
while IFS= read -r line; do
  case "$line" in
    Woman:*) say -v Karen  -r 165 "${line#Woman: }" ;;   # Australian voice
    Man:*)   say -v Daniel -r 165 "${line#Man: }" ;;     # British voice
  esac
done < listening.txt

Run it with bash listen.sh. It prints nothing. You only hear the two voices. We tested it on macOS with these two voices.

Read the questions first. Listen once. Then answer.

  1. What does the student want to book? A. a computer B. a group study room C. a science lab
  2. Which room do they get? Room ___
  3. Why can't they book three hours?
  4. What time will they use the room?
  5. What is the student's number?
  6. What is true about the workshop? A. You must register online. B. It costs a small fee. C. It is on Wednesday evening.
Transcript (open only after you listen) 
Woman: Good morning. How can I help?
Man: Hi. I'd like to book a group study room for Thursday afternoon. There are four of us.
Woman: Let me check. The rooms on the second floor are all taken, I'm afraid. But Room 1B on the ground floor is free from two until five.
Man: Is it big enough for four people?
Woman: Yes. It has six seats and a large screen you can connect a laptop to.
Man: Perfect. We need to practise a presentation. Can we book all three hours?
Woman: The limit is two hours per group, so two until four, or three until five.
Man: Then three until five, please. One of my friends has a lab until half past two.
Woman: Done. I'll need your student number.
Man: It's four, seven, one, nine, three.
Woman: Thanks. By the way, if you're preparing a presentation, there's a free workshop on Wednesday at six about speaking in public. It's in the main hall, and you don't need to register.
Man: Oh, that sounds useful. I might bring the others.
Answers: Listening

1 B. 2 1B. 3 The limit is two hours per group. 4 From three to five (3 to 5 p.m.). 5 47193. 6 C.

In question 4, many people write "2 to 4". The speaker first says both options, then chooses "three until five". In exams, the first number you hear is often not the answer. Wait for the final decision.

Mini mock tests: Writing and Speaking

Writing (25 minutes)

You took an online course on data visualisation, but it was not what you expected. Write an email to the course organiser (150 to 200 words). In your email:

  • say why you joined the course,
  • explain what was wrong,
  • say what you would like the organiser to do.
Scoring guide for Writing (ours, based on common exam criteria)
Criterion (0 to 5)5 means3 means1 means
TaskAll three points, fully developed. The right tone for the reader.All points, but one is thin. The tone slips once or twice.A point is missing or the tone is wrong.
OrganisationClear paragraphs. Linkers join ideas naturally.Paragraphs, but some linkers repeat or feel forced.Hard to follow. No paragraphs.
VocabularyPrecise words and good collocations. Almost no spelling errors.Enough words for the task. Some repetition.Very simple words. Errors block meaning.
GrammarA mix of simple and complex sentences. Few errors.Mostly simple sentences. Errors do not block meaning.Many errors. Meaning is often unclear.

Dear Ms Novak,

I am writing about the online course "Data Visualisation for Beginners", which I finished last week. I joined because I build dashboards at work, and the course page promised practical projects with real data.

Unfortunately, the course was quite different. Most of the videos were about the history of charts, and there was only one short project at the end. In addition, the example files did not open in the current version of the software, so I could not follow two of the lessons. When I asked a question in the forum, nobody answered for ten days.

I would like you to update the example files and add more practical exercises. I would also appreciate a partial refund, since I could not complete a large part of the course.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Kenji Sato

Why 18? Task 5: all three points with details. Organisation 5: one paragraph per point, linkers like "Unfortunately" and "In addition". Vocabulary 4: good phrases like "partial refund", but "quite different" is a little vague. Grammar 4: a good mix of sentences, but no really complex structures.

Speaking (about 10 minutes)

Record yourself on your phone. Do not stop the recording if you make a mistake. Listen the next day and score yourself.

Part 1: short questions (about 20 to 30 seconds each)
  1. What do you do, and what do you like about it?
  2. How do you usually learn new things for work?
  3. What did you do last weekend?
Part 2: a 1-minute talk (1 minute to prepare)

Describe a tool or an app that helps you at work. Say what it is, how you use it, why it helps you and one thing you would change about it.

Part 3: discussion (about 45 seconds each)
  1. Do you think people rely too much on apps today? Why or why not?
  2. How might work tools change in the next ten years?

I'd like to talk about a note-taking app that I use every day at work. I use it to write down tasks during meetings and to keep short guides for things I do only once a month, like updating our servers. The main reason it helps me is search. I can find a note from two years ago in a few seconds, so I don't need to remember everything. It also syncs between my laptop and my phone, which is great when I'm travelling. If I could change one thing, I'd make sharing easier. At the moment, my teammates can't edit my notes, so we sometimes copy text between apps, and that's a bit annoying.

Scoring guide for Speaking (ours, based on common exam criteria)
Criterion (0 to 5)5 means3 means1 means
FluencySpeaks at length with few pauses. Ideas are linked.Keeps going but pauses to find words. Repeats some words.Long pauses. Short, broken answers.
VocabularyPrecise words. Can explain a word they do not know.Enough words for familiar topics.Very limited words.
GrammarA range of structures. Errors are rare.Simple structures mostly correct. Complex ones have errors.Frequent errors, even in simple sentences.
PronunciationEasy to understand. Good stress and rhythm.Mostly clear. Some words need effort.Often hard to understand.

Reading your results

Add up your scores. Then use the table to decide your next step. This is our own guide for practice. It is not an official score conversion.

What your mini mock results mean (our guide)
ResultReading or Listening (out of 6)Writing or Speaking (out of 20)Next step
Secure at B2617 to 20Move to C1 material and official sample tests.
Around B2514 to 16Keep the B1 to B2 plan. Fix your top three errors.
Around B13 or 410 to 13Follow the B1 to B2 plan from week 1.
Below B10 to 20 to 9Follow the A2 to B1 plan first.
  1. Reading 5 out of 6. Listening 4 out of 6.
  2. Writing 15 out of 20. Speaking 11 out of 20.
  3. Reading and writing are around B2. Speaking is around B1.
  4. Plan: B1 to B2, with extra speaking. He records a 2-minute talk every day and does Part 3 discussions with a friend twice a week.

Looking only at the total. "My total is fine, so I am ready." Most exam requirements have a minimum in each skill. Look at your lowest score first.

Exam-day checklist

Many people lose points for reasons that have nothing to do with English: a wrong ID, a late train, a laptop that does not start. The checklist below prevents that. The ETS rules come from its TOEFL test-day pages. Other exams have similar rules, so check yours.

  1. One week before: do one full official sample test under exam timing. Read the rules on the owner's site.
  2. One week before: check that the name on your ID matches your booking exactly. ETS says you cannot test if the names do not match, and you lose the fee.
  3. One day before: check your booking again. ETS asks you to check your account 24 hours before for any change of time or building.
  4. One day before: plan the route and the time. ETS asks you to arrive at least 30 minutes early at a test centre.
  5. The evening before: pack your ID. ETS recommends bringing two forms of ID. Sleep at your normal time.
  6. Test at home: clear the desk, close doors, plug in the computer and close all other apps. Set up the second camera if your exam needs one. Run the owner's system check early, not on the day.
  7. In the test room: no phone and no watch. At an ETS test centre, food and drink are not allowed in the room unless you have an approved health accommodation.
  8. During the test: read each instruction. Watch the timer. Never leave a section empty. If a task goes badly, forget it and start the next one fresh.
  9. After the test: write down which tasks felt hard. You will need these notes if you take the exam again.

On exam morning, warm up your English. Listen to 10 minutes of a podcast and say a few answers aloud. Your first speaking task should not be the first English you speak that day.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for planning and talking about progress
PatternPurposeModelNote
I can + verb, but I still find + noun / -ing + hard.Describe your level honestlyI can read articles, but I still find fast speech hard."Find + noun + adjective": "find it hard".
My weakest skill is + skill, so I will + verb.Set a priorityMy weakest skill is speaking, so I will record myself daily."So" introduces the action.
This week I am going to + verb.Make a short-term planThis week I am going to write two emails."Going to" for plans you already decided.
By + time, I want to be able to + verb.Set a 12-week goalBy March, I want to be able to lead a meeting."Be able to" after "want to".
I have been studying for + time.Say how long you have studiedI have been studying for eight weeks."For" a period, "since" a start point.
It takes about + time + to + verb.Talk about time neededIt takes about 200 hours to move up one level."It takes", not "It needs".
I scored + number + out of + number + in + skill.Report a practice scoreI scored 5 out of 6 in reading."Out of", not "from".
I keep + -ing.Name a repeated mistakeI keep forgetting the -s in "she works"."Keep" + -ing means again and again.
I need to work on + noun / -ing.Name what to improveI need to work on linking my ideas."Work on", not "work in".
If I study + time + a week, I will + verb + by + time.Predict a resultIf I study 12 hours a week, I will be ready by June.Present simple after "if", not "will".

Practice

1. Cambridge says one CEFR level takes about how many guided learning hours?

  • 50
  • 200
  • 1,000

Cambridge gives about 200 hours per level as a guide. The real number depends on the learner.

2. Which study method got a high rating in the 2013 review?

  • Rereading notes
  • Highlighting key sentences
  • Testing yourself

Practice testing and distributed practice got the highest rating. Rereading and highlighting got a low rating.

3. How early does ETS ask you to arrive at a TOEFL test centre?

  • 5 minutes
  • At least 30 minutes
  • 2 hours

ETS asks for at least 30 minutes, to allow time for check-in.

4. I scored 4 out ? 6 in listening.

5. I have been studying ? ten weeks.

6. I keep ? the same mistake with articles.

  1. Mia studies 6 hours a week for 12 weeks. How many hours is that, and is it enough to move from B1 to B2 by Cambridge's guide?
    Answer

    72 hours. B1 to B2 is about 150 to 200 hours. So it is not enough for a full level. She needs about 12 to 16 hours a week, or more weeks.

  2. Write your own goal with two patterns: "My weakest skill is ..., so I will ..." and "By ..., I want to be able to ...".
    Answer

    Model: My weakest skill is writing, so I will write one email every Wednesday and correct it on Friday. By the end of May, I want to be able to write a clear 250-word essay in 40 minutes.

  3. Score this short answer with the Writing guide (Task only): "Dear organiser, I joined the course. It was bad. Please give money back."
    Answer

    Task about 1 or 2. It mentions joining and a refund, but gives no reason for joining and no details of the problem. The tone is too direct for a formal email.

  4. Rewrite the answer above so it scores 4 or 5 for Task (60 to 80 words).
    Answer

    Model: Dear Mr Lane, I joined your data course because I want to build better dashboards at work. Sadly, the course had few practical tasks, and two example files did not open, so I could not finish those lessons. Could you please fix the files and add more exercises? I would also be grateful for a partial refund. Kind regards, Ana Silva.

  5. Plan one study day of 90 minutes for a learner whose weakest skill is listening. Use the five steps of the session carousel.
    Answer

    Model: 10 minutes of flashcards. 30 minutes: a 5-minute podcast at B1 to B2 level, listened to twice, with questions. 30 minutes: shadow 2 minutes of the podcast, then retell it aloud in 1 minute. 15 minutes: compare the retelling with the transcript and note three missed phrases. 5 minutes: log the time and one new phrase.

  6. Hard: Omar's exam needs IELTS 6.5 overall with no band below 6.0 in 12 weeks. His mock results: Reading B2, Listening B2, Writing B2, Speaking B1. What should his plan focus on, and why?
    Answer

    Speaking. It is his only skill near B1, and the "no band below 6.0" rule means one weak skill can stop him. He should keep short daily practice in the other skills but give speaking the most time: daily recordings, weekly feedback with the scoring guide and timed IELTS Speaking tasks from week 9. See IELTS Speaking.

Key takeaways

  • Cambridge's guide: about 200 guided learning hours per CEFR level. Twelve weeks at 12 hours a week gives about 145 hours.
  • Test yourself and spread your study over many days. Rereading and highlighting help little.
  • Use the can-do checklist to find your level in each skill. Give your weakest skill the most time.
  • Each plan has three 4-week blocks, with a check in weeks 1, 4, 8 and 12.
  • Score mini mocks with a clear guide. Look at your lowest skill, not only the total.
  • On exam day, check your ID name, arrive early and never leave a section empty.

Sources

  • Cambridge English: guided learning hours. About 200 hours per level and the cumulative table from A1 to C2 (updated December 2025).
  • Association for Psychological Science: which study strategies make the grade?. A summary of the 2013 review by Dunlosky and colleagues.
  • ETS: TOEFL iBT test day at a test centre. ID rules, arrival time and items not allowed.
  • ETS: TOEFL iBT Home Edition test day. How to prepare your room and computer for a test at home.
  • ETS: TOEFL iBT 2026 specifications. Can-do descriptions for each CEFR level in each skill, which shaped our checklist.
  • Cambridge English: B2 First handbook for teachers. Can-do summaries and writing criteria that our scoring guides follow.

Reading technical English

Engineers read more than they write. Every day you read docs, specs, changelogs, error messages and papers. Each kind of text has its own grammar and its own key words. This chapter teaches you to read them fast and correctly.

  • Recognise the main kinds of technical text and choose how to read each one.
  • Read MUST, SHOULD and MAY in a standard exactly as RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 define them.
  • Read changelogs, error messages and stack traces and find the important line quickly.
  • Find the five parts of a research paper abstract.
  • Use 150 core software words and avoid common false friends.

Kinds of technical text

Look at these five short texts. Each one comes from a different kind of document.

A. Run `pip install queuectl` to install the tool.
B. The client MUST include an API key in every request.
C. ### Fixed  - Crash when a queue name contains a space.
D. error: failed to connect to db:5432: connection refused
E. We propose a new method that reduces review time by 30%.

Text A is a how-to guide. It gives an order. Text B is a specification, or spec. Text C is a changelog. Text D is an error message. Text E comes from a research paper.

Each kind has a different job. So each kind uses different grammar. When you know the kind, you know what to expect.

Four kinds of documentation

Many teams sort their docs with a model called Diátaxis. It has four kinds of documentation. Each kind answers a different need.

The four kinds of documentation in Diátaxis
KindThe reader wants toTypical grammarModel sentence
Tutoriallearn by doingwe + present simple, short stepsNow we add a second route.
How-to guidereach one goal at workimperative: Run, Open, SetSet the timeout to 10 seconds.
Referencelook up a factpresent simple, no subjectReturns the number of items.
Explanationunderstand whyfull sentences, because, soWe use a queue because writes are slow.

Three ways to read

  • Skim: read only the headings, the first lines and the code. Ask: is this page useful?
  • Scan: search for one word or number. Use Ctrl + F. Ask: where is the timeout setting?
  • Read closely: read every word, slowly. Do this for specs, security notes and breaking changes.

Do not read reference docs from top to bottom like a story. Scan for the one function you need. But do read specs and upgrade notes closely. One small word like NOT can change everything.

The grammar of documentation

Here is a short reference entry for an invented Python function.

fetch_user(user_id, *, timeout=30)
    Return the user with the given ID.
    Raises NotFound if no user has this ID.
    timeout: seconds to wait. Defaults to 30. Ignored in test mode.
    Deprecated since 2.3: use get_user() instead.

Most lines have no subject. The hidden subject is "this function". So "Raises NotFound" means "This function raises NotFound". Reference docs are short on purpose.

Two styles: Return and Returns

Python's style guide for docstrings is PEP 257. It asks for a command: "Return the user". Other docs, like Rust and Java, often describe: "Returns the user". Both mean the same thing. Do not read "Returns" as a plural noun. It is a verb.

Common phrases in docs

Doc phrases and what they mean
PhraseMeaningModel
defaults to XX is used if you give no valueThe port defaults to 8080.
is ignoredthe program does not use itThis flag is ignored on Windows.
has no effectnothing changesSetting it twice has no effect.
takes precedence overwins when both are setEnvironment variables take precedence over the config file.
is undefinedanything can happen, do not rely on itThe order of keys is undefined.
out of the boxwith no extra setupIt supports JSON out of the box.
under the hoodinside, where you cannot seeUnder the hood, it uses a thread pool.
at your own riskit may break, and nobody will helpUse internal APIs at your own risk.

Deprecated is very important. A deprecated feature still works today. But it will be removed in a later version. Start to move away from it now.

Docs also use labels: Note (useful extra fact), Warning (you can lose data or time), Tip (a faster way) and Important. Always read a Warning closely.

Long doc sentences often hide simple patterns. Find the main subject and verb first. The chapter The 15 sentence patterns shows the shapes. Linkers like unless, otherwise and however change the meaning. See Linking words.

"Unless" means "if not". "The cache is used unless you pass --no-cache" means: no flag, cache on. Many readers swap the meaning. Read unless, except and otherwise twice.

Must, should and may in standards

Read three lines from an invented API spec.

Line 1: Every request MUST include an API key.

Line 2: The client SHOULD retry after a 503 error.

Line 3: The server MAY compress large responses.

Line 1 is a hard rule. A request without a key is wrong. Line 2 is strong advice. You can skip it, but only for a good reason. Line 3 is a free choice. Some servers compress. Some do not. Clients must work with both.

These capital words come from a document called RFC 2119. It was published in March 1997. It gives each word an exact meaning. A later document, RFC 8174 (May 2017), made one rule clearer. Together they form BCP 14.

The BCP 14 key words
Key wordsMeaning in simple wordsModel
MUST, REQUIRED, SHALLAlways. No exceptions.The token MUST be signed.
MUST NOT, SHALL NOTNever. No exceptions.The server MUST NOT log passwords.
SHOULD, RECOMMENDEDDo it, unless you have a good reason and understand the cost.Clients SHOULD use TLS 1.3.
SHOULD NOT, NOT RECOMMENDEDDo not do it, unless you have a good reason and understand the cost.Servers SHOULD NOT send stack traces to users.
MAY, OPTIONALYour free choice. Others must still work with you.A client MAY cache the response.

The capital letters rule (RFC 8174)

RFC 8174 says the special meaning applies only to words in capital letters. In lowercase, must and may have their normal English meaning. Many RFCs now start with a short standard sentence. It says the key words follow BCP 14 when they appear in all capitals.

Capital letters: BCP 14 meaning

The client MAY retry. (optional feature)

Lowercase: normal English

The server may be slow at night. (a possibility)

RFC 8174 also says something surprising. A spec does not need these words to set a rule. Plain sentences can be rules too. So read the whole spec, not only the capital words.

Use them with care

RFC 2119 asks authors to use these words carefully and not too often. They are for things that matter for interoperability, or to stop harm. A spec full of MUST is hard to follow.

Many specs outside the IETF also point to RFC 2119. Two examples are Semantic Versioning and Conventional Commits. You will meet these words in API guides and design docs too.

SHOULD does not mean "optional". It means "do this, unless you have a real reason not to". MAY in a spec is not a guess about the future. It means "allowed, your choice". The everyday meanings of these modals are in Modal verbs and Hedging and stance.

Find the key words with code

This small script finds BCP 14 key words in a spec. It is case-sensitive, like RFC 8174.

import re

# Longest phrases first, so "MUST NOT" wins over "MUST".
KEYWORDS = ["MUST NOT", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD NOT", "NOT RECOMMENDED",
            "MUST", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHOULD", "RECOMMENDED",
            "MAY", "OPTIONAL"]
PATTERN = re.compile(r"\b(" + "|".join(KEYWORDS) + r")\b")  # case-sensitive

spec = """
Every request MUST include an API key.
The server SHOULD NOT cache error pages.
A client MAY retry the request after 30 seconds.
Clients must be patient. The server may be slow at night.
"""

for number, line in enumerate(spec.strip().splitlines(), start=1):
    found = PATTERN.findall(line)
    print(number, found if found else "no BCP 14 keyword")
1 ['MUST']
2 ['SHOULD NOT']
3 ['MAY']
4 no BCP 14 keyword

Line 4 has must and may, but in lowercase. So they are normal English. The script agrees with RFC 8174.

How an RFC is built

RFCs follow a fixed order. RFC 7322, the RFC style guide, lists it. Once you know the order, you can jump to the part you need.

  1. Abstract: what the document is about, in a few lines.
  2. Status of This Memo: is this a standard, an experiment or just information?
  3. Introduction: the problem and the goal.
  4. Requirements Language: the sentence about BCP 14.
  5. The main body: the rules, often with MUST and SHOULD.
  6. Security Considerations: risks and attacks. Every RFC must have this section.
  7. IANA Considerations: new names or numbers that need to be registered.
  8. References: normative and informative.

Before you implement an RFC, check its status page. A newer RFC may update it or make it obsolete. RFC 2119, for example, is updated by RFC 8174. The status page on the RFC Editor or IETF site shows these links.

Changelogs and version numbers

Here is a short changelog for an invented tool.

# Changelog
All notable changes to this project are documented here.
The format is based on Keep a Changelog. This project
adheres to Semantic Versioning.

## [Unreleased]
### Added
- `--dry-run` flag for the `purge` command.

## [3.0.0] - 2026-10-02
### Removed
- BREAKING: the `watch` command. Use `tail -f` instead.
### Changed
- The default timeout is now 10 s (was 30 s).

## [2.4.1] - 2026-09-12
### Fixed
- Crash when a queue name contains a space.
### Security
- Update the TLS library to fix a certificate check bug.

## [2.4.0] - 2026-08-30
### Deprecated
- The `watch` command. It will be removed in 3.0.0.

The newest version is at the top. Each version has a date in year-month-day form. Changes are grouped by type. This format comes from a popular guide called Keep a Changelog (version 1.1.0).

The six change types in Keep a Changelog
HeadingMeaningShould you worry?
Addednew featuresNo. Read it for new ideas.
Changedexisting features work differentlyMaybe. Defaults may change.
Deprecatedstill works, but will be removedPlan your move now.
RemovedgoneYes. Your code may break.
Fixedbugs fixedGood news. Check your bug is here.
Securitysecurity holes fixedYes. Upgrade soon.

The guide also has an Unreleased section at the top. It shows what is coming next. A yanked release is marked [YANKED]. Do not install it.

Semantic Versioning

Version 3.0.0 has three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. This system is called Semantic Versioning, or SemVer. The current spec is SemVer 2.0.0.

  • MAJOR goes up for a breaking change. 2.4.1 to 3.0.0: read the notes closely.
  • MINOR goes up for new features that are backward compatible. 2.3.0 to 2.4.0.
  • PATCH goes up for backward-compatible bug fixes. 2.4.0 to 2.4.1.
  • Version 0.y.z means early development. Anything may change at any time.
  • 1.0.0-beta.2 is a pre-release. It comes before 1.0.0 and may be unstable.

Deprecated is not removed. A deprecated feature still works. Also, do not confuse deprecated with depreciated. Depreciated means "lost money value", like an old car.

Before a major upgrade, scan the changelog for four words: Removed, BREAKING, Deprecated, Security. Then read those lines closely. Read the rest later.

Error messages

Here are three real messages. We made each error on purpose.

ls: nofile.txt: No such file or directory
KeyError: 'timeout'
thread 'main' (117535749) panicked at panic.rs:4:25:
index out of bounds: the len is 2 but the index is 2

Error messages use a short style. They drop small words like the, is and was. This style is called telegraphic. Read them like newspaper headlines. Put the missing words back in your head.

Error message patterns as full sentences
MessageFull sentence
No such file or directoryThere is no file or folder with this name.
Permission deniedYou are not allowed to do this.
connection refusedThe other machine said no to the connection.
failed to parse configThe program tried to read the config, but it could not.
expected `u32`, found `&str`The code needs a number here, but you gave text.
value moved hereThe value was moved at this line.
unexpected end of fileThe file stopped before the program expected.
`x` is not definedThe name x does not exist here.

The parts of a compiler message

The Rust compiler gives long, helpful messages. Here is a real one.

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `tags`
 --> moved.rs:8:24
  |
6 |     let tags = vec![String::from("urgent")];
  |         ---- move occurs because `tags` has type `Vec<String>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
7 |     let n = send(tags);
  |                  ---- value moved here
8 |     println!("{n} {}", tags.len());
  |                        ^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
note: consider changing this parameter type in function `send` to borrow instead if owning the value isn't necessary
 --> moved.rs:1:15
  |
1 | fn send(tags: Vec<String>) -> usize {
  |    ----       ^^^^^^^^^^^ this parameter takes ownership of the value
  |    |
  |    in this function
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
7 |     let n = send(tags.clone());
  |                      ++++++++

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0382`.
  1. Severity: error, warning, note or help. An error stops the build. A warning does not.
  2. Code: E0382. Search for this code. It gives better results than the message.
  3. Summary: "borrow of moved value". This is the problem in a few words.
  4. Location: moved.rs:8:24 means file, line 8, column 24.
  5. Labels: short notes under the code. They tell a story: moved here, then borrowed here.
  6. Help: one possible fix. It is a suggestion, not an order.

Words like consider and if ... is acceptable are soft. The compiler hedges because it cannot know your goal. Hedging is explained in Hedging and stance.

When you see 30 errors, fix the first one first. Later errors are often caused by the first. Do not start at the bottom of the list.

Reading a stack trace

This Python program reads a config file. The key timeout is missing. I changed the folder name to /home/you/app.

import json

def load_config(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return json.load(f)

def get_timeout(config):
    return config["http"]["timeout"]

def main():
    config = load_config("config.json")
    print(get_timeout(config))

main()
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/app/orders.py", line 14, in <module>
    main()
    ~~~~^^
  File "/home/you/app/orders.py", line 12, in main
    print(get_timeout(config))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/you/app/orders.py", line 8, in get_timeout
    return config["http"]["timeout"]
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'timeout'

A stack trace shows the path to the error. Python calls it a traceback. Each block is one frame. The first line says "most recent call last". So the newest call is at the bottom.

Read the last line

KeyError: 'timeout'. The type is KeyError. The detail is 'timeout'. A dictionary has no key called timeout.

Read the frame above it

Line 8, in get_timeout. This is where the error happened.

Look at the markers

The ^^^ marks show the exact part that failed: the ["timeout"] lookup.

Go up to your own code

Library frames are rarely the cause. Find the highest frame in your own files.

Ask why the data is wrong

The code is fine for a good config. The config file has no timeout. Fix the data, or add a default.

Other languages, other orders

Java prints the newest call at the top. Here is real output from a small invented billing program. It tries to read "12,50" as a whole number.

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: bad invoice
    at Billing.loadInvoice(Billing.java:10)
    at Billing.main(Billing.java:15)
Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12,50"
    at java.base/java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:67)
    at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:668)
    at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:786)
    at Billing.parsePrice(Billing.java:3)
    at Billing.loadInvoice(Billing.java:8)
    ... 1 more

The first line is the outer error: "bad invoice". Caused by shows the deeper error. The deepest "Caused by" is usually the root cause. Here it is the comma in "12,50".

Rust is short by default. A panic prints one place and one message. The note tells you how to see the full trace: set RUST_BACKTRACE=1.

Where to start reading
LanguageNewest callStart reading at
Pythonbottomthe last line, then go up
Javatopthe first line, then the last "Caused by"
Rust panicone line"panicked at", then the message

Learn the verbs of errors. Python and Rust raise or return errors. Java throws exceptions, and code catches them. An unhandled exception is one that nobody caught. A caller is the function that calls another one.

Reading a research paper abstract

Here is an abstract for an invented paper. RevLens is not a real tool.

Code review takes a large share of developer time. Large language models can write review comments, but many comments are generic or wrong. We present RevLens, a review assistant that retrieves similar past reviews from the same repository before it writes a comment. We evaluate RevLens on 4,200 pull requests from 12 open-source projects. Compared with a strong baseline without retrieval, RevLens raises the share of accepted comments from 31% to 44%. An ablation study shows that most of the gain comes from project-specific examples. These results suggest that local context matters more than model size for review tasks.

An abstract is a short summary of a paper. Most abstracts follow the same five moves. If you find the moves, you understand the paper in one minute.

The five moves of an abstract
MoveQuestionIn the RevLens abstract
1. BackgroundWhy is this area important?Code review takes a large share of developer time.
2. GapWhat problem is still open?... many comments are generic or wrong.
3. MethodWhat did they build or do?We present RevLens ... We evaluate ... on 4,200 pull requests.
4. ResultWhat did they find? Numbers?... from 31% to 44%. An ablation study shows ...
5. MeaningWhy does it matter?These results suggest that local context matters more ...

Words you will meet in papers

  • Baseline: the method you compare with. "Outperforms the baseline" means "is better than it".
  • State of the art (SOTA): the best result so far.
  • Ablation study: remove one part, and measure again. It shows which part helps.
  • We propose / We present / We introduce: here comes the new idea.
  • To our knowledge: we did not find older work on this. It is a hedge.
  • Remains an open problem: nobody has solved it yet.

In papers, significant often has a special meaning. "Statistically significant" means the result is probably not chance. It does not always mean "big". A 0.2% gain can be significant. Look at the real number.

Read a paper in this order: title, abstract, figures, conclusion. Then decide if you need the rest. Watch the verbs: shows is strong, suggests is softer. See Hedging and stance.

These 150 words appear again and again in docs, tickets and meetings. They are in ten groups of fifteen. Learn one group a day. Open a group to see the words.

GPUa chip that does many calculations at the same time

Some words have two meanings in tech. Parameter is an input name in code, but in AI it also means a learned weight. Token is a login string on the web, but in AI it is a piece of text. Context tells you which meaning is right.

Do not learn the words as a list only. Write one sentence from your own work for each word. "Our staging cluster has three nodes." The chapter How to grow your vocabulary shows how to review them.

False friends in tech

The test passed eventually, so I am not sure it works.

The test may pass sometimes, so I am not sure it works.

The writer wanted to say "possibly" or "sometimes". In English, eventually means "in the end, after a long time". In German, French and Spanish, a similar word means "possibly". This is a false friend.

False friends from other languages

Common false friends at work
English wordReal English meaningWrong meaning (from)Tech model
actualreal, truecurrent (German aktuell, Spanish actual, Russian актуальный)The actual cause was a full disk.
eventuallyin the endpossibly (German eventuell, French éventuellement)The replicas are eventually consistent.
sensiblereasonable, wisesensitive (German sensibel, French and Spanish sensible)The library has sensible defaults. Never log sensitive data.
accuratecorrect, exactneat, careful (Russian аккуратный)The estimate was accurate within a day.
controlto direct or commandto check (French contrôler)This flag controls the log level.
billion1,000,000,000 (109)1012 (German Billion, French billion)We serve 2 billion requests a month.
claima statement, or a piece of user data in a tokena complaint (Japanese kurēmu)The token has an email claim.
naivesimple, first-try (for an algorithm)sensitive, delicate (Japanese naību)The naive solution is O(n²).

Eventually consistent is a real tech phrase. It means all copies of the data will agree in the end. It does not mean "possibly consistent".

Everyday words with a tech meaning

Everyday meaning

  • argument: a fight with words
  • issue: a problem, or a magazine copy
  • kill: end a life
  • ship: a big boat
  • daemon: (demon) an evil spirit
  • cookie: a sweet biscuit

Tech meaning

  • argument: a value passed to a function
  • issue: a ticket in a tracker, like GitHub Issues
  • kill: stop a process
  • ship: release to users
  • daemon: a program that runs in the background
  • cookie: small data a website stores in your browser

Look-alike words inside English

  • principal (an identity in security, like a user or service) and principle (a basic rule).
  • discrete (separate, as in discrete maths) and discreet (careful, private).
  • affect (a verb: The bug affects login.) and effect (a noun: The fix had no effect.).
  • lose (We lose data.) and loose (not tight: loose coupling).
  • deprecated (will be removed) and depreciated (lost money value).

Do not trust a word because it looks like your language. When a word looks easy but the sentence feels strange, check a learner's dictionary. Check the tech meaning too.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for reading technical English
PatternPurposeModelNote
Subject + MUST / MUST NOT + verbAn absolute rule in a specThe server MUST NOT log passwords.Only capital letters carry the BCP 14 meaning.
Subject + SHOULD + verbStrong advice with rare exceptionsClients SHOULD use TLS 1.3.SHOULD is not "optional". Exceptions need a reason.
Subject + MAY + verbA free choice in a specA client MAY cache the response.Others must still work with you either way.
Return(s) + noun + if + conditionReference docs with a hidden subjectReturns None if the key is missing.The subject is "this function". Returns is a verb.
X defaults to YThe value used when you give noneThe timeout defaults to 30 seconds.Check the default in each new major version.
Deprecated since X: use Y insteadA feature that will be removedDeprecated since 2.3: use get_user().Deprecated still works. Removed does not.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCHRead the risk of an upgrade2.4.1 to 3.0.0 is a major upgrade.A major bump can break your code.
failed to / could not + verb + objectAn action did not workfailed to connect to db:5432The object tells you where to look.
expected X, found YThe code got the wrong kind of valueexpected `u32`, found `&str`X is what the code needs. Y is what you gave.
No such + nounThe thing does not existNo such file or directoryCheck the path and the spelling first.
ErrorType: detail (last line)The end of a Python tracebackKeyError: 'timeout'In Python, start reading at the bottom.
Caused by: ErrorType: detailThe deeper error in a Java traceCaused by: NumberFormatExceptionThe last "Caused by" is often the root cause.
We propose / present + nounThe main idea of a paperWe present RevLens, a review assistant.The next sentences give the method and the results.
X outperforms Y by + numberA result compared with a baselineIt outperforms the baseline by 13 points.Check which baseline and which test set.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

Which kind of documentation uses many imperatives like "Run" and "Set"?

  • Reference
  • How-to guide
  • Explanation

A how-to guide helps you reach one goal. It gives orders, step by step.

A spec says: "The client SHOULD send a request ID." What does this mean?

  • Sending the ID is fully optional.
  • Send it, unless you have a good reason and understand the cost.
  • The client must always send it, with no exceptions.

SHOULD is strong advice. You may skip it only with a real reason.

Which line uses a BCP 14 key word?

  • The server may be busy at noon.
  • Clients must be patient.
  • The server MAY close idle connections.

RFC 8174 says the special meaning is only for words in capital letters.

A library goes from 4.2.7 to 5.0.0. What does SemVer tell you?

  • Only bug fixes.
  • New features, nothing breaks.
  • There are breaking changes. Read the notes closely.

The MAJOR number went up. That means changes that are not backward compatible.

Where do you start reading a Python traceback?

  • At the first line, "Traceback (most recent call last)".
  • At the last line, with the error type and detail.
  • In the middle, at the longest frame.

Python puts the most recent call last. The last line names the error.

"This option is deprecated." What is true?

  • It still works, but it will be removed later.
  • It is already removed.
  • It has lost value, like an old car.

Deprecated means "still here, but plan to stop using it". Depreciated is about money value.

Which sentence uses eventually correctly?

  • Eventually the bug is in the parser, but I am not sure.
  • After three retries, the job eventually finished.
  • We can eventually meet tomorrow, if you are free.

Eventually means "in the end, after some time". It does not mean "possibly".

Fill the gap

Under BCP 14, MUST, REQUIRED and ? all mean an absolute rule.

The port (default) to 8080 if you do not set it.

In SemVer, a backward-compatible bug fix raises the ? number.

In Keep a Changelog, a feature that will be removed soon goes under ?.

The deeper error in a Java stack trace starts with "Caused ?:".

A test that removes one part of a system to measure its effect is an ? study.

Think and write

  1. Write these error messages as full sentences: (a) "Permission denied" (b) "failed to parse config.toml" (c) "connection timed out".
    Answer

    (a) You are not allowed to do this. (b) The program tried to read config.toml, but the file has an error. (c) The program waited for the other machine, but it did not answer in time.

  2. Read the changelog in this chapter. You use the watch command and version 2.4.1. Is the upgrade to 3.0.0 safe?
    Answer

    No, not without changes. Version 3.0.0 removes watch. It was deprecated in 2.4.0. You must change your scripts to use tail -f first. Also, the default timeout changed from 30 s to 10 s. Check that this is fine for you.

  3. A spec says: "Servers SHOULD NOT return stack traces to clients." Your team wants to return them in production. What do you need?
    Answer

    You need a strong, clear reason, and you must understand the risk. Stack traces can show secret details about the system. Most teams show them only in development.

  4. Find the five moves in this abstract: "Log search is slow on large clusters. Existing indexes use too much memory. We design a compressed index for log lines. On 2 TB of logs, it answers queries 5 times faster with 40% less memory. This makes interactive search possible on small machines."
    Answer

    Background: Log search is slow on large clusters. Gap: Existing indexes use too much memory. Method: We design a compressed index. Result: 5 times faster with 40% less memory, on 2 TB. Meaning: interactive search on small machines.

  5. Expert: a design doc says "The service must retry three times" in lowercase. A colleague says this is not a rule because it is not in capital letters. Is the colleague right?
    Model answer

    Not fully. RFC 8174 says lowercase must has its normal English meaning. Normal English must is still a strong word. Also, a document does not need key words to make rules. The best fix is to ask the author. If the doc follows BCP 14, it should say so near the top and use MUST.

Key takeaways

  • Know the kind of text first: tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation, spec, changelog, error or paper.
  • Skim to decide, scan to find, and read closely for specs, warnings and breaking changes.
  • Reference docs hide the subject: "Returns None" means "This function returns None".
  • In BCP 14, MUST is always, SHOULD is normally, MAY is a free choice. Only capital letters count.
  • SemVer: MAJOR can break your code, MINOR adds features, PATCH fixes bugs.
  • Error messages are telegraphic. Add the missing words. Fix the first error first.
  • Python traces put the newest call at the bottom. Java puts it at the top and adds "Caused by".
  • An abstract has five moves: background, gap, method, result, meaning.
  • Watch for false friends like actual, eventually and sensible.

Sources

  • RFC 2119: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels. The IETF document that defines MUST, SHOULD and MAY (1997).
  • RFC 8174: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words. The 2017 update: only capital letters carry the special meaning.
  • RFC 7322: RFC Style Guide. The order of sections in an RFC.
  • Keep a Changelog 1.1.0. Change types, the Unreleased section and yanked releases.
  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0. The meaning of MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH.
  • Diátaxis. The four kinds of documentation.

Writing at work

Software teams work through text. Commits, pull requests, reviews, bug reports and status updates are all writing. Clear writing saves your team hours. Kind writing keeps the team happy. This chapter shows the standard shapes, with before and after examples.

  • Write commit messages with a short imperative subject and a clear body.
  • Write pull request descriptions that explain what changed, why and how to test it.
  • Give code review comments that are kind, clear and labelled by importance.
  • Write bug reports, READMEs, design documents and status updates in standard shapes.
  • Be direct and polite at the same time.

Write for a busy reader

Read two versions of the same message to a team lead.

So yesterday I started looking at the login tests because some of them were red, and I tried a few things, and then I found that the clock on the CI runner is wrong, so maybe we need to fix that, I am not sure who owns it.

The login tests fail because the CI runner's clock is 6 minutes slow. Could the platform team fix the clock? Until then, I have marked the two tests as flaky.

The first version tells a story in time order. The reader must wait for the point. The second version starts with the point. Then it asks for one action. Then it says what you did.

Your reader is busy. They read many messages a day. So every work text should answer three questions fast.

  1. What happened, or what changed?
  2. Why does it matter?
  3. What next? Who must do what?

Many companies call this BLUF, "bottom line up front". The main point goes in the first sentence. Details come after.

Do not write in the order you worked. Write in the order the reader needs. Your journey is interesting to you. The reader wants the result.

Emails have their own openings, closings and tone. See Emails and messages. This chapter is about the texts inside engineering tools.

Commit messages

Here are four real-looking commit messages. Which ones help a reader next year?

fixed stuff

WIP

Updated files.

Changes after review

Fix crash when the cart is empty

Add retry to the payment client

Remove the unused v1 search endpoint

Rename userId to accountId in the API

The "before" messages say nothing. A reader must open the code to learn what changed. The "after" messages say what changed in a few words.

A commit message has three parts. The picture shows them.

The subject line

  • Short. Git's own docs suggest 50 characters or less.
  • Imperative. Write it like an order: "Add", "Fix", "Remove". Not "Added" or "Adding".
  • No full stop at the end.
  • One change. If you need "and", you may need two commits.

Here is a well-known trick. Your subject should complete this sentence: "If applied, this commit will ...". "If applied, this commit will fix crash when the cart is empty." That works. "If applied, this commit will fixed stuff." That does not.

The body

The body explains why. The code already shows what. Git's guide for contributors asks for three things.

  1. The problem with the current code, in the present tense. "The client fails the order on the first 503."
  2. Why your change solves it. "A short retry hides the vendor's deploys."
  3. Other options you rejected, if any. "A longer timeout would slow every request."

Conventional Commits

Many teams use a format called Conventional Commits (version 1.0.0). The subject starts with a type, an optional scope and a colon.

feat(search): add filters by date
fix(auth): refresh the token before it expires
docs: explain the retry settings
refactor(cart)!: store prices as integer cents

BREAKING CHANGE: prices in the API are now in cents.
Common Conventional Commits types
TypeMeaningVersion effect in SemVer
feata new featureMINOR
fixa bug fixPATCH
! or BREAKING CHANGE:old code may stop workingMAJOR
docs, test, refactor, perf, build, ci, chore, styleother common typesnone on their own

Tools can read these prefixes. They can build a changelog and choose the next version number. The version rules are in Reading technical English.

Check your subject with code

import re

def check(message):
    lines = message.split("\n")
    subject = lines[0]
    problems = []
    if len(subject) > 50:
        problems.append(f"subject has {len(subject)} characters (aim for 50)")
    if subject.endswith("."):
        problems.append("subject ends with a full stop")
    # Look at the first word after an optional "type(scope): " prefix.
    first = re.sub(r"^\w+(\(.+?\))?!?:\s*", "", subject).split(" ")[0].lower()
    if first.endswith("ed") or first.endswith("ing"):
        problems.append(f"'{first}' is not imperative (use 'add', 'fix' ...)")
    if len(lines) > 1 and lines[1] != "":
        problems.append("line 2 must be blank")
    return problems or ["looks good"]

messages = [
    "Fixed the bug.",
    "Updating the retry logic in the payment client and the docs",
    "fix(payments): retry card charges on HTTP 503\n\nThe card API returns 503 during deploys.",
]
