for m in messages:
    print(repr(m.split("\n")[0]))
    for p in check(m):
        print("  -", p)
'Fixed the bug.'
  - subject ends with a full stop
  - 'fixed' is not imperative (use 'add', 'fix' ...)
'Updating the retry logic in the payment client and the docs'
  - subject has 59 characters (aim for 50)
  - 'updating' is not imperative (use 'add', 'fix' ...)
'fix(payments): retry card charges on HTTP 503'
  - looks good

This check is rough. A word like "embed" ends in "ed" but is imperative. Use it as a hint, like a linter.

"Update code" and "Fix bug" are too vague. Say which code and which bug. "Fix wrong total when a coupon is 100%" is clear.

Pull request descriptions

Fix bug

Add retry to the payment client for HTTP 503

## Why
The card API returns 503 for a few seconds during its deploys.
Last week 37 orders failed this way.

## What changed
- Retry up to 3 times, with 200 ms, 400 ms and 800 ms waits.
- Retry only on 503. Other errors fail at once, as before.

## How to test
1. Run `make test-payments`.
2. In staging, run the fake vendor with `--fail-first 2`.
   The order should succeed on the third try.

## Risks
A charge could repeat. The idempotency key prevents this.

Closes #412

A pull request, or PR, asks the team to review and merge your change. GitLab calls it a merge request. Google calls it a CL, short for changelist. The description is the first thing a reviewer reads.

The parts of a good description

  • Title: one short sentence that stands alone. Someone who reads only the history should understand it.
  • Why: the problem and its effect. Add numbers if you have them.
  • What changed: a short list, not a copy of the diff.
  • How to test: steps a reviewer can follow.
  • Risks and out of scope: what could go wrong, and what this PR does not do.
  • Links: the issue, the design doc, a screenshot.

On GitHub, words like Closes #412 or Fixes #412 link the PR to an issue. GitHub can close the issue when the PR is merged.

Useful phrases

  • This PR adds / removes / changes ...
  • The main change is in client.py. The rest is tests.
  • Reviewers: please focus on the retry logic.
  • Out of scope: retries for refunds. I will do that in a follow-up.
  • This is a draft. It is not ready for review yet.
  • Depends on #398. Please merge that one first.

Review your own diff before you ask others. Remove debug prints. Check the description again before you merge. The change may have grown during review.

Do not explain every line. The diff already shows what changed. Explain why, and point to the hard part. Also avoid giant PRs. A small PR gets a faster and better review.

Code review comments that are kind and clear

Read three comments on the same line of code.

Why would you use a list here? This is obviously slow.

Hmm, not sure about this.

suggestion: Could we use a set here? We check membership in a loop, so a set makes each check O(1). With 50k users, this matters.

The harsh comment attacks the author. The vague comment gives no reason and no action. The third comment gives a clear idea, a reason and the size of the problem.

Four rules for review comments

  1. Talk about the code, not the person. Say "this function", not "you".
  2. Explain why. Give the reason: speed, safety, readability, a team rule.
  3. Say how important it is. Must it change before merge, or is it a small idea?
  4. Say what is good, too. Real, specific praise teaches as much as criticism.

Label the importance

Google's review guide suggests short labels. Nit is a small point. Optional or Consider is a good idea, not required. FYI is information for the future. A format called Conventional Comments goes further.

Conventional Comments labels
LabelUse it forModel
praisesomething goodpraise: Great test names. They read like a spec.
nitpicka tiny point, about tastenitpick (non-blocking): Double space here.
suggestiona better way, with a reasonsuggestion: Could we extract this into a helper? It appears three times.
issuea real problemissue (blocking): This query has no LIMIT. It can load the whole table.
questionsomething you do not understandquestion: Is this lock needed? I only see one writer.
thoughtan idea for laterthought (non-blocking): We could cache this one day.
todo / chorea small required taskchore: Please add a changelog entry.

The words in brackets are decorations. (blocking) means "please fix before merge". (non-blocking) means "your choice". (if-minor) means "fix it only if it is a small change".

Words to avoid

  • just, simply: "Just use a set" suggests the author missed something easy.
  • obviously, clearly: if it was obvious, the author would have done it.
  • Why didn't you ...?: this sounds like blame. Ask "What do you think about ...?"

Softening is a skill from Hedging and stance. Use could, might and I think on opinions. But keep facts and real bugs clear.

Replying as the author

Reviewer: issue (blocking): This loop can run forever if the API returns an empty page.

Author: Good catch, thank you. Fixed in 4e1c9a2. I added a test for the empty page.

Reviewer: nitpick (non-blocking): I'd call this fetch_all, not get_pages.

Author: I'd like to keep get_pages. The other clients use the same name. Is that OK?

Reviewer: Makes sense. Approved.

Useful replies: "Done.", "Fixed in (commit).", "Good point, changed.", "I disagree, because ...", "Let's talk about this in a quick call." If a reviewer did not understand your code, make the code clearer. A code comment helps future readers more than a review reply.

Too much softening hides real bugs. "Maybe, possibly, we could perhaps think about the null case?" is unclear. A security hole or data loss needs a clear "issue (blocking)".

Bug reports

Login is broken!!! Please fix ASAP. It doesn't work on my phone.

Summary: Login fails with "Invalid token" after password reset

Environment: app 5.12.0 (build 8812), Android 15, Pixel 8
Frequency: always (5 out of 5 tries)

Steps to reproduce
1. Log in as test-user-07.
2. Reset the password from Settings > Security.
3. Log out.
4. Log in with the new password.

Expected result: the home screen opens.
Actual result: the error "Invalid token" appears. No login.

Notes: works on iOS 19 with the same account.
Log: see attached file login-8812.txt, from 14:05 UTC.

A developer can fix a bug faster if they can reproduce it. So the steps are the most important part. The Mozilla bug-writing guide says this too.

The parts of a bug report

  • Summary: about 10 words. Name the problem and when it happens. Do not name your guess at a fix.
  • Environment: version, build, system, device, browser.
  • Frequency: always, sometimes (how often?), or once.
  • Steps to reproduce: numbered, exact, one action per step.
  • Expected result and actual result: what should happen, and what really happens.
  • Evidence: logs, screenshots, the exact error text.

Grammar for bug reports

  • Steps use the imperative: "Open Settings. Tap Security."
  • Actual results use the present simple if it always happens: "The app crashes."
  • Use the past simple for one event: "The app crashed at 14:05."
  • Keep facts and guesses apart: "Possible cause: the old token is still cached." Label the guess.

"It doesn't work" gives no information. What did you do? What did you see? Also, one report should have one bug. Two bugs in one report get lost.

READMEs and design documents

A README is the front door of a project. A design document explains a plan before people build it. Both have standard shapes.

README

# queuectl

A command-line tool to inspect and clean message queues.

## Why
Our queues grow during incidents. queuectl shows the oldest
messages and removes dead ones safely.

## Quick start
    pip install queuectl
    queuectl list --broker localhost:5672

## Getting help
Ask in #queuectl or open an issue.

GitHub's docs say a README should explain what the project does and why it is useful. It should show how to start, where to get help and who maintains it. Put a working example near the top. Many readers copy it first.

Design document

Malte Ubl described design docs at Google in a well-known 2020 post. His usual sections are in the tree above. A big design doc is often 10 to 20 pages. A mini design doc of 1 to 3 pages fits a small change.

  • Context and scope: the situation today, in a few neutral sentences.
  • Goals and non-goals: what the design must do, and what it will not do.
  • The design: an overview first, then details. Focus on the trade-offs.
  • Alternatives considered: other designs and why you rejected them. Ubl calls this one of the most important sections.
  • Cross-cutting concerns: security, privacy and observability.

Language for design docs

Phrases for design documents
JobModel
State a goalUsers can export a report in under 5 seconds.
State a non-goalThis design does not cover mobile clients.
Explain a choiceWe chose Postgres over Redis because we need transactions.
Name a costThe downside is a second database to run.
Reject an optionWe rejected a cron job because it cannot retry single items.
Name a riskThe main risk is lock contention at peak load.
Ask for inputOpen question: who owns the new queue?

An architecture decision record (ADR) is shorter. Michael Nygard proposed it in a 2011 blog post, "Documenting Architecture Decisions". It has five parts: title, status, context, decision and consequences. He suggested one or two pages. Status can be proposed, accepted, deprecated or superseded.

If your design doc sets rules for other teams, you can use MUST, SHOULD and MAY in capital letters. Say near the top that they follow RFC 2119 and RFC 8174. See Reading technical English.

A design doc that shows only the chosen design is weak. Readers ask, "Why not X?" Answer it before they ask, in Alternatives considered.

Status updates

Hi all, this week was busy. We had a lot of meetings and worked on many tickets. There were some problems with the vendor but we are working on it. Hopefully things will be better next week.

Payments migration: weekly update (week 46)

Status: AT RISK. Launch may move from 1 Dec to 8 Dec.

Done
- Moved 70% of card traffic to the new provider.
- Fixed the refund rounding bug (#455).

Next
- Move the last 30% on Tuesday.
- Load test with 2x peak traffic on Thursday.

Risks and blockers
- The vendor has not sent the sandbox keys for refunds.
  Without them, we cannot test refunds.

Ask
- Priya: could you escalate the key request with the vendor?

A status update tells people where a project is. The "after" version starts with the status in one line. Then it gives done, next, risks and one clear request. A reader can stop after line 3 and still know the most important fact.

Many teams use a colour: green (on track), amber or yellow (at risk) and red (off track). This is called RAG status.

Tenses in a status update

Choosing the tense
PartTenseModel
Done, at a known timepast simpleWe moved 70% of traffic on Monday.
Done, result matters nowpresent perfectWe have fixed the rounding bug.
In progresspresent continuousWe are testing refunds.
Planwill / plan to / be going toWe plan to move the rest on Tuesday.
Riskmay / might / couldLaunch may move by one week.

Bad news

Give bad news early, with a plan. Say what happened, the effect, and what you will do. "We will miss 1 December. The new date is 8 December. We are adding a second tester to protect it." Soften the tone, not the facts. See Hedging and stance.

"Hopefully things will be better" is not a plan. Give a date, a number, an owner or an ask. A spoken version of the same update is in Meetings and stand-ups.

Direct but polite

Read three versions of a request.

Review my PR today.

Sorry to bother you, I know you are very busy, I was just wondering if maybe at some point you might possibly have a moment to look at something?

Could you review PR #482 by Thursday? It blocks the release. It is small, about 80 lines.

The first version is an order. It can sound rude. The second version is so soft that the request is lost. The third version is polite and clear. It has a request, a deadline and a reason.

The formula

A good work request has four parts: polite frame + clear action + deadline + reason. "Could you + verb + by + day? + Because or It ...". Linkers like because and so join the reason. See Linking words.

From too direct to direct and polite
Too directDirect and polite
Send me the logs.Could you send me the logs from 14:00 to 15:00?
This is wrong.I think this returns the wrong total when the cart is empty.
No, I can't do it.I can't take this on this week. I could start on Monday.
You forgot the tests.Could we add a test for the empty case?
Answer my question.Any update on the key request? We need it by Friday to test refunds.
Bad idea.I see the benefit. My concern is the extra database. Could we try a queue first?

Do not over-apologise

Many learners start every message with "Sorry". Use "sorry" for real mistakes only. For a normal question, start with the question. "Quick question about the deploy script: does it run migrations?" Use "Thanks for waiting" instead of "Sorry for the delay" when the delay was small.

The first draft

"Hi, sorry, so I was looking at the build and it seems maybe broken since yesterday, not sure why, can someone maybe check?"

Put the point first

"The main build has failed since yesterday at 16:20."

Add the evidence

"The error is 'disk full' on runner ci-04. Link: build 9921."

Make one clear ask

"Could someone from the platform team clean the disk on ci-04?"

Remove extra softeners

The final message: "The main build has failed since yesterday at 16:20. The error is 'disk full' on runner ci-04 (build 9921). Could someone from the platform team clean the disk?"

Teams differ. Some prefer very short, direct messages. Others expect more greeting and softening. Copy the style of good writers on your team. Remote and cross-culture writing is in Presentations and remote work.

Polite is not the same as vague. "Maybe someone could look at it sometime" sounds polite. But nobody will act. Name the person or team, the action and the time.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for writing at work
PatternPurposeModelNote
Verb (imperative) + object + detailCommit subject lineFix crash when the cart is emptyNot "Fixed" or "Fixing". No full stop.
type(scope): descriptionConventional Commits subjectfix(auth): refresh the token earlyAdd ! before the colon for a breaking change.
The current code + verb (present) ...Describe the problem in a commit bodyThe client fails the order on the first 503.Explain why, not only what.
This PR adds / removes / changes + nounOpen a PR descriptionThis PR adds retries to the payment client.Then give Why, How to test and Risks.
Out of scope: + nounSay what a PR or design will not doOut of scope: retries for refunds.Add "follow-up" with a ticket if you plan it.
label (decoration): subjectA clear review commentissue (blocking): This query has no LIMIT.Use blocking only for real problems.
Could we + verb ...? + reasonSuggest a change kindlyCould we use a set here? Lookups are O(1).Always give the reason.
Good catch. Fixed in + commitAnswer a review commentGood catch. Fixed in 4e1c9a2.Thank, act, and point to the fix.
Expected: ... / Actual: ...The core of a bug reportExpected: home screen. Actual: "Invalid token".Keep facts and guesses apart.
We chose X over Y because ...Explain a trade-off in a design docWe chose Postgres over Redis because we need transactions.Also name the cost of X.
This design does not + verbState a non-goalThis design does not cover mobile clients.Non-goals stop scope creep.
Status: colour. + main factOpen a status updateStatus: at risk. Launch may move to 8 Dec.Put the status in the first line.
Could you + verb + by + day? + reasonA direct and polite requestCould you review #482 by Thursday? It blocks the release.Name the action and the deadline.
I can't ... this week. I could ...Say no with an optionI can't take this on this week. I could start Monday.Offer another time or person.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

Which commit subject is best?

  • Fixed a bug in the cart.
  • Fixing stuff
  • Fix wrong total when a coupon is 100%

It is imperative, specific, short and has no full stop.

What should a commit body mainly explain?

  • Every line that changed.
  • Why the change was needed and why this solution.
  • How long the work took.

The diff shows what changed. The body explains why.

In Conventional Commits, which commit leads to a MAJOR version?

  • feat(search): add a date filter
  • fix(auth): handle expired tokens
  • feat(api)!: remove the v1 endpoints

The ! marks a breaking change. A breaking change means MAJOR.

Which review comment is kind and clear?

  • Why didn't you just use a set? This is obviously slow.
  • suggestion: Could we use a set here? We check membership in a loop.
  • Not sure about this.

It talks about the code, gives an action and gives a reason.

What is the most important part of a bug report?

  • The title in capital letters.
  • Exact steps to reproduce the bug.
  • Your guess about the cause.

A developer must reproduce a bug before they can fix it.

Which line belongs in the "Non-goals" section of a design doc?

  • Users can export a report in under 5 seconds.
  • This design does not cover mobile clients.
  • We chose Postgres because we need transactions.

A non-goal says what the project will not do.

Fill the gap

Git's docs suggest a subject line of ? characters or less.

If applied, this commit will ? the unused v1 search endpoint.

issue (?): This loop never ends if the page is empty. Please fix before merge.

Expected result: the home screen opens. ? result: the app crashes.

We chose a queue ? a cron job because it can retry single items.

Status: at ?. The launch may move by one week.

Think and write

  1. Rewrite this commit message: "Updated the code for users and fixed some things."
    Model answer

    Split it into two commits. For example: "Add email check to user sign-up" and "Fix crash when the user name is empty". Each subject is imperative and names one change.

  2. Make this review comment kind and clear: "You forgot error handling. Bad."
    Model answer

    issue (blocking): If the API returns 500, this call throws and the page goes blank. Could we catch the error and show a retry message?

  3. Write a bug summary of about 10 words for this: the app crashes when you upload a photo larger than 20 MB on Android.
    Model answer

    Android app crashes when uploading a photo over 20 MB.

  4. Write a direct but polite request. You need the security team to approve your design doc by Wednesday. The launch depends on it.
    Model answer

    Could the security team review the design doc for the export service by Wednesday? The launch depends on your approval. The main question is in section 4, on token storage.

  5. Write a three-line status update. The search feature is on track. You finished the API. Next week you will build the UI. No blockers.
    Model answer

    Status: on track. We have finished the search API. Next week we will build the UI. No blockers.

  6. Expert: write the "Alternatives considered" paragraph for a design that uses a message queue instead of a nightly cron job.
    Model answer

    We considered a nightly cron job. It is simpler and needs no new service. But it processes all items at once, and one failure stops the batch. It also adds up to 24 hours of delay. We chose a queue because it retries single items and processes them within seconds. The cost is one more service to run and monitor.

Key takeaways

  • Put the main point first. Then the reason. Then the next action.
  • Commit subject: imperative, about 50 characters, no full stop. The body explains why.
  • Conventional Commits: feat is MINOR, fix is PATCH, ! or BREAKING CHANGE is MAJOR.
  • A PR description gives why, what changed, how to test, risks and links.
  • Review comments talk about the code, give a reason and show how important they are.
  • A bug report needs exact steps, expected and actual results, and the environment.
  • A design doc needs goals, non-goals, trade-offs and alternatives considered.
  • A status update starts with the status. Bad news comes early, with a plan.
  • Polite and clear go together: polite frame, clear action, deadline, reason.

Sources

  • Git: Submitting patches. Imperative mood, short subject lines and explaining why in the body.
  • Conventional Commits 1.0.0. Types, scopes, ! and BREAKING CHANGE, and their link to SemVer.
  • Google Engineering Practices. Guides on CL descriptions and on kind, clear review comments with Nit, Optional and FYI labels.
  • Conventional Comments. Labels and decorations for review comments.
  • Mozilla: Bug writing guidelines. Summaries, steps to reproduce, expected and actual results.
  • Malte Ubl: Design Docs at Google. The usual sections of a design doc and typical lengths.

Meetings and stand-ups

Engineers talk in many meetings: stand-ups, planning, design reviews, one-to-ones and incident calls. Each meeting has its own set of phrases. With a few fixed phrases, you can speak clearly even when you feel nervous. This chapter gives you those phrases and shows them in model dialogues.

  • Give a short stand-up update about yesterday, today and blockers.
  • Ask for clarification and check that you understood.
  • Disagree politely and give and receive feedback.
  • Give estimates with the right amount of uncertainty.
  • Speak clearly on an incident call and write useful meeting notes.

The daily stand-up

Ana: Yesterday I finished the export endpoint. Today I'm going to write the tests. No blockers.

Ben: I'm still working on the login bug. I've found the cause, but the fix touches the token library. I'm blocked on a review from the security team.

Chen: Ben, I can ping them after this. Yesterday I paired with Ana on the export. Today I'll start the CSV format. One question for Ana, but we can talk after the stand-up.

A stand-up is a short daily meeting. Each person gives a quick update. People often stand, so the meeting stays short. Many teams use three parts: yesterday, today and blockers. A blocker is something that stops your work.

In Scrum, this meeting is the Daily Scrum. The 2020 Scrum Guide says it is a 15-minute event for the Developers. It happens at the same time and place every working day. Its goal is progress toward the Sprint Goal and a plan for the next day. Older versions of the guide gave three example questions. The 2020 guide lets the team choose the format.

Tenses for a stand-up

Stand-up language by part
PartTenseModels
Yesterdaypast simpleI finished the export endpoint. I fixed two flaky tests.
Result nowpresent perfectI've found the cause. I've opened a PR.
Still in progresspresent continuousI'm still working on the login bug.
Todaygoing to / will / plan toToday I'm going to write the tests. I'll start the CSV format.
Blockerspresent simple and continuousI'm blocked on a review. I'm waiting for the API keys.
Offer helpcan / couldI can help with that. I could pair with you after lunch.

Useful stand-up phrases

  • Quick update from me: ...
  • No change since yesterday. Still on the migration.
  • I'm about halfway through the parser.
  • I need a second pair of eyes on PR #482.
  • No blockers. / One blocker: I don't have access to staging.
  • Can we take this offline? (Let's discuss it after the meeting.)

"I'm blocked" means someone stops you. "I'm blocking" means you stop someone else. Most of the time you mean "I'm blocked on the review" or "I'm blocked by the missing keys".

Do not solve problems in the stand-up. Keep your update under one minute. If a topic needs discussion, say: "Let's talk after the stand-up. Ana and Chen, can you stay?"

Some teams do the stand-up in chat. Each person writes three short lines. The written shape is like a status update in Writing at work. Async teams are covered in Presentations and remote work.

Asking for clarification

Maya: We'll shard the hot partitions and backfill async before the cutover.

You: Sorry, could you say that more slowly? What do you mean by "backfill"?

Maya: Sure. Backfill means we copy the old data into the new tables.

You: Got it. So we copy the old data first, and then we switch traffic. Is that right?

Maya: Yes, exactly.

You asked for help in two steps. First you asked about one word. Then you checked your understanding in your own words. This is called paraphrasing. It is the best way to avoid mistakes.

Four kinds of clarification

Clarification phrases
You needSay
to hear it againSorry, could you say that again? / Could you repeat that, please?
slower speechCould you speak a bit more slowly, please?
a meaningWhat do you mean by "cutover"? / What does SLO stand for?
a choiceDo you mean the staging database or production?
an exampleCould you give me an example?
to see itCould you share your screen? / Could you put the link in the chat?
to checkJust to check: you want the fix today, right? / So, if I understand correctly, ...

Ask early. A question in the first minute is easy. A question after 20 minutes of nodding is hard. Most people are happy to explain a word. Many native speakers also ask what an acronym means.

"Can you repeat?" is incomplete. Repeat needs an object: "Can you repeat that?" Also avoid a bare "What?". It sounds rude. Say "Sorry?" or "Sorry, I missed that."

Do not say "yes" when you did not understand. You may agree to the wrong task. Paraphrase instead: "So I will update the docs by Friday. Is that right?"

Disagreeing politely

Leo: I think we should move the whole service to Kafka this sprint.

You: I see why you want that. Kafka would help with replays. My concern is time. We have two weeks, and nobody on the team has run Kafka before.

Leo: That's fair. But the current queue drops messages.

You: Agreed, that's a real problem. What if we fix the drops first, and plan Kafka for next quarter?

Leo: OK. Let's write that up and ask the team.

You disagreed, but the talk stayed friendly. You did four things in order.

  1. Acknowledge the other idea: "I see why you want that."
  2. State your concern: "My concern is time."
  3. Give evidence: "We have two weeks. Nobody has run Kafka before."
  4. Propose another way: "What if we fix the drops first?"

From soft to strong

Disagreement phrases by strength
StrengthPhrase
Partly agreeI agree with most of that, but ... / That's true for reads. For writes, I'm not sure.
SoftI'm not sure about that. / Have we considered ...? / What if we ...?
ClearI see it differently. / My concern is ... / I'd push back a little on that.
StrongI disagree, and here's why. / I don't think we should ship this today.

Choose the strength by the risk. A naming choice needs a soft phrase. A security hole or data loss needs a clear, strong phrase. Softening tools are in Hedging and stance.

Interrupting and holding the floor

  • Sorry to interrupt, but can I add something?
  • Can I come back to Leo's point?
  • Could I just finish my point?
  • Go ahead. / Sorry, after you.

Some teams use the phrase "disagree and commit". You say your view clearly. Then, when the team decides, you support the decision fully.

"I am not agree" is wrong. Agree is a verb: "I don't agree" or "I disagree". See Error clinic. Also, criticise the idea, not the person. Say "This plan has a risk", not "You are wrong".

Giving and getting feedback

You did great on the incident. / You're careless with reviews.

In Tuesday's incident call, you posted an update every 15 minutes. Support could answer customers without asking us. Thank you.

In the last two PRs, you approved without running the tests. One change broke the build for two hours. Can we talk about how to avoid that?

The specific feedback uses a model called SBI. It comes from the Center for Creative Leadership. It has three parts.

  1. Situation: when and where. "In Tuesday's incident call ..."
  2. Behaviour: what the person did, as a fact you could see. "... you posted an update every 15 minutes."
  3. Impact: the effect on you, the team or the users. "Support could answer customers."

The model has a newer fourth step: Intent. After the impact, you ask a question. "What were you trying to do?" Then you listen. Feedback becomes a two-way talk.

Receiving feedback

  • Thanks for telling me.
  • Can you give me an example?
  • What would you do differently?
  • That's useful. Let me think about it.
  • I didn't see it that way. Here is what I was trying to do.

Feedback in a retrospective

A retrospective, or retro, is a team meeting about how the work went. Common prompts are: What went well? What didn't go well? What will we change? Say actions, not blame. "Next sprint, we'll freeze the scope on day 3."

Do not give feedback about personality: "You are lazy" or "You are careless". Describe the behaviour and its impact. People can change behaviour. They cannot easily change who they are.

Estimates and uncertainty

Product manager: When will the CSV export be ready?

You: My rough estimate is three to five days. Best case Wednesday, worst case next Monday.

Product manager: Why such a wide range?

You: It depends on the billing API. If it supports paging, it's three days. I'll know tomorrow after a short spike. Then I can give you a firmer date.

You gave a range, a reason and a plan to reduce the doubt. A spike is a short investigation. It turns unknowns into facts.

Estimate, target, commitment

  • An estimate is a careful guess: "three to five days".
  • A target is what the business wants: "before the conference".
  • A commitment is a promise: "We will ship on 8 December."

Keep these three apart in your words. "I think three days" is not "I promise three days".

Why early estimates are wide

Steve McConnell describes the Cone of Uncertainty. At the very start, a skilled estimate can be 4 times too high or too low. The range gets smaller as the team makes decisions. The chart shows the high and low limits at each milestone.

McConnell makes two more points. The cone is the best case, for skilled estimators. And it gets narrower only when the team makes decisions. Time alone does not help. So "Give me a week to estimate better" only works if that week answers real questions.

Language for estimates

Phrases for estimates and uncertainty
JobPhrase
Give a rough numberRoughly two weeks. / About three days. / In the region of 20 hours.
Give a rangeThree to five days. / Best case Wednesday, worst case Monday.
Name the conditionAssuming the API supports paging, ... / It depends on the vendor.
Give your confidenceI'm fairly confident about Friday. / I'd say 70% for Friday, 95% for Tuesday.
Say it is earlyThis is a ballpark figure. I'll have a better number after the spike.
Update an estimateThe estimate has changed. It's now five days, because the API has no paging.

A ballpark figure is a very rough number. Many teams also estimate in story points or T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL). These compare tasks with each other, not with hours. In planning poker, everyone shows a number at the same time. Then the people with the highest and lowest numbers explain why.

Two bad answers: "It'll be done tomorrow" when you are not sure, and "I don't know" with no number. Give a range and a condition instead. "Two to four days, depending on the vendor."

Incident calls

An incident call is a live call during an outage. Many people join. Time matters. So the language is short, clear and fixed. Here is part of an invented call.

Sara: This is Sara. I'm the incident commander. Priya is the scribe. What's the customer impact right now?

Tom: Checkout errors are at 30%. Started at 14:05, right after the 14:02 deploy.

Sara: Thanks. Proposal: we roll back the 14:02 deploy now and debug later. Any objections? ... Hearing none, we roll back. Tom, please start the rollback and report back in 10 minutes.

Tom: Rolling back now. I'll report back in 10.

Sara: Kenji, can you post an update on the status page? Say we are investigating checkout errors. Next update in 15 minutes.

Kenji: On it.

Roles on an incident call

Big incidents need clear roles. PagerDuty's public incident response guide lists these.

  • The incident commander (IC) leads and decides. The IC does not fix things directly.
  • The deputy helps the IC, watches the time and can take over.
  • The scribe writes the timeline, actions and decisions.
  • A subject matter expert (SME) knows one system and fixes it.
  • The customer liaison and internal liaison talk to customers and to other teams.

On a small incident, one person can have several roles.

The CAN report

PagerDuty suggests a short status shape for experts called CAN.

  • Condition: "The database is at 95% CPU."
  • Actions: "We need to kill the long report query."
  • Needs: "I need approval from the IC to do it."

Phrases for incident calls

Open the call

"This is Sara. I'm the incident commander. Who's on the call?"

Find the impact

"What's the customer impact? Since when? Which regions?"

Assign work by name

"Tom, please check the deploy. Report back in 10 minutes." Never "Someone check it".

Decide out loud

"Proposal: roll back now. Any objections? Hearing none, we roll back."

Give regular updates

"Status: rollback done. Errors are back to 1%. Next update in 15 minutes."

Hand over clearly

"Leo, you're now the incident commander. Can you confirm?" "Confirmed. I'm IC."

Close the call

"The incident is mitigated. We'll monitor for an hour. The postmortem is on Thursday."

Two words are often confused. To mitigate means to stop the damage, for example with a rollback. To resolve means the real problem is fixed. Many incidents are mitigated in minutes and resolved days later.

Google's SRE book says: declare an incident early. Do it if you need a second team, if customers can see the problem, or if it is unsolved after about an hour of focused work. When command moves to a new person, say it clearly and wait for a "yes". After the incident, many teams write a blameless postmortem. See Hedging and stance for its language.

Do not give long theories on the call. Say what you see, what you are doing and what you need. Also, say numbers and times exactly: "fourteen oh five", "thirty percent".

Running a meeting and taking notes

Here are the notes from an invented design review.

Design review: CSV export
Date: 12 Nov 2026   Attendees: Ana, Ben, Chen, Maya (notes)

Agenda
1. Paging in the billing API
2. File size limits

Decisions
- We will stream the file, not build it in memory.
- Max export size: 1 million rows.

Action items
- Ana: ask the billing team about paging, by Fri 14 Nov.
- Ben: add a size check to the export endpoint, by Tue 18 Nov.

Open questions
- Do we need Excel format? (Maya to ask product)

Good meeting notes have three key parts. Decisions say what the group agreed. Action items say who does what, by when. Open questions say what is still unknown. Notes can be short and telegraphic. But every action item needs an owner and a date.

Phrases for leading a meeting

Phrases for the person who runs the meeting
MomentPhrase
StartLet's get started. The goal today is to decide on paging.
Keep on topicGood point. Let's park that and come back to it at the end.
Invite quiet peopleChen, you know this API well. What do you think?
Watch the timeWe have ten minutes left. Let's move to item 2.
Check agreementSo we agree to stream the file. Does anyone see a problem?
AssignWho can own this? ... Thanks, Ana. By Friday?
CloseTo sum up: two decisions and two actions. I'll send the notes today.

To park a topic means to stop it now and come back later. To take something offline means to discuss it later, with fewer people. These are fixed phrases in meetings. They are polite.

Send the notes the same day. Put decisions and action items at the top. An email version of meeting notes is in Emails and messages.

"We should look into the paging thing" is not an action item. Who? What exactly? By when? Write "Ana: ask the billing team about paging, by Friday."

Model dialogues

Read each dialogue aloud. Notice the fixed phrases. Then practise both roles.

Dialogue 1: a stand-up with a blocker

Lead: OK, let's start. Ana?

Ana: Yesterday I merged the retry PR. Today I'm going to start on refunds. One blocker: I still don't have the sandbox keys.

Lead: Who can help with the keys?

Ben: I can. I'll ask the vendor this morning and let you know by noon.

Ana: Great, thanks. Until then, I'll write the refund tests with mocks.

Lead: Thanks. Ben, you're next.

Dialogue 2: a design review with a disagreement

Maya: For the cache, I propose Redis with a one-hour expiry.

Chen: I like the idea. Just to check: is the price data allowed to be one hour old?

Maya: Good question. I assumed yes.

Chen: I'm not sure that's true. Finance updates prices at noon. A one-hour cache could show the old price.

Maya: Fair point. What if we clear the cache when finance saves a price?

Chen: That works for me. Can we add that to the design doc?

Maya: Yes. Action item for me, by Monday.

Dialogue 3: a one-to-one with feedback

Manager: I'd like to give you some feedback. Is now a good time?

You: Sure.

Manager: In yesterday's planning, you said "two days" for the export. Later it took six. Product had already told a customer.

You: I see. I didn't know the API had no paging.

Manager: That makes sense. What could help next time?

You: I could give a range, and say what it depends on. Maybe "two to six days, depending on paging".

Manager: That would help a lot. Thanks for being open about it.

Dialogue 4: asking for clarification in planning

Product manager: For this sprint, the MVP is SSO plus audit logs.

You: Sorry, could you explain what you mean by audit logs here? All actions, or only admin actions?

Product manager: Only admin actions, for now.

You: OK. So, if I understand correctly, we log admin actions only, and we keep them for how long?

Product manager: One year. Good that you asked.

You: Thanks. I'll add that to the ticket so we don't forget.

An MVP is the smallest useful version of a product. SSO means one login for many apps. Ask about words like these whenever they are unclear.

Job interviews test the same skills. You think aloud, ask for clarification and give estimates. See Job interviews in English. Spoken fluency is in Pronunciation and fluency. The sentence shapes behind these phrases are in The 15 sentence patterns.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for meetings and stand-ups
PatternPurposeModelNote
Yesterday I + past simpleSay what you finishedYesterday I finished the export endpoint.Use I've + past participle for a result now.
Today I'm going to + verbSay your plan for todayToday I'm going to write the tests.Keep it to one or two items.
I'm blocked on / by + nounName a blockerI'm blocked on a security review.Not "I'm blocking". That means you stop others.
What do you mean by + word?Ask about one wordWhat do you mean by "cutover"?Ask early, not after 20 minutes.
So, if I understand correctly, + clauseCheck your understandingSo, if I understand correctly, we copy the data first.End with "Is that right?"
I see + noun / why ... My concern is + nounDisagree politelyI see why you want Kafka. My concern is time.Then give evidence and a proposal.
What if we + verb ...?Propose another wayWhat if we fix the drops first?A question invites discussion.
In + situation, you + past simple. + impactGive specific feedback (SBI)In Tuesday's call, you posted updates every 15 minutes. Support could answer customers.Describe behaviour, not personality.
Number to number + unit, depending on + nounGive an estimate with doubtThree to five days, depending on the billing API.A range is more honest than one number.
I'd say + percent + for + dateState your confidenceI'd say 70% for Friday, 95% for Tuesday.An estimate is not a promise.
Name, please + verb. Report back in + time.Assign work on an incident callTom, please start the rollback. Report back in 10 minutes.Never "someone check it".
Proposal: + action. Any objections?Decide out loudProposal: we roll back now. Any objections?Then say "Hearing none, we ...".
Next update in + timePromise the next statusNext update in 15 minutes.Keep the promise, even with no news.
Name: verb + object, by + dateWrite an action itemAna: ask billing about paging, by Fri 14 Nov.Every action item needs an owner and a date.
Let's park that / take that offlineKeep the meeting on topicGood point. Let's park that until the end.Come back to it, or add an action item.

Practice

Start at the top. The tasks get harder.

Choose the best answer

You cannot work because you are waiting for API keys. What do you say?

  • I'm blocking the API keys.
  • I'm blocked on the API keys.
  • I block for the API keys.

"I'm blocked" means something stops you. "I'm blocking" means you stop others.

How long is the Daily Scrum in the 2020 Scrum Guide?

  • 5 minutes
  • 15 minutes
  • 30 minutes

The guide calls it a 15-minute event for the Developers.

You did not hear the last sentence. What is the best phrase?

  • What?
  • Can you repeat?
  • Sorry, could you say that again?

"What?" sounds rude. "Repeat" needs an object: "repeat that".

Which is the most polite disagreement that is still clear?

  • You are wrong about Kafka.
  • I see why you want Kafka. My concern is that nobody has run it before.
  • Maybe, I don't know, possibly Kafka is perhaps not so good.

It acknowledges the idea, then gives one clear concern with a reason.

Which feedback follows the SBI model?

  • You are a great communicator.
  • In the incident call, you posted updates every 15 minutes, so support could answer customers.
  • Please communicate better in future.

It has a situation, a behaviour you can see and an impact.

Which estimate is best early in a task?

  • It will be done tomorrow, for sure.
  • I don't know.
  • Three to five days, depending on the billing API. I'll know more tomorrow.

A range, a condition and a plan to learn more.

On an incident call, what does the incident commander mainly do?

  • Fixes the database personally.
  • Leads, assigns work and makes decisions.
  • Writes the timeline.

The IC leads and decides. The scribe writes the timeline. Experts fix systems.

Which is a good action item?

  • We should look into paging.
  • Paging: to do.
  • Ana: ask the billing team about paging, by Fri 14 Nov.

It has an owner, a clear action and a date.

Fill the gap

Yesterday I (fix) two flaky tests.

I'm still (work) on the login bug.

What do you ? by "backfill"?

So, if I ? correctly, we switch traffic on Monday.

Three to five days, (depend) on the vendor.

Proposal: we roll back now. Any ??

The rollback stopped the errors. The incident is ?, but the cause is not fixed yet.

Think and speak

  1. Give a stand-up update. Yesterday you reviewed two PRs. Today you will fix the cache bug. You need access to the production logs.
    Model answer

    Yesterday I reviewed two PRs. Today I'm going to fix the cache bug. One blocker: I don't have access to the production logs. Can someone help me with that after the stand-up?

  2. Your colleague says "We'll do a blue-green deploy with a canary." You do not know "canary". Ask and then check your understanding.
    Model answer

    Sorry, what do you mean by "canary" here? ... OK, so we send a small part of the traffic to the new version first, and watch the errors. Is that right?

  3. Disagree politely. Your lead wants to skip tests to ship on Friday. You think this is risky.
    Model answer

    I understand why Friday matters. My concern is the payment code. It has no tests, and a bug there costs real money. What if we ship the UI on Friday and the payment part on Tuesday, with tests?

  4. Give SBI feedback to a teammate. In Monday's code review, they wrote very clear comments with reasons. You learned a lot.
    Model answer

    In Monday's code review, you explained the reason for every comment. I learned a lot about the cache, and I fixed things faster. Thank you.

  5. You are the incident commander. Errors started 5 minutes ago, after a deploy. Open the call and assign two tasks.
    Model answer

    This is Sam. I'm the incident commander. Who's on the call? ... What's the customer impact? ... Proposal: we roll back the last deploy. Any objections? Hearing none. Lena, please start the rollback and report back in 10 minutes. Raj, please update the status page. Next update in 15 minutes.

  6. Expert: a director asks, "Can you commit to 1 March for the new search?" The project has just started. Answer politely and explain the risk.
    Model answer

    I'd rather not commit to a date yet. We're at the very start, so any estimate could be far off, by two times or more. Give us two weeks to agree the scope and build a small prototype. Then I can give you a date with about 80% confidence, and a clear list of what it depends on.

Key takeaways

  • A stand-up update is short: done, next, blockers. Discuss details after the meeting.
  • "I'm blocked on X" means X stops you. Offer help with "I can ..." or "I could ...".
  • Ask for clarification early, then paraphrase: "So, if I understand correctly, ..."
  • Disagree in four steps: acknowledge, concern, evidence, proposal.
  • Use SBI for feedback: situation, behaviour, impact. Then ask about intent.
  • Give estimates as ranges with conditions. An estimate is not a commitment.
  • On incident calls, use roles, names, times and fixed phrases. Decide out loud.
  • Meeting notes need decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions.

Sources

  • The 2020 Scrum Guide. The Daily Scrum: 15 minutes, same time and place, the team chooses the format.
  • PagerDuty Incident Response Guide: Different roles. Incident commander, deputy, scribe, experts, liaisons and the CAN report.
  • Google SRE book: Managing incidents. Roles, clear handoff and when to declare an incident.
  • Steve McConnell: Software Development's Cone of Uncertainty (Construx white paper). The ranges of early estimates and how the cone narrows.
  • Center for Creative Leadership: Situation-Behavior-Impact-Intent. The SBI feedback model and the intent step.

Job interviews in English

A tech interview tests two things at once. It tests your skills, and it tests how clearly you explain them. This chapter gives you the shapes, phrases and ten model answers for every part of a software or AI interview, from "Tell me about yourself" to the salary talk.

  • Introduce yourself in about one minute with a clear present, past and future.
  • Tell work stories with the STAR method and talk about trade-offs.
  • Use clear language in system design and coding interviews, and think aloud.
  • Ask good questions at the end of an interview.
  • Talk about salary with polite phrases and a simple strategy.

The shape of a tech interview

Ana applies for an AI engineer job. In two weeks she has five conversations. Each one has a different goal. If she knows the goal, she can prepare the right English for it.

Recruiter call

About 30 minutes. Your background, why you want the job, dates and sometimes salary. Clear and friendly English matters most here.

Hiring manager

Your future boss. Projects, ways of working and motivation. Expect "Walk me through a project."

Coding round

You solve a problem in a shared editor. You think aloud while you work.

System design round

You design a bigger system on a whiteboard. You ask questions, draw boxes and explain trade-offs.

Behavioural round

"Tell me about a time when..." You answer with short true stories.

Offer

The company makes an offer. You ask questions, maybe negotiate, and then accept or decline.

Many companies use some of these rounds. The names and the order vary. Junior jobs often skip system design. AI jobs may add a round about models, data or evaluation.

A behavioural question asks about your past actions. The idea is simple. Past actions help to predict future actions. A technical question tests what you can do now.

The main tenses in an interview
TenseUse it forExample
Present simpleYour job nowI build data pipelines for a search team.
Present perfectExperience up to nowI have worked with Rust since 2022.
Past simpleStories and finished jobsI found the bug and fixed it the same day.
WouldOptions in a designI would add a cache here.
Will ('ll)Decisions while you codeI'll use a set for the lookups.

"I am working here since 2021" is wrong. Use the present perfect with "since" and "for": "I have worked here since 2021." See The perfect tenses.

Your self-introduction

Almost every interview starts with one question: "Tell me about yourself." Here is a strong answer.

"I'm a backend and AI engineer with five years of experience. Right now I work on a search team at a software company. I build the retrieval part of an AI assistant for support agents. Before that, I spent three years on payment systems. There I learned to care about reliability and clear logs. Last year I led a small project, and we cut the assistant's answer time in half. Now I want to work closer to model evaluation. That's why this role interests me. Your team builds evaluation tools, and that is exactly where I want to grow."

The answer has three parts. Use them in this order.

  1. Present. Who you are now and what you do. Present simple.
  2. Past. One or two earlier jobs and one result. Past simple.
  3. Future. What you want next, and why this job fits. Link it to the company.

Keep it to about one minute. That is around 120 to 150 words. The interviewer will ask for more if they want it. Practise it aloud until it sounds natural, not memorised. The chapter Speaking skills shows how to record and check yourself. Short, simple sentences work best when you are nervous. The basic shapes are in The 15 sentence patterns.

My name is Bat. I was born in 1995. I finished school in 2013. Then I studied at university. My hobbies are football and reading.

I'm a backend engineer with six years of experience. Right now I build APIs for a logistics app. I'm looking for a role with more AI work.

Do not tell your whole life story. Start with your job now, not with your birth or your school. Also say "five years of experience", not "five years experience".

The STAR story method

The interviewer says: "Tell me about a time you solved a hard technical problem." Read this answer. Notice its four parts.

Situation. "Last spring, our document search API became slow every Monday morning. Response times went from 300 milliseconds to over three seconds."

Task. "I was on call that week. My job was to find the cause before the next Monday."

Action. "First, I compared the slow periods with our metrics. The database looked fine, but the cache hit rate dropped to almost zero. Then I checked the cache settings. All entries expired at the same time on Sunday night. So on Monday every request went to the database. I added a small random delay to each expiry time. I also wrote a job that fills the cache before office hours. Finally, I added an alert on the cache hit rate."

Result. "The next Monday, response times stayed under 400 milliseconds. The problem has not come back. Two other teams later used the same fix."

STAR is a shape for behavioural answers. Many university career centres teach it.

  • Situation: the background. Where, when, what was wrong.
  • Task: your goal or your responsibility.
  • Action: what you did, step by step. This is the main part.
  • Result: what happened, with numbers if possible, and what you learned.

The cache hit rate in the story is a good example of a detail. One clear technical detail makes a story believable. Say numbers slowly and stress them. "Three hundred" and "three thousand" must not sound alike. See Pronunciation and fluency.

"I", not "we"

The interviewer wants to hire you, not your team. So say "I" for your own actions. Say "we" only for the team's results. "We launched on time" is fine. "We found the bug" hides your part.

Failure questions

"Tell me about a mistake you made" is also a STAR question. The result here is mainly what you learned and changed.

"In my last job, I trained a model that sorts support tickets by topic. My test accuracy was 94 percent, and I told my manager. But in production, the accuracy was much lower. I looked again and found my mistake. Many tickets were near copies of each other. Some copies were in the training data, and others were in the test data. So the model had already seen the test questions. I told my manager the same day. Then I removed the near copies and split the data by customer. The honest accuracy was 86 percent. Later I raised it to 90 percent with better features. Since then, I always check for data leakage before I report a number."

Data leakage makes a model look better than it is. The story works because it is honest and has a clear lesson.

Do not choose a fake failure, like "I work too hard." Interviewers hear it every day. Choose a real, small mistake. Spend most of the time on how you fixed it.

Build a story bank. Write three to five true stories in STAR notes. Good topics: a hard bug, a mistake, a disagreement, a tight deadline and learning something fast. One story can answer several questions.

Projects and trade-offs

A hiring manager often says: "Walk me through a project you are proud of." Walk me through means: explain it step by step.

"Sure. The project was an assistant that answers questions about our engineering docs. New engineers asked the same questions every week, and senior people lost hours. I was the tech lead, with two other engineers. We used retrieval-augmented generation. In simple words, the system first finds the right parts of the docs. Then a language model writes an answer from those parts, with links. My main part was the retrieval. I tested three ways to split the documents into chunks. Splitting by heading worked best. It raised our 'right source found' score from 71 to 84 percent on our test set. If I did it again, I would build the test set first, not after the first version."

This answer has a problem, a role, a method, one number and one lesson. Retrieval-augmented generation is explained in one simple sentence. Always explain a technical term in plain words. The interviewer may not be an expert in your area.

Next, many interviewers ask about a trade-off.

"In the same project, we had to choose a model for the answers. A large hosted model gave slightly better answers. But it was slower and cost much more per question. A smaller model ran on our own servers. It was about three points worse on our quality score. But it answered in under two seconds. Our users cared most about speed, because they asked questions while coding. So we chose the smaller model. We also kept a fallback. For long, hard questions, the system can still call the large model. The downside is more work. We now monitor two models. I would look at this choice again if the large model became cheaper."

Common trade-offs in software and AI
Trade-offWhat you gain and lose
Latency vs throughputFast single answers, or more answers per second in total
Consistency vs availabilityAlways correct data, or a system that always answers
Quality vs costA bigger model, or a cheaper and faster one
Build vs buyFull control, or a faster start with a ready tool
Speed vs tech debtShip now, or clean code that is easier to change later

Latency is the time for one request. Throughput is how many requests the system handles per second.

Do not only list tools: "We used Python, Kafka and Postgres." Every tool needs a reason. Say "We chose Postgres because we needed transactions."

Senior answers name the cost of a choice, not only the benefit. They say what would change their mind. They also talk about people: who they convinced, and how. Careful words like "I think" and "in our case" help here. See Hedging and stance.

System design language

The interviewer says: "Design a service that summarises long support threads with an AI model." A strong candidate does not draw boxes at once. First, they ask questions.

Candidate: Before I start, can I ask a few questions? Who uses the summaries?

Interviewer: Support agents, inside their ticket tool.

Candidate: How many threads per day? And how fast must a summary appear?

Interviewer: About one million threads a day. Agents should see a summary within five seconds.

Candidate: Thanks. Let me do a quick estimate. One million a day is about twelve per second on average. If the peak is five times higher, that's about sixty per second. Each summary needs one model call. So the model servers are the main cost and the likely bottleneck. I'll draw the high-level design first. Then I'll go deeper into the model part.

A bottleneck is the part that limits the whole system. The quick sum is a back-of-the-envelope estimate. A day has 86,400 seconds. So one million divided by 86,400 is about 11.6, or "about twelve".

The open guide The System Design Primer suggests four steps. Each step has its own phrases.

Four steps and their phrases
StepUseful phrases
1. Requirements and limitsWho are the users? How many requests per second? What matters more here: speed or correctness? Let me assume that...
2. High-level designThe main parts are... Requests go from the client to... This component is responsible for...
3. Core componentsLet me go deeper into... The API looks like this... We store the data in..., because...
4. ScaleThe bottleneck is probably... To handle the peak, I would... One single point of failure is...

When you describe a design, follow the request. Use the present simple and "then". "The API checks the cache. If it finds a summary, it returns it. If not, it puts a job on the queue." Use would for options and will for decisions. "I would consider a second region" is an option. "I'll use a queue" is a decision.

Do not say a tool name without a reason: "I will use Kafka." Say the need first: "We need to absorb peaks, so I'd put a queue here. Kafka or a managed queue would both work."

Coding interviews: thinking aloud

In a coding round, long silence does not help you. The interviewer cannot see your thoughts. Here is a candidate who thinks aloud.

Interviewer: Given a list of request IDs, return the first ID that appears twice.

Candidate: Let me repeat it to check. I return the ID whose second copy comes first. Is that right?

Interviewer: Yes.

Candidate: And if no ID repeats?

Interviewer: Return None.

Candidate: Okay. Let me try an example: A, B, C, B, A. The answer is B, because B repeats before A. A simple way is to compare every pair. That's O of n squared. I think we can do better. I'll keep a set of the IDs I've seen. Set lookups are constant time on average. So the whole thing is O of n time and O of n space. Does that sound okay before I code it?

def first_duplicate(ids):
    seen = set()                 # IDs we have already met
    for request_id in ids:
        if request_id in seen:   # met before: this is the first repeat
            return request_id
        seen.add(request_id)
    return None                  # no ID appears twice

print(first_duplicate(["A", "B", "C", "B", "A"]))
print(first_duplicate(["A", "B"]))
print(first_duplicate([]))
B
None
None

The candidate followed a clear order. You can use it for almost any problem.

  1. Repeat and clarify. "Can the list be empty? Are the IDs strings?"
  2. Try an example. "Let me walk through a small example."
  3. Give the simple solution. "The brute-force way is... It's O of n squared."
  4. Improve it. "We can do better with a hash map."
  5. Code and explain decisions. "I'll return early when I find a repeat."
  6. Test. "Let me run my example through the code. Now an edge case: an empty list."
  7. State the complexity. "Time is O of n. Space is also O of n."

Time complexity is how the running time grows with the input. You need to say it aloud correctly.

How to say complexity aloud
WrittenSaid
O(1)O of one, or constant time
O(log n)O of log n, or logarithmic time
O(n)O of n, or linear time
O(n log n)O of n log n
O(n²)O of n squared, or quadratic time

When you are stuck

  • "Let me think about this for a moment." Then think quietly for a short time.
  • "I'm not sure yet. One idea is... but it fails when..."
  • "Let me draw it out." Drawing often helps with trees and graphs.
  • "Could you give me a small hint?" Asking is better than ten minutes of silence.

Do not read your code letter by letter: "s, e, e, n, equals, set". Explain decisions instead: "I'll use a set, because lookups are fast." And never just say "I don't know" and stop.

Some companies allow AI coding tools in interviews. Others do not. If you are not sure, ask before you start: "Am I allowed to use an AI assistant in this round?"

Questions to ask them

At the end, the interviewer asks: "Do you have any questions for us?" The answer is always yes. Your questions show interest and help you decide.

About the role

What does a normal week look like in this role? What would success look like after six months? What is the hardest part of this job?

About the team and the code

How does the team review code? How often do you deploy? How does on-call work here?

About AI and tools

How do you evaluate model changes before release? Which AI tools does the team use day to day? Who owns the evaluation data?

About growth

How do engineers grow here? Is there a budget for courses or conferences? How do people move between teams?

About next steps

What are the next steps in the process? When can I expect to hear from you? Is there anything about my background you would like me to explain?

Ask each person about their own area. Ask an engineer about code. Ask a manager about goals and growth. Ask the recruiter about the process and dates.

Do not ask things that are on the company website. Also, do not start with holidays or pay in a technical round. Save money questions for the recruiter.

Salary talk

Salary talk feels hard in a second language. But it follows a clear pattern. You need a plan, a few fixed phrases and a calm voice. This book gives no salary numbers. Pay changes fast and differs by country, level and company. Research it yourself before every process.

The strategy

  1. Research first. Use recent data for the job, the level and the location.
  2. Know three numbers. Your ideal number, your target, and your walk-away point. The walk-away point is the lowest offer you would accept. Never say this one.
  3. Let them share first. Ask for the range of the role.
  4. Answer with a range or a position. Base it on research and on the value you bring, not on your personal costs.
  5. Think about the whole package. Base salary, bonus, equity, holidays, remote work and learning budget.
  6. Take time and get it in writing. Never accept a big offer in the first minute.

The EU directive on pay transparency (2023/970) gives job applicants new rights. The employer must share the starting pay or its range, in the job advert or before the interview. The employer also must not ask about your pay history. EU countries had to make this national law by 7 June 2026. Some countries were late. Check the rules in your country. Some places outside the EU have similar rules.

Recruiter: What are your salary expectations?

Candidate: Thanks for asking. First, I'd like to understand the level and the on-call work. Could you share the range for this position?

Recruiter: Sure. The range is [the range].

Candidate: Thank you. That works as a starting point. With my experience of AI systems in production, I'd expect to be in the upper part of that range. Of course, I'll look at the whole package too.

Sometimes a recruiter asks: "What do you earn now?" You can move the talk to the new job, politely.

"I'd prefer to focus on this role. Based on my research for this level, I'm looking for a total package around [your target]."

"Thank you so much for the offer. I'm really excited about the team and the work. Before I decide, I'd like to talk about the base salary. Based on my research for this level and location, and the scope we discussed, I was hoping for something closer to [your target]. Is there any flexibility there? If the base salary is fixed, could we look at the signing bonus or the equity instead? Also, could I have until Friday to decide? And could you send the full offer in writing?"

Notice the soft forms: "I was hoping for", "Is there any flexibility", "could we look at". The past tense in "I was hoping" makes a request softer. These forms are polite but still clear. See Hedging and stance.

Do not give one exact number too early. Do not apologise for asking: "Sorry, I know this is a lot." Never invent another offer, and avoid ultimatums like "Pay me X or I leave."

One more story completes the ten model answers. It is a behavioural question about a disagreement.

"Last year, a teammate wanted to rewrite our ranking service in a new language. I disagreed, because we had a launch in six weeks. I didn't argue in the chat. I asked for a short call. First, I listened to his reasons. The main one was memory use, which was a real problem. Then I suggested a small test. We rewrote only the slowest part and measured it for a week. It used 40 percent less memory. So we agreed on a plan. We kept the old service for the launch and moved the rest step by step after it. The launch was on time. I learned that a small experiment ends a debate faster than opinions."

Disagreement phrases for meetings are in Meetings and stand-ups.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for job interviews
PatternPurposeModelNote
I'm a [role] with [number] years of experience.Start a self-introductionI'm an AI engineer with four years of experience.Say "years of experience", not "years experience".
Right now I + present simpleDescribe your job nowRight now I build search APIs for a retail app.Not "Now I am building" for a long-term job.
I have + past participle + since/forExperience up to nowI have worked with Python for six years.Not "I am working with Python since".
My job was to + verbGive the Task in STARMy job was to find the cause before Monday.Keep the task to one sentence.
First, I... Then I... Finally, I...Give the Action in STARFirst, I checked the metrics. Then I found the cache issue.Say "I" for your own actions.
As a result, + numberGive the Result in STARAs a result, response times stayed under 400 ms.Add a number when you can.
We chose X over Y because...Explain a trade-offWe chose the smaller model over the large one because speed mattered more.Always name the cost too.
If I did it again, I would...Show what you learnedIf I did it again, I would build the test set first.Past simple after "if", "would" in the main part.
Before I start, can I ask...?Clarify requirementsBefore I start, can I ask how many users we expect?Ask before you draw or code.
Let me assume that...State an assumptionLet me assume that reads are ten times more common than writes.Say it aloud so the interviewer can correct you.
That's O of + complexitySay complexity aloudThat's O of n log n because of the sort.Say "O of n squared", not "O n two".
Let me think about this for a moment.Buy thinking timeGood question. Let me think about this for a moment.Then really pause. Do not fill it with "umm".
Could you share the range for this position?Ask about pay firstBefore I give a number, could you share the range for this position?Polite and normal. It is not rude.
Is there any flexibility on...?Negotiate softlyIs there any flexibility on the base salary?Give a reason after it.

Practice

Quick quiz

Which sentence is correct for a self-introduction?

  • I am working here since 2022.
  • I have worked here since 2022.
  • I work here since 2022.

Use the present perfect with "since" for a situation that started in the past and continues now.

In a STAR answer, which part should be the longest?

  • Situation
  • Task
  • Action
  • Result

The Action shows what you did. MIT's guide suggests about 60 percent of the answer.

The interviewer gives you a system design task. What do you say first?

  • I will use Kafka and Redis.
  • Before I start, can I ask a few questions about the users and the load?
  • This is easy. Let me draw it.

Clarify requirements first. Tools come later, with reasons.

How do you say O(n²) aloud?

  • O n two
  • O of n squared
  • O of two n

The small 2 means "squared". You can also say "quadratic time".

Fill the gaps

I'm a data engineer with three years ? experience.

If I did it again, I ? write the tests first.

We chose Postgres ? MongoDB because we needed transactions.

Is there any ? on the base salary?

Think and write

  1. Change this sentence so it shows your own part: "We found the memory leak and fixed it."
    Answer

    "I found the memory leak with a heap profiler. Then I fixed it and added a test." (Use "I" for your actions. Many good answers are possible.)

  2. Write a one-sentence Result with a number for this story: you added an index to a slow database query.
    Answer

    "As a result, the query time dropped from two seconds to 50 milliseconds, and the page loaded much faster." (Use your own real numbers in an interview.)

  3. A recruiter asks: "What is your current salary?" Write a polite answer that moves the talk to the new job.
    Answer

    "I'd prefer to focus on this role. Could you share the range for the position? Based on my research, I'm looking for a total package around [my target]." In the EU, employers must not ask about pay history once the 2023/970 directive is national law in your country.

  4. Write three clarifying questions for this task: "Design a chat app for a company."
    Answer

    Possible questions: How many users, and how many messages per day? Do we need group chats and file sharing? How long do we keep messages? Must messages arrive in order? Do we need search?

  5. Expert. Your story says: "We used a vector database." The interviewer asks "Why?" Give an answer with a reason and a cost.
    Answer

    "We needed to search by meaning, not by exact words, across about two million chunks. A vector database did this fast. The cost was one more system to run and back up. For a smaller data set, I would just use a vector extension in our main database." (A senior answer names the need, the cost and when you would choose differently.)

  6. Expert. Write a 120-word self-introduction for your own next job. Use present, past and future.
    Answer

    Check it with this list. Present: your role and main work now. Past: one earlier job and one result with a number. Future: what you want next and why this company. Short sentences. About one minute when you say it aloud. Record yourself and listen once.

You need a moment to think in a coding round.

"Let me think about this for a moment."

You want to check the problem before you code.

"Let me repeat it to check I understand."

You want to say what you learned from a project.

"If I did it again, I would..."

The recruiter asks for your salary expectations too early.

"Could you share the range for this position?"

You want a better offer, politely.

"Is there any flexibility on the base salary?"

The interviewer asks if you have questions.

"Yes. What would success look like in this role after six months?"

Key takeaways

  • Each round has a goal. Prepare the right English for each one.
  • A self-introduction goes present, past, future, in about one minute.
  • STAR stories spend most of the time on the Action. Say "I" for your own actions.
  • Every technology choice needs a reason and a cost.
  • In system design, ask questions, estimate, then draw. Use "would" for options.
  • In coding rounds, think aloud: clarify, example, simple solution, improve, test, complexity.
  • Always have questions for the interviewer.
  • For salary: research, ask for the range, answer with a range or position, take time, get it in writing.

Sources

  • MIT Career Advising and Professional Development: The STAR method for behavioral interviews. The four parts, the rough time shares and the advice to say "I".
  • Tech Interview Handbook: Coding interview techniques. Clarifying questions, brute force first, then optimise, complexity and testing.
  • The System Design Primer. An open guide with four steps for system design interviews and the main trade-offs.
  • European Commission: Frequently asked questions on the Pay Transparency Directive (2023/970). Pay range before the interview, no pay history questions, transposition by 7 June 2026.
  • UCLA Career Center: Negotiating a compensation package. Research, your key numbers, total compensation and a calm approach.

Presentations and remote work

Engineers present all the time: demos, tech talks, sprint reviews and design reviews. In remote teams, much of the rest of the work happens in writing, across time zones. This chapter gives you the structure, the phrases and a full model talk for both worlds.

  • Plan a talk with a clear opening, body and close.
  • Guide your listeners with signposts, and describe slides and charts.
  • Run a live demo and handle questions calmly.
  • Write clear chat messages and async updates.
  • Plan meetings across time zones and work politely across cultures.

The structure of a talk

Two engineers start a ten-minute demo. Listen to their first sentences.

"Okay, umm, can you see my screen? Sorry for my English. So... this is the dashboard. Here are some numbers..."

"Good morning, everyone. I'm Lin from the search team. Today I'll show you how we made our docs assistant twice as fast. I'll cover three things: the problem, the fix and the lessons. Please keep questions for the end."

The strong start tells the audience four things. Who is speaking. What the talk is about. What comes in what order. And when to ask questions. Now they can relax and follow.

Most good talks have three parts. The opening says what you will say. The body says it. The close says what you said. It sounds like a lot of repetition. But listeners cannot scroll back. Repetition helps them follow.

Know your audience

Who will listen? Engineers, managers or customers? What do they already know?

Write one message

Write the main idea in one sentence. "Our assistant is now twice as fast."

Choose three points

Three to four main points are enough. Give each point an example or a number.

Write the opening

A hook, who you are, the purpose, the outline and when to ask questions.

Write the close

A short summary and one action for the audience. Then thank them and invite questions.

Rehearse aloud

Say it aloud two or three times, with a timer. Cut what is too long.

A hook catches attention. It can be a number, a question or a short story. "Last March, our assistant needed four seconds to answer. Today it needs two."

Do not start with "Sorry for my English." It makes people listen for mistakes. Start with your purpose instead. Your English is good enough if your structure is clear.

Signpost language

Read this part of a talk. The bold words are road signs for the listener.

"So that's the problem. Now let's look at the fix. We made three changes. The first one was a smaller prompt. For example, we sent ten chunks before. Now we send four. The second change was..."

A signpost tells the audience where the talk goes next. Use more signposts in a talk than in writing. Listeners have no headings and no page numbers. The chapter Listening skills shows signposts from the listener's side. Linking words has the basic list.

Signposts for presentations
JobPhrases
Give the outlineI'll cover three things. First... Then... Finally...
Start a pointLet's start with... My first point is...
Finish a pointSo that's the first part. That's all on the problem.
Move onNow let's look at... That brings me to... Moving on to...
Give an exampleFor example... Let me give you an example.
Stress a pointThe key point is... What really matters here is...
Go backAs I said earlier... Remember the chart from the start?
Leave the plan for a momentA quick side note... Back to the main point.
CloseTo sum up... So, the three things to remember are...
Invite questionsThank you. I'm happy to take questions.

The strongest move is a bridge. It closes one part and opens the next in two sentences. "So that's where the time went. Now let's see how we fixed it."

Do not use "So..." or "Next slide" for every change. The audience stops hearing them. Use a bridge at the big changes, and simple words like "also" inside a part.

Stress the signpost and pause after it. "That brings me to... [pause] the lessons." The pause tells the audience that a new part starts. The chapter Pronunciation and fluency explains sentence stress.

Slides and charts

Look at two titles for the same slide.

Topic title

Results

Sentence title

A smaller prompt halved the model time

The second title gives the message. The audience understands the slide in two seconds. Professor Michael Alley at Penn State calls this the assertion-evidence approach. The title is a full sentence. The body is a picture, a chart or a diagram that proves it. His group's studies found that audiences understood and remembered more with these slides.

Describing a chart

Here is a chart from a team update. Read the description under it.

"This chart shows our p95 latency over eight weeks. For the first three weeks, it stayed at about 800 milliseconds. In week 4, we turned on the cache. Latency fell sharply. Then it went down slowly and levelled off at about 320. That's a drop of about 60 percent."

The p95 latency is a common number in engineering talks. Say it as "p ninety-five". The description follows a clear order: what the chart shows, then the trend, then the key change, then one number.

Words for change
UpDownNo changeHow much or how fast
rise, go up, increase, grow, peakfall, go down, drop, decreasestay flat, stay at, level offsharply, slightly, steadily, slowly

Prepositions matter with numbers. "It fell by 500 ms" gives the size of the change. "It fell to 320 ms" gives the new value. "It fell from 820 to 320" gives both.

Do not read your slides aloud word by word. The audience reads faster than you speak. Say the message, then explain the picture. Also, do not say "As you can see" when the chart is small or busy. Point to the exact part: "Look at week 4."

Demo phrases

A live demo is the most exciting part of a tech talk. It is also the part that breaks most often. Good speakers prepare words for every stage.

Phrases for a live demo
StagePhrases
StartI'll share my screen now. Can everyone see the browser window? Let me make the text bigger.
Set the sceneImagine you're a new engineer. You need to rotate an API key.
Do and explainI'm typing a question here. Now I'll click "Ask". Watch the bottom left corner.
Point outNotice that every sentence has a source link. This part is new.
Fill a waitThis takes a few seconds. While it loads, let me explain what happens behind it.
Something breaksThat's not what I expected. Let me try once more. If it fails, I have a short recording.
FinishSo that's the main flow. Let me switch back to the slides.

The key rule: say what you do, and say why it matters. Silent typing feels long to an audience. Ten seconds of silence feels like a minute.

Before the demo

  1. Turn off notifications and close private tabs and chats.
  2. Make the font and the browser zoom large.
  3. Prepare test data. Never show real customer data.
  4. Record a backup video of the demo.
  5. Rehearse the demo with the same network and the same laptop.
