A language model can give a different answer to the same question. Its output is non-deterministic. Say this before the demo: "The model may phrase the answer a bit differently each time." Then a strange answer does not surprise anyone.

Do not apologise again and again when something breaks. Say one calm sentence, try once more, then use your backup. The audience remembers how you react, not the bug.

Handling questions

Listen to a short question and answer at the end of a talk.

Sam: What about the cost?

Lin: Do you mean the cost of the model calls, or the engineering time?

Sam: The model calls.

Lin: Smaller prompts mean fewer tokens, so the cost per question went down too. I don't have the exact number here. I'll post it in the team channel this afternoon. Does that answer your question?

Sam: Yes, thanks.

Lin did four things. She checked the question. She answered briefly. She was honest about a missing number. And she promised a clear next step. Use this order for most questions.

  1. Listen to the end. Do not start your answer in the middle of the question.
  2. Check or repeat it. "So the question is about cost." Online, this also helps people with bad audio.
  3. Answer short. One main point, one reason, maybe one example.
  4. Check. "Does that answer your question?"
Phrases for difficult questions
SituationWhat to say
You did not understandSorry, could you say that again? Do you mean X or Y?
You need a momentGood question. Let me think about that for a second.
You do not knowI don't know, but I'll find out and send it to you today.
Someone disagreesThat's a fair point. Here's how we thought about it.
Two questions in oneYou asked two things. Let me start with the first.
Too long or off topicThat's a bigger topic. Can we take it offline after the talk?
Online audienceLet me check the chat. Priya asks about the cache.

More ways to buy time and to ask for repeats are in Speaking skills.

Take it offline is a common work phrase. It means: talk about it later, in a smaller group. It does not mean "on the internet".

Never guess an answer to look smart. A wrong answer in a talk spreads fast. "I don't know yet" is professional when you add a next step. Also, do not say "Good question" before every answer. Use it once or twice.

Writing for chat and async work

Look at two ways to ask a colleague for help in chat.

09:02 Hi
09:15 Are you there?
09:40 Quick question

Hi Priya, a question about the staging deploy. It fails at the migration step with "relation already exists" (log linked). Did you change the schema yesterday? No rush. Any time before 15:00 UTC is fine.

The first version makes Priya wait for the real question. She may be in another time zone, or busy. The website nohello.net makes the same point: do not send "hello" alone. Put the greeting and the question in one message.

In async work, people do not need to be online at the same time. They read and answer when they can. So every message must stand alone. The reader should not need a call to understand it. Short, complete sentences help readers who use English as a second language. The basic shapes are in The 15 sentence patterns.

Five rules for async messages

  • Lead with the point. Put the main question or decision in the first line. Some teams call this BLUF.
  • Give context. What happened, what you tried, and a link to the log or ticket.
  • Say what you need and by when. "Could you review this by Thursday?"
  • Use structure. Short lines, bullets and one topic per thread.
  • Close the loop. When the problem is solved, say so in the thread.

Docs assistant: weekly update (week 12)

  • Done: smaller prompts are live. Median answer time is now 2.0 s.
  • Next: streaming answers, planned for next Tuesday.
  • Blocked: we need a decision on log retention. @Sara, could you choose option A or B in the doc by Friday?

The update shows three parts that readers look for. Done, next and blocked. Only one person must act, and the message names her and the deadline. The chapter Writing at work has more models for status updates, and Meetings and stand-ups covers live stand-ups.

Async is the default in many remote teams, but not for everything. Use a call for sensitive feedback, for a real emergency, or when a thread goes back and forth many times without a decision. After the call, write the decision in the thread.

Avoid unclear short forms with an international team. "EOD" means "end of day", but whose day? "ASAP" sounds rude and gives no real deadline. Write a time and a time zone instead.

Time zones and politeness across cultures

A manager in New York writes: "Let's meet at 9 tomorrow." Her team is in London, Bengaluru and Tokyo. Whose 9? Whose tomorrow? Tomorrow morning in New York is already night in Tokyo.

Write times that everyone understands

  • Add the time zone, and if possible UTC: "Tuesday 14:00 UTC (10:00 in New York)".
  • Write dates as 2027-03-10. In the US, 03/10 means 10 March. In the UK, it means 3 October.
  • Use a calendar invite. The calendar shows the time in each person's own zone.
  • Rotate meeting times. Then the same people do not always join at night.

The summer time trap

Daylight saving time starts on different dates in different places. In 2027, the US moves its clocks on 14 March. Most of Europe moves them on 28 March. Many countries in Asia, like India and Japan, do not change at all. Look at a weekly meeting that stays at 10:00 in New York.

from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

host = ZoneInfo("America/New_York")   # the meeting is 10:00 in New York
others = {"UTC": "UTC",
          "London": "Europe/London",
          "Bengaluru": "Asia/Kolkata",
          "Tokyo": "Asia/Tokyo"}

for day in ["2027-03-10", "2027-03-17", "2027-03-24", "2027-03-31"]:
    start = datetime.fromisoformat(day + "T10:00").replace(tzinfo=host)
    line = [day]
    for city, zone in others.items():
        local = start.astimezone(ZoneInfo(zone))   # same moment, other zone
        line.append(city + " " + local.strftime("%a %H:%M"))
    print(" | ".join(line))
2027-03-10 | UTC Wed 15:00 | London Wed 15:00 | Bengaluru Wed 20:30 | Tokyo Thu 00:00
2027-03-17 | UTC Wed 14:00 | London Wed 14:00 | Bengaluru Wed 19:30 | Tokyo Wed 23:00
2027-03-24 | UTC Wed 14:00 | London Wed 14:00 | Bengaluru Wed 19:30 | Tokyo Wed 23:00
2027-03-31 | UTC Wed 14:00 | London Wed 15:00 | Bengaluru Wed 19:30 | Tokyo Wed 23:00

For two weeks, the meeting starts one hour earlier in London. Then London goes back to 15:00. But Bengaluru and Tokyo stay one hour earlier all summer. Warn your team before these weeks. The same gap happens in autumn: in 2027, Europe changes on 31 October and the US on 7 November.

Dates for summer time can change when a country changes its law. Do not keep them in your head. Let a calendar or a time zone library do it, like the Python code above.

Politeness across cultures

Your colleague in Amsterdam writes: "This design will not scale." Your colleague in Tokyo writes: "This design is interesting. Maybe we could think about scale a little more." Both mean almost the same thing.

The researcher Erin Meyer uses an idea from the anthropologist Edward Hall. In a low-context culture, people say things clearly and literally. Meyer places the US, Germany and the Netherlands near this end. In a high-context culture, much of the meaning is between the lines. She places Japan, India and France nearer this end. These are averages, not rules about people. Every person and every team is different.

Meyer also shows a surprise. Feedback style is a separate scale. For example, French speakers are high-context in her research, but they often give quite direct negative feedback.

Safe habits for an international team
HabitExample
Be clear about the ask, soft in toneCould you send the logs by 16:00 UTC? Thanks a lot.
Avoid idioms, sarcasm and jokes in writingNot "This is a piece of cake." Say "This is easy."
Explain short forms the first timeWe'll do an RCA (root cause analysis) tomorrow.
Check, do not guessJust to check: do you mean we should stop the release?
Respect local calendarsIn some countries, the work week starts on Sunday. Check holidays too.

Polite English often uses soft forms. "Send me the logs" can sound rude in writing. "Could you send me the logs when you have a moment?" sounds polite. But very soft English can hide the urgency. So add a clear deadline when it matters. See Hedging and stance for softening language.

Very short messages can sound angry in a second language. "Why?" or "No." alone may feel rude. Add a few words: "Could you tell me why? I want to understand the reason."

A full example talk script

Here is a complete short talk for an engineering all-hands meeting. With the demo, it takes about ten minutes. The project and the people are invented. Signposts are in bold. Read it aloud and time yourself.

[Slide 1: "Twice as fast: speeding up our docs assistant"]

"Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining. I'm Lin, and I work on the search team. Last March, our docs assistant needed four seconds to answer a question. Today it needs about two. In the next ten minutes, I'll show you how. Please keep your questions for the end. I'll leave ten minutes for them. You can also post them in the chat."

[Slide 2: "Slow answers drove users away"]

"Let's start with the problem. Four seconds sounds small. But our users ask questions while they code. Four seconds breaks their focus. You can see it on this chart. Weekly users fell by a third in two months."

[Slide 3: Outline]

"I'll cover three things. First, where the time went. Then, the three changes we made. And finally, what we learned, including one mistake."

[Slide 4: "Most of the time went to the model, not to search"]

"So, first: where did the time go? We traced every step of one request. Search took only 300 milliseconds. The model call took almost three seconds. Network and logging took the rest. The key point is this: the model was the bottleneck, not search. We were surprised. We had guessed the opposite."

[Slide 5: "Three changes cut the answer time in half"]

"So that's where the time went. Now let's look at the fix. We made three changes. The first one was a smaller prompt. We used to send ten document chunks to the model. Now we send the best four. That made the model call about twice as fast. The second change was simple. We moved logging out of the request path. The third change was streaming. The assistant now shows the first words after about half a second."

[Slide 6: Live demo]

"Let me show you. I'll switch to the browser. Can everyone see it? Good. One note first: the model may phrase answers a bit differently each time. I'm typing a question: 'How do I rotate the API keys for staging?' Now I'll press Enter. Watch the answer box. The first words appear almost at once. Notice the links under each sentence. Each one goes to the docs page it came from. Let me switch back to the slides."

[Slide 7: "Measure first, and tell people about changes"]

"That brings me to the last part: what we learned. Lesson one: measure before you change anything. Our first guess was wrong. Lesson two: a smaller prompt was not worse. Our quality score stayed the same on our test set of 300 questions. And now the mistake. We turned on streaming without telling the support team. Some users thought the assistant was broken, because the text 'moved'. Next time, we will announce changes first."

[Slide 8: Summary]

"So, to sum up. Slow answers drove users away. Most of the time went to the model. Three changes made the assistant twice as fast. Weekly users are now back above the March level. If you remember one thing, make it this: trace one request from start to end before you optimise. Try it on your own service this week. Thank you. I'm happy to take questions."

Priya: Did you try a cache for common questions?

Lin: Good question. We thought about it. About one question in five is a repeat. But the docs change often, so a cache could give old answers. We'll test a cache with a short expiry time next month.

Tom: Will this work for the other assistants too?

Lin: Probably for the prompt change, yes. The other teams use different models, so I can't promise the same numbers. I'd be happy to look at it with you after the meeting.

Why this script works

  • The hook is a number that changed: four seconds, then two.
  • The outline promises three parts, and the body delivers them in that order.
  • Every slide title is a sentence with the message.
  • Bridges join the parts: "So that's where the time went. Now let's look at the fix."
  • The demo has a warning about the model and clear "watch" and "notice" phrases.
  • The close repeats the main points and gives one action.
  • The answers are short, honest and end with a next step.

The script above has about 480 spoken words. Speaking rates differ a lot between people, and sources give different numbers. At a calm 100 to 130 words per minute, the script fills about four or five minutes. The demo, the pauses and the slide changes fill most of the rest. So time yourself with your own script. Do not trust a general number.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for presentations and remote work
PatternPurposeModelNote
Today I'll show you how / why...State the purposeToday I'll show you how we made the assistant twice as fast.Say it in the first 30 seconds.
I'll cover three things. First... Then... Finally...Give the outlineI'll cover three things: the problem, the fix and the lessons.Keep to three or four points.
So that's X. Now let's look at Y.Bridge two partsSo that's the problem. Now let's look at the fix.Pause after the first sentence.
The key point is...Stress the main ideaThe key point is that the model was the bottleneck.Use it once or twice per talk, not more.
This chart shows...Introduce a chartThis chart shows our p95 latency over eight weeks.Then give the trend, not every number.
It fell from X to Y / by Z.Describe a changeIt fell from 820 to 320 milliseconds."By" is the size. "To" is the new value.
I'm + -ing ... Now I'll...Narrate a demoI'm typing a question. Now I'll press Enter.Never type in silence.
Do you mean X or Y?Check an unclear questionDo you mean the model cost or the engineering time?Better than answering the wrong question.
I don't know, but I'll...Handle an unknown answerI don't know, but I'll post the number in the channel today.Always add a next step and a time.
Hi [name], [question + context]. [Deadline].Ask in chatHi Priya, the staging deploy fails at the migration step. Did you change the schema?Never send "Hi" alone and wait.
Could you [verb] by [time + zone]?Ask with a deadlineCould you review the PR by Thursday 12:00 UTC?Not "ASAP" or "EOD".
[Day] [time] UTC ([local time] in [city])Give a meeting timeTuesday 14:00 UTC (23:00 in Tokyo)Check the summer time weeks.
Just to check: do you mean...?Avoid misunderstandingJust to check: do you mean we should stop the release?Useful with high-context colleagues.

Practice

Quick quiz

Which is the best first sentence after "Good morning, I'm Lin"?

  • Sorry for my English, it's not very good.
  • Today I'll show you how we made our assistant twice as fast.
  • Can you see my screen? Is it okay?

State the purpose early. Apologies and technical checks make a weak start.

Which slide title follows the assertion-evidence approach?

  • Latency
  • Results of week 4
  • The cache cut latency by 60 percent

An assertion-evidence title is a full sentence with the message.

Which chat message is best for an async team?

  • Hi! Are you there?
  • Need help ASAP.
  • Hi Tom, could you check why the nightly job failed? The log is linked. Any time before 10:00 UTC tomorrow is fine.

It has the question, the context and a clear deadline with a time zone.

A weekly meeting is fixed at 10:00 in New York. The US starts summer time two weeks before Europe. What happens in London during those two weeks?

  • The meeting starts one hour earlier.
  • The meeting starts one hour later.
  • Nothing changes.

New York moves its clock forward first. So 10:00 in New York is 14:00 in London, not 15:00, until Europe also changes.

Fill the gaps

Latency fell ? 820 ? 320 milliseconds.

So that's the problem. Now let's look ? the fix.

I don't know, but I'll find ? and send it to you today.

Think and write

  1. Rewrite this chat message for an async team: "hey, the build is broken, can u look asap".
    Answer

    "Hi Ana, the main build fails since this morning at the lint step (link to the log). It blocks the release at 16:00 UTC. Could you take a look before 14:00 UTC? Thanks!" (Many good answers are possible. Include the problem, a link, the impact and a time with a zone.)

  2. Change this topic title into a sentence title: "Error rate".
    Answer

    For example: "The new retry logic halved the error rate." The title should state the message that the chart proves.

  3. Describe this change in one sentence: users went from 4,000 to 3,000 a week.
    Answer

    "Weekly users fell from 4,000 to 3,000, a drop of 25 percent." Or: "Weekly users fell by a quarter."

  4. Someone asks a question you cannot answer: "What is the cost per user per month?" Write your answer.
    Answer

    "I don't have that number with me. I'll check it with the finance team and post it in the channel by tomorrow."

  5. Your demo server stops responding during a talk. Write two calm sentences.
    Answer

    "It looks like the demo server is not responding. Let me show you the recording instead." (One calm sentence, then the backup. No long apology.)

  6. Expert. Your team is in San Francisco, London and Bengaluru. Plan a fair weekly meeting, and write the invite text.
    Answer

    No single time is good for all three. A fair plan rotates two times. For example: "Weekly sync. Week A: Tuesday 16:00 UTC (08:00 San Francisco, 16:00 London, 21:30 Bengaluru). Week B: Wednesday 08:00 UTC (08:00 London, 13:30 Bengaluru, midnight in San Francisco)." In week B, San Francisco watches the recording. These local times are for the northern winter. Check them again in the summer time weeks. Add an agenda doc, record the meeting and write decisions in the thread.

  7. Expert. A colleague from a high-context culture writes: "The plan is interesting. Perhaps we could consider the timeline once more." What might this mean, and how do you reply?
    Answer

    It may mean "I am worried that the timeline is too short." Do not guess. Reply politely and openly: "Thank you. Just to check: do you think the timeline is too tight? I'd really like to hear your concerns. Could we talk for ten minutes tomorrow?"

You finish one part of a talk and start the next.

"So that's the problem. Now let's look at the fix."

A question is not clear.

"Do you mean X or Y?"

You need to wait during a demo.

"This takes a few seconds. While it loads, let me explain..."

A question is too big for the talk.

"That's a bigger topic. Can we take it offline after the talk?"

You give a meeting time to a global team.

"Tuesday 14:00 UTC (23:00 in Tokyo)."

You end a talk.

"To sum up... Thank you. I'm happy to take questions."

Key takeaways

  • A talk has an opening that promises, a body that delivers and a close that repeats.
  • Use more signposts in speech than in writing. A bridge closes one part and opens the next.
  • Slide titles work best as full sentences with the message, supported by a picture.
  • Describe charts in order: what it shows, the trend, the key change, one number.
  • In demos, say what you do and why. Prepare a backup and warn about model output.
  • For questions: listen, check, answer short, check again. Never guess.
  • Async messages stand alone: point first, context, the ask and a deadline with a time zone.
  • Write times with UTC, watch the summer time weeks, and be clear but soft across cultures.

Sources

  • The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, English Language Centre: Delivering an effective academic presentation. Opening, body, close, signposting and handling questions.
  • Penn State: Scientific presentations, the assertion-evidence approach. Sentence titles with visual evidence, and the research behind them.
  • Twist and Doist: What is asynchronous communication?. Context in messages, deadlines, response times and when to meet live.
  • nohello.net. Why you should put your question in the first chat message.
  • Erin Meyer, Harvard Business Review (2014): Navigating the cultural minefield. Low-context and high-context communication and separate feedback styles.
  • Python documentation: zoneinfo. The IANA time zone support used to check the meeting times and summer time dates.
